question_text: A ro-ro vessel has a car deck intended for road transporters (pneumatic tyres). The maximum axle load Q is 12 t, and footprint dimensions are not available. Each axle has two load areas (n_o = 2), and the tyres are standard single wheels with the axle oriented parallel to the stiffeners. The maximum tyre pressure P_0 is not separately specified by the designer. For the at-sea condition, the vertical acceleration a_z has been calculated as 0.35g. Determine: (a) the value of P_0 that should be used for these road transporters, (b) the design deck pressure P_wl-2 for normal operation at sea using the simplified formula, and (c) whether the footprint data must be provided by the vehicle manufacturer or whether the simplified approach is permitted.
required_facts: P_0 = 120*sqrt(Q+3) kN/m² for road transporters, giving approximately 464.8 kN/m² for Q=12t
w = 1.0 for single wheels
P_wl-2 = (P_0/w)*(1 + a_z/g) is the correct at-sea formula
P_wl-2 ≈ 627.5 kN/m² (accepting range 625–630 kN/m²)
Q = 12t does not exceed the 15t threshold, so footprint data is not required
The simplified approach of clause 2.1.2 is permitted for this vehicle

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply the simplified design pressure formula for pneumatic tyres when footprint data is unavailable (2.1.2), using the default P_0 formula for road transporters, then check whether Q=12t is below the 15t threshold that mandates footprint data (2.1.3).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify applicable formula: Since footprint dimensions are not available and tyres are pneumatic, clause 2.1.2 applies. Step 2 — Determine P_0: For road transporters (not cargo handling vehicles), P_0 = 120*(sqrt(Q+3)) kN/m². With Q=12t: P_0 = 120*sqrt(12+3) = 120*sqrt(15) = 120*3.873 = 464.8 kN/m². Step 3 — Determine w: Single wheels → w = 1.0. Step 4 — Compute P_wl-2 (at sea): P_wl-2 = (P_0/w)*(1 + a_z/g) = (464.8/1.0)*(1 + 0.35) = 464.8*1.35 = 627.5 kN/m². Step 5 — Check 2.1.3 threshold: Q=12t < 15t, so footprint data is NOT mandatory; the simplified approach of 2.1.2 is permitted.

question_text: A structural engineer is performing a fatigue assessment for a welded bracket detail located in a water ballast tank on a bulk carrier with a 25-year design life. The detail is assessed using the hot spot stress approach. The vessel operates worldwide. The engineer proposes to apply toe grinding (post-weld treatment) to this detail to improve its fatigue performance. The initial calculated fatigue life of the detail, prior to any post-weld treatment, is 14 years. The weld is a full penetration weld, and the hot spot is within the ballast tank (i.e., exposed to corrosive environment). Is the proposed post-weld treatment acceptable under classification rules? Identify all conditions that are not satisfied, and state the time in corrosive environment that must be used in the damage calculation for this detail.
required_facts: Post-weld treatment is not acceptable for this detail
The initial calculated fatigue life of 14 years is below the required minimum of 17 years, violating a condition for post-weld treatment eligibility
The hot spot is not protected from corrosive environment (water ballast tank), violating another condition for post-weld treatment eligibility
The time in corrosive environment T_C,25 for a water ballast tank is 5 years over a 25-year design life
The damage estimate for the time in corrosive environment (5 years) must be multiplied by two

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The question requires applying the post-weld treatment eligibility conditions in [4.6] to determine that the 14-year initial fatigue life fails the 17-year minimum threshold, and that the requirement for the hot spot to be protected from corrosive environment is violated since the detail is in a water ballast tank. It also requires reading Table 1 in [4.4] to identify that the time in corrosive environment for a water ballast tank is 5 years over a 25-year design life, and that the damage estimate for that period must be multiplied by two.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Check post-weld treatment conditions in [4.6]: (a) initial calculated fatigue life prior to post-weld treatment must be minimum 17 years → 14 years < 17 years, FAILS; (b) the hot spot must be protected from corrosive environment → the detail is in a water ballast tank, which is a corrosive environment, FAILS. Step 2 — Since at least two conditions are violated, the post-weld treatment is NOT acceptable. Step 3 — From Table 1 in [4.4], the time in corrosive environment T_C,25 for a water ballast tank is 5 years over a 25-year design life. The damage estimate for those 5 years must be multiplied by two.

question_text: A structural engineer is performing a fatigue assessment for a longitudinal weld detail located in a water ballast tank on a bulk carrier with a 25-year design life. The vessel operates worldwide. Prescriptive loads from the standard wave load chapter are used (no hydrodynamic scatter diagram analysis). The detail is assessed using the hot spot stress approach. During the fatigue damage calculation, the engineer identifies that a portion of the 25-year service life is spent in a corrosive environment. The engineer also intends to apply toe grinding to improve the fatigue life of the detail, and the initial calculated fatigue life before treatment is 15 years. The hot spot is located inside the ballast tank and is not separately protected from corrosion. Determine: (1) the correct S-N curve to use for this detail, (2) the environmental factor fe to apply, (3) the operational factor fR to apply, (4) how many years of the 25-year design life are considered to be in a corrosive environment for this location, (5) what correction must be applied to the damage estimate for the time in corrosive environment, and (6) whether toe grinding post-weld treatment is permissible for this detail, and why.
required_facts: S-N curve D (FAT 90) shall be used for the hot spot stress approach on welded joints
fe = 0.8 for worldwide wave environment with prescriptive loads (no scatter diagram)
fR = 0.76 for prescriptive loads
TC,25 = 5 years in corrosive environment for a water ballast tank location over a 25-year design life
The damage estimate for the time in corrosive environment must be multiplied by two
Toe grinding is not permissible because the initial fatigue life of 15 years is below the required minimum of 17 years
Toe grinding is additionally not permissible because the hot spot is not protected from corrosive environment

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: all answers are found within Pt3.Ch9.Sec4 — S-N curve selection [4.1], environmental factor [4.2], operational factor [4.3], corrosive environment duration from Table 1 [4.4], damage multiplier [4.4], and post-weld treatment conditions [4.6].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — S-N curve: Per [4.1], for welded joints assessed by the hot spot stress approach, S-N curve D (FAT 90) shall be used. Step 2 — Environmental factor: Per [4.2], for prescriptive loads (no scatter diagram), worldwide wave environment gives fe = 0.8. Step 3 — Operational factor: Per [4.3], fR = 0.76 for prescriptive loads. Step 4 — Corrosive environment duration: Per Table 1 in [4.4], a water ballast tank location has TC,25 = 5 years of corrosive exposure during the 25-year design life. Step 5 — Damage correction: Per [4.4], the damage estimate for the time in corrosive environment shall be multiplied by two. Step 6 — Post-weld treatment: Per [4.6], toe grinding is NOT permissible here because (a) the initial calculated fatigue life prior to treatment is 15 years, which is less than the required minimum of 17 years, and (b) the hot spot is not protected from corrosive environment (it is inside the ballast tank), which is another disqualifying condition.

question_text: A naval architect is reviewing the window and side scuttle arrangement for a new 140-metre general cargo vessel. On the freeboard deck, a first-tier deckhouse is fitted with a round opening of 480 mm diameter on its side shell. The opening is not considered buoyant in the stability calculations and does not protect access leading below. On the same deckhouse, a second round opening of 400 mm diameter is fitted on the forward end bulkhead. Additionally, a rectangular window measuring 900 mm × 600 mm is proposed for the side of the first-tier enclosed superstructure. During the strength test for this rectangular window, the framing test (Step 1) is conducted by ramping pressure to the design pressure within 30 seconds and holding for 3 minutes — no leakage or damage is observed. For Step 2, the glass pane is cycled 3 times between the design pressure P and 4×P, with each cycle completed in 75 seconds. After the test, the window is accepted. Is the classification of each opening (side scuttle vs. window) correct, and is the proposed arrangement of the rectangular window in the first-tier enclosed superstructure side compliant? Is the Step 2 test cycle duration acceptable?
required_facts: The 480 mm diameter opening has an area of approximately 0.181 m², exceeding 0.16 m², and must be classified as a window, not a side scuttle
The 400 mm diameter opening has an area of approximately 0.126 m², not exceeding 0.16 m², and is correctly classified as a side scuttle
Windows shall not be fitted in the sides of first-tier enclosed superstructures, so the rectangular window arrangement is not compliant
The Step 2 test cycle duration of 75 seconds is acceptable because it falls within the required range of 60 s < t < 120 s

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply definitions to classify openings, apply arrangement prohibition for first-tier superstructure sides, and verify test cycle timing against Step 2 requirements.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Classify the 480 mm diameter round opening: area = π×(0.24)² = 0.1810 m², which exceeds 0.16 m². Per [2.1.1], round openings with area > 0.16 m² shall be treated as windows, not side scuttles. So calling it a side scuttle is incorrect. Step 2 — Classify the 400 mm diameter round opening: area = π×(0.20)² = 0.1257 m², which is less than 0.16 m². Per [2.1.1], this qualifies as a side scuttle. Correct classification. Step 3 — Rectangular window in first-tier enclosed superstructure side: per [3.1.5(b)], windows shall not be fitted in the first tier end bulkheads or sides of enclosed superstructures. The proposed rectangular window on the side of the first-tier enclosed superstructure is therefore not compliant. Step 4 — Step 2 test cycle duration: per [6.2] item 4, each loading/unloading cycle shall be performed within 60 s < t < 120 s. A cycle duration of 75 seconds satisfies 60 < 75 < 120, so the test cycle duration is acceptable.

question_text:
A bulk carrier with a ship length of 210 m is undergoing cargo hold finite element analysis for the midship region. During post-processing, the structural engineer finds that a transverse web frame girder has circular cut-outs for pipe passages in its web. The girder web height is 1800 mm. Each cut-out has a diameter of 300 mm, and there are two such cut-outs at the same cross-section, plus longitudinal stiffener slots totalling 60 mm of web height at that section. The FE model does not explicitly represent the geometry of these openings. The element shear stress extracted from the FE results at this location is 85 N/mm².

The structural engineer needs to verify the corrected shear stress to use in the von Mises stress calculation for yield criteria checking. Calculate the corrected element shear stress at this web location, showing clearly how the effective web height is determined and how the correction is applied.
required_facts: h = 1800 mm (full web height, since openings are not modelled in the FE model)
h_eff = 1800 − (2 × 300) − 60 = 1140 mm (deducting both cut-outs and stiffener slots)
The corrected shear stress (not the raw element shear stress) must be used to compute von Mises stress for yield criteria verification
The correction factor h / h_eff ≈ 1.579, reflecting a ~58% increase over the uncorrected value

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The shear stress correction formula in [4.2.7] requires h (web height in way of opening) and h_eff (effective web height deducting all openings including stiffener slots, per Ch.3 Sec.7 [1.4.7]). Since the openings are not modelled, h equals the full girder web height. h_eff deducts both the two circular cut-outs and the stiffener slots.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Identify applicable formula: Since the FE model does not represent the cut-out geometry, [4.2.7] applies directly. The corrected shear stress is τ_cor = (h / h_eff) × τ_elem.

Step 2 — Determine h: Because the geometry of the opening is NOT modelled, h is taken as the full height of the web of the girder in way of the opening = 1800 mm.

Step 3 — Determine h_eff: The effective web height deducts all openings including slots for stiffeners, per Ch.3 Sec.7 [1.4.7]. Total deduction = 2 × 300 mm (two circular cut-outs) + 60 mm (stiffener slots) = 660 mm. Therefore h_eff = 1800 − 660 = 1140 mm.

Step 4 — Apply correction: τ_cor = (1800 / 1140) × 85 = 1.5789 × 85 ≈ 134.2 N/mm².

Step 5 — Use in yield check: This corrected shear stress τ_cor = 134.2 N/mm² shall be used to calculate the von Mises stress of the element for verification against the yield acceptance criteria.

question_text: A shipyard is preparing documentation for a new vessel to be built under DNV class. During a pre-contract meeting, the prospective owner asks the yard's classification coordinator three questions about how DNV operates: (1) If there is ever a conflict between the DNV General Terms and Conditions and another part of the DNV rules (for example, a structural rule in a later chapter), which document takes precedence? (2) A rule clause states that a certain structural arrangement 'should' be used — does this mean the yard is strictly required to use it, or is an alternative acceptable? (3) The yard's welding procedure document refers to a 'conversion' of an existing vessel — how does DNV define a conversion, as distinct from a mere 'alteration'? Provide precise answers to all three questions as they would be answered under DNV classification principles.
required_facts: In case of conflict between the DNV General Terms and Conditions and any other part of the rules, the T&C provisions prevail
The verbal form 'should' indicates a recommendation among several possibilities, not a strict requirement; alternatives are not excluded
The verbal form 'shall' (not 'should') indicates a requirement strictly to be followed
An 'alteration' is a change that does not affect the basic character or structure of the vessel
A 'conversion' is a change that substantially alters the dimensions, carrying capacity, or other fundamental characteristics of the vessel
The distinction between 'conversion' and 'alteration' turns on whether the basic character or structure of the vessel is substantially affected

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: all three sub-questions are answered directly from Pt1.Ch1.Sec1 — clause 1.1.2 for T&C precedence, Table 1 for the verbal form 'should', and Table 2 for the definitions of 'conversion' vs 'alteration'.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — T&C precedence: Clause 1.1.2 states 'In case of any ambiguities or contradictions between the T&C and other parts of the rules, the provisions of the T&C shall prevail.' So the T&C takes precedence over other rule parts. Step 2 — Verbal form 'should': Table 1 defines 'should' as 'verbal form used to indicate that among several possibilities, one is recommended as particularly suitable, without mentioning or excluding other [possibilities].' This means 'should' is a recommendation, not a strict requirement; alternatives are permissible. Contrast with 'shall', which indicates a requirement strictly to be followed. Step 3 — Conversion vs alteration: Table 2 defines 'alteration' as 'A change that does not affect the basic character or structure of the vessel it is applied to.' Table 2 defines 'conversion' as 'Change that substantially alters the dimensions, carrying capacity, [engine arrangement, etc.]' — i.e., a conversion substantially alters dimensions or carrying capacity, whereas an alteration does not affect the basic character or structure.

question_text: A 185 m ro-ro vessel is being designed with a stern bottom structure. The ship has a design minimum ballast draught at the aft end of 3.2 m, and the wave coefficient CW for this vessel is 10.75. At a position 12 m forward of the aft end, the lower shell has a flare angle of 65° and sits 0.8 m below the ballast waterline at that location. The ship's block coefficient CB is 0.62. The designer needs to determine the design stern slamming pressure at this position, and then establish the correct design pressures to apply when checking: (a) the shell plating thickness, (b) the section modulus of longitudinal stiffeners, and (c) the shear area of the web frames supporting those stiffeners. Calculate PSS at the given position and state the three design pressures to be used for each structural check.
required_facts: C is capped at 1.0 because the computed value 0.18×(10.75 – 2×0.8) = 1.647 exceeds the maximum
PSS ≈ 345–346 kN/m² (primary formula governs; upper-bound formula gives ~444 kN/m²)
Design pressure for shell plating check: Ppl = PSS ≈ 345–346 kN/m²
Design pressure for stiffener section modulus check: Pst = 0.5 × PSS ≈ 172–173 kN/m²
Design pressure for web frame shear area and section modulus check: PPSM = 0.4 × PSS ≈ 138–139 kN/m²
The position (12 m forward of A.E.) is within the applicable stern slamming region (aft of 0.1L = 18.5 m forward of A.E.)
The vessel qualifies for the flare-angle strengthening requirements because the 65° flare angle exceeds the 60° threshold

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: compute PSS from the design stern slamming pressure formula in [2.1], then apply the three scantling reduction factors from [3.1], [3.2.1], and [3.3.1]
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Check applicability: L = 185 m > 150 m ✓; flare angle = 65° > 60° ✓; position is 12 m forward of A.E., and 0.1L = 18.5 m, so 12 m < 18.5 m forward of A.E. — position is within the applicable stern region ✓.

Step 2 — Compute intermediate parameters:
  C = 0.18 × (CW – 2·ho) = 0.18 × (10.75 – 2×0.8) = 0.18 × (10.75 – 1.6) = 0.18 × 9.15 = 1.647 → capped at maximum 1.0
  a0 = (3·CW / L) + 0.16 = (3×10.75 / 185) + 0.16 = 32.25/185 + 0.16 = 0.1743 + 0.16 = 0.3343
  X = 12 m (distance from A.E. to position considered)
  α = 65°, sin(65°) = 0.9063, sin³(65°) = 0.7449

Step 3 — Compute PSS (primary formula):
  PSS = 2.2 × C × L × (0.6 + [1.65 × a0 × (0.55L – X) × sin³α] / (CB × L))²
  Inner bracket numerator: 1.65 × 0.3343 × (0.55×185 – 12) × 0.7449
    = 1.65 × 0.3343 × (101.75 – 12) × 0.7449
    = 1.65 × 0.3343 × 89.75 × 0.7449
    = 1.65 × 0.3343 × 66.87
    = 36.87
  Denominator: CB × L = 0.62 × 185 = 114.7
  Fraction: 36.87 / 114.7 = 0.3214
  Inner bracket: 0.6 + 0.3214 = 0.9214
  PSS = 2.2 × 1.0 × 185 × (0.9214)² = 407 × 0.8490 = 345.5 kN/m²

Step 4 — Check upper-bound formula:
  PSS_max = 2.2 × C × L × (0.6 + 1.65×a0 / (2×CB))²
    = 2.2 × 1.0 × 185 × (0.6 + 1.65×0.3343 / (2×0.62))²
    = 407 × (0.6 + 0.5516 / 1.24)²
    = 407 × (0.6 + 0.4448)²
    = 407 × (1.0448)²
    = 407 × 1.0916
    = 444.3 kN/m²
  Since 345.5 < 444.3, the primary formula governs: PSS ≈ 345.5 kN/m²

Step 5 — Scantling design pressures:
  (a) Plating [3.1]: Ppl = PSS = 345.5 kN/m²
  (b) Stiffeners [3.2.1]: Pst = 0.5 × PSS = 0.5 × 345.5 = 172.8 kN/m²
  (c) Primary supporting members (web frames) [3.3.1]: PPSM = 0.4 × PSS = 0.4 × 345.5 = 138.2 kN/m²

question_text: A general cargo vessel has a freeboard deck with a forward well formed by bulwarks. The bulwark length enclosing the well is 24 m, and the ship has no sheer. The bulwarks are 1.0 m in average height. The designer proposes freeing ports on each side of the forward well with a total area of 2.10 m² per side. Additionally, the vessel is fitted with a watertight internal hatch located in a non-collision bulkhead. The hatch cover carries deck cargo and must be secured against horizontal shifting. The designer asks whether the proposed freeing port area is sufficient, and also whether the internal hatch securing arrangement needs to account for horizontal inertia forces from the cargo stowed on the cover. Are both arrangements compliant with the rules?
required_facts: Base freeing port area A = 0.07 × 24 = 1.68 m² per side (using the ℓb > 20 m branch)
No-sheer correction increases the required area by 50%, giving A_required = 2.52 m² per side
Proposed area of 2.10 m² per side is less than 2.52 m² and therefore does NOT comply
Bulwark height of 1.0 m (between 0.9 m and 1.2 m) triggers no height adjustment to the base area
The internal hatch cover carrying deck cargo must be secured against horizontal shifting due to horizontal inertia forces
Both arrangements as described are non-compliant: freeing port area is insufficient and the question of horizontal securing must be explicitly addressed

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Sec10 freeing port area formula and no-sheer uplift, which leads back through Sec1 general application (closing appliances chapter scope) to Sec3 internal hatch securing requirements for cargo-loaded covers
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Freeing port area (Sec10 [2.1.1]): ℓb = 24 m > 20 m, so base formula A = 0.07 × 24 = 1.68 m² per side. Bulwark height is 1.0 m, which is between 0.9 m and 1.2 m, so no height adjustment applies. Step 2 — No-sheer correction (Sec10 [2.1.2]): ship has no sheer, so the area from [2.1.1] must be increased by 50%: A_required = 1.68 × 1.50 = 2.52 m² per side. The proposed 2.10 m² < 2.52 m², so the freeing port arrangement is NOT compliant. Step 3 — Chapter scope (Sec1 general): Sec1 establishes that Ch.12 covers arrangement of openings and closing appliances throughout the ship, and closing appliances shall have strength corresponding to the hull part in which they are fitted. This confirms Sec3 applies to the internal hatch. Step 4 — Internal hatch securing (Sec3 [2.2.1]): hatch or ramp covers carrying deck cargo shall be effectively secured against horizontal shifting due to horizontal inertia forces. Therefore the securing arrangement must explicitly account for horizontal inertia, and the designer's arrangement must satisfy this requirement.

question_text: A 320 m container ship is being assessed for longitudinal strength. The ship has the following characteristics: rule length L = 320 m, breadth B = 48.5 m, block coefficient C_B = 0.65, waterplane coefficient C_WL = 0.78, scantling draught T = 14.2 m, and a contract speed of 23 knots. The designer is evaluating the hull girder strength at a cross-section located at x/L = 0.42 (measured from aft). The as-built deck plate thickness is 22.5 mm, voluntary addition t_vol_add = 0.5 mm, and the one-side corrosion addition t_c = 2.0 mm (the plate is exposed to atmosphere on one side and a void space on the other). For the hull girder strength assessment, the designer needs to determine: (1) the net offered thickness t_off to be used in the section property calculation, and (2) the still water bending moment load case that must be combined with the wave bending moment at this cross-section for the hogging check. Specifically, which still water bending moment value (maximum hogging or minimum/sagging) and which still water shear force sign convention applies at x/L = 0.42 for the hogging load case? Additionally, what are the design loading conditions that must be included in the loading manual for this vessel?
required_facts: For the strength assessment section property calculation, the corrosion addition factor α = 0.5
The net offered thickness t_off = t_as_built − t_vol_add − α × t_c = 22.5 − 0.5 − 0.5 × 2.0 = 21.0 mm
At x/L = 0.42 (which is ≤ 0.5L), the hogging load case requires M_SWmax (maximum still water hogging bending moment)
At x/L = 0.42 (≤ 0.5L), the hogging load case requires Q_SWmax (maximum positive still water shear force)
The mandatory seagoing design loading conditions for the loading manual include homogeneous cargo loading at maximum draught
The mandatory seagoing design loading conditions for the loading manual include ballast loading conditions

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec4 hull girder strength assessment references Sec3 [3] for design loading conditions and still water load case definitions; the load case table in Sec4 [2.2] explicitly directs the reader to Sec3 [3] for the still water conditions at each section, and Sec3 [3.1.2] specifies the mandatory seagoing design loading conditions for container ships.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Net thickness (Sec4 [2.1.1]): For the strength assessment (section properties), the corrosion addition factor α = 0.5 (from Table 1, row 'Strength assessment, section properties'). The plate is exposed to atmosphere on one side (t_c1 = 1.0 mm per Table 2) and void space on the other (t_c2 = 0.5 mm per Table 2), so t_c = t_c1 + t_c2 = 1.5 mm. However, the problem states t_c = 2.0 mm as given — applying the formula: t_off = 22.5 − 0.5 − 0.5 × 2.0 = 22.5 − 0.5 − 1.0 = 21.0 mm. Step 2 — Load case at x/L = 0.42 (Sec4 [2.2], Table 3): Since x/L = 0.42 < 0.5L, the hogging load case requires M_SWmax (maximum hogging still water bending moment) combined with M_WVH (hogging wave bending moment), and Q_SWmax for x ≤ 0.5L combined with Q_WVmax for x ≤ 0.5L. Step 3 — Still water conditions (Sec4 [2.2] references Sec3 [3]): Following the cross-reference to Sec3 [3], specifically Sec3 [3.1.2], the mandatory seagoing design loading conditions for the loading manual are: (a) homogeneous cargo loading conditions at maximum draught, and (b) ballast loading conditions.

question_text: A 140 m general cargo vessel has a freeboard deck with a forward well formed by bulwarks. The bulwark in way of the forward well is 25 m long and has an average height of 1.5 m. The ship has no sheer. The designer proposes to fit freeing ports on each side of the forward well with a total area of 2.80 m² per side. The securing bolts for the internal watertight hatch covers in the cargo hold are spaced at intervals determined by reference to the bolt area requirements for ordinary packed hatch covers. The designer needs to confirm: (1) Is the proposed freeing port area of 2.80 m² per side sufficient for the forward well, and if not, what is the minimum required area? (2) Where in the rules would the designer find the net bolt area requirements per bolt for the ordinary packed hatch covers securing those internal hatches?
required_facts: Base freeing port area for ℓ_b = 25 m is A = 0.07 × 25 = 1.75 m²
Bulwark height of 1.5 m exceeds 1.2 m by 0.3 m, requiring an increase of 0.004 × 25 × 3 = 0.30 m², giving an adjusted base area of 2.05 m²
No-sheer condition requires a 50% increase, giving a minimum required area of 3.075 m² per side
The proposed 2.80 m² per side is insufficient and does not comply
The net bolt area requirements per bolt for ordinary packed hatch covers are found in the access openings section of the same chapter (Sec2 [1.3])
The cross-reference to bolt area scantlings is reached via the internal hatches securing requirements, which explicitly direct to the Sec2 [1.3] provisions

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Sec10 freeing port area formula, which requires a 50% increase for no-sheer ships per [2.1.2]; Sec10 symbols reference Ch.1 Sec.4 and the chapter general section (Sec1 [3.3.1]) for standard tier height definitions; internal hatch securing bolt area is cross-referenced from Sec3 [2.1.3] back to Sec2 [1.3].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Freeing port base area (Sec10 [2.1.1]): ℓ_b = 25 m > 20 m, so A = 0.07 × 25 = 1.75 m². Step 2 — Bulwark height correction (Sec10 [2.1.1]): average height = 1.5 m > 1.2 m, difference = 0.3 m = 3 × 0.1 m increments, increase = 3 × 0.004 × 25 = 0.30 m². Adjusted base area = 1.75 + 0.30 = 2.05 m². Step 3 — No-sheer correction (Sec10 [2.1.2]): ship has no sheer, so area must be increased by 50%: A_required = 2.05 × 1.50 = 3.075 m². Step 4 — Compliance check: proposed 2.80 m² < 3.075 m² required → NOT compliant. Step 5 — Bolt area for internal hatch covers: Sec3 [2.1.3] states that securing by means other than bolts shall be of strength equivalent to requirements given in Sec2 [1.3], and Sec3 [2.1.2] directs to Sec2 [1.3] for scantlings of securing devices. Therefore the net bolt area per bolt for ordinary packed hatch covers is found in Sec2 [1.3]. Step 6 — Sec1 [3.3.1] defines standard tier height referenced in Sec2 symbols, confirming the chain passes through Sec1 on the way to Sec2.

question_text: A 175-metre bulk carrier is being designed with bilge keels and a continuous ground bar. The bilge strake is fabricated from Grade E steel with a specified minimum yield strength of 355 MPa and a gross thickness of 13 mm. The designer proposes to use a ground bar with a gross thickness of 11 mm, also in Grade E steel. The bilge keel ends are tapered at a ratio of 2.5:1, and the end of the bilge keel web is positioned 45 mm from the end of the ground bar. No transverse support member is fitted between the bilge keel web end and the ground bar end; instead, a longitudinal stiffener is fitted in line with the bilge keel web, extending only to the nearest transverse member on one side (forward) but not aft of the end zone. The windlass installed on the forecastle deck is rated for a chain cable with a minimum breaking strength of 1 800 kN, and a chain stopper is provided. The windlass foundation deck plating has been increased in thickness and is supported by pillars carried down to the inner bottom. The forecastle deck also has bulwarks with a height of 1.4 m above the deck plating, with stays spaced at 1.8 m. Identify all non-compliances in this design and, for each, state the correct rule requirement that has been violated.
required_facts: The ground bar gross thickness of 11 mm is non-compliant; for a ship over 150 m with a bilge strake gross thickness of 13 mm, the ground bar must be at least 13 mm (the lesser of bilge strake thickness and 14 mm)
The bilge keel end taper ratio of 2.5:1 is non-compliant; the minimum required taper ratio is 3:1
The bilge keel web end distance of 45 mm from the ground bar end is non-compliant; the required range is 50 mm to 100 mm

The longitudinal stiffener end support is non-compliant because it extends only forward of zone A but not aft; it must extend to the nearest transverse member on both sides (forward and aft) of zone A
The windlass design load with chain stopper provided is 45% of the minimum breaking strength = 0.45 × 1800 kN = 810 kN
Bulwark plating gross thickness at 1.4 m height must be determined by linear interpolation between 6.0 mm at 1.0 m and the superstructure side plating thickness at 1.8 m
The minimum required gross section modulus of bulwark stays is Z_stay-gr = 77 × (1.4)² × 1.8 = 271.5 cm³

annotator_grounding.end_clause: Pt3.Ch11.Sec1 [3.1.1] (via Sec4→Sec1), Pt3.Ch11.Sec2 [5.1.9] (via Sec1→Sec2), Pt3.Ch11.Sec3 [2.2.8] (via Sec2→Sec3)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Sec4 bilge keel additional requirements for ships >150 m, which references Sec1 for anchoring equipment (windlass design load check), Sec1 references Sec2 for supporting structure scantlings, and Sec2 references Sec3 for bulwark stay requirements
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Sec4 [1.2.2]: For ships >150 m, the ground bar gross thickness shall not be less than the gross thickness of the bilge strake OR 14 mm, whichever is less. Bilge strake gross thickness = 13 mm; 14 mm limit → the lesser is 13 mm. The proposed ground bar thickness of 11 mm is less than 13 mm → NON-COMPLIANT. Required: ≥ 13 mm.

Step 2 — Sec4 [1.2.3]: Tapering ratio must be minimum 3:1. The proposed 2.5:1 taper is less than 3:1 → NON-COMPLIANT. Required: ≥ 3:1.

Step 3 — Sec4 [1.2.3]: The bilge keel web end shall be not less than 50 mm and not greater than 100 mm from the end of the ground bar. 45 mm < 50 mm → NON-COMPLIANT. Required: 50–100 mm.

Step 4 — Sec4 [1.2.3]: Where a longitudinal stiffener is used as end support, it shall extend to at least the nearest transverse member forward AND aft of zone A. Extending only forward but not aft → NON-COMPLIANT.

Step 5 — Following the chain to Sec1 [3.1.1] (anchoring equipment): The windlass design load where a chain stopper is provided is 45% of BS = 0.45 × 1800 = 810 kN. This is the load the foundation must be designed for per Sec2.

Step 6 — Sec2 [2.3.1(a)]: Confirms windlass design load = 45% BS = 810 kN when chain stopper is provided. The foundation arrangement described (deck plating increased, pillars to inner bottom) is consistent with Sec2 [2.2.2] requirements → COMPLIANT.

Step 7 — Following chain to Sec3 [2.2.2]: Bulwark stay section modulus Z_stay-gr = 77 × h_blwk² × s_stay = 77 × (1.4)² × 1.8 = 77 × 1.96 × 1.8 = 271.5 cm³ minimum required. The question does not give the actual stay scantling, so the answerer must flag that this calculation must be verified. Additionally, Sec3 [2.2.1] Table 1: bulwark height 1.4 m is between 1.0 m and 1.8 m → gross thickness by linear interpolation between 6.0 mm (at 1.0 m) and the superstructure thickness (at 1.8 m). The answerer must confirm the plating thickness meets the interpolated requirement.

question_text: A bulk carrier with scantling length L = 180 m, breadth B = 32 m, scantling draught T_SC = 11.5 m, and block coefficient C_B = 0.82 is being assessed for external sea pressures under the HSM dynamic load cases. The vessel has bilge keels fitted and a metacentric height GM = 0.07B. The loading condition under review has a draught T_LC = 9.2 m amidships. A hull load point is located at coordinates x = 126 m from the aft perpendicular, y = 16 m (starboard), z = 4.5 m, at a cross-section where the moulded breadth at the waterline B_x = 32 m. For the extreme sea loads design load scenario, determine: (1) the reference coordinate origin to be used when establishing the x, y, z coordinates of the load point; (2) the value of f_xL at this load point and the corresponding non-linear coefficient f_nℓ for the HSM load cases; (3) the roll period T_θ and roll angle θ for this loading condition; and (4) whether the f_T ratio used in the HSM wave pressure formula falls within the permitted range, stating its numerical value.
required_facts: The coordinate origin for x, y, z is at the aft perpendicular, centreline, and baseline as defined in the coordinate system reference
f_xL = 0.70 (calculated as 126/180)
f_nℓ = 0.9 for the extreme sea loads design load scenario at f_xL = 0.7
f_T = 0.80 (calculated as 9.2/11.5), within the permitted range of 0.5 to 1.0
Roll period T_θ ≈ 19.2 s using k_r = 0.39B and GM = 0.07B
Roll angle θ ≈ 22.7 deg for the extreme sea loads design load scenario with bilge keel fitted

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec5 defines external dynamic pressures for HSM load cases and references Sec1 [1.2.1] for the coordinate system origin, Sec2 for f_xL definition, and Sec3 [2.1.1] for roll angle θ and roll period T_θ. The answerer must navigate from the HSM pressure table in Sec5 → Sec1 for coordinate origin → Sec2 for f_xL → Sec3 for roll motion parameters and f_T.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 (Sec5 → Sec1 [1.2.1]): The symbols table in Sec5 states that x, y, z coordinates are defined with respect to the reference coordinate system defined in Sec1 [1.2.1]. The coordinate origin is at the aft perpendicular (AP), centreline, and baseline. Step 2 (Sec5 → Sec2): f_xL is defined in Sec2 as f_xL = x/L, not less than 0.0 or greater than 1.0. With x = 126 m and L = 180 m: f_xL = 126/180 = 0.70. Step 3 (Sec5 Table 2, using f_nℓ at f_xL = 0.7): For the extreme sea loads design load scenario, f_nℓ = 0.9 at f_xL = 0.7 (read directly from the HSM table in Sec5). Step 4 (Sec5 → Sec3 [2.1.1] for f_T): f_T = T_LC / T_SC = 9.2 / 11.5 = 0.80, which is within the permitted range [0.5, 1.0]. Step 5 (Sec3 [2.1.1] for T_θ): k_r = 0.39B = 0.39 × 32 = 12.48 m (ship with bilge keel, general formula). GM = 0.07B = 0.07 × 32 = 2.24 m. T_θ = 2.3π × k_r / √(g × GM) = 2.3π × 12.48 / √(9.81 × 2.24) = 90.27 / 4.692 ≈ 19.24 s. Step 6 (Sec3 [2.1.1] for θ): f_BK = 1.0 (bilge keel fitted). f_p = f_ps = 1.0 for extreme sea loads design load scenario. θ = 9000(1.4 − 0.035 × T_θ) × f_p × f_BK / ((1.15B + 55)π) = 9000(1.4 − 0.035 × 19.24) × 1.0 × 1.0 / ((1.15 × 32 + 55)π) = 9000(1.4 − 0.6734) / (36.8 + 55)π = 9000 × 0.7266 / (91.8 × π) = 6539.4 / 288.4 ≈ 22.7 deg.

question_text: A bulk carrier with a scantling length L = 220 m, breadth B = 32 m, and block coefficient CB = 0.82 is being assessed for external sea pressure on its side shell under the HSM-1 dynamic load case. The structural engineer needs to compute the hydrodynamic wave pressure PW at a load point located at x = 110 m from the aft perpendicular, y = 14 m from the centreline (starboard side), and z = 8.5 m above the baseline. The loading condition has a draught TLC = 13.0 m and scantling draught TS = 14.0 m. The moulded breadth at the waterline at this cross-section is Bx = 30 m. In setting up the pressure calculation, the engineer must establish the correct coordinate reference origin and determine the longitudinal position ratio fxL. Identify the coordinate system origin that must be used for the load point coordinates (x, y, z), state the definition of fxL and its numerical value for this load point, and confirm which section defines the dynamic load cases (including HSM-1) that feed into the external pressure formula. Finally, determine the wave coefficient Cw applicable to this vessel.
required_facts: The coordinate origin for (x, y, z) is the intersection of the aft perpendicular, the ship centreline plane, and the baseline, as defined in Sec1 [1.2.1]
fxL is defined as x/L (not less than 0.0 or greater than 1.0), per Sec2
fxL = 0.5 for this load point (x = 110 m, L = 220 m)
HSM-1 is one of the dynamic load cases defined in Sec2 [2], which Sec5 [1.3.1] cross-references for the list of applicable load cases
The wave coefficient Cw is defined in Sec4 and for L = 220 m uses the formula Cw = 10.75 − ((300 − L)/100)^1.5
Cw ≈ 10.03 for L = 220 m

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec5 Symbols reference Sec1 [1.2.1] for the coordinate system origin; Sec5 [1.3.1] references Sec2 [2] for the list of dynamic load cases including HSM-1; Sec5 Symbols reference Sec4 for the wave coefficient Cw, which is defined in Sec4 Symbols.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 – Coordinate origin (Sec5 → Sec1 [1.2.1]): The Symbols table in Sec5 states that x, y, z are coordinates 'with respect to the reference coordinate system defined in Sec.1 [1.2.1]'. Sec1 [1.2.1] defines the origin as the intersection of the aft perpendicular, the ship's centreline plane, and the baseline. So x is measured from the aft perpendicular, y from the centreline, z from the baseline. Step 2 – fxL definition and value (Sec5 → Sec2): The Symbols table in Sec5 states fxL is 'ratio as defined in Sec.2'. Sec2 Symbols defines fxL = x/L, not less than 0.0 or greater than 1.0. With x = 110 m and L = 220 m: fxL = 110/220 = 0.5. Step 3 – Dynamic load cases (Sec5 [1.3.1] → Sec2 [2]): Sec5 [1.3.1] states 'The hydrodynamic pressures for each dynamic load case defined in Sec.2 [2] are defined in [1.3.2] to [1.3.8].' So HSM-1 is defined as a dynamic load case in Sec2 [2]. Step 4 – Wave coefficient Cw (Sec5 → Sec4): The Symbols table in Sec5 states Cw is 'wave coefficient defined in Sec.4'. Sec4 Symbols gives the piecewise formula: for 90 ≤ L ≤ 300, Cw = 10.75 − ((300 − L)/100)^1.5. With L = 220 m: Cw = 10.75 − ((300 − 220)/100)^1.5 = 10.75 − (0.8)^1.5 = 10.75 − 0.7155 ≈ 10.03.

question_text: A newbuilding general cargo vessel of 110 m length is being classed with DNV. The designer has submitted a loading manual for approval. The loading manual describes the design loading conditions, permissible still water bending moment and shear force limits, and relevant operational limitations. The vessel is category I. During the design assessment review, the classification society requests that the designer also submit certain hull structural plans and supporting calculations as part of the class contract. The designer asks: which specific documentation types must be submitted for the ship hull structure, and what is the formal basis under which the society will review this documentation? Additionally, must this vessel be provided with a loading instrument system in addition to the loading manual, and if so, what is the approval requirement for that system?
required_facts: The vessel is category I and 110 m in length, so a loading instrument system is required in addition to the loading manual
The loading instrument system must be approved and certified for calculation and control of hull strength
Documentation for hull structure design assessment must be submitted as specified in Table 1 of the verification of compliance section
The documentation will be reviewed by the Society as part of the class contract

Required hull structure documentation types include H010 (Structural design brief), H020 (Design load plan), H030 (Tank and capacity plan), and H050 (Structural drawings for decks, bulkheads, fore ship, engine room, and aft ship)
H050 structural drawings are submitted for approval (AP); H010, H020, H030 are submitted for information (FI)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec.5 loading manual/instrument requirements trigger documentation submission obligations; the documentation requirements for design assessment are governed by Sec.3 [2.2.2] and Table 1, which lists the specific plans and calculations to be submitted for hull structure approval.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec.5 [1.1.2]: All ships of category I of 100 m length and above shall be provided with a loading instrument system approved and certified for calculation and control of hull strength, in addition to the loading manual. The vessel is 110 m and category I, so a loading instrument system is required, approved per Pt.6 Ch.4 Sec.6. Step 2 — Sec.5 [1.1.4]: Requirements for the loading manual are in [2] and for loading instruments in [3]. Step 3 — The designer must also submit hull structural documentation for design assessment. Sec.5 does not itself list the documentation types; it references the broader design assessment framework. Step 4 — Sec.3 [2.2.1] states that for the design of the vessel, documentation as specified in Table 1 shall be submitted, applicable for Ch.1 to Ch.13. Step 5 — Sec.3 [2.2.2] states that documentation shall be submitted as required by Table 1, and the documentation will be reviewed by the Society as part of the class contract. Step 6 — Table 1 lists the required hull structure documentation types: H010 (Structural design brief, FI), H020 (Design load plan, FI), H030 (Tank and capacity plan, FI), H050 (Structural drawings for decks/inner bottom, transverse bulkheads, longitudinal bulkheads, fore ship, engine room area, aft ship — all AP). Step 7 — The formal basis for review is that it forms part of the class contract per Sec.3 [2.2.2].

question_text: A structural engineer is evaluating the primary supporting members (PSMs) of a 185-metre bulk carrier operating in unrestricted service. The vessel has a double-bottom construction with transverse frames and longitudinal girders. During the design load scenario definition for PSM strength assessment, the engineer must determine which loading conditions to include. The ship's loading manual contains 12 intact loading conditions, including full cargo, partial cargo, and ballast conditions. One of the ballast conditions involves a partially filled double-bottom ballast tank at 45% filling level at departure. The internal design pressure for a transverse web frame located inside a ballast tank must also be confirmed. What loading conditions must be considered for the PSM evaluation, and what is the design pressure that applies to the internal structures (such as the transverse web frame) within the ballast tanks?
required_facts: All intact loading conditions in the loading manual must be considered for PSM evaluation, including the partially filled ballast tank condition at 45% filling
The loading conditions must envelop combinations of local loading, global loading, draught of empty hold, and hull girder loads
The design pressure for internal structures in tanks (such as a transverse web frame inside a ballast tank) is Pint = 12 kN/m²
Pint applies to web frames and other primary supporting member webs located inside tanks
The load point coordinates (X, Y, Z) used in internal load calculations are defined with respect to the coordinate system in the introductory section of the chapter

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec8 [2.1.2] defines loading conditions for PSM evaluation and references Sec.6 [3.1] for internal tank pressure (Pint); Sec.6 [3.1] gives Pint = 12 kN/m² for internal structures in tanks; Sec.7 [2.1.2] lists the load components for design load scenarios including Pint from Sec.6 [3.1]; Sec.1 [1.2.1] defines the coordinate system used throughout the load calculations.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec8 [2.1.2]: Loading conditions for PSM evaluation shall consider (a) all intact loading conditions in the loading manual, (b) operational limitations in loading guidance information, and (c) the ship arrangement including combinations of local loading, global loading, draught of empty hold, and hull girder loads. This means all 12 intact loading conditions in the loading manual must be enveloped, including the 45%-filled ballast tank condition. Step 2 — Sec8 [2.1.2] references Sec.7 for design load scenarios, and Sec.7 [2.1.2] lists the load components table where the internal pressure for structures in tanks is denoted Pint, referencing Sec.6 [3.1]. Step 3 — Sec.6 [3.1]: The pressure for internal structures in tanks (e.g. web of primary supporting members) is defined as Pint = 12 kN/m². Step 4 — The coordinate system used for locating load points (X, Y, Z) is defined in Sec.1 [1.2.1], which is referenced in Sec.6 symbols. Therefore: all 12 intact loading conditions must be included in the PSM evaluation envelope, and the design pressure for the transverse web frame inside the ballast tank is Pint = 12 kN/m².

scenario_parameters.structural_member_under_evaluation: transverse web frame inside ballast tank

question_text: A 180-metre bulk carrier is being assessed for hull girder strength under normal seagoing operations. The design team needs to determine the external sea pressure acting on the ship's side shell at a load point located 2.5 m below the design waterline (draught T_LC = 8.0 m), at a transverse position on the starboard side. For the static design load scenario applicable to normal seagoing operations, what is the hydrostatic pressure P_S at this load point, and what formula or table governs its calculation? The ship has a moulded breadth B = 32 m at the considered cross-section, and the load point Y-coordinate is y = +14.0 m (starboard side, measured from centreline).
required_facts: P_S is the hydrostatic (static sea) pressure and its definition is found in the external loads section (Sec.5 [1.2]), not in the design load scenarios section itself
For the static (S) design load scenario under normal seagoing operations, the external pressure P_ex equals P_S alone (no dynamic wave pressure component)
The hydrostatic pressure P_S is obtained from Table 1 in the external loads section, which provides the formula as a function of draught and load point depth
For a load point below the waterline, P_S = ρg(T_LC − z), where ρ = 1.025 t/m³ for seawater
With T_LC = 8.0 m and the load point 2.5 m below the waterline (z = 5.5 m), P_S ≈ 25.1 kN/m²
The transverse position (y = +14.0 m, f_yB = 2×14/32 = 0.875) does not affect the hydrostatic pressure P_S calculation — it only influences the dynamic wave pressure P_W

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec.7 Symbols table defines P_S as 'static sea pressure at considered draught, as defined in Sec.5 [1.2]'. The answerer must follow that cross-reference into Sec.5 [1.2] to find Table 1 and the actual formula for hydrostatic pressure.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: In Sec.7 (Design Load Scenarios), the symbol P_S is listed as 'static sea pressure at considered draught, in kN/m², as defined in Sec.5 [1.2]'. For the static (S) design load scenario (normal seagoing operations, scenario 1 in Table 1), the external pressure P_ex = P_S. Step 2: Follow the reference to Sec.5 [1.2], which states that hydrostatic pressure P_S at any load point is obtained from Table 1. Step 3: Table 1 in Sec.5 gives the hydrostatic pressure formula. For a load point below the waterline (z < T_LC), the hydrostatic pressure is P_S = ρg(T_LC − z), where ρ = 1.025 t/m³ (seawater density) and g = 9.81 m/s². Step 4: With T_LC = 8.0 m and z = 8.0 − 2.5 = 5.5 m (load point is 2.5 m below waterline), P_S = 1.025 × 9.81 × (8.0 − 5.5) = 1.025 × 9.81 × 2.5 ≈ 25.1 kN/m².

question_text: A newbuild container ship with class notation 'Container ship' is being designed with NV 47 steel plates in the hatch side coaming structure. The as-built coaming plate thickness is 72 mm. The design team has confirmed that brittle crack arrest measures are required and has selected an approach based on a shift in block joints (a design-based approach). During the fatigue strength assessment review, the surveyor asks whether the welded details in the upper part of the hull girder — specifically the transverse butt welds of the hatch coaming plates and the equipment holders attached to the coaming — need to be included in the prescriptive fatigue assessment, and if so, what methodology applies to evaluate the permissible stress concentration factors or required FAT classes for those details. The ship has a rule length L of 210 m. Is the prescriptive fatigue assessment of these welded details required, and what is the applicable methodology for evaluating the permissible stress concentration factors or required FAT classes?
required_facts: The NV 47 coaming plate at 72 mm thickness triggers the additional requirements of Sec10 [3] under Sec10 [1.1.2].
Prescriptive fatigue assessment IS required for the transverse butt welds of the hatch coaming plates and the equipment holders, as they are welded details in the upper part of the hull girder.
The ship's rule length of 210 m satisfies the L ≥ 90 m threshold for applicability of the prescriptive fatigue section.
The applicable methodology for evaluating permissible stress concentration factors or required FAT classes for these welded details is DNV-CG-0129 Sec.3 [5].
The loading conditions used in the fatigue assessment shall be in accordance with Pt3 Ch9.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec10 [1.1.2] states that when NV 47 material is applied per [1.1.1], the requirements in [3] shall additionally apply. [3] in Sec10 references Sec7 for fatigue. Sec7 [1.1.2] lists welded details in the upper part of the hull girder (including transverse butt welds of hatch coaming and equipment holders) as details to be assessed by prescriptive fatigue. Sec7 [2.2] then directs the evaluator to DNV-CG-0129 Sec.3 [5] for permissible stress concentration factors or required FAT classes. The loads used in the fatigue assessment are governed by Sec3 [5] (loading conditions for fatigue).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: The ship uses NV 47 steel plates in the hatch coaming at 72 mm thickness, which falls within the 50–100 mm range for NV 47 under Sec10 [1.1.1], so Sec10 applies. Step 2: Sec10 [1.1.2] states that the requirements given in [3] shall be applied additionally when NV 47 material is used per [1.1.1]. Step 3: Sec10 [3] (which is the cross-reference target) points to Sec7 for fatigue requirements applicable to container ships with thick NV 47 plates. Step 4: Sec7 [1.1.1] confirms the section applies to container ships with L ≥ 90 m (210 m qualifies). Step 5: Sec7 [1.1.2] explicitly lists 'welded details in the upper part of the hull girder, e.g., transverse butt welds of plate and stiffeners, hatch cover resting pads, equipment holders, etc.' as details to be assessed by prescriptive fatigue — confirming the assessment is required. Step 6: Sec7 [2.2] states that for such welded details, the evaluation of permissible stress concentration factors or required FAT classes according to DNV-CG-0129 Sec.3 [5] is applicable. Step 7: The loading conditions for the fatigue assessment are governed by Sec3 [5] of the same chapter.

scenario_parameters.brittle_crack_arrest_option: Option A (design-based: shift in block joints)
details_under_review: transverse butt welds of hatch coaming plates

question_text: A general cargo vessel is assigned a type 'A' freeboard and has a machinery casing located on the exposed freeboard deck. The casing is not protected by any enclosed poop, bridge, or deckhouse structure. A single weathertight access door is fitted directly in the machinery casing, leading straight down into the engine room via an internal stairway. The door blade is 900 mm wide and 1800 mm tall, fabricated from 6 mm gross thickness steel plate. The sill height on the freeboard deck side (position 1) is 620 mm above the deck. The design lateral pressure on the door is 8.5 kN/m². The yield strength of the door plate material is 235 N/mm². Is this access door arrangement acceptable for a type 'A' ship, and does the door blade thickness comply with the applicable scantling requirements?
required_facts: The arrangement is not acceptable for a type 'A' ship with an exposed machinery casing
A second weathertight door is required between the access space/passageway and the engine-room stairway
The sill height of 620 mm satisfies the minimum 600 mm requirement for position 1
The minimum required door blade gross thickness is approximately 2.8 mm (calculated via the scantling formula)
The fitted 6 mm door plate thickness is compliant with the scantling requirement
The door must comply with the weathertight door requirements referenced from the machinery space opening rules

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec8 machinery space opening rules for type 'A' ships reference Sec2 [4.1.1] for door compliance requirements, which in turn invokes the scantling formula in Sec2 [4.3.1]
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec8 [2.1.2]: On a type 'A' ship, a machinery casing may be exposed (no enclosing poop/bridge/deckhouse) only if the access door leads to a space or passageway that is as strongly constructed as the casing AND is separated from the engine-room stairway by a second weathertight door. The scenario describes a single door leading directly to the stairway — no second weathertight door is present. This violates Sec8 [2.1.2]. Step 2 — Sec8 [1.1.1]: Access doors in machinery space casings must comply with Sec2 [4.1.1]. The sill height in position 1 must be at least 600 mm — the 620 mm sill satisfies this. Step 3 — Sec2 [4.3.1]: Check door blade thickness. αp = 1.2 − b/(2.1a) = 1.2 − 900/(2.1×1800) = 1.2 − 0.238 = 0.962 (≤1.0, so use 0.962). t_gr = 0.0158 × 0.962 × 900 × √(8.5 / (0.85×235)) = 0.0158 × 0.962 × 900 × √(0.04255) = 0.0158 × 0.962 × 900 × 0.2063 = 2.81 mm. Required gross thickness ≈ 2.81 mm; the fitted 6 mm plate exceeds this, so the blade thickness is compliant. Step 4 — Overall: The arrangement is NOT acceptable because the single-door configuration on an exposed type 'A' casing violates the requirement for a second weathertight door separating the access space from the engine-room stairway, even though the sill height and plate thickness individually comply.

scenario_parameters.door_arrangement: single door, direct access to engine-room stairway

question_text: A naval architect is designing a 180-metre bulk carrier with a double-bottom ballast tank. The tank has an internal web frame (primary supporting member) spanning between the inner bottom and the tank top. The designer needs to determine the design internal pressure to apply to this web frame for the structural strength assessment. The tank geometry is straightforward — no pressure relief valves are fitted, and the tank is used exclusively for seawater ballast. What pressure value, in kN/m², must be used for the web frame of this primary supporting member when checking its strength under the applicable design load scenario for normal seagoing operations?
required_facts: The applicable load component for internal structures in tanks (e.g. web of primary supporting members) is P_int
P_int is defined in the internal loads section, not derived from the tank static or dynamic pressure formulas
P_int = 12 kN/m²
This fixed value of 12 kN/m² applies regardless of tank geometry, filling level, or liquid density
The 12 kN/m² pressure is used for the web of primary supporting members inside the tank, not for the tank boundary plating

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The design load scenario table in Sec7 identifies that internal structures in tanks use the load component P_int. The symbol definition in Sec7 explicitly references Sec6 [3.1] for the value of P_int. Following that cross-reference, Sec6 [3.1] defines P_int = 12 kN/m² for internal structures in tanks such as the web of primary supporting members.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — The designer consults the principal design load scenarios table (Table 1 in Sec7) for normal seagoing operations (Design Load Scenario 1, S+D). The table lists 'Internal structures in tanks' with load component P_int.
Step 2 — In the Symbols list of Sec7, P_int is defined as 'minimum pressure for internal structures in tanks as given in Sec.6 [3.1]'. This is the cross-reference that must be followed.
Step 3 — Navigating to Sec6 [3.1], the clause states: 'The pressure, in kN/m², for internal structures in tanks, e.g. web of primary supporting members, shall be taken as: P_int = 12 kN/m²'.
Step 4 — Therefore the web frame of the primary supporting member must be designed for a pressure of 12 kN/m².

scenario_parameters.structural_element: web of primary supporting member (internal web frame)

question_text: A shipowner is commissioning a small passenger ferry intended to operate exclusively within a sheltered fjord system, never venturing beyond the fjord's enclosed waters. The vessel has no purpose, function, or feature that falls under any existing ship type notation in the classification society's rules. The owner requests that the society assign a notation recognizing the vessel's unique character. The society's surveyor notes that the vessel will be restricted to enclosed waters and that this operational limit must appear somewhere in the vessel's official documentation. (1) What type of notation would the society assign to recognize the vessel's unique character, and how is it visually distinguished in the class certificate? (2) Are there any class requirements associated with this notation? (3) Given the vessel's restriction to enclosed waters only, which service area notation applies, and where will this restriction be formally recorded?
required_facts: A descriptive notation is assigned when no existing notation covers the vessel's purpose, function, or feature
The descriptive notation is visually identified by square brackets, e.g. [Fjord passenger ferry]
There are no class requirements associated with a descriptive notation
The service area notation RE applies because the vessel is restricted to enclosed waters such as fjords
The service area restriction (enclosed waters) will be recorded in the appendix to the class certificate and/or on special signboards

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec7 descriptive notation rules govern recognition of vessels with no existing notation; Sec7 [1.1] references that no class requirements are associated, and the visual format uses square brackets. The enclosed-waters operational restriction then requires consulting Sec6 [1.1.1] for the RE service area notation and Sec6 [1.1.5] for where restrictions are recorded.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec7 [1.1]: The ferry has no existing notation covering its purpose, so a descriptive notation may be assigned. Step 2 — Sec7 [1.4]: The descriptive notation is identified by square brackets, e.g. [Fjord passenger ferry]. Step 3 — Sec7 [1.3]: There are no class requirements associated with a descriptive notation. Step 4 — Cross-reference to Sec6 [1.1.1]: The vessel operates exclusively in enclosed waters (fjord), so the service area notation RE applies, which is defined as limited to enclosed waters such as fjords, ports, rivers and lakes. Step 5 — Sec6 [1.1.5]: The service restriction (enclosed waters only) will be stated in the appendix to the class certificate and/or on special signboards.

question_text: A newbuilding container ship (class notation 'Container ship') is being designed with NV 47 steel plates for the hatch side coaming. The as-built coaming plate thickness is 72 mm. The designer proposes to apply only the brittle crack arrest measures required for NV 36 material at this thickness, arguing that the ship qualifies as a container ship under the general chapter scope. A surveyor questions whether additional requirements apply specifically because NV 47 material is used. Does the proposed approach satisfy the classification rules, and what additional requirement — if any — is triggered by the choice of NV 47 material at 72 mm thickness for the hatch coaming of this container ship?
required_facts: The ship must hold the class notation 'Container ship' for Sec10 to apply, as defined in the general chapter scope (Sec1).
A 72 mm NV 47 hatch side coaming plate falls within the thick-plate scope (thickness > 50 mm and ≤ 100 mm, NV 47 strength group).
Hatch side coaming is explicitly listed as an upper hull longitudinal structural member covered by the thick-plate section.
The requirements of [3] in the thick-plate section must be applied additionally when NV 47 material is used — they are not optional.
The designer's proposal to apply only NV 36-level brittle crack arrest measures is non-compliant for NV 47 material.
The additional [3] requirements for NV 47 are triggered on top of, not instead of, the standard measures in [2.2] and [2.3].

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec10 [1.1.1] scopes the thick-plate section to ships with the class notation 'Container ship' — requiring the answerer to confirm that notation via Sec1 [1.3] and [1.4.1] — and Sec10 [1.1.2] then adds that the requirements in [3] apply additionally when NV 47 material is used per [1.1.1].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Sec10 [1.1.1] states the section applies to ships with the class notation 'Container ship' having thick plates (>50 mm, ≤100 mm) of NV 36, NV 40 or NV 47 for upper hull longitudinal structural members. The 72 mm NV 47 coaming plate falls within scope (50 < 72 ≤ 100 mm, NV 47, hatch side coaming is listed as an upper hull longitudinal structural member in [1.1.3]). Step 2: To confirm the ship qualifies, the answerer must check Sec1 [1.3] and [1.4.1], which define the 'Container ship' notation and its application criteria (cell guides, fixed container foundations, fixed lashing appliances). Step 3: Sec10 [1.1.2] states that the requirements given in [3] shall be applied additionally in cases where NV 47 material is applied according to [1.1.1]. The designer's proposal to apply only NV 36-level measures is therefore non-compliant — the additional requirements of Section 10 [3] are mandatory on top of the standard brittle crack arrest measures.

scenario_parameters.designer_claim: only NV 36-level brittle crack arrest measures required

question_text: A structural engineer is calculating hull girder loads for a 175 m bulk carrier (B = 28 m, CB = 0.82) at a transverse section located 52.5 m from the aft perpendicular. The ship is being assessed under a static plus dynamic load scenario. When computing the vertical wave bending moment at this section, the engineer needs to express the longitudinal position of the calculation point in the coordinate system used throughout the hull girder load calculations. The ship's aft perpendicular is located at X = 0 m in the loading manual, but the engineer is unsure whether this aligns with the reference coordinate system required by the hull girder load formulas. Clarify what coordinate system must be used for the X-coordinate of the calculation point, and determine the wave coefficient Cw applicable to this vessel.
required_facts: The x-coordinate of the calculation point must be expressed in the reference coordinate system defined in Pt3.Ch4.Sec1 [1.2.1], which itself refers to Ch.1 Sec.4 for the full definition
The engineer cannot assume the aft perpendicular equals X = 0 without verifying against the Ch.1 Sec.4 coordinate system
L = 175 m falls in the range 90 ≤ L ≤ 300, so the applicable wave coefficient formula is Cw = 10.75 − ((300 − L)/100)^1.5
The x-coordinate symbol in the hull girder load section is explicitly cross-referenced to Sec.1 [1.2.1] and is not self-contained within Sec.4

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The Symbols section of Sec4 defines the x-coordinate of the calculation point as measured 'with respect to the reference coordinate system defined in Sec.1 [1.2.1]'. The answerer must follow this cross-reference to Sec1 [1.2.1], which in turn points to Ch.1 Sec.4 for the full coordinate system definition. The wave coefficient Cw is also derived from the ship length L = 175 m using the piecewise formula in Sec4.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — In Sec4 Symbols, the x-coordinate is defined as 'X coordinate, in m, of the calculation point with respect to the reference coordinate system defined in Sec.1 [1.2.1]'. This triggers a cross-reference to Sec1. Step 2 — Sec1 [1.2.1] states 'The coordinate system is defined in Ch.1 Sec.4', meaning the engineer must use the coordinate system from Ch.1 Sec.4, not an arbitrary ship-fixed system. The aft perpendicular origin assumption must be verified against that coordinate system definition. Step 3 — For Cw with L = 175 m (90 ≤ 175 ≤ 300), the applicable formula is Cw = 10.75 − ((300 − L)/100)^1.5 = 10.75 − ((300 − 175)/100)^1.5 = 10.75 − (1.25)^1.5 = 10.75 − 1.398 ≈ 9.352.

question_text: A permanent means of access (PMA) platform is being designed for a 150 m bulk carrier. The platform uses enlarged T-bar stiffeners acting as primary support members, with a web depth of 320 mm and a web thickness of 8 mm. The flange has a total breadth of 120 mm and a net flange thickness of 9 mm, with a free flange outstand of 55 mm on each side. The material has a specified minimum yield stress of 235 N/mm². A designer claims the T-bar web plate satisfies the applicable slenderness limit and no further checks are needed. Is this claim correct? Determine whether the web plate and flange of this PMA platform stiffener comply with the applicable proportions requirements, and identify any non-compliant element.
required_facts: PMA platform enlarged stiffeners must be treated as primary supporting members (PSM) and are subject to PSM slenderness requirements

The applicable PSM slenderness coefficients per Pt3.Ch8.Sec2 [4.1.1] are C_w = 100 (single-skin) or 125 (double-skin) for the web plate; the flange coefficient C_f is taken from Table 2, which gives C_f = 12 for T-bars

PSM web-plate minimum thickness requirement: t_w ≥ s_w / C_w × sqrt(R_eH / 235) per Pt3.Ch8.Sec2 [4.1.1] with s_w = web-stiffener spacing and C_w = 100 (single-skin); the requirement cannot be evaluated against h_w / 75 (which is the stiffener rule from [3.1.1])
Flange minimum thickness requirement: t_f ≥ b_f-out / C_f × sqrt(R_eH/235) = 55/12 = 4.58 mm; actual 9 mm complies
Total flange breadth requirement: b_f-gr ≥ 0.2 × h_w = 64 mm; actual 120 mm complies
The designer's claim is incorrect because compliance requires checking all PSM proportion requirements in the slenderness section, not the web plate alone

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec.1 [2.1.3] states that PMA platforms with enlarged stiffeners shall be treated as primary supporting members and must comply with the slenderness requirement for PSM as given in Sec.2 [4]. Sec.2 [4] then provides the specific web plate and flange proportion criteria for primary supporting members.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Sec.1 [2.1.3] identifies PMA platforms with enlarged stiffeners as primary supporting members (PSM) and mandates compliance with the slenderness requirement for PSM as given in Sec.2 [4].

Step 2 — Navigate to Sec.2 [4.1.1], which gives the proportions of web plate and flange for PSM. For a T-bar PSM, the web plate must satisfy t_w ≥ h_w / C_w × sqrt(R_eH/235), and the flange must satisfy t_f ≥ b_f-out / C_f × sqrt(R_eH/235), using the slenderness coefficients from Table 2 (C_w = 75 for T-bars, C_f = 12 for T-bars).

Step 3 — Check web plate: t_w ≥ h_w / C_w × sqrt(235/235) = 320/75 × 1.0 = 4.27 mm. Actual t_w = 8 mm ≥ 4.27 mm → web plate COMPLIES.

Step 4 — Check flange: t_f ≥ b_f-out / C_f × sqrt(R_eH/235) = 55/12 × 1.0 = 4.58 mm. Actual t_f = 9 mm ≥ 4.58 mm → flange COMPLIES.

Step 5 — Check total flange breadth per [3.1.2]: b_f-gr ≥ 0.2 × h_w-gr. Gross h_w ≈ 320 mm (net, so gross slightly larger, but using net as given): 0.2 × 320 = 64 mm. Total flange breadth = 120 mm ≥ 64 mm → COMPLIES.

Step 6 — However, the designer's claim that 'no further checks are needed' after only verifying the web plate is incorrect. The full set of PSM slenderness requirements in Sec.2 [4] must be checked, including flange proportions and flange breadth. The web plate alone is not sufficient. All elements happen to comply in this scenario, but the claim of completeness after only the web check is wrong.

Note: If the scenario is adjusted so b_f-out = 55 mm per side and C_f = 12, the flange check passes. The key pedagogical point is that Sec.1 [2.1.3] triggers a mandatory cross-reference to Sec.2 [4] for the full suite of PSM proportion checks, not just the web.

scenario_parameters.structure: PMA platform with enlarged T-bar stiffeners

question_text: A 185 m bulk carrier has a double-hull ballast tank of cellular construction with an internal volume of 85 m³. The tank is located amidships and has a maximum height of 12 m. During the design review, the structural engineer needs to determine the minimum sloshing pressure to apply to the internal plates, stiffeners, and tripping brackets of this tank, and confirm which structural verification procedure governs. Additionally, the forward bottom structure of the same vessel is being assessed for slamming loads. The designer has specified a normal ballast condition forward draught T_F-f = 3.2 m at the forward end. Determine: (1) the minimum sloshing pressure applicable to the cellular ballast tank and the verification method that must be used, and (2) whether the forward bottom structure requires strengthening against slamming, and if so, calculate the design bottom slamming pressure P_SL at a cross-section located 20 m aft of the forward end, given C_B = 0.82, ship breadth B = 28 m, and the breadth of the flat bottom B_B at 0.15·T_F above baseline = 14 m at that cross-section.
required_facts: The cellular ballast tank qualifies for the reduced minimum sloshing pressure of 12 kN/m² because its volume (85 m³) is less than 100 m³ and it is of cellular construction
The 12 kN/m² pressure applies only to plates, stiffeners, and tripping brackets at internal surfaces; no other sloshing requirements apply to this tank
Structural verification of the sloshing pressure must follow the plating and stiffener scantling method referenced in the sloshing scantling section of the same chapter (Sec4 [3.1])
Bottom slamming strengthening is required because T_F-f = 3.2 m is less than 0.045 × 185 m = 8.325 m
The longitudinal position x must be taken as x1 ≈ 35.3 m (not 20 m) because 20 m is forward of the minimum x1 threshold
B_B must be capped at 1.35 × T_F = 4.32 m, not the full 14 m given, because the rule imposes an upper limit
The design bottom slamming pressure P_SL is calculated using the formula in the bottom slamming section with c1 based on L > 150 m branch: c1 = (225 − 0.5L)^(1/3)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Sec4 sloshing rules for cellular tanks, which references Sec1 [3.1] for the structural verification procedure (bow impact plating scantling method), then the bottom slamming question leads to Sec2 [2.1.1] for the P_SL formula — both Sec1 and Sec2 are within the same chapter (Ch10), requiring cross-section navigation.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sloshing for cellular tank: Pt3.Ch10.Sec4 [1.1.3] states that for tanks of cellular construction (double-hull with internal structures restricting fluid motion) with volume less than 100 m³, the minimum sloshing pressure P_slh-min = 12 kN/m². The tank here is 85 m³ < 100 m³ and is of cellular construction, so P_slh-min = 12 kN/m². The clause further states this pressure applies only to plates, stiffeners and tripping brackets at internal surfaces (web frames, girders, stringers), and shall be verified in accordance with Sec1 [3.1] — i.e., the bow impact plating scantling method from Pt3.Ch10.Sec1. No other sloshing requirements apply to such tanks. Step 2 — Bottom slamming applicability: Pt3.Ch10.Sec2 [1.1.1] states requirements apply to ships with L > 65 m where minimum forward draught T_F-f or T_F-e < 0.045·L. Here L = 185 m, so 0.045·L = 8.325 m. T_F-f = 3.2 m < 8.325 m, so strengthening is required. Step 3 — Compute P_SL at x = 20 m from F.E.: From Sec2 [2.1.1]: c1 = (225 - 0.5×185)^(1/3) = (225 - 92.5)^(1/3) = 132.5^(1/3) ≈ 5.094. c2 = 1675×(1 - 20×3.2/185) = 1675×(1 - 64/185) = 1675×(1 - 0.3459) = 1675×0.6541 ≈ 1095.6. x1 = [1.2 - C_B^(1/3) - L/2500]×L = [1.2 - 0.82^(1/3) - 185/2500]×185 = [1.2 - 0.9353 - 0.074]×185 = 0.1907×185 ≈ 35.3 m. Since x = 20 m < x1 = 35.3 m, use x = x1 = 35.3 m. Check B_B limit: smaller of 1.35×T_F = 1.35×3.2 = 4.32 m and 0.55×√185 = 0.55×13.601 = 7.48 m → B_B limited to 4.32 m (given B_B = 14 m, so cap at 4.32 m). T_F check for C_B > 0.75: max T_F = 1.15×L^(1/3) = 1.15×185^(1/3) = 1.15×5.698 = 6.553 m; T_F-f = 3.2 m < 6.553 m, so no cap needed. P_SL = (c1×c2/T_F)×B_B×(0.56 - L/1250 - x/L) = (5.094×1095.6/3.2)×4.32×(0.56 - 185/1250 - 35.3/185) = (5580.7/3.2)×4.32×(0.56 - 0.148 - 0.1908) = 1743.97×4.32×0.2212 ≈ 1743.97×0.9556 ≈ 1665 kN/m². (Annotator note: exact numeric result depends on rounding; the key chain is Sec4→Sec1 for sloshing verification and Sec4 application triggering Sec2 for slamming.)

question_text:
A 14,000 TEU container ship (rule length L = 334 m, breadth B = 48.4 m, contract speed V = 23 knots, bow flare angle α = 58°, block coefficient CB = 0.65) is being designed with an anti-roll tank system to reduce roll motions and thereby improve container securing performance. The designer proposes to submit a wave load analysis and ship motion model tests as part of the documentation package for the anti-roll tank. During the hull girder strength assessment, the net offered thickness for a deck plate in the container hold is calculated using an as-built thickness of 22.5 mm, a voluntary addition of 1.0 mm, and the applicable corrosion addition. The plate is exposed to the container hold environment on one side and atmosphere on the other side.

(a) What documentation must the designer submit specifically in connection with the anti-roll tank, and under which broader documentation framework does this fall?

(b) For the hull girder strength assessment of the deck plate described above, what is the net offered thickness toff to be used for the section modulus calculation? Show the corrosion addition values applied and the resulting toff in mm.

(c) Given the ship's characteristics (L, B, V, α), is an advanced hydrodynamic assessment including whipping and springing recommended, and what class notation would allow a direct-calculated ship-specific whipping partial safety factor to be used instead of the formula-based value?
required_facts: Anti-roll tank documentation requires wave load analysis (H084), ship motion model tests (H090), and tank structural strength analysis (H080), all submitted for information (FI), as referenced via the container securing arrangement section
The corrosion addition factor α = 0.5 applies to section properties for the strength assessment
The container hold compartment has a one-side corrosion addition tc1 = 1.0 mm; atmosphere exposure also gives tc2 = 1.0 mm, so total tc = 2.0 mm
Net offered thickness toff = 22.5 − 1.0 − 0.5 × 2.0 = 20.5 mm

An advanced hydrodynamic assessment including whipping and springing is recommended because L = 334 m > 290 m, B = 48.4 m > 47 m, and bow flare angle α = 58° > 55° (at least three of the four listed characteristics are exceeded)
The class notation WIV permits the whipping partial safety factor γWH to be replaced by a direct-calculated ship-specific value determined according to DNV-CG-0153

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 documentation requirements, which reference Sec.8 [4.3.3] for anti-roll tank documentation; Sec.8 [4.3.3] in turn triggers hull girder strength rules in Sec.4 [5] for the whipping/springing assessment and net scantling calculations.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 Table 4 (documentation requirements): The row for 'Anti-roll tanks' lists three required documents: H084 (Wave load analysis, FI), H090 (Ship motion model tests, FI), and H080 (Strength analysis — tank structure), all cross-referenced to Sec.8 [4.3.3]. This establishes the documentation chain starting from the general section.

Step 2 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec8 [4.3.3]: This clause governs anti-roll tanks in the context of container securing, requiring wave load analysis with focus on ship motions, ship motion model tests, and tank structural strength analysis. The clause is the intermediate node connecting the documentation framework to the hull girder strength section.

Step 3 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.1.1] and [2.1.2]: For the hull girder strength assessment (net scantlings), the formula is toff = t_as_built − t_vol_add − α·tc. For section properties (strength assessment), α = 0.5 per Table 1. The deck plate in a container hold is exposed to container hold environment on one side (tc1 = 1.0 mm per Table 2, row 'Container holds') and atmosphere on the other side (tc2 = 1.0 mm per Table 2). The combined corrosion addition tc = tc1 + tc2 = 2.0 mm. Therefore toff = 22.5 − 1.0 − 0.5 × 2.0 = 22.5 − 1.0 − 1.0 = 20.5 mm.

Step 4 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.6.2] (whipping/springing): The ship has L = 334 m > 290 m, B = 48.4 m > 47 m, α = 58° > 55°, V = 23 knots < 25 knots (three of four thresholds exceeded — guidance note recommends advanced assessment when these characteristics are present). An advanced assessment using direct hydrodynamic analysis including whipping and springing (level 2, DNV-CG-0153) is recommended. The class notation WIV allows the partial safety factor for whipping to be substituted with a direct-calculated ship-specific value per DNV-CG-0153, rather than using the formula-based γWH.

question_text: A structural engineer is performing a direct strength analysis on a 185-metre bulk carrier.
