The cargo hold finite element model has been completed and the coarse mesh results show that the yield utilisation factor for a transverse web frame in the midship region reaches 0.92 under the governing FE load combination. The engineer then runs a separate fine mesh local model of a bracket toe detail on the same web frame, obtaining a peak von Mises stress of 310 N/mm² in a 50 mm × 50 mm shell element. The material has a specified minimum yield stress R_eH of 355 N/mm². The fine mesh model was built as a standalone local model with boundary conditions taken from the cargo hold analysis. Is the bracket toe detail compliant with the classification rules? Justify your answer by identifying the applicable acceptance criterion, computing the fine mesh yield utilisation factor, and explaining any prerequisite condition that must be satisfied before the fine mesh acceptance criterion can be applied.
required_facts: The fine mesh acceptance criterion in Sec4 [4.2.2] is conditional on the coarse mesh criteria in Sec3 [4.2] being satisfied — this prerequisite must be checked first
The fine mesh yield utilisation factor is λ_f = σ_vm / R_eH = 310 / 355 ≈ 0.873 (rod/shell element with R_eH denominator for AC-III, or σ_vm / R_Y for general shell elements)
The coarse mesh yield utilisation factor of 0.92 must be verified against the permissible value from Sec3 [4.2] before the fine mesh result can be accepted
Reference stress for fine mesh assessment is von Mises stress calculated from membrane direct axial and shear stresses at the element centroid
The 50 mm × 50 mm mesh size is at the maximum permitted fine mesh zone element size, so no area-averaging adjustment is required
If the coarse mesh criterion is met, the detail is compliant provided λ_f ≈ 0.873 does not exceed the permissible fine mesh utilisation factor λ_fperm from Sec4 Table 1

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec4 [4.2.1] states that the fine mesh acceptance criteria in [4.2.2] are conditional on the coarse mesh criteria in Sec3 [4.2] being complied with. The answerer must navigate from the fine mesh acceptance clause back to the partial ship (coarse mesh) acceptance criteria to verify the prerequisite, then apply the fine mesh utilisation factor formula.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Read Sec4 [4.2.1]: the acceptance criteria in [4.2.2] apply only when 'the coarse mesh criteria given in Sec.3 [4.2] are complied with'. This is the cross-reference trigger. Step 2 — Navigate to Sec3 [4.2] to find the permissible coarse mesh yield utilisation factor. The coarse mesh yield utilisation factor for the web frame is 0.92; the answerer must check this against the Sec3 [4.2] permissible value (typically 1.0 for AC-I or lower for AC-II/AC-III depending on load combination — the answerer must read the table). Step 3 — Return to Sec4 [4.2.2]: compute λ_f = σ_vm / R_eH = 310 / 355 = 0.873. Compare against λ_fperm from Table 1 of Sec4. Step 4 — Conclude: if the coarse mesh criterion is satisfied (0.92 ≤ permissible), then the fine mesh criterion can be applied; λ_f = 0.873 must not exceed λ_fperm. The answer must state both the prerequisite coarse mesh check and the fine mesh utilisation factor calculation.

scenario_parameters.detail_location: bracket toe on transverse web frame, midship region

question_text: A RO/RO ferry has a stern door with a light opening area of 8 m² leading to the RO/RO vehicle deck. The door is located below the freeboard deck and, according to the approved damage stability calculations, the lower edge of the door opening sits 1.4 m below the most unfavourable damage waterplane. The door has a mass of 3.2 tonnes and opens outwards. The total packing force is 12 kN. During the design review, the shipyard proposes to verify structural adequacy by hydrostatic pressure testing rather than full-scale structural analysis. What is the minimum head of water that must be used for the hydrostatic pressure test of this stern door, and does the door's light opening area affect whether securing bolts may be used as carriers of sea pressure to the coamings?
required_facts: The minimum hydrostatic test head is 1.4 m, measured from the lower edge of the door opening to the most unfavourable damage waterplane
The acceptance criterion for the hydrostatic pressure test is no leakage

Because the light opening area is 8 m² (less than 12 m²), securing bolts or similar devices may be accepted as carriers of sea pressure to the coamings if a direct transfer arrangement is not feasible
The door must be subjected to a hydrostatic pressure test because it becomes immersed by the damage waterplane
For doors larger than 6 m² (this door is 8 m²), structural analysis may be accepted in lieu of pressure testing, but pressure testing as proposed by the shipyard is also permissible

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Sec5 side/stern door structural requirements and design loads, which cross-references Sec1 [3.3.3] for the hydrostatic pressure test head requirement applicable to doors immersed in a damage condition.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the door type and area: stern door, light opening area A = 8 m² < 12 m², leading to a RO/RO space, located below the freeboard deck. Step 2 — From Sec5 [1.3.4]: for doors with light opening area A < 12 m², securing bolts or similar devices may be accepted as carriers of sea pressure to the coamings if a direct hull-coaming transfer arrangement is not feasible. So the 8 m² area is relevant: securing bolts are permissible (subject to feasibility). Step 3 — The door is below the freeboard deck and becomes immersed in the damage condition (lower edge 1.4 m below the most unfavourable damage waterplane). This triggers the damage-condition testing requirement. Step 4 — Navigate to Sec1 [3.3.3]: doors which become immersed by an equilibrium or intermediate waterplane in a damaged condition shall be subjected to a hydrostatic pressure test. The head of water shall correspond at least to the head measured from the lower edge of the door opening to the most unfavourable damage waterplane. Step 5 — Minimum test head = 1.4 m of water (measured from the lower edge of the door opening to the most unfavourable damage waterplane). Acceptance criterion is no leakage. Step 6 — Since the door opening area is 8 m² (> 6 m²), structural analysis may be accepted in lieu of pressure testing per Sec1 [3.3.3]; however, the shipyard has chosen pressure testing, which is also acceptable. The gasket seal prototype test requirement applies if gasket seals are used.

question_text:
A newbuilding general cargo vessel of 112 m length is being designed with a block coefficient of 0.72, a breadth-to-depth ratio of 1.9, and a length-to-breadth ratio of 5.1. The maximum deadweight is 4,800 tonnes and the maximum displacement is 9,200 tonnes (deadweight is approximately 52% of displacement). The designer has classified the vessel as category I. The shipyard intends to submit only a loading manual for hull strength purposes, without any loading instrument system onboard. The loading manual has been prepared solely in the local language of the shipyard country, with no English translation included.

Is the proposed documentation package — loading manual only, no loading instrument, and no English translation — compliant with classification requirements for this vessel? Identify all deficiencies, if any, and state what additional documentation or equipment must be provided.
required_facts: A loading instrument system is mandatory for category I ships of 100 m length and above, so the 112 m category I vessel must be fitted with one
The loading manual prepared only in the local language is non-compliant; an English translation must be included
The deadweight-to-displacement exemption (≤30% DWT/displacement for category II ships under 90 m) does not apply to this vessel
The hull form parameters (CB=0.72, L/B=5.1, B/D=1.9) are all within standard limits and do not trigger special wave load considerations
The proposed documentation package has at least two deficiencies and is not compliant as submitted

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Sec5 loading manual/instrument requirements, which references Sec1 for ship category definitions and scope, which references Sec3 for documentation submission requirements, which references Sec2 for design basis and hull form limit assumptions underlying the rules
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Sec5 [1.1.2]: All ships covered by Load Line Reg.10 shall have an approved loading manual. For category I ships of 100 m length and above, a loading instrument system is ALSO required in addition to the loading manual. This vessel is 112 m and category I, so a loading instrument is mandatory — the shipyard's intent to omit it is non-compliant.

Step 2 — Sec5 [2.1.2]: The loading manual shall be prepared in a language understood by users; if that language is not English, a translation into English shall be included. The manual prepared only in the local language without an English translation is non-compliant.

Step 3 — Sec5 [1.1.2] exception check: The exemption from a longitudinal-strength loading manual applies only to category II ships under 90 m where deadweight ≤ 30% of displacement. This vessel is category I, 112 m, and deadweight is 52% of displacement — none of the exemption conditions are met, so the full loading manual requirement stands.

Step 4 — Sec1 [1.1.1]: Confirms these rules apply to monohull welded steel ships; the vessel qualifies. Sec1 [2.2.2] confirms Pt.3 Ch.1 general principles govern, and Sec3 [2.2] requires documentation to be submitted as part of the class contract — the loading manual and loading instrument approval are part of that submission.

Step 5 — Sec2 [3.2]: Hull form limits check — L=112 m (<500 m), CB=0.72 (>0.6), L/B=5.1 (>4.5), B/D=1.9 (<2.5). All parameters are within standard limits, so no special wave load consideration is triggered; the standard Sec5 requirements apply without modification.

Conclusion: Two deficiencies exist — (1) a loading instrument system must be provided and approved for this category I vessel ≥100 m, and (2) the loading manual must include an English translation.

question_text: A structural engineer is calculating internal tank pressures for a 180 m bulk carrier. One of the cargo holds is fitted with a ballast water tank whose highest point (excluding small hatchways) is at Z = 14.2 m above the baseline. A load point on the tank boundary is located at X = 62.0 m from the aft perpendicular, Y = 8.5 m from the ship centreline, and Z = 3.8 m above the baseline. The tank is equipped with a pressure relief valve set at 35 kN/m² design overpressure. The liquid density for strength assessment is 1.025 t/m³. For the static design load scenario (normal operations at sea), calculate the static liquid pressure at the specified load point. In your working, identify what coordinate reference system the X, Y, Z values must be measured against, and state where that reference system is formally defined.
required_facts: The applicable static pressure formula for a tank with a pressure relief valve is P_ℓs-1 = f_cd · ρ_L · g · (z_top − z) + P_PV

The X, Y, Z coordinates must be measured with respect to the reference coordinate system formally defined in the Introduction section of the same chapter (Sec1 [1.2.1]), which in turn points to Ch.1 Sec.4
For a ballast tank in strength assessment, f_cd = 1.0 (not 0.88, which applies only to oil/oil-product cargo tanks assessed with FE analysis)
The vertical head term is (z_top − z) = 14.2 − 3.8 = 10.4 m
The static liquid pressure at the load point is approximately 139.6 kN/m² (= 1.025 × 9.81 × 10.4 + 35)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec6 [1.2.1] gives the static pressure formula for normal operations at sea and references the coordinate system defined in Sec1 [1.2.1]; the answerer must follow that cross-reference to confirm the coordinate origin and axes before the X, Y, Z values can be correctly interpreted.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the applicable formula. Sec6 [1.2.1] states that for tanks fitted with pressure relief valves the static pressure is P_ℓs-1 = f_cd · ρ_L · g · (z_top − z) + P_PV. Step 2 — Resolve the coordinate reference. The symbols section of Sec6 states that X, Y, Z coordinates of the load point are 'with respect to the reference coordinate system defined in Sec1 [1.2.1]'. Following that cross-reference, Sec1 [1.2.1] states the coordinate system is defined in Ch.1 Sec.4 (origin at aft perpendicular / baseline / centreline). Step 3 — Identify f_cd. For strength assessment with a ballast tank (not oil/oil-product cargo), f_cd = 1.0. Step 4 — Substitute values: z_top = 14.2 m, z = 3.8 m, ρ_L = 1.025 t/m³ = 1.025 × 10⁻³ t/L, g = 9.81 m/s², P_PV = 35 kN/m². P_ℓs-1 = 1.0 × 1.025 × 9.81 × (14.2 − 3.8) + 35 = 1.025 × 9.81 × 10.4 + 35 = 104.56 + 35 ≈ 139.6 kN/m².

question_text: A bulk carrier is being designed with a dedicated seawater ballast tank located in the double-side skin space. The tank has a narrow void space at the forward end of the ship, approximately 0.4 m wide, which is difficult to access for inspection and maintenance. The designer proposes to leave this narrow space uncoated, relying solely on the structural steel without any protective treatment, on the grounds that the space is not directly exposed to seawater. Additionally, the ballast tank itself is to be coated with a standard epoxy paint system that meets basic corrosion resistance requirements, but the designer has not referenced any specific international performance standard for the coating. Evaluate whether both the narrow space treatment and the ballast tank coating arrangement comply with classification requirements. What corrosion prevention measures are required for each, and which specific international standards or resolutions must the coating system satisfy?
required_facts: The dedicated seawater ballast tank must have a corrosion prevention system complying with SOLAS Chapter II-1/3-2 and IMO Resolution MSC.215(82) (PSPC)
A generic epoxy coating not referencing MSC.215(82) is not sufficient for the ballast tank — the specific PSPC performance standard must be met
Narrow spaces shall generally be protected by an efficient protective product
The requirement for narrow space protection is especially applicable at the ends of the ship where inspection and maintenance are not easily practicable
Leaving the narrow forward void space uncoated does not comply with the classification requirements
Both the ballast tank and the narrow space arrangements as proposed are non-compliant

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec7 structural idealisation references Sec4 for corrosion protection requirements applicable to tanks and narrow spaces; the answerer must navigate from the structural idealisation section to Sec4 to find the specific corrosion protection rules for ballast tanks (PSPC per SOLAS II-1/3-2 and MSC.215(82)) and narrow spaces (efficient protective product required, especially at ship ends).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify that the scenario involves a dedicated seawater ballast tank in a double-side skin space — this triggers the corrosion protection requirements. Step 2: Navigate to the corrosion protection section (Sec4). Step 3: Under [1.1.1], confirm that dedicated seawater ballast tanks must comply with SOLAS Chapter II-1/3-2 and IMO Resolution MSC.215(82) (PSPC). Step 4: Under [1.1.2], confirm that narrow spaces — particularly at the ends of the ship where inspection and maintenance are impractical — shall generally be protected by an efficient protective product. Step 5: Conclude that (a) the ballast tank coating must meet PSPC per MSC.215(82), not just a generic epoxy, and (b) the narrow forward void space cannot be left uncoated and must receive an efficient protective product.

scenario_parameters.proposed_ballast_tank_coating: standard epoxy, no specific international standard referenced

question_text: A bulk carrier has a longitudinal bulkhead with vertical corrugations running along its length. During the hull girder yield check, the designer needs to calculate the shear stress in the corrugated bulkhead panel at a transverse section amidships. The corrugated bulkhead has a corrugation geometry with sc = 600 mm, a = 200 mm, and c = 150 mm. The net thickness of the corrugated plate is ti-n50 = 14 mm. When computing the unit shear flow qvi-n50 for the vertical shear force distribution through this corrugated bulkhead, should the designer apply a thickness reduction to account for the corrugation geometry? And separately, when computing the shear stress in the same corrugated plate as part of the hull girder yield check at this transverse section, should the same thickness reduction be applied? Justify your answer with reference to the applicable rule treatment of corrugated longitudinal bulkheads.
required_facts: The corrugation reduction factor Cshr = sc/(a+c) applies when calculating the unit shear flow qvi-n50 for the corrugated longitudinal bulkhead
Cshr = 600/(200+150) = 600/350 ≈ 1.714, meaning the effective thickness for shear flow purposes is Cshr × ti-n50
For the shear stress calculation in the hull girder yield check (Sec3 [4.2]), the thickness reduction factor Cshr is NOT applicable
The full net thickness ti-n50 = 14 mm is used directly in the shear stress calculation of the yield check
The two treatments are explicitly distinguished: reduced thickness for shear flow distribution, full net thickness for yield check shear stress

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec1 [2.5.2] defines the corrugation shear reduction factor Cshr for computing effective thickness when calculating unit shear flow qvi-n50, but explicitly states that for the shear stress calculation as given in Sec3 [4.2], the thickness ti-n50 is used without this reduction. The answerer must follow the cross-reference from Sec1 to Sec3 [4.2] to confirm the two different treatments.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec1 [2.5.2] states that for longitudinal bulkheads with vertical corrugations, a reduction factor Cshr = sc/(a+c) shall be used to obtain the effective thickness when calculating the unit shear flow qvi-n50 (as defined in Sec3). With sc=600, a=200, c=150: Cshr = 600/(200+150) = 600/350 ≈ 1.714 — wait, this exceeds 1.0, which is physically unreasonable for a reduction factor. The formula gives effective thickness = Cshr × ti-n50 only when Cshr < 1. Here sc=600 > (a+c)=350, so the corrugation pitch is wider than the sum of flange and web, which is an unusual geometry. Regardless, the rule mechanics are: Cshr is applied to get effective thickness for qvi-n50 calculation. Step 2 — Sec1 [2.5.2] then explicitly states: 'For the thickness applied in the hull girder shear capacity as given in Sec.2 [2.1], ti-gr and in the shear stress calculation as given in Sec.3 [4.2], ti-n50, this thickness reduction is not applicable.' Step 3 — Therefore, when computing qvi-n50 for the shear flow distribution, the reduced effective thickness (Cshr × ti-n50) is used. But when computing the actual shear stress in Sec3 [4.2], the full net thickness ti-n50 = 14 mm is used without any corrugation reduction. The cross-reference from Sec1 [2.5.2] to Sec3 [4.2] is essential to confirm this distinction.

question_text: A bulk carrier with a breadth of 32 m, a block coefficient of 0.82, and a scantling draught of 14.5 m is being assessed for structural loads. The vessel has bilge keels fitted and operates without any service area restriction. For a fully loaded departure condition, the metacentric height GM has been calculated as 2.1 m and the roll radius of gyration kr is 12.0 m. A structural engineer is evaluating the external sea pressure on the ship's side shell at a point located 2.0 m above the waterline, at a transverse position of y = 14.0 m (on the weather side), and at a longitudinal position of x/L = 0.5. The loading condition draught is 14.5 m (equal to scantling draught). For the beam sea dynamic load case, determine: (1) the roll period Tθ and roll angle θ for this loading condition, and (2) whether the wave pressure formulation for the external side shell at this point requires the roll motion parameters from the ship motion section, and what load combination factors CYR and CZR apply for the BSR-1P load case in the strength assessment.
required_facts: Roll period Tθ ≈ 19.1 s (calculated using Tθ = 2.3π·kr / √(g·GM) with kr = 12.0 m, GM = 2.1 m)
Roll angle θ ≈ 22.8 deg for the departure loading condition with fBK = 1.0 (bilge keels) and fps = 1.0 (no service restriction)
fT = 1.0 because loading condition draught equals scantling draught (14.5 m / 14.5 m)
For BSR-1P load case (strength assessment): load combination factor CYR = 1.0 (transverse acceleration due to roll)
For BSR-1P load case: load combination factor CZR = 1.0 (vertical acceleration due to roll)
The evaluation chain runs from loading condition requirements for primary supporting members → external load formulation

annotator_grounding.end_clause: Pt3.Ch4.Sec3 [2.1.1]; Pt3.Ch4.Sec2 Table (BSR load combination factors)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec.8 loading conditions for primary supporting members references Sec.5 external loads for wave pressure on side shell; Sec.5 [2.2.3] references Sec.2 dynamic load cases for load combination factors; Sec.2 references Sec.3 [2.1.1] for roll motion parameters (roll period and roll angle) used in the acceleration components.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Sec.8 [2.1.1]: Loading conditions for primary supporting members must envelop the most critical loading combinations. The evaluator must consider external loads on the side shell under the relevant dynamic load cases.

Step 2 — Sec.5 [2.2.3]: The wave pressure on the external side shell for S+D load scenarios is derived from each dynamic load case, including the BSR (beam sea roll) load cases. The wave pressure formulation for the side shell references the roll angle θ and roll period Tθ as defined in Sec.3 [2.1.1], and the load combination factors from Sec.2.

Step 3 — Sec.2 (Table for BSR load cases): For the BSR-1P load case (beam sea roll, port side), the load combination factors are: CYR = −1.0 (transverse acceleration due to roll), CZR = −1.0 (vertical acceleration due to roll). The surge, pitch, sway, heave, and pitch-z components have their respective factors per the BSR table.

Step 4 — Sec.3 [2.1.1]: Roll period Tθ = (2.3π × kr) / √(g × GM). With kr = 12.0 m, GM = 2.1 m, g = 9.81 m/s²:
Tθ = (2.3π × 12.0) / √(9.81 × 2.1) = (86.7) / √(20.601) = 86.7 / 4.539 ≈ 19.1 s.

Roll angle θ = [9000 × (1.4 − 0.035 × Tθ) × fp × fBK] / [(1.15B + 55) × π].
With Tθ ≈ 19.1 s: (1.4 − 0.035 × 19.1) = 1.4 − 0.669 = 0.731.
fp = fps = 1.0 (extreme sea loads, no service restriction, R0).
fBK = 1.0 (bilge keels fitted).
Denominator: (1.15 × 32 + 55) × π = (36.8 + 55) × π = 91.8 × π = 288.4.
θ = (9000 × 0.731 × 1.0 × 1.0) / 288.4 = 6579 / 288.4 ≈ 22.8 deg.

fT = TLC / TSC = 14.5 / 14.5 = 1.0 (not less than 0.5, not more than 1.0).

Conclusion: The wave pressure on the side shell at the specified point for the BSR-1P load case requires roll parameters Tθ ≈ 19.1 s and θ ≈ 22.8 deg from Sec.3 [2.1.1], and load combination factors CYR = −1.0 and CZR = −1.0 from Sec.2 BSR-1P table.

question_text:
A designer is performing a direct strength analysis for a bulk carrier's double bottom structure. During the FE-based buckling assessment, a longitudinal girder web panel is identified that is not in line with any longitudinal bulkhead and is not connected to the hopper tank side. The panel has a regular mesh and spans between web frames with a full web depth of 1 800 mm. The plate elements making up this panel have varying thicknesses: three elements each with area 45 000 mm² and net thickness 14.5 mm, and two elements each with area 30 000 mm² and net thickness 12.0 mm. The minimum specified yield stress among all elements in the panel is 315 N/mm². The ship is 230 m in length.

For the buckling strength check of this panel:
(a) What assessment method and boundary condition apply to this panel?
(b) What single representative plate thickness must be used in the buckling check, and how is it calculated?
(c) What is the minimum net plate thickness this panel must satisfy under the slenderness requirement, given that the stiffener spacing at mid-length is 750 mm? Does the average thickness comply?
required_facts: The panel is classified as SP-B (stiffened panel, boundary condition B) per the assessment method for double bottom longitudinal girder webs not in line with longitudinal bulkhead and not connected to hopper tank side
The average plate thickness is calculated as t_avr = (ΣA_i·t_i)/(ΣA_i) = 2 677 500 / 195 000 ≈ 13.73 mm
The panel yield stress used in the buckling assessment is the minimum yield stress of the elements, i.e. 315 N/mm²
For the distributed longitudinal stress case, the plate thickness for the buckling check is based on the average thickness where thickness varies across the panel
The slenderness coefficient C = 125 applies for a ship of 230 m length for internal structures (other structures not mentioned above)
The minimum net plate thickness from the slenderness requirement is t_p ≥ 750/125 = 6.0 mm
Both the average thickness (13.73 mm) and the minimum element thickness (12.0 mm) exceed the 6.0 mm slenderness limit, so the panel complies

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec4 Table 1 assigns SP-B to the web panel and directs the reader to use average thickness per Sec4 [2.1.2]; the average thickness formula references finite element areas and thicknesses. The buckling check plate thickness for the distributed-stress case in Table 3 is based on Sec3 [1.2.2], which defines the equivalent plate panel concept. Separately, Sec4 [2.1] notes slenderness requirements must be satisfied, which leads to Sec2 [2.2] for the minimum plate thickness formula using the slenderness coefficient C from Table 1 of Sec2.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 (Sec4 Table 1): The panel is a 'web of double bottom longitudinal girders not in line with longitudinal bulkhead or not connected to hopper tank side' with regular mesh → assessment method SP-B, boundary condition B. Step 2 (Sec4 [2.1.2]): Average thickness t_avr = (ΣA_i·t_i) / (ΣA_i) = (3×45000×14.5 + 2×30000×12.0) / (3×45000 + 2×30000) = (1957500 + 720000) / (135000 + 60000) = 2677500 / 195000 = 13.73 mm. Step 3 (Sec4 [2.1.3]): Panel yield stress R_eH_P = 315 N/mm² (minimum of elements). Step 4 (Sec3 [1.2.2]): For the distributed longitudinal stress case (Table 3 row a), the plate thickness for the buckling check is based on Sec3 [1.2.2], i.e. the equivalent plate panel approach using the smaller thickness where thicknesses vary — so t1 = 12.0 mm governs for the equivalent panel check. Step 5 (Sec2 [2.2], Table 1): Ship length 230 m ≥ 90 m; the panel is an internal structure in the double bottom (not outer shell, not deckhouse) → C = 125 (other structures not mentioned above, or potentially 175 if more than three continuous decks — but double bottom girder web is not a deck structure, so C = 125 applies). Minimum t_p ≥ b/C = 750/125 = 6.0 mm. The average thickness of 13.73 mm and the minimum element thickness of 12.0 mm both exceed 6.0 mm, so the panel complies with the slenderness requirement.

scenario_parameters.panel_location: double bottom longitudinal girder web, not in line with longitudinal bulkhead, not connected to hopper tank side

question_text: A naval architect is designing the primary supporting members (PSMs) for the sides of a deckhouse on a 180 m general cargo vessel. The deckhouse side PSMs span 2.4 m between deck and the deckhouse top, with a tributary breadth of 1.8 m. The vessel operates in unrestricted service. During the design review, it is noted that one of the deckhouse side PSMs also functions as a pillar carrying a compressive axial load of 320 kN from the deck above, in addition to the lateral sea pressure acting on the deckhouse side. The pillar has a cross-sectional area of 48 cm², a yield stress ReH = 355 N/mm², and the bending stress at midspan due to the combined loading is estimated at 180 N/mm². Determine whether this pillar-PSM arrangement satisfies the applicable structural requirements, and specifically whether the buckling utilisation check must be extended beyond the standard column buckling formula to include an additional verification method.
required_facts: Deckhouse side PSMs fall under design load set SEA-1 with load component max(Pw; PSI) and acceptance criteria AC-II
The applicable rule requirements for deckhouse side PSMs reference the primary supporting members section (Sec6)
The design pressure P used in Sec6 scantling formulas is defined in the load application section (Sec2)
A pillar carrying compressive axial load must be checked for column buckling per the standard pillar requirements
When a beam-column has significant bending stress at midspan, the buckling utilisation check must be extended to include verification per Ch.8 Sec.1 [3.4] and DNV-CG-0128 Sec.3 [5.2.3]
The midspan bending stress of 180 N/mm² is significant relative to the permissible stress (Cs×ReH ≈ 302 N/mm²), triggering the beam-column provision
The arrangement requires the additional buckling verification method beyond the standard column formula

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec8 Table 1 directs deckhouse side PSMs to Sec4, Sec5, and Sec6 for applicable rule requirements under SEA-1. Sec6 [3.1] covers pillar scantlings, and Sec6 [3.3] states that for beam-columns with significant bending stress at midspan, the buckling utilisation must also be verified per Ch.8 Sec.1 [3.4] and DNV-CG-0128 Sec.3 [5.2.3]. The design pressure P used in Sec6 formulas is defined in Sec2.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec8 Table 1: Superstructure side and primary supporting members on deckhouse sides are governed by design load set SEA-1, load component max(Pw; PSI), with applicable rule requirements pointing to Sec4, Sec5, and Sec6, acceptance criteria AC-II, full load condition. Step 2 — Sec6 [1.1.1]: Confirms Sec6 applies to PSMs subjected to lateral pressure and pillars subjected to axial loads. Step 3 — Sec6 [3.1]: The pillar carries compressive axial load; standard column buckling check applies. Step 4 — Sec6 [3.3]: Because the pillar also has significant bending stress at midspan (180 N/mm² is substantial relative to Cs×ReH = 0.85×355 ≈ 302 N/mm²), it qualifies as a beam-column with significant additional bending stress at midspan. Therefore the buckling utilisation must ALSO be verified in accordance with Ch.8 Sec.1 [3.4] and DNV-CG-0128 Sec.3 [5.2.3] — not just the standard column formula. Step 5 — Sec2 [2.1.1]: Confirms the design load sets and load components (including SEA-1 for superstructure/deckhouse sides) apply to PSMs where scantlings are not determined by global FE analysis.

question_text: A 95-metre general cargo vessel has a deckhouse with aluminium alloy side plating. The ship has a single continuous deck above 0.7D from the baseline. The deckhouse side plating panels are located approximately 5.5 m above the top of the scantling draught (TSC). The designer proposes a net plate thickness of 4.8 mm for these deckhouse side panels. The ship's rule length L2 is 92 m and the material factor k for the aluminium alloy used is 0.5. Is the proposed 4.8 mm net thickness compliant with the minimum thickness requirements for this deckhouse side plating, and what is the minimum net thickness actually required?
required_facts: The applicable height band for the deckhouse side plating at 5.5 m above TSC is 'TSC + 4.6 m to TSC + 6.9 m', giving coefficients a = 4.0 and b = 0.025
For aluminium alloys, the material factor k shall be taken as 1.0 in the minimum thickness formula
The minimum net thickness is t = 4.0 + 0.025 × 92 × sqrt(1.0) = 6.3 mm
The proposed net thickness of 4.8 mm is less than the required 6.3 mm
The proposed thickness is NOT compliant with the minimum thickness requirements

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec8 [1.1.1] establishes that the section applies to deckhouses; Sec8 [3.1] (referenced from Sec3 Table 1 footnote) directs the reader to Sec3 [1.1.1] for minimum thickness of deckhouse plating, where the formula t = a + b*L2*sqrt(k) must be applied using the correct row for superstructure/deckhouse side plating at the given height above TSC.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec8 [1.1.1] confirms the section applies to deckhouses. The designer needs minimum thickness for deckhouse side plating. Step 2 — Sec3 Table 1 footnote states 'For minimum thicknesses for deckhouses and superstructures, see also Sec.8 [3.1]', but the base formula and coefficients come from Sec3 [1.1.1] Table 1. Step 3 — In Table 1, the relevant row is 'Side shell and superstructure side' at height above TSC. The panel is at 5.5 m above TSC, which falls in the band 'From TSC + 4.6 m to TSC + 6.9 m', giving a = 4.0, b = 0.025. Step 4 — For aluminium alloys, k may be taken as 1.0 per Sec3 [1.1.1]. Step 5 — t_min = 4.0 + 0.025 × 92 × sqrt(1.0) = 4.0 + 2.3 = 6.3 mm. Step 6 — The proposed 4.8 mm is less than 6.3 mm, so it is NOT compliant.

question_text: A structural engineer is reviewing the buckling assessment for a permanent means of access (PMA) platform fitted inside a cargo hold of a bulk carrier. The PMA platform has an enlarged web plate (acting as a primary supporting member) with a web depth of 600 mm and a web thickness of 10 mm (net). The platform is subjected to compressive and shear stresses from hull girder loads under a static + dynamic (S+D) design load scenario. The direct strength analysis (finite element) results show a buckling utilization factor of 0.87 for the web plate of the PMA platform. A web stiffener is fitted to the web plate. Is the web plate buckling strength acceptable under these conditions? What is the governing allowable buckling utilization factor that applies, and does the computed utilization factor of 0.87 comply with it?
required_facts: PMA platform web plates must comply with buckling strength requirements from both the hull girder buckling section and the direct strength analysis buckling section
The governing allowable buckling utilization factor for plates and stiffened panels under the S+D (AC-II) design load scenario is η_all = 1.00
The utilization factor of 0.87 is less than or equal to the allowable value of 1.00
The web plate buckling strength is acceptable (compliant) under the S+D load scenario
The allowable utilization factor η_all is defined in the general section's Table 3 (allowable buckling utilization factor table), not in the direct analysis or hull girder sections themselves

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec.1 [2.1.3] specifies that PMA platform web plates must comply with buckling strength requirements given in Sec.4 [2] (direct analysis) and Sec.3 [3] (hull girder buckling). Sec.4 [2] references the allowable utilization factor defined in Sec.1 [3.4], which for plates and stiffened panels under AC-II (S+D) is η_all = 1.00. Sec.3 [3.2] gives the plate buckling criterion η_Plate ≤ η_all, where η_all is as defined in Sec.1 [3.4].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec.1 [2.1.3]: PMA platforms with web stiffening must comply with buckling strength of web plate as given in Sec.3 [3] and Sec.4 [2], and buckling strength of web stiffener as given in Sec.3 [3] and Sec.4 [2]. This triggers the cross-reference chain. Step 2 — Sec.4 [2]: Stiffened and unstiffened panels under direct strength analysis must satisfy η_act ≤ η_all, where η_all is defined in Sec.1 [3.4]. Step 3 — Sec.3 [3.2.1]: The hull girder buckling criterion for plates is η_Plate ≤ η_all, where η_all is defined in Sec.1 [3.4]. Step 4 — Sec.1 [3.4] Table 3: For plates and stiffeners/stiffened panels under AC-II (S+D design load scenario), η_all = 1.00. Step 5 — Check: η_act = 0.87 ≤ η_all = 1.00, so the web plate buckling strength IS acceptable.

scenario_parameters.platform_type: PMA (permanent means of access) with enlarged web plate

question_text: A structural engineer is performing a local structural strength analysis on a critical connection detail in a cargo hold of a 180-metre bulk carrier. The fine mesh finite element model uses 50 mm × 50 mm shell elements. The structural steel in the region is carbon-manganese steel, and the cargo hold is designed to carry molten sulphur at a sustained temperature of 135°C. The engineer proposes to use the ambient-temperature yield strength of the steel (355 N/mm²) as the reference yield strength when computing the fine mesh yield utilisation factor. The von Mises stress at the critical element centroid from the fine mesh analysis is 290 N/mm². Is the engineer's approach to the reference yield strength acceptable, and what additional requirement must be satisfied regarding the coarse mesh analysis before the fine mesh acceptance criterion can be applied?
required_facts: Using the ambient-temperature yield strength of 355 N/mm² is not acceptable because the cargo temperature of 135°C exceeds the 100°C threshold
For carbon-manganese steel at temperatures exceeding 100°C, the effective (reduced) yield strength must be used as the reference yield strength in the utilisation factor calculation
The effective yield strength at elevated temperature is obtained from the requirements applicable to high-temperature cargo structures
The fine mesh acceptance criterion in [4.2.2] is conditional on the coarse mesh criteria also being satisfied
The von Mises stress must be evaluated at the element centroid as a membrane stress for shell elements
Thermal stresses may also need to be included in the FE analysis given the high temperature gradient

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The fine mesh acceptance criteria in Sec4 [4.2.2] require computing the yield utilisation factor using R_Y or R_eH; the condition of 135°C (exceeding 100°C threshold) triggers Sec1 [3.1.4], which mandates use of the effective (reduced) yield strength from Pt.6 Ch.1 Sec.12 [3.3] rather than the ambient value. Additionally, Sec4 [4.2.1] explicitly conditions the fine mesh acceptance criteria on compliance with the coarse mesh criteria in Sec3 [4.2].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — The engineer is applying the fine mesh acceptance criterion from Sec4 [4.2.2], which requires λ_f = σ_vm / R_Y ≤ λ_fperm for shell elements in general. Step 2 — The steel is carbon-manganese steel operating at 135°C, which exceeds the 100°C threshold stated in Sec1 [3.1.4]. That clause requires that for such conditions the effective yield strength from Pt.6 Ch.1 Sec.12 [3.3] be used instead of the ambient yield strength. Therefore using 355 N/mm² is not acceptable; the reduced effective yield strength at 135°C must be substituted as R_Y. Step 3 — Sec4 [4.2.1] states that the acceptance criteria in [4.2.2] are based on the condition that the coarse mesh criteria given in Sec3 [4.2] are complied with, so that compliance is a prerequisite.

question_text:
A naval architect is designing a 160-metre general cargo ship (L2 = 160 m, k = 1.0) with a two-deck deckhouse structure located amidships. The deckhouse has a front bulkhead and side walls. One of the primary supporting members (PSM) inside the deckhouse — a transverse web frame on the deckhouse side — has a proposed net web thickness of 6.0 mm. The deckhouse sits entirely above 0.7D from the baseline, and the ship has exactly two continuous decks arranged above 0.7D.

The designer also needs to verify the section modulus of this same PSM, which is subjected to lateral sea pressure. The PSM spans 2.4 m between supports (effective bending span), supports a tributary breadth of 1.8 m, and the governing design pressure from the applicable load set is 12.5 kN/m². The PSM is to be checked under the acceptance criterion corresponding to the dynamic load scenario (AC-II).

For the section modulus calculation, the hull girder longitudinal stress at the load calculation point is 28 N/mm², and the yield strength ReH = 235 N/mm². The bending moment distribution factor fbdg = 12 (simply supported ends).

(a) Is the proposed net web thickness of 6.0 mm for this deckhouse PSM compliant with the minimum thickness rule? Show the minimum required net thickness.
(b) What is the minimum required section modulus for this PSM, in cm³, under the governing load set? Identify which design load set and acceptance criterion apply to the deckhouse side PSM under sea pressure loading.
(c) Does the hull girder longitudinal stress level at this location affect the method by which the section modulus requirement must be verified?
required_facts: Minimum required net web thickness for this PSM is 6.1 mm (using a=4.5, b=0.01, L2=160, k=1.0), so the proposed 6.0 mm is non-compliant
The 'more than 2 continuous decks above 0.7D' row in Table 3 does NOT apply because the ship has exactly two such decks, not more than two
The applicable design load set for the deckhouse side PSM under sea pressure is SEA-1 with acceptance criterion AC-II
The minimum required section modulus is approximately 54.1 cm³ (using Cs=0.85 for AC-II, fbdg=12, P=12.5 kN/m², S=1.8 m, ℓ_bdg=2.4 m, ReH=235 N/mm²)
Since the hull girder longitudinal stress (28 N/mm²) does not exceed 0.15 × ReH (35.25 N/mm²), the standard section modulus formula applies and FE analysis is not required
The hull girder longitudinal stress σ_hg for the static load component S is taken as the stress due to vertical still water bending moment

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec.3 Table 3 minimum thickness for PSM in deckhouses references Sec.8 [3.1] for deckhouse-specific rules; Sec.8 Table 1 defines the applicable design load set (SEA-1, AC-II) for deckhouse side PSMs and references Sec.6 for scantling requirements; Sec.6 [2.1.1] section modulus formula references Sec.2 [1] for hull girder stress and Sec.2 [2] for design load sets.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Minimum thickness (Sec.3 → Sec.8 [3.1]): From Sec.3 Table 3, PSM in deckhouses and superstructures (and decks for vessels with more than 2 continuous decks above 0.7D) uses a=4.5, b=0.01. However, the ship has exactly two continuous decks above 0.7D, not MORE than two, so this row does NOT apply. The applicable row is 'PSM in general': a=4.5, b=0.01. t_min = 4.5 + 0.01 × 160 × sqrt(1.0) = 4.5 + 1.6 = 6.1 mm. The proposed 6.0 mm is NON-COMPLIANT by 0.1 mm. Note: Sec.3 also directs the designer to 'see also Sec.8 [3.1]' for deckhouse minimum thicknesses, confirming the deckhouse-specific check path. Step 2 — Applicable load set (Sec.8 Table 1): For 'Superstructure side and primary supporting members on deckhouse sides and bulkheads', the applicable design load set is SEA-1, design load scenario 2, load component max(Pw; PSI), acceptance criterion AC-II, full load condition. This is the governing load set for the PSM section modulus check. Step 3 — Section modulus (Sec.6 [2.1.1] → Sec.2 [1]): Z = 1000 × |P| × S × ℓ_bdg² / (fbdg × Cs × ReH). For AC-II: Cs = 0.85. Z = 1000 × 12.5 × 1.8 × (2.4)² / (12 × 0.85 × 235) = 1000 × 12.5 × 1.8 × 5.76 / 2397 = 129600 / 2397 ≈ 54.1 cm³. Step 4 — Hull girder stress check (Sec.6 [1.1.2]): σ_hg = 28 N/mm², ReH = 235 N/mm², 0.15 × ReH = 35.25 N/mm². Since 28 < 35.25, the hull girder longitudinal stress does NOT exceed 0.15 ReH, so the standard section modulus formula of [2.1.1] remains applicable and FE analysis or the alternative [2.2] method is not required.

question_text:
A 320-metre bulk carrier is being assessed for hull girder buckling. The upper deck plating consists of longitudinally stiffened panels. In a region of the deck where the plate thickness changes across the width of an elementary plate panel, the narrower strip has a net thickness of 18 mm over a width of 400 mm, and the wider strip has a net thickness of 22 mm over a width of 600 mm. Both strips are made of the same steel grade with a minimum yield stress of 355 N/mm².

The direct strength analysis FE model for this region uses finite elements of varying size. Across the buckling panel, five finite elements are identified with the following individual plate areas and net thicknesses: element 1 — area 0.12 m², thickness 18 mm; element 2 — area 0.18 m², thickness 18 mm; element 3 — area 0.20 m², thickness 22 mm; element 4 — area 0.15 m², thickness 22 mm; element 5 — area 0.10 m², thickness 22 mm.

For the hull girder buckling check of the deck panel (not the direct strength analysis), determine the equivalent plate panel width to be used in the buckling assessment, and state the plate thickness to be paired with it. Then, for the direct strength analysis buckling check of the same region, determine the average plate thickness to be used. In both cases, state the yield stress to be applied in the buckling assessment.
required_facts: Equivalent plate panel width b_eq ≈ 844 mm (accepting 840–845 mm), paired with the smaller net thickness t1 = 18 mm, for the hull girder buckling check
The formula used is b_eq = l1 + l2*(t1/t2)^1.5 with l1 = 400 mm, l2 = 600 mm, t1 = 18 mm, t2 = 22 mm
Average plate thickness for the direct strength analysis buckling check is t_avr = 20.4 mm, calculated as the area-weighted mean of the five finite elements
The yield stress applied in both the hull girder buckling check and the direct strength analysis buckling check is 355 N/mm², taken as the minimum (here uniform) yield stress across the panel
The hull girder buckling check and the direct strength analysis buckling check use different methods for handling thickness variation: equivalent width approach vs. area-weighted average thickness

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec4 [2.1.2] defines the area-weighted average thickness for direct strength analysis panels; Sec4 [2.1.3] defines yield stress as the minimum within the panel. The hull girder buckling check (Sec3) uses a different approach: Sec3 [1.2.1] defines an equivalent plate panel width formula b_eq = l1 + l2*(t1/t2)^1.5 paired with the smaller thickness t1, and Sec3 [1.2.3] requires the minimum yield strength for mixed materials (here same material so 355 N/mm² applies directly).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Hull girder buckling check (Sec3 path): Identify t1 = 18 mm (smaller), t2 = 22 mm (larger), l1 = 400 mm, l2 = 600 mm. Apply Sec3 [1.2.1]: b_eq = 400 + 600*(18/22)^1.5. Compute (18/22) = 0.8182; (0.8182)^1.5 = 0.8182 * sqrt(0.8182) = 0.8182 * 0.9046 = 0.7401. So b_eq = 400 + 600*0.7401 = 400 + 444.1 = 844.1 mm. This equivalent width is paired with t1 = 18 mm. Per Sec3 [1.2.3], minimum yield stress = 355 N/mm² (same material throughout). Step 2 — Direct strength analysis buckling check (Sec4 path): Apply Sec4 [2.1.2] area-weighted average: t_avr = (0.12*18 + 0.18*18 + 0.20*22 + 0.15*22 + 0.10*22) / (0.12+0.18+0.20+0.15+0.10). Numerator = 2.16 + 3.24 + 4.40 + 3.30 + 2.20 = 15.30. Denominator = 0.75. t_avr = 15.30/0.75 = 20.4 mm. Per Sec4 [2.1.3], yield stress = minimum of all element yield stresses = 355 N/mm² (all same grade).

question_text: A 320 m container ship is being designed with side shell framing in the midship region. The structural arrangement omits intermediate stringers between the main deck and the double bottom, resulting in relatively large unsupported spans between transverse web frames. During the fatigue assessment of the longitudinal stiffener end connections in this region, the designer notes that no global finite element analysis has been performed for this vessel, but a similar ship of comparable length and framing arrangement was analyzed previously. The relative displacements from that similar ship's FE analysis are proposed for use in calculating the additional stresses at the stiffener end connections. The design team needs to determine: (a) whether additional stresses due to relative deflections must be considered for this side structure arrangement, (b) what method must be used to calculate those additional stresses, and (c) under what conditions the relative displacements from the previously analyzed similar ship may be substituted for project-specific FE results.
required_facts: Additional stresses due to relative deflections must be considered because the side structure has relatively low lateral bending stiffness resulting from omission of stringers
The additional stresses shall be calculated using the method described in DNV-CG-0129 Sec.4 [7], based on relative displacements from global or cargo hold FE analysis
Relative displacements from a previously analyzed similar ship may be used only when no FE results are available for the specific ship
The Society (classification society) — not the designer — decides whether the previously analyzed ship qualifies as 'similar' to the specific ship
The ship's 320 m rule length exceeds the 90 m minimum threshold, confirming the prescriptive fatigue assessment requirements apply

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec7 fatigue rules for longitudinal stiffener end connections reference DNV-CG-0129 Sec.4 [7] for the calculation method of additional stresses due to relative displacement; the trigger condition (low lateral bending stiffness from omitted stringers) is established in Sec7 [2.1.1], and the cross-reference to the calculation procedure and the similarity condition for substitute FE results is in Sec7 [2.1.2]
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Confirm applicability: The ship is 320 m, which exceeds the 90 m threshold, so the fatigue assessment requirements of this section apply. Step 2 — Identify trigger: Sec7 [2.1.1] states that for side structures with relatively low lateral bending stiffness (e.g. due to omission of stringers or reduced number of transverse web frames), additional stresses due to relative deflections of supporting transverses shall be considered. The omission of intermediate stringers directly triggers this requirement. Step 3 — Calculation method: Sec7 [2.1.2] mandates that the additional stresses due to relative displacement shall be calculated as described in DNV-CG-0129 Sec.4 [7], based on relative displacements taken from global or cargo hold FE analysis. Step 4 — Substitute FE results: Sec7 [2.1.2] explicitly permits use of relative displacements from a similar ship if no FE results are available for the specific ship, but only if the Society decides that the previously analyzed ship can be considered similar to the specific ship. The designer cannot unilaterally make this determination.

scenario_parameters.framing_arrangement: no intermediate stringers between main deck and double bottom
scenario_parameters.fatigue_detail_type: longitudinal stiffener end connections to transverse web frames

question_text: A structural engineer is performing a direct strength analysis on a bulk carrier's double bottom structure. During the finite element analysis, a longitudinal girder web panel in the double bottom is identified as being subjected to combined compressive and shear stresses. The panel is classified under acceptance criterion AC-II with a combined static and dynamic design load scenario (S+D). The computed buckling utilization factor for this panel comes out to η_act = 0.97. The panel is a plate-type structural member (not a strut or pillar). Is this panel compliant with the buckling strength requirements, and what is the maximum allowable buckling utilization factor that applies to this panel?
required_facts: The allowable buckling utilization factor η_all for plates and stiffened panels under AC-II (S+D load scenario) is 1.00
The panel is compliant because η_act = 0.97 does not exceed η_all = 1.00
The acceptance criterion requires η_act ≤ η_all
The utilization factor η is defined as the ratio of applied loads to the corresponding ultimate capacity or buckling strength
The η_all value is obtained from the allowable buckling utilization factor table applicable to plates and stiffeners, not the strut/pillar row

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec4 defines η_all by reference to Sec1 [3.4]; Sec3 [3.2.1] defines the utilization factor η; Sec1 [3.4] Table 3 gives the allowable values by structural member type and acceptance criterion
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec4 Symbols block states η_all = allowable buckling utilization factor, as defined in Sec1 [3.4]. This forces the reader to leave Sec4 and go to Sec1. Step 2 — Sec3 [3.2.1] defines the utilization factor η as the ratio between applied loads and corresponding ultimate capacity or buckling strength, confirming η_act = 0.97 is the quantity to compare. Step 3 — Sec1 [3.4] Table 3 gives allowable buckling utilization factors: for 'Plates and stiffeners/stiffened panels' under AC-II (S+D), η_all = 1.00. Step 4 — Acceptance criterion from Sec1 [3.3.1]: η_act ≤ η_all → 0.97 ≤ 1.00, so the panel IS compliant. The answer requires navigating from Sec4 → Sec3 [3.2.1] for the utilization factor definition, then Sec4 → Sec1 [3.4] for the allowable value.

scenario_parameters.structural_element: double bottom longitudinal girder web panel

question_text: A 180 m bulk carrier has a machinery space with a raised platform used for equipment access. The platform is non-exposed and located inside the machinery space. The designer proposes a static distributed load of 6.0 kN/m² for this platform. A concentrated unit load also needs to be determined for a single piece of equipment placed on the platform. The ship's scantling draught is 11.5 m and the current loading condition draught is 9.2 m. Is the proposed static distributed load of 6.0 kN/m² acceptable for this machinery space platform, and what is the minimum static distributed load that must be applied? Additionally, which dynamic load cases must be considered when assessing the platform under the dynamic load scenarios, and how many distinct equivalent design waves are defined for the beam sea roll motion cases?
required_facts: The proposed static distributed load of 6.0 kN/m² is NOT acceptable for a machinery space platform.
The minimum static distributed load for platforms in machinery space is 8 kN/m² (0.8 t/m²).
The distributed load calculation method is referenced from the external loads section (Sec5 [2.3.1]).
Concentrated forces on the platform must be calculated per Sec5 [2.3.2].
There are 4 distinct beam sea roll motion equivalent design waves: BSR-1P, BSR-2P, BSR-1S, and BSR-2S.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec6 [2.1] states that loads on non-exposed decks (including machinery space platforms) are given in Sec5 [2.3], except that for machinery space platforms the loads in Sec6 [2.2] and [2.3] apply. Sec6 [2.2] sets the minimum static distributed load for machinery space platforms at 8 kN/m² and directs distributed load calculation to Sec5 [2.3.1]. Sec6 [2.3] directs concentrated force calculation to Sec5 [2.3.2]. The dynamic load cases to be applied come from Sec2 [1.1], which defines all EDWs including BSR cases (4 beam sea roll EDWs: BSR-1P, BSR-2P, BSR-1S, BSR-2S).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec6 [2.1]: The platform is non-exposed and in the machinery space. The section states that for accommodation decks, wheelhouse decks, and platforms in machinery space, the loads defined in [2.2] and [2.3] of Sec6 apply (not Sec5 [2.3] directly). Step 2 — Sec6 [2.2]: The minimum static distributed load for platforms in machinery space is 8 kN/m². The proposed 6.0 kN/m² is below this threshold and therefore NOT acceptable. The minimum required value is 8 kN/m². The section also references Sec5 [2.3.1] for the calculation method of distributed loads. Step 3 — Sec6 [2.3]: Concentrated forces on non-exposed decks shall be calculated according to Sec5 [2.3.2]. Step 4 — Sec2 [1.1]: The dynamic load cases include BSR load cases: BSR-1P, BSR-2P (port side waves) and BSR-1S, BSR-2S (starboard side waves) — totalling 4 distinct beam sea roll EDWs. These must be considered for the dynamic load scenarios applied to the platform structural assessment.

question_text: A 180 m bulk carrier is operating in a normal ballast condition with a minimum forward draught at the forward end of 3.8 m. The block coefficient is 0.82. The designer has proposed a stern frame fabricated from steel plates. During the design review, the question arises whether the forward bottom structure requires strengthening against bottom slamming, and if so, what design bottom slamming pressure applies at a cross-section located 30 m aft of the forward end. Additionally, the stern frame material specification and construction standard must be confirmed. For the bottom slamming pressure calculation, assume the breadth of the bottom at 0.15 T_F above the baseline at the cross-section considered is 22 m, and the block coefficient C_B = 0.82. Is the forward bottom structure required to be strengthened against bottom slamming, and if so, what is the design bottom slamming pressure at the cross-section 30 m from the forward end? Also confirm whether the proposed fabricated steel plate stern frame is acceptable under the applicable rules.
required_facts: Bottom slamming strengthening is required because T_F-f = 3.8 m is less than 0.045 × 180 = 8.1 m
Since C_B = 0.82 > 0.75, T_F is capped at 1.15 × L^(1/3) ≈ 6.49 m, but 3.8 m governs
The longitudinal position x = 30 m is less than x1 ≈ 34.7 m, so x must be taken as x1 in the pressure formula
B_B is capped at 1.35 × T_F ≈ 5.13 m (not the geometric breadth of 22 m)
The design bottom slamming pressure P_SL at the cross-section is approximately 1490–1500 kN/m²
A fabricated steel plate stern frame is explicitly acceptable under the rules; no special consideration is required for this construction type

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec6 stern frame clause [2.1.1] confirms fabricated plate stern frames are acceptable and references Ch3 Sec1 for material specs. Separately, the bottom slamming applicability check starts at Sec1 [1.1.1] (bow impact application), which cross-references Sec2 [2.1.1] for the bottom slamming pressure formula and applicability threshold (T_F < 0.045L).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Stern frame: Pt3.Ch10.Sec6 [2.1.1] states stern frames may be fabricated from steel plates or cast steel with hollow section; fabricated plate construction is explicitly permitted. Material specifications are governed by Ch3 Sec1.

Step 2 — Bottom slamming applicability (Sec2 [1.1.1]): The rule applies to ships with L > 65 m where the minimum forward draught T_F < 0.045L. Here L = 180 m, so threshold = 0.045 × 180 = 8.1 m. The given T_F-f = 3.8 m < 8.1 m, so bottom slamming strengthening IS required.

Step 3 — Check T_F cap for C_B > 0.75: Since C_B = 0.82 > 0.75, T_F shall not be taken greater than 1.15 × L^(1/3) = 1.15 × 180^(1/3) = 1.15 × 5.646 = 6.49 m. Since 3.8 m < 6.49 m, T_F = 3.8 m governs.

Step 4 — Compute c1: L = 180 m > 150 m, so c1 = (225 − 0.5 × 180)^(1/3) = (225 − 90)^(1/3) = 135^(1/3) = 5.129.

Step 5 — Compute c2: c2 = 1675 × (1 − 20 × T_F / L) = 1675 × (1 − 20 × 3.8 / 180) = 1675 × (1 − 0.4222) = 1675 × 0.5778 = 967.8.

Step 6 — Compute x1 (minimum x): x1 = [1.2 − C_B^(1/3) − L/2500] × L = [1.2 − 0.82^(1/3) − 180/2500] × 180 = [1.2 − 0.9353 − 0.072] × 180 = 0.1927 × 180 = 34.7 m. Since x = 30 m < x1 = 34.7 m, x shall be taken as x1 = 34.7 m.

Step 7 — Check B_B cap: B_B shall not exceed the smaller of 1.35 × T_F = 1.35 × 3.8 = 5.13 m and 0.55 × √L = 0.55 × √180 = 0.55 × 13.416 = 7.38 m. So B_B_max = 5.13 m. Given B_B = 22 m >> 5.13 m, B_B is capped at 5.13 m.

Step 8 — Compute P_SL: P_SL = (c1 × c2 / T_F) × B_B × (0.56 − L/1250 − x/L) = (5.129 × 967.8 / 3.8) × 5.13 × (0.56 − 180/1250 − 34.7/180) = (4963.5 / 3.8) × 5.13 × (0.56 − 0.144 − 0.1928) = 1306.2 × 5.13 × 0.2232 = 1306.2 × 1.145 = 1495.6 kN/m².

question_text: A 180-metre bulk carrier has a permanent means of access (PMA) platform fitted inside a cargo hold, supported by enlarged stiffeners acting as primary supporting members. The platform web plate is 600 mm deep and 8 mm thick (net). The web has no intermediate stiffeners fitted. The material has a specified minimum yield stress of 235 N/mm². The designer proposes to omit tripping brackets at the platform ends, arguing that the web plate slenderness is acceptable. Is the web plate slenderness acceptable without tripping brackets, and what is the minimum net web thickness required to satisfy the applicable slenderness limit for this primary supporting member web plate?
required_facts: PMA platforms with enlarged stiffeners are classified as primary supporting members (PSMs)
The minimum net web thickness from the PSM slenderness requirement is determined by s_w/C_w × sqrt(R_eH/235), with C_w = 100 elsewhere or 125 for double skin construction.
The proposed 8 mm net thickness is not the exact slenderness limit under the applicable PSM rule
Omission of tripping brackets is only permitted if the hull girder buckling strength of the web plate is separately demonstrated to comply
Both the slenderness check (Sec.2) and the hull girder buckling check (Sec.3) must be satisfied for the PMA platform web plate
The designer cannot omit tripping brackets based solely on slenderness compliance — the buckling strength check per the hull girder buckling requirements is also mandatory

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec.1 [2.1.3] identifies PMA platforms as PSMs and directs to Sec.3 [3] for web plate buckling strength and Sec.2 [4] for slenderness requirements. Sec.2 [4.1.1] gives the PSM web plate slenderness formula. Sec.3 [3] governs whether tripping brackets may be omitted.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec.1 [2.1.3]: PMA platforms with enlarged stiffeners are treated as primary supporting members (PSMs). The clause states that tripping brackets per Sec.2 [5] may be omitted only if buckling strength per Sec.3 [3] is complied with. This creates two parallel paths: (a) check slenderness per Sec.2 [4] and (b) check hull girder buckling per Sec.3 [3]. Step 2 — Sec.2 [4.1.1]: The PSM web plate slenderness requirement is t_w ≥ h_w / C_w × sqrt(R_eH / 235). For a primary supporting member web plate, C_w = 75 (from Table 2 for angle/T-bar type, applicable to PSM web). With h_w = 600 mm and R_eH = 235 N/mm²: t_w_min = 600 / 75 × sqrt(235/235) = 8.0 mm. The proposed 8 mm net thickness exactly meets the minimum slenderness limit. Step 3 — Sec.3 [3]: The hull girder buckling check of the web plate must also be satisfied. If the Sec.3 [3] buckling check is passed, tripping brackets may be omitted per Sec.1 [2.1.3]. If not, tripping brackets are required per Sec.2 [5]. The slenderness alone (8 mm being exactly at the limit) does not by itself permit omission of tripping brackets — the Sec.3 [3] buckling strength check must additionally be demonstrated.

question_text: A newbuilding container ship (150 m LOA) is being designed with fixed cell guides in the cargo holds and fixed lashing eye plates on the upper deck. The designer has prepared hull support structures for both the container support fittings and the lashing eye plates. For the lashing eye plate support structures, the designer proposes to use the lashing certified safe working load (SWL) of 250 kN as the sole design load basis, without including any reaction forces from container stacks. The container securing arrangement plan has been submitted, and the ship is equipped with fixed container foundations on the inner bottom and fixed appliances for stowage and lashing on the upper deck. Is the proposed design load basis for the lashing eye plate hull support structures compliant with the classification rules? Additionally, what documentation must be submitted as part of the container securing arrangement plan, and what is the minimum metacentric height (GM) requirement that must be reflected in that plan?
required_facts: Hull support structures for lashing eye plates must be strengthened with respect to the lashings' certified safe working load (SWL) of 250 kN — this part of the design basis is compliant.

Design loads for hull support structures for container securing structures must also be taken in accordance with Sec8 [6], not solely from the SWL; the proposed basis is incomplete if it omits the Sec8 [6] load components.
A container securing arrangement plan must be submitted for approval (documentation type H190).
The container stowage plan (Z030) must be submitted for information.
The container securing arrangement plan must include a minimum one metacentric height (GM) value.
The GM value included in the plan shall not be less than the minimum GM value in the approved trim and stability booklet for the respective draught.
The ship qualifies for the 'Container ship' class notation as it has cell guides, fixed container foundations on the inner bottom, and fixed lashing appliances on the upper deck.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec9 governs hull support structures and references Sec8 [6] for design loads on securing structures; Sec8 [1.1.1] references Sec1 [2.1] for the container securing arrangement plan submission requirements including the GM requirement.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec9 [3.1.2] states that hull support structures for lashing eye plates shall be strengthened with respect to the lashings' certified SWL. This confirms the 250 kN SWL basis is required. Step 2 — Sec9 [3.3] states that design loads acting on hull support structures for container securing structures shall be taken in accordance with Sec8 [6]. The answerer must navigate to Sec8 [6] to confirm what those loads entail and whether the SWL-only basis is sufficient or whether additional load components from Sec8 [6] must also be considered. Step 3 — Sec8 [1.1.1] requires a container securing arrangement plan to be submitted according to Sec1 [2.1], and specifies that the plan shall include minimum one metacentric height GM value, which shall not be less than the minimum GM in the approved trim and stability booklet for the respective draught. Step 4 — Sec1 [2.1] (documentation table) lists the required documentation including H190 – Container securing arrangement plan (for approval) and Z030 – Arrangement plan (container stowage plan, for information). The chain requires the answerer to traverse Sec9 → Sec8 → Sec1 to fully answer both parts of the question.

question_focus: design load completeness for lashing eye plate supports
container securing arrangement plan documentation requirements

question_text: A 175-metre general cargo vessel is being fitted with bilge keels. The ground bar connecting the shell plating to the bilge keel web has a gross thickness of 12 mm, while the bilge strake gross thickness is 14 mm. The bilge keel ends are tapered at a ratio of 2.5:1, and the end of the bilge keel web is positioned 45 mm from the end of the ground bar. No transverse or longitudinal support members are fitted inside the hull at the bilge keel ends. The windlass foundation on the forecastle deck is supported by a pillar-and-girder arrangement carried down to the tank top. The windlass is rated for a chain cable with a minimum breaking strength of 1,800 kN, and a chain stopper is fitted. The deck plating under the windlass has been increased in thickness. Is the bilge keel arrangement compliant with the classification rules for a vessel of this length? Identify all non-compliant aspects and state the minimum permissible ground bar gross thickness for this vessel.
required_facts: The 150 m threshold is exceeded (175 m), so the additional bilge keel requirements for ships above 150 m apply
The minimum ground bar gross thickness is 14 mm (lesser of bilge strake thickness 14 mm and 14 mm limit), making the proposed 12 mm non-compliant
The taper ratio of 2.5:1 is non-compliant; the minimum required ratio is 3:1
The bilge keel web end distance of 45 mm is non-compliant; it must be not less than 50 mm from the end of the ground bar
The absence of transverse or longitudinal internal support members at the bilge keel ends is non-compliant
The windlass foundation design load (chain stopper fitted) is 45% of BS = 810 kN

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Pt3.Ch11.Sec4 bilge keel appendage requirements for ships above 150 m, which triggers the additional requirements in Sec4 [1.2]. Those requirements reference ground bar thickness, taper ratio, web end positioning, and internal support members. The windlass foundation design cross-references Sec2 for supporting structure scantlings, which in turn references Sec1 for the chain stopper load case.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec4 [1.2] applies because the vessel is 175 m, which exceeds the 150 m threshold. Step 2 — Sec4 [1.2.2]: ground bar gross thickness shall not be less than the gross thickness of the bilge strake (14 mm) or 14 mm, whichever is less. The lesser value is 14 mm, so the minimum is 14 mm. The proposed 12 mm is non-compliant. Step 3 — Sec4 [1.2.3]: tapering ratio must be minimum 3:1. The proposed 2.5:1 is non-compliant. Step 4 — Sec4 [1.2.3]: the bilge keel web end must be not less than 50 mm and not greater than 100 mm from the end of the ground bar. The proposed 45 mm is below the 50 mm minimum — non-compliant. Step 5 — Sec4 [1.2.3]: ends of the bilge keel and ground bar shall be supported by either transverse or longitudinal members inside the hull. No such members are fitted — non-compliant. Step 6 — For the windlass, Sec2 [2.1] applies to the supporting structure. Sec2 [2.3.1](a): where a chain stopper is provided, the design load for the windlass foundation is 45% of BS = 0.45 × 1,800 = 810 kN. This is the load case to be used for foundation strength assessment.

question_text: A chemical tanker has the following characteristics: length L = 148 m, breadth B = 22.4 m, block coefficient C_B = 0.74, scantling draught T_SC = 9.2 m, and metacentric height GM = 0.12 × B. The vessel has bilge keels fitted. One of the cargo tanks has an effective sloshing length ℓ_slh = 20.5 m and an effective sloshing breadth b_slh = 10.8 m. The tank height h_tk = 14.0 m. The tank is intended to carry a heavy liquid cargo with a maximum liquid cargo density ρ_max-LM = 1.55 t/m³ at 98% fill. The designer proposes to restrict filling to a partial level when carrying this heavy cargo. Determine: (1) the cargo density ρ_L to be used for sloshing assessment of this cargo tank, (2) the factor f_cd applicable to this case, (3) the maximum permissible filling height h_part in metres for the partial filling restriction, and (4) whether the tank dimensions require sloshing calculations for both longitudinal and transverse liquid motion to be performed.
required_facts: ρ_L = 1.55 t/m³ (because ρ_max-LM = 1.55 t/m³ > 1.025 t/m³, so ρ_L = ρ_max-LM for strength assessment)
f_cd = 1.0 (the 0.88 reduction applies only to oil/oil products with ρ_L ≤ 1.025 t/m³; this heavy chemical cargo does not qualify)
Longitudinal sloshing calculations are required because ℓ_slh = 20.5 m > 0.03L = 4.44 m
Transverse sloshing calculations are required because b_slh = 10.8 m > 0.32B = 7.17 m
ρ_part must not be taken less than ρ_L = 1.55 t/m³ per the definition in Ch.4 Sec.6

annotator_grounding.end_clause: Pt3.Ch4.Sec6 (ρ_L, ρ_part, f_cd definitions) → Pt3.Ch4.Sec3 (roll period / accelerations, not directly needed but ρ_L definition chain passes through Sec6 which references Sec3 for accelerations)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch10.Sec4 [1.2.1] defines h_part using ρ_L, f_cd, and ρ_part, all of which are defined in Pt3.Ch4.Sec6. Pt3.Ch4.Sec6 in turn defines the liquid density ρ_L for strength assessment and the factor f_cd, and references Pt3.Ch4.Sec3 for the acceleration values used in internal load calculations that underpin the density definitions.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Start at Pt3.Ch10.Sec4 [1.2.1]: The formula for maximum permissible filling height is h_part = (h_tk × ρ_L × f_cd) / ρ_part. The symbols ρ_L, f_cd, and ρ_part are all stated as 'defined in Ch.4 Sec.6', requiring a cross-chapter lookup.

Step 2 — Go to Pt3.Ch4.Sec6: 
  • ρ_L for strength assessment: since ρ_max-LM = 1.55 t/m³ > 1.025, the rule states ρ_L = ρ_max-LM = 1.55 t/m³.
  • ρ_part: maximum permissible high liquid cargo density associated with partial filling, not less than ρ_L = 1.55 t/m³. The designer must specify ρ_part; for this scenario ρ_part = ρ_max-LM = 1.55 t/m³ (the tank is being assessed for the case where it carries the heavy cargo at partial fill, so ρ_part = 1.55 t/m³).
  • f_cd: since this is NOT oil or oil product cargo with ρ_L ≤ 1.025 t/m³ (it is a heavy chemical cargo with ρ_L = 1.55 t/m³), f_cd = 1.0 (the 0.88 reduction only applies to oil/oil products with ρ_L ≤ 1.025 t/m³ under FE analysis).

Step 3 — Back to Pt3.Ch10.Sec4 [1.2.1]: Compute h_part:
  h_part = (14.0 × 1.55 × 1.0) / 1.55 = 14.0 m
  This equals h_tk, meaning the partial filling restriction does not reduce the required fill height below the full tank height in this degenerate case where ρ_part = ρ_L. The formula is still required to be applied.

Step 4 — Check sloshing applicability (Pt3.Ch10.Sec4 [1.1.2]):
  • Longitudinal: ℓ_slh = 20.5 m; 0.03L = 0.03 × 148 = 4.44 m. Since 20.5 m > 4.44 m, longitudinal sloshing calculations ARE required.
  • Transverse: b_slh = 10.8 m; 0.32B = 0.32 × 22.4 = 7.17 m. Since 10.8 m > 7.17 m, transverse sloshing calculations ARE required.
  Both directions must be assessed.

Step 5 — Pt3.Ch4.Sec3 is the end of the chain: Sec6 references Sec3 [3.2] for the accelerations (a_x, a_y, a_z at the tank CoG) used in the internal pressure formulas of Sec6. The roll period T_θ and roll angle θ from Sec3 [2.1.1] feed into the dynamic internal pressures that establish the design loads underpinning the density and f_cd framework. For the roll period: T_θ = 2.3π k_r / √(g·GM), with k_r = 0.39B = 0.39 × 22.4 = 8.736 m (general), GM = 0.12B = 0.12 × 22.4 = 2.688 m (tanker default not applicable here since GM is given as 0.12B per scenario — actually for tankers GM = 0.12B is the default, consistent). T_θ = 2.3π × 8.736 / √(9.81 × 2.688) = 63.12 / 5.133 ≈ 12.3 s. This confirms the motion environment used in Sec6 internal load derivations.

question_text: A 175 m general cargo vessel with service area notation R2 is being designed with a pronounced flare bow. At the forward perpendicular region, the flare angle α is measured as 52° at 0.10L from the forward end, and 44° at 0.15L from the forward end. The ship has no bilge keel, a beam B = 26 m, block coefficient CB = 0.65, scantling draught TSC = 9.2 m, and metacentric height GM = 0.07B. The design speed V = 15 knots. For the bow impact pressure calculation at a point on the side shell located 3.5 m above the waterline at scantling draught, with a flare angle α = 52° and a waterplane half-angle β = 35°, determine: (1) what is the correct longitudinal extent of the bow impact strengthening zone, and (2) what value of the reduction factor fr should be used in the bow impact pressure formula, and what is the resulting value of the coefficient C (before applying the 0 to 1.0 cap) given CW = 10.75 and ho = 3.5 m?
required_facts: The bow impact strengthening zone must be extended to 0.20L from the forward end because α > 40° at both 0.10L and 0.15L
The reduction factor fr = 0.8 for service area notation R2 (20% reduction), obtained from the ship motions and accelerations section
The raw coefficient C = 0.18 × (fr × CW − 0.5 × ho) = 0.18 × (0.8 × 10.75 − 0.5 × 3.5) = 1.233 before capping
The effective coefficient C is capped at 1.0 (maximum allowed value)
The first extension trigger is α = 52° > 40° at 0.10L, requiring extension from 0.10L to 0.15L
The second extension trigger is α = 44° > 40° at 0.15L, requiring further extension from 0.15L to 0.20L

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Bow impact section defines the extent of strengthening based on flare angle thresholds at 0.10L and 0.15L, and the bow impact pressure formula references fr from Ch.4 Sec.3, where fr depends on the service area notation (R2 = 0.8).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Extent of strengthening (Pt3.Ch10.Sec1 [1.1.3]): The base zone is forward of 0.10L from F.E. Since α = 52° > 40° at 0.10L, the zone must be extended to 0.15L. Since α = 44° > 40° at 0.15L, the zone must be further extended to 0.20L from F.E. Therefore the bow impact strengthening zone extends to 0.20L from the forward end. Step 2 — Reduction factor fr (Pt3.Ch4.Sec3): The bow impact pressure formula uses C = 0.18(fr·CW − 0.5·ho). The parameter fr is the reduction factor related to service restrictions, defined in Pt3.Ch4.Sec3. For service area notation R2, fr = 0.8 (20% reduction). Step 3 — Compute C: C = 0.18 × (0.8 × 10.75 − 0.5 × 3.5) = 0.18 × (8.60 − 1.75) = 0.18 × 6.85 = 1.233. Since C is capped at maximum 1.0, the effective C = 1.0. The raw (uncapped) value is 1.233.

question_text: A 175 m general cargo vessel is being designed with a pronounced flared bow. The ship has a scantling draught of 9.2 m and a minimum design ballast draught of 4.1 m. At 0.10L from the forward end, the flare angle is measured at 44°. At 0.15L from the forward end, the flare angle is 38°. The bow region contains transversely framed shell plating supported by primary supporting members spaced at 3.6 m apart. A structural analyst needs to determine the required extent of the bow impact strengthening zone and, when sizing the side shell plating in that zone, must correctly identify the value of S (primary supporting member spacing) to use in the scantling formula. What is the longitudinal extent of the bow impact strengthening zone, and what value of S applies when calculating the shell plating thickness in this zone?
required_facts: The flare angle at 0.10L (44°) exceeds 40°, triggering extension of the bow impact zone from 0.10L to 0.15L
The flare angle at 0.15L (38°) does not exceed 40°, so no further extension to 0.20L is required
The longitudinal extent of the bow impact strengthening zone is 0.15L from the forward end
The vertical extent runs from the minimum design ballast draught T_BAL = 4.1 m up to the forecastle deck
S in the shell plating scantling formula is the primary supporting member spacing as defined in the structural idealisation rules
S = 3.6 m for this vessel

annotator_grounding.end_clause: Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 (symbols/definitions for T_BAL), Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [2.1.1] (definition of S as PSM spacing)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch10.Sec1 [1.1.3] governs the extent of bow impact strengthening and references Ch.1 Sec.4 for the definition of T_BAL. The scantling formula for shell plating in Pt3.Ch10.Sec1 [3.1.1] uses the symbol S (PSM spacing), which is defined in Ch.3 Sec.7 [1.2.2]. The answerer must follow both cross-references to correctly resolve the extent rule and the spacing parameter.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Determine extent of bow impact zone (Pt3.Ch10.Sec1 [1.1.3]): The base requirement is that strengthening extends forward of 0.1L from the F.E. Since the flare angle at 0.10L is 44° > 40°, the zone must be extended to 0.15L. Check 0.15L: flare angle is 38° which is NOT greater than 40°, so no further extension to 0.20L is triggered. Therefore the bow impact strengthening zone extends from 0.15L forward of the F.E. down to T_BAL (4.1 m) and up to the forecastle deck. Step 2 — Resolve T_BAL definition: The clause references Ch.1 Sec.4 [3.1.6] for the definition of T_BAL (minimum design ballast draught). This confirms T_BAL = 4.1 m as given. Step 3 — Identify S for the plating formula: The scantling formula in Pt3.Ch10.Sec1 [3.1.1] uses S = primary supporting member spacing.
