The footnote/table in that section directs the reader to Ch.3 Sec.7 [1.2.2] for the definition of S. Per Ch.3 Sec.7 [1.2.2], S is the PSM spacing in metres. Therefore S = 3.6 m.

question_text: A 180 m general cargo vessel (block coefficient CB = 0.72, scantling draught TSC = 9.5 m, breadth B = 28 m) has a centreline cargo oil tank with an effective sloshing length ℓslh = 25.2 m and an effective sloshing breadth bslh = 8.4 m. The tank height htk = 14 m. The designer needs to determine the roll period Tθ and roll angle θ to compute the transverse sloshing pressure. The roll radius of gyration kr is estimated at 11.5 m and the metacentric height GM = 1.8 m. The loading condition draught TLC = 8.0 m. For the transverse acceleration component used in the sloshing pressure calculation, what is the numerical value of the common acceleration parameter a0, and does the effective sloshing breadth of this tank require the designer to perform an additional liquid impact assessment beyond the standard sloshing load check? Show all intermediate values needed to reach your conclusions.
required_facts: The roll period formula Tθ = 2.3πkr/√(gGM) gives Tθ ≈ 19.8 s
The breadth threshold for additional liquid impact assessment is 0.56·B = 15.68 m; bslh = 8.4 m does NOT exceed this threshold
The length threshold band is 0.13L = 23.4 m to 0.16L = 28.8 m; ℓslh = 25.2 m falls within this band, triggering the additional liquid impact assessment requirement
An additional liquid impact assessment IS required for this tank due to the effective sloshing length condition, even though the breadth condition is not met
Symbol definitions for CB, L, B, TLC, TSC are drawn from the primary symbols and ship main data tables in the general definitions section of Part 3

annotator_grounding.end_clause: Pt3.Ch4.Sec3 [2.1.1] → Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 2 (L, B, CB definitions) and Table 3 (material/ship data symbols)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch10.Sec4 sloshing section references Ch.1 Sec.4 for undefined symbols (including L, B, CB) and references Ch.4 Sec.3 for ship motions/accelerations (roll period, roll angle, acceleration parameter a0). Ch.4 Sec.3 in turn references Ch.1 Sec.4 for symbol definitions (CB, TLC, TSC, kr, GM). The answerer must navigate from the sloshing section to the motions chapter to compute a0, then back to the sloshing section threshold check (bslh > 0.56B) to determine whether liquid impact assessment is required.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Identify that the sloshing section (Pt3.Ch10.Sec4) states 'For symbols not defined in this section, see Ch.1 Sec.4', and that the transverse sloshing pressure Pslh-t depends on ship motion parameters defined in Pt3.Ch4.Sec3.
Step 2 — Navigate to Pt3.Ch4.Sec3 Symbols section. The common acceleration parameter a0 is defined as: a0 = (1.58 − 0.47·CB)·(2.4/√L + 34/L − 600/L²). With L = 180 m and CB = 0.72: a0 = (1.58 − 0.47×0.72)·(2.4/√180 + 34/180 − 600/180²) = (1.58 − 0.3384)·(2.4/13.416 + 0.1889 − 0.01852) = 1.2416·(0.17890 + 0.18889 − 0.01852) = 1.2416 × 0.34927 ≈ 0.4337.
Step 3 — Roll period from Pt3.Ch4.Sec3 [2.1.1]: Tθ = 2·kr/√GM = 2×11.5/√1.8 = 23.0/1.3416 ≈ 17.14 s. Roll angle θ from [2.1.1] formula (depends on Tθ and a0 per the rule table/formula in that clause).
Step 4 — Return to Pt3.Ch10.Sec4 [1.1.5]: additional liquid impact assessment is required when bslh > 0.56·B. Check: 0.56×28 = 15.68 m. Since bslh = 8.4 m < 15.68 m, the breadth threshold is NOT exceeded. Also check length threshold: 0.13L = 23.4 m, 0.16L = 28.8 m. Since ℓslh = 25.2 m and 23.4 < 25.2 ≤ 28.8, the length condition IS triggered, so additional liquid impact assessment IS required.
Step 5 — Symbol definitions for L, B, CB, TSC, TLC confirmed via Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Tables 1–3.

question_text: A 180 m LNG carrier is being designed with a cargo tank that has an effective sloshing length of 25.2 m (i.e., 0.14L) and an effective sloshing breadth of 32.4 m (i.e., 0.18B). The tank volume is 22,000 m³. The ship has a scantling draught of 11.5 m, a block coefficient CB = 0.72, and a metacentric height GM = 4.2 m in the ballast loading condition. The roll period in the ballast condition is 14.8 s and the roll angle is 22°. The designer is performing a fatigue assessment of the tank boundary structural details and needs to determine the correct operational factor fR to apply to the prescriptive loads used in the fatigue calculation. What value of fR should be used, and what additional liquid impact load assessment is triggered by the tank geometry?
required_facts: The effective sloshing length ℓ_slh = 0.14L satisfies the condition 0.13L < ℓ_slh ≤ 0.16L, triggering an additional liquid impact load assessment
The liquid impact load assessment per [2.4] is required in addition to (not instead of) the standard sloshing load checks
The effective sloshing breadth of 0.18B does not exceed 0.56B, so the breadth criterion alone would not trigger the additional assessment
The roll period and roll angle used in the sloshing and fatigue load calculations are prescribed quantities defined in Ch.4 Sec.3 [2.1.1]
The operational factor for fatigue assessment using prescriptive loads is fR = 0.76
fR = 0.76 applies specifically to prescriptive loads calculated in Ch.4; direct wave load analysis requires special consideration

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Pt3.Ch10.Sec4 sloshing/liquid impact requirements, which reference Ch.4 Sec.3 for ship motions/accelerations (roll period and angle used to characterise the dynamic environment), and the fatigue assessment of tank details leads to Ch.9 Sec.4 for the operational factor fR applicable to prescriptive loads.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt3.Ch10.Sec4 [1.1.5]: The effective sloshing length ℓ_slh = 25.2 m = 0.14L, which satisfies 0.13L < ℓ_slh ≤ 0.16L. The effective sloshing breadth b_slh = 32.4 m = 0.18B, which does NOT exceed 0.56B. Therefore, the condition on sloshing length alone triggers the requirement for an additional liquid impact load assessment in accordance with [2.4], in addition to the standard sloshing loads [2.1]–[2.3]. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch4.Sec3 [2.1.1]: The roll period T_θ and roll angle θ are defined here. The given values (T_θ = 14.8 s, θ = 22°) are the prescriptive motion parameters that feed into the sloshing and fatigue load calculations. This cross-reference is needed to confirm the motion parameters are correctly sourced from Ch.4 Sec.3 rather than assumed arbitrarily. Step 3 — Pt3.Ch9.Sec4 [4.3]: For the fatigue assessment of the tank boundary details, the prescriptive loads are calculated using Ch.4. The operational factor to apply is fR = 0.76, as specified in Ch.9 Sec.4 [4.3] for prescriptive loads.

question_text: A Norwegian marine research institute is commissioning a new vessel designed to deploy and recover autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) in Arctic waters. The vessel has no direct equivalent in standard ship type categories — it is neither a pure offshore service vessel nor a survey ship, but a purpose-built AUV tender with a dedicated moonpool, integrated AUV hangar, and real-time subsea data relay systems. The owner wishes to have this unique purpose formally recognized in the vessel's class certificate issued by DNV. They have been told that a descriptive notation may be assigned, and they want to understand: (1) whether there are any specific technical or design requirements they must satisfy to obtain this notation, (2) how the notation will appear in the class certificate, and (3) whether DNV, as the classifying society, is authorized to assign such a notation alongside standard class notations for the same vessel.
required_facts: A descriptive notation may be assigned to vessels whose purpose, function, or feature is not covered by existing notations.
There are no class requirements associated with a descriptive notation.
The descriptive notation must be requested from DNV (the Society) — it is not automatically assigned.
The descriptive notation will appear in the class certificate enclosed in square brackets, e.g. [AUV tender].
DNV is the Society authorized to carry out classification services, including assignment of such notations, as established by its organizational mandate.
A descriptive notation can be assigned alongside standard class notations (construction symbol, main class, ship type, additional class notations) for the same vessel.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt1.Ch2.Sec7 establishes that a descriptive notation may be assigned for vessels with purpose not covered by existing notations, with no class requirements attached, and identified by square brackets. Pt1.Ch2.Sec1 [1.1.4] cross-references Ch.1 Sec.1 [2.2.5] for the Society's authority to assign optional notations under special consideration. Pt1.Ch1.Sec1 [1.1.1] establishes DNV's organizational identity and authority as the Society carrying out classification services.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — The AUV tender does not fit any existing ship type notation (Sec.3) or additional class notation (Sec.4), so the owner looks to Pt1.Ch2.Sec7 for descriptive notations. Sec7 [1.1] confirms this applies to vessels with purpose not covered by existing notations. Step 2 — Sec7 [1.3] explicitly states there are NO class requirements associated with a descriptive notation, answering question (1). Step 3 — Sec7 [1.4] states the notation is identified by square brackets, e.g. [AUV tender], answering question (2). Step 4 — To confirm DNV's authority to assign this alongside standard notations, the chain leads to Pt1.Ch2.Sec1 [1.1.4], which states that optional class notations may, upon special consideration, be assigned to a vessel. That clause cross-references Ch.1 Sec.1 [2.2.5]. Step 5 — Pt1.Ch1.Sec1 [1.1.1] establishes that DNV is the Society carrying out classification and verification services, confirming its authority to assign such notations, answering question (3).

scenario_parameters.vessel_type: AUV tender (purpose-built, no standard category equivalent)

question_text: A naval architect is designing bilge keels for a 175-metre bulk carrier. The bilge strake is made from Grade E36 steel with a specified minimum yield strength of 355 N/mm² and a gross thickness of 16 mm. The proposed ground bar has a gross thickness of 14 mm and is made from Grade A36 steel (also 355 N/mm² yield strength). The bilge keel web ends are positioned 60 mm from the ends of the ground bar. The ground bar runs continuously along the bilge keel length, and the ends of both the ground bar and bilge keel web are tapered with a ratio of 2.5:1. A transverse support member is fitted between the end of the bilge keel web and the end of the ground bar. During the design review, the following questions arise: (1) Is the proposed ground bar thickness compliant? (2) Is the taper ratio at the ends acceptable? (3) Is the material grade of the ground bar acceptable given the material class requirement for a bilge strake? To answer question (3), the reviewer needs to determine what 'material class' means in the context of these rules — specifically, what symbol is used for the material factor that distinguishes steel grades, and what its units are.
required_facts: The ship is 175 m, which exceeds 150 m, so the additional bilge keel requirements apply
The ground bar thickness of 14 mm is compliant because the minimum is the lesser of the bilge strake thickness (16 mm) and 14 mm, giving a minimum of 14 mm
The taper ratio of 2.5:1 is NOT compliant — the minimum required taper ratio is 3:1
The bilge keel web end position of 60 mm is compliant as it falls within the required 50–100 mm range from the ground bar end
The material factor symbol 'k' (dimensionless) is defined in the general symbols section and is used to distinguish steel material grades/classes

The ground bar must be of the same material class as the bilge strake; Grade A36 and Grade E36 may differ in material class despite having the same yield strength, requiring verification against the material class tables

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Bilge keel appendage rules for ships >150m reference specific thickness and taper requirements, and material class requirements that point back to the general symbols section for the definition of the material factor 'k'
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Identify ship length: 175 m > 150 m, so the additional requirements of Pt3.Ch11.Sec4 [1.2] apply.

Step 2 — Check ground bar thickness (clause [1.2.2]): The gross thickness of the ground bar shall not be less than the gross thickness of the bilge strake OR 14 mm, whichever is LESS. Bilge strake gross thickness = 16 mm; 14 mm limit applies (lesser of 16 mm and 14 mm is 14 mm). Proposed ground bar thickness = 14 mm. This is exactly at the minimum — compliant.

Step 3 — Check taper ratio (clause [1.2.3]): Tapering shall be gradual with a minimum ratio of 3:1. The proposed ratio is 2.5:1, which is less than the required 3:1 minimum. This is NOT compliant.

Step 4 — Check bilge keel web end position (clause [1.2.3]): The end of the bilge keel web shall be not less than 50 mm and not greater than 100 mm from the end of the ground bar. Proposed = 60 mm. This is within the 50–100 mm range — compliant.

Step 5 — Material class requirement (clause [1.1.4]): The ground bar shall be of the same material class as a bilge strake according to Ch.3 Sec.1 Table 3 and Table 9. To understand what distinguishes material classes (e.g., Grade A vs Grade E), the reviewer must consult the symbols section referenced at the top of Pt3.Ch11.Sec4: 'For symbols not defined in this section, see Ch.1 Sec.4.' In Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 3 (Materials), the material factor symbol is 'k' (dimensionless, units: '-'), which differentiates steel grades. Grade A36 and Grade E36 both have the same yield strength (355 N/mm²) but may differ in material class (notch toughness/temperature requirements). The material class of the bilge strake (Grade E36) is typically a higher class than Grade A36 due to toughness requirements at lower temperatures. Therefore the ground bar material (Grade A36) may not satisfy the same material class as the bilge strake (Grade E36) — this requires verification against Ch.3 Sec.1 Table 3 and Table 9.

question_text: A 180 m general cargo vessel is being designed with a weathertight door fitted in a companionway on the freeboard deck (position 1). The door blade is a flat steel panel with the following dimensions: plate panel breadth b = 400 mm, plate panel length a = 900 mm. The design lateral pressure P at the load calculation point is 12.5 kN/m². The steel used has a minimum yield stress R_eH = 235 N/mm². The designer proposes a gross door blade thickness of 5.5 mm. Is this thickness sufficient to meet the classification requirements for weathertight doors, and what is the minimum required gross thickness?
required_facts: The applicable formula for minimum gross door blade thickness is t_gr = 0.0158 * alpha_p * b * sqrt(|P| / (0.85 * R_eH))
The aspect ratio correction factor alpha_p = 1.2 - b/(2.1*a) = 1.2 - 400/(2.1*900) ≈ 0.988, which is less than 1.0 and is used as-is
The minimum required gross thickness t_gr ≈ 1.56 mm
The proposed thickness of 5.5 mm exceeds the minimum required thickness of approximately 1.56 mm
The arrangement is compliant with the classification requirements for weathertight door blade thickness
The design pressure P must be determined at the load calculation point for the relevant design load set, per the internal loads framework referenced by the door scantling rules

annotator_grounding.end_clause: Pt3.Ch4.Sec6 (internal loads section, referenced for design pressure P definition and load calculation point)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The weathertight door scantling formula in Pt3.Ch12.Sec2 [4.3.1] requires the design pressure P, which is defined by reference to Ch.6 Sec.2 [2] and the load calculation point defined in Ch.3 Sec.7 [2.2]. The aspect ratio correction factor alpha_p must also be computed from the panel dimensions before applying the thickness formula.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the applicable scantling formula from the weathertight door requirements: t_gr = 0.0158 * alpha_p * b * sqrt(|P| / (0.85 * R_eH)). Step 2 — Compute the aspect ratio correction factor: alpha_p = 1.2 - b/(2.1*a) = 1.2 - 400/(2.1*900) = 1.2 - 0.2116 = 0.9884, which is less than 1.0 so use 0.9884. Step 3 — Substitute values: t_gr = 0.0158 * 0.9884 * 400 * sqrt(12.5 / (0.85 * 235)) = 0.0158 * 0.9884 * 400 * sqrt(12.5 / 199.75) = 0.0158 * 0.9884 * 400 * sqrt(0.06257) = 0.0158 * 0.9884 * 400 * 0.2502 = 0.0158 * 0.9884 * 100.08 = 0.0158 * 98.96 = 1.564 mm. Wait — recalculate carefully: 0.0158 * 0.9884 = 0.015617; 0.015617 * 400 = 6.2468; sqrt(12.5/199.75) = sqrt(0.06257) = 0.25015; t_gr = 6.2468 * 0.25015 = 1.563 mm. Step 4 — The minimum required gross thickness is approximately 1.56 mm. The proposed thickness of 5.5 mm exceeds this minimum, so the arrangement is compliant. Note: The design pressure P = 12.5 kN/m² is taken as given by the designer consistent with the load definitions in Ch.6 Sec.2 [2] for the relevant design load set, evaluated at the load calculation point per Ch.3 Sec.7 [2.2] — this cross-reference to Ch.4 Sec.6 internal loads framework is what makes the question a cross-chapter chain.

question_text: A ro-ro vessel has a car deck fitted with transverse primary supporting members (girders) spanning 4.2 m between web frames. The deck is designed to carry heavy road transporters with a maximum axle load of 22 t. The girders are fabricated from steel with a specified minimum yield stress of 355 N/mm². During the design review, the structural engineer needs to verify the scantlings of these girders under the most severe vehicle loading condition at sea. The permissible stress coefficient to be applied when checking the section modulus of these girders is under debate — one engineer argues it should be 0.70, while another argues it should be 0.85. The girders are being assessed under Assessment Condition II (AC-II). Additionally, the symbol Q appears in the wheel load calculation formulas, but a junior engineer is unsure whether Q in that context refers to the maximum axle load or to shear force, since the same letter appears in the general symbols table with a different meaning. Clarify the correct permissible stress coefficient for the girder section modulus check under AC-II, and explain how the symbol Q is resolved between the wheel load section and the general symbols definitions.
required_facts: The allowable stresses for girders under vehicle loading are governed by Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 [2.2], as referenced from the wheel load girder scantling requirements.
The permissible stress coefficient Cs for section modulus of primary supporting members under AC-II is 0.85.
Cs = 0.70 applies only to AC-I, not AC-II or AC-III.
The symbol Q in the wheel load section is locally defined as maximum axle load in tonnes, overriding the general symbol definition.
The general symbols table (Ch.1 Sec.4 Table 1) defines Q as shear force in kN, but this applies only where Q is not locally redefined.
The local symbol definition in the wheel load section takes precedence over the general definition in Ch.1 Sec.4 for that section's formulas.
For heavy vehicles with axle load exceeding 15 t (here 22 t), footprint data must be provided for the pressure calculation.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch10.Sec5 [3.3.1] directs the designer to Ch.6 Sec.6 [2.2] for allowable stresses on vehicle-loaded girders; Ch.6 Sec.6 [2.1.1] defines the permissible stress coefficient Cs; Ch.6 Sec.6 opens with 'For symbols not defined in this section, see Ch.1 Sec.4', which is where the general symbol table lives — and that table defines Q as shear force, while Pt3.Ch10.Sec5 locally redefines Q as maximum axle load.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt3.Ch10.Sec5 [3.3.1] states: 'The scantlings of girders shall be specially considered based on the most severe condition of moving or stowed vehicles. Allowable stresses are as given in Ch.6 Sec.6 [2.2].' This is the first hop, directing the reader to Ch.6 Sec.6. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 [2.1.1] gives the section modulus formula and defines Cs: Cs = 0.70 for AC-I, Cs = 0.85 for AC-II and AC-III. Therefore under AC-II the correct coefficient is 0.85. Step 3 — The symbol conflict: Pt3.Ch10.Sec5 opens its Symbols block with 'For symbols not defined in this section, see Ch.1 Sec.4', and then locally defines Q = maximum axle load, in t. Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 1 defines Q = shear force, in kN. Because Pt3.Ch10.Sec5 provides a local definition of Q, that local definition takes precedence within the wheel load section; the general definition in Ch.1 Sec.4 applies only for symbols NOT defined locally. Hence Q = maximum axle load (in t) when used in the wheel load pressure formulas of Pt3.Ch10.Sec5.

question_text: A 185 m bulk carrier is being designed with a pronounced flare in the bow region. At 0.13L from the forward end, the flare angle α is measured at 43°. The designer has proposed to limit the bow impact strengthening zone to 0.15L from the forward end. A cargo hold finite element analysis has been carried out for the midship region. The FE model includes longitudinal shell envelope panels and double bottom floors. During the buckling assessment of the FE results, the designer proposes to use boundary condition SP-B for the double bottom floors, with panel dimensions defined as length equal to full web depth and width between primary supporting members. Is the proposed extent of the bow impact strengthening zone compliant, and is the proposed boundary condition for the double bottom floors in the buckling assessment correct? Justify your answer with reference to the applicable thresholds and boundary condition assignments.
required_facts: The bow impact strengthening zone must extend to at least 0.15L from the forward end because the flare angle α = 43° exceeds the 40° threshold, triggering the first extension rule
The proposed extent of 0.15L is the minimum compliant extent, provided the flare angle does not also exceed 40° at 0.15L (which would require further extension to 0.20L)
All structural elements in the cargo hold FE analysis must be assessed for buckling in accordance with the requirements of the direct strength analysis buckling section
Double bottom floors must be assigned boundary condition SP-A, not SP-B, in the buckling assessment
The correct panel definition for double bottom floors is: length = full web depth, width = between primary supporting members
The designer's proposed boundary condition SP-B for double bottom floors is non-compliant

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch10.Sec1 [1.1.3] defines the bow impact strengthening extent rules based on flare angle thresholds, and references the need for FE analysis. Pt3.Ch7.Sec3 [4.3] mandates that all structural elements in the cargo hold FE analysis be assessed against buckling as defined in Ch.8 Sec.4. Pt3.Ch8.Sec4 [2.1.1] Table 1 specifies that double bottom floors shall use boundary condition SP-A (not SP-B), with panel defined as length = full web depth and width between primary supporting members.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Bow impact extent (Pt3.Ch10.Sec1 [1.1.3]): The base strengthening zone is forward of 0.1L from FE. If flare angle α > 40° at 0.10L from FE, the zone extends to 0.15L. If α > 40° at 0.15L from FE, it must extend further to 0.20L. Here α = 43° > 40° is measured at 0.13L (i.e., between 0.10L and 0.15L). The first threshold is triggered (α > 40° at 0.10L), so the zone must extend to at least 0.15L. The question states the designer limits to 0.15L. To determine if 0.15L is sufficient, we must check whether α > 40° also applies at 0.15L. The scenario only states α = 43° at 0.13L; no value is given at 0.15L. However, the designer's proposal of 0.15L is the minimum required by the first trigger, so it is compliant provided α does not exceed 40° at 0.15L — the scenario does not state it does, so 0.15L is the correct minimum extent. Step 2 — Buckling assessment linkage (Pt3.Ch7.Sec3 [4.3]): The cargo hold FE analysis results must be assessed for buckling as defined in Ch.8 Sec.4. Step 3 — Boundary condition for double bottom floors (Pt3.Ch8.Sec4 [2.1.1] Table 1): Table 1 explicitly assigns SP-A (not SP-B) to double bottom floors, with panel defined as length = full web depth and width between primary supporting members. The designer's proposal of SP-B is therefore incorrect; SP-A must be used.

question_text: A 180 m general cargo vessel is being designed with a double-bottom ballast tank amidships. The tank has its highest point at z_top = 14.2 m above the keel reference, and the load point under assessment is located at z = 2.1 m. The tank is fitted with a pressure relief valve set at 45 kN/m². The liquid density for strength assessment is 1.025 t/m³. During the structural design review, the designer must determine the correct static internal pressure to apply at the load point for the static (S) design load scenario, and also confirm what minimum pressure value must be applied to the web of a primary supporting member located inside this ballast tank. What are the two pressure values the designer must use, and is the static pressure at the load point governed by the pressure relief valve arrangement?
required_facts: The static internal pressure for the water ballast tank boundary at the load point uses the formula P_ℓs-3 = ρ_L × g × (z_top − z) + P_0 because it follows the water-ballast-tank branch rather than the pressure-relief-valve cargo-tank branch
f_cd = 1.0 applies for ballast tanks (not oil cargo with ρ_L ≤ 1.025)
The pressure relief valve arrangement does not govern the static pressure formula for this ballast tank (PPV branch not selected)
The minimum pressure for internal structures in tanks (e.g. the PSM web) is P_int = 12 kN/m²
The two pressures are distinct: ~146.7 kN/m² for the tank boundary load point and 12 kN/m² for the internal structural member web

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch1.Sec2 establishes that structural strength must be checked against the design load scenarios; Pt3.Ch4.Sec7 defines the design load scenarios table and specifies that for boundaries of water ballast tanks under the static (S) scenario the internal pressure is P_ℓs-1, referencing Sec.6; Pt3.Ch4.Sec6 [1.2.1] gives the formula for P_ℓs-1 (with the pressure relief valve branch), and Sec.6 [3.1] gives the fixed minimum pressure P_int = 12 kN/m² for internal structures in tanks.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt3.Ch1.Sec2 [3.1.3]: ships must be designed to withstand environmental and loading conditions; structural strength checked per the rules including load scenarios. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch4.Sec7 design load scenarios table: for 'Boundaries of water ballast tanks' under the Static (S) column, the design internal pressure is P_ℓs-1. The table also shows that for 'Internal structures in tanks' the applicable pressure is P_int (no dynamic component in the S scenario column). Step 3 — Pt3.Ch4.Sec6 [1.2.1]: P_ℓs-1 for tanks with pressure relief valves = f_cd × ρ_L × g × (z_top − z) + P_PV. With f_cd = 1.0 (ballast tank, not oil cargo with ρ_L ≤ 1.025), ρ_L = 1.025 t/m³, g = 9.81 m/s², z_top = 14.2 m, z = 2.1 m, P_PV = 45 kN/m²: P_ℓs-1 = 1.0 × 1.025 × 9.81 × (14.2 − 2.1) + 45 = 1.025 × 9.81 × 12.1 + 45 = 121.6 + 45 ≈ 166.6 kN/m². Step 4 — Pt3.Ch4.Sec6 [3.1]: for internal structures in tanks (e.g. web of primary supporting members), P_int = 12 kN/m² (fixed value, irrespective of tank geometry). Conclusion: static pressure at load point ≈ 166.6 kN/m² (governed by the PV arrangement formula); minimum pressure for PSM web inside the tank = 12 kN/m².

question_text:
A 175 m general cargo vessel is being designed with a pronounced bow flare. At 0.10L from the forward end, the flare angle is 45°, and at 0.15L from the forward end, the flare angle is 42°. The bow region includes several primary supporting members (web frames) spanning transversely across the flared shell. One such web frame has an effective bending span of 2.8 m and supports shell plating over a spacing S between adjacent primary supporting members of 3.2 m. The design bow impact pressure P_FB at the load calculation point has been calculated as 185 kN/m². The web frame is fabricated from steel with yield strength R_eH = 315 N/mm², and the assessment condition is AC-I. The load calculation point for this web frame is defined as the midpoint of the member's effective bending span.

Determine: (1) what is the required extent of the bow impact strengthening zone along the ship's length, and (2) what is the minimum required section modulus Z (in cm³) of the primary supporting web frame resisting the bow impact pressure, using the appropriate bending moment distribution factor for a simply supported member?
required_facts: Because the flare angle at 0.10L exceeds 40°, the bow impact strengthening zone must be extended to at least 0.15L from the forward end
Because the flare angle at 0.15L also exceeds 40°, the zone must be further extended to 0.20L from the forward end
The bending moment distribution factor f_bdg for a simply supported member would be 8 from the formula, but the rule imposes a minimum of 10, so f_bdg = 10 must be used
The load calculation point is defined as the midpoint of the effective bending span per the structural idealisation rules
The permissible stress coefficient C_s = 0.70 for AC-I
The minimum required section modulus Z ≈ 2104 cm³ using Z = 1000 * |P| * S * ℓ_bdg² / (f_bdg * C_s * R_eH)

annotator_grounding.end_clause: Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 [2.1.1], Table 1 — which references Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [4.1] for the load calculation point definition
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch10.Sec1 governs bow impact strengthening extent and scantling requirements for primary supporting members; the PSM section modulus formula in Pt3.Ch10.Sec1 [3.2.1] uses fbdg from Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 Table 1, and the spacing S and load calculation point are defined in Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [1.2.2] and [4.1] respectively.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Strengthening extent (Pt3.Ch10.Sec1 [1.1.3]): The base rule requires strengthening forward of 0.1L. Since the flare angle at 0.10L is 45° > 40°, the zone must extend to 0.15L. Since the flare angle at 0.15L is 42° > 40°, the zone must further extend to 0.20L from the forward end. Final answer: bow impact strengthening extends to 0.20L from F.E.

Step 2 — Section modulus of PSM (Pt3.Ch10.Sec1 [3.2.1] → Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 [2.1.1]): The section modulus formula is Z = 1000 * |P| * S * ℓ_bdg² / (f_bdg * C_s * R_eH). The bending moment distribution factor f_bdg is taken from Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 Table 1; for a simply supported member (both ends simply supported, n_s = 0), f_bdg = 8*(1 + 0/2) = 8, but the rule states f_bdg shall not be taken less than 10, so f_bdg = 10. C_s = 0.70 for AC-I. The load calculation point is defined in Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [4.1] as the midpoint of the effective bending span, confirming P_FB = 185 kN/m² applies there. Substituting: Z = 1000 * 185 * 3.2 * (2.8)² / (10 * 0.70 * 315) = 1000 * 185 * 3.2 * 7.84 / 2205 = 1000 * 4638.08 / 2205 ≈ 2104 cm³.

question_text: A bulk carrier with ESP notation has a No. 1 cargo hatch cover fitted with stoppers to resist longitudinal forces from the forward end. The ship has no forecastle fitted. The stopper and its supporting structure are fabricated from high-strength steel with a specified minimum yield stress of 355 N/mm² and an ultimate tensile strength of 490 N/mm². The designer proposes to check the stopper welds using an allowable equivalent stress of 284 N/mm². Is this allowable stress correct, and what design pressure must the No. 1 hatch cover stoppers be designed to resist for longitudinal forces at the forward end?
required_facts: The ship is a Type-2 vessel (bulk carrier with ESP notation), so the Type-2 stopper requirements apply
No. 1 hatch cover with no forecastle must be designed for a longitudinal forward-end stopper pressure of 230 kN/m²
The effective yield strength R_eH must be taken as min[R_eH_nominal; 0.7 R_m] = min[355; 343] = 343 N/mm²
The allowable equivalent stress in stopper weld throats is 0.8 × R_eH = 0.8 × 343 = 274.4 N/mm²
The designer's proposed allowable of 284 N/mm² is incorrect because it uses the nominal yield stress instead of the effective yield strength
The 175 kN/m² reduced pressure for No. 1 hatch cover is only permitted when a forecastle is fitted in accordance with UR S28, which is not the case here

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Pt3.Ch12.Sec4 [6.2.4] which specifies stopper design pressures for Type-2 ships and references allowable stress of 0.8 R_eH; to evaluate R_eH the answerer must go to Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.2] to find the material factor k and confirm the effective yield strength definition, and also check the symbol definition in Pt3.Ch12.Sec4 Symbols where R_eH = min[R_eH; 0.7 R_m].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify ship type: bulk carrier with ESP notation → Type-2 ship per Pt3.Ch12.Sec4 [1.2]. Step 2 — Identify applicable design pressure: No. 1 hatch cover, no forecastle fitted → longitudinal stopper pressure = 230 kN/m² (the 175 kN/m² reduction only applies when a forecastle is fitted per UR S28). Step 3 — Determine allowable stress for stopper welds: Pt3.Ch12.Sec4 [6.2.4] states equivalent stress in throat of stopper welds shall not exceed 0.8 R_eH. Step 4 — Determine R_eH: per the Symbols in Pt3.Ch12.Sec4, R_eH = min[R_eH_material; 0.7 R_m] = min[355; 0.7×490] = min[355; 343] = 343 N/mm². Step 5 — Compute allowable: 0.8 × 343 = 274.4 N/mm². Step 6 — Check designer's value: designer proposed 284 N/mm², which would correspond to 0.8 × 355 = 284 N/mm², incorrectly using the nominal yield stress rather than the effective yield strength R_eH = min[R_eH; 0.7 R_m]. The correct allowable is 274.4 N/mm², so the designer's value is unconservative and incorrect. Cross-reference to Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.4] confirms that for AH36/DH36 steel R_eH = 355 N/mm² and R_m = 490 N/mm², validating the material properties used.

question_text: A 180 m general cargo vessel is being designed with a pronounced bow flare. At 0.12L from the forward end, the flare angle is 45°. The bow region shell stiffeners in the impact zone are fitted at a spacing of 600 mm and span 2.4 m between primary supporting members. The stiffeners are unsymmetrical flat-bar profiles welded to the shell plating. Due to the hull form geometry, the angle between the web plate of these stiffeners and the attached shell plating is 44°. The designer proposes to omit tripping brackets entirely in this region, arguing that the stiffener spacing is sufficient to prevent lateral-torsional buckling. As part of the structural review, the buckling utilization factor for these stiffeners under the combined static and dynamic (S+D) load case is calculated to be 0.87. Is the proposed arrangement acceptable? Specifically: (1) must tripping brackets be fitted for these stiffeners, and if so at what maximum spacing; (2) what is the allowable buckling utilization factor for the S+D acceptance criterion; and (3) is the calculated utilization factor of 0.87 compliant?
required_facts: The flare angle of 45° at 0.12L exceeds 40°, so the bow impact strengthening zone must be extended to at least 0.15L from the forward end
Tripping brackets must be fitted because the stiffener web-to-plating angle (44°) is less than 50°
Maximum tripping bracket spacing is 4 × stiffener spacing = 4 × 600 mm = 2400 mm
For an unsymmetrical stiffener with web-to-plating angle less than 50°, the face plate shall be fitted on the open angle side
The allowable buckling utilization factor for plates, stiffeners, and stiffened panels under AC-II S+D loading is 1.00
The calculated utilization factor of 0.87 is compliant (0.87 < 1.00)
The proposed arrangement of omitting tripping brackets entirely is not acceptable

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Bow impact zone requirements (Ch.10 Sec.1) note that obstructions such as knuckles require additional reinforcement including carlings; the buckling chapter (Ch.8 Sec.1 Table 3) defines allowable utilization factors; and the detail design chapter (Ch.3 Sec.6) mandates tripping brackets when the stiffener-to-plating angle is less than 50°, specifying maximum spacing and face-plate orientation.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Bow impact zone applicability: The flare angle at 0.12L is 45° > 40°, so the bow impact strengthening area must be extended to at least 0.15L from the forward end (Pt3.Ch10.Sec1 [1.1.3]). The stiffeners at 0.12L therefore fall within the strengthened bow impact zone. Step 2 — Tripping bracket requirement: Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [3.1.2] states that where the angle between the web plate of a stiffener and the attached plating is less than 50°, tripping brackets or carlings shall be fitted spaced not more than 4 times the stiffener spacing. With stiffener spacing of 600 mm, the maximum tripping bracket spacing is 4 × 600 = 2400 mm. Since the span is 2.4 m, at least one intermediate tripping bracket is required (or brackets at each end). The proposal to omit tripping brackets is therefore not acceptable. Additionally, because the stiffener is unsymmetrical and the angle is less than 50°, the face plate shall be fitted on the open angle side. Step 3 — Allowable buckling utilization factor: Per Pt3.Ch8.Sec1 [3.4] Table 3, for acceptance criterion AC-II under S+D loading, the allowable buckling utilization factor η_a = 0.90. Step 4 — Compliance check: The calculated utilization factor of 0.87 < 0.90, so the buckling utilization is compliant with the S+D criterion, provided the tripping bracket deficiency is corrected.

question_text: A newbuilding general cargo vessel has a length of 95 m and a maximum deadweight of 2,800 tonnes, with a maximum displacement of 6,500 tonnes. The vessel is classed as a category II ship. The designer has prepared a loading manual based on preliminary ship data, but the final lightship weight came in 3.5% heavier than the preliminary value used, shifting the still water bending moments by approximately 2.8% above the originally approved values. The designer argues that since the vessel is under 100 m, no loading instrument is required, and that the loading manual does not need to be resubmitted. Additionally, the structural drawings show a main deck plate with a net required thickness of 11.1 mm. The corrosion addition for this location is 1.8 mm. The shipyard proposes to order plates at an as-built thickness of 13.0 mm, with no voluntary addition declared. Is the designer correct that the loading manual does not need to be updated and resubmitted? And does the proposed deck plate as-built thickness of 13.0 mm satisfy the gross scantling compliance requirement?
required_facts: The loading manual must be updated and resubmitted because the change in still water bending moments (2.8%) exceeds the 2% tolerance threshold
The gross required thickness t_gr = min(11.1 + 1.8 ; 1.25 × 11.1) = min(12.9 ; 13.875) = 12.9 mm, which rounds to 13.0 mm
The gross offered thickness t_gr_off = 13.0 − 0 = 13.0 mm (no voluntary addition)
The deck plate as-built thickness of 13.0 mm satisfies gross scantling compliance since t_gr_off (13.0 mm) ≥ t_gr (13.0 mm)
The designer is incorrect that the loading manual does not need resubmission

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec5 loading manual requirements trigger a re-approval threshold check (2% rule), which in turn requires applying the net scantling approach from Ch3 Sec2 to verify gross scantling compliance of the proposed plate thickness.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt3.Ch1.Sec5 [1.1.2]: The vessel is 95 m, category II, and deadweight is 2,800 t vs displacement 6,500 t, giving DWT/displacement = 43%, which exceeds 30%. Therefore the exemption for category II ships under 90 m with DWT ≤ 30% displacement does NOT apply here anyway (vessel is 95 m, above 90 m threshold), so a loading manual considering longitudinal strength IS required. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch1.Sec5 [2.1.2]: The loading manual shall be based on final ship data. Modifications resulting in changes to lightship weight require the manual to be updated and re-approved UNLESS the resulting still water bending moments and shear forces do not differ from originally approved data by more than 2%. Here the deviation is 2.8%, which exceeds the 2% tolerance. Therefore the loading manual MUST be updated and resubmitted — the designer is incorrect. Step 3 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec2 [1.2.1]: Gross required thickness t_gr = min(t + t_c ; 1.25t) = min(11.1 + 1.8 ; 1.25 × 11.1) = min(12.9 ; 13.875) = 12.9 mm. Rounded to nearest 0.5 mm: 13.0 mm. Step 4 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec2 [1.2.2]: Gross offered thickness t_gr_off = t_as_built − t_vol_add = 13.0 − 0 = 13.0 mm. Step 5 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec2 [1.3.2]: Compliance requires t_gr_off ≥ t_gr, i.e. 13.0 mm ≥ 13.0 mm. The condition is exactly met, so the proposed as-built thickness of 13.0 mm is compliant.

question_text: A RO/RO ferry has a stern door that also serves as a vehicle ramp. The door opens inward and leads directly to the RO/RO cargo space. The door opening area is 18 m², and the door mass is 12 t. The total packing force is 15 kN. The deepest equilibrium waterline in the damaged condition is 0.8 m above the load point of the door. During the structural design review, the designer needs to determine: (1) the design force F₁ that the securing bolts, supporting members, and surrounding structure must be designed to withstand; and (2) what symbol definitions must be used for the variables in the design force formula — specifically, what is the standard unit and meaning of the symbol 'P' as used in the general rules, and what is the value of ρ (density of seawater) to be used in any hydrostatic calculations. Is the door arrangement subject to the additional design load requirements applicable to RO/RO spaces, and what is the numerical value of F₁ in kN?
required_facts: The stern door leads to a RO/RO space, so the additional design load requirements of the relevant clause apply
Pe = 10 × h_b = 10 × 0.8 = 8 kN/m², but the minimum value of 25 kN/m² governs, so Pe = 25 kN/m²
The symbol P is defined in the general symbols table as pressure with units kN/m²
The density of seawater ρ is taken equal to 1.025 t/m³ per the primary symbols definitions
F₁ applies because the door opens inward

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch12.Sec5 [1.4.1] states that [1.4.3] applies only to doors leading to RO/RO or special category spaces as defined in Ch.1 Sec.4; the answerer must navigate to Ch.1 Sec.4 to confirm the definition of 'special category spaces' and RO/RO spaces, and also to resolve the standard symbol definitions (P in kN/m², ρ = 1.025 t/m³) needed to compute Pe and F₁.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt3.Ch12.Sec5 [1.4.1]: The clause states that [1.4.3] applies only to doors leading to RO/RO spaces or special category spaces 'as defined in Ch.1 Sec.4'. The stern door leads to the RO/RO cargo space, so [1.4.3] applies. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch12.Sec5 [1.4.3]: For a door opening inward, F₁ = A·Pe + Fp. Pe = 10·h_b (minimum 25 kN/m²). h_b = 0.8 m, so Pe = 10 × 0.8 = 8 kN/m², which is below the minimum of 25 kN/m², so Pe = 25 kN/m². A = 18 m², Fp = 15 kN. F₁ = 18 × 25 + 15 = 450 + 15 = 465 kN. Step 3 — Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 1: The symbol P is defined as 'pressure' with units kN/m². ρ (density of seawater) = 1.025 t/m³ per Table 1. These definitions confirm the units used in the Pe calculation. Step 4 — Conclusion: The arrangement is subject to the additional design loads; F₁ = 465 kN.

scenario_parameters.door_type: stern door / vehicle ramp, opens inward

question_text: A 180 m general cargo vessel is being designed with a fabricated stern frame. The designer proposes to use cast steel for the stern frame construction. The material certificate shows the cast steel has a specified minimum yield stress of 355 N/mm² and a tensile strength of 510 N/mm². The designer wants to confirm: (1) whether this material is acceptable for the stern frame, (2) what material grade category this steel falls under, and (3) what material factor k applies when calculating scantlings for this component. Is the proposed cast steel acceptable, and what is the correct value of k to use in scantling calculations?
required_facts: Cast steel is explicitly permitted for stern frames, with material specifications governed by Ch.3 Sec.1
ReH = 355 N/mm² places this steel in the high strength (HT) category, since 235 < 355 ≤ 390 N/mm²
The steel is cast steel with Rm >= 400
The material factor k = 0.72 applies for ReH = 355 N/mm² per Table 2
The proposed cast steel is acceptable for the stern frame application

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch10.Sec6 [2.1.1] states that for applicable material specifications and steel grades for stern frames, see Ch.3 Sec.1. Ch.3 Sec.1 [2.1.4] defines steel grade categories and [2.2] gives the material factor k table.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Pt3.Ch10.Sec6 [2.1.1] explicitly states 'For applicable material specifications and steel grades, see Ch.3 Sec.1.' This triggers the cross-reference. Step 2: Navigate to Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.4], which defines steel categories: normal strength (ReH = 235 N/mm²), high strength (235 < ReH ≤ 390 N/mm²), and extra high strength (ReH > 390 N/mm²). With ReH = 355 N/mm², the cast steel falls in the high strength category (HT), grade designation AH/DH/EH/FH series — specifically A36/D36/E36/F36 range. Step 3: Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.2] Table 2 gives k = 0.72 for ReH = 355 N/mm². Step 4: The material is acceptable for stern frame use (cast steel is explicitly permitted per [2.1.1]), and k = 0.72 applies to scantling calculations.

question_text: A naval architect is designing a 95-metre general cargo vessel with a conventional diesel-mechanical propulsion plant. The ship has no damage stability calculations on file. The design includes a collision bulkhead, an aft peak bulkhead, and bulkheads at each end of the engine room. The designer proposes a total of 4 transverse watertight bulkheads for the vessel. The design documentation references a symbol 'T_LL' used in the minimum bow height calculation, but the subdivision arrangement drawing does not define this symbol locally. Where should the designer look to find the definition of T_LL, and is the proposed number of 4 transverse watertight bulkheads sufficient for this vessel?
required_facts: Symbols not defined in the subdivision arrangement section are defined in Ch.1 Sec.4 of the same Part
T_LL is defined as the draught at 85% of the least moulded freeboard depth (D_LL)
For a vessel of 95 m length with no damage stability calculations, the applicable length band is 85 < L ≤ 105 m
Table 1 requires a minimum of 4 transverse watertight bulkheads for an engine-room-aft arrangement in this length band, or 5 bulkheads for an elsewhere arrangement
The proposed count of 4 bulkheads is only sufficient if the engine room is located aft; otherwise a minimum of 5 is required

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch2.Sec2 states that symbols not defined locally are found in Ch.1 Sec.4; the answerer must navigate there to find T_LL defined as the draught at 85% of the least moulded freeboard depth. Separately, Pt3.Ch2.Sec2 Table 1 gives the minimum bulkhead count for a 95m ship (falling in the 85 < L ≤ 105 range) as 4 bulkheads with engine room aft, or 5 bulkheads elsewhere — the proposed count of 4 must be checked against this table.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: The symbols preamble of Pt3.Ch2.Sec2 explicitly states 'For symbols not defined in this section, see Ch.1 Sec.4.' The designer must therefore consult Ch.1 Sec.4 to find T_LL. Step 2: In Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 2 (Ship's main data), T_LL is defined as 'the draught in m at 85% of the least moulded freeboard depth, D_LL'. Step 3: For the bulkhead count, Pt3.Ch2.Sec2 [1.1.4] applies because no damage stability calculations have been carried out. Table 1 shows that for 85 < L ≤ 105 m, the minimum number of transverse watertight bulkheads is 4 (engine room aft arrangement) or 5 (elsewhere arrangement). At L = 95 m the ship falls in this band. Step 4: The proposed 4 bulkheads meets the minimum only if the engine room is aft; if the engine room is not aft, 5 bulkheads are required and the proposal is non-compliant.

question_text: A shipowner is applying for DNV class on a newly built 165-metre general dry cargo vessel with five cargo holds, designed to carry solid bulk cargoes with a maximum cargo density of 1.75 t/m³. The designer proposes to assign the class notation HC(B) without any additional density qualifier. During the design review, a question arises about whether a maximum cargo density notation is required, and if so, what that notation would be. Additionally, the review team wants to confirm the precise meaning of the word 'shall' as used in the mandatory notation requirements — specifically whether it denotes a strict obligation or merely a recommendation. What class notations are mandatory for this vessel, and what is the correct interpretation of the verbal form used to express those mandatory requirements?
required_facts: HC(B) is a mandatory class notation for this vessel because it is a general dry cargo ship with L ≥ 150 m and at least five cargo holds designed for solid bulk cargoes
The Maximum cargo density notation (1.75 t/m³) is mandatory because the vessel has HC(B) and the design density 1.75 t/m³ is less than 3.0 t/m³
The proposed assignment of HC(B) alone without the density qualifier is not sufficient — the density notation must also be assigned
The verbal form 'shall' as used in the mandatory notation requirements denotes a requirement strictly to be followed, not merely a recommendation
The definition of 'shall' is found in the verbal forms table in the classification principles section of the rules

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Pt1.Ch2.Sec4 which identifies mandatory additional class notations for vessel types and references the concept of mandatory requirements; the verbal form 'shall' used in those mandatory requirements is defined in Pt1.Ch1.Sec1 Table 1 (verbal forms normative table).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — From Pt1.Ch2.Sec4 Table 1: A 165m general dry cargo vessel with five cargo holds designed for solid bulk cargoes meets the threshold for mandatory HC notation (L ≥ 150 m, minimum five cargo holds). HC(B) is appropriate for cargoes of density ≥ 1.0 t/m³ with all holds loaded. Step 2 — Still in Table 1: The 'Maximum cargo density' notation (ρ) is listed as mandatory for vessels with HC(A), HC(B), or HC(B*) designed for a maximum cargo density < 3.0 t/m³. Since 1.75 t/m³ < 3.0 t/m³, the notation 'Maximum cargo density 1.75' is mandatory alongside HC(B). Step 3 — The mandatory requirements use the verbal form 'shall'. To confirm what this means, the reader must follow the cross-reference to Pt1.Ch1.Sec1 [1.2.1] Table 1 (Verbal forms normative), which defines 'shall' as 'verbal form used to indicate a requirement strictly to be followed' — i.e., a strict obligation, not a recommendation.

question_text: A structural engineer is performing a fatigue assessment for a 180-metre bulk carrier operating worldwide. The ship's side shell plating in the midship region includes a welded longitudinal stiffener connection located in a water ballast tank. The designer proposes to use prescriptive wave loads from the standard load calculation procedure (not a direct hydrodynamic analysis) and applies a world wide wave environment scatter diagram. During the fatigue calculation, the designer uses an operational factor of 0.85 and an environmental factor of 0.75 for the prescriptive loads. The total external sea pressure Pex at a load point on the side shell at z = 4.5 m below the waterline is being evaluated for the static plus dynamic design load scenario. Is the designer's choice of operational factor and environmental factor correct for this scenario? What values should be used, and how does the symbol Pex relate to the load components used in the calculation?
required_facts: The operational factor fR for prescriptive loads calculated using the standard Ch.4 procedure shall be 0.76, not 0.85 as proposed by the designer.
The environmental factor fe for world wide wave environment with prescriptive loads shall be 0.8, not 0.75 as proposed by the designer.
Pex (total external sea pressure) is composed of hydrostatic pressure PS and dynamic wave pressure PW for the static plus dynamic (S+D) design load scenario.
The correct value fR = 0.76 is specified for prescriptive loads and requires special consideration when combined with direct wave load analysis.
The fe = 1.0 value applies only to the North Atlantic wave environment (or when a hydrodynamic scatter diagram analysis is used), not to world wide operation.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The symbol Pex is defined in Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 4 with a cross-reference to Ch.4 Sec.5 [1.1], which defines how total external sea pressure is composed of hydrostatic and wave pressure components and also references fR from Ch.9 Sec.4 [4.3]. Ch.9 Sec.4 [4.3] specifies the correct operational factor fR = 0.76 for prescriptive loads, and Ch.9 Sec.4 [4.2] specifies fe = 0.8 for world wide wave environment.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — The designer needs to verify the load factors used. The symbol Pex (total sea pressure) appears in Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 4 with a reference to Ch.4 Sec.5 [1.1]. Step 2 — Ch.4 Sec.5 [1.1] defines Pex = PS + PW for the static plus dynamic (S+D) design load scenario, where PS is hydrostatic pressure and PW is wave pressure. The section also lists fR (factor related to operational profile) as defined in Ch.9 Sec.4 [4.3]. Step 3 — Ch.9 Sec.4 [4.3] states that for prescriptive loads calculated in Ch.4, the operational factor shall be fR = 0.76. The designer's value of 0.85 is therefore incorrect. Step 4 — Ch.9 Sec.4 [4.2] states that for prescriptive loads in a world wide wave environment, the environmental factor fe = 0.8 shall be used (fe = 1.0 for North Atlantic). The designer's value of 0.75 is also incorrect. Step 5 — The guidance note in [4.3] clarifies that fR = 0.76 applies to prescriptive loads and will be specially considered when combined with direct wave load analysis results.

scenario_parameters.structural_location: side shell longitudinal stiffener connection in water ballast tank

question_text: A 95 m general cargo vessel (category II ship) has a maximum deadweight of 2,800 tonnes and a maximum displacement of 8,500 tonnes. The vessel's loading manual was approved two years ago based on final ship data. The shipowner has since made modifications to the ballast tank arrangement, resulting in a change to the buoyancy distribution. Recalculations show that the still water bending moment at the critical section has increased by 1.8% compared to the originally approved value, and the still water shear force has increased by 2.3% compared to the originally approved value. The naval architect must determine whether the loading manual requires re-approval and resubmission. Additionally, the loading manual currently includes departure and arrival conditions for the standard cargo loading case, but the operator intends to perform ballasting during the voyage. What intermediate conditions must be documented in the loading manual for this ballasting operation, and what filling levels must be investigated for any ballast tanks that will be partially filled during the voyage?
required_facts: The loading manual must be re-approved and resubmitted because the still water shear force increase of 2.3% exceeds the 2% threshold, even though the SWBM increase of 1.8% is within the 2% limit
The loading computer system must also be updated and re-approved when the loading manual is re-approved

Both the still water bending moment AND shear force (and draughts) must each individually remain within 2% of originally approved values for resubmission to be waived — it is not sufficient that only one criterion is met
For the ballasting operation during voyage, the loading manual must include calculations for the intermediate condition just before and just after each ballasting or de-ballasting operation

In cargo loading conditions, for any peak ballast tank intended to be partially filled during the voyage, the still water bending moment and shear force must be calculated with those tanks assumed empty, full, and partially filled at the intended level

In cargo loading conditions, where multiple forepeak tanks are intended to be partially filled, all combinations of empty, full, or partially filled at intended level for those tanks must be investigated

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch1.Sec5 [2.1.2] defines the 2% threshold for re-approval of the loading manual and references Ch.4 Sec.8 for loading conditions; Pt3.Ch1.Sec5 [2.1.3] explicitly references Ch.4 Sec.8 for the design loading conditions to be included; Ch.4 Sec.8 [1.1.2] specifies intermediate ballasting conditions and Ch.4 Sec.8 [1.2.1] specifies the filling level combinations required for partially filled ballast tanks
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Start at Pt3.Ch1.Sec5 [2.1.2]: The condition for not requiring resubmission is that resulting draughts, still water bending moments AND shear forces must ALL be within 2% of originally approved data. The SWBM increase of 1.8% is within 2%, but the shear force increase of 2.3% exceeds the 2% threshold. Therefore, the loading manual must be updated and re-approved, and the loading computer system must also be updated and re-approved. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch1.Sec5 [2.1.3] states that loading conditions shall be as defined in Ch.4 Sec.8, directing the reader to the intermediate section. Step 3 — At Pt3.Ch4.Sec8 [1.1.2]: Where ballasting and/or de-ballasting is intended during voyage, calculations of the intermediate condition just before and just after ballasting/de-ballasting shall be submitted and included in the loading manual. Step 4 — At Pt3.Ch4.Sec8 [1.2.1]: For ballast loading conditions involving partially filled ballast tanks, all combinations of empty, full, and partially filled at intended level must be investigated for each such tank. Where multiple tanks are intended to be partially filled, all combinations of empty, full or partially filled at intended level for those tanks shall be investigated. Step 5 — Note also from Pt3.Ch1.Sec5 [1.1.2]: This vessel at 95 m length is category II, and its deadweight ratio is 2800/8500 = 32.9%, which exceeds 30% of maximum displacement, so a loading manual considering longitudinal strength IS required (the exemption for category II ships under 90 m with DWT ≤ 30% displacement does not apply here since the vessel is 95 m, above the 90 m threshold).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation_note: The 95 m length also means the vessel is above the 90 m threshold, so the category II exemption from longitudinal strength loading manual does not apply regardless of the DWT ratio.

scenario_parameters.modification_type: ballast tank arrangement / buoyancy distribution change

question_text: A general cargo vessel of 105 m in length and 8,200 tonnes maximum displacement is being designed for unrestricted ocean service. The ship is classified as category I. The designer has prepared a loading manual covering all standard cargo and ballast conditions, but has not included a loading instrument system onboard, arguing that the vessel's relatively modest size and simple loading patterns make such a system unnecessary. The loading manual documents permissible still water bending moments and shear forces, and all loading conditions are based on final ship data. During the design review, the structural assessment team is evaluating the design load scenarios for strength assessment. For a normal seagoing operation load case, the team needs to confirm the correct combination of hull girder loads to apply: specifically, whether the vertical bending moment (VBM) for this scenario should use only the permissible still water bending moment Msw, or the combined value Msw + Mwv-LC, and similarly whether the vertical shear force (VSF) should be Qsw alone or Qsw + Qwv-LC. Is the designer's decision to omit the loading instrument system compliant with classification requirements, and what are the correct hull girder load combinations for VBM and VSF in the normal seagoing operation design load scenario?
required_facts: The loading instrument system is mandatory for this vessel because it is category I and 105 m in length, which meets or exceeds the 100 m threshold.
The designer's decision to omit the loading instrument system is not compliant with classification requirements.
Minimum requirements apply irrespective of other considerations and cannot be overridden by the designer's judgment about loading simplicity.
For normal seagoing operation (Design Load Scenario 1), VBM = Msw + Mwv-LC (still water bending moment combined with vertical wave bending moment).
For normal seagoing operation (Design Load Scenario 1), VSF = Qsw + Qwv-LC (still water shear force combined with vertical wave shear force).
The normal seagoing scenario is an S+D (static + dynamic) load scenario, not a static-only scenario.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec5 [1.1.2] mandates a loading instrument for category I ships of 100 m and above; Sec5 references rule principles in Sec2 [5.2] for minimum requirements context; Pt3.Ch4.Sec7 Table 1 defines the design load scenarios and specifies the correct hull girder load combinations for normal seagoing operation.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt3.Ch1.Sec5 [1.1.2]: 'All ships of category I of 100 m length and above shall in addition to the loading manual be provided with a loading instrument system approved and certified for calculation and control of hull strength.' The vessel is 105 m and category I, so it exceeds the 100 m threshold. The loading instrument is mandatory; the designer's omission is non-compliant. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch1.Sec2 [5.2]: Minimum requirements apply irrespective of all other requirements; scantlings or provisions below minimum requirements may only be accepted on a case-by-case basis. This reinforces that the loading instrument requirement is a minimum that cannot be waived by the designer's judgment alone. Step 3 — Pt3.Ch4.Sec7 Table 1: For Design Load Scenario 1 (Normal operations at sea), the hull girder loads are: VBM = Msw + Mwv-LC (combined still water and wave vertical bending moment), VSF = Qsw + Qwv-LC (combined still water and wave vertical shear force). The static-only values Msw and Qsw alone are not sufficient for the seagoing S+D scenario.

question_text:
A 95-metre general cargo vessel is being fitted with an anchor windlass on the exposed forecastle deck. The forecastle deck is located 7.5 m above the summer load waterline. The windlass foundation is a custom-fabricated steel pedestal welded directly to the deck plating; it is not selected from any accepted industry standard. The pedestal is fabricated from normal-strength steel with a specified minimum yield stress of 235 N/mm². The weld connecting the pedestal base plate to the deck plating is a continuous fillet weld with a leg length of 8 mm. The as-built thickness of the deck plating (the abutting plate) is 14 mm.

During the design review, the following questions arise:
1. What corrosion addition must be applied to the pedestal and its foundation when determining net scantlings for strength assessment?
2. For the fillet weld connecting the pedestal base plate to the deck plating, what is the minimum required throat thickness, and what value of R_eH_weld must be used in the weld strength calculation?
3. Is the proposed 8 mm leg length fillet weld likely to satisfy the weld strength requirements, given the design loads from the anchoring operation (the windlass is fitted with a chain stopper, and the chain cable has a minimum breaking strength of 1 200 kN)?
required_facts: Design load for windlass with chain stopper = 45% of BS = 0.45 × 1200 kN = 540 kN
Corrosion addition t_c = 2.0 mm for custom (non-standard) pedestals and foundations on deck
Strength assessment is based on net scantlings (as-built thickness minus t_c)
R_eH_weld = 305 N/mm² for welding of normal-strength steel with R_eH = 235 N/mm²
Gap allowance t_gap = 2.0 mm for as-built plate thickness of 14 mm (≥ 12 mm)
Effective throat thickness = (leg length − t_gap) × cos(45°) ≈ (8 − 2.0) × 0.707 ≈ 4.24 mm

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch11.Sec2 governs the supporting structure and foundations for anchor windlasses, specifying design loads (45% of BS when chain stopper is provided), acceptance criteria referencing net scantlings, and corrosion additions for custom pedestals (2.0 mm per Sec2 [5.8.1]). The weld design for the pedestal-to-deck connection must then follow Pt3.Ch13.Sec1, which provides the weld factor, throat thickness formula, and R_eH_weld values for normal-strength steel.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Identify applicable design load: windlass with chain stopper → load = 45% × BS = 0.45 × 1200 = 540 kN (Pt3.Ch11.Sec2 [2.3.1a]).
Step 2 — Corrosion addition: the pedestal is a custom fabrication not from an accepted industry standard → t_c = 2.0 mm (Pt3.Ch11.Sec2 [5.8.1]).
Step 3 — Strength assessment uses net scantlings (as-built minus t_c) per Pt3.Ch11.Sec2 [2.4.1].
Step 4 — For the fillet weld, navigate to Pt3.Ch13.Sec1. The abutting plate is normal-strength steel with R_eH = 235 N/mm², so R_eH_weld = 305 N/mm² (Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 Symbols).
Step 5 — Throat thickness: t_throat = l × cos(45°) = 8 × 0.707 ≈ 5.66 mm, rounded to 5.5 mm net after gap allowance. The gap allowance t_gap for t_as-built = 14 mm (between 12 mm and upper bound) = 2.0 mm, so effective throat = (8 − 2.0) × 0.707 ≈ 4.24 mm (Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [2.5.3] and symbols).
Step 6 — The weld must be assessed against the 540 kN design load using the effective weld area and permissible stress derived from R_eH_weld = 305 N/mm²; the adequacy of the 8 mm leg length depends on the pedestal base plate perimeter and load distribution, but the answerer must confirm the throat calculation and material parameters.

question_text:
A structural engineer is reviewing the intersection detail where longitudinal shell stiffeners pass through a transverse web frame on a 145-metre bulk carrier. The cut-outs in the web frame are 420 mm deep, and the transverse web frame has a total web depth of 900 mm. No lug or collar plates are fitted at these cut-outs. The cut-out breadth is 60 mm, and the corners are currently detailed with a radius of 10 mm. The location is below the scantling draught, and the calculated direct stress in the web stiffener is 72% of the permissible value.

(a) Is the cut-out depth arrangement acceptable without lug or collar plates, and what condition, if any, must be satisfied for it to be accepted?
(b) What is the minimum corner radius required for the cut-out corners, and does the current 10 mm radius comply?
(c) Is a soft heel with keyhole required at this intersection, and why or why not?

In your answer, identify the relevant stress symbol used for the web stiffener direct stress and state its standard unit as defined in the general rules symbols table.
required_facts: Cut-out depth ratio is 46.7% (420/900), which does not exceed the 50% limit, so the arrangement is acceptable without lug or collar plates (subject to no high-stress area triggers)
Minimum corner radius R = max(20% × 60 mm, 25 mm) = 25 mm; the current 10 mm radius does NOT comply
Corner radius upper limit is 50 mm; the required minimum of 25 mm applies here
Soft heel with keyhole is NOT required because the calculated direct stress (72% of permissible) does not exceed the 80% threshold
The symbol for direct stress in the PSM web stiffener is σ (or σ_w), with unit N/mm², as defined in the general symbols table in the primary symbols section of the rules

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch6.Sec7 governs cut-out arrangement and web stiffener details; the section header explicitly states 'For symbols not defined in this section, see Ch.1 Sec.4', so the answerer must navigate to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 to confirm the symbol σ_w (direct stress, N/mm²) and its unit.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Cut-out depth check (Pt3.Ch6.Sec7 [1.1.2]): Cut-out depth = 420 mm; PSM web depth = 900 mm; ratio = 420/900 = 46.7%, which is less than 50%. Therefore the cut-out depth is within the 50% limit and is acceptable without lug or collar plates, provided no other trigger (cross-tie ends, bulkhead stools, high-stress areas) applies. No additional shear/buckling check is mandated at this depth.

Step 2 — Corner radius check (Pt3.Ch6.Sec7 [1.1.6]): Minimum R = max(20% × b, 25 mm) = max(0.20 × 60, 25) = max(12, 25) = 25 mm. Upper cap is 50 mm. Current R = 10 mm < 25 mm → NON-COMPLIANT. Minimum required corner radius is 25 mm.

Step 3 — Soft heel requirement (Pt3.Ch6.Sec7 [1.1.5]): Location is below scantling draught T_sc (shell longitudinals), so the clause applies. Soft heel with keyhole is required only when calculated direct stress σ_w exceeds 80% of permissible value. Here σ_w = 72% of permissible < 80% threshold → soft heel is NOT required.

Step 4 — Symbol and unit lookup (Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 1): Pt3.Ch6.Sec7 preamble states 'For symbols not defined in this section, see Ch.1 Sec.4'. The symbol σ_w is the direct stress in the PSM web stiffener. The general symbol σ = normal stress, unit N/mm², as defined in Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 1.

question_text: A 185 m general cargo vessel is being designed with a transversely framed double bottom in the engine room. The designer proposes to fit solid floors at every second frame (frame spacing 600 mm, so floors at 1200 mm centres) under the main engine seating, arguing that the double bottom is supported by two continuous longitudinal girders running the full length of the engine room. The engine room extends 18 m in length. Additionally, a web frame in the engine room side structure is proposed at 5.5 times the frame spacing. A primary supporting member (floor girder) in the engine room has a span of 4.2 m, a tributary breadth of 2.8 m, and is subjected to a design pressure of 35 kN/m² under the AC-II load set. The designer calculates a required section modulus of 1 850 cm³ using load model A (both ends fixed, uniformly distributed load). Is the proposed floor spacing under the main engine acceptable, is the web frame spacing in the side structure acceptable, and is the section modulus calculation for the floor girder correct? Provide the minimum required section modulus.
required_facts: Floor spacing under the main engine must be at every frame (600 mm), not every second frame; the proposed 1200 mm spacing is not acceptable
The exception for greater floor spacing applies only forward and aft of the engine seating, not directly under the main engine
Web frame spacing in the engine room side structure must not exceed 5 times the frame spacing; 5.5 × frame spacing is not acceptable without a partial structural analysis
The section modulus formula for primary supporting members is Z = 1000 × |P| × S × ℓbdg² / (fbdg × Cs × ReH)
For load model A at mid-span, fbdg = 24.0; Cs = 0.85 for AC-II
The correct required section modulus at mid-span is approximately 361 cm³ (assuming ReH = 235 N/mm²), not 1 850 cm³
The designer's section modulus value of 1 850 cm³ is incorrect

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch3.Sec5 establishes engine room structural arrangement requirements (floor spacing under main engine, web frame spacing in side structure), and the floor girder scantling check requires navigating to Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 for the primary supporting member section modulus formula and the correct fbdg factor for the chosen load model.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Floor spacing under main engine: Pt3.Ch3.Sec5 [5.1.6] states that solid floors shall be fitted at every frame under the main engine and thrust bearing. The proposed spacing of every second frame (1200 mm) is therefore NOT acceptable; floors must be at every frame (600 mm centres). The exception for greater spacing applies only forward and aft of the engine/bearing seatings, not directly under them, and only when supported by effective longitudinal girders — but this exception does not override the 'every frame' requirement directly under the engine. Step 2 — Web frame spacing in side structure: Pt3.Ch3.Sec5 [5.2] states web frames shall be spaced not more than 5 times the frame spacing apart. The proposed 5.5 × frame spacing exceeds this limit and is NOT acceptable unless a partial ship structural analysis per Ch.7 Sec.3 is carried out. Step 3 — Section modulus of floor girder: Navigate to Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 [2.1.1]. The formula is Z = 1000 × |P| × S × ℓbdg² / (fbdg × Cs × ReH). For load model A (both ends fixed, UDL), fbdg at mid-span = 24.0 (from Table 1). Cs = 0.85 for AC-II. Assuming ReH = 235 N/mm² (mild steel): Z = 1000 × 35 × 2.8 × 4.2² / (24.0 × 0.85 × 235) = 1000 × 35 × 2.8 × 17.64 / (4794) = 1 728 720 / 4794 ≈ 360.6 cm³. The designer's value of 1 850 cm³ is incorrect — they likely used fbdg = 12 (support position factor) instead of 24 for mid-span, or made an error in the formula. The correct mid-span section modulus is approximately 361 cm³. If the support position governs (fbdg = 12), Z ≈ 721 cm³, still far below 1 850 cm³. The designer's figure of 1 850 cm³ is not reproducible from the formula with any standard fbdg value from Table 1 for load model A, suggesting an error in the calculation.

question_text:
A 95-metre bulk carrier is being designed for unrestricted service. In the normal ballast condition, the minimum forward draught at the forward perpendicular is 2.8 m. The block coefficient CB is 0.72. The designer is evaluating whether the forward bottom structure requires strengthening against bottom slamming, and if so, what the design bottom slamming pressure PSL is at a cross-section located 22 m aft of the forward perpendicular, where the breadth of the bottom at 0.15 TF above the baseline is 9.5 m.

Additionally, the ship has a double bottom fitted throughout the cargo hold region. The inner bottom height above the keel is being determined. The ship's moulded breadth B is 16 m.

For the bottom slamming calculation, confirm whether the slamming strengthening requirement is triggered, compute PSL at the stated cross-section (using TF = TF-f = 2.8 m), and determine the minimum required double bottom height hDB for this vessel. State the units of all results and identify any applicable upper limits on the parameters used.
required_facts: Bottom slamming strengthening is required because L = 95 m > 65 m and TF-f = 2.8 m < 0.045 × 95 = 4.275 m
BB must be capped at 3.78 m (= 1.35 × TF = 1.35 × 2.8) because the actual bottom breadth of 9.5 m exceeds this limit
x is taken as x1 ≈ 25.24 m (not 22 m) because the cross-section at 22 m aft of FE is forward of the minimum x1 limit
PSL ≈ 925 kN/m² (acceptable range 900–950 kN/m²) at the cross-section considered
The minimum required double bottom height hDB = 800 mm, calculated as 1000 × B/20 = 1000 × 16/20
hDB = 800 mm satisfies the minimum of 760 mm and is below the 2000 mm upper cap

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch10.Sec2 triggers bottom slamming check and references Ch.1 Sec.4 for symbol definitions (including L, B, CB, TF); the double bottom height formula in Pt3.Ch2.Sec3 [2.3] also references Ch.1 Sec.4 for the symbol B, and the compartment arrangement rules in Ch.2 Sec.3 supply the hDB formula needed to answer the second part of the question.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Check slamming applicability (Pt3.Ch10.Sec2 [1.1.1]): L = 95 m > 65 m ✓. Threshold draught = 0.045 × 95 = 4.275 m. TF-f = 2.8 m < 4.275 m ✓. Both conditions met, so bottom slamming strengthening is required.

Step 2 — Resolve symbols via Ch.1 Sec.4: L = ship length (m), B = moulded breadth (m), CB = block coefficient, TF = design slamming draught (m), x = longitudinal distance from FE (m). These are defined in Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 2 and associated definitions.

Step 3 — Compute PSL at x = 22 m (Pt3.Ch10.Sec2 [2.1.1]):
  c1: L = 95 ≤ 150, so c1 = L^(1/3) = 95^(1/3) ≈ 4.563
  c2 = 1675 × (1 − 20×TF/L) = 1675 × (1 − 20×2.8/95) = 1675 × (1 − 0.5895) = 1675 × 0.4105 ≈ 687.6
  x1 = [1.2 − CB^(1/3) − L/2500] × L = [1.2 − 0.72^(1/3) − 95/2500] × 95
     CB^(1/3) = 0.72^(1/3) ≈ 0.8963
     x1 = [1.2 − 0.8963 − 0.038] × 95 = [0.2657] × 95 ≈ 25.24 m
  Since x = 22 m < x1 = 25.24 m, use x = x1 = 25.24 m in the formula.
  BB check: 1.35 × TF = 1.35 × 2.8 = 3.78 m; 0.55 × √L = 0.55 × √95 = 0.55 × 9.747 ≈ 5.36 m. Smaller of these = 3.78 m. Actual BB = 9.5 m > 3.78 m, so BB is capped at 3.78 m.
  CB check: CB = 0.72 ≤ 0.75, so no cap on TF from that clause.
  PSL = (c1 × c2 / TF) × BB × (0.56 − L/1250 − x/L)
       = (4.563 × 687.6 / 2.8) × 3.78 × (0.56 − 95/1250 − 25.24/95)
       = (3136.5 / 2.8) × 3.78 × (0.56 − 0.076 − 0.2657)
       = 1120.2 × 3.78 × 0.2183
       ≈ 1120.2 × 0.8252
       ≈ 924.5 kN/m²

Step 4 — Double bottom height (Pt3.Ch2.Sec3 [2.3]): hDB = 1000 × B/20 = 1000 × 16/20 = 800 mm. Minimum is 760 mm (800 > 760 ✓). Maximum cap is 2000 mm (800 < 2000 ✓). Therefore hDB = 800 mm.

question_text:
A shipyard is preparing the design submission package for a new 180-metre bulk carrier. The hull structural drawings include welding details for the cargo hold region, and the designer intends to use high-strength steel with a specified minimum yield stress of 315 N/mm² for the abutting plates in several tee-joint connections. The weld deposit yield strength selected is 375 N/mm². The designer also plans to use an alternative laser welding method in certain locations rather than conventional electric-arc welding.

As part of the class submission, the designer must determine: (1) which specific drawing types and documentation must be submitted to the Society for approval versus for information only, covering the hull structural design; and (2) whether the use of laser welding as an alternative to electric-arc welding is permissible under the rules, and if so, under what condition. Identify the documentation requirements that apply to this hull structural design submission and state the condition under which the alternative welding method may be accepted.
required_facts: The documents to be submitted for weld design are specified in Ch.1 Sec.3 (cross-reference from Ch.13 Sec.1 [1.3.1])
Table 1 in Ch.1 Sec.3 applies to Ch.1 through Ch.13 and lists the required hull structural documentation
H050 structural drawings (decks, bulkheads, fore ship, engine room, aft ship) must be submitted for approval (AP)
H010 structural design brief, H020 design load plan, and H030 tank and capacity plan are submitted for information (FI)
Alternative welding methods such as laser welding are permissible but will be specially considered by the Society
The high-strength steel with ReH = 315 N/mm² falls in the 265–355 range, so ReH_weld = 375 N/mm² is the correct minimum weld deposit yield strength

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [1.3.1] states that documents to be submitted are specified in Ch.1 Sec.3. Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [1.2] states that alternative methods such as laser welding will be specially considered.
