The answerer must follow the cross-reference from Ch.13 to Ch.1 Sec.3 to find Table 1, which lists the specific documentation types (H010, H020, H030, H050 series) and their AP (approval) or FI (for information) status.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Read Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [1.3.1] — it says 'The documents to be submitted are specified in Ch.1 Sec.3.' This is the cross-reference trigger. Step 2: Navigate to Pt3.Ch1.Sec3 [2.2.1] and Table 1, which lists documentation requirements applicable for Ch.1 to Ch.13. Step 3: From Table 1, identify that for ship hull structure the required submissions include: H010 Structural design brief (FI), H020 Design load plan (FI), H030 Tank and capacity plan (FI), and H050 Structural drawings for decks/inner bottom, transverse bulkheads, longitudinal bulkheads, fore ship, engine room area, and aft ship — all marked AP (for approval). Step 4: Return to Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [1.2] — alternative methods such as laser welding 'will be specially considered', meaning they are permissible but require special consideration by the Society rather than automatic acceptance.

question_text: A ro-ro vessel has a car deck fitted with transverse girders supporting wheel loads from heavy road transporters. Each transporter has a maximum axle load of 22 t. The transverse girders span 4.8 m between web frames and are spaced 2.4 m apart. The girders are simply supported at both ends (no end fixity). A structural engineer proposes using a permissible stress coefficient of 0.70 for the girder scantling check under the at-sea load condition. The design load set for this condition is classified as AC-II. Is the proposed permissible stress coefficient acceptable for sizing the section modulus of these primary supporting members, and what value should be used if it is not?
required_facts: The permissible stress coefficient Cs = 0.70 applies only to AC-I load sets
For AC-II (and AC-III) load sets, Cs = 0.85 must be used for section modulus sizing
The proposed value of 0.70 is not acceptable for an AC-II design load set
The correct permissible stress coefficient to use is Cs = 0.85
The allowable stress criteria for vehicle-load girders are governed by the primary supporting member rules, not the wheel-load chapter alone

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch10.Sec5 [3.3.1] states that allowable stresses for girders supporting vehicle loads are as given in Ch.6 Sec.6 [2.2]. Ch.6 Sec.6 [2.1.1] defines the permissible stress coefficient Cs: 0.70 for AC-I, and 0.85 for AC-II and AC-III. Since the design load set is AC-II, the correct Cs is 0.85, not 0.70.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Pt3.Ch10.Sec5 [3.3.1] specifies that scantlings of girders for vehicle loads shall be specially considered based on the most severe condition, and that allowable stresses are as given in Ch.6 Sec.6 [2.2]. Step 2: Navigate to Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 [2.1.1], which gives the section modulus formula for primary supporting members and defines Cs: Cs = 0.70 for AC-I, Cs = 0.85 for AC-II and AC-III. Step 3: The at-sea load condition is classified as AC-II, so Cs = 0.85 must be used. The proposed value of 0.70 (which applies only to AC-I) is therefore not acceptable.

question_text: A structural engineer is sizing longitudinal stiffeners on the inner bottom of a bulk carrier. The stiffeners are supported by transverse floors spaced 2.4 m apart (full length ℓ = 2.4 m). The stiffener spacing s = 750 mm. At one end, a bracket is fitted to the free edge of the stiffener with an effective bracket arm of 180 mm, reducing the bending span. At the other end, no bracket is fitted. The stiffener web makes an angle of 80° with the attached plating. For the structural idealisation, the engineer needs to determine: (1) the effective bending span ℓ_bdg to use in strength calculations, (2) the maximum permissible effective shear span ℓ_shr, and (3) the correct symbol to use for the density of seawater when computing hydrostatic pressure on the inner bottom plating. What are the correct values and symbol?
required_facts: ℓ_bdg = 2.4 m because a bracket fitted on one side only of the PSM does not reduce the effective bending span
Maximum permissible ℓ_shr = 2.025 m, derived from ℓ − s/2000 = 2.4 − 750/2000
φ_w is taken as 90° because the actual angle (80°) is greater than or equal to 75°
The seawater density symbol is ρ, found by following the cross-reference from the Sec.7 Symbols preamble to Ch.1 Sec.4
ρ = 1.025 t/m³ as defined in the primary symbols table

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 defines structural idealisation of stiffeners including effective bending and shear spans, and its Symbols section explicitly defers to Ch.1 Sec.4 for symbols not defined locally — the answerer must follow that cross-reference to find the seawater density symbol ρ and its value.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Effective bending span (Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [1.1.2]): The bracket is fitted to the free edge on one side only. Per [1.1.2], in single skin structures a bracket on one side only means the effective bending span is taken as the total span between PSMs. Therefore ℓ_bdg = ℓ = 2.4 m (bracket on one side only does not reduce the bending span). Step 2 — Effective shear span (Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [1.1.4]): The upper bound formula applies regardless of support detail: ℓ_shr ≤ ℓ − s/2000 = 2.4 − 750/2000 = 2.4 − 0.375 = 2.025 m. The bracket on the free edge may further reduce ℓ_shr, but the maximum permissible value is 2.025 m. Step 3 — Web angle: φ_w = 80° which is ≥ 75°, so per the Symbols section of Pt3.Ch3.Sec7, φ_w shall be taken equal to 90°. Step 4 — Seawater density symbol: The Symbols section of Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 states 'For symbols not defined in this section, see Ch.1 Sec.4.' Seawater density is not defined in Sec.7's local symbol list, so the engineer must go to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 1, which defines ρ = density of seawater = 1.025 t/m³.

question_text: A general cargo vessel has a moulded length of 82 m, a maximum deadweight of 2,800 tonnes, and a maximum displacement of 5,200 tonnes at scantling draught. The ship is classed as a category II vessel. The designer is preparing the loading guidance documentation package and wants to confirm whether a loading manual that addresses longitudinal strength is required for this ship. Additionally, the designer needs to confirm which symbols and definitions govern the calculation of still water bending moments and shear forces referenced in that loading manual. Is a longitudinal-strength loading manual required for this vessel, and what standard symbol set applies to the permissible still water bending moment and shear force limits stated in the manual?
required_facts: The exemption from a longitudinal-strength loading manual for category II ships requires BOTH length less than 90 m AND maximum deadweight not exceeding 30% of maximum displacement.
The deadweight-to-displacement ratio for this vessel is approximately 53.8% (2,800 / 5,200), which exceeds the 30% threshold.
Because the 30% deadweight/displacement condition is not met, the exemption does not apply and a loading manual addressing longitudinal strength IS required.
The permissible still water bending moment limit uses symbol M (units kNm) and the shear force limit uses symbol Q (units kN), as defined in the primary symbols table.

The symbol set governing still water bending moments and shear forces in the loading manual is the same symbol set used for external sea pressure load calculations (P in kN/m², with ρ = 1.025 t/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s²).
The ship's 82 m length alone would satisfy the length condition (< 90 m), but the deadweight ratio condition is the binding constraint that triggers the requirement.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec5 [1.1.2] states that a longitudinal-strength loading manual is not required for a category II ship with length less than 90 m where maximum deadweight does not exceed 30% of maximum displacement. That same clause cross-references Sec4 [3.1.7] for the category II exemption condition. The loading manual content requirements (Sec5 [2.1.1]) reference permissible still water bending moment and shear force limits, whose symbols (M, Q) are defined in Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [1.1.1] Table 1. The external load expressions used in hull strength calculations (including the sea pressure formula in Pt3.Ch4.Sec5 [1.1]) rely on those same symbol definitions.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Start at the loading manual application clause (Pt3.Ch1.Sec5 [1.1.2]): it states that a loading manual considering longitudinal strength is NOT required for a category II ship with length less than 90 m where maximum deadweight does not exceed 30% of maximum displacement. Step 2 — Check the numeric threshold: ship length = 82 m < 90 m threshold. Deadweight ratio = 2,800 / 5,200 = 53.8%, which EXCEEDS the 30% limit. Therefore the exemption does NOT apply, and a longitudinal-strength loading manual IS required. Step 3 — The exemption condition cross-references Sec4 [3.1.7] for the category II definition and the deadweight/displacement ratio criterion. Step 4 — The loading manual must state permissible limits of still water bending moments (M, kNm) and shear forces (Q, kN) as defined in Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 1 (primary symbols). Step 5 — The external sea pressure loads (P, kN/m²) used in hull strength assessment are defined in Pt3.Ch4.Sec5 [1.1], and the symbols used there (P, M, Q, ρ, g, T_LC, etc.) are all drawn from the same Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 symbol table.

question_text: A bulk carrier of length 160 m and breadth 28 m is fitted with an anchor windlass on the forecastle deck. The forecastle deck is located 14 m above the summer load waterline. The windlass is positioned 32 m aft of the forward perpendicular. A chain stopper is provided. The minimum breaking strength (BS) of the chain cable is 1 800 kN. The ship has a block coefficient CB = 0.82, a metacentric height GM = 0.07B, and operates without service restriction (R0). The windlass foundation is a custom fabricated steel pedestal (not selected from an accepted industry standard) and the designer proposes to use a net scantling approach for the strength check. The ship's scantling draught TSC = 11.0 m and the loading condition draught TLC = 9.5 m. The vertical position of the windlass centre of gravity is z = 16.5 m above the keel, and the ship's rotation centre R is to be determined from the draught values. For the green sea load case, the projected area of the windlass normal to the shaft axis is Ax = 3.2 m² and parallel to the shaft axis is Ay = 1.8 m², with a shape factor f = 1.0. The designer intends to assess the foundation strength using beam theory. Determine: (1) the design load to be applied to the windlass foundation for the anchoring operation load case, (2) whether the green sea load case applies to this windlass installation and, if so, the two independent green sea forces Px and Py, (3) the permissible normal stress and shear stress for the beam theory strength assessment, expressed in terms of the material yield stress ReH, and (4) the envelope transverse acceleration ay-env acting at the windlass location, given that the roll acceleration aroll is to be computed using the standard motion formulas for the ship's parameters.
required_facts: Anchoring design load for windlass with chain stopper = 45% of BS = 810 kN
Green sea load case applies because forecastle deck height (14 m) is less than min(0.1L, 22 m) = 16 m above summer load waterline and windlass is within forward 0.25L of a ship ≥ 80 m
Green sea force normal to shaft axis Px = 640 kN
Green sea force parallel to shaft axis Py = 270 kN
Permissible normal stress (beam theory) = 1.0 ReH
Permissible shear stress (beam theory) = 0.6 ReH
Envelope transverse acceleration ay-env must be derived from Pt3.Ch4.Sec3 [3.3.2] using aroll-y = aroll × (z − R) and the envelope combination ay-env = sqrt(asway^2 + (g sinθ + aroll-y)^2)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The windlass supporting structure section (Pt3.Ch11.Sec2) specifies anchoring design loads, green sea applicability criteria, and acceptance criteria referencing corrosion addition from Ch.3 Sec.3. For the envelope transverse acceleration needed to characterise dynamic loads on the foundation, the answerer must follow the cross-reference to Pt3.Ch4.Sec3 [3.3.2] to compute ay-env = sqrt((aroll-y)^2 + (0.5*g*sin(theta))^2) at the windlass location, using the roll motion parameters derived from the ship's GM and roll period.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Anchoring load: Chain stopper is provided, so per [2.3.1](a) the windlass design load = 45% × BS = 0.45 × 1800 = 810 kN. Step 2 — Green sea applicability: Per [2.5.1], the requirement applies when (i) windlass is on an exposed deck over the forward 0.25L, (ii) ship length ≥ 80 m, and (iii) deck height < min(0.1L, 22 m) above summer load waterline. Here 0.25L = 40 m; windlass is at 32 m aft of FP, so within forward 0.25L. Ship length 160 m ≥ 80 m. Threshold = min(0.1×160, 22) = min(16, 22) = 16 m. Forecastle deck is at 14 m < 16 m, so green sea load case APPLIES. Px = 200 × Ax = 200 × 3.2 = 640 kN; Py = 150 × Ay × f = 150 × 1.8 × 1.0 = 270 kN. Step 3 — Acceptance criteria per [2.4.2](a): Normal stress ≤ 1.0 ReH; Shear stress ≤ 0.6 ReH. Step 4 — Envelope transverse acceleration: Navigate to Pt3.Ch4.Sec3 [3.3.2]. aroll-y = aroll × (z − R). First compute R = min(D/4 + TLC/2, D/2). Assuming D ≈ TSC + freeboard; with the given data the answerer uses R = min(D/4 + 9.5/2, D/2). Then compute roll period Tθ = 2.3π×kr/sqrt(g×GM) with kr = 0.39B = 0.39×28 = 10.92 m, GM = 0.07×28 = 1.96 m; Tθ = 2.3π×10.92/sqrt(9.81×1.96) ≈ 56.5 s. Roll angle θ from formula. aroll = (π/Tθ)^2 × θ_rad × (z−R). ay-env = sqrt(aroll-y^2 + (0.5g sinθ)^2) per [3.3.2].

question_text:
A bulk carrier of 185 m rule length is being designed with large deck openings (the total breadth of hatchways exceeds 70% of the ship's breadth). The strength deck has a series of cargo hatchways, and the designer proposes a hatch corner arrangement where the corner plate has a gross thickness of 18 mm, while the adjacent longitudinal deck girder plate has a gross thickness of 22 mm. The hatch corner is located at a longitudinal position of x/L = 0.55 from the aft perpendicular, and the relevant cross deck strip breadth (bQ) is 3.2 m. The longitudinal deck girder breadth alongside the hatchway (bL) is 2.8 m. The hatch corner plate material has a yield stress of 355 N/mm² (material factor k = 0.72). A stiffener web passes through the hatch corner region and is knuckled within its span; the designer has not fitted any tripping bracket or equivalent support at the knuckle. Additionally, the internal deck plating panels between hatchways have a stiffener spacing of 680 mm and are fabricated from steel with ReH = 235 N/mm². The ship's length is 185 m.

(a) Is the omission of tripping brackets at the knuckled stiffener web compliant with the structural detailing requirements, and what specific support arrangements are mandatory?
(b) For the internal deck plating panels between hatchways, what is the minimum net plate thickness required to satisfy the slenderness requirement, and which slenderness coefficient C applies?
(c) For the hatch corner on the strength deck at x/L = 0.55, what is the minimum required corner radius r (in metres), using the HC2 corner type formula (corner between a transverse deck strip and a closed area), and is the proposed corner plate thickness arrangement acceptable given the ratio tD/ti?
required_facts: The omission of tripping brackets at the knuckled stiffener web is non-compliant; a tripping bracket or equivalent must be fitted both to support the face plate and to support the knuckled web section.

For internal deck plating panels on a ship of L = 185 m (≥ 90 m), the applicable slenderness coefficient C = 100 for strength deck plating, giving a minimum net plate thickness of tp ≥ 680/100 = 6.8 mm.

The ship qualifies as having large deck openings, which triggers the requirement to apply the hatch corner radius formula from the bulk carrier/large-opening rules rather than the general rules alone.
For the HC2 hatch corner type, c1 = 0.4 × bQ = 0.4 × 3.2 = 1.28 m, and the minimum radius r_min = 0.15 m applies for strength deck corners.

The plate thickness ratio tD/ti = 22/18 ≈ 1.22 exceeds the upper limit of 1.0 specified in the hatch corner formula, meaning the corner plate arrangement is not acceptable and the corner plate thickness must be increased to at least equal the adjacent deck girder plate thickness (22 mm).
The fD coefficient for the strength deck at L = 185 m is fD = 0.25 + 185/2000 = 0.3425, and at x/L = 0.55 the distribution factor cs = 1.0.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Starting from weld design and structural detailing in Pt3.Ch13, the chain passes through slenderness requirements in Pt3.Ch8.Sec2, then detail design rules for knuckles and hatch corners in Pt3.Ch3.Sec6, which explicitly cross-references Pt5.Ch2 for ships with large deck openings, landing at the hatch corner radius formula in Pt5.Ch2.Sec2 [2.1.1].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 (Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 → Pt3.Ch8.Sec2): The structural design of the deck panels requires checking slenderness. Pt3.Ch8.Sec2 Table 1 gives slenderness coefficient C for plate panels. For a ship of L = 185 m (≥ 90 m), internal structures with more than three continuous decks (except tank/watertight boundaries) use C = 175; however, the cross-deck strip between hatchways is classified as 'other structures not mentioned above' or strength deck plating, so C = 100 applies for outer shell including strength deck for L ≥ 90 m. The minimum net plate thickness is tp ≥ b/C = 680/100 = 6.8 mm. Step 2 (Pt3.Ch8.Sec2 → Pt3.Ch3.Sec6): Pt3.Ch8.Sec2 [1.1] notes that requirements may reference Sec.3 and Sec.4, and the detail design rules in Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 govern knuckles and hatch corners. Per Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [2.1.1(g)], when a stiffener or primary supporting member is knuckled within the length of the span, effective support shall be provided by fitting a tripping bracket or equivalent for the face plate and for the knuckled web section. The omission of tripping brackets is therefore non-compliant. Step 3 (Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 → Pt5.Ch2.Sec2): Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [7.3.5] states that for ships with large deck openings, hatch corners shall be specially considered per Pt.5 Ch.1 and Pt.5 Ch.2. This triggers the cross-volume reference. In Pt5.Ch2.Sec2 [2.1.1], for HC2 corner type: c1 = 0.4 × bQ = 0.4 × 3.2 = 1.28 m. The fD coefficient for the strength deck: fD = 0.25 + L13/2000 = 0.25 + 185/2000 = 0.25 + 0.0925 = 0.3425. At x/L = 0.55 (within 0.3 ≤ x/L < 0.7), cs = 1.0. The c2 coefficient requires MT, Iy-gr, zD, zO which are ship-specific; the question focuses on the c1 component and the minimum radius. r_min = 0.15 m for strength deck corners. So r ≥ c1 · c2 with r ≥ 0.15 m. For the HC2 formula, r ≥ 0.4 × bQ = 1.28 m (before c2 scaling), but c2 modifies this based on bending moment and section properties. The plate thickness ratio check: tD/ti = 22/18 = 1.222, but the rule requires 1.0 ≥ tD/ti ≥ 0.65, meaning ti must be ≥ tD. Here tD/ti = 22/18 > 1.0, which violates the upper bound of the ratio constraint, making the arrangement non-compliant as the corner plate is thinner than the adjacent deck girder plate beyond the permitted ratio.

question_text: A newbuild 310-metre container ship (class notation 'Container ship') is being designed with upper deck plating and hatch side coaming fabricated from NV 47 steel. The hatch coaming plates have an as-built thickness of 68 mm. During the design review, the shipyard proposes to apply ISO 5817 quality level C welding throughout the entire upper hull longitudinal structure, arguing that this meets the general minimum standard. The fatigue engineer also notes that the bottom plating welds are specified to ISO 5817 level C. A separate concern is raised about the coaming top plate longitudinals, which are also 68 mm NV 47 material — the shipyard asks whether these members fall within the scope of the thick-plate regime and whether any additional measures beyond the standard brittle crack arrest design are triggered. Assess whether the proposed ISO 5817 level C welding quality is acceptable for the upper hull longitudinal structure of this vessel, identify which structural members are covered by the thick-plate requirements, and state what additional requirement is triggered by the choice of NV 47 material at 68 mm thickness.
required_facts: ISO 5817 level C is NOT acceptable for the upper hull longitudinal structure of a container ship; ISO 5817 level B is required within 0.4L amidships

The definition of upper hull longitudinal structural members includes the uppermost strake of longitudinal bulkhead, sheer strake, upper deck, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate, and all attached longitudinals
The coaming top plate longitudinals at 68 mm NV 47 fall within the thick-plate regime (thickness >50 mm and ≤100 mm, NV 47 steel, Container ship notation)

The thick-plate section applies to Container ship notation vessels with NV 36, NV 40, and NV 47 steel plates of thickness exceeding 50 mm but not greater than 100 mm in upper hull longitudinal structural members
Because NV 47 material is used, the additional requirements (beyond standard brittle crack arrest design) specified for NV 47 application are triggered
Bottom plating welds at ISO 5817 level C are acceptable (the level B requirement applies only to the upper hull longitudinal structure)

annotator_grounding.start_clause: Pt3.Ch9.Sec5 [1] (special consideration for fatigue, innovative or specific ship types)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Fatigue workmanship rules (Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2]) require ISO 5817 level B for container ships in the upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships; that clause cross-references Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3] to define which members are 'upper hull longitudinal structural members'; Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.1] triggers the thick-plate regime for NV 47 plates >50 mm and ≤100 mm; [1.1.2] then requires the additional measures in [3] when NV 47 material is used; Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 confirms the Container ship notation scope.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2]: The general minimum is ISO 5817 level C for all ship types, BUT for container ships the upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships must meet ISO 5817 level B. The shipyard's proposal of level C for the upper hull is therefore non-compliant for this container ship. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2] references Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3] to define 'upper hull longitudinal structural members': these are the uppermost strake of longitudinal bulkhead, sheer strake, upper deck, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate, and all attached longitudinals. The coaming top plate longitudinals at 68 mm NV 47 are explicitly included. Step 3 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.1]: The thick-plate section applies to Container ship notation vessels with plates of NV 36/40/47 steel, thickness >50 mm and ≤100 mm, in upper hull longitudinal structural members. At 68 mm the coaming and coaming top plate longitudinals fall squarely within scope. Step 4 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.2]: Where NV 47 material is applied per [1.1.1], the additional requirements of [3] (brittle crack arrest design measures beyond the standard options) shall also be applied. This is an extra obligation on top of the standard brittle crack arrest design required for all thick-plate members. Step 5 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.3]: Confirms the vessel qualifies as a Container ship (cell guides, fixed container foundations, fixed lashing appliances), so all the above applies.

question_text:
A newbuild container ship (170 m in length, class notation 'Container ship') is being designed with bilge keels. The bilge keel is of closed type and is attached to the bilge strake. A ground bar is fitted between the shell plate and the bilge keel. At the bilge keel ends, the ground bar and bilge keel web are tapered with a ratio of 4:1. The upper hull longitudinal structural members — specifically the hatch side coaming — are fabricated from NV 47 steel with an as-built plate thickness of 65 mm. The designer proposes to use fillet welds at the bilge keel end-to-ground-bar connection with a leg length of 6 mm, and the abutting plate (ground bar) has an as-built thickness of 10 mm. No brittle crack arrest measures have been incorporated into the cargo hold region for the hatch coaming structure.

(a) Are the bilge keel end tapering and welding arrangements compliant with the applicable rules for a ship of this length?
(b) What is the minimum fillet weld gap allowance (t_gap) that must be used when sizing the fillet weld at the bilge keel end connection, given the ground bar as-built thickness?
(c) Is the omission of brittle crack arrest measures for the hatch coaming acceptable, and what is the basis for that determination?
required_facts: The 4:1 tapering ratio at the bilge keel ends is compliant because the minimum required ratio is 3:1 for ships longer than 150 m.
The welding requirements for the bilge keel end connection are governed by the weld joint design rules referenced from the bilge keel section.
With a ground bar as-built thickness of 10 mm (between 6 mm and 12 mm), the minimum fillet weld gap allowance t_gap must be determined by linear interpolation, yielding approximately 1.67 mm.
The ship's 'Container ship' class notation brings the thick steel plate requirements into scope for upper hull longitudinal structural members.
The hatch side coaming fabricated from NV 47 steel at 65 mm thickness falls within the 50–100 mm range and triggers mandatory brittle crack arrest measures.
Omission of brittle crack arrest measures (Option A or Option B) in the cargo hold region for the hatch coaming is not acceptable under the applicable rules.
The material grade selection for thick plates must also comply with the material grade selection rules referenced within the thick plate section.

annotator_grounding.end_clause: Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [5.1] (weld gap allowance); Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [3.2.4] (brittle crack arrest table); Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.1] and [1.4.1] (container ship notation scope)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch11.Sec4 bilge keel end requirements reference Ch.13 Sec.1 [5.1] for welding; Ch.13 Sec.1 defines t_gap for fillet welds based on as-built thickness. Separately, the container ship class notation (established in Pt5.Ch2.Sec1) triggers Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 for thick NV 47 plates, which mandates brittle crack arrest measures via Table 1 thresholds.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt3.Ch11.Sec4 [1.2.3]: Ship is 170 m > 150 m, so additional requirements apply. Tapering ratio of 4:1 satisfies the minimum 3:1 requirement. Welding requirements are directed to Ch.13 Sec.1 [5.1]. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [5.1] (weld gap allowance symbol definition): Ground bar as-built thickness = 10 mm, which falls in the range 6.0 mm < t_as-built < 12.0 mm, so t_gap is determined by linear interpolation between 1.0 mm (at 6 mm) and 2.0 mm (at 12 mm). At 10 mm: t_gap = 1.0 + (10-6)/(12-6) × (2.0-1.0) = 1.0 + 0.667 = 1.667 mm ≈ 1.67 mm. Step 3 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.1]/[1.4.1]: The ship has the class notation 'Container ship', which brings Pt5.Ch2 into scope. Step 4 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.1]: Section applies to Container ship notation with thick plates (50 mm < t ≤ 100 mm) of NV 36, NV 40, or NV 47 for upper hull longitudinal structural members. Hatch side coaming at 65 mm NV 47 qualifies. Step 5 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [3.2.4] (Table 1 threshold check): NV 47 at 65 mm exceeds the threshold in Table 1 for the hatch coaming structure, so brittle crack arrest measures (Option A or Option B) are mandatory within the cargo hold region. Omission is not acceptable.

question_text: A 9,500 TEU container ship (L = 320 m, B = 48.2 m, CB = 0.65, CWL = 0.82) is being designed with containers stowed on deck using cross lashings. The designer proposes to use upper corner castings instead of lower corner castings for attaching single lashing rods. The loading manual currently includes only two seagoing conditions: a homogeneous full-load departure condition and a ballast arrival condition. The ship's approved trim and stability booklet specifies a minimum GM of 0.45 m at the scantling draught; the container securing arrangement plan lists a single GM value of 0.42 m for that draught. Is the proposed lashing attachment arrangement acceptable, and is the set of loading conditions in the loading manual sufficient for classification? Identify any deficiencies and state what corrections are required.
required_facts: Using upper corner castings for single lashings requires a reduction in allowable lashing loads per the applicable guidance; without applying that reduction the arrangement is non-compliant.
The GM value in the container securing arrangement plan (0.42 m) is less than the minimum GM in the approved trim and stability booklet (0.45 m), which is not permitted.
Each seagoing design loading condition must be evaluated at both departure and arrival; the loading manual is missing the full-load arrival condition and the ballast departure condition.
The standard container-ship loading conditions (homogeneous full load and ballast) are required in the loading manual and are present, but are incomplete without both departure and arrival variants.

Three corrections are required: (1) apply reduced allowable lashing loads or revert to lower corner castings, (2) update the securing plan GM to ≥ 0.45 m, (3) add the missing departure/arrival loading condition variants to the loading manual.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Pt5.Ch2.Sec8 container securing rules: upper corner casting lashing triggers an allowable load reduction per DNV-CG-0060 Sec.3 [2], and the GM in the securing plan must not be less than the minimum GM in the approved stability booklet. The loading conditions requirement in Sec8 [1.1.1] references Sec3 [3.1.1], which in turn requires compliance with the standard loading conditions of Pt3.Ch4.Sec8 [1.1.1] — meaning both departure and arrival conditions are needed for each design loading condition, and the container-ship-specific conditions (homogeneous full load and ballast) must also be present.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Lashing attachment (Pt5.Ch2.Sec8 [2.3.4]): Single lashings must be fitted to lower corner castings. If upper corner castings are used instead, the allowable lashing loads shall be decreased per DNV-CG-0060 Sec.3 [2]. The question does not state that reduced allowable loads have been applied, so the arrangement as described (upper castings, no load reduction applied) is non-compliant. Correction: either revert to lower corner castings, or apply the required reduction to allowable lashing loads and re-verify the strength evaluation.

Step 2 — GM value in securing plan (Pt5.Ch2.Sec8 [1.1.1]): The container securing arrangement plan must include at least one GM value, and that GM shall not be less than the minimum GM in the approved trim and stability booklet for the respective draught. The plan lists GM = 0.42 m, but the booklet minimum is 0.45 m. This is non-compliant; the plan must be corrected to use GM ≥ 0.45 m.

Step 3 — Loading conditions (Pt5.Ch2.Sec8 [1.1.1] → Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [3.1.1] and [3.1.2]): The container securing arrangement plan must comply with the strength evaluation per Sec8 [8.1], and the standard design loading conditions per Sec3 [3.1.1] must be considered in addition to those in Pt3.Ch4.Sec8 [1.1.1]. Sec3 [3.1.2] requires the loading manual to include homogeneous cargo loading at maximum draught and ballast loading conditions — both present. However, Pt3.Ch4.Sec8 [1.1.1] requires each design loading condition to be evaluated at both departure and arrival. The loading manual only has a departure full-load condition and an arrival ballast condition; it is missing the full-load arrival condition and the ballast departure condition. Correction: add the missing departure/arrival variants so all four conditions are covered.

question_text:
A 14,000 TEU container ship (L = 366 m, B = 51 m, CB = 0.64, CWL = 0.82) is being designed for unrestricted ocean service. During a harbour loading operation, the ship is in a sagging condition with a calculated still water bending moment of 9,800,000 kNm at the midship section. The vertical wave bending moment at that section for seagoing conditions is 4,200,000 kNm (sagging). The container securing arrangement plan submitted for approval includes a minimum GM value of 0.45 m, while the approved trim and stability booklet specifies a minimum GM of 0.52 m at the corresponding draught. Additionally, the lashing computer installed on board was tested only on the primary nominated computer — the second nominated computer was not tested because it holds a type approval certificate from the manufacturer.

Two compliance questions arise:

1. Is the container securing arrangement plan acceptable as submitted, given the GM values stated above?

2. For the harbour loading condition described, determine whether the still water bending moment of 9,800,000 kNm (sagging) is permissible. The permissible seagoing sagging still water bending moment Msw at midship is 7,500,000 kNm, and the permissible seagoing hogging still water bending moment is 6,800,000 kNm. Show the applicable criterion and state whether the harbour condition is compliant.
required_facts: The container securing arrangement plan is not acceptable because the plan GM of 0.45 m is less than the minimum GM of 0.52 m specified in the approved trim and stability booklet
The lashing computer certification is acceptable because the second nominated computer holds a type approval certificate, so testing on both computers is not required

The permissible harbour/sheltered water sagging bending moment criterion is M_sw-p ≤ f_har-M × M_wv + M_sw, with f_har-M = 0.9 per Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2.3.1] (in lieu of the Pt3.Ch5.Sec2 default f_har = 0.5 for non-container ships)
The permissible harbour sagging bending moment evaluates to 0.9 × 4,200,000 + 7,500,000 = 11,280,000 kNm
The applied harbour sagging moment of 9,800,000 kNm does not exceed the permissible value of 11,280,000 kNm
The harbour loading condition is compliant

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec8 [1.1.1] governs the container securing arrangement plan and requires the GM in the plan to not be less than the minimum GM in the approved trim and stability booklet — this flags the first non-compliance. Sec8 [1.1.2] and [9.6.2] govern lashing computer certification and state that where hardware is type approved, testing on the second nominated computer is not required — this determines the second item is compliant. The harbour bending moment question requires navigating from Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2] (which states hull girder loads for container ships are per Pt.3 Ch.4 except as modified in Sec.3) and then to Pt3.Ch5.Sec2 [1.7], which gives the permissible still water bending moment criterion for harbour/sheltered water operations: Msw-p ≤ (fhar × Mwv + Msw), where fhar = 0.5.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — GM check (Pt5.Ch2.Sec8 [1.1.1]): The plan GM of 0.45 m is less than the booklet minimum of 0.52 m. The rule requires the plan GM shall not be less than the minimum GM in the approved trim and stability booklet. Therefore the plan is NOT acceptable as submitted.

Step 2 — Lashing computer certification (Pt5.Ch2.Sec8 [9.6.2]): The rule states that where the hardware IS type approved, the test need only be carried out on the first nominated computer (not both). Since the second computer holds a type approval certificate, testing only the primary computer is acceptable. This item is compliant.

Step 3 — Harbour bending moment (chain hop to Pt3.Ch5.Sec2 [1.7] via Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2]): Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [1] states loads shall be per Pt.3 Ch.4 except as given in Sec.3. Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2.1] provides guidance on still water loads but the permissible harbour criterion is in Pt3.Ch5.Sec2 [1.7]. The criterion is: Msw-p ≤ fhar × |Mwv| + Msw, where fhar = 0.5 (unless otherwise defined in Pt.5, and Pt.5 Ch.2 does not redefine it). For sagging: Msw-p ≤ 0.5 × 4,200,000 + 7,500,000 = 2,100,000 + 7,500,000 = 9,600,000 kNm. The calculated harbour sagging moment is 9,800,000 kNm > 9,600,000 kNm. Therefore the harbour loading condition is NOT compliant.

question_text:
A newbuild 220-metre container ship is being designed with cell guides in the cargo holds and fixed lashing bridges on the upper deck. During the structural design review, the naval architect proposes using a mixed-material approach for the inner bottom longitudinal stiffeners: the plate flange of each stiffener is fabricated from normal-strength steel with a specified minimum yield stress of 235 N/mm², while the stiffener web is fabricated from high-strength steel with a specified minimum yield stress of 355 N/mm². The design team argues this is acceptable because the plate flange still meets the minimum grade requirements for the ship's length and service area.

For one of these inner bottom longitudinal stiffeners under a loaded container stack, the following parameters apply:
- Net section modulus required by calculation: Z = 480 cm³
- Actual net elastic section modulus: Za = 510 cm³
- The stiffener is an L-profile (unsymmetrical)
- Hull girder longitudinal stress at the load calculation point: σhg = −45 N/mm² (compression)
- Lateral pressure acts on the plate side
- The stiffener has fixed ends
- Effective bending span: ℓbdg = 2.8 m
- Stiffener spacing: s = 0.75 m
- Design pressure: P = 28 kN/m²

Is the proposed mixed-material arrangement for the stiffener flange and web permissible under classification rules, and if an additional yield capacity check of the plate flange is required, what permissible bending stress coefficient Cs applies to this stiffener when computing the minimum required net section modulus? Show your reasoning.
required_facts: The mixed-material arrangement (plate flange at 235 N/mm², web at 355 N/mm²) triggers an additional yield capacity check of the plate flange because the plate flange has a lower minimum yield strength than the connected stiffener web
The requirement for this additional check originates from the materials clause applicable to rolled steels for hull structures (Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.2])
For the additional plate flange check, ReH = 235 N/mm² (the plate flange yield stress) must be used in the section modulus formula, not the web value of 355 N/mm²

The stiffener has fixed ends, hull girder stress is compressive (negative), and lateral pressure acts on the plate side — this combination selects the branch Cs = βs − (αs·σhg/ReH) from Table 3 of the stiffener section modulus requirements
The factor fu = 1.15 applies because the stiffener is an unsymmetrical L-profile
The Cs coefficient is not simply Cs-max; it is reduced due to the compressive hull girder stress combined with pressure on the plate side for a fixed-end stiffener

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Container ship rules (Pt5.Ch2.Sec1) direct undefined terms to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [3] for definitions and symbols. Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 leads to material rules in Pt3.Ch3.Sec1, which at clause 2.1.2 flags that when plate flange yield strength is lower than the connected stiffener/PSM, an additional yield capacity check per Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4] is required. Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.2] then provides the section modulus formula and Table 3 defines the permissible bending stress coefficient Cs for the specific combination of hull girder stress sign, load side, and end fixity.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Entry via Pt5.Ch2.Sec1: The ship is a container ship under Pt5.Ch2. Sec1 [1.5] states that for definitions not defined in that section, see Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [3]. This directs the analyst to the general symbols and definitions chapter for any term or material concept not locally defined.

Step 2 — Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 to Pt3.Ch3.Sec1: Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 provides primary symbols (Table 1) including ReH (specified minimum yield stress). The material-specific rules for rolled steels are in Pt3.Ch3.Sec1. Clause 2.1.2 explicitly states: 'The rules generally assume material in flange and web have the same minimum yield strength. When material in plate flange has a lower minimum yield strength than connected stiffener or PSM, then additional check of yield capacity of plate flange may be required, see Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4].' Since the plate flange is 235 N/mm² and the web is 355 N/mm², this condition is triggered — the mixed-material arrangement is not straightforwardly permissible without the additional check.

Step 3 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.2] → Pt3.Ch6.Sec5 [1.1.4] and [1.1.2]: The cross-reference leads to Ch.6 Sec.5. Clause [1.1.2] gives the section modulus formula Z = (fu |P| s ℓbdg²) / (fbdg Cs ReH). For the additional plate flange check, ReH of the plate flange (235 N/mm²) must be used. Table 3 of Ch.6 Sec.5 defines Cs based on: (a) end fixity — fixed ends apply, (b) sign of hull girder stress — compression (negative σhg = −45 N/mm²), (c) which side lateral pressure acts on — plate side. For a fixed-end stiffener with compression hull girder stress and pressure on the plate side, Table 3 gives Cs = βs − (αs·σhg/ReH), not to exceed Cs-max. The specific numeric value requires reading Table 4 for αs, βs, Cs-max for AC-I/AC-II/AC-III, but the key finding is that Cs is reduced from its maximum value due to the compressive hull girder stress acting on the plate side for a fixed stiffener — this is the formula branch that must be selected from Table 3.

scenario_parameters.ship_type: container ship with cell guides and lashing bridges

question_text:
A 310 m container ship (L = 310 m, B = 48.2 m, CB = 0.65, CWL = 0.88) is being assessed for harbour/sheltered water operations. The ship carries a maximum of 14,000 TEU (each container mass G = 14 t). During a harbour loading sequence, the vertical still water bending moment at the midship section is calculated as 6,800,000 kNm in hogging. The vertical wave bending moment at the same section under seagoing conditions is 4,200,000 kNm in hogging. The hull section modulus at the deck is 42.5 m³ (gross), and the permissible normal stress for the deck material (high-strength steel, ReH = 355 N/mm²) gives a permissible seagoing still water bending moment Msw of 7,500,000 kNm in hogging.

A designer proposes to accept the 6,800,000 kNm harbour hogging moment without further restriction, arguing that harbour operations are less severe than seagoing and no additional check is needed beyond confirming the value is below the seagoing Msw.

Is the proposed harbour bending moment of 6,800,000 kNm acceptable? Show the applicable harbour/sheltered water permissible bending moment limit and state whether the design is compliant.
required_facts: The harbour/sheltered water bending moment check for a container ship must be performed per the rule referencing Pt3 vertical hull girder bending strength, not simply compared to the seagoing Msw alone
The applicable harbour correction factor for container ships is f_har-M = 0.9, not the default f_har = 0.5
The permissible harbour hogging bending moment is Msw-p ≤ Msw + f_har-M × |Mwv| = 7,500,000 + 0.9 × 4,200,000 = 11,280,000 kNm
The proposed harbour moment of 6,800,000 kNm is less than 11,280,000 kNm and is therefore compliant
The designer's reasoning is incorrect — a dedicated harbour bending moment check is mandatory for container ships, and the container-ship-specific correction factor f_har-M = 0.9 must be applied
The wave bending moment Mwv used in the harbour check must be taken with the same sign as the considered still water bending moment (hogging in this case)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2.3.1] directs harbour/sheltered bending moment compliance to Pt3.Ch5.Sec2 [1.7] with a container-ship-specific correction factor f_har-M = 0.9. Pt3.Ch5.Sec2 [1.7] gives the general harbour permissible bending moment formula involving Msw, Mwv, and f_har. The container ship rule overrides the default f_har = 0.5 with f_har-M = 0.9.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Identify the applicable rule for harbour bending moment on a container ship. Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2.3.1] states that the permissible hull girder bending moment for harbour/sheltered operations shall comply with Pt3.Ch5.Sec2 [1.7], applying a correction factor f_har-M = 0.9 (overriding the default f_har = 0.5 from Pt3.Ch5.Sec2 symbols).

Step 2 — Apply Pt3.Ch5.Sec2 [1.7]. The permissible still water bending moment for harbour/sheltered operations in hogging is: Msw-p ≤ Msw + f_har · |Mwv|, where f_har is taken as f_har-M = 0.9 per Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2.3.1].

Step 3 — Compute the limit: Msw-p ≤ 7,500,000 + 0.9 × 4,200,000 = 7,500,000 + 3,780,000 = 11,280,000 kNm.

Step 4 — Compare: The proposed harbour moment is 6,800,000 kNm < 11,280,000 kNm, so the moment is within the permissible limit.

Step 5 — Identify the designer's error: The designer's argument that 'no additional check is needed' is wrong — a specific harbour check IS required per Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2.3.1] referencing Pt3.Ch5.Sec2 [1.7], and the correction factor f_har-M = 0.9 (not the default 0.5) must be used for container ships. However, numerically the proposed value happens to be compliant.

Note: The chain also passes through Pt3.Ch4.Sec3 for the underlying motion/acceleration definitions that feed into the wave bending moment Mwv used in the formula, confirming the cross-volume dependency.

question_text: A new 280-metre container ship is being designed with fixed cell guides at the bulkheads, fixed container foundations on the inner bottom, and fixed lashing appliances on the upper deck. The ship will carry standard ISO containers only — no bulk dry cargo. During the structural design review, the naval architect is sizing a transverse primary supporting member (floor/web frame) in the double-bottom region that is subjected to lateral sea pressure. The member spans 3.6 m between its supports (full length between primary supporting members), with symmetrical brackets fitted to both sides of each supporting web. The brackets reduce the effective bending span by 0.15 m at each end. The PSM spacing S is 3.6 m, the design pressure P at the load calculation point is 85 kN/m², and the member is to be assessed under Assessment Condition AC-I. The hull girder longitudinal stress at this member's location is confirmed to be less than 0.15 R_eH. The steel has a specified minimum yield stress R_eH of 315 N/mm². The attached plating has a net thickness of 14 mm and the PSM web-to-plate angle is 90°. Using load model A (both ends fixed, uniformly distributed load), determine: (a) the effective bending span ℓ_bdg to be used in the section modulus calculation, (b) the minimum required section modulus Z of this primary supporting member, and (c) whether the section modulus requirement at the support positions uses a different bending moment distribution factor than at mid-span, and if so, what value applies at the supports.
required_facts: The effective bending span ℓ_bdg = 3.30 m (full span 3.6 m reduced by 0.15 m bracket deduction at each end, per structural idealisation rules for PSMs with brackets on both sides)
The permissible stress coefficient C_s = 0.70 for AC-I
The bending moment distribution factor at mid-span for load model A is f_bdg = 24.0

The Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 [2.1.1] prescriptive section-modulus formula does not apply to this member because Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 [1.1.2] excludes double-skin primary supporting members and Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [1.3.2] identifies double-bottom floors / web frames as double-skin sections; the section modulus must instead be assessed by direct strength / FE analysis per Ch.6 Sec.6 [1.1.2]

The same exclusion in Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 [1.1.2] applies at the support positions: the f_bdg = 12.0 support-region branch of the [2.1.1] formula does not apply to a double-skin double-bottom PSM; no support-region [2.1.1] requirement can be claimed
The section modulus shall be based on the effective breadth of attached plating b_eff as defined in the structural idealisation section

The [2.1.1] section modulus formula is not applicable here because Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 [1.1.2] excludes double-skin PSMs and Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [1.3.2] classifies double-bottom floors / web frames as double-skin sections, even though the hull-girder longitudinal stress is below 0.15 R_eH

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 establishes that container ship hull rules are supplementary to main class (Pt.3) rules, and directs undefined terms to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [3]. Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 provides the symbol definitions (R_eH, P, S, etc.) needed for the formula. Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 defines the structural idealisation rules for effective bending span of PSMs ([1.1.8]) and effective breadth of attached plating ([1.3.2]), and the procedure for calculating section modulus ([1.4.6]). Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 [2.1.1] gives the section modulus formula Z = 1000|P|S·ℓ_bdg²/(f_bdg·C_s·R_eH) and Table 1 for f_bdg values under load model A.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Establish applicability: The ship has cell guides, fixed foundations, and lashing appliances → qualifies as a Container ship under Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.3]. Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.2] states these rules are supplementary to main class rules (Pt.3). Step 2 — Definitions: Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.5] directs to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [3] for undefined terms; symbols such as R_eH, P, S are defined there. Step 3 — Effective bending span: Per Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [1.1.8] (effective bending span of PSMs), with symmetrical brackets fitted to both sides of the supporting web, the effective bending span ℓ_bdg = 3.6 − 0.15 − 0.15 = 3.30 m. Step 4 — Applicability of [2.1.1]: Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 [1.1.2] states the section modulus requirement in [2.1.1] is NOT applicable for double skin PSMs or for longitudinal PSMs with hull girder stress > 0.15 R_eH. This is a transverse PSM (web frame/floor) and hull girder stress < 0.15 R_eH, so [2.1.1] applies. Step 5 — Section modulus formula: Z = 1000 × |P| × S × ℓ_bdg² / (f_bdg × C_s × R_eH). For AC-I: C_s = 0.70. Load model A, mid-span: f_bdg2 = 24.0 (from Table 1). Z = 1000 × 85 × 3.6 × (3.30)² / (24.0 × 0.70 × 315) = 1000 × 85 × 3.6 × 10.89 / (5292) = 1000 × 3332.34 / 5292 ≈ 629.7 cm³. Step 6 — Support positions: Per Table 1 Note 1 and Note 3, within 0.2·ℓ_bdg from each end (i.e., within 0.2 × 3.30 = 0.66 m of each support), f_bdg = f_bdg1 = f_bdg3 = 12.0 for load model A. However, Note 3 states f_bdg at supports shall not be taken greater than 12, so f_bdg = 12.0 at supports. Z_support = 1000 × 85 × 3.6 × (3.30)² / (12.0 × 0.70 × 315) = 3332340 / 2646 ≈ 1259.4 cm³. The support section modulus requirement is therefore larger (≈1259 cm³) than the mid-span requirement (≈630 cm³), governed by f_bdg = 12 at supports vs f_bdg = 24 at mid-span.

scenario_parameters.ship_type: container ship with cell guides, fixed foundations, lashing appliances
scenario_parameters.PSM_type: transverse primary supporting member (web frame/floor) in double-bottom

question_text:
A newbuild 310-metre container ship is being designed with a class notation 'Container ship'. The structural design team proposes to use extra high strength steel with a specified minimum yield stress of 460 N/mm² (grade A47/D47) for the longitudinal hull girder members amidships. The steel supplier has also offered an alternative grade with a specified minimum yield stress of 500 N/mm² at a competitive price. The design team wants to confirm which of these two steel grades can be used without requiring special case-by-case approval from the classification society.

Additionally, the structural drawings show a deck plate flange with a specified minimum yield stress of 355 N/mm² connected to a longitudinal stiffener web with a specified minimum yield stress of 460 N/mm². The designer claims no additional yield capacity check is needed for the plate flange because the stiffener spacing is within normal limits.

For each of the two steel grades (460 N/mm² and 500 N/mm²), state whether it may be used without special approval, and identify whether the designer's claim about the mixed-yield-strength connection is correct.
required_facts: The 460 N/mm² (A47/D47) extra high strength steel may be used without special case-by-case approval because the ship holds the class notation 'Container ship'
The 500 N/mm² steel grade (ReH > 460 N/mm²) requires case-by-case consideration and cannot be used without special approval from the Society
The rules assume flange and web material have the same minimum yield strength; a lower-yield plate flange connected to a higher-yield stiffener triggers an additional yield capacity check
The designer's claim that no additional check is needed for the mixed-yield connection (355 N/mm² flange / 460 N/mm² stiffener) is incorrect
The 'Container ship' class notation is the gating condition that unlocks use of 460 N/mm² EHS steel; other ship types must seek case-by-case approval even for this grade

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 defines the 'Container ship' class notation and for definitions refers to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [3]; Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 symbols section refers back to Ch.1 Sec.4 for undefined symbols and uses EPP/plate panel definitions that feed into Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.1] and [2.1.2]; Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.5] restricts 460 N/mm² EHS steel to Container ship notation and flags 500 N/mm² as case-by-case; Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.2] requires additional yield capacity check when plate flange has lower yield than connected stiffener or PSM.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.3] and [1.4.1] establish that the ship carries the class notation 'Container ship'. Step 2 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.5] directs the reader to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [3] for definitions not defined locally, confirming the chain leads into Pt3. Step 3 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 symbols preamble states 'For symbols not defined in this section, see Ch.1 Sec.4', and its structural idealisation rules (EPP dimensions [2.1.1]) feed into material grade application checks in Pt3.Ch3.Sec1. Step 4 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.5] states: the application of EHS steel with ReH = 460 N/mm² is LIMITED to ships with the class notation 'Container ship' as defined in Pt.5 Ch.2 — so 460 N/mm² is permitted without special approval for this ship. However, EHS steel with ReH > 460 N/mm² (i.e. the 500 N/mm² grade) will be considered on a case-by-case basis — so it requires special approval. Step 5 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.2] states: the rules generally assume material in flange and web have the same minimum yield strength; when the plate flange has a LOWER minimum yield strength than the connected stiffener or PSM, an additional check of yield capacity of the plate flange MAY be required (see Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4]). The designer's claim is therefore incorrect — the mixed-yield connection (355 N/mm² flange + 460 N/mm² stiffener) does trigger the requirement for an additional yield capacity check of the plate flange.

question_text: A newbuilding 300m container ship has inner bottom plating in a cargo hold. The shipyard proposes an as-built plate thickness of 14.5 mm for this plating. The corrosion addition applicable to this location is 3.0 mm, and the shipyard has declared a voluntary addition (owner's extra margin) of 0.5 mm. The net required thickness calculated from structural analysis is 11.0 mm. Does the proposed scantling comply with the classification rules? Show your derivation of the gross required thickness, the gross offered thickness, and the net offered thickness, and state whether each compliance criterion is satisfied.
required_facts: Gross required thickness t_gr = min(t + tc, 1.25t) = min(14.0, 13.75) = 13.75 mm, rounded to 14.0 mm
Gross offered thickness t_gr_off = t_as_built − t_vol_add = 14.5 − 0.5 = 14.0 mm
Net offered thickness t_off = t_gr_off − tc = 14.0 − 3.0 = 11.0 mm
Compliance criterion: gross offered thickness (14.0 mm) must be ≥ gross required thickness (14.0 mm) — criterion is exactly met
Net offered thickness (11.0 mm) equals the net required thickness (11.0 mm) — criterion is exactly met
The proposed scantling is compliant with the rules, with zero margin on both criteria
The voluntary addition of 0.5 mm is excluded from the gross offered thickness and does not contribute to structural compliance

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 establishes that the container ship rules are supplementary to main class rules and directs to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [3] for definitions; Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 provides the symbol framework used throughout Pt3; Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [2.1.1] defines the elementary plate panel geometry and references Sec.2 for scantling compliance; Pt3.Ch3.Sec2 [1.3.2] contains the actual compliance criteria for gross and net scantlings.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Entry via Pt5.Ch2.Sec1: The ship is a container ship, so Pt5.Ch2 applies. Sec1 [1.2] states these rules are supplementary to main class (Pt3). Sec1 [1.5] directs to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [3] for definitions not defined locally. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [3]: Provides the symbol definitions (t, tc, t_vol_add, t_as_built, t_gr, t_gr_off, t_off) used in the scantling compliance chain. Step 3 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [2.1.1]: Structural idealisation of the elementary plate panel; the section header references Sec.2 for scantling compliance of plating. Step 4 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec2 [1.3.2]: Apply the three formulae and compliance criteria: (a) Gross required thickness: t_gr = min(t + tc ; 1.25t) = min(11.0 + 3.0 ; 1.25 × 11.0) = min(14.0 ; 13.75) = 13.75 mm → rounded to nearest 0.5 mm per [1.3.1] = 14.0 mm. (b) Gross offered thickness: t_gr_off = t_as_built − t_vol_add = 14.5 − 0.5 = 14.0 mm. (c) Net offered thickness: t_off = t_gr_off − tc = 14.0 − 3.0 = 11.0 mm. Compliance check per [1.3.2]: t_gr_off (14.0 mm) ≥ t_gr (14.0 mm) → exactly satisfied, compliant. Net offered thickness t_off (11.0 mm) ≥ net required thickness t (11.0 mm) → exactly satisfied, compliant. Conclusion: the proposed scantling is compliant, but only marginally — there is zero spare margin on both gross and net criteria.

question_text: A newbuilding container ship has a rule length of 310 m, a moulded breadth of 48.2 m, and a contract speed of 23 knots at design draft. The ship is fitted with cell guides, fixed container foundations on the inner bottom, and fixed lashing appliances on the upper deck. During the design review, the naval architect is evaluating the hull girder ultimate strength at a cross-section located at 0.25L from the aft perpendicular. The permissible still water bending moment at that section is 8,400,000 kNm (hogging) and the vertical wave bending moment is 5,200,000 kNm (hogging). The proposed hull cross-section yields a vertical hull girder ultimate bending capacity M_U of 22,500,000 kNm. The cargo holds at this section are empty in the governing loading condition, and the ship does not carry a HC(A), HC(B*), or HC(M) class notation. Does the cross-section satisfy the hull girder ultimate strength criterion in hogging, and what is the governing partial safety factor γ_R that must be applied to M_U?
required_facts: The 0.25L location is a mandatory hull girder ultimate strength check location for container ships with large deck openings
γ_DB = 1.1 for hogging (empty holds but no HC(A)/HC(B*)/HC(M) notation, so the 1.25 factor does not apply)
Allowable moment M_U / γ_R = 22,500,000 / 1.155 ≈ 19,480,000 kNm
The criterion M ≤ M_U / γ_R must be re-checked by comparing M with M_U / γ_R using the Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.6.2]-corrected values of the applied bending moment and γ_R

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The ship qualifies as a container ship under Pt5.Ch2.Sec1, triggering Pt5.Ch2.Sec8 documentation requirements (wave load analysis reference at [4.3.3]), which in turn points to Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 for hull girder strength assessment, which explicitly defers to Pt3.Ch5 and specifies that for container ships the ultimate strength check locations include 0.25L and 0.75L per Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [1.1.2]; the checking criterion and partial safety factors are then applied per Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [2.1.2] and [2.2.1].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.3]: The vessel meets all three criteria (cell guides, fixed foundations, fixed lashing appliances), so it is classified as a container ship and the chapter applies. Step 2 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec8 [4.3.3] (via Sec1 documentation table): The wave load analysis and anti-roll tank documentation references point to Sec.8 [4.3.3], confirming the ship's motion and structural analysis scope. Step 3 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [5]: Hull girder strength shall be carried out in accordance with Pt.3 Ch.5, with Sec.4 specifying additional or replacement requirements. Step 4 — Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [1.1.2]: For container ships with large deck openings, ultimate strength must be checked at or near 0.25L and 0.75L — the 0.25L section is therefore a mandatory check location. Step 5 — Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [2.1.2]: The criterion is M ≤ M_U / γ_R, where γ_R = γ_M × γ_DB. Step 6 — γ_M = 1.1 (general value). Step 7 — γ_DB for hogging: the holds are empty but the ship does NOT carry HC(A), HC(B*), or HC(M), so γ_DB = 1.1 (not 1.25). Step 8 — γ_R = 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.21. Step 9 — Allowable moment = 22,500,000 / 1.21 = 18,595,041 kNm. Step 10 — Applied moment M = γ_S × M_sw-U + γ_W × M_wv = 1.0 × 8,400,000 + 1.2 × 5,200,000 = 8,400,000 + 6,240,000 = 14,640,000 kNm. Step 11 — 14,640,000 ≤ 18,595,041: criterion is satisfied.

question_text: A newbuilding container ship has a rule length of 320 m and a contract speed of 22 knots. The upper deck plating in the cargo hold region amidships is fabricated from NV 47 steel with an as-built thickness of 68 mm. The hatch side coaming plates are also NV 47 with an as-built thickness of 72 mm. During the design review, the structural fabrication quality standard for the upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships is being established. The designer proposes applying ISO 5817 quality level C throughout, citing that this is the standard minimum for all ship types. Is this proposal acceptable for this vessel, and what welding quality level must actually be applied to the upper hull longitudinal structure in the 0.4L amidships region? Additionally, for the hull girder strength assessment of this vessel, what corrosion addition factor α should be used when determining the net offered thickness of the upper deck plating for the buckling capacity check, and what is the applicable one-side corrosion addition tc for the upper deck (exposed to atmosphere)?
required_facts: ISO 5817 quality level C is not acceptable for the upper hull longitudinal structure of this container ship within 0.4L amidships; ISO 5817 quality level B is required

The upper deck plating and hatch side coaming are classified as upper hull longitudinal structural members, which include the upper deck, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate, sheer strake, uppermost strake of longitudinal bulkhead, and attached longitudinals

The NV 47 plates with thickness 68 mm and 72 mm (both >50 mm and ≤100 mm) fall within the scope of the thick steel plate requirements for container ships, reinforcing the level B welding quality requirement
For the hull girder buckling capacity check, the corrosion addition factor α = 1.0
The one-side corrosion addition tc for the upper deck exposed to atmosphere is 1.0 mm
The net offered thickness formula is t_off = t_as_built − t_vol_add − α·tc, with α = 1.0 for buckling capacity

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Pt3.Ch9.Sec5 (special fatigue considerations), which leads to Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2] (workmanship/welding quality), which references Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3] to define 'upper hull longitudinal structural members' for container ships, and separately the hull girder strength assessment for container ships is governed by Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.1] for corrosion addition factors.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2] states that ISO 5817 quality level C is the minimum for all ship types, BUT ISO 5817 quality level B shall be applied to container ships for the upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships and critical areas. Step 2 — The definition of 'upper hull longitudinal structural members' is given by Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3]: it includes the uppermost strake of longitudinal bulkhead, sheer strake, upper deck, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate and all attached longitudinals. The 68 mm NV 47 upper deck and 72 mm NV 47 hatch side coaming both fall within this definition and within the thickness range (>50 mm, ≤100 mm) covered by Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.1]. Therefore the designer's proposal of ISO 5817 level C is NOT acceptable; ISO 5817 level B is required for these members within 0.4L amidships. Step 3 — For the hull girder strength assessment per Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.1.1], the net offered thickness uses α from Table 1. For buckling capacity, α = 1.0. Step 4 — Per Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.1.2] and Table 2, the upper deck exposed to atmosphere has a one-side corrosion addition tc = 1.0 mm. However, Table 2 also notes that container holds have tc = 1.0 mm. The upper deck exposed to atmosphere is tc = 1.0 mm per Table 2.

question_text: A 310 m bulk carrier with large deck openings is being designed with five cargo holds. The strength deck has a series of cargo hatchways, and at one hatch corner located 0.45L from the aft perpendicular, the hatch corner sits between a longitudinal deck strip and a closed area (HC1 type). The longitudinal deck girder alongside the hatchway has a breadth b_L = 2.8 m, and the relevant length of large deck openings forward and aft of the superstructure is 180 m. The rule length L is 310 m. The gross plate thickness of the longitudinal structural member is t_D = 18 mm, and the hatchway corner plate gross thickness is t_i = 16 mm. The gross moment of inertia of the hull section at the hatch corner (without insert plate) is I_y-gr = 980 m⁴, the total longitudinal bending moment at the relevant cross deck strip is M_T = 8,500,000 kNm, the hatchway corner is located at z_D = 22.5 m above baseline, and the neutral axis is at z_O = 10.2 m above baseline. The material factor k_i = 1.0. The designer proposes a hatch corner radius of r = 0.55 m with no insert plate. Evaluate whether this arrangement is compliant, and determine the minimum required corner radius. Additionally, identify what structural detailing requirements apply to the knuckle formed at the hatch coaming-to-deck connection, given that the knuckle is located within 0.6L and the nearest support stiffening is currently 65 mm away from the knuckle line.
required_facts: The minimum required hatch corner radius is approximately r ≥ 1.09 m (from r ≥ c1·c2 ≈ 1.792 × 0.610)
The proposed radius of 0.55 m is non-compliant as it is less than the required minimum
Insert plates are required at the hatch corner because the calculated radius exceeds the proposed radius
The f_D coefficient for the strength deck equals 0.40 (using L13 = 300 m capped value)
The knuckle-to-support-stiffening distance of 65 mm exceeds the 50 mm maximum permitted within 0.6L and is non-compliant
The support stiffening at the knuckle must be repositioned to no more than 50 mm from the knuckle line
The t_D/t_i ratio of 18/16 = 1.125 is capped at 1.0 per the rule constraint

annotator_grounding.start_clause: Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 (structural idealisation context, leading to design load scenario and detail design)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The bulk carrier with large deck openings triggers Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [7.3.5] which directs to Pt5.Ch2 for hatch corner treatment; Pt5.Ch2.Sec2 [2.1.1] provides the hatch corner radius formula referencing hull girder loads from Pt3.Ch8.Sec4 boundary conditions; Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [6.1.4] governs the knuckle detailing at the coaming connection.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify ship type trigger: The vessel is a bulk carrier with large deck openings (L=310m). Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [7.3.5] states that for ships with large deck openings, hatch corners shall be specially considered on the basis of stresses due to longitudinal hull girder bending, torsion and transverse loads, and directs the designer to Pt.5 Ch.1 and Pt.5 Ch.2. Step 2 — Navigate to Pt5.Ch2.Sec2 [2.1.1]: This clause provides the hatch corner radius formula r ≥ c1·c2 with r ≥ r_min. For HC1 type (between longitudinal deck strip and closed area): c1 = (f_D + ℓ/750)·b_L. Compute f_D: for strength deck hatch corners, f_D = 0.25 + L13/2000, where L13 = min(max(L,100),300) = 300 m, so f_D = 0.25 + 300/2000 = 0.25 + 0.15 = 0.40. Then c1 = (0.40 + 180/750)·2.8 = (0.40 + 0.24)·2.8 = 0.64·2.8 = 1.792. Step 3 — Compute c2: c_s at x/L=0.45 (within 0.3≤x/L<0.7) → c_s = 1.0. c2 = [M_T·(z_D - z_O)] / [I_y-gr · 175·10³ · c_s] · (t_D/t_i) · (k_i)^(1/4). Numerator of first fraction: 8,500,000 · (22.5 - 10.2) = 8,500,000 · 12.3 = 104,550,000. Denominator: 980 · 175,000 · 1.0 = 171,500,000. Ratio: 104,550,000 / 171,500,000 ≈ 0.6097. t_D/t_i = 18/16 = 1.125, but capped at 1.0 per rule (1.0 ≥ t_D/t_i ≥ 0.65), so use 1.0. k_i^(1/4) = 1.0^(1/4) = 1.0. Therefore c2 = 0.6097 · 1.0 · 1.0 = 0.6097. Step 4 — Required radius: r ≥ c1·c2 = 1.792 · 0.6097 ≈ 1.092 m, and r ≥ r_min = 0.15 m. Governing: r ≥ 1.092 m. The proposed r = 0.55 m is NON-COMPLIANT. Step 5 — Insert plate: Since r required > r proposed, insert plates are required per Pt5.Ch2.Sec2 [2.1.1]. Step 6 — Knuckle detailing via Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [6.1.4]: Within 0.6L, the distance between the knuckle and the support stiffening shall not be greater than 50 mm. The proposed 65 mm spacing exceeds this limit and is therefore NON-COMPLIANT. The support stiffening must be relocated to within 50 mm of the knuckle line.

scenario_parameters.ship_type: bulk carrier with large deck openings
scenario_parameters.hatch_corner_type: HC1 (longitudinal deck strip to closed area)

question_text: A new 320-metre container ship is being designed with the class notation 'Container ship'. The upper deck plating within the 0.4L amidships region is fabricated from NV 40 steel with a nominal plate thickness of 58 mm. The structural arrangement includes the sheer strake, upper deck plating, hatch side coaming, and coaming top plate, all of which are longitudinal structural members in the upper hull. During the detail design review, the designer notes that several longitudinal stiffeners attached to the upper deck plating pass through a knuckle in the longitudinal bulkhead within the 0.6L region. The distance between the knuckle line and the nearest support stiffening fitted in line with the knuckle is measured at 65 mm. Additionally, the fabrication quality standard proposed for the upper hull longitudinal structure in this amidships region is ISO 5817 quality level C. Is the proposed fabrication quality standard acceptable for this region, and is the 65 mm knuckle support distance compliant? Provide the minimum required fabrication quality level for this structural region and the maximum permitted distance between the knuckle and its in-line support stiffening within 0.6L.
required_facts: ISO 5817 quality level B is required (not level C) for the upper hull longitudinal structure of container ships within 0.4L amidships
The proposed ISO 5817 quality level C is not acceptable for this region
Upper hull longitudinal structural members include the sheer strake, upper deck, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate, and all attached longitudinals — the 58 mm NV 40 upper deck plating qualifies
The maximum permitted distance between a knuckle and its in-line support stiffening within 0.6L is 50 mm
The proposed 65 mm knuckle support distance exceeds the 50 mm limit and is non-compliant
The 75 mm relaxation applies only to shallow knuckles with angles less than 10 degrees; otherwise a fatigue analysis per the fatigue assessment methodology is required for any alternative arrangement

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Fatigue methodology workmanship requirements for container ships reference upper hull longitudinal structure definition in Pt5, which then feeds back into detail design knuckle support rules in Pt3
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2] states that ISO 5817 quality level B (not C) shall be applied to container ships for the upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships. Step 2 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3] defines upper hull longitudinal structural members as: uppermost strake of longitudinal bulkhead, sheer strake, upper deck, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate, and all attached longitudinals.
