question_text:
A newbuilding container ship of 320 m rule length is being designed with the class notation 'Container ship'. The upper deck plating within the 0.4L amidships region is fabricated from NV 47 steel with an as-built thickness of 68 mm. The hatch side coaming plates in the same region are also NV 47 with a thickness of 72 mm. During the design review, the following questions arise:

1. What ISO 5817 weld quality level must be applied to the upper hull longitudinal structure in the 0.4L amidships region for this vessel, and why does it differ from the general requirement for other ship types?

2. For the hull girder strength assessment of this container ship, the designer proposes to use the permissible still water shear force Qsw at a transverse section located at x/L = 0.45 (i.e., within the 0.4L amidships region). The loading manual shows a maximum still water shear force of 28,500 kN at this section. The total hull girder shear capacity QR at this section has been calculated as 31,200 kN, and no shear force correction ΔQmdf applies. Is the proposed loading condition compliant with the hull girder shear strength requirement?

3. The scantlings of the continuous hull girder longitudinal strength members — including the upper deck plating and hatch side coaming — are maintained at full thickness throughout the 0.4L amidships region. The designer intends to begin tapering these scantlings at exactly x/L = 0.30 from amidships (i.e., at the boundary of the 0.4L region). Is this arrangement acceptable under the applicable rules, and what flexibility, if any, exists regarding the longitudinal extent of these scantlings?
required_facts: ISO 5817 quality level B (not level C) must be applied to the upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships for this container ship
Upper hull longitudinal structural members include the upper deck plating and hatch side coaming, as defined by the container ship rules for very thick steel plates
The NV 47 plates exceeding 50 mm thickness in the upper hull qualify as critical areas, reinforcing the level B requirement

The still water shear force of 28,500 kN must be compared against the reduced hull girder shear capacity Q_R - |Qwv| under Pt3.Ch5.Sec2 [2.2.1], rather than directly against the total shear capacity of 31,200 kN
Scantlings of continuous hull girder longitudinal strength members shall generally be maintained within the full 0.4L amidships region
Gradual reduction of scantlings towards the end of the 0.4L region is permissible in special cases, provided it does not inhibit the vessel's loading flexibility

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 workmanship requirement which mandates ISO 5817 level B for container ships in the upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships, referencing Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3] for the definition of upper hull longitudinal structural members. Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.4.2] governs hull girder shear strength for container ships and references Pt3.Ch5.Sec2 [2.4.2] for the permissible still water shear force definition and compliance check. Pt3.Ch5.Sec2 [1.1.1] governs the longitudinal extent of hull girder scantlings.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — ISO 5817 weld quality: Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2] states that ISO 5817 quality level C applies to all ship types, but level B is required for container ships for the upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships. The reference to Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3] defines 'upper hull longitudinal structural members' as including the uppermost strake of longitudinal bulkhead, sheer strake, upper deck, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate and all attached longitudinals. Since the upper deck and hatch side coaming are explicitly listed, ISO 5817 level B applies. The NV 47 material with thickness 68–72 mm (exceeding 50 mm) also qualifies these as 'critical areas' per the guidance note in Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2]. Step 2 — Hull girder shear compliance: Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [1] states hull girder strength assessment shall be carried out in accordance with Pt3.Ch5, with additional requirements in lieu of particular Pt3.Ch5 requirements. Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.4.2] references Pt3.Ch5.Sec2 [2.4.2] for the permissible still water shear force Qsw. The compliance criterion from Pt3.Ch5.Sec2 [2.4] requires that the still water shear force for the considered loading condition does not exceed the permissible value, which is bounded by QR (and ΔQmdf correction if applicable). Here Qsw-Lcd = 28,500 kN < QR = 31,200 kN with no ΔQmdf correction, so the arrangement is compliant. Step 3 — Longitudinal extent of scantlings: Pt3.Ch5.Sec2 [1.1.1] states that scantlings of all continuous hull girder longitudinal strength members shall generally be maintained within 0.4L amidships. However, in special cases based on ship type, hull form and loading conditions, scantlings may be gradually reduced towards the end of the 0.4L part. The designer's intent to begin tapering at exactly the boundary of the 0.4L region is generally acceptable, but the rule notes that gradual reduction towards the end of the 0.4L part is permissible in special cases — meaning the taper should not inhibit loading flexibility.

question_text: A 175 m container ship is being designed with containers stacked on the weather deck. The forward-most container stack is positioned 24 m aft of the forward end of the ship. The designer is evaluating whether a wave breaker is required and, if so, what structural requirements apply to it. The ship's weather deck at the wave breaker location has a transverse span of 22 m between hatch coamings. For the wave breaker plating, the designer proposes using a vehicle with a maximum axle load Q = 8 t, with two load areas per axle, individual footprint dimensions of a₁ = 200 mm and b₁ = 150 mm, and the ship operates in a sea state where the vertical acceleration aₙ = 3.2 m/s². Separately, the designer needs to determine the design deck pressure for normal operation at sea for a cargo-handling vehicle with pneumatic tyres where footprint data is not available, with maximum tyre pressure P₀ = 1000 kN/m², axle load Q = 6 t, and single wheels (w = 1.0, n₀ = 2). Is a wave breaker required for this vessel, and what is the design deck pressure Pwl-2 (in kN/m²) for normal operation at sea for the pneumatic-tyre vehicle described?
required_facts: A wave breaker is required because the forward-most container position (24 m from F.E.) is forward of the 0.15L threshold (0.15 × 175 m = 26.25 m from F.E.)
The wave breaker requirement is triggered when containers are carried above the weather deck forward of 0.15L from the forward end
For the pneumatic-tyre vehicle, the design deck pressure formula for normal operation at sea is Pwl-2 = (P₀/w) × (1 + aₙ/g)
Pwl-2 for the pneumatic-tyre vehicle equals approximately 1326 kN/m² using P₀ = 1000 kN/m², w = 1.0, aₙ = 3.2 m/s², g = 9.81 m/s²
For vehicles with axle load Q > 15 t, footprint data must be provided; Q = 6 t and Q = 8 t are both below this threshold so the standard formulas apply
The wave breaker structural requirements are governed by the special hull structures rules referenced from the container ship local scantlings section

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec5 [5.1.1] triggers the wave breaker requirement for container ships with deck cargo forward of 0.15L from FE, then references Pt3.Ch10.Sec6 [10] for wave breaker construction requirements, which in turn points to Pt3.Ch10.Sec5 for wheel loading design pressures applicable to the wave breaker deck structure.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Check wave breaker trigger (Pt5.Ch2.Sec5 [5.1.1]): The rule states that if containers are carried above the weather deck at a location forward of 0.15L from the forward end (F.E.), a wave breaker shall be fitted. For L = 175 m, 0.15L = 0.15 × 175 = 26.25 m from F.E. The forward-most container stack is at 24 m aft of F.E., which is less than 26.25 m, so the position IS forward of the 0.15L limit. Therefore a wave breaker IS required. Step 2 — Wave breaker construction reference: Pt5.Ch2.Sec5 [5.1.1] directs the designer to Pt3.Ch10.Sec6 [10] for the wave breaker requirements. Step 3 — Wheel loading design pressure (Pt3.Ch10.Sec5 [2.1.1]): For the vehicle with known footprint data, Pwl-2 = Q/(n₀·a₁·b₁) × (g + aₙ) × 10⁶. With Q = 8 t = 8000 kg, n₀ = 2, a₁ = 200 mm, b₁ = 150 mm, g = 9.81 m/s², aₙ = 3.2 m/s²: Pwl-2 = 8/(2 × 200 × 150) × (9.81 + 3.2) × 10⁶ = 8/(60000) × 13.01 × 10⁶ = 1734.7 kN/m². Step 4 — Pneumatic tyre vehicle (Pt3.Ch10.Sec5 [2.1.2]): Pwl-2 = (P₀/w) × (1 + aₙ/g). With P₀ = 1000 kN/m², w = 1.0, aₙ = 3.2 m/s², g = 9.81 m/s²: Pwl-2 = (1000/1.0) × (1 + 3.2/9.81) = 1000 × (1 + 0.326) = 1000 × 1.326 = 1326 kN/m².

question_text: A 320-metre container ship (L = 320 m, B = 48.5 m, CB = 0.65, CWL = 0.82, scantling draught T = 14.2 m) is being designed for unrestricted ocean service. The ship has a pronounced bow flare: the projected horizontal deck area extending from 0.8L forward is ADK = 1 840 m², the corresponding waterplane area at scantling draught over the same region is AWL = 1 510 m², and the vertical distance from the waterline to the uppermost deck at the forward end is zf = 9.4 m. The designer needs to determine the vertical wave bending moments for strength assessment at the midship cross-section (x/L = 0.5). As part of the same structural review, the designer must also verify the external sea pressure acting on a shell plate located at the midship cross-section, at a depth of z = 6.0 m below the baseline, on the starboard side at y = +18.0 m (Bx = 38.0 m at that cross-section), for the HSM-1 dynamic load case under the extreme sea loads design load scenario. The scantling draught load case reference draught is TLC = 14.2 m. Determine: (a) the hogging and sagging vertical wave bending moments at x/L = 0.5 for strength assessment, and (b) whether the external dynamic (wave) pressure PW for the HSM-1 load case at the specified shell plate location is zero or non-zero, and explain why.
required_facts: The container-ship-specific vertical wave bending moment formula from Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2.2.3] applies, not the general Pt3.Ch4 formula, because Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2.2.1] states it is used in lieu of the Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 [3] values
The wave parameter C ≈ 0.987 because L = 320 m is less than Lref ≈ 407.5 m (computed using CWL = 0.82)
The distribution factor cM = 1.0 at x/L = 0.5 for both hogging and sagging conditions
The bow flare coefficient fBow ≈ 0.549, yielding fNL-Sag ≈ 1.339 (greater than the 1.0 minimum) and fNL-Hog ≈ 0.897 (less than the 1.1 cap)
The hogging wave bending moment MWV-Hog is approximately +6 700 000 kNm and the sagging moment MWV-Sag is approximately −10 010 000 kNm at x/L = 0.5 for strength assessment with f_R = 0.85
For the HSM-1 load case, the external dynamic wave pressure PW at the shell plate is calculated per Sec.5 [1.3.2] and Table 2.
The external pressure rules for HSM load cases are found in Pt3.Ch4.Sec5 [1.3.2], reached by following the general loads reference in Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [1] back to Pt3.Ch4

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2.2.3] gives the container-ship-specific vertical wave bending moment formula and references fR from Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 [3.1.1]; the same Sec3 [1] states that static and dynamic loads shall be per Pt3.Ch4 except where overridden. For external sea pressure the answerer must follow the general loads framework back to Pt3.Ch4.Sec5 [1.3.2] (HSM load case hydrodynamic pressures), which is the end node of the chain via Pt3.Ch4.Sec8 [1] (loading conditions) establishing the design load scenario context.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 – Identify ship type and applicable load rules: The vessel is a container ship, so Pt5.Ch2 applies. Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [1] states that static and dynamic loads shall be per Pt3.Ch4 except where overridden by Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 itself. Step 2 – Vertical wave bending moment (part a): Use Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2.2.3] formulas. First compute Lref = 315 × CWL^(−1.3) = 315 × 0.82^(−1.3). CWL^(−1.3): ln(0.82)=−0.1985, ×(−1.3)=+0.2581, exp=1.2944. Lref = 315 × 1.2944 ≈ 407.5 m. Since L=320 < Lref=407.5, use C = 1 − 1.50×(1 − √(320/407.5))^2.2. √(320/407.5)=√0.7853=0.8862. (1−0.8862)=0.1138. 0.1138^2.2: ln(0.1138)=−2.172, ×2.2=−4.779, exp=0.00843. C = 1 − 1.50×0.00843 = 1 − 0.01265 ≈ 0.987. Distribution factor cM at x/L=0.5 (hogging): from Table 1, range 0.35≤x/L<0.55 → cM=1.0. Distribution factor cM at x/L=0.5 (sagging): range 0.35≤x/L<0.6 → cM=1.0. Bow flare coefficient fBow = (ADK − AWL)/(0.2 × L × zf) = (1840−1510)/(0.2×320×9.4) = 330/601.6 = 0.549. fNL-Hog = 0.3×(CB/CWL)×√T = 0.3×(0.65/0.82)×√14.2 = 0.3×0.7927×3.768 = 0.897; not greater than 1.1 → fNL-Hog = 0.897. fNL-Sag = 4.5×(1+0.2×fBow)/(CWL×√CB×L^0.3) = 4.5×(1+0.2×0.549)/(0.82×√0.65×320^0.3). √0.65=0.8062. 320^0.3: ln320=5.768, ×0.3=1.730, exp=5.641. Denominator=0.82×0.8062×5.641=3.731. Numerator=4.5×1.1098=4.994. fNL-Sag=4.994/3.731=1.339; not less than 1.0 → fNL-Sag=1.339. For fR and fp: fR is taken from Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 [3.1.1] for strength assessment (unrestricted service, fR=1.0 typically); fp is given in Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [3.1.1]. With fR=1.0, fp=1.0 (standard), cM=1.0, C≈0.987, CWL=0.82, L=320, B=48.5: (B/L)^0.8=(48.5/320)^0.8=0.1516^0.8; ln(0.1516)=−1.887, ×0.8=−1.510, exp=0.2211. MWV-Hog = +1.5×1.0×1.0×320³×0.987×1.0×0.82×0.2211×0.897 = +1.5×3.2768×10⁷×0.987×0.82×0.2211×0.897. Compute: 1.5×3.2768e7=4.9152e7; ×0.987=4.851e7; ×0.82=3.978e7; ×0.2211=8.797e6; ×0.897≈7.891e6 kNm ≈ 7 891 000 kNm. MWV-Sag = −1.5×1.0×1.0×320³×0.987×1.0×0.82×0.2211×1.339 = −(4.851e7×0.82×0.2211×1.339) = −(3.978e7×0.2211×1.339) = −(8.797e6×1.339) ≈ −11 779 000 kNm ≈ −11 779 MNm. Step 3 – External sea pressure for HSM-1 (part b): The answerer must follow the chain from Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [1] → Pt3.Ch4 → Pt3.Ch4.Sec5 [1.3.2]. From Table 2 of Pt3.Ch4.Sec5, for HSM-1: PW = 0.0 when z ≥ TLC (above waterline), and PW = PW,WL − ρg(z − TLC) when z < TLC. Here z = 6.0 m < TLC = 14.2 m, so PW is non-zero; PW = PW,WL − ρg(6.0 − 14.2) = PW,WL + ρg×8.2. Since (z − TLC) is negative, the term −ρg(z−TLC) is positive, meaning the wave pressure below the waterline is PW,WL plus a hydrostatic-like increment. The plate is submerged (z < TLC), so PW ≠ 0 for HSM-1.

question_text: A 320-metre bulk carrier with large deck openings is being designed with a series of cargo hatchways on the strength deck. At one hatch corner located between a longitudinal deck strip and a closed area (type HC1), the following parameters apply: rule length L = 320 m, breadth of the longitudinal deck girder alongside the hatchway b_L = 3.2 m, breadth of the cross deck strip b_Q = 2.8 m, the hatch corner is positioned at x/L = 0.55 from the aft perpendicular, and the relevant large deck opening length forward and aft of the superstructure ℓ = 48 m. The gross thickness of the hatchway corner plate t_i = 22 mm, the gross plate thickness of the longitudinal structural member t_D = 20 mm, the total longitudinal bending moment M_T = 8 500 000 kNm, the distance of the hatch corner from baseline z_D = 18.5 m, the neutral axis height z_O = 9.2 m, the gross moment of inertia I_y-gr = 420 m⁴, and the material factor k_i = 1.0. The structural designer proposes a hatch corner radius of r = 1.20 m and no insert plate. The double bottom floors in the FE model are assessed using boundary condition SP-A with the panel defined as full web depth between primary supporting members. During the direct strength analysis, a longitudinal deck panel adjacent to the hatch corner shows a plate thickness that varies across the panel: three finite elements with areas 0.18 m², 0.22 m², and 0.15 m² and net thicknesses 18 mm, 20 mm, and 17 mm respectively. The slenderness check for this internal deck plate (vessel length ≥ 90 m, not a tank or watertight boundary, more than three continuous decks) uses a stiffener spacing b = 680 mm. Is the proposed hatch corner radius compliant, and is the plate slenderness of the deck panel acceptable? Provide the minimum required corner radius, the average plate thickness for buckling assessment, and the minimum plate thickness required by the slenderness criterion.
required_facts: The average plate thickness for buckling assessment is approximately 18.5 mm (computed as area-weighted average of the three finite elements)
The minimum plate thickness from the slenderness criterion is approximately 3.9 mm (b/C = 680/175), so the deck panel slenderness is acceptable
The slenderness coefficient C = 175 applies for internal structures in a vessel with more than three continuous decks and L ≥ 90 m
The hatch corner radius formula must be applied because the vessel has large deck openings, requiring special consideration per the detail design rules referencing the ship-type rules
The minimum required hatch corner radius is approximately 1.45 m (r = c_1 × c_2 ≈ 1.485 × 0.977)
The proposed radius of 1.20 m is not compliant — it is less than the required minimum of approximately 1.45 m
An insert plate is required at the hatch corner since the radius requirement is not met

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Buckling assessment of deck panels near hatch corners in a bulk carrier with large deck openings triggers: (1) average thickness calculation per Pt3.Ch8.Sec4 [2.1.2], (2) slenderness check per Pt3.Ch8.Sec2 [2.2] with coefficient from Table 1, (3) detail design reference for hatch corners of ships with large deck openings per Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [7.3.5] pointing to Pt5.Ch2, (4) hatch corner radius formula per Pt5.Ch2.Sec2 [2.1.1]
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Average plate thickness (Pt3.Ch8.Sec4 [2.1.2]): t_avr = (0.18×18 + 0.22×20 + 0.15×17) / (0.18+0.22+0.15) = (3.24 + 4.40 + 2.55) / 0.55 = 10.19 / 0.55 = 18.53 mm. Step 2 — Slenderness check (Pt3.Ch8.Sec2 [2.2], Table 1): For internal structures with more than three continuous decks, vessel length ≥ 90 m, C = 175. Minimum t_p = b/C = 680/175 = 3.89 mm. The average thickness 18.53 mm >> 3.89 mm, so slenderness is satisfied. Step 3 — Hatch corner identification (Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [7.3.5]): The vessel has large deck openings; hatch corners shall be specially considered per Pt5.Ch2. Step 4 — Hatch corner radius (Pt5.Ch2.Sec2 [2.1.1]): Compute f_D for strength deck hatch corner: L_13 = min(max(320,100),300) = 300 m. f_D = 0.25 + 300/2000 = 0.25 + 0.15 = 0.40. c_1 for HC1 type = (f_D + ℓ/750)·b_L = (0.40 + 48/750)×3.2 = (0.40 + 0.064)×3.2 = 0.464×3.2 = 1.485. Compute c_s at x/L = 0.55 (0.3 ≤ x/L < 0.7): c_s = 1.0. Check t_D/t_i = 20/22 = 0.909, within [0.65, 1.0]. c_2 = [M_T×(z_D - z_O)] / [I_y-gr × 175×10³ × c_s] × (t_D/t_i) × k_i^(1/4) = [8500000×(18.5−9.2)] / [420×175000×1.0] × (20/22) × 1.0 = [8500000×9.3] / [73500000] × 0.909 = 79050000/73500000 × 0.909 = 1.0755 × 0.909 = 0.977. r_required = c_1 × c_2 = 1.485 × 0.977 = 1.451 m, with r_min = 0.15 m. Since r_required = 1.451 m > proposed r = 1.20 m, the proposed radius is NOT compliant. An insert plate is also required.

scenario_parameters.ship_type: bulk carrier with large deck openings
scenario_parameters.hatch_corner_type: HC1 (longitudinal deck strip to closed area)
scenario_parameters.deck_type: internal, vessel with more than three continuous decks

question_text:
A 185-metre container ship (class notation 'Container ship') is under design review. The upper hull structure in the cargo hold region includes hatch side coaming plates of NV 47 steel with an as-built thickness of 68 mm. The longitudinal stiffeners on the inner bottom and shell envelope run through cut-outs in the transverse primary supporting members (PSMs) of the bow area. At one location forward of 0.1L from the forward end, the shell plating has a flare angle of 47° at 0.10L and 43° at 0.15L from the forward end. The bow impact strengthening extent must be determined.

Separately, at a transverse PSM in the cargo hold region, longitudinal stiffeners pass through cut-outs that are 58% of the PSM web depth. No lug or collar plates are fitted at these cut-outs. The cut-out breadth is 90 mm. The designer proposes to use a corner radius R = 18 mm at the cut-out corners.

For the fillet welds connecting these stiffeners to the PSM web, the stiffeners are subject to bow impact loads. The abutting plate is normal strength steel (ReH = 235 N/mm²) with an as-built thickness of 14 mm.

(a) What is the required longitudinal extent of bow impact strengthening for this vessel?
(b) Is the cut-out arrangement (depth 58% of PSM web depth, no lug/collar plate, R = 18 mm) compliant? If not, what is the minimum acceptable corner radius?
(c) For the fillet welds connecting stiffeners to the PSM under bow impact loading, which weld sizing procedure applies, and what is the minimum specified yield stress of the weld deposit (ReH_weld) that must be used?
required_facts: Bow impact strengthening must extend to 0.20L (37 m) from the forward end because flare angle exceeds 40° at both 0.10L and 0.15L
The cut-out depth of 58% of PSM web depth exceeds the 50% limit and is non-compliant without demonstrated shear strength and buckling capacity
The minimum required corner radius R is 25 mm (= max(20% × 90 mm, 25 mm)); the proposed R = 18 mm is non-compliant
For fillet welds under bow impact loading, weld sizing is governed by Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [2.5.6] as referenced from the stiffener-PSM connection rules
For normal strength steel (ReH = 235 N/mm²), the minimum weld deposit yield stress is ReH_weld = 305 N/mm²
Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 applies to this vessel (Container ship notation, NV 47 steel, 68 mm thickness in range 50–100 mm), and the additional requirements for NV 47 material must also be applied

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Bow impact extent rules (Pt3.Ch10.Sec1) trigger extended strengthening zone based on flare angles; cut-out rules at PSM intersections (Pt3.Ch6.Sec7) govern depth limits and corner radii; stiffener-to-PSM weld sizing under bow impact is referred from Pt3.Ch6.Sec7 [1.3.4] to Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [2.5.4]; the container ship NV47 thick plate rules (Pt5.Ch2.Sec10) apply additionally for the hatch coaming.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 (Pt3.Ch10.Sec1 [1.1.3]): The base extent is 0.1L from F.E. Since flare angle α = 47° > 40° at 0.10L, the extent must be extended to 0.15L. Since α = 43° > 40° at 0.15L, the extent must be further extended to 0.20L. Therefore the bow impact strengthening extends to 0.20L from F.E. (= 37 m on a 185 m ship).

Step 2 (Pt3.Ch6.Sec7 [1.1.2]): Cut-out depth is 58% of PSM web depth, which exceeds the 50% limit. Without lug or collar plate, this is not permitted unless shear strength and buckling capacity are demonstrated sufficient. The arrangement as described (no lug/collar, no demonstrated capacity) is non-compliant.

Step 3 (Pt3.Ch6.Sec7 [1.1.6]): Minimum corner radius R = max(20% × b, 25 mm) = max(0.20 × 90 mm, 25 mm) = max(18 mm, 25 mm) = 25 mm. The proposed R = 18 mm is less than 25 mm and is therefore non-compliant. Minimum required R = 25 mm.

Step 4 (Pt3.Ch6.Sec7 [1.3.4] → Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [2.5.4]): For stiffener-to-PSM fillet welds under bow impact loads, Pt3.Ch6.Sec7 [1.3.4] directs the designer to size welds per Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [2.5.4]. For normal strength steel with ReH = 235 N/mm², the minimum weld deposit yield stress is ReH_weld = 305 N/mm².

Step 5 (Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.1], [1.1.2]): The vessel has class notation 'Container ship' with NV 47 hatch coaming plates of 68 mm thickness (50 mm < 68 mm ≤ 100 mm). Therefore Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 applies, and additionally the requirements of [3] (for NV 47 material) must be applied.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation_note: The cross-volume link is: Pt3.Ch6.Sec7 [1.3.4] references Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [2.5.4] for weld sizing under bow impact; and Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 applies as an overlay for the container ship NV47 thick plate requirements.

question_text: A 280 m container ship is being designed with a cargo hold finite element analysis covering the midship region. The structural engineer has completed the FE model and is now performing yield strength verification for the primary supporting members, including the inner bottom plating and double bottom girders. The mesh size used throughout the cargo hold model is the standard s×s mesh. At one location on a double bottom girder web, the calculated von Mises stress from the FE analysis is 285 N/mm² under a design load combination involving a head sea equivalent design wave that maximises the vertical wave bending moment amidships, combined with a sagging still water bending moment. The material yield stress is 315 N/mm². The load case uses 100% of the permissible still water bending moment and the dynamic load case is applied at scantling draught. Is the yield criterion satisfied at this location, and what acceptance criterion value (in N/mm²) must the von Mises stress not exceed for this load combination?
required_facts: Yield verification for cargo hold FE analysis of container ships must follow the acceptance criteria for partial ship structural analysis (cargo hold analysis) as referenced from the container ship rules
The HSM-2 dynamic load case is defined as the head sea equivalent design wave that maximises the vertical wave bending moment amidships

The acceptance criterion for von Mises stress under the standard design load combination at 100% permissible SWBM is η × ReH, where η = 1.0 for primary supporting members under full design load combinations
The acceptance criterion value is 315 N/mm² (= 1.0 × 315 N/mm²)
The calculated von Mises stress of 285 N/mm² does not exceed 315 N/mm², so the yield criterion is satisfied
The standard s×s cargo hold mesh shell stress result is evaluated at element centroids rather than using area-weighted averaging in this case

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec6 [2.4.1] directs yield verification to Pt3.Ch7.Sec3 [4.2], which defines the acceptance criteria for von Mises stress in cargo hold FE analysis including the usage factor and load combination factors; the dynamic load case (HSM-2) is defined in Pt3.Ch4.Sec2 as the head sea EDW that maximises vertical wave bending moment amidships, which is required to identify the correct load combination factor and usage factor tier applicable to the yield check.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec6 [2.4.1]: For a container ship cargo hold FE analysis, yield verification of primary supporting members shall be carried out according to Pt3.Ch7.Sec3 [4.2]. This is the mandatory cross-reference from the container ship rules to the general FE yield acceptance criteria. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch7.Sec3 [4.2]: The yield acceptance criterion for cargo hold mesh (s×s) requires that the area-weighted von Mises stress in the evaluation area does not exceed a usage-factor-adjusted yield stress. For the standard cargo hold mesh under a full design load combination (100% SWBM, dynamic load case at scantling draught), the acceptance criterion is η × ReH, where η is the usage factor. For primary supporting members under the standard design load combinations (which include the HSM-2 dynamic load case), the usage factor η = 1.0 applies, giving an acceptance criterion of 1.0 × 315 = 315 N/mm². Step 3 — Pt3.Ch4.Sec2 [1.1]: The HSM-2 load case is defined as the head sea EDW that maximises the vertical wave bending moment amidships. This confirms the load case described in the scenario is a standard design load case (not a special or reduced load case), so the full usage factor applies without reduction. Step 4 — Conclusion: The acceptance criterion is 315 N/mm². The calculated von Mises stress of 285 N/mm² is less than 315 N/mm², so the yield criterion is satisfied at this location.

scenario_parameters.analysis_type: cargo hold FE analysis, midship region
scenario_parameters.structural_member: double bottom girder web (primary supporting member)
scenario_parameters.dynamic_load_case: HSM-2 (head sea, maximises vertical wave bending moment amidships)

question_text: A naval architect is performing a fatigue assessment of the deck longitudinals amidships on a 280 m container ship with a waterplane coefficient CWL = 0.78, beam B = 42 m, block coefficient CB = 0.65, and scantling draught T = 13.5 m. The bow flare shape coefficient fBow has been calculated as 0.35. The ship operates worldwide and the fatigue loads are being derived using the prescriptive load approach. For the vertical wave bending moment used in the fatigue assessment, the designer proposes to use fNL-Hog = 0.30 × (CB/CWL) × √T and fNL-Sag = 4.5 × (1 + 0.2 × fBow) / (CWL × √CB × L^0.3), with an operational factor fR = 1.0. Is this approach correct? Determine the correct values of fNL-Hog, fNL-Sag, and fR that must be used for the fatigue vertical wave bending moment calculation, and compute the numerical values for this ship.
required_facts: For fatigue assessment of the vertical wave bending moment, fNL-Hog = 1.0 (the non-linear strength expression must NOT be used)
For fatigue assessment of the vertical wave bending moment, fNL-Sag = 1.0 (the non-linear strength expression must NOT be used)
The operational factor fR for fatigue assessment is obtained from the fatigue chapter (Pt3 Ch9), not set to 1.0
fR = 0.76 for prescriptive loads in worldwide wave environment fatigue assessment
The designer's proposed fR = 1.0 is incorrect for a worldwide-trading ship using prescriptive loads
The designer's proposed non-linear expressions for fNL-Hog and fNL-Sag are the strength-assessment branches and must not be applied in fatigue calculations

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 defines the vertical wave bending moment formula for container ships and specifies that for fatigue assessment fR is taken from Pt3.Ch9.Sec4 [4.3], and that fNL-Hog = 1.0 and fNL-Sag = 1.0 for fatigue (not the strength-assessment non-linear expressions). The answerer must navigate from the container-ship load section into the fatigue chapter to retrieve fR = 0.76.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2.2.3]: The vertical wave bending moment formula for container ships gives MWV-Hog and MWV-Sag. The formula contains fR, fNL-Hog, and fNL-Sag. The section explicitly states two branches for each non-linear factor: one for strength assessment and one for fatigue assessment. For fatigue assessment: fNL-Hog = 1.0 (not the expression 0.3×CB/CWL×√T) and fNL-Sag = 1.0 (not the expression 4.5×(1+0.2fBow)/(CWL×√CB×L^0.3)). Step 2 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2.2.3] also states that fR for fatigue assessment shall be taken as given in Pt3.Ch9.Sec4 [4.3]. Step 3 — Pt3.Ch9.Sec4 [4.3]: For prescriptive loads calculated in Ch.4, the operational factor fR = 0.76. Therefore the designer's proposal is incorrect on all three counts: fNL-Hog should be 1.0 (not the non-linear expression), fNL-Sag should be 1.0 (not the non-linear expression), and fR should be 0.76 (not 1.0).

question_text:
A 185-metre container ship is being designed with longitudinal stiffeners in the upper hull region. The hatch coaming top plate is 92 mm thick and made of NV 36 steel (specified minimum yield stress 355 N/mm²). The plate flange of these longitudinal stiffeners has a lower minimum yield strength than the connected stiffeners themselves. The stiffener web depth is 280 mm and the actual net web thickness is 9 mm. The stiffener is a flat bar profile.

The designer needs to verify two things:
1. Given the mixed yield strength between the plate flange and the stiffener, does the rules require any additional check beyond the standard yield capacity assessment for these stiffeners?
2. For the flat bar stiffener web, what is the maximum permissible web depth-to-thickness ratio, and does the 280 mm × 9 mm web satisfy the slenderness requirement?

State whether the arrangement is compliant, identify any additional checks triggered by the material mismatch, and calculate the limiting web thickness for the given web depth.
required_facts: The 92 mm NV 36 coaming top plate falls within the additional NDT scope for container ship upper hull longitudinal structural members (85 < t ≤ 100 mm, NV 36)
When the plate flange has a lower minimum yield strength than the connected stiffener, an additional yield capacity check of the plate flange is required
The slenderness coefficient Cw for a flat bar stiffener is 22 (or 26 if laterally loaded and not participating in hull girder bending)
The minimum required net web thickness is t_w ≥ (280/22) × sqrt(355/235) ≈ 15.65 mm
The actual web thickness of 9 mm does not satisfy the slenderness requirement
The arrangement is non-compliant — both the slenderness check fails and an additional plate flange yield capacity check is triggered

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The NDT and material requirements for NV 36 upper hull structure (Pt1.Ch3.Sec3) lead to material application rules in Pt3.Ch3.Sec1, which at clause [2.1.2] explicitly flags that when plate flange yield strength is lower than the connected stiffener, an additional yield capacity check is required per Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4]. That stiffener strength check in Pt3.Ch6.Sec5 references stiffener geometry parameters (hw) as shown in Ch.8 Sec.2, which contains the slenderness requirements for flat bar stiffeners (Cw = 22).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Pt1.Ch3.Sec3 [2.1.3]: The 92 mm NV 36 coaming top plate (85 < t ≤ 100 mm, NV 36) falls within the additional NDT scope for upper hull longitudinal structural members of container ships. This flags the structure as subject to heightened scrutiny and directs attention to material and structural requirements.

Step 2 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.2]: The rules state that when the plate flange has a lower minimum yield strength than the connected stiffener or PSM, an additional check of yield capacity of the plate flange may be required, with the cross-reference pointing explicitly to Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4]. This is the gating condition triggered by the mixed-yield scenario described.

Step 3 — Pt3.Ch6.Sec5 [1.1.4]: This clause governs the yield capacity check for stiffeners where the plate flange yield strength differs from the stiffener. The stiffener web thickness formula and combined stress coefficient Cm are evaluated here. The geometry parameter hw (web depth) is referenced as shown in Ch.8 Sec.2.

Step 4 — Pt3.Ch8.Sec2 [3.1.1]: For flat bar stiffeners, the slenderness coefficient Cw = 22 (standard) or Cw = 26 for laterally loaded flat bars not participating in hull girder bending. Using Cw = 22 and ReH = 355 N/mm² for the stiffener material:
  t_w ≥ (hw / Cw) × sqrt(ReH / 235)
  t_w ≥ (280 / 22) × sqrt(355 / 235)
  t_w ≥ 12.727 × 1.230
  t_w ≥ 15.65 mm

The actual web thickness of 9 mm is less than the required 15.65 mm, so the flat bar stiffener does NOT satisfy the slenderness requirement. The arrangement is non-compliant, and an additional yield capacity check of the plate flange is also required due to the material mismatch.

question_text:
A naval architect is designing a 185-metre container ship with a hatch coaming structure. The upper hull longitudinal structural members include a hatch side coaming plate with a leading plate thickness of 92 mm made of NV 36 steel, and horizontal coaming plates of 88 mm thickness made of NV 40 steel. The coaming structure incorporates longitudinal stiffeners with T-bar profiles. The flange plate of these stiffeners has a specified minimum yield strength of 235 N/mm², while the connected primary supporting member web is fabricated from steel with a minimum yield strength of 355 N/mm².

For the stiffener scantling check, the designer needs to determine the effective shear span. The stiffener has a full length of 3.2 m between primary supporting members, a stiffener spacing of 800 mm, and brackets are fitted to the free edge of the stiffener at one end only. No brackets are fitted to the attached plating on the opposite side.

Given this arrangement:
1. Which NDT requirements apply to the block-to-block butt joints of the hatch side coaming plate and the horizontal coaming plates, and what minimum testing extents (MT/PT and RT/UT percentages) are required?
2. Does the difference in yield strength between the stiffener flange plate and the connected PSM web trigger any additional design check, and if so, what is that check?
3. What is the maximum permissible effective shear span for the longitudinal stiffener described above?
required_facts: The 92 mm NV 36 hatch side coaming plate meets the threshold of 85 < t ≤ 100 mm for NV 36, triggering the additional container ship NDT requirements
The 88 mm NV 40 horizontal coaming plate meets the threshold of 50 < t ≤ 100 mm for NV 40, also triggering the additional container ship NDT requirements
Block-to-block butt joints of both plates require 100% MT/PT and 100% RT/UT (UT only, not RT) testing

The lower yield strength of the stiffener flange plate (235 N/mm²) compared to the connected PSM web (355 N/mm²) triggers an additional yield capacity check of the plate flange per the materials section cross-reference to the stiffener strength requirements
The maximum permissible effective shear span is 2.8 m, calculated as ℓ - s/2000 = 3.2 - 800/2000 = 2.8 m

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Pt1.Ch3.Sec3 NDT requirements for container ship upper hull structural members, which triggers material grade and thickness thresholds; Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.2] flags that mismatched yield strengths between flange and web require additional yield capacity check per Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4]; Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4] references Ch.3 Sec.7 [1.1.4] for effective shear span definition and [1.4.3] for effective shear depth used in the web thickness formula.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 (Pt1.Ch3.Sec3 Table 1): The hatch side coaming leading plate is 92 mm of NV 36. The threshold for NV 36 is 85 < t ≤ 100 mm, so 92 mm qualifies. The horizontal coaming plate is 88 mm of NV 40, and the threshold for NV 40 is 50 < t ≤ 100 mm, so 88 mm also qualifies. Both plates therefore fall under the 'Additional for container ships' row in Table 1. For all block-to-block butt joints of upper hull longitudinal structural members: MT/PT = 100%, RT/UT = 100% (UT only, not RT, per footnote 3). Step 2 (Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.2]): The stiffener flange plate has ReH = 235 N/mm² (normal strength) while the PSM web has ReH = 355 N/mm² (high strength). Since the plate flange has a lower minimum yield strength than the connected PSM, Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.2] explicitly states that an additional check of yield capacity of the plate flange may be required, and directs the designer to Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4]. Step 3 (Pt3.Ch6.Sec5 [1.1.4] → Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [1.1.4]): The effective shear span formula from Ch.3 Sec.7 [1.1.4] is: ℓ_shr ≤ ℓ - s/2000. With ℓ = 3.2 m and s = 800 mm: ℓ_shr ≤ 3.2 - 800/2000 = 3.2 - 0.4 = 2.8 m. Since brackets are fitted to the free edge at one end only (not both ends), the bracket reduction applies only at that one end, but the formula cap of ℓ - s/2000 = 2.8 m is the maximum permissible effective shear span regardless.

scenario_parameters.bracket_arrangement: free edge bracket at one end only, no bracket on opposite attached plating side

question_text: A 310-metre container ship is being designed with a midship section that includes a vertically corrugated longitudinal bulkhead running the full length of the cargo hold region. The designer proposes to include the full cross-sectional area of the vertical corrugations in the hull girder section modulus calculation. The ship has a scantling draft of 14.5 m, a breadth of 48.2 m, and a contract speed of 24 knots at 85% MCR with 15% sea margin. The as-built deck plate thickness is 22 mm, the voluntary addition is 1 mm, and the deck is exposed to atmosphere on one side and a container hold on the other side (treated as a void space). Using the net thickness approach required for this vessel type, calculate the net offered thickness of the deck plate for the hull girder strength assessment (section properties), and determine whether the proposed inclusion of the vertical corrugation area in the section modulus is acceptable. State clearly what area contribution, if any, the corrugated bulkhead may make to the hull girder transverse section.
required_facts: The net offered thickness of the deck plate for section properties is t_off = 20.25 mm
The corrosion addition factor α = 0.5 applies for strength assessment section properties
The total corrosion addition tc = 1.5 mm (1.0 mm atmosphere side + 0.5 mm void space side)
Vertical corrugations of a longitudinal bulkhead shall NOT be included in the hull girder transverse section for bending
The corrugated bulkhead is not effective for hull girder bending and its corrugation area must be excluded from the section modulus
The corrugated bulkhead may contribute to hull girder shear force capacity, but not to bending section modulus

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 mandates hull girder strength per Pt3.Ch5 with net scantlings; the net thickness formula uses corrosion addition factor α=0.5 for section properties in strength assessment, and tc from Table 2; following the Pt3.Ch5 reference leads to Sec2 for bending/shear strength (which references Sec1 for section characteristics), and Sec1 [2.5] explicitly excludes vertical corrugations from the hull girder transverse section area.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.1.1]: For a container ship, hull girder strength uses the net thickness approach. The net offered thickness is t_off = t_as_built − t_vol_add − α·tc. For strength assessment (section properties), α = 0.5 (Table 1). Step 2 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.1.2] + Table 2: The deck plate is exposed to atmosphere on one side (tc1 = 1.0 mm) and a void/dry space on the other (tc2 = 0.5 mm). The total corrosion addition tc = tc1 + tc2 = 1.0 + 0.5 = 1.5 mm. Step 3 — Apply formula: t_off = 22 − 1 − 0.5 × 1.5 = 22 − 1 − 0.75 = 20.25 mm. Step 4 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [1]: Hull girder strength shall be carried out in accordance with Pt3.Ch5. Step 5 — Pt3.Ch5.Sec2 [1.5]: Higher-strength steel and section property rules reference Sec1 for the definition of contributing members. Step 6 — Pt3.Ch5.Sec1 [2.5.1]: For longitudinal bulkheads with vertical corrugations, the vertical corrugations shall NOT be included in the hull girder transverse section. Vertically corrugated longitudinal bulkheads are not effective for hull girder bending (though they are effective for shear). Therefore the designer's proposal to include the full corrugation area in the section modulus is not acceptable; the vertical corrugations must be excluded entirely from the bending section modulus calculation.

scenario_parameters.deck_side_2_exposure: void/dry space (container hold treated as void)

question_text: A new 320-metre container ship is being designed with the class notation 'Container ship'. The upper deck plating within the 0.4L amidships region is fabricated from NV 47 steel with an as-built thickness of 62 mm. The hatch side coaming plates in the same region are also NV 47, 58 mm thick. During the structural detail design review, the designer proposes a longitudinal shallow knuckle (angle of 7 degrees) in the upper deck plating within 0.6L amidships, where the distance between the knuckle and the nearest support stiffening fitted in line with the knuckle is 80 mm. Additionally, the hatch corners of this vessel — which has large deck openings — are to be assessed. (1) What ISO 5817 weld quality level is required for the upper hull longitudinal structural members in the 0.4L amidships region, and which specific structural members are included in this category? (2) Is the proposed 80 mm knuckle-to-support distance for the shallow longitudinal knuckle compliant, and what is the maximum permitted distance? (3) What additional design consideration is triggered for the hatch corners given the nature of this vessel's deck openings, and which load types must be included in that assessment?
required_facts: ISO 5817 quality level B is required for the upper hull longitudinal structural members within 0.4L amidships for this container ship
Upper hull longitudinal structural members include: uppermost strake of longitudinal bulkhead, sheer strake, upper deck, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate, and all attached longitudinals
The proposed 80 mm knuckle-to-support distance is non-compliant for a shallow longitudinal knuckle (angle < 10 degrees) within 0.6L
The maximum permitted distance between a shallow knuckle and its in-line support stiffening within 0.6L is 75 mm
Hatch corners of ships with large deck openings must be specially assessed for stresses from longitudinal hull girder bending, torsion, and transverse loads
The definition of 'large deck openings' must be verified against the primary symbols and definitions table in the general rules chapter

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2] mandates ISO 5817 level B for container ship upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships and references Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3] for the definition of those members; Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3] lists the specific structural members; the detail design of the knuckle is governed by Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [6.3.6] (shallow knuckle distance limit of 75 mm within 0.6L); and hatch corners of ships with large deck openings per Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [7.3.5] must be specially considered using the definition of 'large deck openings' from Ch.1 Sec.4 Table 7.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Start at Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2]: The fatigue methodology section states that ISO 5817 quality level B applies to container ships for 'upper hull longitudinal structure, see Pt.5 Ch.2 Sec.10 [1.1.3], within 0.4L amidships' and critical areas. The vessel is a 320 m container ship with NV 47 steel plates of 62 mm and 58 mm thickness, both exceeding 50 mm, placing them squarely in the critical area definition (ReH ≥ 390 N/mm² or thickness > 50 mm). ISO 5817 level B is therefore required. Step 2 — Follow reference to Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3]: This clause defines 'upper hull longitudinal structural members' as: uppermost strake of longitudinal bulkhead, sheer strake, upper deck, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate, and all attached longitudinals. Both the upper deck plating and hatch side coaming plates fall within this definition, confirming ISO 5817 level B applies to both. Step 3 — Move to Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [6.3.6] for the knuckle detail: The section on detail design states that for shallow knuckles (angles less than 10 degrees), the distance between the knuckle and the support stiffening in line with the knuckle shall not exceed 75 mm within 0.6L. The proposed 80 mm distance exceeds this 75 mm limit, so the arrangement is non-compliant. The maximum permitted distance for a shallow knuckle (7 degrees < 10 degrees) within 0.6L is 75 mm. Step 4 — Follow to Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [7.3.5] and then Ch.1 Sec.4 Table 7: For ships with large deck openings (as defined in Ch.1 Sec.4 Table 7), hatch corners must be specially considered on the basis of stresses due to longitudinal hull girder bending, torsion, and transverse loads, with reference to Pt.5 Ch.1 and Pt.5 Ch.2. The answerer must consult Ch.1 Sec.4 Table 7 to confirm whether this vessel qualifies as having 'large deck openings', and then apply the special hatch corner assessment requirement.

question_text: A newbuilding container ship of 285 m length is being designed with bilge keels. The bilge keel is of closed type, and a ground bar is fitted between the shell plate and the bilge keel. The ground bar and bilge keel ends are tapered with a ratio of 3:1. The shell plating in way of the bilge strake is fabricated from NV 36 steel (yield strength 355 N/mm², material factor k = 0.72). The designer proposes to use NV 36 steel for both the ground bar and the bilge keel web. The as-built thickness of the bilge strake is 22 mm, and the proposed ground bar as-built thickness is 18 mm. Additionally, the upper deck and hatch side coaming of this container ship are fabricated from NV 47 steel plates with an as-built thickness of 68 mm. The welding procedure for these thick plates uses standard toughness weld deposits with ReH_weld = 400 N/mm². Is the proposed design compliant with classification requirements? Specifically: (a) is the ground bar thickness acceptable, (b) are the welding requirements for the bilge keel ends satisfied, and (c) what additional measures are required for the NV 47 thick plate welded connections in the upper hull?
required_facts: The ground bar minimum gross thickness requirement for a ship over 150 m is the lesser of the bilge strake gross thickness (22 mm) or 14 mm, giving a minimum of 14 mm; the proposed 18 mm is compliant
Pt3.Ch11.Sec4 [1.1.3] requires the bilge keel end welding to comply with the weld joint design rules in Ch.13 Sec.1 [5.1], which the designer must verify
For NV 36 steel (ReH = 355 N/mm²), the weld deposit must have ReH_weld ≥ 375 N/mm²
The container ship's NV 47 upper hull plates at 68 mm thickness (50 mm < t ≤ 100 mm) trigger the thick plate application requirements of Pt5.Ch2.Sec10
Because NV 47 material is used, the additional requirements of Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [3] apply in addition to the general thick plate measures

Brittle crack arrest design measures (Option A or Option B) must be implemented in the cargo hold region for the NV 47 thick plate welded connections; standard toughness weld deposits alone are not sufficient

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Bilge keel appendage rules in Pt3.Ch11.Sec4 reference welding requirements in Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [5.1]; the container ship class notation triggers Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 for thick NV47 plates, which at [3.2.4] imposes additional weld quality requirements beyond the base welding design rules in Pt3.Ch13.Sec1
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt3.Ch11.Sec4 [1.2.2]: Ship length is 285 m > 150 m, so the additional requirements apply. The gross thickness of the ground bar shall not be less than the gross thickness of the bilge strake or 14 mm, whichever is less. Bilge strake gross thickness = 22 mm; 14 mm is less than 22 mm, so the ground bar gross thickness must be ≥ 14 mm. The proposed 18 mm as-built thickness satisfies this minimum (18 mm ≥ 14 mm), so the ground bar thickness is acceptable. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch11.Sec4 [1.1.3]: The ground bar and bilge keel shall be tapered or rounded towards the bilge keel ends, and the clause explicitly cross-references Ch.13 Sec.1 [5.1] for welding requirements at the bilge keel ends. The answerer must navigate to Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [5.1] to determine the applicable weld joint design requirements for the tapered ends, including fillet weld sizing and the weld factor f_weld applicable to the bilge strake connection. Step 3 — Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [5.1]: This section governs the design of weld joints for hull structures. For the bilge keel ground bar connection to the bilge strake (NV 36, k = 0.72, ReH = 355 N/mm²), the weld deposit yield strength ReH_weld must be ≥ 375 N/mm² for high-strength steels with ReH from 265 to 355 N/mm². The designer must confirm the weld consumables meet this minimum. Step 4 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.1]: The ship has the class notation Container ship, and the upper hull longitudinal structural members (upper deck, hatch side coaming) use NV 47 steel at 68 mm thickness. Since 50 mm < 68 mm ≤ 100 mm and the steel strength group is NV 47, this section applies. Step 5 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.2]: Because NV 47 material is applied per [1.1.1], the additional requirements of [3] must also be applied. Step 6 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [3.2.4]: This sub-clause imposes specific additional weld quality requirements for NV 47 thick plates, including requirements for high-toughness weld deposits and enhanced NDT, which go beyond the base Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 requirements. The standard toughness weld deposits proposed by the designer are insufficient; brittle crack arrest design measures (Option A or Option B per [2.2.1]) must be implemented within the cargo hold region.

question_text:
A 185 m general cargo vessel (summer load waterline draught 9.2 m, breadth 28 m) is being designed for DNV class. The construction contract between the owner and the shipbuilder was signed on 14 March 2023. During detailed design review in late 2024, the naval architect proposes to relocate a sanitary discharge pipe that originates from a space below the freeboard deck. The pipe exits through the shell plating, and the inboard end of the discharge is located 1.6 m above the summer load waterline (i.e., 0.0086 L above the SWL). The discharge passes through a first-tier deckhouse on the freeboard deck; the deckhouse has an access door on the weather side. The side scuttles fitted to this first-tier deckhouse are round, each with a clear opening area of 0.12 m², and no hinged inside deadlights are fitted to them.

(a) How many non-return valves are required for this discharge arrangement, and is a positive means of closing from above the freeboard deck required? State the threshold distances that govern your answer.

(b) The access door in the deckhouse is referenced as a condition for the discharge valve requirements to apply. What weathertightness standard must that door meet, and what is the minimum gross plate thickness formula that governs its blade design?

(c) Are the side scuttles in this first-tier deckhouse required to be fitted with hinged inside deadlights? Justify your answer based on the nature of the space and the size of the openings.

(d) The owner asks whether the 2024 rule amendments (issued after the contract date) must be applied to this vessel. What rule governs which edition of the rules applies, and what is the general principle?
required_facts: 0.01L = 1.85 m and 0.02L = 3.70 m for L = 185 m; the inboard end at 1.6 m does not exceed 0.01L, so one automatic non-return valve with positive means of closing from above the freeboard deck is required
The discharge valve requirements apply only when the deckhouse door complies with the weathertight door standard in the access-openings section (Sec2 [4.1.1])
The weathertight door blade gross thickness is calculated by t_gr = 0.0158 · αp · b · sqrt(|P| / (0.85 · ReH))
Side scuttles with area 0.12 m² are classified as side scuttles (not windows) because 0.12 m² < 0.16 m²
Hinged inside deadlights are required on side scuttles in first-tier deckhouses on the freeboard deck that protect openings leading below or are considered buoyant in stability calculations
The rules in force at the date of contract for construction (14 March 2023) apply; 2024 amendments do not automatically apply to this vessel

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec9 [1.1.1] triggers valve requirements for discharges from spaces below freeboard deck passing through deckhouses whose doors comply with Sec2 [4.1.1]; Sec2 [4.1.1] governs weathertight door scantlings and references Sec6 [3.1] for deadlight requirements on side scuttles in first-tier deckhouses; Sec6 [3.1] references Pt1.Ch1.Sec2 [1.3] for which rule edition applies.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Pt3.Ch12.Sec9 [1.1.1]: The discharge originates below the freeboard deck and exits through the shell. The inboard end is 1.6 m above SWL. For L=185 m: 0.01L = 1.85 m; 0.02L = 3.70 m. Since 1.6 m < 1.85 m (i.e., the vertical distance does NOT exceed 0.01L), the general requirement applies: one automatic non-return valve WITH a positive means of closing from above the freeboard deck is required. The two-valve-without-positive-closing option is not available because the 0.01L threshold is not met.

Step 2 — Pt3.Ch12.Sec9 [1.1.1] cross-reference to Pt3.Ch12.Sec2 [4.1.1]: The applicability of the discharge valve rule is conditioned on the deckhouse door complying with Sec2 [4.1.1]. Sec2 [4.1.1] sets the weathertight door standard for doors in deckhouses/companionways on the freeboard deck. The door blade gross thickness is governed by: t_gr = 0.0158 · αp · b · sqrt(|P| / (0.85 · ReH)), and stiffener section modulus by Z_gr = |P| · s · ℓ_bdg² / (7.6 · ReH). The door must meet this scantling standard to satisfy the cross-reference condition in Sec9.

Step 3 — Pt3.Ch12.Sec2 [4.1.1] cross-reference to Pt3.Ch12.Sec6 [3.1]: Sec6 [3.1.1] requires hinged inside deadlights on side scuttles fitted to (b) spaces within the first tier of enclosed superstructures and (c) first-tier deckhouses on the freeboard deck protecting openings leading below or considered buoyant in stability calculations. The deckhouse in question is a first-tier deckhouse on the freeboard deck. The side scuttles have area 0.12 m² < 0.16 m², so they are classified as side scuttles (not windows) per Sec6 [2.1.1]. Therefore hinged inside deadlights ARE required.

Step 4 — Pt3.Ch12.Sec6 [3.1] cross-reference to Pt1.Ch1.Sec2 [1.3]: Sec6 references Pt1.Ch1.Sec2 [1.3] for the applicable rule edition. Per Pt1.Ch1.Sec2 [1.3.1], the rules in force at the date of 'contract for construction' generally apply. The contract was signed 14 March 2023, so the 2023 rules apply. Rule amendments issued in 2024 do not automatically apply to this vessel unless the Society and parties agree otherwise.

question_text: A newbuild container ship of 320 m length is being designed with class notation 'Container ship'. The upper deck plating within the 0.4L amidships region is fabricated from NV 47 steel with an as-built thickness of 62 mm. The hatch side coaming plates in the same region are also NV 47 steel at 58 mm thickness. During the design review, the structural engineer proposes applying ISO 5817 quality level C for all welded joints in the upper hull longitudinal structure, arguing that this is the standard minimum requirement for all ship types. The shipyard also asks whether the 62 mm upper deck plates and 58 mm coaming plates fall within the scope of any special application requirements for thick steel plates in container ships. (1) Is the proposed ISO 5817 quality level C acceptable for the upper hull longitudinal structure of this container ship within the 0.4L amidships region, or is a higher quality level required? (2) Do the upper deck plating and hatch side coaming plates fall within the scope of the thick-plate application rules for container ships, and what structural members are considered part of the upper hull longitudinal structure for this purpose?
required_facts: ISO 5817 quality level B (not C) is required for the upper hull longitudinal structure of a container ship within the 0.4L amidships region

The definition of upper hull longitudinal structural members includes: uppermost strake of longitudinal bulkhead, sheer strake, upper deck, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate, and all attached longitudinals
Both the 62 mm upper deck plates and 58 mm hatch side coaming plates are upper hull longitudinal structural members and fall within the thick-plate application scope
The thick-plate rules apply to container ships with NV 36, NV 40, or NV 47 steel plates with thickness exceeding 50 mm but not greater than 100 mm in upper hull longitudinal structural members
The proposed ISO 5817 quality level C is not acceptable for these members in this container ship

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2] specifies that ISO 5817 quality level B (not C) applies to container ships for upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships, and cross-references Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3] for the definition of 'upper hull longitudinal structural members'. Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.1] then establishes the thick-plate application scope (50–100 mm, NV 36/40/47, container ships), and [1.1.3] defines which members are included.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: The fatigue methodology section (Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2]) states that ISO 5817 quality level C is the minimum for all ship types, BUT for container ships, ISO 5817 quality level B shall be applied to the upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships and critical areas. The reference for the definition of 'upper hull longitudinal structural members' is explicitly given as Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3]. Step 2: Following that cross-reference to Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3], upper hull longitudinal structural members are defined as: uppermost strake of longitudinal bulkhead, sheer strake, upper deck, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate, and all attached longitudinals. Step 3: Therefore, the upper deck plating (62 mm) and hatch side coaming (58 mm) are both upper hull longitudinal structural members. Step 4: Since both are NV 47 steel with thickness between 50 mm and 100 mm, they fall squarely within the scope of Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.1], which applies to container ships with thick plates (>50 mm, ≤100 mm) of NV 36, NV 40, or NV 47 for upper hull longitudinal structural members. Step 5: Conclusion — ISO 5817 quality level C is NOT acceptable for these members; level B is required. Both the 62 mm deck plates and 58 mm coaming plates are within the thick-plate application scope.

question_text: A new 310-metre container ship is being designed with the class notation 'Container ship'. The upper deck plating within the 0.4L amidships region is fabricated from NV 40 steel with an as-built thickness of 58 mm. The hatch side coaming plates in the same region are also NV 40, 62 mm thick. During the design review, the structural engineer proposes applying ISO 5817 quality level C to all welded joints in the upper hull longitudinal structure, arguing that this is the standard minimum requirement for all ship types. A second engineer disagrees and insists a higher weld quality level is mandatory for this vessel type and region. Which engineer is correct, what weld quality level must be applied to the upper hull longitudinal structure of this container ship within the 0.4L amidships region, and does the hatch side coaming qualify as part of the upper hull longitudinal structure subject to this requirement?

The second engineer is correct; quality level C is insufficient for this vessel type and region
The definition of upper hull longitudinal structural members must be taken from the container ship-specific rules (Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3])
Hatch side coaming is explicitly listed as an upper hull longitudinal structural member and is therefore subject to the ISO 5817 level B requirement
The 58 mm upper deck plates and 62 mm coaming plates also qualify as critical areas (thickness exceeding 50 mm), reinforcing the level B requirement
The 'Container ship' class notation confirms these supplementary container ship rules apply to this vessel

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2] states that ISO 5817 quality level B (not C) shall be applied to container ships for upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships, and cross-references Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3] to define what 'upper hull longitudinal structural members' means. Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3] explicitly lists hatch side coaming as one of those members. Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 establishes that this chapter applies to ships intended for carriage of containers, confirming the vessel type triggers these requirements.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2]: The workmanship clause states that ISO 5817 quality level C is the minimum for all ship types, BUT for container ships, ISO 5817 quality level B shall be applied to the upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships and critical areas. The first engineer is therefore wrong. Step 2 — The clause in Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2] cross-references Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3] to define what constitutes 'upper hull longitudinal structural members'. Step 3 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3] defines upper hull longitudinal structural members as: uppermost strake of longitudinal bulkhead, sheer strake, upper deck, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate, and all attached longitudinals. Step 4 — The hatch side coaming is explicitly listed in Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3], so it is part of the upper hull longitudinal structure. Step 5 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.1] confirms this chapter applies to ships intended for carriage of containers, so the 'Container ship' notation vessel is subject to these rules. Step 6 — The 58 mm upper deck plates and 62 mm coaming plates both exceed 50 mm, which also makes them 'critical areas' per the guidance note in Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2] (thickness > 50 mm). question_text:
A 145-metre general cargo vessel is being designed with a raised forecastle deck. The forward exposed freeboard deck has a continuous bulwark running 28 metres along each side, forming a well between the forecastle break and the forward deckhouse. The bulwark has an average height of 1.35 metres above sheathing. The designer proposes to fit openings in the bulwark using vertical bars spaced 230 mm apart rather than horizontal rails, and also intends to use this same bulwark arrangement to satisfy deck drainage requirements. The ship has standard sheer throughout.

The classification surveyor raises two concerns: first, whether the vertical-bar opening arrangement in the bulwark is acceptable as a substitute for horizontal protection courses; and second, whether the freeing port area provided on each side of the well is sufficient. The designer has calculated a total freeing port area of 2.10 m² per side for this well.

Is the vertical-bar arrangement acceptable, and is the proposed freeing port area of 2.10 m² per side compliant? If not, what is the minimum required freeing port area per side, accounting for the bulwark height?
required_facts: Vertical bars spaced approximately 230 mm apart are acceptable in lieu of horizontal rails for bulwark openings
The applicable freeing port area formula for ℓ_b > 20 m is A = 0.07 × ℓ_b, giving a base area of 1.96 m² per side
The bulwark height of 1.35 m exceeds the 1.2 m threshold by 0.15 m, requiring an area increase of 0.168 m² per side
The minimum required freeing port area per side is 2.128 m²
The proposed freeing port area of 2.10 m² per side is NOT compliant (falls short by approximately 0.028 m²)
The applicable rules are those in force at the date of contract for construction

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Pt3.Ch11.Sec2 (supporting structure / deck fittings), which in its FEA acceptance criteria references DNV-CG-0127 Sec.3 [2.2.8] for web openings. Pt3.Ch11.Sec3 [2.1.2] governs bulwark openings and references Ch.12 Sec.10 [6.1] for the horizontal-course protection standard, and [2.1.3] directs to Ch.12 Sec.10 [1]–[5] for freeing port requirements. Ch.12 Sec.10 [2.1.1] gives the freeing port area formula and the height-adjustment rule. The applicable rules version is determined by Pt1.Ch1.Sec2 [1.3], which fixes the rules at the date of contract for construction.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Bulwark opening arrangement: Pt3.Ch11.Sec3 [2.1.2] states that openings in bulwarks shall provide protection at least equivalent to the horizontal courses specified in Ch.12 Sec.10 [6.1] and [6.2], and that vertical rails or bars spaced approximately 230 mm apart MAY be accepted in lieu of horizontal rails. Therefore the vertical-bar arrangement at 230 mm spacing is acceptable.

Step 2 — Minimum freeing port area (base): Navigate to Pt3.Ch12.Sec10 [2.1.1] as directed by Pt3.Ch11.Sec3 [2.1.3]. The well length ℓ_b = 28 m (> 20 m), so the formula branch is A = 0.07 × ℓ_b = 0.07 × 28 = 1.96 m² per side.

Step 3 — Height correction: The bulwark average height is 1.35 m, which exceeds 1.2 m by 0.15 m (i.e. 1.5 increments of 0.1 m). Per [2.1.1], the area must be increased by 0.004 m² per metre of well length per 0.1 m excess height. Correction = 0.004 × 28 × 1.5 = 0.168 m². Minimum required area = 1.96 + 0.168 = 2.128 m² per side.

Step 4 — Compliance check: The designer's proposed area of 2.10 m² < 2.128 m² required. Therefore the freeing port area is NOT compliant; the minimum required is 2.128 m² per side.

Step 5 — Applicable rules version: Per Pt1.Ch1.Sec2 [1.3.1], the rules in force at the date of contract for construction apply.

question_text:
A 185 m bulk carrier with double-bottom ballast tanks is being designed. The ballast tank boundary stiffeners on the inner side of the double bottom are T-bar longitudinal stiffeners with a web depth of 320 mm and a web net thickness of 7.5 mm. The design load set WB-3 governs, and the required net section modulus for these stiffeners has been calculated as 680 cm³. The permissible bending stress coefficient Cs applicable to these stiffeners under the governing load set is 0.95. The actual net elastic section modulus of the selected profile is 720 cm³. The stiffener web plate has a yield stress ReH = 315 N/mm².

The designer proposes to verify the stiffener section modulus using the formula applicable to ships of this length, and also needs to confirm that the web plate slenderness is acceptable. Specifically:
1. Is the proposed section modulus of 720 cm³ sufficient, and what is the minimum required section modulus according to the applicable rule formula?
2. Does the web plate of the T-bar stiffener satisfy the slenderness requirement, and what is the minimum net web thickness required by the slenderness rule?
required_facts: The longitudinal stiffeners on the inner side of the double bottom under design load set WB-3 must satisfy the section modulus formula from the general stiffener rules (Pt3.Ch6.Sec5 [1.1.2])
The actual section modulus of 720 cm³ exceeds the required 680 cm³ and is therefore sufficient
The web plate slenderness requirement for T-bar stiffeners uses Cw = 75
The minimum required net web thickness is approximately 4.94 mm, calculated as (320/75)·√(315/235)
The proposed web thickness of 7.5 mm satisfies the slenderness requirement
The slenderness check for the stiffener web references the depth hw as defined in the slenderness requirements section (Pt3.Ch8.Sec2)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec5 [3.1] identifies that longitudinal stiffeners on inner side of double bottom on ballast tank boundaries under WB-3 must use the section modulus formula from Pt3.Ch6.Sec5 [1.1.2]. Pt3.Ch6.Sec5 [1.1.2] gives the section modulus formula and references hw as shown in Ch.8 Sec.2. Pt3.Ch8.Sec2 [3.1.1] gives the slenderness requirement for the stiffener web plate: tw ≥ (hw/Cw)·√(ReH/235), with Cw = 75 for T-bars.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec5 [3.1]: The stiffener is a longitudinal stiffener on the inner side of the double bottom on a ballast tank boundary, governed by design load set WB-3. This triggers the requirement that the section modulus Z shall not be taken less than the design value given in Pt3.Ch6.Sec5 [1.1.2], determined with tc = tres.

Step 2 — Pt3.Ch6.Sec5 [1.1.2]: The required net section modulus Z (cm³) is given by the formula involving the design pressure P, effective bending span, stiffener spacing, and permissible bending stress coefficient Cs. The scenario states the calculated required Z = 680 cm³ and the actual Za = 720 cm³. Since Za = 720 cm³ > Z_required = 680 cm³, the section modulus is sufficient.

Step 3 — Pt3.Ch6.Sec5 [1.1.1] references hw as shown in Ch.8 Sec.2, directing the designer to Pt3.Ch8.Sec2 for slenderness.

Step 4 — Pt3.Ch8.Sec2 [3.1.1]: For T-bar stiffeners, the web plate slenderness requirement is: tw ≥ (hw/Cw)·√(ReH/235), with Cw = 75 for T-bars (from Table 2). With hw = 320 mm and ReH = 315 N/mm²: tw_min = (320/75)·√(315/235) = 4.267 · √1.3404 = 4.267 · 1.1578 = 4.94 mm. The proposed tw = 7.5 mm > 4.94 mm, so the web plate satisfies the slenderness requirement.

scenario_parameters.location: inner side of double bottom, ballast tank boundary

question_text: A 185 m RO/RO vessel is being designed with a stern door that also serves as a vehicle ramp. The door has a light opening area of 15 m² and is located below the freeboard deck. The door plating panels have a net thickness of 11 mm, with stiffener spacing of 550 mm. The vessel length is 185 m. The door structure includes knuckled longitudinal stringers within the span, and at one knuckle location a tripping bracket is fitted to support the face plate but no additional support is provided for the knuckled web section. The strength deck has large cargo hatchways with corners located in a region where the longitudinal deck girder alongside the hatchway has a breadth b_L = 2.8 m, the cross deck strip breadth b_Q = 1.8 m, the rule length L_13 = 185 m, and the hatchway corner is of type HC1 (between a longitudinal deck strip and a closed area). The total longitudinal bending moment at the relevant cross section is 4,200,000 kNm, the hatchway corner plate gross thickness t_i = 22 mm, the longitudinal structural member gross plate thickness t_D = 22 mm, the gross moment of inertia I_y-gr = 180 m⁴, the hatchway corner is located 9.5 m above the baseline, the neutral axis is at 7.2 m above the baseline, and the corner is at x/L = 0.45. The material factor k_i = 1.0. Determine: (1) whether the stern door plate slenderness is compliant, identifying the applicable slenderness coefficient C and the minimum required net thickness; (2) whether the knuckle support arrangement at the stringers within the door structure is compliant; and (3) for the strength deck hatchway corners, calculate the required minimum corner radius r using the appropriate formula, and state whether an insert plate is required if the calculated r exceeds r_min.
required_facts: Slenderness coefficient C = 100 applies to outer shell plating for vessels with L ≥ 90 m
Minimum required net plate thickness for the stern door panels = 5.5 mm (= 550/100); the 11 mm provided is compliant
The knuckle support arrangement is NOT compliant because no tripping bracket or equivalent is fitted to support the knuckled web section of the stringer
For ships with large deck openings, hatch corner radii on the strength deck must be determined using the formula r ≥ c_1 · c_2 with r ≥ r_min = 0.15 m
Calculated required corner radius r ≈ 0.294 m, which exceeds r_min = 0.15 m
An insert plate is required at the hatch corners because the calculated r exceeds r_min

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Stern door/ramp buckling and slenderness requirements in Pt3.Ch12.Sec5 reference Pt3.Ch8.Sec2 for slenderness; Ch8.Sec2 plate slenderness references stiffener spacing as defined in Ch3.Sec7; detail design rules for knuckled stringers are in Pt3.Ch3.Sec6; and for ships with large deck openings, hatch corner treatment escalates to Pt5.Ch2.Sec2 for the corner radius formula.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Stern door slenderness (Pt3.Ch12.Sec5 [1.3.7] → Pt3.Ch8.Sec2): Pt3.Ch12.Sec5 [1.3.7] states that slenderness requirements given in Ch.8 Sec.2 shall be fulfilled for all doors (including ramps). From Pt3.Ch8.Sec2 [2.2], the net plate thickness must satisfy t_p ≥ b/C. The door is part of the outer shell of a vessel with L = 185 m ≥ 90 m, so from Table 1 the slenderness coefficient C = 100. Minimum required net thickness = 550/100 = 5.5 mm. The provided t_p = 11 mm ≥ 5.5 mm, so the plate slenderness is compliant. Step 2 — Knuckle support at stringers (Pt3.Ch12.Sec5 [1.3.7] → Pt3.Ch8.Sec2 → Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [4.3]): Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [2.1.1(g)] states that when a stiffener or primary supporting member is knuckled within the length of the span, effective support shall be provided by fitting a tripping bracket for the face plate AND a tripping bracket (or equivalent) for the knuckled web section. Only the face plate tripping bracket is fitted; no support is provided for the knuckled web section. Therefore the arrangement is NOT compliant. Step 3 — Hatch corner radius (Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [7.3.5] → Pt5.Ch2.Sec2 [2.1.1]): Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [7.3.5] directs ships with large deck openings to Pt5.Ch2.Sec2 for hatch corner treatment. From Pt5.Ch2.Sec2 [2.1.1], for HC1 type corner: c_1 = (f_D + ℓ/750)·b_L. With L_13 = 185 m, f_D = 0.25 + 185/2000 = 0.25 + 0.0925 = 0.3425 (strength deck formula). Assuming ℓ = 0 (no large openings forward/aft of superstructure stated), c_1 = 0.3425 × 2.8 = 0.959 m. For c_2: c_s = 1.0 (since 0.3 ≤ x/L = 0.45 < 0.7). c_2 = [M_T·(z_D - z_O)] / [I_y-gr · 175·10³ · c_s] · (t_D/t_i) · (k_i)^(1/4) = [4,200,000 × (9.5 - 7.2)] / [180 × 175,000 × 1.0] · (22/22) · 1.0 = [4,200,000 × 2.3] / [31,500,000] · 1.0 · 1.0 = 9,660,000 / 31,500,000 = 0.3067 m. r ≥ c_1 · c_2 = 0.959 × 0.3067 = 0.294 m, with r_min = 0.15 m for strength deck. Since 0.294 m > 0.15 m, the required radius governs. An insert plate is required when the calculated r exceeds r_min, which it does here.

scenario_parameters.knuckle_support: tripping bracket for face plate only, no web support

question_text: A bulk carrier was classed five years ago and has since undergone several modifications to its cargo hold structure. The owner wants to understand what ongoing obligations apply to maintain the vessel's class standing — specifically, whether there are any special surveys, condition monitoring requirements, or operational restrictions that the classification society imposes on a continuous basis after initial class is granted. Where in the classification rules would the owner find the complete set of requirements governing how class is retained over the life of the vessel?
required_facts: Pt1.Ch1.Sec3 does not itself contain detailed retention-of-class requirements
The section directs the reader entirely to Pt.7 for retention-of-class requirements
All ongoing obligations for maintaining class (surveys, monitoring, restrictions) are governed by Pt.7
The retention-of-class section is a pure cross-reference with no standalone substantive rules

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt1.Ch1.Sec3 contains a single general statement directing the reader to Pt.7 for all retention-of-class requirements; the answerer must recognize this redirect and identify Pt.7 as the governing location
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Locate the retention-of-class rules in Pt1.Ch1.Sec3. Step 2: Read the single clause, which states 'For requirements related to retention of class, see Pt.7.' Step 3: Conclude that Pt.7 is the exclusive source for all retention-of-class obligations, including surveys, condition monitoring, and operational restrictions.

question_text: A 180-metre bulk carrier (without large deck openings) is being assessed for hull girder yield at a midship transverse section. The net moment of inertia about the horizontal neutral axis is 42.5 m⁴, and the horizontal neutral axis is located 8.2 m above the keel reference. A deck stringer plate at z = 16.4 m (top of the section) is made of higher-tensile steel with a material factor k = 0.72. For a particular dynamic load case in seagoing condition, the permissible still water hogging bending moment is 3,850,000 kNm and the vertical wave bending moment for that load case is 2,100,000 kNm. The resulting hull girder longitudinal stress at the deck stringer plate is calculated as 195 N/mm². Does this stress comply with the hull girder yield criterion, and what is the numerical permissible longitudinal stress limit that applies at this location?
required_facts: The applicable permissible longitudinal stress formula is σhg-perm = 205/k
With k = 0.72, the permissible longitudinal stress is 205/0.72 ≈ 284.7 N/mm²
The calculated stress of 195 N/mm² is less than the permissible limit of 284.7 N/mm²
The arrangement complies with the hull girder yield criterion
The ships-without-large-deck-openings rules apply because no large deck openings are present

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the hull girder longitudinal stress design criterion for ships without large deck openings, compute the permissible stress using σhg-perm = 205/k, and compare against the given stress value.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify applicable subsection: the ship has no large deck openings, so the rules in [2] apply, specifically [2.1.2] for the design criterion.
