Step 2 — Compute permissible longitudinal stress: σhg-perm = 205/k = 205/0.72 = 284.7 N/mm². Step 3 — Apply criterion: |σhg| ≤ σhg-perm → |195| ≤ 284.7 → 195 ≤ 284.7. Step 4 — Conclusion: the stress of 195 N/mm² is below the permissible limit of 284.7 N/mm², so the arrangement complies with the hull girder yield criterion.

question_text: A 180 m bulk carrier has a double-bottom ballast tank adjacent to the outer shell on the port side. The tank is intended to carry seawater ballast. A designer is checking the scantlings of the outer shell plating in way of this tank. The ship's scantling draught is 11.2 m and the ballast draught is 6.8 m. For the static and dynamic pressure combination to be applied to the outer shell plating in way of this ballast tank, should the designer use the net difference between internal ballast pressure and external sea pressure, or should the two pressures be considered independently? Identify the correct pressure combination approach and state which design load sets from the standard design load set table apply to this outer shell element, including the acceptance criteria class for each.
required_facts: Because the compartment adjacent to the outer shell is intended to carry liquids (ballast tank), the net difference between internal pressure and external sea pressure shall be used — not independent consideration of the two pressures.
The applicable design load sets for the outer shell in way of a ballast tank include SEA-1 (PS + PW at TSC, AC-II) and SEA-2 (PS at TSC, AC-I) for the sea-pressure-dominated cases.

Load sets TK-1/WB-1 (Pls-1 + Pld − (PS + PW), ballast draught, AC-II), TK-2/WB-3 (max(Pls-4; Pls-ST) − PS, ballast draught, AC-III), and TK-3/WB-4 (Pls-3 − PS, ballast draught, AC-I) apply, with the subtraction terms reflecting the net-difference rule.
Independent consideration of internal and external pressures would only apply if the adjacent compartment were NOT intended to carry liquids.
Five load sets in total apply to the outer shell element: SEA-1, SEA-2, TK-1/WB-1, TK-2/WB-3, and TK-3/WB-4.

annotator_grounding.end_clause: Pt3.Ch6.Sec2 [1.3.1], Table 1 (External shell rows: SEA-1, SEA-2, TK-1/WB-1, TK-2/WB-3, TK-3/WB-4)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pressure combination rule in [1.3.1] governs whether net or independent pressures apply; then Table 1 external shell rows identify the applicable load sets and acceptance criteria.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the element: outer shell plating adjacent to a ballast tank (a compartment intended to carry liquids). Step 2 — Apply [1.3.1] first paragraph: 'If the compartment adjacent to the outer shell is intended to carry liquids, the static and dynamic lateral pressures to be considered are the differences between the internal pressures and the external sea pressures at the corresponding draught.' Since the ballast tank IS intended to carry liquids, the net difference approach applies — not independent pressures. Step 3 — Move to Table 1, External shell (excluding external decks) rows: SEA-1: load component (PS + PW), draught TSC, full load scenario, AC-II. SEA-2: load component PS, draught TSC, AC-I. TK-1 or WB-1: load component Pls-1 + Pld − PS, draught TBAL, ballast scenario, AC-II. TK-2 or WB-3: load component Pls-ST − PS, draught TBAL, AC-III. TK-3 or WB-4: load component Pls-3 − PS, draught TBAL, AC-I. Step 4 — Note that the subtraction of PS in the tank/ballast load sets (TK-1/WB-1, TK-2/WB-3, TK-3/WB-4) is the direct implementation of the net-difference rule from [1.3.1]: internal liquid pressure minus external sea pressure. Step 5 — Confirm: because the compartment carries liquids, the second paragraph of [1.3.1] (independent consideration) does NOT apply here.

scenario_parameters.adjacent_compartment: double-bottom ballast tank (intended to carry liquids)
scenario_parameters.question_focus: pressure combination approach and applicable design load sets

question_text: A 14,000 TEU container ship is being designed with containers stowed in cell guides within the cargo holds. The inner bottom in way of the cell guide footprints has no doubler plates fitted. Additionally, the hatchway coamings in way of the transverse strut connections of the cell guides have not been locally strengthened, and the cell guide lower sections are welded directly to the deck plating edges at the hatchway openings. The design team has calculated reaction forces from container stacks acting on the container support fittings under two load combinations: (LC1) transverse loading with vertical load Fv1, transverse horizontal load Fq, and wind loads included; (LC2) longitudinal/vertical loading with vertical load Fv2, longitudinal horizontal load Fl, and no wind loads. The lashing eye plates on deck are designed for a certified safe working load (SWL) of 250 kN per lashing point, but the hull support structures beneath them have been sized for only 200 kN. Identify all non-compliances in this arrangement and state what corrective measures are required.
required_facts: The hatchway coamings must be strengthened in way of the transverse and longitudinal strut connections of the cell guides — the current arrangement without such strengthening is non-compliant.
Cell guides must not be welded to deck plating edges in way of the hatchways — the current welded arrangement is non-compliant and must be corrected.
Doubler plates must be fitted at the cell guide footprints on the inner bottom — the absence of doubler plates is non-compliant.
Hull support structures for lashing eye plates must be sized to the certified SWL of the lashings (250 kN); sizing them for only 200 kN is non-compliant and the structures must be upgraded to 250 kN.

The two load combinations used (LC1: Fv1 + Fq + wind; LC2: Fv2 + Fl, no wind) correctly match the required load combinations for hull support structures of container support fittings and are compliant.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question exercising three distinct atomic requirements within Pt5.Ch2.Sec9: the cell guide strut connection strengthening requirement (2.2.1), the prohibition on welding cell guides to deck plating edges at hatchways (2.2.1), the doubler plate requirement for cell guide footprints on inner bottom (2.2.2), and the SWL-based strengthening requirement for lashing eye plate hull support structures (3.1.2).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Check 2.2.1 first sentence: hatchway coamings shall be strengthened in way of connections of transverse and longitudinal struts of cell guides. The scenario states coamings have NOT been strengthened → non-compliant. Step 2 — Check 2.2.1 second sentence: cell guides shall NOT be welded to deck plating edges in way of hatchways. The scenario states they ARE welded there → non-compliant. Step 3 — Check 2.2.2: for containers stowed in cell guides in hold, doubler plates shall be arranged for the footprints on inner bottom or stringers. The scenario states no doubler plates are fitted → non-compliant. Step 4 — Check 3.1.2: hull support structures for lashing eye plates shall be strengthened with respect to the lashings' certified SWL. SWL = 250 kN but structures sized for only 200 kN → non-compliant; structures must be upgraded to match 250 kN SWL. Step 5 — Confirm LC1 and LC2 load combinations match Table 1 (they do, so that part of the design is compliant). Total: four non-compliances identified.

question_text: A bulk carrier is assigned a freeboard less than that based on Table B in the ICLL (i.e., it receives a reduced freeboard). The ship has a machinery space casing located in Position 1 on the exposed freeboard deck. The casing is not protected by any adjacent structure such as a poop deck or deckhouse. A single weathertight access door is fitted in the casing, with an outer sill height of 600 mm above the deck. No inner door or inner sill is provided. Is this arrangement compliant with the applicable requirements, and if not, what specific additional features must be provided?
required_facts: The ship is assigned a freeboard less than Table B, which triggers the enhanced requirement for machinery space casing access
Double doors are required for the casing access opening
An inner sill of 230 mm must be provided in addition to the outer sill of 600 mm
The existing arrangement (single door, no inner sill) is NOT compliant
The outer sill of 600 mm alone satisfies the baseline Position 1 sill height requirement but is insufficient given the reduced freeboard assignment

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: the ship is assigned a freeboard less than Table B (reduced freeboard), which triggers the special requirement in [1.1.3] for double doors and an inner sill of 230 mm in addition to the outer sill of 600 mm. The scenario tests whether the answerer recognises the gating condition (freeboard less than Table B) and the resulting mandatory arrangement.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the casing location: Position 1, unprotected by other structures. Step 2 — Check [1.1.1]: access door sill must be at least 600 mm in Position 1. The 600 mm outer sill satisfies this baseline requirement. Step 3 — Check [1.1.3]: because the ship is assigned a freeboard LESS than that based on Table B in the ICLL, double doors are required and an inner sill of 230 mm must be provided in conjunction with the outer sill of 600 mm. Step 4 — The current arrangement has only a single door and no inner sill, so it does NOT comply with [1.1.3]. The required additions are: (a) a second (inner) door, and (b) an inner sill of 230 mm.

question_text: A general cargo vessel has a well formed by bulwarks on the freeboard deck between a forecastle and a midship deckhouse. The bulwark along this well is 28 m long and has an average height of 1.5 m. The ship has standard sheer in way of the well. Determine the minimum required freeing port area (in m²) on each side of the ship for this well, accounting for the bulwark height.
required_facts: The formula A = 0.07 × ℓb applies because ℓb = 28 m exceeds 20 m
Base freeing port area = 1.96 m² per side
Bulwark height of 1.5 m exceeds the 1.2 m threshold, triggering an area increase
Height excess = 0.3 m (3 increments of 0.1 m), each adding 0.004 × 28 = 0.112 m²
Total height correction = 0.336 m²
Minimum required freeing port area = 2.296 m² per side

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the freeing port area formula for ℓb > 20 m, then apply the height correction for bulwarks exceeding 1.2 m average height.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Select formula branch: ℓb = 28 m > 20 m, so use A = 0.07 × ℓb = 0.07 × 28 = 1.96 m².
Step 2 — Check bulwark height correction: average height = 1.5 m > 1.2 m, so an increase applies. Difference = 1.5 − 1.2 = 0.3 m, which is 3 increments of 0.1 m. Increase per increment = 0.004 m² per metre of well length per 0.1 m difference = 0.004 × 28 = 0.112 m² per increment. Total increase = 3 × 0.112 = 0.336 m².
Step 3 — Final area: A_total = 1.96 + 0.336 = 2.296 m² per side.

question_text: A newbuild container ship is being designed with a hatch side coaming structure. The coaming plates are made from NV 47 steel with an as-built thickness of 72 mm. The upper deck plating is also NV 47 with a thickness of 68 mm. At one block-to-block joint, the hatch coaming plate and the upper deck plate butt welds are aligned in a straight line with no shift between them. Does this section's scope apply to this vessel, and are any special brittle crack arrest countermeasures required for the hatch coaming structure? If so, which option(s) — design-based or welding-quality-based — must be implemented, and does the NV 47 material trigger any additional requirements beyond those applicable to NV 36 or NV 40 steel of the same thickness?
required_facts: The section applies because the vessel is a container ship with NV 47 steel coaming plates of 72 mm thickness, which is within the 50–100 mm range covered by 1.1.1
The hatch coaming as-built thickness of 72 mm is the controlling parameter for Table 1, and since it exceeds the minimum threshold, countermeasures are required
For NV 47 steel at 72 mm, Table 1 requires brittle crack arrest countermeasures including both design-based (Option A) and/or welding-quality-based (Option B) measures
Because NV 47 material is applied, the additional requirements of section [3] must also be implemented — these are not required for NV 36 or NV 40 at the same thickness
The straight-line alignment of the hatch coaming and upper deck butt welds with no shift qualifies them as block butt joints, placing them within the scope of brittle crack arrest design requirements

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Check scope applicability (1.1.1: container ship, NV 47, thickness 50–100 mm), then determine controlling parameter for Table 1 (hatch coaming as-built thickness = 72 mm), then read Table 1 to identify which measures apply for NV 47 at 72 mm, then apply 1.1.2 for the NV 47 additional requirements from [3], then note 2.2.4 regarding straight-line butt joints counted as block butt joints.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Scope check (1.1.1): The vessel has class notation 'Container ship', uses NV 47 steel, and the coaming plate thickness is 72 mm, which is >50 mm and ≤100 mm. All conditions of 1.1.1 are met, so this section applies. Step 2 — Controlling parameter (2.2.1 / Table 1): The thickness and steel strength group of the hatch coaming structure are the controlling parameters. The as-built hatch coaming thickness is 72 mm (>50 mm threshold), so countermeasures are not waived. Step 3 — Table 1 lookup: For NV 47 steel at 72 mm leading plate thickness, Table 1 specifies which measures (1 through 5) apply. Based on the table structure described, NV 47 at this thickness range triggers Measures 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 (all measures), meaning both Option A (design-based: shift in block joints, crack arrest plates/holes) and Option B (welding quality: high toughness welds + increased NDT) countermeasures are required. Step 4 — NV 47 additional requirements (1.1.2): Because NV 47 material is used per 1.1.1, the requirements in [3] must additionally be applied — these go beyond what is required for NV 36 or NV 40 at the same thickness. Step 5 — Straight-line joint (2.2.4 guidance note): The butt welds of the hatch coaming plate and upper deck plate are aligned in a straight line with no shift, which per the guidance note classifies them as block butt joints regardless of whether they are assembly or sub-assembly joints, confirming they are within scope of the brittle crack arrest design requirements.

question_text: A naval architect is designing a deckhouse side panel for a vessel. The panel is a flat plate with a length (longer dimension) of 800 mm and a breadth (shorter dimension) of 400 mm. The design pressure PA for the deckhouse side under the SEA-1 load set is 35 kN/m². The plate is made of ordinary mild steel. Using the correction factor for panel aspect ratio αp, calculate the value of αp for this panel and determine whether the computed value must be capped before use in scantling calculations.
required_facts: αp = 1.2 − b/(2.1·a) where a is the longer panel dimension and b is the shorter dimension
Substituting a = 800 mm and b = 400 mm gives αp = 1.2 − 400/1680 ≈ 0.962
The computed value 0.962 is less than 1.0, so the cap of 1.0 does not apply
αp is used directly as ≈ 0.962 in subsequent scantling calculations
The relevant design pressure for the deckhouse side panel under SEA-1 is PA

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: read the αp formula from the Symbols block, substitute a=800 mm and b=400 mm, compute the result, then apply the stated upper-bound cap of 1.0.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 – Identify the formula from the Symbols block: αp = 1.2 − b/(2.1·a), not to be taken greater than 1.0. Step 2 – Substitute a = 800 mm, b = 400 mm: αp = 1.2 − 400/(2.1 × 800) = 1.2 − 400/1680 = 1.2 − 0.2381 = 0.9619. Step 3 – Compare with cap: 0.9619 < 1.0, so the cap does NOT apply; the value is used as computed. Step 4 – Note that PA (deckhouse side, SEA-1) is the relevant design pressure per Table 1 for deckhouse side plate and stiffeners.

question_text: A 180 m general cargo vessel is being designed with a pronounced flare bow. The ship has a forecastle deck. At a station 0.12L forward of the forward end, the measured flare angle α is 44°. Further aft, at a station 0.17L from the forward end, the flare angle α is 42°. At a station 0.22L from the forward end, the flare angle α is 38°. The minimum design ballast draught T_BAL is 4.2 m. Determine the longitudinal extent of the bow impact strengthening zone that must be applied to this vessel, clearly stating the forward and aft limits and the vertical extent.
required_facts: The base bow impact strengthening zone starts at 0.1L (18 m) from the forward end
Because the flare angle exceeds 40° at 0.10L from F.E., the zone is extended to 0.15L (27 m) from F.E.
Because the flare angle exceeds 40° at 0.15L from F.E., the zone is further extended to 0.20L (36 m) from F.E.
Because the flare angle at 0.20L from F.E. is 38° (not greater than 40°), no further extension to 0.25L is required
The final longitudinal extent of the bow impact strengthening zone is forward of 0.20L (36 m) from the forward end
The vertical extent runs from the minimum design ballast draught T_BAL (4.2 m) up to the forecastle deck
Aft of 0.1L from F.E., bow impact strengthening is only required where the flare angle exceeds 5°

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the stepped extension rules in [1.1.3] sequentially — base zone is 0.1L, first extension to 0.15L triggered if α > 40° at 0.10L, second extension to 0.20L triggered if α > 40° at 0.15L, third extension to 0.25L would require α > 40° at 0.20L. Vertical extent runs from T_BAL to forecastle deck.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Base zone is forward of 0.1L from F.E. (= 18 m from F.E. for a 180 m ship). Step 2: Check first extension trigger — is α > 40° at 0.10L from F.E.? The scenario states α = 44° at 0.12L, but the rule checks at 0.10L. However, the question places the measurement at 0.12L; the answerer must note the rule checks at 0.10L. For the purposes of this question the flare at 0.10L is implicitly captured by the 0.12L station being > 40°, so the zone extends to 0.15L (= 27 m). Step 3: Check second extension trigger — is α > 40° at 0.15L from F.E.? The scenario states α = 42° at 0.17L ≈ 0.15L station, which is > 40°, so the zone extends further to 0.20L (= 36 m). Step 4: Check third extension trigger — is α > 40° at 0.20L from F.E.? The scenario states α = 38° at 0.22L ≈ 0.20L station, which is NOT > 40°, so no further extension. Final longitudinal extent: forward of 0.20L from F.E. (= 36 m from F.E.). Vertical extent: from T_BAL (4.2 m) up to the forecastle deck. Aft of 0.1L, strengthening applies only where α > 5°.

question_text: A bulk carrier of 185 m length operates on unrestricted service with a single deck arrangement. At the transverse section located at the forward end of the engine room, the permissible still water bending moment in hogging is 4 200 000 kNm and the vertical wave bending moment in hogging is 2 800 000 kNm. The computed vertical hull girder ultimate bending capacity M_U at this section is 11 500 000 kNm. The vessel has class notation HC(B*) and its loading manual includes alternate loading conditions with empty cargo holds. Does this section satisfy the hull girder ultimate strength criterion in hogging, and what is the numerical value of the total partial safety factor γ_R that must be applied to M_U?
required_facts: The section applies because L = 185 m > 150 m, unrestricted service, and single deck arrangement all satisfy the applicability conditions
The design bending moment M = 7 560 000 kNm (computed as 1.0 × 4 200 000 + 1.2 × 2 800 000)
γ_DB = 1.25 in hogging because the vessel has class notation HC(B*) with empty cargo holds
The allowable capacity M_U / γ_R = 8 363 636 kNm (approximately 8 364 000 kNm)
The criterion M ≤ M_U / γ_R is satisfied (7 560 000 kNm ≤ 8 363 636 kNm)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: verify applicability (L > 150 m, unrestricted service, single deck), compute M from γ_S·M_sw-U + γ_W·M_wv, determine γ_DB for hogging with HC(B*) notation and empty holds, compute γ_R = γ_M · γ_DB, then check M ≤ M_U / γ_R
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Applicability check [1.1.1]: L = 185 m > 150 m ✓, unrestricted service ✓, single deck ✓. The section applies. The forward end of the engine room is an explicitly listed check location [1.1.2].

Step 2 — Compute design bending moment M [2.2.1]: M = γ_S · M_sw-U + γ_W · M_wv = 1.0 × 4 200 000 + 1.2 × 2 800 000 = 4 200 000 + 3 360 000 = 7 560 000 kNm.

Step 3 — Determine γ_DB [2.1.2]: The vessel has class notation HC(B*) and the loading manual includes alternate loading conditions with empty cargo holds. The rule states γ_DB = 1.25 for vessels with empty cargo holds and class notation HC(A) or HC(B*), or HC(M) if alternate loading conditions are included in the loading manual. HC(B*) with empty holds qualifies → γ_DB = 1.25 (hogging).

Step 4 — Compute γ_R [2.1.2]: γ_R = γ_M × γ_DB = 1.1 × 1.25 = 1.375.

Step 5 — Check criterion [2.1.2]: M_U / γ_R = 11 500 000 / 1.375 = 8 363 636 kNm. Since M = 7 560 000 kNm ≤ 8 363 636 kNm, the criterion is satisfied.

question_text:
A general cargo ship has a rule length L2 of 148 m and is constructed in steel with a material factor k = 1.0. During the structural review, the following net thicknesses are proposed for various structural elements:

1. Keel plating: 11.5 mm
2. Side shell plating at a location 3.2 m above the top of continuous superstructure (TSC): 9.8 mm
3. Weather deck plating (strength deck, not sheltered, contributing to hull girder longitudinal strength): 9.2 mm
4. Watertight transverse bulkhead (not contributing to longitudinal strength): 5.0 mm
5. Bottom centreline girder in the cargo area (below a longitudinal bulkhead): 9.4 mm
6. A floor in the aft peak tank (reduced floor type): 9.2 mm

For each element, determine whether the proposed net thickness meets the minimum requirement. Identify any elements that are non-compliant and state the minimum required net thickness for each.
required_facts: Keel plating minimum required thickness is 12.4 mm; proposed 11.5 mm is non-compliant
Side shell plating at 3.2 m above TSC minimum required thickness is approximately 9.78 mm; proposed 9.8 mm is compliant
Weather deck (strength deck) minimum required thickness is 7.46 mm; proposed 9.2 mm is compliant
Watertight transverse bulkhead not contributing to longitudinal strength has its minimum thickness capped at 5.0 mm by footnote; proposed 5.0 mm is compliant
Bottom centreline girder in cargo area below longitudinal bulkhead minimum required thickness is 9.44 mm; proposed 9.4 mm is non-compliant
Floor in aft peak tank (reduced floor) minimum required thickness is 8.70 mm; proposed 9.2 mm is compliant

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question requiring application of Table 1 (plating), Table 2 footnotes, and Table 3 (primary supporting members) within Pt3.Ch6.Sec3, including footnote conditions for watertight bulkheads and aft peak tank floors.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Formula: t = a + b * L2 * sqrt(k), with k=1.0 and L2=148 m.

1. Keel plating (Table 1, Shell — Keel): a=5.0, b=0.05 → t_min = 5.0 + 0.05*148*1.0 = 5.0 + 7.4 = 12.4 mm. Proposed 11.5 mm < 12.4 mm → NON-COMPLIANT.

2. Side shell at 3.2 m above TSC (Table 1, Side shell — 'From TSC to TSC+4.6 m'): a=4.6 (reading the table row for side shell from upper end of bilge to TSC+4.6 m), b=0.035 → t_min = 4.6 + 0.035*148 = 4.6 + 5.18 = 9.78 mm. Proposed 9.8 mm ≥ 9.78 mm → COMPLIANT (marginally).

3. Weather deck (strength deck, Table 1, Deck — Weather deck): a=4.5 (from the deck row for weather/strength deck boundary for cargo tanks etc. — actually the weather deck row gives a=4.5, b=0.02 for weather deck and strength deck) → t_min = 4.5 + 0.02*148 = 4.5 + 2.96 = 7.46 mm. Proposed 9.2 mm ≥ 7.46 mm → COMPLIANT.

4. Watertight transverse bulkhead not contributing to longitudinal strength (Table 1, Bulkheads — Watertight bulkheads): a=4.5, b=0.01 → t_min = 4.5 + 0.01*148 = 4.5 + 1.48 = 5.98 mm. However, footnote 8 states: 'For transverse watertight bulkhead and longitudinal watertight bulkhead not contributing to longitudinal strength, net minimum thickness need not be taken greater than 5.0 mm.' So t_min is capped at 5.0 mm. Proposed 5.0 mm = 5.0 mm → COMPLIANT (exactly at the capped minimum).

5. Bottom centreline girder in cargo area below longitudinal bulkhead (Table 3, PSM): a=5.0, b=0.03 → t_min = 5.0 + 0.03*148 = 5.0 + 4.44 = 9.44 mm. Proposed 9.4 mm < 9.44 mm → NON-COMPLIANT.

6. Floor in aft peak tank (reduced floor, Table 3): a=5.0, b=0.025 (footnote 1 applies) → t_min = 5.0 + 0.025*148 = 5.0 + 3.70 = 8.70 mm. Proposed 9.2 mm ≥ 8.70 mm → COMPLIANT.

question_text: A naval architect is reviewing the structural design package for a new 180-metre general cargo vessel built from welded steel with a conventional single-hull monohull form and a standard transverse framing arrangement. The vessel has been assigned the class notation CSR by the classification society. The designer intends to use the hull structure requirements from the main class hull chapters (covering general arrangement, structural design principles, loads, hull girder strength, local scantlings, FEA, buckling, fatigue, special requirements, hull equipment, openings, and welding) as the sole basis for demonstrating compliance. The rudder arrangement and stability booklet are being prepared separately under dedicated chapters. Is the designer's approach to rule compliance complete and correct? Identify any gaps in the proposed compliance strategy.
required_facts: For a vessel with class notation CSR, the separate CSR requirements replace Pt.3 Ch.1 through Ch.13
Ch.14 (Rudders and steering) and Ch.15 (Stability) still apply to CSR ships and are not replaced
The exceptions retained from Ch.1–Ch.13 for CSR ships are limited to certification requirements in Sec.3 [4] and documentation requirements in Sec.3 [2.2] not specified in CSR
The designer's plan to use the standard Pt.3 Ch.1–Ch.13 chapters as the hull structure compliance basis is incorrect for a CSR-notated vessel
The compliance gap is the failure to apply the separate CSR hull structure requirements in place of Ch.1–Ch.13

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: the CSR notation clause in Pt3.Ch1.Sec1 [1.1.2] specifies exactly which Pt.3 chapters are replaced by CSR requirements and which are retained, so the answerer must identify the gap between what the designer proposes and what the rule actually requires.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the vessel type: monohull welded steel, class notation CSR. Step 2 — Locate the CSR application rule: Pt3.Ch1.Sec1 [1.1.2] states that for CSR ships, separate CSR requirements replace Ch.1 through Ch.13, EXCEPT for (a) certification requirements in Sec.3 [4] and (b) documentation requirements for items in Sec.3 [2.2] not specified in CSR. Ch.14 (Rudders and steering) and Ch.15 (Stability) also apply to CSR ships. Step 3 — Evaluate the designer's plan: the designer correctly plans to use Ch.14 and Ch.15. However, the designer incorrectly proposes to use Ch.1–Ch.13 as the compliance basis; for a CSR vessel those chapters are replaced by the separate CSR requirements (with the narrow exceptions for Sec.3 [4] and Sec.3 [2.2]). The gap is that the designer must apply the CSR requirements for hull structure (Ch.1–Ch.13 equivalent) rather than the standard Pt.3 chapters, and must also ensure the Sec.3 certification and documentation exceptions are addressed.

scenario_parameters.designer_proposed_chapters: Ch.1 to Ch.13 (standard Pt.3), Ch.14, Ch.15
scenario_parameters.threshold_tested: CSR notation triggers replacement of Ch.1–Ch.13 with separate CSR requirements

question_text: A bulk carrier has a ship length L = 220 m, breadth B = 32 m, and block coefficient C_B = 0.82. The designer needs to determine the minimum permissible still water bending moment in the hogging condition at the midship region (x = 0.5L) for seagoing operations, to be used as a guidance value at the preliminary design stage. The vertical wave bending moment for strength assessment amidships in hogging condition (M_wv-h-mid) has been calculated as 1,850,000 kNm. What is the minimum permissible still water hogging bending moment M_sw-h-min at midship, and what wave coefficient C_w applies to this vessel?
required_facts: f_sw = 1.0 at x = 0.5L because 0.3L ≤ x ≤ 0.7L
M_sw-h-min = f_sw × (171 × C_w × L² × B × (C_B + 0.7) × 10^-3 − M_wv-h-mid)
M_sw-h-min ≈ 2,189,500 kNm (accepting ±5,000 kNm rounding tolerance)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: determine C_w from the piecewise formula for L=220m (falls in 90≤L≤300 branch), then apply f_sw=1.0 at midship (0.3L≤x≤0.7L), then compute M_sw-h-min using the hogging formula.

question_text: A 95-metre general cargo vessel has a flat bar stiffener installed on a tight floor inside a ballast tank. The stiffener web depth is 180 mm and the net web thickness is 6 mm. The stiffener material has a specified minimum yield stress of 235 N/mm². The double bottom girders are arranged at every 3rd longitudinal spacing. Does this flat bar stiffener comply with the web slenderness requirement, and what is the maximum permissible web depth-to-thickness ratio for this specific arrangement?
required_facts: The applicable slenderness coefficient Cw for this flat bar is 30, not the base value of 22
The Cw = 30 applies because all three conditions are met: flat bar on tight floors, inside ballast tank, and double bottom girders at every 3rd longitudinal spacing
The minimum required web thickness is hw/Cw * sqrt(ReH/235) = 180/30 * 1.0 = 6.0 mm
The actual net web thickness of 6 mm exactly meets the minimum requirement
The stiffener is compliant (just at the limit)
The maximum permissible web depth-to-thickness ratio for this arrangement is 30

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply stiffener web slenderness formula from [3.1.1](a), then identify the correct Cw from Table 2 for a flat bar stiffener on tight floors inside a ballast tank with girders at every 3rd longitudinal spacing (footnote 4: Cw = 30), then check hw/tw against the threshold.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify stiffener type — flat bar. Step 2: Go to Table 2 for flat bars. Base Cw = 22. Step 3: Check footnote 4: Cw = 30 applies when the flat bar stiffener is on tight floors AND arranged inside ballast tank AND double bottom girders are at every 3rd longitudinal spacing. All three conditions are met here. Step 4: Apply formula from [3.1.1](a): tw >= hw/Cw * sqrt(ReH/235). With ReH = 235 N/mm², sqrt(235/235) = 1.0, so tw >= hw/Cw = 180/30 = 6.0 mm. Step 5: The actual tw = 6 mm, which exactly meets the minimum requirement (6 >= 6.0). The stiffener is just compliant. The maximum permissible hw/tw ratio is Cw = 30, giving hw_max = 30 * 6 = 180 mm for this thickness.

question_text: A bulk carrier with a scantling length of 180 m, breadth of 32 m, and block coefficient CB = 0.82 is being assessed for strength under the extreme sea loads design load scenario. The vessel has service area notation R2 and is fitted with bilge keels. The metacentric height GM has not been calculated, so default values are to be used. The loading condition draught TLC is 9.5 m and the scantling draught TSC is 12.0 m. Calculate the roll angle θ (in degrees) for this strength assessment, and determine whether the heading correction factor fβ takes the value 1.0 or 0.8 for a BSR load case under this scenario.
required_facts: fβ = 0.8 for BSR load cases under the extreme sea loads design load scenario
fr = 0.8 for service area notation R2
fps = fr = 0.8 for extreme sea loads design load scenario with service restriction
fp = fps = 0.8 for strength assessment
fBK = 1.0 because the ship is fitted with bilge keels

GM = 0.25 × B = 0.25 × 32 = 8.0 m, taken from Pt5.Ch1.Sec2 [5.1.2] Table 4 for the bulk-carrier homogeneous-heavy-cargo, partially filled, full-load condition (Pt5 overrides the Pt3.Ch4.Sec3 generic default GM = 0.07 × B for ships with class notation Bulk carrier or Ore carrier)

Roll angle θ must be re-derived using the bulk-carrier-specific k_r = 0.42 × B = 13.44 m (Pt5.Ch1.Sec2 [5.1.2] Table 4) together with GM = 8.0 m and the Pt3.Ch4.Sec3 roll-angle formula; the generic-default-based value of ≈18° derived from k_r = 0.39B / GM = 0.07B is not applicable for a bulk carrier

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Roll angle formula requires fps for strength assessment, which depends on design load scenario and service restriction notation; fβ for BSR load case is explicitly 0.8; fr for R2 is 0.8; fps = fr = 0.8 for extreme sea loads with service restriction; GM default for bulk carrier uses general formula GM = 0.07B; fBK = 1.0 for bilge keel; kr = 0.39B in general (bulk carrier kr/GM defined in Pt5 but default general values apply here since no Pt5 override is invoked in the question context).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — fβ: The question asks about a BSR load case under extreme sea loads design load scenario. From the symbols section, fβ = 0.8 for BSR and BSP load cases for the extreme sea loads design load scenario. Answer: fβ = 0.8.

Step 2 — fps: For strength assessment under extreme sea loads design load scenario for a vessel with service restriction (R2 notation), fps = fr. From the fr table, R2 = 0.8 reduction → fr = 0.8. Therefore fps = 0.8.

Step 3 — fp: For strength assessment, fp = fps = 0.8.

Step 4 — fBK: Ship is fitted with bilge keels → fBK = 1.0.

Step 5 — GM: GM not calculated; general default GM = 0.07B = 0.07 × 32 = 2.24 m. Check minimum: 0.05B = 0.05 × 32 = 1.6 m. 2.24 > 1.6, so GM = 2.24 m.

Step 6 — kr: Default kr = 0.39B = 0.39 × 32 = 12.48 m.

Step 7 — Tθ: Tθ = (2.3π × kr) / √(g × GM) = (2.3π × 12.48) / √(9.81 × 2.24) = (90.13) / √(21.974) = 90.13 / 4.688 ≈ 19.23 s.

Step 8 — θ: θ = [9000 × (1.4 − 0.035 × Tθ) × fp × fBK] / [(1.15B + 55) × π]
= [9000 × (1.4 − 0.035 × 19.23) × 0.8 × 1.0] / [(1.15 × 32 + 55) × π]
= [9000 × (1.4 − 0.6731) × 0.8] / [(36.8 + 55) × π]
= [9000 × 0.7269 × 0.8] / [91.8 × π]
= [5233.7] / [288.4]
≈ 18.15 deg.

question_text: A 175-metre general dry cargo vessel is being designed to carry solid bulk cargoes. The vessel has five cargo holds and is intended to operate at a scantling draught with all holds loaded. The designer proposes to assign the vessel a class notation that reflects its bulk cargo carrying capability, but the maximum cargo density of the intended cargoes is 2.4 t/m³. Does the vessel require a mandatory additional class notation related to its maximum cargo density, and if so, what is the specific notation that must be assigned?
required_facts: The vessel qualifies for mandatory HC(B) notation because it is a general dry cargo ship with L ≥ 150 m, at least five cargo holds, and all holds loaded at scantling draught
The 'Maximum cargo density ρ' notation is mandatory for vessels with HC(B) notation when the maximum cargo density is less than 3.0 t/m³
The vessel's maximum cargo density of 2.4 t/m³ is less than the 3.0 t/m³ threshold, triggering the mandatory notation
The required notation is 'Maximum cargo density (2.4)' with ρ = 2.4 t/m³
Design requirements for the Maximum cargo density notation reference Pt.6 Ch.1 Sec.4 and DNV-RU-SHIP-CSR Sec.1

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The vessel's characteristics (general dry cargo, L ≥ 150 m, five cargo holds, all holds loaded at scantling draught) trigger mandatory HC(B) notation. HC(B) vessels designed for a maximum cargo density less than 3.0 t/m³ must also carry the mandatory 'Maximum cargo density ρ' notation, where ρ = 2.4 t/m³.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify vessel type — general dry cargo ship, L = 175 m ≥ 150 m, five cargo holds, all holds loaded at scantling draught. Step 2: From Table 1, HC(B) is defined as 'Strengthened to carry dry bulk cargoes of density ≥ 1.0 t/m³ with all holds loaded at scantling draught'. The mandatory application column states HC with qualifiers A, B, B*, C or M are mandatory for 'General dry cargo ship designed for carriage of solid bulk cargoes, with L ≥ 150 m, having minimum five cargo holds'. This vessel qualifies for mandatory HC(B). Step 3: From Table 1, the 'Maximum cargo density ρ' notation is mandatory for 'vessels with class notation BC(A), BC(B), HC(A), HC(B) or HC(B*) designed for a maximum cargo density < 3.0 t/m³'. The vessel has HC(B) and its maximum cargo density is 2.4 t/m³ < 3.0 t/m³. Therefore the Maximum cargo density notation is mandatory. Step 4: The notation to be assigned is 'Maximum cargo density (2.4)' where ρ = 2.4 t/m³.

scenario_parameters.loading_condition: all holds loaded at scantling draught

question_text: A structural engineer is reviewing the load assessment plan for a new 180-metre bulk carrier. The design team has prepared two separate assessment packages: one for hull girder ultimate strength and one for fatigue life of the side shell longitudinals. For the strength package, the team proposes using wave-induced dynamic loads calibrated to a probability level of 10⁻⁵, arguing this is conservative enough for a bulk carrier trading in the North Atlantic. For the fatigue package, the team proposes using loads at a probability level of 10⁻⁴, citing similarity to other projects. A reviewer flags both probability levels as incorrect. What are the correct probability levels that must be used for the wave-induced dynamic loads in the strength assessment and in the fatigue assessment respectively, and are the proposed levels acceptable?
required_facts: The correct probability level for wave-induced dynamic loads in the strength assessment is 10⁻⁸
The correct probability level for loads in the fatigue assessment is 10⁻²
The proposed strength assessment probability level of 10⁻⁵ is not acceptable
The proposed fatigue assessment probability level of 10⁻⁴ is not acceptable
Strength assessment excludes fatigue criteria

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-clause question: Pt3.Ch4.Sec1 [1.1.3] directly defines the required probability levels for strength assessment (10⁻⁸) and fatigue assessment (10⁻²).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the relevant clause: Pt3.Ch4.Sec1 [1.1.3] 'Probability level for strength and fatigue assessments' states: strength assessment wave-induced dynamic loads are at a probability level of 10⁻⁸; fatigue assessment loads correspond to a probability level of 10⁻². Step 2 — Compare proposed values: the team proposed 10⁻⁵ for strength (incorrect; must be 10⁻⁸) and 10⁻⁴ for fatigue (incorrect; must be 10⁻²). Step 3 — Conclusion: both proposed probability levels are non-compliant and must be corrected.

question_text: A newly built bulk carrier has a double bottom structure. During the design review, the inner bottom plating manholes in the cargo holds are assessed. The manhole covers fitted in the inner bottom plating within the cargo holds are plain steel plates welded flush, with no additional protective measures applied. The edges of the manholes are ground smooth, and reinforcement rings are welded around each manhole opening in the inner bottom plating. Is this arrangement fully compliant with the classification rules for access to double bottom compartments, and if not, which specific element is non-compliant?
required_facts: The arrangement is not fully compliant with the classification rules.
Smooth manhole edges satisfy the requirement for smooth edges.
Reinforcement rings on inner bottom plating manholes satisfy that specific requirement.
Manhole covers in the inner bottom plating within cargo holds must be effectively protected.
Plain flush-welded steel plates with no additional protective measures do not constitute effective protection of the manhole covers.
The non-compliant element is the lack of effective protection on the manhole covers in the cargo hold inner bottom plating.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-clause question: Pt3.Ch2.Sec4 [1.2.1] specifies requirements for manholes in double bottom compartments, including smooth edges, reinforcement rings on inner bottom plating manholes, and effective protection of manhole covers in cargo holds.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify the applicable rule for double bottom access — Pt3.Ch2.Sec4 [1.2.1]. Step 2: Check each requirement in [1.2.1]: (a) manholes shall be cut in inner bottom, floors and longitudinal girders — satisfied; (b) edges of manholes shall be smooth — satisfied (edges are ground smooth); (c) manholes in inner bottom plating shall have reinforcement rings — satisfied (rings are welded); (d) manhole covers in inner bottom plating in cargo holds shall be effectively protected — NOT satisfied (plain flush-welded steel plates with no additional protective measures do not constitute 'effective protection'). Step 3: Conclude the arrangement is non-compliant because the manhole covers in the cargo hold inner bottom plating are not effectively protected.

scenario_parameters.manhole_cover_protection: plain flush-welded steel, no additional protection
scenario_parameters.location: inner bottom plating in cargo holds

question_text: A horizontal stiffener on a transverse bulkhead of a 75 m general cargo vessel is being designed. The stiffener is a flat bar profile, continuous with fixed ends, spanning an effective bending span of 2.4 m and an effective shear span of 2.3 m. The design lateral pressure at the load calculation point is 18.5 kN/m² (acting on the plate side), the stiffener spacing is 0.65 m, the effective shear depth is 180 mm, and the material yield strength ReH is 235 N/mm². The hull girder longitudinal stress at the load calculation point is +42 N/mm² (tension). The acceptance criteria being applied is AC-II. Determine the minimum required net web thickness tw for this stiffener.
required_facts: Cm = 1.0 because the ship length is less than 90 m and the profile is a flat bar
fshr = 0.5 for a horizontal stiffener with fixed ends (from Table 1)
Ct = 0.90 for AC-II acceptance criteria (from Table 2)
tw = (Cm × fshr × |P| × s × ℓshr) / (dshr × Ct × τeH) ≈ 0.63 mm

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the web thickness formula in Sec5 [1.1.1], selecting correct fshr from Table 1 for a horizontal stiffener with fixed ends, Ct from Table 2 for AC-II, and Cm = 1.0 because ship length < 90 m and profile is a flat bar.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Identify Cm: Ship length is 75 m (< 90 m) AND profile is a flat bar. Per [1.1.1], Cm = 1.0 for ships of length less than 90 m and for flat bars and bulb profiles. So Cm = 1.0.

Step 2 — Identify fshr from Table 1: The stiffener is horizontal and continuous with fixed ends. From Table 1, for 'Horizontal stiffeners' under 'continuous stiffeners with fixed ends', fshr = 0.5.

Step 3 — Identify Ct from Table 2: Acceptance criteria is AC-II. From Table 2, Ct = 0.90 for all stiffeners under AC-II.

Step 4 — Compute τeH: τeH = ReH / √3 = 235 / 1.7321 = 135.67 N/mm².

Step 5 — Apply the web thickness formula:
tw = (Cm × fshr × |P| × s × ℓshr) / (dshr × Ct × τeH)
= (1.0 × 0.5 × 18.5 × 0.65 × 2.3) / (0.180 × 0.90 × 135.67)

Numerator: 1.0 × 0.5 × 18.5 × 0.65 × 2.3 = 0.5 × 18.5 × 1.495 = 0.5 × 27.6575 = 13.829 kN/m (units consistent when s in m, ℓshr in m, P in kN/m², dshr in m)
= 13.829

Denominator: 0.180 × 0.90 × 135.67 = 0.162 × 135.67 = 21.978

tw = 13.829 / 21.978 = 0.629 mm

Note: checking unit consistency — P [kN/m²] × s [m] × ℓshr [m] gives kN/m; dshr [m] × τeH [N/mm² = kN/m² × 10³ ... need to reconcile]. The formula as written in the rule uses dshr in mm and τeH in N/mm², with P in kN/m², s in m, ℓshr in m, giving tw in mm:

tw = (Cm × fshr × |P| × s × ℓshr) / (dshr × Ct × τeH)
= (1.0 × 0.5 × 18.5 × 0.65 × 2.3) / (180 × 0.90 × 135.67)

Numerator: 13.829 (kN/m² × m × m = kN)
Denominator: 180 × 0.90 × 135.67 = 21,978.5 (mm × N/mm² = N = 10⁻³ kN × 10³ ... )

Applying the standard DNV unit convention where the formula yields tw in mm with P in kN/m², s in m, ℓshr in m, dshr in mm, τeH in N/mm²:

tw = (1.0 × 0.5 × 18.5 × 0.65 × 2.3 × 1000) / (180 × 0.90 × 135.67)
= 13829 / 21978.5
= 0.629 mm

So tw_min ≈ 0.63 mm. This is a very thin result driven by the small pressure and short span; the governing minimum will typically come from other criteria (e.g. minimum thickness rules), but the formula-derived value is ~0.63 mm.

scenario_parameters.stiffener_type: flat bar, horizontal, continuous, fixed ends

question_text: A ro-ro ferry has a stern door that also serves as a vehicle ramp. The door has a light opening area of 9 m². The door leads directly into an enclosed ro-ro cargo space. During the structural design review, the naval architect proposes to use securing bolts as the primary means of transferring sea pressure to the hull coamings, rather than arranging direct load transfer through the coaming structure. Is this arrangement acceptable under classification rules? Additionally, the door/ramp is intended to be used in harbour condition — does this trigger any additional structural check beyond the standard sea pressure assessment, and if so, what type of check is required?
required_facts: The light opening area of 9 m² is less than the 12 m² threshold, so direct sea pressure transfer to coamings is not mandatory
Securing bolts are acceptable as carriers of sea pressure to the coamings for doors with A < 12 m², provided direct transfer is not feasible
Because the door also acts as a vehicle ramp used in harbour condition, an additional buckling check is required
The additional buckling check required for ramps in harbour condition is per Ch.8 Sec.4
Standard slenderness requirements per Ch.8 Sec.2 must also be fulfilled regardless of ramp function

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: check the 12 m² threshold in [1.3.3] vs [1.3.4] to determine whether securing bolts are permissible, then check [1.3.7] for the ramp-in-harbour buckling requirement.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Threshold check for sea pressure transfer: [1.3.3] states that doors with light opening area A ≥ 12 m² must transfer sea pressure directly to hull coamings. [1.3.4] states that for doors with A < 12 m², securing bolts or similar devices may be accepted as carriers of sea pressure to the coamings, if direct transfer is not feasible. The door has A = 9 m², which is less than 12 m², so securing bolts are permissible (subject to the condition that direct transfer is not feasible). Step 2 — Ramp in harbour buckling check: [1.3.7] states that an additional buckling check according to Ch.8 Sec.4 is only required for doors acting as ramps in harbour condition. Since this door also serves as a vehicle ramp and is used in harbour condition, the additional buckling check is triggered. The standard slenderness requirements of Ch.8 Sec.2 also apply per [1.3.7].

question_text: A seagoing bulk carrier is being assessed for hull girder strength at a transverse section amidships. The designer has identified the following load components to apply for the normal seagoing operation design load scenario: vertical bending moment equal to Msw + Mwv-LC, horizontal bending moment equal to Mwh-LC, vertical shear force equal to Qsw + Qwv-LC, and torsional moment equal to Mst + Mwt-LC. The external shell pressure on the underwater hull is taken as PS + PW, and the boundaries of water ballast tanks are loaded with Pℓs-1 + Pℓd. For the internal structures inside those ballast tanks, the designer proposes to apply a pressure of Pℓs-1 + Pℓd as well, reasoning that internal structures should see the same load as the tank boundaries. Is this combination of load components correct for the normal seagoing operation scenario, and specifically, is the proposed pressure for internal structures inside the ballast tanks consistent with the principal design load scenarios?
required_facts: Design Load Scenario 2 (Normal operation at sea) is an S+D (Static + Dynamic) scenario
Hull girder loads VBM = Msw + Mwv-LC, HBM = Mwh-LC, VSF = Qsw + Qwv-LC, and TM = Mst + Mwt-LC are all correct for Scenario 2
External shell pressure PS + PW is correct for scenario 2
Boundaries of water ballast tanks loaded with Pℓs-1 + Pℓd is correct for scenario 2
Internal structures in tanks must use Pint (not Pℓs-1 + Pℓd) for scenario 1
The designer's proposed pressure for internal structures inside ballast tanks is incorrect

annotator_grounding.end_clause: Pt3.Ch4.Sec7 Table 1 (Load scenario 1 — Normal operation at sea)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: the answerer must read Table 1 in Pt3.Ch4.Sec7 and identify the correct load components for Design Load Scenario 1 (Normal operation at sea, S+D), then check each proposed load component against the table, specifically noting that internal structures in tanks use Pint (not Pℓs-1 + Pℓd) for scenario 1.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify Design Load Scenario 1 as 'Normal operation at sea' — this is an S+D (Static + Dynamic) scenario. Step 2: Check each proposed hull girder load against Table 1, column 1: VBM = Msw + Mwv-LC ✓, HBM = Mwh-LC ✓, VSF = Qsw + Qwv-LC ✓, TM = Mst + Mwt-LC ✓. Step 3: Check external shell pressure: PS + PW ✓. Step 4: Check boundaries of water ballast tanks: Pℓs-1 + Pℓd ✓. Step 5: Check internal structures in tanks for scenario 1: Table 1 shows Pint for internal structures in tanks under scenario 1 (Normal operation at sea), NOT Pℓs-1 + Pℓd. The designer's proposal to use Pℓs-1 + Pℓd for internal structures is therefore incorrect — the correct pressure is Pint (minimum pressure for internal structures in tanks).

question_text: A structural engineer is performing a fine mesh finite element analysis on a critical bracket toe detail of a bulk carrier. The fine mesh zone uses a uniform element size of 30 mm × 30 mm. At the location of interest, the individual element von Mises stresses (evaluated at element centroids) are as follows across a 2×2 group of elements: 320 N/mm², 345 N/mm², 310 N/mm², and 365 N/mm². All four elements have equal area. The material yield strength R_Y is 355 N/mm², and the applicable permissible fine mesh utilisation factor λ_fperm is 1.0 (Acceptance Criteria class AC-I). The analysis uses shell elements (not rod elements), and this is not an AC-III condition. Does the detail comply with the acceptance criteria, and what is the governing von Mises stress value that must be compared against the permissible limit?
required_facts: Because the mesh size (30 mm × 30 mm) is smaller than the standard 50 mm × 50 mm, an area-weighted average von Mises stress must be computed over an area equal to 50 mm × 50 mm before comparison with the permissible limit
The area-weighted average von Mises stress σ_vm-av = (320 + 345 + 310 + 365) / 4 = 335 N/mm²
The fine mesh yield utilisation factor λ_f = 335 / 355 ≈ 0.944
λ_f = 0.944 does not exceed the AC-I permitted value λ_fperm = 1.36f_f or 1.2f_f, depending on weld adjacency, so the detail complies with the acceptance criteria
The governing stress for comparison is 335 N/mm² (the averaged value), not the peak element stress of 365 N/mm²

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The question targets the mesh-size averaging rule: when mesh size is smaller than the standard 50 mm × 50 mm, the engineer must compute a weighted-average von Mises stress over an area equivalent to 50 mm × 50 mm before comparing to the permissible stress. This requires reading clause 4.2.2(a) (trigger: mesh < 50 mm), then applying the weighted-average formula in 4.2.2(b), then checking against λ_fperm.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify reference stress: per [4.1], reference stress is von Mises stress σ_vm evaluated at element centroid using membrane direct axial and shear stresses. Step 2 — Note mesh size: 30 mm × 30 mm < 50 mm × 50 mm, so per [4.2.2(a)], an average von Mises stress over an area equal to 50 mm × 50 mm must be used instead of the peak element stress. Step 3 — Compute average: per [4.2.2(b)], σ_vm-av = Σ(A_i × σ_vm-i) / Σ(A_i). All elements have equal area, so σ_vm-av = (320 + 345 + 310 + 365) / 4 = 1340 / 4 = 335 N/mm². Step 4 — Compute utilisation factor: λ_f = σ_vm / R_Y = 335 / 355 = 0.944. Step 5 — Check acceptance: λ_f = 0.944 ≤ λ_fperm = 1.0 → the detail complies. The governing stress is 335 N/mm² (the area-weighted average), NOT the peak element stress of 365 N/mm².

question_text: A 180-metre bulk carrier has a double-side skin space running along the cargo hold region. The shipyard proposes to leave a narrow void space at the forward end of the ship, approximately 400 mm wide between two structural members, without any protective coating or corrosion prevention treatment, on the basis that the space is too tight to apply coating during construction and will be sealed off permanently. Is this arrangement acceptable under classification rules, and what corrosion protection requirement applies to this space?
required_facts: The 400 mm void qualifies as a narrow space subject to corrosion protection requirements.
Narrow spaces shall generally be protected by an efficient protective product.
The forward end of the ship is explicitly identified as a location where the requirement is particularly important due to inaccessibility for inspection and maintenance.
The shipyard's proposal to leave the space uncoated is not acceptable under the rules.
The inaccessibility of the space does not exempt it from protection — it reinforces the need for protection.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: the narrow space at the forward end of the ship triggers Pt3.Ch3.Sec4 [1.1.2], which specifically addresses narrow spaces and their corrosion protection requirement, with particular emphasis on ends of the ship where inspections and maintenance are not easily practicable due to inaccessibility.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify the space as a 'narrow space' — a 400 mm wide void between structural members qualifies as a narrow space. Step 2: Apply Pt3.Ch3.Sec4 [1.1.2]: narrow spaces shall generally be protected by an efficient protective product. Step 3: Note the specific aggravating condition — the space is at the forward end of the ship, which is explicitly called out in [1.1.2] as a location where inspections and maintenance are not easily practicable due to inaccessibility. Step 4: Conclude that the shipyard's proposal to leave the space uncoated is not acceptable; an efficient protective product must be applied, and the forward-end location makes this requirement even more critical, not less.

scenario_parameters.space_type: narrow void space in double-side skin region

question_text: A tank access hatch on the freeboard deck of a bulk carrier has a rectangular cover measuring 0.65 m × 0.85 m (area = 0.5525 m²). The cover is made of mild steel and is secured to the coaming by bolts spaced 420 mm apart along the long sides, with the corner bolts located 230 mm from each corner. The designer proposes a gross plate thickness of 11.5 mm for the cover. Is this hatch cover arrangement compliant with classification requirements? Identify all aspects that are non-compliant and state the minimum required values.
required_facts: The minimum required gross thickness for a hatch cover with area ≥ 0.5 m² is 12.5 mm
The proposed thickness of 11.5 mm is less than the required 12.5 mm and is therefore non-compliant
Stiffening is not required because the hatch area (0.5525 m²) does not exceed 1.25 m²
The maximum permitted fastening spacing is 380 mm; the proposed 420 mm spacing exceeds this limit and is non-compliant
The corner fastening distance of 230 mm is within the 250 mm maximum and is compliant

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question exercising three sub-rules within Sec7: minimum cover thickness for area ≥ 0.5 m² (2.1.2), stiffening requirement for area > 1.25 m² (2.1.3), and fastening spacing/corner distance limits (2.1.4)
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Thickness check per [2.1.2]: Cover area = 0.5525 m², which is ≥ 0.5 m², so minimum gross thickness = 12.5 mm. Proposed thickness of 11.5 mm is less than 12.5 mm → NON-COMPLIANT. Step 2 — Stiffening check per [2.1.3]: Area = 0.5525 m² < 1.25 m², so stiffening is NOT required → compliant on this point. Step 3 — Fastening spacing per [2.1.4]: Maximum allowed spacing = 380 mm; proposed spacing = 420 mm → NON-COMPLIANT. Step 4 — Corner distance per [2.1.4]: Maximum allowed = 250 mm from corners; proposed = 230 mm → COMPLIANT.

question_text: A structural engineer is performing a fatigue assessment for a welded bracket detail located in a water ballast tank on a bulk carrier with a 25-year design life. The detail is assessed using the hot spot stress approach. The vessel operates exclusively in worldwide trade (not North Atlantic). Prescriptive loads from the standard load calculation method are used — no hydrodynamic scatter diagram analysis has been performed. The detail is located at a longitudinal end connection and the initial calculated fatigue life before any post-weld treatment is 14 years. The designer proposes applying weld toe grinding to improve the fatigue life of this detail. (1) What S-N curve must be used for this welded detail? (2) What environmental factor fe applies? (3) How many years of the 25-year design life must be treated as time in corrosive environment, and what adjustment must be made to the damage estimate for that period? (4) Is the proposed weld toe grinding acceptable under the applicable rules, and if not, why not?
required_facts: S-N curve D (FAT 90) must be used for the hot spot stress approach on welded joints
fe = 0.8 applies for worldwide wave environment with prescriptive loads
Time in corrosive environment TC,25 = 5 years for a water ballast tank over a 25-year design life
The damage estimate for the 5 years in corrosive environment must be multiplied by two
Weld toe grinding is NOT acceptable because post-weld treatment is not applicable to longitudinal end connections
Weld toe grinding is also NOT acceptable because the initial fatigue life of 14 years is below the required minimum of 17 years prior to post-weld treatment

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question covering S-N curve selection (4.1), environmental factor (4.2), corrosive environment time and damage multiplier (4.4 + Table 1), and post-weld treatment eligibility conditions (4.6)
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — S-N curve (4.1): For welded joints assessed by hot spot stress approach, S-N curve D (FAT 90) shall be used. Step 2 — Environmental factor (4.2): For prescriptive loads (not scatter diagram), worldwide wave environment → fe = 0.8. Step 3 — Corrosive environment (4.4 + Table 1): Water ballast tank → TC,25 = 5 years out of TD = 25 years. The S-N curves from 4.1 can be used for both periods, but the damage estimate for the 5 years in corrosive environment shall be multiplied by two. Step 4 — Post-weld treatment (4.6): Two conditions are violated: (a) post-weld treatment is NOT applicable to longitudinal end connections — this detail is at a longitudinal end connection; (b) the initial calculated fatigue life prior to post-weld treatment must be minimum 17 years, but here it is only 14 years. Therefore the proposed weld toe grinding is NOT acceptable.

scenario_parameters.detail_location: water ballast tank, longitudinal end connection

question_text: A transverse web frame in a bulk carrier has a depth of 1200 mm. Longitudinal stiffeners pass through cut-outs in this web frame. One of the cut-outs has a depth of 620 mm and a breadth of 90 mm, with no lug or collar plate fitted. The cut-out has square corners (corner radius R = 0 mm). Is this arrangement compliant with classification rules? If not, identify all violations and state the minimum required corner radius R for the cut-out.
required_facts: The 50% depth limit for cut-outs without lug or collar plate equals 600 mm (50% of 1200 mm PSM depth)
The cut-out depth of 620 mm exceeds the 600 mm limit, so the arrangement is non-compliant under [1.1.2] unless shear and buckling capacity are verified
The minimum corner radius R is the greater of 20% of cut-out breadth b or 25 mm
20% of b = 20% × 90 mm = 18 mm, which is less than 25 mm, so the governing minimum is 25 mm
The actual corner radius R = 0 mm violates the minimum requirement of 25 mm
The arrangement has two violations: cut-out depth exceeds 50% limit and corner radii are non-compliant

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: check cut-out depth limit against PSM depth (1.1.2), then check corner radius requirement (1.1.6)
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Apply [1.1.2]: The total depth of cut-outs without lug or collar plate shall not exceed 50% of the depth of the primary supporting member. PSM depth = 1200 mm, so limit = 0.50 × 1200 = 600 mm. The actual cut-out depth is 620 mm > 600 mm. Therefore the cut-out depth VIOLATES [1.1.2] unless shear strength and buckling capacity are demonstrated to be sufficient. Step 2 — Apply [1.1.6]: Corner radii R shall be at least the greater of (a) 20% of the breadth b of the cut-out, or (b) 25 mm, but need not exceed 50 mm. Cut-out breadth b = 90 mm. 20% × 90 = 18 mm. Since 18 mm < 25 mm, the governing minimum is 25 mm. The actual R = 0 mm, which violates [1.1.6]. Minimum required R = 25 mm.

question_text:
A small passenger ferry operates exclusively on a sheltered inland lake, never venturing into open sea. The vessel's designer intends to assign it a service area notation that reflects this operational profile. The class certificate appendix will record the service area restrictions accordingly. During a design review, the following three questions arise:

1. Which service area notation is appropriate for this vessel, and what is the corresponding significant wave height coefficient (expressed in terms of Cw)?
2. The ferry is flagged under Norway and will operate under Norwegian domestic requirements as a local trade vessel. How should the service area notation appear on the class certificate?
3. The designer also wants to understand which aspects of the vessel's design may be modified as a result of this restricted service area notation compared to a vessel built for unrestricted trade — list all categories of design modifications that the rules identify as potentially affected.
required_facts: The correct service area notation for an inland lake (enclosed waters) is RE
The significant wave height for RE is 0.4Cw, where Cw is the wave coefficient
With Norwegian flag under local trade provisions, the notation on the class certificate must be written as RE(nor)
Design hull girder loads may be modified under a restricted service area notation
Design pressures on shell, weather decks, superstructures and deckhouses may be modified
Anchoring and mooring equipment requirements may be modified
Stability requirements may be modified

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: identify RE notation from Table 1 for enclosed waters, read HS coefficient, then apply 1.1.3 for flag-state parenthetical notation, then list 1.1.2 modification categories
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Clause 1.1.1 states that the notation RE is limited to enclosed waters such as fjords, ports, rivers and lakes. An inland lake qualifies. From Table 1, RE corresponds to a significant wave height of 0.4Cw. Step 2 — Clause 1.1.3 states that when a flag administration's domestic requirements are applied under local trade provisions, the flag state is indicated in parentheses after the service area notation using lower-case ISO 3166 country codes. Norway's ISO 3166 alpha-3/alpha-2 code used in the example is 'nor', so the notation becomes RE(nor). Step 3 — Clause 1.1.2 lists four categories of design that may be modified: (a) design hull girder loads, (b) design pressures on shell, weather decks, superstructures and deckhouses, (c) anchoring and mooring equipment, (d) stability.

question_text: A container ship is fitted with a lashing computer system that has just been installed on board. The hardware has not been type approved. During the onboard certification test, the numerical output from the lashing computer system for one of the test conditions differs from the approved test conditions by 0.8% of the strength limit. The ship has two nominated computers. The surveyor is present. (a) Can a lashing computer certificate be issued based on this test result? (b) On how many computers must the test be carried out before the certificate can be issued?
required_facts: The 1% acceptance criterion is: |(software result – independent calculation)| / strength limit ≤ ±1%

For onboard certification per [9.6.2], any numerical difference between the installed system output and the approved test conditions prevents certificate issuance, so a 0.8% deviation is by itself a basis for refusal even though it satisfies the ±1% software-approval criterion in [9.5.8]
Because the hardware is not type approved, the test must be carried out on both the first and the second nominated computer
The test must be completed on two computers before the certificate can be issued
Both nominated computers must be identified on the lashing computer certificate

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The question requires applying the 1% acceptance criterion from [9.5.8] to determine whether the 0.8% deviation is within tolerance, then applying the hardware type-approval condition in [9.6.2] to determine how many computers must be tested.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Apply [9.5.8]: The acceptance criterion states the difference between software results and independent calculations shall not be greater than 1% of the strength limit: |(Results from software) – (Results from independent calculations)| / (Strength limits) ≤ ±1%. The observed deviation is 0.8%, which is within the ±1% limit. Therefore the numerical output is acceptable and does NOT prevent certificate issuance on that ground. Step 2 — Apply [9.6.2] hardware condition: 'Where the hardware is not type approved, the test shall be carried out on both the first and the second nominated computer prior to the issuance of the lashing computer certificate.' Since the hardware is not type approved, the test must be performed on both nominated computers (i.e., two computers). Step 3 — Conclusion: (a) A certificate can be issued provided the test is also successfully completed on the second nominated computer, because the 0.8% deviation is within the 1% tolerance. (b) The test must be carried out on both nominated computers — two computers in total.

question_text: A newly built general cargo vessel has a length L_LL of 22 m and is intended to operate without any service restrictions. The owner wants to know whether the vessel must comply with the intact stability requirements under the main class rules. Additionally, the vessel has a loading instrument system installed onboard — does this trigger any specific compliance requirement, and if so, what standard must that system meet?
required_facts: The stability requirements apply only to vessels with L_LL of 24 m and above
The vessel's L_LL of 22 m is below the 24 m threshold, so the vessel does not need to comply with the stability requirements of this section under the main class
The presence of a loading instrument system onboard triggers a specific compliance requirement
The loading instrument system must be in accordance with the requirements in Pt.6 Ch.4 Sec.6

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: check the length threshold in [1.1.1] (24 m minimum) to determine applicability, then check [1.1.4] for the loading instrument system requirement.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Apply [1.1.1]: The stability requirements apply to all vessels with L_LL of 24 m and above. This vessel has L_LL = 22 m, which is below the 24 m threshold. Therefore the vessel does NOT fall under the mandatory stability requirements of this section for the main class. Step 2 — Apply [1.1.4]: Regardless of the length threshold question, [1.1.4] states that if a loading instrument system is installed onboard, it shall be in accordance with the requirements given in Pt.6 Ch.4 Sec.6. Since the vessel has such a system installed, that cross-reference requirement is triggered and the system must comply with Pt.6 Ch.4 Sec.6.

question_text: During a direct strength analysis of a bulk carrier, a finite element model of the double bottom structure includes a longitudinal girder web panel that is NOT in line with any longitudinal bulkhead and is NOT connected to the hopper tank side. The panel is composed of 4 finite elements with the following net thicknesses and areas: element 1 has area 0.012 m² and thickness 14.0 mm; element 2 has area 0.018 m² and thickness 16.0 mm; element 3 has area 0.015 m² and thickness 13.5 mm; element 4 has area 0.010 m² and thickness 15.0 mm. The elements are made of two different steel grades: elements 1 and 3 have a specified yield stress of 315 MPa, while elements 2 and 4 have a specified yield stress of 355 MPa. For the buckling assessment of this panel: (a) which boundary condition category (A or B) applies, (b) what is the average thickness t_avr to be used in the buckling check, and (c) what yield stress R_eH_P must be used for the panel?
required_facts: Boundary condition B (SP-B) applies to the web of double bottom longitudinal girders not in line with a longitudinal bulkhead and not connected to hopper tank side
t_avr is calculated as the area-weighted average: Σ(A_i × t_i) / Σ(A_i)
t_avr = 14.70 mm (numerator 0.8085 m²·mm, denominator 0.055 m²)
R_eH_P is taken as the minimum specified yield stress among all elements in the panel
R_eH_P = 315 MPa

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: Table 1 determines boundary condition (SP-B for double bottom longitudinal girder web not in line with longitudinal bulkhead), clause 2.1.2 gives the area-weighted average thickness formula, clause 2.1.3 gives the minimum yield stress rule.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Boundary condition: From Table 1, 'Web of double bottom longitudinal girders not in line with longitudinal bulkhead or not connected to hopper tank side' maps to assessment method SP-B (with superscript 5), which corresponds to Boundary Condition B. Step 2 — Average thickness: Apply formula t_avr = Σ(A_i × t_i) / Σ(A_i). Numerator = (0.012×14.0) + (0.018×16.0) + (0.015×13.5) + (0.010×15.0) = 0.168 + 0.288 + 0.2025 + 0.150 = 0.8085 m²·mm. Denominator = 0.012 + 0.018 + 0.015 + 0.010 = 0.055 m². t_avr = 0.8085 / 0.055 = 14.70 mm (rounded to 2 decimal places). Step 3 — Yield stress: Per clause 2.1.3, R_eH_P is the MINIMUM of the specified yield stresses of elements within the panel. Elements 1 and 3 have 315 MPa, elements 2 and 4 have 355 MPa. Minimum = 315 MPa.

scenario_parameters.structural_element: double bottom longitudinal girder web, not in line with longitudinal bulkhead, not connected to hopper tank side

question_text: A structural engineer is reviewing the fabrication quality requirements for a 310-metre container ship currently in the design approval stage. The vessel has a declared yield strength of 390 N/mm² for the upper deck longitudinal plating, with plate thicknesses of 55 mm in the region between 0.2L forward of midship and 0.2L aft of midship. The fabrication team proposes to apply ISO 5817 quality level C uniformly across all structural areas of the vessel, citing that this meets the minimum standard for all ship types. Is this proposal acceptable for the upper hull longitudinal structure in the specified amidships region, and what is the correct quality level that must be applied there?
required_facts: The proposal to apply ISO 5817 quality level C uniformly is not acceptable for the upper hull longitudinal structure in the amidships region
ISO 5817 quality level B is required for container ships in the upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships for critical areas
The region described (between 0.2L forward and 0.2L aft of midship) falls within the 0.4L amidships zone
The plating qualifies as a critical area because its yield strength R_eH = 390 N/mm² meets the threshold of ≥ 390 N/mm²
The plating also qualifies as a critical area because its thickness of 55 mm exceeds the 50 mm threshold stated in the guidance note
ISO 5817 quality level C remains the correct minimum for all other areas of the vessel not meeting the container ship exception criteria

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The workmanship clause in Sec3 [2] establishes that ISO 5817 level C is the baseline for all ship types, but container ships require level B for upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships. The guidance note defines 'critical areas' as those with yield strength ≥ 390 N/mm² or thickness > 50 mm — both thresholds are met here.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: The baseline rule states ISO 5817 quality level C applies to all ship types. Step 2: An exception exists for container ships — ISO 5817 quality level B is required for upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships for critical areas. Step 3: The vessel is a container ship, so the exception is triggered. Step 4: The region described (±0.2L from midship = within 0.4L amidships) falls within the specified zone. Step 5: The guidance note defines critical areas as those with yield strength R_eH ≥ 390 N/mm² OR thickness > 50 mm. Step 6: The plating has R_eH = 390 N/mm² (meets the ≥ 390 threshold) AND thickness = 55 mm (exceeds 50 mm threshold). Step 7: Both criteria independently confirm this is a critical area. Step 8: Therefore ISO 5817 quality level B is required, not level C. The proposal to apply level C uniformly is not acceptable for this region.

scenario_parameters.region: 0.2L forward to 0.2L aft of midship (within 0.4L amidships)

question_text: During detail design review of a bulk carrier, a naval architect is evaluating a longitudinal shell knuckle located within the 0.6L midship region. The knuckle angle is 7 degrees (a shallow knuckle). The nearest support stiffening fitted in line with the knuckle is positioned 68 mm away from the knuckle line. Is this arrangement compliant with the classification rules? If not, what is the maximum permissible distance, and under what alternative condition could the 68 mm distance potentially be accepted?
required_facts: A knuckle angle of 7 degrees qualifies as a shallow knuckle because it is less than 10 degrees
For shallow knuckles, the maximum permissible distance between the knuckle and the support stiffening is 75 mm
The general (non-shallow) limit within 0.6L is 50 mm, but this does not apply here
The proposed distance of 68 mm is less than 75 mm, so the arrangement is compliant
An alternative arrangement with a distance exceeding 75 mm may be accepted based on fatigue analysis in accordance with Ch.9

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-clause question: apply the distance threshold rule for shallow knuckles within 0.6L, check the 7-degree angle against the shallow-knuckle definition (less than 10 degrees), compare the 68 mm distance against the 75 mm limit for shallow knuckles, and identify the fatigue-analysis alternative.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify knuckle type: the knuckle angle is 7 degrees, which is less than 10 degrees, so this qualifies as a shallow knuckle per clause 2.1.1(f). Step 2 — Apply the shallow-knuckle distance limit: for shallow knuckles (angles less than 10 degrees), the maximum permissible distance between the knuckle and the support stiffening in line with the knuckle is 75 mm (not the general 50 mm limit, which applies to non-shallow knuckles within 0.6L). Step 3 — Check compliance: the proposed distance is 68 mm, which is less than 75 mm, so the arrangement IS compliant. Step 4 — Alternative: even if the distance exceeded 75 mm, an alternative arrangement could be accepted based on a fatigue analysis in accordance with Ch.9.

question_text: A structural designer is sizing a flat bar stiffener located inside a ballast water tank on a carbon-manganese steel bulk carrier. The stiffener web is fully immersed in the ballast water environment, but its connection to the attached plating is at the inner bottom, which forms the boundary between the ballast tank below and a dry void space above. The gross offered thickness of the stiffener web is 12 mm. Calculate the total corrosion addition t_c that must be applied to this stiffener, and determine whether the calculated value needs to be capped. Use t_res = 0.5 mm.
required_facts: The stiffener web uses the boundary-member branch based on its connection to attached plating, giving t_c = 1.0 + 1.0 + 0.5 = 2.5 mm before capping
The connection to attached plating at the inner bottom boundary (ballast tank / void space) gives t_c = 1.0 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 2.0 mm
Per the stiffener-connection rule, the boundary value, not the 2.5 mm internal-member value, governs for the web
The cap t_c_max = 0.2 × 12 mm = 2.4 mm
Since 2.0 mm is below 2.4 mm, the total corrosion addition remains t_c = 2.0 mm
t_res = 0.5 mm is included in all corrosion addition calculations regardless of environment

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: determine corrosion addition for a stiffener whose web is in a ballast water tank but whose connection to plating is at the inner bottom boundary between ballast tank and void space. Apply stiffener rule (1.2.6), multi-value rule (1.2.7), and cap rule (1.2.5).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the stiffener rule (1.2.6): the corrosion addition of a stiffener is determined according to the location of its connection to the attached plating. The connection is at the inner bottom, which is the boundary between the ballast water tank (below) and a dry void space (above). Step 2 — Determine t_c1 and t_c2 for the inner bottom plate boundary: side 1 (ballast water tank) → Table 1 gives t_c1 = 1.0 mm; side 2 (void space, upper surface of deck/bottom plate) → Table 1 gives t_c2 = 0.5 mm (upper surface of decks or bottom plate of void/dry space). Step 3 — Apply formula 1.2.1 for a boundary member: t_c = t_c1 + t_c2 + t_res = 1.0 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 2.0 mm. Step 4 — However, per 1.2.6, the stiffener corrosion addition is determined by the location of its connection to the attached plating. The stiffener web itself is exposed to ballast water on both sides (it is an internal member within the ballast tank). Per 1.2.2 for an internal member: t_c = 2*t_c1 + t_res = 2*1.0 + 0.5 = 2.5 mm. Step 5 — Per 1.2.7, when a stiffener is affected by more than one value, the largest applies. The web (internal to ballast tank) gives 2.5 mm; the connection zone (boundary) gives 2.0 mm. Largest = 2.5 mm applies to the web. Step 6 — Check cap per 1.2.5: t_c_max = 0.2 * t_gr_off = 0.2 * 12 = 2.4 mm. Since 2.5 mm > 2.4 mm, the value must be capped at 2.4 mm.

scenario_parameters.connection_location: inner bottom (boundary between ballast tank and void space above)
