annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply the simplified design pressure formula for pneumatic tyres when footprint data is unavailable (2.1.2), using the default P_0 formula for road transporters, then check whether Q=12t is below the 15t threshold that mandates footprint data (2.1.3).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify applicable formula: Since footprint dimensions are not available and tyres are pneumatic, clause 2.1.2 applies. Step 2 — Determine P_0: For road transporters (not cargo handling vehicles), P_0 = 120*(sqrt(Q+3)) kN/m². With Q=12t: P_0 = 120*sqrt(12+3) = 120*sqrt(15) = 120*3.873 = 464.8 kN/m². Step 3 — Determine w: Single wheels → w = 1.0. Step 4 — Compute P_wl-2 (at sea): P_wl-2 = (P_0/w)*(1 + a_z/g) = (464.8/1.0)*(1 + 0.35) = 464.8*1.35 = 627.5 kN/m². Step 5 — Check 2.1.3 threshold: Q=12t < 15t, so footprint data is NOT mandatory; the simplified approach of 2.1.2 is permitted.

question_text: A structural engineer is reviewing the buckling assessment for a stiffened deck panel on a bulk carrier. The panel is part of the continuous inner deck plating (not a web of a primary supporting member). During a static loading condition (design load scenario AC-I, still water only), the calculated buckling utilization factor for the panel is 0.83. Is the panel's buckling strength considered acceptable under the classification rules, and what is the maximum allowable buckling utilization factor that applies in this case?
required_facts: The applicable structural member category is 'Plates and stiffeners/stiffened panels'
The design load scenario is AC-I (still water, S loads only)
The allowable buckling utilization factor η_all = 0.80 for plates/stiffened panels under AC-I
The acceptance criterion requires η_act ≤ η_all
η_act = 0.83 exceeds η_all = 0.80, so the panel fails the buckling check
The η_all = 0.85 exception does not apply because harbour/special operations loads are not involved

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the buckling acceptance criterion from [3.3.1] (η_act ≤ η_all), then look up η_all for plates/stiffened panels under AC-I from Table 3.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the structural member type: the panel is continuous inner deck plating, which falls under 'Plates and stiffeners/stiffened panels' in Table 3. Step 2 — Identify the boundary condition context: continuous large panels use Boundary Condition A (all edges forced to remain straight), consistent with the plate/stiffened panel category. Step 3 — Identify the design load scenario: AC-I corresponds to still-water (S) loads only. Step 4 — Look up η_all from Table 3: for Plates and stiffeners/stiffened panels under AC-I (S), η_all = 0.80. Note: the footnote 3 exception (η_all = 0.85) applies only when hull girder permissible loads for harbour or special operations are applied, which is not the case here. Step 5 — Apply acceptance criterion from [3.3.1]: η_act (0.83) ≤ η_all (0.80)? No, 0.83 > 0.80. Step 6 — Conclusion: the panel does NOT have acceptable buckling strength; it fails the AC-I criterion by a margin of 0.03.

question_text: During the newbuilding design review of a bulk carrier, a structural engineer is checking compliance for a deck plating panel. The net required thickness calculated from structural analysis is 14.2 mm, and the applicable corrosion addition for that location is 3.0 mm. The shipyard proposes to install plates with an as-built thickness of 18.5 mm, and the owner has declared a voluntary corrosion margin of 0.5 mm on top of the rule-required corrosion addition. Determine: (1) the gross required thickness for this panel, (2) the gross offered thickness, (3) the net offered thickness, and (4) whether the proposed plating is compliant with the classification rules.
required_facts: The gross offered thickness (18.0 mm) is greater than or equal to the gross required thickness (17.0 mm)
The proposed plating is compliant with the classification rules
The voluntary addition (0.5 mm) is excluded from the gross offered thickness and does not count toward rule compliance

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question exercising the three scantling definitions (gross required, gross offered, net offered) and the compliance check, all within Pt3.Ch3.Sec2
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Gross required thickness [1.2.1]: t_gr = min(t + t_c ; 1.25t) = min(14.2 + 3.0 ; 1.25 × 14.2) = min(17.2 ; 17.75) = 17.2 mm. Round to nearest 0.5 mm per [1.3.1]: 17.0 ≤ 17.2 < 17.25, so t_gr = 17.0 mm. Step 2 — Gross offered thickness [1.2.2]: t_gr_off = t_as_built − t_vol_add = 18.5 − 0.5 = 18.0 mm. Step 3 — Net offered thickness [1.2.3]: t_off = t_gr_off − t_c = 18.0 − 3.0 = 15.0 mm. Step 4 — Compliance [1.3.2]: t_gr_off (18.0 mm) ≥ t_gr (17.0 mm), so the plating is compliant.

question_text: A shipbuilder based in a country where DNV has no prior record of completed classification projects is preparing to build a new 8,500 GT general cargo vessel for a Norwegian owner. The owner and shipbuilder signed the main construction contract on 1 March 2024. Six months later, on 1 September 2024, they signed an amendment to the original contract adding two additional sister vessels of the same design. The shipbuilder intends to subcontract the propulsion machinery package to a specialist manufacturer. The subcontractor's integration work will be managed entirely by the subcontractor without direct oversight from the main builder. The shipbuilder has not yet submitted any documentation to the classification society. Identify (a) what the shipbuilder must demonstrate before the Society will proceed with classification, (b) which rules apply to the two additional vessels added by the amendment, and (c) whether the proposed arrangement for subcontracted propulsion integration is acceptable under classification requirements.
required_facts: The shipbuilder, being unfamiliar to the Society, must provide evidence of capability to successfully manage classification projects before classification proceeds
The builder retains full responsibility for integration even when the integration task is subcontracted, and must ensure proper interaction between all involved parties
The proposed arrangement where the subcontractor manages integration entirely without builder oversight is not acceptable under the rules
The two additional vessels added by the 1 September 2024 amendment have a date of 'contract for construction' of 1 September 2024, not 1 March 2024
The amendment is treated as a 'new contract' for the additional vessels, so the rules in force on 1 September 2024 apply to those vessels

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question exercising three distinct sub-rules within Sec2: the unfamiliar builder evidence requirement (1.2.1), the builder's non-delegable integration responsibility (1.2.3), and the contract-amendment date rule for additional vessels (1.3.2 item 3)
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Clause 1.2.1: The shipbuilder is unfamiliar to the Society. The rule requires them to provide evidence of capability to successfully manage classification projects (e.g., prior successful classification with another society, or similar design projects). Without this, the Society may decline the request per 1.1.1. Step 2 — Clause 1.2.3: The builder has full responsibility for integration of and between systems, equipment, components and the vessel. If integration is subcontracted, the builder must ensure proper interaction between all involved parties — the builder cannot simply hand off integration responsibility entirely to the subcontractor. The proposed arrangement (subcontractor managing integration without builder oversight) is therefore not acceptable as stated; the builder must ensure proper interaction. Step 3 — Clause 1.3.2 item 3: The two additional vessels were added by an amendment signed on 1 September 2024, not by the original contract of 1 March 2024. Under item 3, an amendment adding additional vessels is treated as a 'new contract', so the date of 'contract for construction' for those two vessels is 1 September 2024, and the rules in force on that date apply to them.

question_text: A vessel has a plate stem with horizontal stringers spaced 1.8 m apart. The ship has a length L = 120 m and the stem plating is constructed from ordinary mild steel (k = 1.0). The designer proposes a net plate thickness of 14 mm for the region from 0.6 m below the lowest ballast draft up to T_SC + 0.6 m. Is this thickness compliant, and what is the minimum required net thickness for this region? Additionally, what is the upper cap on net thickness that the rules impose regardless of the formula result?
required_facts: minimum required net thickness t ≈ 16.24 mm (accepting 16.2–16.3 mm)
formula used: t = (0.6 + 0.4·S_B)(0.08L + 2.7)√k with S_B = 1.8 m, L = 120 m, k = 1.0
upper cap on net thickness is 22√k − 1 = 21 mm
the formula result (≈16.24 mm) is below the cap, so the cap does not govern
proposed thickness of 14 mm is less than the required 16.24 mm and is therefore not compliant

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the plate stem thickness formula and the upper-bound cap directly from Sec6 [1.1.1]
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the applicable formula from Pt3.Ch10.Sec6 [1.1.1]: t = (0.6 + 0.4·S_B)(0.08L + 2.7)√k. Step 2 — Substitute values: S_B = 1.8 m, L = 120 m, k = 1.0. t = (0.6 + 0.4×1.8)(0.08×120 + 2.7)×√1.0 = (0.6 + 0.72)(9.6 + 2.7)×1 = 1.32 × 12.3 = 16.236 mm. Step 3 — Apply the upper cap: t_max = 22√k − 1 = 22×1 − 1 = 21 mm. Step 4 — The formula gives 16.24 mm (rounded to 2 d.p.), which is below the cap of 21 mm, so the governing minimum is 16.24 mm. Step 5 — The proposed thickness of 14 mm is less than 16.24 mm, so it is NOT compliant.

question_text: A newly built sea-going vessel is designed to carry containers as its primary cargo. The ship is fitted with cell guides at the bulkheads, fixed container foundations on the inner bottom, and fixed lashing appliances on the upper deck and hatch covers. The owner also wants to transport dry bulk grain in the cargo holds during return voyages to improve commercial utilisation. Additionally, the owner requests the class notation 'RSD' to be assigned to the vessel. Under the applicable classification rules, (a) is the proposed dual-purpose operation — containers outbound, dry bulk grain inbound — permissible, and (b) what ship type notation will the vessel receive, and what does the 'RSD' notation specifically require?
required_facts: The transport of dry cargo in bulk is explicitly not permitted under the applicable rules for container ships.

The vessel qualifies for the ship type notation 'Container ship' because it meets all three physical characteristics: cell guides at bulkheads, fixed container foundations on the inner bottom, and fixed lashing appliances on the upper deck and/or hatch covers.
The 'RSD' additional notation requires a global finite element strength analysis.
The 'RSD' notation is applicable to ships holding the 'Container ship' notation.
Break bulk cargo on the inner bottom may be accepted on a case-by-case basis, but this exception does not extend to dry bulk grain.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 application scope (1.3) explicitly prohibits dry bulk carriage; ship type notation (1.4.1 Table 1) assigns 'Container ship'; additional notation RSD (1.4.2 Table 2) requires global finite element strength analysis per Pt.6 Ch.1 Sec.8.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Check application scope (Sec1 [1.3]): The rules apply to sea-going ships primarily intended for container carriage with cell guides, fixed foundations, and fixed lashing appliances — all present. However, [1.3] explicitly states 'The transport of dry cargo in bulk is not permitted.' Therefore the proposed grain voyages are not permissible under these rules. Step 2 — Ship type notation (Sec1 [1.4.1], Table 1): A ship built in compliance with the requirements of this section is assigned the notation 'Container ship'. Step 3 — Additional notation RSD (Sec1 [1.4.2], Table 2): The RSD notation covers 'Requirements for global finite element strength analysis' and applies to ships with the notation 'Container ship', with the design requirements referenced to Pt.6 Ch.1 Sec.8.

question_text: A shipowner is commissioning a new vessel designed to serve as a floating marine biology research station, equipped with underwater observation chambers, specimen collection systems, and onboard laboratory facilities. The vessel does not fit any of the standard ship type categories recognized by the classification society. The owner wants the vessel's classification certificate to reflect its unique purpose and function. The owner asks whether the classification society can formally recognize this vessel's purpose in its class notation, what the notation would look like on the certificate, and whether any specific technical class requirements are attached to this type of notation.
required_facts: A descriptive notation can be assigned when the vessel's purpose or function is not covered by existing notations
The descriptive notation is assigned upon request to the classification society
There are no class requirements associated with a descriptive notation
The descriptive notation is identified on the certificate by use of square brackets, e.g. [Marine biology research station]

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: the vessel's purpose is not covered by existing notations, so a descriptive notation applies under Sec7. All four sub-clauses are needed to fully answer the question.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — [1.1]: The vessel's purpose (floating marine biology research station) is not covered by existing ship type notations, so a descriptive notation may be assigned to recognize it. Step 2 — [1.2]: The descriptive notation is assigned upon request to the Society; the owner must formally request it. Step 3 — [1.3]: There are no class requirements associated with a descriptive notation — so no technical rules are triggered by the notation itself. Step 4 — [1.4]: The notation appears on the certificate enclosed in square brackets, e.g. [Research vessel] or in this case something like [Marine biology research station].

scenario_parameters.special_features: underwater observation chambers, specimen collection systems, onboard laboratory

question_text: A structural engineer is reviewing the midship section of a 180 m bulk carrier. At the midship transverse section, the bottom shell plating and inner bottom plating are steel, but the upper deck plating is made of an aluminium alloy with a Young's modulus of 70,000 N/mm². The deck plating has a gross sectional area of 0.045 m². Additionally, the section contains two elliptical openings in the upper deck: one measuring 2.8 m in length and 1.0 m in breadth, and another measuring 2.2 m in length and 0.8 m in breadth. There are also three circular manholes in the inner bottom, each 0.5 m in diameter, spaced 1.2 m apart from each other in the transverse direction. The ship breadth B is 32 m and there are no large openings in the bottom area. Determine: (1) the steel-equivalent sectional area of the aluminium deck plating that may be included in the hull girder transverse section calculation; (2) which of the deck openings must be deducted from the sectional area used in the hull girder moment of inertia and section modulus; and (3) whether the inner bottom manholes need to be deducted, given that their combined breadth in the transverse section is 1.5 m.
required_facts: CE = 70000 / 206000 ≈ 0.3398, giving a steel-equivalent deck area of approximately 0.0153 m²
The first elliptical deck opening (2.8 m × 1.0 m) is a large opening because its length exceeds 2.5 m, and must be deducted from the hull girder section modulus and moment of inertia
The second elliptical deck opening (2.2 m × 0.8 m) is a small opening because neither dimension exceeds the large-opening thresholds
The three inner bottom manholes (0.5 m diameter) are small openings and are isolated (spaced 1.2 m ≥ 1.0 m apart)
The deduction-free breadth limit for the inner bottom is 0.06 × (32 − 0) = 1.92 m; the combined manhole breadth of 1.5 m does not exceed this limit, so no deduction is required

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single section, multiple sub-rules: apply the CE factor for non-steel material (2.6), classify openings using the definitions in (2.7), apply mandatory deduction for large openings (2.8), and check the deduction-free threshold for small isolated openings (2.9).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Steel-equivalent area of aluminium deck (clause 2.6): CE = E / (2.06×10^5) = 70,000 / 206,000 = 0.3398. Steel-equivalent area = 0.3398 × 0.045 m² = 0.01529 m² ≈ 0.0153 m².

Step 2 — Classify deck openings (clause 2.7a): Large openings are elliptical openings exceeding 2.5 m in length OR 1.2 m in breadth. Opening 1: 2.8 m length > 2.5 m → LARGE. Opening 2: 2.2 m length ≤ 2.5 m AND 0.8 m breadth ≤ 1.2 m → NOT large → small opening.

Step 3 — Deduction of large openings (clause 2.8): Opening 1 is a large opening and must be deducted from the sectional area used in hull girder moment of inertia and section modulus.

Step 4 — Isolated small openings in inner bottom (clauses 2.7c and 2.9): The three manholes are 0.5 m diameter each → circular openings ≤ 0.9 m → small openings. They are spaced 1.2 m apart ≥ 1.0 m → isolated. Check deduction-free limit: 0.06(B − Σb) = 0.06(32 − 0) = 1.92 m (Σb = 0 since no large openings in bottom area). Sum of manhole breadths = 3 × 0.5 = 1.5 m ≤ 1.92 m → no deduction required for the inner bottom manholes.

question_text: A vessel operator is reviewing the in-operation class notations assigned to their fleet. Vessel A is a general cargo ship currently in service with no offshore operations. The operator wants to know whether the PMS(M) notation is mandatory for this vessel, and whether the vessel qualifies to apply for the PMS(CBM) notation without first holding any other PMS qualifier. Separately, Vessel B is an offshore drilling unit that already holds PMS(M) and the DRILL additional class notation. The operator asks whether Vessel B is eligible to apply for PMS(D), and if so, what prerequisite conditions must be satisfied. Provide a clear determination for both vessels.
required_facts: PMS(M) is NOT mandatory for a general cargo vessel in service
PMS(CBM) requires the vessel to have already obtained PMS(M) as a prerequisite
Vessel A cannot apply for PMS(CBM) without first holding PMS(M)
PMS(D) requires the offshore unit to hold both PMS(M) and the additional class notation DRILL
Vessel B satisfies both prerequisites (PMS(M) and DRILL) and is therefore eligible for PMS(D)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: Table 1 of Sec5 defines PMS qualifiers (M, D, P, CBM), their mandatory status, and the application conditions for each qualifier, including prerequisite holdings.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — PMS(M) mandatory status: Table 1 shows PMS(M) is marked 'Mandatory: no', so it is NOT mandatory for Vessel A (a general cargo ship in service). Step 2 — PMS(CBM) eligibility without prior qualifier: Table 1 states PMS(CBM) applies to 'any vessel and offshore unit that has obtained PMS(M)' for machinery/thrusters. Therefore Vessel A cannot apply for PMS(CBM) without first holding PMS(M) — PMS(M) is a prerequisite. Step 3 — PMS(D) eligibility for Vessel B: Table 1 states PMS(D) applies to 'Any offshore unit that has obtained PMS(M) and additional class notation DRILL'. Vessel B holds both PMS(M) and DRILL, so it satisfies both prerequisites and is eligible for PMS(D).

scenario_parameters.query_1: Is PMS(M) mandatory for Vessel A?
scenario_parameters.query_2: Can Vessel A apply for PMS(CBM) without any prior PMS qualifier?
scenario_parameters.query_3: Is Vessel B eligible for PMS(D) and what are the prerequisites?

question_text: A 12,000 GT general cargo vessel was constructed entirely under the oversight of Bureau Veritas and held a BV class certificate for 8 years. The owner now wishes to transfer the vessel to DNV class. DNV has reviewed the vessel's construction records and existing class notations, and considers the BV notations to have equivalent intent to its own. The owner asks whether the vessel can receive the DNV construction symbol '⊞' (the boxed hash mark indicating Society-supervised construction) and the main class notation '1A'. What construction symbol, if any, will DNV assign to this vessel, and is the vessel eligible for the '1A' main class notation?
required_facts: The vessel will NOT receive the ⊞ construction symbol because it was not built under DNV supervision
The vessel will receive the ✦ (dotted/alternative) construction symbol, assigned to vessels built under a recognized society and later classed with DNV
Bureau Veritas must be a classification society recognized by DNV for [1.1.2] to apply
The vessel is eligible for the '1A' main class notation despite being originally classed with another society
DNV will assign class notations it considers equivalent in intent to the original BV notations

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Determine which construction symbol applies based on how the vessel was built and classed, then determine eligibility for 1A main class notation for vessels originally classed with another society.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Check [1.1.1] — the ⊞ symbol is reserved for vessels built under the Society's (DNV's) own supervision. This vessel was built under BV supervision, so ⊞ does NOT apply. Step 2: Check [1.1.2] — the ✦ (dotted hash) symbol applies to vessels built under a recognized classification society and later assigned class with the Society. BV is a recognized society, and the vessel is being transferred to DNV class, so the ✦ symbol applies. The equivalent class notations will be assigned. Step 3: Check [1.1.3] — confirms that vessels not covered by [1.1.1] or [1.1.2] receive no construction symbol; this vessel is covered by [1.1.2] so it does receive a symbol. Step 4: Check [2.1.2] — the 1A main class notation will also be assigned to vessels designed and constructed in accordance with the rules of another classification society and later assigned class with the Society. This vessel qualifies, so 1A is assignable.

question_text: A new RO/RO ferry is being designed with a stern door that leads directly to the RO/RO vehicle deck. The design team has prepared an operating and maintenance manual (OMM) for the stern door. The manual includes: main particulars of the vessel, a key plan of the door equipment, manufacturer's recommended testing procedures, limiting heel and trim conditions for door operations, emergency operating instructions, a maintenance schedule with acceptance/rejection criteria, and a register of inspections covering repairs and renewals. However, the manual does not include a description of the central power pack or the bridge panel, and it omits the manufacturer's maintenance procedures. The manual has been submitted for approval. Is the submitted OMM content sufficient to meet classification requirements, and if not, what specific items are missing?
required_facts: The stern door leading to a RO/RO space requires an operating and maintenance manual (OMM)
The OMM is not sufficient — it is missing required content
Description of the central power pack is a required item under equipment description and is missing
Description of the bridge panel is a required item under equipment description and is missing
Manufacturer's maintenance procedures are a required item under the maintenance section and are missing
The OMM must be submitted for approval and the inclusion of maintenance information (inspections, trouble-shooting, acceptance/rejection criteria) must be verified

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Stern door leading to RO/RO space triggers OMM requirement under 3.2.1, then 3.2.2 specifies the required content checklist, and 3.2.3 requires submission for approval with verification of maintenance information
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify that a stern door leading to a RO/RO space triggers the OMM requirement per 3.2.1. Step 2: Check the required content list in 3.2.2 against what the manual contains. Under (a) description of equipment, the manual must include descriptions of bow doors, inner bow doors, bow ramp/doors, side doors, stern doors, central power pack, engine control room panel, and bridge panel — the central power pack and bridge panel descriptions are missing. Under (c) maintenance, manufacturer's maintenance procedures are explicitly required but omitted. Step 3: Per 3.2.3, the OMM must be submitted for approval and must include necessary information on inspections, trouble-shooting, and acceptance/rejection criteria in the maintenance part — the scenario states acceptance/rejection criteria are present but manufacturer's maintenance procedures are absent, so 3.2.3 verification would fail on that item.

items_present: limiting heel and trim for door operations

question_text: A 175 m bulk carrier is being designed with a cargo hold arrangement. The structural engineer is setting up the finite element model for the midship cargo hold analysis. The proposed FE model covers only two cargo hold lengths (the mid-hold plus one adjacent hold), and the transverse bulkheads at both ends of the model are retained in the model. The model includes only the port side of the ship for efficiency, and the superstructure above the upper deck in way of the machinery space is included. Is this FE model configuration compliant with the classification rules? Identify each aspect of the model setup that is non-compliant and state what the correct requirement is for each.
required_facts: The cargo hold analysis is mandatory because the ship length (175 m) exceeds 150 m and the ship has a cargo hold arrangement
The longitudinal extent of the FE model must cover three cargo hold lengths — a two-hold model is non-compliant
Both port and starboard sides of the ship must be modelled — a port-side-only model is non-compliant
The transverse bulkheads at the ends of the model may be omitted (their retention is not a violation of the extent rule)
The superstructure in way of machinery space is not required to be included in the model (its inclusion is unnecessary per the rules)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Ship length >150 m with cargo hold arrangement triggers mandatory cargo hold analysis per [1.3.1], then [2.2.2] defines the specific FE model extent requirements for that analysis
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Check [1.3.1] — L=175 m > 150 m and ship has cargo hold arrangement, so cargo hold analysis of midship region is mandatory. Step 2: Apply [2.2.2] to evaluate the proposed model. [2.2.2] states: (a) longitudinal extent shall cover THREE cargo hold lengths — the proposed two-hold model is non-compliant; (b) transverse bulkheads and webframes at the ENDS of the model CAN BE OMITTED — retaining them is not a violation but the extent is still wrong; (c) BOTH port and starboard sides shall be modelled — port-side-only model is non-compliant; (d) superstructure or deckhouse in way of machinery space is NOT required to be included — including it is not a violation per se, but the rule explicitly excludes it, so it is unnecessary and the model deviates from standard practice. Non-compliances: (1) model extent is two holds, must be three; (2) only port side modelled, both sides required.

question_text: A newbuild container ship has a hatch coaming top plate that is 92 mm thick and made of NV 47 steel. The shipyard's NDT plan covers the block-to-block butt joints of the upper hull longitudinal structural members. For the transversely orientated full penetration plate butt welds at these block joints, the plan specifies 20% MT and 20% UT. A surveyor questions whether the UT requirement is correct and whether MT alone would suffice for these welds. Additionally, for the longitudinally orientated weld joints within approximately 250 mm of the block-to-block joints, the plan specifies 20% UT. Is the NDT plan compliant with the minimum requirements, and if not, which specific test method percentages are incorrect?
required_facts: NV 47 at 92 mm falls within the 50 < t ≤ 100 mm threshold, triggering the additional container ship NDT requirements in Table 1
For transversely orientated full penetration plate butt welds, the required NDT is 20% UT (RT/UT column) and 20% MT/PT; it is not UT only.
Footnote 3 specifies that only UT shall be performed for the 20% RT/UT entry, so RT is excluded
For longitudinally orientated weld joints within ~250 mm of block-to-block joints, the required NDT is 20% MT only (MT/PT column); RT/UT is not required (shown as '--')
The plan's 20% MT on transversely orientated full penetration butt welds is required by the MT/PT 20 row in Table 1.
The plan's 20% UT on longitudinally orientated joints near block joints is incorrect; 20% MT is required instead
Footnote 1 mandates MT (not PT) for ferromagnetic materials where magnetic particle testing is specified

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Table 1 additional container ship row for NV 47 with 50 < t ≤ 100 mm specifies MT/PT and RT/UT percentages for different weld orientations; footnotes constrain which methods apply
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify the plate as NV 47 at 92 mm thickness, which falls in the 50 < t ≤ 100 mm band — the 'Additional for container ships' row of Table 1 applies. Step 2: For transversely or vertically orientated full penetration weld joints (plate butt welds), Table 1 shows MT/PT = '--' and RT/UT = 20%. Footnote 3 states 'Only UT shall be performed', so RT is excluded. Therefore the correct requirement is 20% UT only, with 0% MT. The plan's 20% MT is incorrect (MT is not required/permitted here per the '--' entry), but the 20% UT is correct. Step 3: For longitudinally orientated weld joints in the vicinity of block-to-block joints (~250 mm), Table 1 shows MT/PT = 20% and RT/UT = '--'. This means 20% MT is required and no UT is required. The plan's specification of 20% UT for these welds is incorrect — it should be 20% MT, not UT. Step 4: Footnote 1 confirms only MT (not PT) for ferromagnetic materials; NV 47 steel is ferromagnetic. Footnote 8 confirms this scope applies for the full length of the coaming structure.

scenario_parameters.structure: hatch coaming top plate, upper hull longitudinal structural member
scenario_parameters.weld_type_1: transversely orientated full penetration plate butt weld at block joint
scenario_parameters.weld_type_2: longitudinally orientated weld joint within ~250 mm of block-to-block joint

question_text: A designer is sizing the bottom shell plating for a bulk carrier. The plate panel in question is transversely stiffened, located on the outer bottom, and is part of the 'other longitudinal members' category (not a watertight boundary). The panel has a breadth b = 800 mm and a length a = 2400 mm. The design pressure for the governing load set is P = 180 kN/m². The hull girder longitudinal stress at the load calculation point is σ_hg = +55 N/mm² (hogging, tensile on bottom). The material yield stress is R_eH = 315 N/mm². Calculate the required net thickness of this plate panel.
required_facts: From Table 1, for 'other longitudinal members / transverse stiffened plating': β_a = 1.10, α_a = 1.00, C_a-max = 1.00
C_a = 1.10 − 1.00×(55/315) ≈ 0.925, which is below C_a-max = 1.00 so no cap applies

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section: apply the lateral pressure plating formula, compute α_p from panel aspect ratio, look up β_a and α_a from Table 1 for 'other longitudinal members / transverse stiffened plating', compute C_a with the hull girder stress correction, cap at C_a-max, then evaluate t.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Panel aspect ratio correction α_p: α_p = 1.2 − b/(2.1·a) = 1.2 − 800/(2.1×2400) = 1.2 − 800/5040 = 1.2 − 0.1587 = 1.0413. Since α_p must not exceed 1.0, cap at α_p = 1.0. Step 2 — Coefficients from Table 1 for 'Other longitudinal members, Transverse stiffened plating': β_a = 1.10, α_a = 1.00, C_a-max = 1.00. Step 3 — Compute C_a: C_a = β_a − α_a·(σ_hg / R_eH) = 1.10 − 1.00×(55/315) = 1.10 − 0.1746 = 0.9254. Check against C_a-max = 1.00: 0.9254 < 1.00, so C_a = 0.9254. Step 4 — Apply thickness formula: t = 0.0158 × α_p × b × √(|P| / (C_a × R_eH)) = 0.0158 × 1.0 × 800 × √(180 / (0.9254 × 315)) = 12.64 × √(180 / 291.5) = 12.64 × √0.6175 = 12.64 × 0.7858 = 9.93 mm. Required net thickness ≈ 9.93 mm.

question_text: A bulk carrier with ESP notation has its No. 1 cargo hold hatch cover fitted with stoppers to resist longitudinal forces on the forward end. The ship has no forecastle fitted. The stopper material has a specified minimum yield strength ReH of 355 N/mm². A designer proposes that the stoppers and their supporting structures be designed for a forward-end longitudinal pressure of 175 kN/m². Is this design pressure acceptable for the No. 1 hatch cover, and what is the maximum allowable equivalent stress in the stopper welds (throat) and supporting structures?
required_facts: The ship is a Type-2 ship (bulk carrier with ESP notation)
The required design pressure for No. 1 hatch cover longitudinal forward-end stoppers is 230 kN/m², not 175 kN/m²
The 175 kN/m² reduction is only permitted when a forecastle is fitted per UR S28; since no forecastle is fitted, 175 kN/m² is not acceptable
The proposed design pressure of 175 kN/m² is non-compliant for the No. 1 hatch cover
The maximum allowable equivalent stress in stopper welds (throat) and supporting structures is 0.8 × ReH = 0.8 × 355 = 284 N/mm²

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Type-2 ship stopper requirements for No. 1 hatch cover longitudinal pressure, with no forecastle fitted, and allowable stress calculation from ReH
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify ship type. A bulk carrier with ESP notation is a Type-2 ship per the definitions in this section. Step 2: Apply Type-2 specific stopper requirements in [6.2.4]. For Type-2 ships, all hatch covers must resist transverse forces from 175 kN/m². For longitudinal forces on the forward end: all hatch covers except No. 1 must resist 175 kN/m²; No. 1 hatch cover must resist 230 kN/m². Step 3: Check forecastle exception. The 230 kN/m² for No. 1 may be reduced to 175 kN/m² only when a forecastle is fitted in accordance with UR S28. Since no forecastle is fitted, the reduction does not apply. Therefore 175 kN/m² is NOT acceptable for No. 1 hatch cover — the required pressure is 230 kN/m². Step 4: Allowable stress. Per [6.2.4], the equivalent stress in stoppers/supporting structures and in the throat of stopper welds shall not exceed 0.8 × ReH = 0.8 × 355 = 284 N/mm².

question_text: A general cargo vessel is fitted with a weathertight door on the exposed freeboard deck that provides access to a space below the freeboard deck. The door blade is a flat steel plate panel with a breadth b = 400 mm and a length a = 800 mm. The design lateral pressure P at the load calculation point is 12.5 kN/m². The steel used has a minimum yield stress R_eH = 235 N/mm². Calculate the minimum required gross thickness t_gr of the door blade in mm, and determine whether a gross thickness of 6 mm is compliant.
required_facts: αp = 1.2 - b/(2.1·a) = 1.2 - 400/(2.1×800) ≈ 0.962, which is less than 1.0 so the computed value is used
Substituted values give t_gr ≈ 1.52 mm
The proposed gross thickness of 6 mm exceeds the minimum required thickness of approximately 1.52 mm
The 6 mm door blade is compliant with the scantling requirement

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the door blade thickness formula in Sec2 [4.3.1], first computing the aspect ratio correction factor αp from the panel dimensions, then substituting into the thickness formula.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Compute αp: αp = 1.2 - b/(2.1·a) = 1.2 - 400/(2.1×800) = 1.2 - 400/1680 = 1.2 - 0.2381 = 0.9619. Since 0.9619 < 1.0, use αp = 0.9619. Step 2 — Apply thickness formula: t_gr = 0.0158 × αp × b × sqrt(|P| / (0.85 × R_eH)) = 0.0158 × 0.9619 × 400 × sqrt(12.5 / (0.85 × 235)) = 0.0158 × 0.9619 × 400 × sqrt(12.5 / 199.75) = 0.0158 × 0.9619 × 400 × sqrt(0.06257) = 0.0158 × 0.9619 × 400 × 0.25015 = 0.0158 × 0.9619 × 100.06 = 0.0158 × 96.27 = 1.521 mm. Wait — recheck: 0.0158 × 0.9619 = 0.015198; × 400 = 6.079; × 0.25015 = 1.521 mm. Step 3 — Compliance check: required t_gr ≈ 1.52 mm; proposed 6 mm >> 1.52 mm, so the 6 mm plate is compliant. Note: the low pressure value (12.5 kN/m²) yields a modest thickness requirement, confirming the 6 mm plate has significant margin.

question_text: A manufacturer of a fire damper actuator system intends to supply units directly from stock to multiple DNV-classed vessels without submitting design documentation for each individual vessel. The manufacturer has an established quality control system with documented traceability, qualified personnel, and appropriate facilities. They have also provided a written declaration confirming the product contains no asbestos and meets SOLAS Ch.II-1/3-5.2 requirements. The manufacturer claims that because the product is a standard, routinely manufactured component, no product certificate is required for each delivery — only a single approval covering the design is sufficient. Is this claim correct under DNV classification rules, and what approval procedure must the manufacturer follow for products manufactured for stock?
required_facts: Products manufactured for stock shall normally be type approved (not case-by-case plan approval).
Type approval is the mandatory procedure the manufacturer must follow for stock components.
For certain products where only type approval is required, no product certificate (survey) is needed per the rules.
The manufacturer's claim is conditionally correct only if the applicable chapter designates the product as requiring type approval only — it is not a blanket exemption.
The asbestos-free declaration is a prerequisite for certificate issuance but does not replace the type approval requirement.
For type approved products, design plans need not be resubmitted for each vessel unless stated as a condition on the type approval certificate.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The question targets Sec4 [2.3.6] (products for stock shall normally be type approved) and [2.3.4] (for certain products, only type approval is required and no product certificate is needed), testing whether the answerer can correctly identify the applicable approval procedure and the condition under which no product certificate is required.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: The manufacturer supplies standard, routinely manufactured components from stock to multiple vessels — this triggers [2.3.6]: 'Products and systems manufactured for stock shall normally be type approved.' Step 2: The manufacturer's claim that no product certificate is required must be checked against [2.3.4]: 'For certain products and systems, as defined in applicable chapters of the rules, only type approval is required. For these products and systems no survey is required, i.e. no product certificate is required.' Step 3: Therefore, the manufacturer's claim is conditionally correct — IF the applicable chapter of the rules designates this product as one requiring only type approval, then no product certificate is needed. However, the mandatory procedure for stock products is type approval per [2.3.6]. Step 4: The asbestos-free declaration and quality control requirements of [1.2.2] and [1.2.3] are prerequisites for certificate issuance and are satisfied here, but do not substitute for the type approval procedure.

scenario_parameters.supply_model: manufactured for stock, supplied to multiple DNV-classed vessels
scenario_parameters.quality_system: documented traceability, qualified personnel, suitable facilities
scenario_parameters.manufacturer_claim: no product certificate required per delivery; single design approval sufficient

question_text: A shipyard has a contract for construction signed on 15 March 2022 for a two-island container ship. The design team is reviewing the structural calculations and wants to know whether the revised bi-moment calculation formula applies to this vessel. The ship is a newbuild. Does the retroactive requirement for the bi-moment formula apply to this contract, and what is the basis for that determination?
required_facts: The retroactive bi-moment formula requirement has an entry into force date of 2022-01-01
The contract date of 15 March 2022 is on or after the entry into force date of 2022-01-01
The retroactive requirement applies to newbuilds with contract for construction date on or after the entry into force date
The retroactive requirement therefore applies to this vessel
The valid until date for this retroactive requirement is 2022-12-31

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Determine applicability of retroactive bi-moment formula requirement by checking contract date against entry into force date in Table 1
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify the vessel type — two-island container ship — and the topic of interest — bi-moment calculation formula revision (Sec.2 row in Table 1). Step 2: Read the scope clause: retroactive requirements apply to newbuilds and conversions with contract for construction date on or after the entry into force date. Step 3: From Table 1, the entry into force date for the bi-moment revision is 2022-01-01. Step 4: The contract date is 15 March 2022, which is on or after 2022-01-01. Step 5: Therefore the retroactive requirement applies. Step 6: Also note the valid until date is 2022-12-31, meaning after that date the requirement is covered by the regular rules (Pt.3 Ch.5 Sec.3 Edition July 2022), but for a contract signed in March 2022 the retroactive version is the applicable one.

question_text: A naval architect is computing the net offered thickness for a deck plate that forms part of the hull girder of a 310-metre container ship. The plate is located in a ballast water tank. The as-built thickness is 22.0 mm, the voluntary addition for extra corrosion protection is 0.5 mm, and the one-side corrosion addition tc for the ballast water tank boundary is 1.0 mm per side. The designer intends to use this net thickness value for a hull girder ultimate strength assessment. What is the correct corrosion addition factor α that must be applied in the net thickness formula for this specific assessment type, and what is the resulting net offered thickness toff in mm?
required_facts: α = 0.5 for hull girder ultimate strength section properties assessment
tc = 2.0 mm (1.0 mm per side × 2 sides for ballast water tank)
The corrosion addition factor α differs by assessment type: α = 1.0 for buckling capacity but α = 0.5 for section properties in ultimate strength
Ballast water tank one-side corrosion addition is 1.0 mm per Table 2

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply the net scantlings formula using the corrosion addition factor α from Table 1 (which varies by assessment type) and the corrosion addition tc from Table 2 (which varies by compartment type). For hull girder ultimate strength, α = 0.5; for a ballast water tank, tc = 1.0 mm per side, so tc = tc1 + tc2 = 2.0 mm total.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the assessment type: the question asks about hull girder ultimate strength assessment. Step 2 — Look up α in Table 1: for 'Hull girder ultimate strength', the row shows α = 0.5 for section properties and buckling/collapse capacity. The applicable α for section properties in ultimate strength is 0.5. Step 3 — Look up tc in Table 2: the plate is in a ballast water tank, so one-side corrosion addition = 1.0 mm. Since the plate has two sides both exposed to ballast water, tc = tc1 + tc2 = 1.0 + 1.0 = 2.0 mm. Step 4 — Apply the formula: toff = tas_built − tvol_add − α·tc = 22.0 − 0.5 − 0.5 × 2.0 = 22.0 − 0.5 − 1.0 = 20.5 mm.

question_text: A ballast tank on a bulk carrier has its volumetric centre of gravity at coordinates (xG, yG, zG) = (120.0 m, 4.5 m, 8.2 m) and the load point under assessment is at (x, y, z) = (120.0 m, 4.5 m, 8.2 m) — i.e. the load point coincides with the tank's centre of gravity. The tank top is at z_top = 14.0 m, the tank is fitted with a pressure/vacuum relief valve set to a design overpressure of 30 kN/m². For the static (S) design load scenario during normal operations at sea, calculate the internal liquid pressure P_ℓs at the load point. The tank carries seawater ballast (density 1.025 t/m³). Show whether the pressure relief valve term or the non-PV formula applies, and state the numerical result.
required_facts: The PV-valve branch of the static pressure formula applies: P_ℓs-1 = f_cd · ρ_L · g · (z_top − z) + P_PV
f_cd = 1.0 because the tank is a ballast tank (not an oil/oil-product cargo tank with ρ_L ≤ 1.025)
ρ_L = 1.025 t/m³ for ballast tanks in strength assessment
P_PV = 30 kN/m² is within the permissible range of 25–70 kN/m²

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the static liquid pressure formula for normal operations at sea from Sec6 [1.2.1], selecting the correct branch (PV-valve fitted vs. other cases), then substitute the given numeric values.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify applicable formula branch: the tank is fitted with a pressure relief valve, so the formula is P_ℓs-1 = f_cd · ρ_L · g · (z_top − z) + P_PV. Step 2 — Determine f_cd: the tank is a ballast tank (seawater, ρ_L = 1.025 t/m³), not an oil/oil-product cargo tank, so f_cd = 1.0 (the f_cd = 0.88 reduction applies only to strength FE analysis of oil/oil-product cargo tanks with ρ_L ≤ 1.025). Step 3 — Substitute values: z_top = 14.0 m, z = 8.2 m, so (z_top − z) = 5.8 m; ρ_L = 1.025 t/m³; g = 9.81 m/s²; P_PV = 30 kN/m². P_ℓs-1 = 1.0 × 1.025 × 9.81 × 5.8 + 30 = 1.025 × 9.81 × 5.8 + 30 = 58.33 + 30 = 88.33 kN/m² (approximately). Step 4 — Verify P_PV bounds: 30 kN/m² is within the allowed range of 25–70 kN/m², so no issue. Result: P_ℓs ≈ 88.3 kN/m².

question_text: A bulk carrier has a deck plate panel in the midship region with a longitudinal stiffening arrangement. The panel consists of two strakes joined by a transverse butt weld: the narrower strake has a net plate thickness of 16 mm and a width of 400 mm, while the wider strake has a net plate thickness of 20 mm and a width of 600 mm. Under the governing hull girder load combination, the hull girder bending stress σ_hg = 150 N/mm² and the hull girder shear stress τ_hg = 60 N/mm². The allowable buckling utilization factor η_all = 0.87. For the buckling check of this plate panel, what equivalent plate panel width b_eq should be used, and which stress combination (stress combination 1 or stress combination 2) produces the higher shear stress input τ for the buckling assessment?
required_facts: The smaller net plate thickness t1 = 16 mm is used together with b_eq for the buckling check
For a longitudinal stiffening arrangement, stress combination 2 applies τ = τ_hg = 60 N/mm²
Stress combination 1 applies τ = 0.7 × τ_hg = 42 N/mm², which is lower
Stress combination 2 produces the higher shear stress input for the buckling assessment

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply the equivalent plate panel formula from [1.2.1] using the two strake widths and thicknesses, then identify the correct stress combination from [2.2] for a longitudinal stiffening arrangement.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Equivalent plate panel width [1.2.1]: The smaller thickness is t1 = 16 mm with ℓ1 = 400 mm; the greater thickness is t2 = 20 mm with ℓ2 = 600 mm. Apply b_eq = ℓ1 + ℓ2 × (t1/t2)^1.5 = 400 + 600 × (16/20)^1.5 = 400 + 600 × (0.8)^1.5 = 400 + 600 × 0.7155 = 400 + 429.3 ≈ 829 mm. Step 2 — Stress combinations [2.2a] for longitudinal stiffening: Stress combination 1 gives τ = 0.7 × τ_hg = 0.7 × 60 = 42 N/mm²; Stress combination 2 gives τ = τ_hg = 60 N/mm². Therefore stress combination 2 produces the higher shear stress input τ = 60 N/mm² for the buckling assessment.

question_text: A naval architect is reviewing the design basis documentation for a new bulk carrier with a design life of 20 years. The ship has a length L = 220 m, breadth B = 32 m, depth D = 18 m, and block coefficient C_B = 0.82. The designer proposes that the structural assessment is valid down to a lowest mean daily average air temperature of -10°C, and the ship will trade exclusively in the North Atlantic. The design basis document has been prepared but no formal notification of changes has been issued since the initial submission. Is the proposed 20-year design life acceptable under classification rules, and does the proposed minimum air temperature of -10°C require any additional class notation?
required_facts: The minimum required design life is 25 years, so the proposed 20-year design life is not acceptable
The design temperature threshold for the DAT notation is 'below and including -10°C'
A lowest mean daily average air temperature of exactly -10°C triggers the requirement for the additional class notation DAT
The DAT notation requirements are covered in Pt.6 Ch.6
All hull form parameters (L, B, D, C_B) are within the standard rule limits and do not require special wave load consideration

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: check design life minimum (3.4) and design temperature threshold (3.5.4) within Pt3.Ch1.Sec2
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Design life: Clause 3.4 states a design life of MINIMUM 25 years shall be applied. The proposed 20-year design life is below this minimum and is therefore NOT acceptable. Step 2 — Design temperature: Clause 3.5.4 states the rules assume validity down to a lowest mean daily average air temperature of -10°C. Ships intended to operate in areas with lower mean daily average temperature (BELOW AND INCLUDING -10°C) are subject to the additional class notation DAT per Pt.6 Ch.6. The proposed temperature is exactly -10°C, which falls within the 'below and including -10°C' trigger condition, so the DAT notation IS required. Step 3 — Hull form check: L/B = 220/32 = 6.875 > 4.5 ✓; B/D = 32/18 = 1.78 < 2.5 ✓; C_B = 0.82 > 0.6 ✓; L = 220 m < 500 m ✓. All hull form parameters are within standard limits, so no special wave load consideration is triggered by geometry alone (though L > 90 m with all parameters in range is fine). Step 4 — Design basis documentation: Clause 3.1.2 requires that all changes to the design basis be formally advised; the absence of any change notifications is consistent with the rules only if no changes have occurred.

question_text: An engineer is setting up a finite element model for a 185-metre bulk carrier that holds the ESP class notation. The structural team plans to use four-node isotropic shell elements throughout the model, but for a slender deck plate panel with high transverse utilization they want to switch to anisotropic elements to capture the stress distribution more accurately. They propose using an imperfection factor X = 0.05 for the anisotropic material model. Additionally, the web plates of the primary supporting members (PSMs) in the cargo hold region will also be modelled with anisotropic elements to simplify the mesh transition. The ship operates a cargo hold that occasionally carries heated cargo, and the structural steel in one compartment is expected to reach 115°C during loaded voyages. The team intends to use the standard yield strength values throughout without any temperature correction. Identify all the non-compliances in this FE modelling approach and state the correct requirements that must be applied.
required_facts: The imperfection factor X for anisotropic material models must equal 0.1, not 0.05 — the proposed value of 0.05 is non-compliant.
The web of primary supporting members must always be modelled with isotropic material properties; using anisotropic elements for PSM webs is not permitted.
For carbon-manganese steel exceeding 100°C (here 115°C), the standard yield strength cannot be used — the effective (temperature-reduced) yield strength must be applied.
Because the ship holds ESP notation, the FE model must be based on net scantlings (not gross scantlings).
There are three distinct non-compliances: wrong imperfection factor, anisotropic PSM webs, and uncorrected yield strength at elevated temperature.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question exercising two sub-rules within Pt3.Ch7.Sec1: the imperfection factor threshold in [3.1.3] (X must equal 0.1, not 0.05), the mandatory isotropic modelling requirement for PSM webs in [3.1.3], and the temperature-corrected yield strength requirement in [3.1.4] for steel exceeding 100°C.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Net scantling: The ship has ESP notation, so the FE model must be based on net scantlings (Sec1 [2.1]). Step 2 — Anisotropic element imperfection factor: Sec1 [3.1.3] states the imperfection factor X shall equal 0.1. The proposed value of 0.05 is non-compliant. Step 3 — Mandatory isotropic structures: Sec1 [3.1.3] explicitly lists 'web of primary supporting members' as a structure that shall ALWAYS be modelled with isotropic material properties. Using anisotropic elements for PSM webs is non-compliant. Step 4 — High-temperature yield strength: Sec1 [3.1.4] states that for carbon-manganese steels subjected to temperatures exceeding 100°C, the effective yield strength as given in Pt.6 Ch.1 Sec.12 [3.3] shall be used. At 115°C the standard yield strength cannot be used; the temperature-reduced effective yield strength is mandatory.

scenario_parameters.element_type: four-node isotropic shell (general) + anisotropic (slender panel and PSM webs)

question_text: A naval architect is preparing the class notation string for a new offshore service vessel being submitted to a classification society. The vessel will be assigned the following notations: the standard construction symbol, main class notation 1A, ship type notation Offshore service vessel (AHTS), and several additional class notations including E0, NAUT(OSV), LFL, HELDK(S, H), SF, Ice(1A), Winterized, and Clean(Design). The designer writes the notation string and includes qualifiers for NAUT, HELDK, and Ice. For the NAUT notation, the designer writes it as NAUT[OSV] using square brackets. For HELDK, the designer writes HELDK(S H) omitting the comma and space between qualifiers. For Ice, the designer writes Ice(1A) correctly. Are the qualifier formatting conventions for NAUT and HELDK correct as written, and what is the proper way to express each?
required_facts: Qualifiers must be indicated in parentheses, not square brackets
NAUT[OSV] is incorrectly formatted; the correct form is NAUT(OSV)
Multiple qualifiers must be separated by comma and space
HELDK(S H) is incorrectly formatted; the correct form is HELDK(S, H)
Ice(1A) is correctly formatted as it uses parentheses and has only one qualifier

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: clause 1.1.5 defines the formatting rules for qualifiers — they follow immediately after the class notation in parentheses (not square brackets), and multiple qualifiers are separated by comma and space.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify the relevant rule for qualifier formatting. Clause 1.1.5 states: 'Qualifiers follow immediately after a class notation and are indicated in parenthesis. Multiple qualifiers are separated by comma and space.' Step 2: Check NAUT[OSV] — square brackets are used instead of parentheses. This is incorrect; the correct form is NAUT(OSV). Step 3: Check HELDK(S H) — the two qualifiers S and H are separated by a space only, missing the required comma. The correct form is HELDK(S, H). Step 4: Ice(1A) uses parentheses with a single qualifier — no comma needed — so it is correctly formatted.

question_text: A structural engineer is reviewing the symbol definitions used in a ship's structural calculation report. The report uses the symbol 'RY' to represent a stress value of 235 N/mm² for a steel with material factor k = 1.0, and separately uses 'ReH' to represent the specified minimum yield stress of 355 N/mm² for a higher-strength steel grade. The report also lists 'τY' as the nominal shear yield stress. Based on standard classification rule definitions, is the value assigned to RY correct for k = 1.0, and what is the correct formula that defines τY in terms of RY?
required_facts: RY is defined as the nominal yield stress equal to 235/k (N/mm²)
For k = 1.0, RY = 235/1.0 = 235 N/mm², so the report's value is correct
τY is the nominal shear yield stress defined in Table 3 of the Materials symbols
τY is taken equal to RY/√3 (i.e., the shear yield stress formula based on von Mises criterion)
ReH is a distinct symbol representing the specified minimum yield stress from material certificates, not a nominal rule-defined value like RY

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: the answerer must locate the Materials symbol table (Table 3) in Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 and read the definitions of RY and τY directly, then verify the numeric value for k=1.0
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Locate Table 3 (Materials) in Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [2.2]. Step 2: Find RY — defined as 'nominal yield stress, taken equal to 235/k' with units N/mm². For k = 1.0, RY = 235/1.0 = 235 N/mm². The report's value of 235 N/mm² is therefore correct. Step 3: Find τY — defined as 'nominal shear yield stress, taken equal to RY/√3' (the table entry reads 'taken equal to' with the shear yield formula, which by standard structural convention is RY/√3). The answerer must confirm the formula from the table entry for τY.

question_text: A 175 m ro-ro vessel is being designed with a stern bottom structure. The lower shell in the stern region has a flare angle of 65°. The design minimum ballast draught at the aft end is 3.2 m, and the shell at the position being evaluated sits 0.8 m below the ballast waterline. The position under review is located 12 m forward of the aft end. The vessel's block coefficient C_B is 0.62, and the wave coefficient C_W for this vessel is 10.5. For the stern bottom plating at this location, what design pressure should be used for the plating scantling check, and what pressure should be used for sizing the stiffeners and their connection areas to supporting members such as floors and girders?
required_facts: The vessel qualifies for stern slamming requirements because L = 175 m exceeds the 150 m threshold
The flare angle of 65° exceeds 60°, triggering the high-flare strengthening requirements applicable to ro-ro vessels
The design stern slamming pressure P_SS is approximately 329 kN/m² (acceptable range 320–340 kN/m²)
The plating scantling pressure P_pl equals P_SS (full stern slamming pressure, approximately 329 kN/m²)
The stiffener design pressure P_st equals 0.5 × P_SS, approximately 165 kN/m²
The connection area pressure for stiffener supports also equals 0.5 × P_SS, approximately 165 kN/m²

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Ship length > 150 m triggers applicability; flare angle > 60° triggers the high-flare vessel requirements; compute P_SS from the design formula using given parameters; apply P_pl = P_SS for plating and P_st = 0.5 P_SS for stiffeners and connection areas.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Applicability check [1.1.1]: L = 175 m > 150 m, so stern slamming requirements apply. Step 2 — High-flare check [1.1.2]: flare angle = 65° > 60°, and vessel is a ro-ro, so strengthening per [3.1], [3.2.1], and [3.3.1] is required. Step 3 — Location check [1.1.3]: position is 12 m forward of A.E., and 0.1L = 17.5 m, so the position (12 m < 17.5 m forward of A.E.) is within the applicable stern region. Step 4 — Compute C: h_o = -0.8 m (shell is 0.8 m below waterline, so h_o is negative since positive is downwards and shell is below waterline — actually h_o is vertical distance positive downwards from waterline T_BA to shell; shell is below waterline so h_o = +0.8 m). C = 0.18 × (C_W − 2 h_o) = 0.18 × (10.5 − 2 × 0.8) = 0.18 × (10.5 − 1.6) = 0.18 × 8.9 = 1.602, capped at maximum 1.0. So C = 1.0. Step 5 — Compute a_0: a_0 = (3 × C_W / L) + 0.16 = (3 × 10.5 / 175) + 0.16 = (31.5 / 175) + 0.16 = 0.18 + 0.16 = 0.34. Step 6 — Compute P_SS (main formula): X = 12 m, α = 65°. P_SS = 2.2 × C × L × (0.6 + (1.65 × a_0 × (0.55L − X) × sin³α) / (C_B × L))². = 2.2 × 1.0 × 175 × (0.6 + (1.65 × 0.34 × (0.55 × 175 − 12) × sin³(65°)) / (0.62 × 175))². 0.55 × 175 = 96.25; 96.25 − 12 = 84.25. sin(65°) ≈ 0.9063; sin³(65°) ≈ 0.7451. Numerator: 1.65 × 0.34 × 84.25 × 0.7451 = 0.561 × 84.25 × 0.7451 = 0.561 × 62.77 ≈ 35.22. Denominator: 0.62 × 175 = 108.5. Fraction: 35.22 / 108.5 ≈ 0.3247. Inner term: 0.6 + 0.3247 = 0.9247. Squared: 0.9247² ≈ 0.8551. P_SS = 2.2 × 1.0 × 175 × 0.8551 = 385 × 0.8551 ≈ 329.2 kN/m². Step 7 — Check upper bound formula: P_SS_max = 2.2 × C × L × (0.6 + 1.65 × a_0 / (2 × C_B))³ — wait, the upper bound uses a cube not a square, and uses a_0 not a. Checking: (0.6 + 1.65 × 0.34 / (2 × 0.62))³ = (0.6 + 0.561 / 1.24)³ = (0.6 + 0.4524)³ = (1.0524)³ ≈ 1.165. P_SS_max = 2.2 × 1.0 × 175 × 1.165 ≈ 448.8 kN/m². Since 329.2 < 448.8, the main formula governs: P_SS ≈ 329 kN/m². Step 8 — Plating pressure [3.1]: P_pl = P_SS ≈ 329 kN/m². Step 9 — Stiffener pressure [3.2.1]: P_st = 0.5 × P_SS ≈ 165 kN/m². Step 10 — Connection area pressure [3.2.2]: P = 0.5 × P_SS ≈ 165 kN/m².

question_text: A designer is sizing a watertight hatch located in a transverse watertight bulkhead (not the collision bulkhead) of a cargo vessel. The hatch plate panel has a calculated design pressure of 45 kN/m² acting on it. The designer proposes to use a plate thickness that satisfies the general plate strength formula with a capacity reduction factor Ca = 0.8. Is this value of Ca acceptable for this hatch location, and what is the correct value of Ca that must be used?
required_facts: Ca = 0.8 is only applicable for a door or hatch located in the collision bulkhead
For a door or hatch in any other bulkhead (non-collision), Ca = 1.0 must be used
The proposed Ca = 0.8 is not acceptable for this hatch location
The correct value of Ca for this hatch is 1.0
The hatch plate thickness must in no case be less than the minimum thickness required for the adjacent bulkhead

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: the answerer must locate the internal watertight door/hatch strength requirements, identify the Ca factor table for plates, and determine the correct value based on bulkhead type (collision vs. other).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the structural element: a watertight hatch in a transverse watertight bulkhead that is NOT the collision bulkhead. Step 2 — Navigate to the strength requirements for internal watertight doors and hatches (Pt3.Ch12.Sec3 [4.3.1]), which states they shall be designed with strength equivalent to the surrounding structure and shall withstand design pressure from both sides. Step 3 — Go to [4.3.2] which specifies the Ca values for plates: Ca = 0.8 for door/hatch in collision bulkhead, Ca = 1.0 for door/hatch in other bulkheads. Step 4 — Since this hatch is in a non-collision bulkhead ('other bulkheads'), the correct Ca = 1.0. The proposed Ca = 0.8 is only permitted for hatches in the collision bulkhead. Therefore the proposed value is NOT acceptable; the correct value is Ca = 1.0.

question_text: A naval architect is reviewing the window and side scuttle arrangement for a new general cargo vessel. On the shell plating of the first tier of an enclosed superstructure, there is a round opening with a diameter of 480 mm. The designer has classified this opening as a 'side scuttle' and has not fitted any deadlight or storm cover, arguing that the opening is circular and therefore qualifies as a side scuttle rather than a window. Is this classification correct, and what fitting requirement applies to this opening based on its location?
required_facts: The area of the 480 mm diameter circular opening is approximately 0.181 m², which exceeds the 0.16 m² threshold
Round or oval openings with area exceeding 0.16 m² must be treated as windows, not side scuttles
The designer's classification of the opening as a side scuttle is incorrect
Windows are prohibited in the sides of first tier enclosed superstructures
The opening is non-compliant and cannot be permitted in this location regardless of deadlight fitting

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply the area-based definition threshold to classify the opening, then apply the arrangement rule for the determined classification at that location.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Classify the opening: Per [2.1.1], a side scuttle is a round or oval opening with area not exceeding 0.16 m². A 480 mm diameter circle has area = π × (0.24)² = 0.1810 m², which exceeds 0.16 m². Per [2.1.1], round or oval openings with area exceeding 0.16 m² shall be treated as windows. Therefore the designer's classification as a side scuttle is incorrect — this is a window. Step 2 — Apply arrangement rule for windows: Per [3.1.5], windows shall not be fitted in the first tier end bulkheads or sides of enclosed superstructures (clause b). The opening is on the shell of the first tier of an enclosed superstructure, which falls squarely under this prohibition. Therefore the window is not permitted in this location at all, regardless of whether a deadlight is fitted.

scenario_parameters.location: shell plating, first tier of enclosed superstructure

question_text: A shipyard is welding a 14 mm thick steel plate (normal strength steel, ReH = 235 N/mm²) to a tank boundary structure using fillet welds. The weld deposit has a specified minimum yield stress of 305 N/mm². The designer proposes to use a fillet weld gap allowance (tgap) of 1.5 mm for this connection. Is this gap allowance acceptable under classification rules? What is the minimum permissible tgap for this plate thickness, and how should it be determined?
required_facts: t_as-built = 14 mm, which is ≥ 12.0 mm
minimum tgap = 2.0 mm for t_as-built ≥ 12.0 mm
proposed tgap of 1.5 mm is less than the required 2.0 mm
the arrangement is not acceptable as proposed
linear interpolation applies only for 6.0 mm < t_as-built < 12.0 mm, which does not apply here

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: the tgap symbol definition in Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 specifies threshold values at 6 mm and 12 mm plate thickness, with linear interpolation in between. The plate is 14 mm thick, which falls above the 12 mm threshold, so tgap must not be less than 2.0 mm. The proposed 1.5 mm is non-compliant.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify the plate thickness: t_as-built = 14 mm. Step 2: Apply the tgap rule from the Symbols table: tgap ≥ 2.0 mm for t_as-built ≥ 12.0 mm; tgap ≥ 1.0 mm for t_as-built ≤ 6.0 mm; linear interpolation for 6.0 mm < t_as-built < 12.0 mm. Step 3: Since 14 mm ≥ 12.0 mm, the minimum tgap = 2.0 mm. Step 4: The proposed tgap of 1.5 mm < 2.0 mm, so the arrangement is not acceptable.

question_text: A container ship has a ship length L = 280 m, breadth B = 42 m, block coefficient C_B = 0.65, and waterplane coefficient C_WL = 0.82. The scantling draught is T = 13.5 m. For strength assessment at the midship section (x/L = 0.5), calculate the vertical wave hogging bending moment M_WV-Hog. Use f_R = 1.0, f_p = 1.0. Is the non-linear hogging correction factor f_NL-Hog capped at its upper limit, and what is the final value of f_NL-Hog to be used?
required_facts: f_NL-Hog is NOT capped because 0.874 < 1.1 upper limit for strength assessment
L_ref for vertical wave bending moments = 315 * C_WL^(-1.3) ≈ 407.7 m, so L < L_ref and the first branch of C applies
Wave parameter C ≈ 0.969
Distribution factor c_M = 1.0 at x/L = 0.5 (hogging, range 0.35 ≤ x/L < 0.55)
M_WV-Hog ≈ 5,010,000 kNm (approximately 5.0 × 10^6 kNm)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the vertical wave bending moment formula for hogging at x/L=0.5, compute f_NL-Hog, check against the cap of 1.1, read c_M from Table 1, then assemble M_WV-Hog.

question_text: A general cargo vessel of 82 m in length is being designed with a maximum deadweight of 1,850 tonnes and a maximum displacement of 4,200 tonnes. The vessel falls under category II classification. The designer is preparing the documentation package and wants to know whether an approved loading manual is required for this vessel, and if so, whether that loading manual must address longitudinal strength considerations.
required_facts: An approved loading manual is required because the vessel is covered by Reg.10 of the International Convention on Load Lines
The category II exemption from longitudinal strength in the loading manual requires both length < 90 m AND deadweight ≤ 30% of maximum displacement
The deadweight ratio is 1,850 / 4,200 ≈ 44%, which exceeds the 30% threshold
The longitudinal strength exemption does NOT apply to this vessel
The loading manual must therefore include longitudinal strength (permissible still water bending moments and shear forces)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the category II exemption threshold check in 1.1.2 — a loading manual is required (vessel is covered by Load Lines Reg.10), but the longitudinal strength component is exempt only if length < 90 m AND deadweight ≤ 30% of maximum displacement.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Determine whether a loading manual is required at all: the vessel is covered by Reg.10 of the International Convention on Load Lines, so an approved loading manual is required per 1.1.2 paragraph 1. Step 2 — Check the longitudinal-strength exemption for category II ships: the exemption applies when (a) the ship is category II, (b) length < 90 m, and (c) maximum deadweight does not exceed 30% of maximum displacement. Step 3 — Apply the numbers: length = 82 m < 90 m ✓; deadweight ratio = 1,850 / 4,200 = 44.0%, which exceeds the 30% threshold ✗. Step 4 — Conclusion: because the deadweight ratio (44%) exceeds 30%, the exemption does not apply, and the loading manual must include longitudinal strength considerations even though the vessel is category II and under 90 m.

question_text: A naval architect is performing a fatigue assessment for a novel semi-submersible heavy-lift vessel with a non-conventional hull form. The structural detail under review is a highly stressed node at the intersection of a pontoon column and the main deck box girder. The designer proposes to use the standard wave-induced stress procedure from the class guideline DNV-CG-0129 without any modifications. The classification society's surveyor raises concerns that: (1) the prescriptive stress formulations in the rules may not be applicable to this unconventional geometry, and (2) the detail is located in a safety-critical area where failure would have severe consequences for the vessel's structural integrity. Given these concerns, can the standard procedure be applied as-is, and what additional measures may the classification society require for this fatigue assessment?
required_facts: The standard DNV-CG-0129 procedure cannot be applied as-is for an innovative hull design without special consideration by the Society.
For innovative hull designs, the required scope of fatigue evaluation will be specially considered on a case-by-case basis.
Because the prescriptive stress formulations are not regarded as applicable to this unconventional geometry, the Society may require directly calculated loads or the use of FE models.
For a safety-critical structural detail, a reduced permissible cumulative fatigue damage may be required based on consideration of criticality.
Additional verification by fracture mechanics may be required for the critical detail.
The Society may request additional details to be assessed beyond the standard procedure.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: Pt3.Ch9.Sec5 General — special considerations for innovative hull designs and critical structural details where standard procedures may not apply
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify that the vessel is an innovative/non-conventional hull design (semi-submersible heavy-lift), which triggers the special consideration clause. Step 2: Pt3.Ch9.Sec5 [1] states that for innovative hull designs, the required scope of fatigue evaluation will be specially considered — so the standard DNV-CG-0129 procedure cannot simply be applied as-is without review. Step 3: Because the prescriptive stress formulations are not regarded as applicable for this specific structure/geometry, the Society may require directly calculated loads or the use of FE models. Step 4: Because the detail is in a safety-critical location, a reduced permissible cumulative fatigue damage may be required based on consideration of criticality. Step 5: Additionally, the Society may request additional details to be assessed, and additional verification by fracture mechanics may be required for this critical detail. Step 6: Conclusion: the standard procedure cannot be applied as-is; the Society has authority to require FE models, directly calculated loads, reduced permissible damage, and fracture mechanics verification.

scenario_parameters.detail_location: pontoon column to main deck box girder intersection node
scenario_parameters.proposed_procedure: standard DNV-CG-0129 wave-induced stress method, unmodified
scenario_parameters.criticality: safety-critical — failure has severe structural integrity consequences
scenario_parameters.surveyor_concern_1: prescriptive stress formulations not applicable to unconventional geometry
scenario_parameters.surveyor_concern_2: high criticality of the structural detail

question_text: A bulk carrier was classed with a major classification society five years ago and has since undergone several structural repairs and one change of ownership. The vessel's current operator wants to confirm whether the classification society's rules governing the ongoing validity of the ship's class certificate — including any periodic surveys, condition monitoring, or compliance obligations that must be met to keep the class in force — fall under the general classification requirements or are addressed in a dedicated part of the ruleset. Where in the rules should the operator look to find all requirements that must be satisfied to retain the vessel's class, and are those requirements contained within the general classification principles section?
required_facts: The retention-of-class requirements are not contained within the general classification principles section
All requirements for retaining class are located in Part 7 of the rules
The general classification section provides only a cross-reference redirect to Part 7
The operator must consult Part 7 to find survey, monitoring, and compliance obligations for keeping class in force

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt1.Ch1.Sec3 contains only a single-sentence redirect: all retention-of-class requirements are in Pt.7, not in the general classification section.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Read Pt1.Ch1.Sec3 'Retention of Class'. Step 2: The entire section states 'For requirements related to retention of class, see Pt.7.' Step 3: Conclude that the general classification principles section (Pt1) does NOT contain the substantive retention-of-class rules — they are wholly located in Pt.7. The operator must consult Pt.7 for all periodic survey, condition monitoring, and compliance obligations needed to keep class in force.

question_text: A 180-metre bulk carrier (without large deck openings) is being assessed for hull girder yield at a midship transverse section. The net moment of inertia about the horizontal neutral axis is 42.5 m⁴, and the horizontal neutral axis is located 8.2 m above the keel reference. A deck stringer plate at z = 16.4 m (top of the section) is made of mild steel (k = 1.0). For a particular dynamic load case in seagoing condition, the permissible still water hogging bending moment is 3,800,000 kNm and the vertical wave bending moment for that load case is 2,100,000 kNm. The still water component of the longitudinal stress at the deck stringer plate is +85 N/mm² (hogging). Calculate the total hull girder longitudinal stress σ_hg at the deck stringer plate for this dynamic load case, determine the permissible longitudinal stress, and state whether the design criterion is satisfied.
required_facts: The applicable formula is σ_hg = σ_hg-sw + σ_hg-dyn, where σ_hg-dyn = σ_wv-LC + σ_wh-LC
The vertical distance from the neutral axis to the deck stringer plate is 16.4 − 8.2 = 8.2 m
σ_wv-LC at the deck stringer plate ≈ 405 N/mm² (computed as Mwv-LC × (z − zn-n50) / Iy-n50)
Total hull girder longitudinal stress σ_hg ≈ 490 N/mm²
Permissible longitudinal stress σ_hg-perm = 205 / k = 205 N/mm² for mild steel (k = 1.0)
The design criterion |σ_hg| ≤ σ_hg-perm is NOT satisfied (490 N/mm² > 205 N/mm²)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the hull girder longitudinal stress definition formula (σ_hg = σ_hg-sw + σ_hg-dyn) and then check against the permissible stress criterion (|σ_hg| ≤ σ_hg-perm = 205/k).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Identify the ship type: no large deck openings → use [2.1.1] and [2.1.2].

Step 2 — Compute the dynamic (wave) component of longitudinal stress at the deck stringer plate (z = 16.4 m, zn-n50 = 8.2 m, so the distance from neutral axis = 16.4 − 8.2 = 8.2 m):
  σ_wv-LC = Mwv-LC × (z − zn-n50) / Iy-n50
           = 2,100,000 kNm × 8.2 m / 42.5 m⁴
           = 17,220,000 / 42.5
           = 405,176 kN/m² ≈ 405.2 N/mm²  (hogging wave → positive at deck)

Step 3 — No horizontal wave bending moment is given (σ_wh-LC = 0 for this scenario), so:
  σ_hg-dyn = σ_wv-LC + σ_wh-LC = 405.2 + 0 = 405.2 N/mm²

Step 4 — Total longitudinal stress:
  σ_hg = σ_hg-sw + σ_hg-dyn = 85 + 405.2 = 490.2 N/mm²

Step 5 — Permissible longitudinal stress (mild steel, k = 1.0):
  σ_hg-perm = 205 / k = 205 / 1.0 = 205 N/mm²

Step 6 — Design criterion check:
  |σ_hg| = 490.2 N/mm² > σ_hg-perm = 205 N/mm²  → criterion NOT satisfied.

scenario_parameters.ship_type: bulk carrier, no large deck openings

question_text: A 180-metre bulk carrier has a double-bottom ballast tank adjacent to the outer shell on the port side. The tank is intended to carry seawater ballast. During a structural assessment of the outer shell plating in the bottom region, the designer is evaluating the net lateral pressure to apply for the primary supporting member scantling check. The ship's ballast draught is T_BAL = 5.8 m. The internal static liquid pressure P_ls-ST has been calculated as 42 kN/m², the internal dynamic pressure P_ld as 18 kN/m², and the external hydrostatic sea pressure P_S at the location under consideration is 31 kN/m². The wave pressure P_W at the same location is 12 kN/m². For the AC-III load set applicable to this tank boundary, what net lateral pressure should be applied to the outer shell plating, and which load combination governs?
required_facts: Because the compartment adjacent to the outer shell is intended to carry liquids, the net pressure is the difference between internal and external pressures (not considered independently)
