The applicable load set for AC-III on the external shell adjacent to a tank is TK-2 or WB-3
The load component for this set is P_ls-ST minus P_S (static internal pressure minus hydrostatic sea pressure)
Net lateral pressure = 42 - 31 = 11 kN/m²
The dynamic pressures P_ld and P_W are not included in the AC-III (TK-2/WB-3) load combination for the outer shell

annotator_grounding.end_clause: Pt3.Ch6.Sec2 [1.3.1], Table 1 (TK-2 or WB-3 row for external shell)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The outer shell is adjacent to a liquid-carrying compartment, so [1.3.1] first paragraph applies: net pressure = internal minus external. Then Table 1 identifies the correct load set (TK-2/WB-3 for AC-III) and confirms the pressure expression P_ls-ST - P_S for the external shell.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify pressure combination rule: Per [1.3.1], because the compartment adjacent to the outer shell IS intended to carry liquids (ballast tank), the net lateral pressure is the difference between internal and external pressures. Step 2 — Identify the applicable load set from Table 1: For the external shell (excluding external decks), the AC-III load set corresponds to TK-2 or WB-3, with load component P_ls-ST - P_S. Step 3 — Apply the formula: Net pressure = P_ls-ST - P_S = 42 - 31 = 11 kN/m². Step 4 — Confirm P_ld and P_W are not added here: The AC-III set uses only the static internal pressure P_ls-ST minus the static external sea pressure P_S; the dynamic components P_ld and P_W are not part of this load set. Step 5 — Conclusion: The governing net lateral pressure for the AC-III check on the outer shell plating adjacent to the ballast tank is 11 kN/m², using load set TK-2/WB-3.

question_text: A 14,000 TEU container ship is being designed with containers stowed in cell guides within the cargo hold. The inner bottom has doubler plates arranged at the container footprint locations. The cell guide transverse struts connect directly to the hatchway coaming, and the longitudinal struts are welded to the deck plating edge at the hatchway opening. The lashing eye plates on deck are designed for a certified safe working load (SWL) of 250 kN per lashing point, but the hull support structures beneath them have been sized for a design load of 200 kN. For the on-deck container stacks, the designer has calculated reaction forces under two load cases: (1) transverse loading with vertical load Fv1, transverse horizontal load Fq, and wind loads included; (2) longitudinal/vertical loading with vertical load Fv2, longitudinal horizontal load Fl, and wind loads included in both cases. The strength evaluation of all hull support structures uses gross scantlings throughout. Identify all non-compliant aspects of this design and explain what corrections are required.
required_facts: Strength evaluation must use net scantlings, not gross scantlings — use of gross scantlings is non-compliant
Cell guides must not be welded to deck plating edges in way of hatchways — the longitudinal strut weld to the deck plating edge at the hatchway is non-compliant
Hull support structures for lashing eye plates must be sized for the certified SWL of 250 kN, not the reduced 200 kN design load
Load combination 2 (longitudinal/vertical loading) must NOT include wind loads — including wind in LC2 is non-compliant
The doubler plate arrangement at inner bottom footprints for cell-guide-stowed containers is compliant with the rules

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question requiring the answerer to apply multiple sub-clauses within Pt5.Ch2.Sec9 to identify four distinct non-compliances in the described design
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Clause [2.1]: Strength evaluation must be based on NET scantlings, not gross scantlings. The scenario states gross scantlings are used → non-compliant. Step 2 — Clause [2.2.1]: Hatchway coamings shall be strengthened in way of connections of transverse AND longitudinal struts of cell guides (compliant for transverse struts connecting to coaming). However, the second sentence of [2.2.1] states cell guides shall NOT be welded to deck plating edges in way of hatchways. The scenario states longitudinal struts are welded to the deck plating edge at the hatchway opening → non-compliant. Step 3 — Clause [2.2.2]: For containers stowed in cell guides in hold, doubler plates shall be arranged for footprints on inner bottom or stringers. The scenario states doubler plates are arranged → compliant. Step 4 — Clause [3.1.2]: Hull support structures for lashing eye plates shall be strengthened with respect to the lashings' certified SWL (250 kN). The structures are sized for only 200 kN → non-compliant. Step 5 — Clause [3.2.1] Table 1: Load combination 2 (longitudinal/vertical loading) specifies NO wind loads. The scenario includes wind loads in both load cases → non-compliant for LC2.

scenario_parameters.cell_guide_longitudinal_strut_attachment: welded to deck plating edge at hatchway

question_text: A bulk carrier has a longitudinally stiffened bottom shell plate panel in the midship region. The plate panel consists of two strakes joined by a longitudinal weld: the inner strake has a net thickness t1 = 16 mm and width ℓ1 = 900 mm, while the outer strake has a net thickness t2 = 20 mm and width ℓ2 = 600 mm. Both strakes are made of the same steel grade (ReH = 315 N/mm²). The hull girder vertical still water bending stress at this location is σhg-sw = 85 N/mm² (hogging, compressive at bottom) and the hull girder shear stress is τhg = 40 N/mm². The allowable buckling utilization factor ηall = 0.9. For the buckling check of this plate panel under the longitudinal stiffening arrangement, determine: (1) the equivalent plate panel width beq to be used in the buckling assessment, and (2) the two stress combinations (σx, σy, τ) that must be applied to the elementary plate panel.
required_facts: beq = ℓ1 + ℓ2 × (t1/t2)^1.5 is the correct formula for equivalent plate panel width
beq ≈ 1329 mm (accepting 1329–1330 mm)
The buckling check uses beq combined with the smaller thickness t1 = 16 mm
Stress combination 1 (longitudinal): σx = 85 N/mm², σy = 0, τ = 28 N/mm²
Stress combination 2 (longitudinal): σx = 59.5 N/mm², σy = 0, τ = 40 N/mm²
Both stress combinations must satisfy the buckling criterion ηPlate ≤ 0.9

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the equivalent plate panel width formula from [1.2.1] using the given thickness and width values, then read off the longitudinal stiffening stress combinations from [2.2].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Equivalent plate panel width [1.2.1]: beq = ℓ1 + ℓ2 × (t1/t2)^1.5 = 900 + 600 × (16/20)^1.5. Compute (16/20) = 0.8; (0.8)^1.5 = 0.8 × sqrt(0.8) = 0.8 × 0.8944 = 0.7155. So beq = 900 + 600 × 0.7155 = 900 + 429.3 = 1329.3 mm ≈ 1329 mm. The buckling check is then performed using beq = 1329 mm combined with the smaller thickness t1 = 16 mm. Step 2 — Stress combinations for longitudinal stiffening arrangement [2.2a]: Combination 1: σx = σhg = 85 N/mm², σy = 0, τ = 0.7 × 40 = 28 N/mm². Combination 2: σx = 0.7 × 85 = 59.5 N/mm², σy = 0, τ = 40 N/mm². Both combinations must satisfy ηPlate ≤ ηall = 0.9.

question_text: A naval architect is sizing the bottom shell plating for a bulk carrier. The plate panel in question is longitudinally stiffened, with a panel breadth b = 820 mm and panel length a = 2600 mm. The design pressure at the load calculation point is P = 95 kN/m². The material yield strength is ReH = 315 N/mm². The hull girder longitudinal stress at the load calculation point is σhg = +62 N/mm² (hogging, tensile on the bottom). Determine the required net thickness of this plate panel, showing the calculation of the aspect ratio correction factor αp, the permissible bending stress coefficient Ca, and the final thickness t.
required_facts: Table 1 row for 'Other longitudinal members, longitudinal stiffened plating' gives βa = 1.10, αa = 0.50, Ca-max = 1.00
The hull girder stress reduces Ca slightly but the cap at Ca-max = 1.00 is the binding constraint

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the plating thickness formula in Sec4 [1.1.1], compute αp from the panel aspect ratio, look up βa, αa, Ca-max from Table 1 for longitudinally stiffened plating (bottom shell = 'other longitudinal members'), compute Ca accounting for hull girder stress, then evaluate the thickness formula.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Aspect ratio correction factor αp: αp = 1.2 − b/(2.1a) = 1.2 − 820/(2.1 × 2600) = 1.2 − 820/5460 = 1.2 − 0.1502 = 1.0498. Since 1.0498 > 1.0, cap at αp = 1.0. Step 2 — Table 1 lookup: Bottom shell plating is longitudinally stiffened and falls under 'Other longitudinal members' → βa = 1.10, αa = 0.50, Ca-max = 1.00. Step 3 — Permissible bending stress coefficient Ca: Ca = βa − αa × (σhg / ReH) = 1.10 − 0.50 × (62 / 315) = 1.10 − 0.50 × 0.1968 = 1.10 − 0.0984 = 1.0016. Check against Ca-max = 1.00 → Ca is capped at 1.00. Step 4 — Net thickness: t = 0.0158 × αp × b × sqrt(|P| / (Ca × ReH)) = 0.0158 × 1.0 × 820 × sqrt(95 / (1.00 × 315)) = 12.956 × sqrt(0.30159) = 12.956 × 0.5492 = 7.11 mm.

question_text: A 95 m general cargo vessel (category II) has a maximum deadweight of 2,800 tonnes and a maximum displacement of 7,500 tonnes. The ship is classed and falls under the International Convention on Load Lines. The owner asks whether a loading manual is required, and if so, whether it also needs to address longitudinal strength. Additionally, the owner wants to know if an approved loading instrument system for hull strength calculation is required for this vessel. Provide a clear determination for each of the three questions.
required_facts: A loading manual is required because the ship is covered by Load Lines Reg. 10
The category II exemption from longitudinal strength in the loading manual does not apply because the ship length (95 m) is not less than 90 m
The deadweight ratio is approximately 37.3% (2800/7500), which also independently exceeds the 30% threshold, confirming the exemption fails
The loading manual must therefore address longitudinal strength
A loading instrument system for hull strength is NOT required because the ship is category II and below 100 m in length

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section reasoning: apply the loading manual requirement (all Load Lines ships), then check the category II exemption threshold for longitudinal strength (length < 90 m AND deadweight ≤ 30% displacement), then check the loading instrument threshold (category I ships ≥ 100 m only).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Loading manual required? The ship is classed and covered by Load Lines Reg. 10, so yes, an approved loading manual is required per [1.1.2] first paragraph. Step 2 — Must the loading manual address longitudinal strength? The exemption applies to a category II ship with length less than 90 m where maximum deadweight does not exceed 30% of maximum displacement. Check: length = 95 m, which is NOT less than 90 m. Therefore the exemption does NOT apply, and the loading manual must consider longitudinal strength. (Even if length were under 90 m, deadweight ratio = 2800/7500 = 37.3%, which exceeds 30%, so the exemption would still fail on that criterion alone.) Step 3 — Loading instrument required? Per [1.1.2] third paragraph and [3.1.1], a loading instrument system is required only for category I ships of 100 m length and above. This vessel is 95 m and category II, so no loading instrument is required.

question_text: A general cargo vessel has a weathertight door fitted in a deckhouse on the freeboard deck. The door blade is a flat steel plate with no stiffeners, spanning a clear opening of 600 mm wide by 1800 mm tall. The design lateral pressure at the load calculation point is 12.5 kN/m². The steel used has a minimum yield stress ReH = 235 N/mm². The door panel aspect ratio gives a = 1800 mm and b = 600 mm. Calculate the minimum required gross plate thickness for the door blade. Is a 6 mm gross thickness plate compliant with this requirement?
required_facts: Formula used: t_gr = 0.0158 × αp × b × sqrt(|P| / (0.85 × ReH))
Minimum required gross thickness t_gr ≈ 2.37 mm
The proposed 6 mm plate thickness exceeds the minimum requirement
The 6 mm door blade is compliant with the scantling requirement

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the door blade thickness formula in Sec2 [4.3.1], using the aspect ratio correction factor αp defined in the Symbols block of the same section
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Compute αp: αp = 1.2 - b/(2.1·a) = 1.2 - 600/(2.1×1800) = 1.2 - 600/3780 = 1.2 - 0.1587 = 1.0413. Since αp must not exceed 1.0, cap it at αp = 1.0. Step 2 — Apply thickness formula from [4.3.1]: t_gr = 0.0158 × αp × b × sqrt(|P| / (0.85 × ReH)) = 0.0158 × 1.0 × 600 × sqrt(12.5 / (0.85 × 235)) = 9.48 × sqrt(12.5 / 199.75) = 9.48 × sqrt(0.06257) = 9.48 × 0.2501 = 2.37 mm. Step 3 — Compare: required t_gr ≈ 2.37 mm; proposed 6 mm plate exceeds this, so the 6 mm plate IS compliant.

question_text:
A naval architect is reviewing the window and side scuttle arrangement for a new 140-metre general cargo vessel. On the freeboard deck, a first-tier deckhouse is fitted with a round opening of 480 mm diameter on its forward end bulkhead. The opening is intended to be a fixed (non-opening) light with toughened safety glass. The vessel's stability booklet treats this deckhouse as buoyant in the stability calculations.

Separately, on the second tier of the superstructure, a rectangular window measuring 900 mm × 600 mm is fitted in the side shell plating. The superstructure at this location protects direct access to a companionway leading below decks. The designer proposes to fit only a hinged inside deadlight to this window, with no external storm cover.

For the strength test of the second-tier window, the designer proposes to apply the test pressure to the design pressure level, hold for 3 minutes, then perform 3 loading/unloading cycles between the design pressure P and 4×P. The window is located 1.2 Cw above the waterline at scantling draft.

(1) Is the round opening on the forward end bulkhead of the first-tier deckhouse classified as a side scuttle or a window, and is its installation in that location compliant with the rules?
(2) Is the proposed deadlight arrangement for the second-tier side shell window compliant?
(3) Is the proposed strength test procedure for the second-tier window — specifically Step 2 (the cyclic loading) — required by the rules, given the window's position?
required_facts: The round opening has an area of approximately 0.181 m², which exceeds the 0.16 m² threshold, so it is classified as a window, not a side scuttle
Windows are prohibited in the first-tier end bulkheads of enclosed superstructures and in first-tier deckhouses considered buoyant in stability calculations, so the installation is non-compliant
A hinged inside deadlight capable of being secured weathertight is the required fitting for second-tier side shell windows protecting direct access below, so the proposed arrangement is compliant
Step 2 cyclic loading is exempt only for windows at 1.7 Cw or more above the waterline at scantling draft; at 1.2 Cw the window is below this threshold, so Step 2 is required

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question requiring classification of opening type by area threshold, application of location-based prohibition on windows in first-tier end bulkheads, deadlight requirements for second-tier side shell windows, and interpretation of the Step 2 test exemption based on vertical position relative to 1.7 Cw.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Classify the round opening: diameter 480 mm → area = π×(0.24)² = 0.1810 m², which exceeds 0.16 m². Per [2.1.1], round openings exceeding 0.16 m² are treated as windows, not side scuttles. Per [2.1.2], this is confirmed as a window.

Step 2 — Check installation location: Per [3.1.5](b), windows shall NOT be fitted in the first tier end bulkheads or sides of enclosed superstructures. The deckhouse is treated as buoyant in stability calculations, which per [3.1.5](c) also prohibits windows in first-tier deckhouses considered buoyant. The opening is on the forward end bulkhead of a first-tier deckhouse — this is non-compliant regardless of whether it is fixed or opening.

Step 3 — Second-tier window deadlight compliance: Per [3.1.6], side scuttles and windows at the side shell in the second tier shall be provided with hinged inside deadlights capable of being closed and secured weathertight, if the superstructure protects direct access to an opening leading below. The proposed hinged inside deadlight satisfies this requirement — compliant.

Step 4 — Step 2 cyclic test requirement: Per [6.2] item 4, the guidance note states that Step 2 is NOT required for windows located in superstructure and deckhouse sides from 1.7 Cw above WL at scantling draft. The window is at 1.2 Cw above WL, which is BELOW the 1.7 Cw threshold. Therefore Step 2 IS required, and the designer's procedure is correct in including it.

scenario_parameters.window_location_first_tier: forward end bulkhead of first-tier deckhouse
scenario_parameters.second_tier_window_location: side shell, second tier, protecting direct access below

question_text: A 145-meter bulk carrier is being designed with transverse web frames acting as primary supporting members in the cargo hold region. At one intersection, a longitudinal stiffener passes through the web frame via a cut-out. The cut-out has a depth of 210 mm, the primary supporting member web depth at that location is 380 mm, and no lug or collar plate is fitted. The cut-out has a rectangular profile with a breadth of 90 mm and sharp 90-degree corners (corner radius R = 0 mm). The intersection is not in a high-stress area and is not in way of cross-tie ends or bulkhead stools. Is this cut-out arrangement compliant with the classification rules? If not, identify all non-compliances and state the minimum required corner radius R for the cut-out.
required_facts: The 50% depth limit for cut-outs without lug or collar plate is 190 mm (50% of 380 mm PSM web depth)
The cut-out depth of 210 mm exceeds the 190 mm limit, making the arrangement non-compliant under [1.1.2] unless shear strength and buckling capacity are verified
The minimum corner radius R is the greater of 20% of cut-out breadth b or 25 mm
20% of 90 mm breadth = 18 mm, which is less than 25 mm, so R_min = 25 mm
The actual corner radius of 0 mm is non-compliant; the minimum required is 25 mm
Corner radius R need not exceed 50 mm per the rules

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: both the cut-out depth limit and the corner radius requirement are found within Pt3.Ch6.Sec7. The answerer must apply [1.1.2] to check the 50% depth rule, then apply [1.1.6] to determine the minimum corner radius.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Check cut-out depth limit per [1.1.2]: The rule states the total depth of cut-outs without lug or collar plate shall not exceed 50% of the PSM web depth. 50% of 380 mm = 190 mm. The actual cut-out depth is 210 mm, which exceeds 190 mm. Since no lug or collar plate is fitted, this is non-compliant unless shear strength and buckling capacity are demonstrated to be sufficient. Step 2 — Check corner radius per [1.1.6]: The rule requires corner radii R to be at least the greater of (a) 20% of the cut-out breadth b, or (b) 25 mm, but R need not exceed 50 mm. 20% of 90 mm = 18 mm. The greater of 18 mm and 25 mm is 25 mm. Therefore R_min = 25 mm. The actual R = 0 mm, which is non-compliant. Two non-compliances exist: (1) cut-out depth 210 mm exceeds the 50% limit of 190 mm with no lug/collar plate fitted, and (2) corner radius of 0 mm is below the required minimum of 25 mm.

question_text: A structural engineer is preparing a finite element model for a 185-metre bulk carrier with class notation ESP. The ship will be analysed under four loading conditions: fully loaded, 60% cargo fill (partly loaded), ballast, and during cargo discharge. The FE model uses four-node isotropic shell elements throughout, except for two slender plate panels in the double-bottom region that have high utilisation in the transverse direction — these panels have an aspect ratio of 6:1 and are modelled with anisotropic material properties using an imperfection factor X = 0.15. The engineer proposes to use gross scantlings for the entire FE model, including the buckling capacity assessment, on the grounds that the ship has not yet been assigned its final class notation. Is the proposed modelling approach compliant with the classification rules? Specifically: (1) which scantling basis must be used for the FE model and for the buckling capacity assessment given the ESP notation, (2) is the imperfection factor X = 0.15 acceptable for the anisotropic panels, and (3) are all four proposed loading conditions appropriate for the analysis?
required_facts: FE models for ships with ESP notation must use net scantlings, not gross scantlings
Buckling capacity assessment must also be based on net scantlings (not gross) regardless of notation assignment status
The prescribed imperfection factor for anisotropic elements is X = 0.1; the value X = 0.15 is not compliant
All four proposed loading conditions (fully loaded, partly loaded/60% fill, ballast, during discharge) are appropriate and align with the required load scenarios
The overall modelling approach is non-compliant due to both the incorrect scantling basis and the incorrect imperfection factor

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: all three sub-questions are answered directly within Pt3.Ch7.Sec1 — net scantling rule for ESP ships (Sec1 [2.1]), anisotropic imperfection factor requirement (Sec1 [3.1.3]), and load scenario requirements (Sec1 [1.3.1]).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Scantling basis: Sec1 [2.1] states that FE models for ships with class notation ESP shall be based on net scantling as defined in Ch.3 Sec.2 Table 1, and that buckling capacity assessment shall also be based on net scantling. The engineer's proposal to use gross scantlings is therefore non-compliant on both counts. Step 2 — Imperfection factor: Sec1 [3.1.3] specifies that when anisotropic elements are used, the imperfection factor shall be X = 0.1. The engineer has used X = 0.15, which does not comply with the prescribed value. Step 3 — Load scenarios: Sec1 [1.3.1] lists fully loaded, partly loaded, ballasted, and during loading/discharging as the required loading conditions. All four conditions proposed by the engineer (fully loaded, 60% fill, ballast, discharge) map directly onto these four categories and are therefore appropriate.

question_text:
A transverse web frame in the cargo hold of a bulk carrier spans between two longitudinal girders. The frame is modeled as a beam with both ends fixed (continuous over supports) and carries a uniform lateral pressure of 85 kN/m² over a tributary breadth of 2.4 m. The effective bending span is 4.2 m and the effective shear span is 4.0 m. The material has a minimum yield stress ReH = 315 N/mm² and the design load set is classified as AC-II. The hull girder longitudinal stress at this member is 28 N/mm², which is well below 0.15·ReH.

Determine: (a) the minimum required section modulus Z in cm³ for the mid-span position, and (b) the minimum required shear area Ashr in cm².
required_facts: Load model A (fixed-fixed ends) applies, giving fbdg2 = 24.0 at mid-span and fshr = 0.50 at supports
Cs = 0.85 and Ct = 0.85 for AC-II
The standard section modulus formula is applicable because hull girder longitudinal stress (28 N/mm²) is less than 0.15·ReH (47.25 N/mm²)
Minimum required section modulus Z ≈ 560 cm³ (mid-span)
τeH = ReH / √3 ≈ 181.8 N/mm²
Minimum required shear area Ashr ≈ 26.4 cm²

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the section modulus formula [2.1.1] and shear area formula [2.1.2] from Pt3.Ch6.Sec6, selecting the correct fbdg and fshr from Table 1 for a fixed-fixed (load model A) beam, and using Cs = Ct = 0.85 for AC-II.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Identify load model from Table 1. Both ends fixed with uniform load corresponds to load model A (fixed-fixed). For mid-span (position 2): fbdg2 = 24.0. For shear at support (position 1 or 3): fshr = 0.50.

Step 2 — Check applicability of [2.1.1]. The hull girder longitudinal stress is 28 N/mm²; 0.15 × 315 = 47.25 N/mm². Since 28 < 47.25, the standard formula applies (not the FE/[2.2] route).

Step 3 — Section modulus [2.1.1]:
Z = 1000 × |P| × S × ℓbdg² / (fbdg × Cs × ReH)
Z = 1000 × 85 × 2.4 × (4.2)² / (24.0 × 0.85 × 315)
Numerator: 1000 × 85 × 2.4 × 17.64 = 1000 × 85 × 42.336 = 3,598,560
Denominator: 24.0 × 0.85 × 315 = 6,426
Z = 3,598,560 / 6,426 ≈ 560.1 cm³

Step 4 — Shear area [2.1.2]:
Ashr = 10 × fshr × |P| × S × ℓshr / (Ct × τeH)
τeH = ReH / √3 = 315 / 1.732 ≈ 181.8 N/mm²
Ashr = 10 × 0.50 × 85 × 2.4 × 4.0 / (0.85 × 181.8)
Numerator: 10 × 0.50 × 85 × 2.4 × 4.0 = 10 × 0.50 × 816 = 4,080
Denominator: 0.85 × 181.8 = 154.53
Ashr = 4,080 / 154.53 ≈ 26.4 cm²

question_text: A new RO/RO passenger ferry is being designed with a bow door and an inner bow door, both leading to the RO/RO vehicle deck. However, the manual does not include a description of the central power pack or the bridge panel equipment, and the register of inspections section only lists planned inspection intervals but does not specifically mention inspection of locking, securing, and supporting devices. Is the OMM as described compliant with classification requirements, and what specific items are missing or deficient?

The description of the central power pack is missing and is a required content item
The description of the bridge panel equipment is missing and is a required content item
The limiting heel and trim of the ship for loading/unloading and for door operations must be included in the service conditions section but is absent
The register of inspections must specifically include inspection of locking, securing, and supporting devices — listing only planned intervals is insufficient
The OMM as described is not compliant with classification requirements

Step 3: Check [3.2.2](b) — service conditions including limiting heel/trim for loading/unloading, limiting heel/trim for door operations, operating instructions, and emergency operating instructions. The scenario states only planned intervals are listed without specific mention of locking/securing/supporting device inspections — this is a deficiency. question_text: A bulk carrier of 185 m length operates on unrestricted service with a single cargo deck. At the midship cross-section, the permissible still water bending moment is 4 200 000 kNm in hogging and 3 800 000 kNm in sagging. The vertical wave bending moment at that section is 2 500 000 kNm in hogging and 2 100 000 kNm in sagging. The vessel has class notation HC(A) and its loading manual includes alternate loading conditions with empty cargo holds. Calculate the combined vertical bending moment M for both hogging and sagging conditions, determine the minimum required hull girder ultimate bending capacity MU for each condition, and state whether the partial safety factor γDB = 1.25 or 1.1 applies in hogging.
required_facts: Hogging combined bending moment M = 7 200 000 kNm (= 1.0 × 4 200 000 + 1.2 × 2 500 000)
Sagging combined bending moment M = 6 320 000 kNm (= 1.0 × 3 800 000 + 1.2 × 2 100 000)
γDB = 1.25 applies in hogging because the vessel has class notation HC(A) and alternate loading conditions with empty cargo holds are included in the loading manual
Minimum required MU in hogging ≥ 9 900 000 kNm
Minimum required MU in sagging ≥ 6 952 000 kNm

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the hull girder ultimate strength checking criteria within Pt3.Ch5.Sec4, selecting the correct γDB branch for an HC(A) vessel with alternate loading conditions in hogging, and computing M and the MU lower bound from the criteria formula.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Check applicability [1.1.1]: L = 185 m > 150 m, unrestricted service, single deck → section applies.

Step 2 — Compute M per [2.2.1]: M = γS·Msw-U + γW·Mwv, with γS = 1.0 and γW = 1.2.
  Hogging: M_hog = 1.0 × 4 200 000 + 1.2 × 2 500 000 = 4 200 000 + 3 000 000 = 7 200 000 kNm.
  Sagging: M_sag = 1.0 × 3 800 000 + 1.2 × 2 100 000 = 3 800 000 + 2 520 000 = 6 320 000 kNm.

Step 3 — Determine γDB per [2.1.2]:
  Hogging: vessel has class notation HC(A) AND alternate loading conditions with empty cargo holds are included in the loading manual → γDB = 1.25.
  Sagging: γDB = 1.0 (always).

Step 4 — Compute γR = γM × γDB, with γM = 1.1:
  Hogging: γR = 1.1 × 1.25 = 1.375.
  Sagging: γR = 1.1 × 1.0 = 1.1.

Step 5 — Apply criterion M ≤ MU / γR, rearranged to MU ≥ M × γR:
  Hogging: MU ≥ 7 200 000 × 1.375 = 9 900 000 kNm.
  Sagging: MU ≥ 6 320 000 × 1.1 = 6 952 000 kNm.

question_text: A RO/RO ferry has a stern door that opens inwards and leads directly to the enclosed RO/RO vehicle deck. The door has a light opening area of 9.5 m² and a mass of 4.2 tonnes. The door sill is located 180 mm above the uppermost load line. From the ship's damage stability calculations, the deepest equilibrium waterline in damaged condition is 1.8 m above the load point of the door. The total packing force is 12 kN. A designer proposes to use securing bolts as the primary means of transferring sea pressure to the coamings, without fitting a direct hull coaming load path. Is this structural arrangement acceptable, and what is the minimum design force (in kN) that the securing bolts and closing devices must be designed to resist?
required_facts: The securing bolt arrangement is acceptable because the light opening area A = 9.5 m² is less than the 12 m² threshold
The door leads to a RO/RO space and opens inwards, so the F1 formula applies: F1 = A·Pe + Fp
Pe = 10·hb = 10 × 1.8 = 18 kN/m², but the minimum value of 25 kN/m² governs
The securing bolts and closing devices must be designed to resist a minimum force of 249.5 kN

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: check door area against 12 m² threshold for securing bolt acceptability ([1.3.4]), then apply the F1 formula for inward-opening doors leading to RO/RO spaces ([1.4.3])
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Structural arrangement acceptability: Per [1.3.4], securing bolts may be accepted as carriers of sea pressure to the coamings only for doors with light opening area A < 12 m². Here A = 9.5 m² < 12 m², so the securing bolt arrangement is acceptable (provided the direct load path per [1.3.3] is not feasible). Step 2 — Design force: The door leads to an enclosed RO/RO space, so [1.4.3] applies. The door opens inwards, so F1 applies: F1 = A·Pe + Fp. Pe = 10·hb = 10 × 1.8 = 18 kN/m², with minimum 25 kN/m² — since 18 < 25, Pe = 25 kN/m². F1 = 9.5 × 25 + 12 = 237.5 + 12 = 249.5 kN. The securing bolts and closing devices must be designed for at least 249.5 kN.

question_text: A 180 m cargo ship (not a tanker) has a beam B of 32 m. The naval architect proposes a double bottom with an inner bottom height of 1 500 mm above the keel line, measured vertically. The double bottom extends from the collision bulkhead to the aft peak bulkhead. In the cargo hold area, small drainage wells are cut into the double bottom tank; the deepest well bottom sits 480 mm above the keel line. Is the proposed double bottom arrangement fully compliant with classification requirements? Identify any non-compliant element and state the minimum permissible value(s) that must be met.
required_facts: h_DB = 1 600 mm (calculated as 1000 × 32 / 20)
The proposed inner bottom height of 1 500 mm is less than the required 1 600 mm and is therefore non-compliant
For L_LL ≥ 80 m the drainage well bottom must be at least 500 mm or half the required double bottom height above the keel plane
Half the required double bottom height = 800 mm, which governs over the 500 mm minimum
The proposed well depth of 480 mm above the keel is less than 800 mm and is therefore non-compliant
Both the inner bottom height and the drainage well arrangement must be corrected for compliance

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the double bottom height formula in [2.3] to check the proposed 1 500 mm height, then check the drainage well depth against the [2.4] threshold (500 mm or half h_DB, whichever is greater).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Required double bottom height (Sec3 [2.3]): h_DB = 1000 × B / 20 = 1000 × 32 / 20 = 1 600 mm. The maximum cap is 2 000 mm, so h_DB = 1 600 mm applies. The proposed height of 1 500 mm is LESS than 1 600 mm → NON-COMPLIANT. Step 2 — Drainage well depth (Sec3 [2.4]): The ship has L_LL = 180 m ≥ 80 m, so the rule applies. The vertical distance from the well bottom to the keel plane must not be less than 500 mm OR half the required double bottom height (1 600 / 2 = 800 mm), whichever is the more stringent. The rule states 'not less than 500 mm or half the required double bottom height', meaning the larger of the two governs: 800 mm. The proposed well bottom is at 480 mm, which is less than 800 mm → NON-COMPLIANT.

question_text: A newbuilding bulk carrier has a deck plating panel where the net required thickness calculated from structural analysis is 14.2 mm. The corrosion addition for this panel is 3.0 mm. The shipyard proposes to install plates with an as-built thickness of 18.5 mm, including a voluntary builder's extra margin of 0.5 mm added beyond the corrosion addition. A surveyor needs to verify whether this plating arrangement is compliant. What is the gross required thickness for this panel (rounded to the nearest half millimetre), what is the gross offered thickness, and does the arrangement satisfy the scantling compliance requirement?
required_facts: The gross required thickness rounded to the nearest half millimetre is 17.0 mm
t_gr_off = t_as_built − t_vol_add = 18.5 − 0.5 = 18.0 mm
The voluntary addition (0.5 mm) is deducted from the as-built thickness to obtain the gross offered thickness and does not contribute to compliance
t_gr_off (18.0 mm) ≥ t_gr rounded (17.0 mm), so the arrangement is compliant

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply gross required thickness formula, then gross offered thickness formula, then rounding rule, then compliance check — all within Pt3.Ch3.Sec2
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Gross required thickness [1.2.1]: t_gr = min(t + t_c ; 1.25t) = min(14.2 + 3.0 ; 1.25 × 14.2) = min(17.2 ; 17.75) = 17.2 mm. Step 2 — Rounding [1.3.1]: 17.2 mm falls in the range 17.0 ≤ t_gr < 17.25, so rounded gross required thickness = 17.0 mm. (Actually 17.2 falls in 17.0 ≤ t_gr < 17.25 → rounds to 17.0 mm.) Step 3 — Gross offered thickness [1.2.2]: t_gr_off = t_as_built − t_vol_add = 18.5 − 0.5 = 18.0 mm. Step 4 — Compliance [1.3.2]: t_gr_off (18.0 mm) ≥ t_gr rounded (17.0 mm) → compliant. Note: the voluntary addition of 0.5 mm is correctly excluded from the gross offered thickness per [1.2.2]; it does not count toward compliance.

question_text: A naval architect is checking the scantlings of a 110-metre general cargo vessel. One of the transverse web frames in the cargo hold uses a flat bar stiffener on a tight floor. The stiffener is arranged inside a ballast tank, and double bottom girders are arranged at every 3rd longitudinal spacing. The flat bar stiffener has a web depth h_w of 180 mm and a net web thickness t_w of 6 mm. Does this stiffener satisfy the slenderness requirement for its web plate, and what is the minimum net web thickness required?
required_facts: The applicable slenderness coefficient C_w is 30, not 22, because the flat bar stiffener is on a tight floor inside a ballast tank with double bottom girders at every 3rd longitudinal spacing
The minimum net web thickness formula is t_w ≥ (h_w / C_w) × sqrt(R_eH / 235)
With C_w = 30, h_w = 180 mm, and R_eH = 235 N/mm², the minimum required t_w = 6.0 mm
The provided t_w of 6 mm exactly meets the minimum requirement and is therefore compliant

If the default C_w = 22 for flat bars had been used instead, the minimum t_w would be 180/22 ≈ 8.18 mm, which would make the stiffener non-compliant — so correct identification of the footnote 4 condition is critical

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply stiffener web slenderness formula using the special C_w value from Table 2 footnote 4 for flat bar stiffeners on tight floors inside ballast tanks with girders at every 3rd longitudinal spacing
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify stiffener type — flat bar stiffener on a tight floor, arranged inside a ballast tank, with double bottom girders at every 3rd longitudinal spacing. This triggers footnote 4 of Table 2, which gives C_w = 30 (instead of the default C_w = 22 for flat bars). Step 2: The vessel is 110 m, so R_eH is the material yield stress. The question does not specify material, so assume standard mild steel R_eH = 235 N/mm². Step 3: Apply the web slenderness formula from [3.1.1] a): t_w ≥ (h_w / C_w) × sqrt(R_eH / 235). With C_w = 30, h_w = 180 mm, R_eH = 235 N/mm²: t_w_min = (180 / 30) × sqrt(235/235) = 6.0 × 1.0 = 6.0 mm. Step 4: The provided t_w = 6 mm equals exactly the minimum required value of 6.0 mm, so the stiffener just satisfies the requirement.

question_text: A newly built 185-metre sea-going vessel is designed to carry containers as its primary cargo. The ship is fitted with cell guides at the transverse bulkheads, fixed container foundations welded to the inner bottom, and fixed lashing fittings on the upper deck and hatch covers. The owner also wants to carry occasional break-bulk cargo on the inner bottom and, separately, intends to load grain in bulk in one of the cargo holds during return voyages. The designer is preparing the classification submission and needs to know: (1) which ship type class notation will be assigned to this vessel, (2) whether the break-bulk carriage on the inner bottom is permissible under the rules, (3) whether the bulk grain carriage is permissible, and (4) which compliance document type and issuing authority are required for the container securing equipment fitted on board.
required_facts: The vessel qualifies for the ship type notation 'Container ship'
Break-bulk carriage on the inner bottom may be accepted on a case-by-case basis (not automatically permitted or prohibited)
The transport of dry cargo in bulk is not permitted for this vessel type
Container securing equipment requires a Product Certificate (PC)
The Product Certificate for container securing equipment must be issued by the Society (DNV)
The applicable compliance standard for container securing equipment is DNV-CP-0068

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: all answers are found within Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 by applying the application criteria in 1.3, the ship type notation table in 1.4.1, and the certification requirements table in 2.2.1.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 – Check application criteria (Sec1 [1.3]): the vessel has cell guides at bulkheads, fixed container foundations on the inner bottom, and fixed lashing appliances on the upper deck/hatch covers → all three characteristics are met, so the chapter applies. Step 2 – Ship type notation (Sec1 [1.4.1], Table 1): a ship built in compliance with the requirements of this section is assigned the notation 'Container ship'. Step 3 – Break-bulk on inner bottom (Sec1 [1.3]): 'The transport of other cargo, i.e. break bulk on the inner bottom, may be accepted on a case by case basis.' → permissible subject to case-by-case approval, not automatically prohibited. Step 4 – Dry bulk carriage (Sec1 [1.3]): 'The transport of dry cargo in bulk is not permitted.' → bulk grain carriage is explicitly prohibited. Step 5 – Compliance document for container securing equipment (Sec1 [2.2.1], Table 5): container securing equipment requires a Product Certificate (PC) issued by the Society, with compliance standard DNV-CP-0068.

question_text: A structural engineer is performing a fatigue assessment for a longitudinal weld detail located in a water ballast tank of a bulk carrier. The vessel operates worldwide and the fatigue loads are calculated using the prescriptive method. The detail is assessed using the hot spot stress approach. After running the fatigue calculation, the engineer finds that the initial (pre-treatment) calculated fatigue life for this detail is 19 years. The engineer proposes to apply weld toe grinding to improve the fatigue life, and the weld is a full penetration weld. The hot spot is confirmed to be protected from corrosive environment. Is the proposed post-weld treatment acceptable under classification rules? Additionally, what environmental factor f_e should be used in the fatigue damage calculation, and what is the time in corrosive environment T_C,25 that must be accounted for over the 25-year design life for this ballast tank detail?
required_facts: f_e = 0.8 for worldwide wave environment with prescriptive loads
T_C,25 = 5 years for a water ballast tank over the 25-year design life
The fatigue damage estimate for the time in corrosive environment must be multiplied by two
Post-weld treatment is acceptable because the initial fatigue life of 19 years meets the minimum threshold of 17 years
The full penetration weld and corrosion-protected hot spot satisfy the post-weld treatment conditions in [4.6]
S-N curve D (FAT 90) shall be used for the hot spot stress approach

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: all required facts are contained within Pt3.Ch9.Sec4 — environmental factor from [4.2], corrosive environment time from Table 1, and post-weld treatment conditions from [4.6].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Environmental factor [4.2]: Prescriptive loads, worldwide wave environment → f_e = 0.8. Step 2 — Corrosive environment time, Table 1: Water ballast tank → T_C,25 = 5 years over 25-year design life; damage estimate for this period must be multiplied by two. Step 3 — Post-weld treatment acceptability [4.6]: Conditions checked: (a) detail assessed by FE analysis — assumed yes (hot spot approach implies FE); (b) full penetration weld — yes; (c) hot spot protected from corrosive environment — yes (stated); (d) initial calculated fatigue life prior to treatment must be minimum 17 years — 19 years ≥ 17 years, so this condition is satisfied; (e) post-weld treatment not applicable to longitudinal end connections — this is a longitudinal weld detail but not stated to be an end connection, so acceptable; (f) not a cargo hold with mechanical damage risk — it is a ballast tank, so acceptable. All conditions are met → post-weld treatment (toe grinding) is acceptable.

question_text: A general cargo vessel has a freeboard deck well formed by bulwarks on the weather deck. The bulwark runs for 24 metres along the well and has an average height of 1.5 metres. The ship has no sheer in way of this well. What is the minimum required freeing port area, in m², on each side of the ship for this well?
required_facts: Base formula A = 0.07 × ℓb applies because ℓb = 24 m > 20 m, giving A = 1.68 m²
Bulwark height of 1.5 m exceeds 1.2 m threshold, triggering an area increase of 0.004 m² per metre of well length per 0.1 m excess
Height excess = 0.3 m (3 increments), so height correction = 3 × 0.004 × 24 = 0.288 m²
Height-adjusted area = 1.68 + 0.288 = 1.968 m²
No-sheer condition requires a 50% increase to the calculated area
Minimum required freeing port area per side = 1.968 × 1.50 = 2.952 m²

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the freeing port area formula for ℓb > 20 m, then apply the bulwark height correction for height > 1.2 m, then apply the 50% increase for no sheer per [2.1.2].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Base area from [2.1.1]: ℓb = 24 m > 20 m, so A = 0.07 × 24 = 1.68 m².
Step 2 — Bulwark height correction: average height = 1.5 m > 1.2 m, difference = 1.5 − 1.2 = 0.3 m, which is 3 increments of 0.1 m. Increase = 3 × 0.004 × 24 = 0.288 m². Adjusted area = 1.68 + 0.288 = 1.968 m².
Step 3 — No-sheer correction from [2.1.2]: area shall be increased by 50%. Final area = 1.968 × 1.50 = 2.952 m².

scenario_parameters.L_constraint: ℓb = 24 m assumed ≤ 0.7L, so no cap applied

question_text: A structural engineer is performing a fine mesh finite element analysis on a critical bracket toe detail in a bulk carrier. The fine mesh model uses a uniform element size of 30 mm × 30 mm throughout the fine mesh zone. At the bracket toe, the highest-stressed shell element shows a von Mises stress of 285 N/mm². The surrounding elements within the equivalent 50 mm × 50 mm averaging area have the following von Mises stresses and areas: element 1 (285 N/mm², 900 mm²), element 2 (260 N/mm², 900 mm²), element 3 (240 N/mm², 900 mm²), element 4 (210 N/mm², 900 mm²). The material yield strength R_Y = 355 N/mm² and the permissible fine mesh utilisation factor λ_fperm = 1.0 for the applicable acceptance criteria class. Is the structural detail compliant, and what is the governing von Mises stress used in the assessment?
required_facts: Because the mesh size (30 mm × 30 mm) is smaller than the reference 50 mm × 50 mm, stress averaging over an equivalent 50 mm × 50 mm area is required before comparing to the permissible stress
The area-weighted average von Mises stress is 248.75 N/mm² (not the peak element value of 285 N/mm²)
The fine mesh yield utilisation factor λ_f = 248.75 / 355 ≈ 0.70
λ_f (0.70) does not exceed λ_fperm (1.0), so the detail is compliant
Stress averaging uses the formula σ_vm-av = Σ(A_i × σ_vm-i) / Σ(A_i) weighted by element areas

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: fine mesh acceptance criteria in Pt3.Ch7.Sec4 [4.2.2], requiring application of the stress-averaging formula when mesh size is smaller than 50 mm × 50 mm, then checking the utilisation factor against the permissible value.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Recognise that the mesh size (30 mm × 30 mm) is smaller than the reference mesh size (50 mm × 50 mm). Per [4.2.2](a), when a smaller mesh size is used, an average von Mises stress over an area equal to the specified 50 mm × 50 mm mesh size must be used instead of the peak element stress. Step 2 — Apply the area-weighted average formula from [4.2.2](b): σ_vm-av = Σ(A_i × σ_vm-i) / Σ(A_i). With four elements each of area 900 mm²: σ_vm-av = (900×285 + 900×260 + 900×240 + 900×210) / (4×900) = (256500 + 234000 + 216000 + 189000) / 3600 = 895500 / 3600 = 248.75 N/mm². Step 3 — Compute the fine mesh yield utilisation factor: λ_f = σ_vm-av / R_Y = 248.75 / 355 = 0.700. Step 4 — Check against permissible: λ_f (0.700) ≤ λ_fperm (1.0). The detail is compliant. The governing stress is the averaged value of 248.75 N/mm², not the peak element stress of 285 N/mm².

question_text: A container ship is being designed with cell guides in the cargo hold. The cell guides are to be welded directly to the deck plating edges in way of the hatchways for structural continuity. Additionally, containers will be stowed in cell guides in the hold, and the designer proposes to omit doubler plates at the foot prints on the inner bottom, arguing that the inner bottom plating is already at maximum scantling. The hull support structures for lashing eye plates are sized to a safe working load of 150 kN per lashing point. For the strength evaluation of the hull support structures for container support fittings, the designer intends to use only the vertical load Fv1 and horizontal transverse load Fq for all load combinations, omitting the longitudinal/vertical load combination entirely. Are any of these design decisions non-compliant with classification rules, and if so, which ones and why?
required_facts: Welding cell guides to deck plating edges in way of hatchways is explicitly prohibited and the arrangement is non-compliant
Doubler plates are mandatory at foot prints on the inner bottom (or stringers) for containers stowed in cell guides in hold, so omitting them is non-compliant
Two load combinations are required for hull support structures for container support fittings: LC1 (transverse: Fv1 + Fq + wind) and LC2 (longitudinal/vertical: Fv2 + Fl, no wind)
Omitting LC2 (longitudinal/vertical load combination) from the strength evaluation is non-compliant
Hull support structures for lashing eye plates must be strengthened with respect to the lashings' certified safe working load (SWL)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: all required reasoning is within Pt5.Ch2.Sec9. The answerer must identify three distinct non-compliances: (1) cell guides welded to deck plating edges at hatchways is explicitly prohibited, (2) omitting doubler plates at foot prints for in-hold cell guide containers is explicitly required, (3) omitting the longitudinal/vertical load combination (LC2: Fv2 + Fl) violates Table 1 which mandates two load combinations for container support fitting hull structures.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Check cell guide welding arrangement: Sec9 [2.2.1] explicitly states 'The cell guides shall not be welded to deck plating edges in way of the hatchways.' The proposed welding is therefore non-compliant. Step 2 — Check doubler plates: Sec9 [2.2.2] states 'For containers stowed in cell guides in hold, doubler plates shall be arranged for the foot prints on inner bottom or stringers.' Omitting them is non-compliant regardless of scantling arguments. Step 3 — Check load combinations: Sec9 Table 1 lists two mandatory load combinations for hull support structures for container support fittings: LC1 (transverse loading: Fv1, Fq, with wind) and LC2 (longitudinal/vertical loading: Fv2, Fl, no wind). Using only LC1 and omitting LC2 is non-compliant. Step 4 — Check lashing eye plate sizing: Sec9 [3.1.2] states hull support structures for lashing eye plates shall be strengthened with respect to the lashings' certified SWL — this is a requirement on the structure being adequate for the SWL, not a prohibition on any particular SWL value, so the 150 kN SWL itself is not inherently non-compliant as long as the structure is designed accordingly.

scenario_parameters.cell_guide_welding: proposed at deck plating edges in way of hatchways
scenario_parameters.doubler_plates: omitted at inner bottom foot prints

question_text: A structural designer is selecting rolled steel for the main deck plating of a 145-metre bulk carrier. Option B steel (ReH = 390 N/mm²) is classified as high strength hull structural steel, grade family AH/DH/EH/FH (A40/D40/E40/F40)
Material factor k for Option A (ReH = 355 N/mm²) is 0.72
Material factor k for Option B (ReH = 390 N/mm²) is 0.66 with fatigue assessment or 0.68 without fatigue assessment (as stated in Table 2)
The mixed-strength arrangement — lower-yield flange (355 N/mm²) connected to higher-yield stiffener (390 N/mm²) — triggers an additional yield capacity check of the plate flange

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: classify steel grades per 2.1.4, look up material factor k from Table 2 per 2.2, and identify the mixed-strength flange/web check triggered by 2.1.2.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Classify Option A (ReH = 355 N/mm²): Per 2.1.4, normal strength is ReH = 235 N/mm²; high strength is 235 < ReH ≤ 390 N/mm²; extra high strength is ReH > 390 N/mm². ReH = 355 N/mm² falls in the high strength range. Grade family is AH/DH/EH/FH (specifically A36/D36/E36/F36 per Table 1). Tensile strength 510 N/mm² is within the specified range 490–630 N/mm² for 355-grade steel — consistent. Step 2 — Classify Option B (ReH = 390 N/mm²): ReH = 390 N/mm² satisfies 235 < ReH ≤ 390 N/mm², so it is also high strength. Grade family is AH/DH/EH/FH (specifically A40/D40/E40/F40 per Table 1). Tensile strength 530 N/mm² is within the specified range 510–660 N/mm² — consistent. Step 3 — Material factor k from Table 2: For Option A (ReH = 355 N/mm²), k = 0.72. For Option B (ReH = 390 N/mm²), k = 0.66 (linear interpolation between 355 → 0.72 and 390 → 0.66 per Table 2). Step 4 — Mixed-strength arrangement: Per 2.1.2, when the plate flange has a lower minimum yield strength than the connected stiffener or PSM, an additional check of the yield capacity of the plate flange may be required, with reference to Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4]. Here Option A (355 N/mm²) flange is lower than Option B (390 N/mm²) stiffener web, so this additional yield capacity check is triggered.

scenario_parameters.mixed_arrangement: Option A flange + Option B stiffener web

question_text: A naval architect is preparing the class notation string for a new offshore service vessel being submitted to a classification society. The vessel will be assigned the following notations: the standard construction symbol, main class notation 1A, ship type notation Offshore service vessel (AHTS), and several additional class notations including E0, NAUT(OSV), LFL, HELDK(S, H), SF, Ice(1A), Winterized, and Clean(Design). The designer also wants to include a survey arrangement notation TMON. When writing the formal class notation string in the submission documents, how should qualifiers such as (OSV), (S, H), and (1A) be formatted relative to their parent class notations, and what is the correct way to separate multiple qualifiers belonging to the same class notation?
required_facts: Qualifiers are placed in parentheses immediately after the class notation they belong to, with no space between the notation name and the opening parenthesis.
Multiple qualifiers belonging to the same class notation are separated by a comma followed by a space inside the parentheses.
HELDK with qualifiers S and H is correctly written as HELDK(S, H).
NAUT with qualifier OSV is correctly written as NAUT(OSV).
Ice with qualifier 1A is correctly written as Ice(1A).
Class notations and their qualifiers are shown in bold in formal documentation.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: qualifier formatting rules are fully defined in Pt1.Ch2.Sec1 [1.1.5] and [1.1.6], with Table 1 providing concrete examples of the notation string for an offshore service vessel.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the relevant rule: Pt1.Ch2.Sec1 [1.1.5] states that qualifiers follow immediately after a class notation and are indicated in parenthesis, and that multiple qualifiers are separated by comma and space. Step 2 — Apply to NAUT(OSV): single qualifier, so written as NAUT(OSV) with no comma needed. Step 3 — Apply to HELDK(S, H): two qualifiers S and H, so written as HELDK(S, H) with a comma and space between them inside the parentheses. Step 4 — Apply to Ice(1A): single qualifier, written as Ice(1A). Step 5 — Confirm via Table 1 (Example 3) which shows exactly this notation string for an offshore service vessel: NAUT(OSV), HELDK(S, H), Ice(1A), confirming the formatting. Step 6 — Conclude: qualifiers are placed in parentheses immediately after the notation name, and when a notation carries more than one qualifier they are separated by ', ' (comma followed by space) within the same set of parentheses.

question_text: A shipowner signs a contract with a shipbuilder on 15 March 2022 to build a series of five identical bulk carriers (hull numbers 101–105). The contract explicitly includes an option for two additional vessels (hull numbers 106–107). The option for hull numbers 106–107 is exercised on 20 April 2023 — that is, 13 months after the original contract was signed. The owner then requests that hull number 107 be redesigned as a chemical tanker rather than a bulk carrier, and a revised contract for hull 107 is signed on 10 September 2023. For classification purposes: (a) What is the date of 'contract for construction' that governs the applicable rules for hull numbers 101–105? (b) Are hull numbers 106–107 considered part of the original series, and what date of 'contract for construction' applies to them? (c) What date of 'contract for construction' applies to hull number 107 as a chemical tanker?
required_facts: The date of 'contract for construction' for hull numbers 101–105 is 15 March 2022
Hull numbers 106–107 are NOT part of the original series because the option was exercised 13 months after contract signing, exceeding the 1-year limit
The date of 'contract for construction' for hull numbers 106–107 (as bulk carriers) is 20 April 2023, treated as a new contract
Because hull 107's ship type was changed to a chemical tanker via a revised contract, the date of 'contract for construction' for hull 107 is 10 September 2023
The 1-year option exercise deadline is measured from the date the original series contract was signed

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question requiring careful application of the multi-part definition of 'contract for construction' in clause 1.3.2, covering series vessels, option exercise timing, contract amendments, and ship-type changes.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 (hulls 101–105): Per 1.3.2 item 2, the date of 'contract for construction' for a series of vessels is the date the contract to build the series is signed — 15 March 2022. All five hulls share this date. Step 2 (hulls 106–107 as optional vessels): Per 1.3.2 item 2, optional vessels are part of the same series only if the option is exercised not later than 1 year after the original contract was signed. The option was exercised on 20 April 2023, which is 13 months after 15 March 2022 — exceeding the 1-year limit. Therefore hulls 106–107 are NOT part of the original series. Per 1.3.2 item 3, the amendment adding them is treated as a 'new contract', so the date of 'contract for construction' for hulls 106–107 is 20 April 2023. Step 3 (hull 107 as chemical tanker): Per 1.3.2 item 4, when a contract is amended to change the ship type, the date of 'contract for construction' for that vessel is the date the revised or new contract is signed — 10 September 2023.

question_text: A 185-metre general cargo vessel is being designed with a large moonpool located at 62 metres forward of the aft perpendicular. The moonpool opening measures 8 m × 6 m and creates a significant structural discontinuity in the main deck and inner bottom. The ship's designer is preparing the fatigue assessment plan for classification. Two structural details are under review: (1) the longitudinal stiffener end connections at the transverse frames within the midship region, and (2) the deck plating and coaming structure immediately surrounding the moonpool opening. For each detail, state whether fatigue assessment is mandatory or discretionary under the main class requirements, and explain the basis for each determination.
required_facts: The 0.5L amidships zone for a 185 m vessel spans from 46.25 m to 138.75 m from the aft perpendicular, and the moonpool at 62 m from aft lies within this zone.
Fatigue assessment of longitudinal stiffener end connections at frames and transverse bulkheads within 0.5L amidships is mandatory (prescriptive fatigue assessment is required).
Fatigue assessment of the moonpool structure is discretionary, not automatically mandatory — it may be required on a case-by-case basis.
The moonpool/large opening is explicitly cited as an example of a structural discontinuity that can cause high longitudinal stresses, making it a candidate for case-by-case fatigue assessment.
The distinction between the two details is that clause [1] uses 'shall' (mandatory) while clause [2] uses 'may' (discretionary/case-by-case).

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: both details fall within 0.5L amidships; longitudinal stiffener end connections are mandatorily assessed under [1], while the moonpool structure is a named example of a high-stress discontinuity detail assessed on a case-by-case basis under [2].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Establish the 0.5L amidships zone. L = 185 m, so 0.5L = 92.5 m centred amidships. The amidships zone runs from 0.25L = 46.25 m from aft to 0.75L = 138.75 m from aft. The moonpool at 62 m from aft falls within this zone. Step 2 — Detail (1): Longitudinal stiffener end connections at frames within 0.5L amidships. Pt3.Ch9.Sec2 [1] states these 'shall be assessed based on prescriptive fatigue assessment' — mandatory, no discretion. Step 3 — Detail (2): The moonpool opening is explicitly listed in the guidance note to Pt3.Ch9.Sec2 [2] as an example of a detail with high longitudinal stresses caused by structural discontinuities. Clause [2] states fatigue assessment 'may be required on a case-by-case basis' — discretionary, subject to the classification society's judgment.

details_under_review: longitudinal stiffener end connections at transverse frames

question_text: A newly built 180-metre bulk carrier has two dedicated seawater ballast tanks and a number of narrow void spaces at the bow and stern regions. The shipyard proposes the following corrosion protection arrangements: (1) the dedicated seawater ballast tanks will be coated with a standard epoxy paint system applied in the shipyard, but the shipyard does not intend to follow the IMO PSPC performance standard (MSC.215(82)) on the grounds that the vessel is not required to comply with SOLAS Chapter II-1/3-2; (2) the narrow void spaces at the forward and aft ends of the ship will be left uncoated because the shipyard argues that 'narrow spaces' are not explicitly listed as mandatory coating areas in the structural rules. Assess whether each of these two proposed arrangements is acceptable under classification rules, giving reasons for each conclusion.
required_facts: Dedicated seawater ballast tanks exposed to a corrosive environment must have an efficient corrosion prevention system.

For vessels subject to PSPC requirements, the corrosion prevention system for dedicated seawater ballast tanks must comply with SOLAS Chapter II-1/3-2 and IMO Resolution MSC.215(82); a non-PSPC-compliant coating is not acceptable for such vessels.
Narrow spaces must generally be protected by an efficient protective product.
The requirement for protecting narrow spaces applies particularly at the ends of the ship (bow and stern) where inspection and maintenance are difficult due to inaccessibility.
Leaving the narrow void spaces at the forward and aft ends uncoated is not acceptable under the classification rules.
The shipyard's argument that narrow spaces are not explicitly listed as mandatory coating areas is incorrect; clause 1.1.2 explicitly requires their protection.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: both sub-clauses of Pt3.Ch3.Sec4 are needed. Clause 1.1.1 governs dedicated seawater ballast tanks (PSPC requirement) and clause 1.1.2 governs narrow spaces at ship ends.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 – Dedicated seawater ballast tanks: Clause 1.1.1 states that for vessels following PSPC requirements, dedicated seawater ballast tanks shall have an efficient corrosion prevention system in accordance with SOLAS Chapter II-1/3-2 and IMO Resolution MSC.215(82). The shipyard's claim that the vessel is not subject to SOLAS II-1/3-2 may or may not be valid depending on flag/class, but the classification rule itself mandates compliance with PSPC for vessels that do follow PSPC requirements. If the vessel is subject to PSPC (which a bulk carrier of this size typically is), the arrangement of applying a non-PSPC-compliant coating is not acceptable. Step 2 – Narrow spaces at bow and stern: Clause 1.1.2 states that narrow spaces shall generally be protected by an efficient protective product, particularly at the ends of the ship where inspections and maintenance are not easily practicable due to their inaccessibility. The shipyard's argument that narrow spaces are not mandatory is incorrect; the rule explicitly requires protection for narrow spaces, with special emphasis on ship ends. Leaving them uncoated is therefore not acceptable.

scenario_parameters.shipyard_claim_1: vessel not subject to SOLAS II-1/3-2

question_text: A bulk carrier has a rectangular tank access hatchway on the freeboard deck with plan dimensions of 1.0 m × 1.4 m (area = 1.40 m²). The proposed hatch cover is made of mild steel and has a gross thickness of 11.0 mm. The cover is secured to the coaming by bolts spaced 360 mm apart, with the nearest bolt 230 mm from each corner. Is this hatch cover arrangement fully compliant with classification requirements? Identify any non-compliant aspects and state the minimum required gross thickness for this cover.
required_facts: Minimum required gross thickness is 12.5 mm because the hatch cover area (1.40 m²) is at or above the 0.5 m² threshold
The proposed 11.0 mm gross thickness is non-compliant (less than the required 12.5 mm)
The hatch cover must be stiffened because the hatchway area (1.40 m²) exceeds 1.25 m²
Bolt spacing of 360 mm is compliant (does not exceed the 380 mm maximum)
Corner bolt distance of 230 mm is compliant (does not exceed the 250 mm maximum)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the hatch cover thickness formula (linear interpolation for area between 0.25 m² and 0.5 m² thresholds — but area is 1.40 m², above 0.5 m², so t_gr = 12.5 mm), check stiffening requirement (area > 1.25 m²), and verify fastening spacing and corner distance rules.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Thickness (2.1.2): The hatch cover area is 1.40 m², which is above the 0.5 m² threshold, so the minimum gross thickness is t_gr = 12.5 mm. The proposed 11.0 mm is less than 12.5 mm → NON-COMPLIANT. Step 2 — Stiffening (2.1.3): The area 1.40 m² exceeds 1.25 m², so the hatch cover must be stiffened. The scenario does not mention stiffening → must be flagged. Step 3 — Fastening spacing (2.1.4): Bolts are spaced 360 mm apart, which is ≤ 380 mm → COMPLIANT. Corner distance is 230 mm, which is ≤ 250 mm → COMPLIANT. Summary: The cover fails on minimum thickness (11.0 mm < 12.5 mm required) and must also be stiffened because area > 1.25 m². Fastening spacing and corner distances are acceptable.

question_text: A general cargo vessel has a bulwark fitted at the boundary of an exposed freeboard deck. The bulwark height, measured from the top of the deck plating to the top of the rail, is 1.4 m. Bulwark stays are spaced at 1.8 m apart. The designer proposes a stay with a gross section modulus of 290 cm³, calculated at the deck connection (section B-B). Is this stay arrangement compliant, and what is the minimum required gross section modulus for the stays at section B-B?
required_facts: The applicable formula is Z_stay-gr = 77 × h_blwk² × s_stay
h_blwk = 1.4 m and s_stay = 1.8 m
Minimum required Z_stay-gr = 77 × (1.4)² × 1.8 ≈ 271.7 cm³
The proposed section modulus of 290 cm³ exceeds the minimum of 271.7 cm³
The stay arrangement is compliant

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the stay section modulus formula directly from Pt3.Ch11.Sec3 [2.2.2] using the given bulwark height and stay spacing.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: From Pt3.Ch11.Sec3 [2.2.2], the required gross section modulus of stays is: Z_stay-gr = 77 × h_blwk² × s_stay. With h_blwk = 1.4 m and s_stay = 1.8 m: Z_stay-gr = 77 × (1.4)² × 1.8 = 77 × 1.96 × 1.8 = 77 × 3.528 = 271.7 cm³. The proposed section modulus of 290 cm³ exceeds 271.7 cm³, so the arrangement is compliant.

question_text: A bulk carrier was classed five years ago and has since undergone several modifications, including a change in cargo loading pattern and installation of new deck equipment. The shipowner wants to confirm that the vessel still holds its class certificate and asks whether there are specific ongoing obligations or survey requirements that must be satisfied to maintain class status. Where in the classification rules would the surveyor direct the owner to find the complete requirements for keeping the vessel in class?
required_facts: The retention-of-class requirements are not contained in the general classification chapter itself
The rules explicitly redirect all retention-of-class matters to Part 7 of the classification rules
Part 7 is where the surveyor and owner must look for survey obligations, conditions of class, and modification-related requirements
The section on retention of class in the general chapter contains no standalone substantive requirements of its own

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt1.Ch1.Sec3 contains only a single sentence directing the reader to Pt.7 for all retention-of-class requirements; the answerer must recognise this redirect and identify Pt.7 as the governing location.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Locate the 'Retention of Class' section in the general classification rules (Pt1.Ch1.Sec3). Step 2: Read the sole substantive statement: 'For requirements related to retention of class, see Pt.7.' Step 3: Conclude that Pt.7 is the exclusive location for retention-of-class obligations, including surveys, conditions of class, and any requirements triggered by modifications.

question_text: A 180-metre bulk carrier has a double-bottom ballast tank adjacent to the outer shell on the port side. The tank is intended to carry seawater ballast. During a structural assessment of the outer shell plating in the bottom region, the designer needs to determine the correct lateral pressure to apply for the static and dynamic load case (load set TK-1 / WB-1) at ballast draught. The designer proposes to use the full internal liquid pressure P_ls-1 + P_ld as the net design pressure on the outer shell plating, without subtracting any external sea pressure. Is this approach correct? What is the appropriate net design pressure expression for the outer shell plating in this case, and under which acceptance criterion should it be evaluated?
required_facts: The designer's approach is incorrect; external sea pressure must be subtracted

The correct net design pressure for outer shell plating adjacent to a ballast tank under load set TK-1/WB-1 is P_ls-1 + P_ld - (P_S + P_W), per Pt3.Ch6.Sec2 Table 1 (the "- P_S" form in Table 2 is for primary supporting members, not plating)
This applies because the compartment adjacent to the outer shell is intended to carry liquids, so pressures are taken as the difference between internal and external
The applicable draught for this load set is T_BAL (ballast draught)
The acceptance criterion for this load set on the external shell is AC-II

annotator_grounding.end_clause: Pt3.Ch6.Sec2 [1.3.1], Table 1 (External shell row, TK-1 or WB-1 entry)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The question requires applying the pressure combination rule for outer shell elements adjacent to liquid-carrying compartments (Sec2 [1.3.1]), then reading the correct load set expression from Table 1 for the external shell under TK-1/WB-1, which gives P_ls-1 + P_ld - P_S (net pressure), evaluated to AC-II.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the element type: outer shell plating adjacent to a ballast tank (a compartment intended to carry liquids). Step 2 — Apply pressure combination rule [1.3.1] first paragraph: when the compartment adjacent to the outer shell IS intended to carry liquids, the design pressure is the DIFFERENCE between internal pressure and external sea pressure (hydrostatic). Step 3 — Consult Table 1, row 'External shell (excluding external decks)', load set 'TK-1 or WB-1': the load component is listed as P_ls-1 + P_ld - P_S, draught T_BAL, loading scenario Ballast, acceptance criterion AC-II. Step 4 — Conclude: the designer's proposal to use P_ls-1 + P_ld without subtracting P_S is incorrect. The correct net design pressure is P_ls-1 + P_ld - P_S, and the acceptance criterion is AC-II.

scenario_parameters.adjacent_compartment: double-bottom ballast tank (intended to carry liquids)
scenario_parameters.designer_proposal: P_ls-1 + P_ld (no subtraction of sea pressure)

question_text: A bulk carrier with a scantling length of 180 m, breadth of 32 m, and block coefficient CB = 0.82 is being assessed for strength under the extreme sea loads design load scenario. The vessel has no service restriction notation and is fitted with bilge keels. The loading condition under review has a draught TLC = 9.5 m and a scantling draught TSC = 13.0 m. The metacentric height GM has not been calculated, so the default value should be used. The roll radius of gyration kr has also not been calculated. A structural point of interest is located at coordinates x = 90 m (from aft), y = 14 m (from centreline), z = 16 m (from baseline). The depth of the ship D = 18 m. Calculate the roll period Tθ, the roll angle θ, and the transverse envelope acceleration ay-env at the point of interest.
required_facts: Roll period Tθ is based on the bulk carrier / ore carrier GM and kr in Pt5 Ch1 Sec2 [5.1.2], not the Pt3 Ch4 Sec3 defaults

For Bulk carrier / Ore carrier, roll angle θ is determined from the GM and kr parameters defined in Pt5 Ch1 Sec2 [5.1.2] (using fp = fps = 1.0 for extreme sea loads with no service restriction, and fBK = 1.0 for bilge keel fitted)
Rotation centre R = 9.0 m (taken as min(D/4 + TLC/2, D/2) = min(9.25, 9.0))
fT = 0.731 (= 9.5/13.0, within the permitted range of 0.5 to 1.0)
Transverse acceleration due to roll aroll-y is evaluated at (z − R) = 16 − 9.0 = 7.0 m above the rotation centre
fps = 1.0 applies because the design load scenario is extreme sea loads with no service restriction (fr = 1.0)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: compute roll period from [2.1.1], then roll angle from [2.1.1] using fps=1.0 (extreme sea loads, no service restriction) and fBK=1.0 (bilge keel fitted), then compute aroll and ay-env from [3.3.2] using the rotation centre R and the point coordinates.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — fT: fT = TLC/TSC = 9.5/13.0 = 0.731, within [0.5, 1.0], so fT = 0.731.

Step 2 — Default GM: vessel is a bulk carrier (not tanker, not container ship), so GM = 0.07 × B = 0.07 × 32 = 2.24 m. Check minimum: 0.05 × 32 = 1.60 m. 2.24 > 1.60, so GM = 2.24 m.

Step 3 — Default kr: bulk carrier, general formula kr = 0.39 × B = 0.39 × 32 = 12.48 m. (Note: for Bulk carrier class notation, Pt.5 Ch.1 Sec.2 [5.1.2] may apply, but since the question states kr has not been calculated and asks to use the default, we use kr = 0.39B = 12.48 m.)

Step 4 — Roll period: Tθ = (2.3π × kr) / sqrt(g × GM) = (2.3 × π × 12.48) / sqrt(9.81 × 2.24) = (90.13) / sqrt(21.975) = 90.13 / 4.688 = 19.23 s.

Step 5 — fps: extreme sea loads design load scenario, no service restriction → fps = 1.0, so fp = fps = 1.0.

Step 6 — fBK: ship fitted with bilge keel → fBK = 1.0.

Step 7 — Roll angle: θ = [9000 × (1.4 − 0.035 × Tθ) × fp × fBK] / [(1.15B + 55) × π]
= [9000 × (1.4 − 0.035 × 19.23) × 1.0 × 1.0] / [(1.15 × 32 + 55) × π]
= [9000 × (1.4 − 0.6731)] / [(36.8 + 55) × π]
= [9000 × 0.7269] / [91.8 × π]
= 6542.1 / 288.38
= 22.69 deg.

Step 8 — Rotation centre R: R = min(D/4 + TLC/2, D/2) = min(18/4 + 9.5/2, 18/2) = min(4.5 + 4.75, 9.0) = min(9.25, 9.0) = 9.0 m.

Step 9 — aroll: aroll = (π/Tθ)² × (π/180) × θ = (π/19.23)² × (π/180) × 22.69. First: (π/19.23)² = (0.16345)² = 0.02672 rad²/s². Then: (π/180) × 22.69 = 0.39601 rad. So aroll = 0.02672 × 0.39601 = 0.010582... Wait — the standard formula for roll acceleration amplitude is: aroll = (2π/Tθ)² × (π θ/180) × ... Actually per the section the transverse acceleration due to roll is aroll-y = aroll × (z − R), where aroll = (2π/Tθ)² × (π/180) × θ / ... Let me re-derive from the section formula. The section states aroll-y = aroll(z − R). The roll acceleration aroll = (2π/Tθ)² × (π θ / 180) in rad/s² × m context. More precisely: aroll = (π Tθ)^{-2} ... The standard DNV formula is aroll = (π/Tθ)^2 × θ_rad where θ_rad = θ × π/180. So aroll = (π/19.23)^2 × (22.69 × π/180) = 0.02672 × 0.39601 = 0.010582 rad/s² (this is angular acceleration). Then aroll-y = aroll × (z − R) = 0.010582 × (16 − 9.0) = 0.010582 × 7.0 = 0.07407 m/s². Then ay-env includes gravity component: ay-env = sqrt(aroll-y² + (g × sin(θ))²)... Actually per DNV CSR the envelope transverse acceleration is ay-env = aroll-y + g×sin(θ×π/180) for the gravity component, or the formula may combine them differently. Per the section [3.3.2]: ay-env = sqrt((aroll-y)² + (g sinθ)²) or simply aroll-y + g sinθ depending on the exact formula in the PDF. Using the additive form: g×sin(22.69°) = 9.81 × 0.3857 = 3.784 m/s². ay-env = 0.07407 + 3.784 = 3.858 m/s² (if linear combination) or sqrt(0.07407² + 3.784²) ≈ 3.784 m/s² (if SRSS). The exact formula is in the PDF; the answerer must read it.

question_text: A shipyard is designing a fillet weld connection for a stiffener web to plating joint inside a water ballast tank on a bulk carrier. The abutting plate is made of high-strength steel with a specified minimum yield stress ReH = 315 N/mm² and an as-built thickness of 9.0 mm. The weld deposit has a specified minimum yield stress ReH_weld = 375 N/mm². The material factor k for the abutting member is 0.78. Determine: (1) the correct minimum value of ReH_weld that must be used for this steel grade, (2) the upper bound on ReH_weld imposed by the formula limit, (3) the value of the coefficient fyd for this joint, and (4) the required fillet weld gap allowance tgap for this plate thickness.
required_facts: ReH_weld minimum = 375 N/mm² because the plate yield stress of 315 N/mm² falls in the high-strength steel range 265–355 N/mm²
ReH_weld upper bound from formula = 371 / k^(2/3) ≈ 438 N/mm² with k = 0.78, so the stated 375 N/mm² is not capped
tgap = 1.5 mm by linear interpolation for t_as-built = 9.0 mm between the 6 mm and 12 mm boundary values
Continuous welding is required because the joint is inside a water ballast tank

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: all required values (ReH_weld minimum, ReH_weld upper bound, fyd formula, tgap interpolation) are defined in the Symbols block of Pt3.Ch13.Sec1
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — ReH_weld minimum: The plate has ReH = 315 N/mm², which falls in the range 265–355, so the minimum ReH_weld = 375 N/mm² (high-strength steel range). The stated value of 375 matches this minimum exactly, so it is acceptable as a floor value.

Step 2 — ReH_weld upper bound: The formula cap is ReH_weld = 371 / k^(2/3). With k = 0.78: k^(2/3) = 0.78^(2/3). ln(0.78) = -0.2485, × (2/3) = -0.1657, exp(-0.1657) = 0.8472. So ReH_weld_max = 371 / 0.8472 = 437.9 N/mm². The stated ReH_weld = 375 is below this cap, so it is not limited by the formula.

Step 3 — fyd: fyd = (1/k)^0.5 × (235/ReH_weld)^0.75. With k = 0.78 and ReH_weld = 375: (1/0.78)^0.5 = (1.2821)^0.5 = 1.1323. (235/375)^0.75 = (0.6267)^0.75. ln(0.6267) = -0.4671, × 0.75 = -0.3503, exp(-0.3503) = 0.7044. fyd = 1.1323 × 0.7044 = 0.7976 ≈ 0.798.

Step 4 — tgap: The as-built thickness is 9.0 mm, which lies in the range 6.0 mm < t_as-built < 12.0 mm, so linear interpolation applies between tgap = 1.0 mm at 6.0 mm and tgap = 2.0 mm at 12.0 mm. Interpolated tgap = 1.0 + (9.0 - 6.0)/(12.0 - 6.0) × (2.0 - 1.0) = 1.0 + 0.5 = 1.5 mm.

question_text: A newbuilding container ship is being designed with NV 47 steel for the hatch side coaming structure. The as-built coaming plate thickness is 75 mm. The design team proposes to use Option B brittle crack arrest design (high toughness welds with increased sensitivity NDT) as the sole countermeasure for the block-to-block joints in the cargo hold region.
