question_text: A steel bulk carrier (material factor k = 1.0) is being assessed for hull girder yield at a midship transverse section. The section has a net moment of inertia about the horizontal neutral axis Iy-n50 = 180 m⁴, and the horizontal neutral axis is located at zn-n50 = 7.2 m above the keel. The uppermost deck plating is at z = 14.8 m, and the keel plate is at z = 0 m. For the critical dynamic load case under consideration, the following moments act at this section: permissible still water hogging bending moment Msw-h = 4,200,000 kNm, vertical wave bending moment Mwv-LC = +2,800,000 kNm (hogging), and horizontal wave bending moment Mwh-LC = 0 kNm. The ship has no large deck openings. Determine whether the hull girder longitudinal stress at the deck (uppermost point) satisfies the yield criterion, and state the permissible longitudinal stress. Show the computed stress and whether the section is compliant.
required_facts: The permissible hull girder longitudinal stress is σhg-perm = 205 N/mm² (for k = 1.0)
The distance from the neutral axis to the deck is 7.6 m (= 14.8 − 7.2)
The still water bending stress at the deck is approximately 177.3 N/mm²
The dynamic wave bending stress at the deck is approximately 118.2 N/mm²
The total hull girder longitudinal stress at the deck is approximately 295.5 N/mm²
The computed stress exceeds the permissible value, so the section is NOT compliant with the yield criterion

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the hull girder longitudinal stress formula for ships without large deck openings, compute σhg at the deck point, then compare against the permissible stress σhg-perm = 205/k.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify applicable formula (no large deck openings → [2.1.1]): σhg = σhg-sw + σhg-dyn, where σhg-sw = Msw-h × (z − zn-n50) / Iy-n50 (hogging, so use Msw-h) and σhg-dyn = σwv-LC + σwh-LC. Step 2 — Compute distance from neutral axis to deck: z_deck − zn-n50 = 14.8 − 7.2 = 7.6 m. Step 3 — Compute still water stress at deck: σhg-sw = (4,200,000 kNm × 7.6 m) / 180 m⁴. Convert: 4,200,000 kNm = 4,200,000 × 10³ Nm = 4.2 × 10⁹ Nm; Iy-n50 = 180 m⁴. σhg-sw = (4.2 × 10⁹ × 7.6) / 180 = 3.192 × 10¹⁰ / 180 = 1.773 × 10⁸ N/m² = 177.3 N/mm². Step 4 — Compute dynamic wave stress at deck: σwv-LC = (Mwv-LC × (z − zn-n50)) / Iy-n50 = (2,800,000 × 10³ × 7.6) / 180 = 2.128 × 10¹⁰ / 180 = 1.182 × 10⁸ N/m² = 118.2 N/mm². σwh-LC = 0. σhg-dyn = 118.2 N/mm². Step 5 — Total stress: σhg = 177.3 + 118.2 = 295.5 N/mm². Step 6 — Permissible stress [2.1.2]: σhg-perm = 205 / k = 205 / 1.0 = 205 N/mm². Step 7 — Check: |σhg| = 295.5 N/mm² > 205 N/mm² → NOT compliant.

question_text: A 180 m general cargo vessel has a deep ballast tank amidships with the following characteristics: effective sloshing length ℓ_slh = 5.0 m, effective sloshing breadth b_slh = 18.5 m, ship breadth B = 32 m, and ship length L = 180 m. The tank volume is 420 m³ and it is not of cellular construction. The designer wants to know: (1) Is a full sloshing pressure assessment required for both longitudinal and transverse liquid motion, or can either be waived? (2) What minimum sloshing pressure must be used for plates, stiffeners, and tripping brackets at all internal surfaces, and which verification procedure applies? (3) Does the tank's effective sloshing breadth trigger any additional liquid impact assessment requirement beyond the standard sloshing loads?
required_facts: Longitudinal sloshing pressure P_slh-l calculations are NOT required because ℓ_slh = 5.0 m is less than 0.03L = 5.4 m
Transverse sloshing pressure P_slh-t calculations ARE required because b_slh = 18.5 m exceeds 0.32B = 10.24 m
The minimum sloshing pressure P_slh-min = 20 kN/m² applies (tank volume 420 m³ > 100 m³ and not cellular construction)

The 20 kN/m² minimum pressure applies to plates, stiffeners and tripping brackets at all internal surfaces including web frames, girders, stringers and wash bulkheads, verified per the plate/stiffener strength check procedure
An additional liquid impact assessment is required because b_slh = 18.5 m exceeds 0.56B = 17.92 m

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply threshold checks in [1.1.2] to determine which sloshing pressure calculations are required, apply [1.1.4] for minimum pressure (tank > 100 m³, not cellular), and apply [1.1.5] to check whether b_slh > 0.56B triggers additional liquid impact assessment.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Check [1.1.2] longitudinal waiver: ℓ_slh = 5.0 m vs 0.03L = 0.03 × 180 = 5.4 m. Since 5.0 < 5.4 m, calculations involving P_slh-l are NOT required (longitudinal sloshing pressure waived). Step 2 — Check [1.1.2] transverse waiver: b_slh = 18.5 m vs 0.32B = 0.32 × 32 = 10.24 m. Since 18.5 > 10.24 m, calculations involving P_slh-t ARE required (transverse sloshing pressure cannot be waived). Step 3 — Determine minimum sloshing pressure: tank volume = 420 m³ > 100 m³ and not cellular construction, so [1.1.3] does not apply. Per [1.1.4], P_slh-min = 20 kN/m² applies to plates, stiffeners and tripping brackets at all internal surfaces (web frames, girders, stringers, wash bulkheads), verified per [3.1]. Step 4 — Check [1.1.5] for additional liquid impact assessment: b_slh = 18.5 m vs 0.56B = 0.56 × 32 = 17.92 m. Since 18.5 > 17.92 m, the effective sloshing breadth exceeds 0.56B, so an additional assessment with liquid impact loads per [2.4] is required, in addition to the standard sloshing loads.

question_text: A shipyard is designing a 165-metre general dry cargo vessel intended to carry solid bulk cargoes. The vessel has six cargo holds and will operate at a scantling draught. The design team is evaluating which additional class notations are mandatory for this vessel. They note that the vessel is not designed to IACS Common Structural Rules (CSR) standards. During the design review, the following questions arise: (1) Is an HC-type notation mandatory for this vessel, and if so, which qualifier (A, B, B*, C, or M) is the minimum mandatory qualifier? (2) The vessel's cargo holds are designed so that all holds can be loaded simultaneously at scantling draught, but the vessel is not strengthened to carry any hold empty at scantling draught. Does this design trigger a specific HC qualifier, and is that qualifier mandatory? (3) If the design is later upgraded so that alternate holds can be empty at scantling draught (but not any arbitrary hold), which qualifier would then apply, and does the mandatory status change?
required_facts: HC notation is mandatory for this vessel because it is a general dry cargo ship designed for solid bulk carriage with L = 165 m ≥ 150 m and six cargo holds (≥ 5 holds).
For the base design where all holds are loaded at scantling draught, the applicable mandatory qualifier is HC(B).
HC(B) covers strengthening for dry bulk cargoes of density ≥ 1.0 t/m3 with all holds loaded, and includes HC(C) capability.
For the upgraded design where specified (alternate) holds can be empty at scantling draught, the applicable qualifier is HC(A).
HC(A) is defined as strengthened for dry bulk cargoes of density ≥ 1.0 t/m3 with specified holds empty at scantling draught, in addition to HC(B).
HC(A) is also mandatory (not optional) for this vessel type and size under the same mandatory applicability conditions.
The non-CSR status of the vessel does not affect the mandatory HC notation requirement under Table 1; CSR-specific notations (BC) are separate and listed in Table 2.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: Table 1 of Pt1.Ch2.Sec4 defines HC qualifiers A, B, B*, C, M and their mandatory applicability conditions for general dry cargo ships with L ≥ 150 m and minimum five cargo holds.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Identify vessel type and size: 165 m general dry cargo vessel with six cargo holds carrying solid bulk cargoes. L = 165 m ≥ 150 m and holds ≥ 5, so the mandatory HC notation condition is triggered per Table 1.

Step 2 — Determine which HC qualifier applies to the base design (all holds loaded, no hold empty at scantling draught): HC(C) is defined as 'Strengthened to carry dry bulk cargoes of density < 1.0 t/m3.' HC(B) is 'Strengthened to carry dry bulk cargoes of density ≥ 1.0 t/m3 with all holds loaded, in addition to HC(C).' Since the vessel has all holds loaded at scantling draught and is not strengthened for any hold empty, the applicable qualifier is HC(B) (which includes HC(C) capability). HC(B) is mandatory for a general dry cargo ship with L ≥ 150 m and ≥ 5 holds.

Step 3 — Upgraded design with alternate holds empty: HC(A) is 'Strengthened to carry dry bulk cargoes of density ≥ 1.0 t/m3 with specified holds empty at scantling draught, in addition to HC(B).' This matches the upgraded scenario where specified (alternate) holds can be empty. HC(A) is also mandatory under the same conditions.

Step 4 — Confirm mandatory status: Table 1 states HC with one of qualifiers A, B, B*, C or M is mandatory for 'General dry cargo ship designed for carriage of solid bulk cargoes, with L ≥ 150 m' having minimum five cargo holds. The vessel meets all these criteria, so the notation is mandatory in both design scenarios.

scenario_parameters.base_design_hold_loading: all holds loaded at scantling draught
scenario_parameters.upgraded_design_hold_loading: alternate (specified) holds empty at scantling draught

question_text: A 12,000 GT general cargo vessel is being designed with a conventional balanced spade rudder made of carbon steel. The designer proposes to omit a rudder carrier, relying instead on the lower rudder bearing alone to support the full weight of the rudder. The rudder bearings are located in a sealed housing that requires partial disassembly of the stern tube arrangement to access. The maximum ahead service speed is 15 knots and the maximum astern speed is 6 knots. The rudder stock is connected to the steering gear via a flanged coupling, and the bolts for this coupling are supplied with a manufacturer's material declaration (MD) rather than a type approval certificate (TAC). Is this rudder arrangement compliant with classification requirements? Identify all non-compliant aspects of the proposed design.
required_facts: Omitting the rudder carrier is non-compliant; effective means (e.g. a rudder carrier on the upper rudder stock) must be provided to support rudder weight without excessive bearing pressure
The bearing arrangement is non-compliant because all rudder bearings must be accessible for wear measurement without lifting or dismantling the rudder
The flanged coupling bolts are non-compliant; they require a type approval certificate (TAC) issued by the Society, not a manufacturer's material declaration (MD)
The rudder material (carbon steel) and rudder type (conventional balanced spade) are acceptable under the rules, which apply to steel rudders of ordinary profile types
Maximum ahead service speed and maximum astern speed must be specified — these are provided (15 kn ahead, 6 kn astern) and satisfy the definition requirement

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: all required checks are within Pt3.Ch14.Sec1 — design considerations for rudder carrier (1.5.1), bearing accessibility (1.5.2), and compliance document requirements for flanged coupling bolts (Table 2 / 1.4.1)
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Clause 1.5.1 requires effective means for supporting the weight of the rudder without excessive bearing pressure, e.g. by a rudder carrier attached to the upper part of the rudder stock. Omitting the rudder carrier and relying solely on the lower bearing is non-compliant. Step 2 — Clause 1.5.2 requires all rudder bearings to be accessible for measuring of wear WITHOUT lifting or dismantling the rudder. The sealed housing requiring partial disassembly of the stern tube arrangement violates this requirement. Step 3 — Table 2 (Compliance documents) specifies that bolts for flanged couplings must have a TAC (type approval certificate) issued by the Society. The designer has provided only an MD (material declaration) from the manufacturer, which is the correct document type for synthetic bushings, not for flanged coupling bolts. This is non-compliant. Result: three distinct non-compliances identified, all within Pt3.Ch14.Sec1.

scenario_parameters.bearing_access: requires partial disassembly of stern tube arrangement

question_text: A 310-metre container ship is being assessed for hull girder ultimate strength. The ship has a contract speed of 26 knots (specified at 85% MCR and 15% sea margin), a breadth of 50 m, and a bow flare angle of 58°. The design team is computing the net offered thickness for a deck plate that is as-built 22.0 mm thick, with a voluntary addition of 0.5 mm. The plate borders a ballast water tank on one side and a void space on the other. For the ultimate strength assessment, what is the corrosion addition factor α that applies, what is the total corrosion addition tc for this plate, and what is the resulting net offered thickness toff? Additionally, should the design team consider an advanced assessment (level 2) based on direct hydrodynamic analysis including whipping and springing for this vessel?
required_facts: α = 0.5 for hull girder ultimate strength assessment (from Table 1, section properties and buckling/collapse capacity rows)
tc = 1.5 mm, combining ballast water tank side (tc1 = 1.0 mm) and void space side (tc2 = 0.5 mm)
toff = 20.75 mm, calculated as 22.0 − 0.5 − 0.5 × 1.5
All four guidance-note thresholds are exceeded: L > 290 m, B > 47 m, bow flare angle > 55°, V > 25 knots
An advanced assessment (level 2) using direct hydrodynamic analysis including whipping and springing per DNV-CG-0153 is recommended

annotator_grounding.end_clause: Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.1.1], [2.1.2], Table 1, Table 2, guidance note under [2.6.2]
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply Table 1 to find α for hull girder ultimate strength, apply Table 2 to find tc1 and tc2 for the two compartment types, compute tc per Pt3.Ch3.Sec3 combination rule (tc = tc1 + tc2), then apply the toff formula. Also check the guidance note thresholds for advanced assessment recommendation.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Corrosion addition factor α: From Table 1, for hull girder ultimate strength (section properties and buckling/collapse capacity), α = 0.5 for both. The question asks about the ultimate strength assessment, so α = 0.5.

Step 2 — Corrosion addition tc: The plate has one side exposed to a ballast water tank (tc1 = 1.0 mm per Table 2) and the other side exposed to a void space (tc2 = 0.5 mm per Table 2). Per Pt3.Ch3.Sec3, tc = tc1 + tc2 = 1.0 + 0.5 = 1.5 mm.

Step 3 — Net offered thickness: toff = t_as_built − t_vol_add − α·tc = 22.0 − 0.5 − 0.5 × 1.5 = 22.0 − 0.5 − 0.75 = 20.75 mm.

Step 4 — Advanced assessment recommendation: Check guidance note thresholds: L = 310 m > 290 m ✓, B = 50 m > 47 m ✓, bow flare angle α = 58° > 55° ✓, V = 26 knots > 25 knots ✓. All four criteria are exceeded, so an advanced assessment using direct hydrodynamic analysis including whipping and springing (level 2) per DNV-CG-0153 is recommended.

question_text: A bulk carrier has a longitudinally stiffened bottom shell plate panel spanning between two transverse frames. The plate panel consists of two strakes joined by a longitudinal butt weld: the inner strake has a net thickness of 16 mm over a width of 320 mm, and the outer strake has a net thickness of 20 mm over a width of 180 mm. Both strakes are made of the same steel grade with a yield strength of 315 N/mm². The hull girder vertical still water bending moment produces a compressive bending stress of 85 N/mm² at this location, and the hull girder shear stress at this section is 40 N/mm². For the buckling check of this plate panel under the longitudinal stiffening arrangement, determine: (1) the equivalent plate panel width to be used in the buckling assessment, and (2) the two stress combinations (σx, σy, τ) that must be applied to the elementary plate panel.
required_facts: b_eq ≈ 448.8 mm (using formula b_eq = ℓ1 + ℓ2 × (t1/t2)^1.5 with t1=16 mm, t2=20 mm, ℓ1=320 mm, ℓ2=180 mm)
The buckling check uses the smaller plate thickness t1 = 16 mm combined with b_eq
Stress combination 1 (longitudinal): σx = 85 N/mm², σy = 0, τ = 28 N/mm²
Stress combination 2 (longitudinal): σx = 59.5 N/mm², σy = 0, τ = 40 N/mm²
Both stress combinations must be checked and the panel must satisfy η_Plate ≤ η_all for each

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply the equivalent plate panel width formula from [1.2.1] using the two strake widths and thicknesses, then apply the longitudinal stiffening stress combinations from [2.2]
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Equivalent plate panel width [1.2.1]: The smaller thickness is t1 = 16 mm with width ℓ1 = 320 mm; the greater thickness is t2 = 20 mm with width ℓ2 = 180 mm. Apply: b_eq = ℓ1 + ℓ2 × (t1/t2)^1.5 = 320 + 180 × (16/20)^1.5. Compute (16/20)^1.5 = (0.8)^1.5 = 0.8 × √0.8 = 0.8 × 0.8944 = 0.7155. So b_eq = 320 + 180 × 0.7155 = 320 + 128.8 = 448.8 mm. Step 2 — Stress combinations [2.2], longitudinal stiffening arrangement: σhg = 85 N/mm² (compressive), τhg = 40 N/mm². Combination 1: σx = σhg = 85 N/mm², σy = 0, τ = 0.7 × 40 = 28 N/mm². Combination 2: σx = 0.7 × 85 = 59.5 N/mm², σy = 0, τ = τhg = 40 N/mm².

question_text: A naval architect is sizing the bottom shell plating for a bulk carrier. The plate panel in question is longitudinally stiffened, with a panel breadth b = 820 mm and panel length a = 2600 mm. The design pressure at the load calculation point is P = 95 kN/m². The hull girder longitudinal stress at that point is σ_hg = +62 N/mm² (hogging, tensile on the bottom). The steel yield strength is R_eH = 315 N/mm². Determine the minimum net thickness required for this plate panel, showing the calculation of the aspect ratio correction factor α_p and the permissible bending stress coefficient C_a.
required_facts: Table 1 row for 'Other longitudinal members, Longitudinal stiffened plating' gives β_a = 1.10, α_a = 0.50, C_a-max = 1.00
Minimum net thickness t ≈ 7.1 mm

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the plating thickness formula in Sec4 [1.1.1], compute α_p from the panel aspect ratio, look up β_a, α_a, and C_a-max from Table 1 for longitudinally stiffened plating under 'Other longitudinal members', then compute C_a and finally t.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Aspect ratio correction factor α_p:
  α_p = 1.2 − b/(2.1·a) = 1.2 − 820/(2.1×2600) = 1.2 − 820/5460 = 1.2 − 0.1502 = 1.0498
  Since 1.0498 > 1.0, cap at α_p = 1.0.

Step 2 — Table 1 lookup for 'Other longitudinal members, Longitudinal stiffened plating':
  β_a = 1.10, α_a = 0.50, C_a-max = 1.00.

Step 3 — Permissible bending stress coefficient C_a:
  C_a = β_a − α_a·(σ_hg / R_eH) = 1.10 − 0.50×(62/315) = 1.10 − 0.50×0.1968 = 1.10 − 0.0984 = 1.0016
  Since 1.0016 > C_a-max = 1.00, cap at C_a = 1.00.

Step 4 — Net thickness:
  t = 0.0158 × α_p × b × √(|P| / (C_a × R_eH))
  t = 0.0158 × 1.0 × 820 × √(95 / (1.00 × 315))
  t = 12.956 × √(0.30159)
  t = 12.956 × 0.5492
  t = 7.12 mm

Minimum net thickness required ≈ 7.12 mm.

question_text: A 95 m general cargo vessel (category II) has a maximum deadweight of 2,800 tonnes and a maximum displacement of 8,500 tonnes. The ship is classed and falls under the International Convention on Load Lines. The shipowner asks whether a loading manual is required for this vessel, and if so, whether a loading instrument system (loading computer) must also be provided onboard. Provide a clear determination for both requirements, showing the relevant thresholds and how the ship's parameters compare to them.
required_facts: A loading manual is required because the ship is 95 m, which is not less than 90 m, so the category II exemption from the longitudinal-strength loading manual does not apply.
The deadweight ratio is approximately 32.9% (2,800 / 8,500), which also exceeds the 30% threshold, providing a second independent reason the exemption fails.
The loading manual exemption requires BOTH length < 90 m AND deadweight ≤ 30% of maximum displacement; failing either condition means the exemption is unavailable.
A loading instrument system (loading computer) is NOT required because that obligation applies only to category I ships of 100 m length and above.
The ship at 95 m is below the 100 m threshold for mandatory loading instrument systems, and it is category II, not category I.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply the loading manual exemption condition for category II ships under 90 m with deadweight ≤ 30% of displacement, then check the loading instrument threshold of 100 m for category I ships.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Loading manual requirement: The ship is 95 m, which is ≥ 65 m, so it falls under the general requirement for an approved loading manual per [1.1.2]. The exemption from a longitudinal-strength loading manual applies only to category II ships with length < 90 m AND deadweight ≤ 30% of maximum displacement. This ship is 95 m, which is NOT less than 90 m, so the exemption does not apply regardless of the deadweight ratio. A loading manual is therefore required. (For completeness: 2,800 / 8,500 = 32.9%, which also exceeds the 30% threshold, so the ship would fail both conditions of the exemption even if it were shorter.) Step 2 — Loading instrument requirement: A loading instrument system is mandatory for all category I ships of 100 m length and above. This ship is 95 m and is category II, so neither condition is met. No loading instrument system is required.

question_text: A general cargo vessel has a weathertight door fitted in a deckhouse on the freeboard deck. The door blade is a flat steel plate with no stiffeners, spanning a clear opening of 600 mm wide by 1800 mm tall. The design lateral pressure at the load calculation point is 12.5 kN/m². The steel used has a minimum yield stress ReH = 235 N/mm². The door panel dimensions are: plate panel breadth b = 600 mm, plate panel length a = 1800 mm. Calculate the minimum required gross thickness of the door blade. Is a door blade with a gross thickness of 8 mm compliant with this requirement?
required_facts: αp is calculated as 1.2 - b/(2.1·a) = 1.2 - 600/(2.1×1800) ≈ 1.041, which must be capped at 1.0
The minimum required gross thickness formula is t_gr = 0.0158 × αp × b × sqrt(|P| / (0.85 × ReH))
Substituting αp = 1.0, b = 600 mm, P = 12.5 kN/m², ReH = 235 N/mm² gives t_gr ≈ 2.37 mm
A door blade gross thickness of 8 mm exceeds the minimum required 2.37 mm and is therefore compliant
The aspect ratio correction factor αp must not be taken greater than 1.0 per the symbols definition

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section question: apply the door blade thickness formula in [4.3.1], first computing the aspect ratio correction factor αp from the symbols block, then substituting into the thickness formula.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Compute αp: αp = 1.2 - b/(2.1·a) = 1.2 - 600/(2.1×1800) = 1.2 - 600/3780 = 1.2 - 0.1587 = 1.0413. Since αp must not exceed 1.0, cap it at αp = 1.0. Step 2 — Apply thickness formula: t_gr = 0.0158 × αp × b × sqrt(|P| / (0.85 × ReH)) = 0.0158 × 1.0 × 600 × sqrt(12.5 / (0.85 × 235)) = 9.48 × sqrt(12.5 / 199.75) = 9.48 × sqrt(0.06257) = 9.48 × 0.2502 = 2.37 mm. Wait — units check: b is in mm per the symbols block, P in kN/m², ReH in N/mm². sqrt(kN/m² / (N/mm²)) = sqrt(kN/m² × mm²/N) = sqrt(1000 N/m² × mm²/N) = sqrt(1000 × 10^-6 m²/m²) — dimensionless after unit conversion. The formula is empirical and self-consistent as written. t_gr = 0.0158 × 1.0 × 600 × sqrt(12.5/199.75) = 9.48 × 0.2502 ≈ 2.37 mm. Step 3 — Compare: 8 mm >> 2.37 mm, so the 8 mm door blade is compliant. Note: the aspect ratio correction αp was capped at 1.0 because the raw value (1.041) exceeded the maximum.

question_text:
A general cargo ship with a rule length L of 148 m and material factor k = 1.0 is being designed. A transverse watertight bulkhead separates a water ballast tank from an adjacent dry cargo hold. The bulkhead is transversely stiffened. The design pressure P acting on the bulkhead panel is 28 kN/m², the panel breadth b is 820 mm, the panel length a is 1 050 mm, and the hull girder longitudinal stress σ_hg at the load calculation point is 55 N/mm² (compressive). The yield strength R_eH of the steel is 235 N/mm².

A designer proposes a net plate thickness of 7.2 mm for this bulkhead panel. The bulkhead also carries a primary supporting member (a horizontal stringer) spanning 4.8 m between supports, with a tributary breadth S of 2.4 m. The stringer web has a proposed net thickness of 6.5 mm.

Determine whether the proposed net thickness of 7.2 mm for the bulkhead plating is acceptable, and whether the proposed net web thickness of 6.5 mm for the stringer satisfies the applicable minimum thickness requirement. Show all governing thickness values.

The pressure-formula-derived required net plating thickness is approximately 3.98 mm
The minimum net plating thickness from the absolute minimum requirements for a water ballast tank bulkhead is 6.72 mm (using a = 4.5, b = 0.015, L2 = 148 m), which governs
The proposed bulkhead plating thickness of 7.2 mm satisfies both the pressure formula and the minimum thickness requirement and is therefore acceptable
The minimum net web thickness for the PSM stringer at a tank boundary is also 6.72 mm (a = 4.5, b = 0.015, L2 = 148 m)
The proposed stringer web thickness of 6.5 mm is less than the required minimum of 6.72 mm and is therefore NOT acceptable

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec4 plating formula gives the pressure-based required thickness for the bulkhead panel; Sec6 PSM section references minimum thickness requirements; Sec3 provides the absolute minimum thickness floors for both plating (Table 1) and PSM web plating (Table 3) that must not be undercut regardless of the pressure calculation.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Plating thickness from Sec4 [1.1.1]: Panel is a transverse boundary between a ballast tank and a dry cargo hold, transversely stiffened → from Table 1: β_a = 1.10, α_a = 1.00, C_a-max = 1.00. Compute C_a = 1.10 − 1.00 × (55/235) = 1.10 − 0.2340 = 0.866, which is less than C_a-max = 1.00, so C_a = 0.866. Aspect ratio correction: α_p = 1.2 − b/(2.1a) = 1.2 − 820/(2.1 × 1050) = 1.2 − 0.3719 = 0.828, not greater than 1.0, so α_p = 0.828. Required thickness: t = 0.0158 × 0.828 × 820 × √(28 / (0.866 × 235)) = 0.0158 × 0.828 × 820 × √(0.13745) = 0.0158 × 679.0 × 0.3708 = 3.977 mm ≈ 3.98 mm from pressure formula. Step 2 — Minimum plating thickness from Sec3 [1.1.1] Table 1: Bulkhead is a boundary for a water ballast tank → a = 4.5, b_coeff = 0.015. t_min = 4.5 + 0.015 × L2 × √k, where L2 = min(L, 300) = 148 m, k = 1.0. t_min = 4.5 + 0.015 × 148 × 1.0 = 4.5 + 2.22 = 6.72 mm. The minimum thickness of 6.72 mm governs over the pressure-derived 3.98 mm. The proposed 7.2 mm exceeds 6.72 mm → plating is acceptable. Step 3 — Minimum stringer web thickness from Sec3 [3.1.1] Table 3: The stringer is a PSM at a tank boundary (ballast tank) → a = 4.5, b_coeff = 0.015. t_min_PSM = 4.5 + 0.015 × 148 × 1.0 = 6.72 mm. Additionally, Sec3 [2.1] requires the stiffener/PSM web net thickness to be not less than 40% of the net required thickness of the attached plating (determined per Sec4). The attached plating required thickness from Sec4 is 3.98 mm (pressure-based), but the governing plating thickness is 6.72 mm (minimum). The 40% rule references the Sec4-derived thickness: 0.40 × 3.98 = 1.59 mm, which is not governing. The PSM minimum from Table 3 is 6.72 mm. The proposed 6.5 mm is less than 6.72 mm → the stringer web thickness is NOT acceptable and must be increased to at least 6.72 mm.

scenario_parameters.bulkhead_type: transverse watertight, ballast tank / dry cargo hold boundary

question_text:
A 185-metre bulk carrier (ESP notation) has a deckhouse with side plating that is longitudinally stiffened. The deckhouse side plating panels have a breadth b = 480 mm and a length a = 720 mm. The design sea pressure acting on the deckhouse side is PA = 12.5 kN/m². The material yield strength ReH = 235 N/mm², and the hull girder longitudinal stress at the load calculation point is σhg = 60 N/mm². The ship's length L2 = 185 m and material factor k = 1.0.

The designer proposes a net plate thickness of 7.0 mm for the deckhouse side plating. A pillar inside the deckhouse is also under review: it is a beam-column with a compressive axial load Fpill = 420 kN, a net cross-section area Apill = 28 cm², and a significant bending stress of 45 N/mm² at midspan due to an eccentric deck load. The pillar has an effective length of 3.2 m and a radius of gyration of 38 mm.

Is the proposed 7.0 mm net thickness for the deckhouse side plating acceptable, and does the pillar arrangement require any additional buckling verification beyond the standard axial compression check? Provide the governing minimum thickness and identify all checks that must be satisfied for the pillar.
required_facts: The pressure-based net thickness from the lateral pressure formula is approximately 3.1–3.2 mm, which is not the governing criterion
The minimum thickness for deckhouse side plating per the minimum thickness requirements (referencing deckhouse/superstructure rules) is approximately 5.85 mm (using a = 4.0, b = 0.01, L2 = 185 m)
The proposed 7.0 mm net thickness is acceptable as it exceeds the governing minimum of approximately 5.85 mm
The pillar standard axial compression buckling check per Ch.8 Sec.4 [5.1] must be performed with σav = 150 N/mm²
Because the midspan bending stress (45 N/mm²) is significant, the beam-column combined axial-plus-bending buckling check is also required
The additional beam-column check must be carried out in accordance with Ch.8 Sec.1 [3.4] and DNV-CG-0128 Sec.3 [5.2.3]

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec.4 plating thickness formula → Sec.3 minimum thickness (including Sec.8 reference for deckhouse minimum thickness per Sec.3 Table 1 footnote) → Sec.8 [3.1] which directs deckhouse minimum thickness back to Sec.3 → Sec.6 [3.3] for beam-column combined load buckling check
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 (Sec.4 [1.1.1]): Compute the pressure-based net thickness for the deckhouse side plating. Panel aspect ratio correction: αp = 1.2 − 480/(2.1×720) = 1.2 − 0.317 = 0.883 (< 1.0, so use 0.883). For deckhouse side plating under SEA-1 / AC-II, the plating is longitudinally stiffened. From Table 1 of Sec.4, for 'Other longitudinal members, Longitudinal stiffened plating': βa = 1.10, αa = 0.50, Ca-max = 1.00. Ca = 1.10 − 0.50×(60/235) = 1.10 − 0.1277 = 0.972, which is less than Ca-max = 1.00, so Ca = 0.972. t = 0.0158 × 0.883 × 480 × sqrt(12.5 / (0.972 × 235)) = 0.0158 × 0.883 × 480 × sqrt(0.05472) = 0.0158 × 0.883 × 480 × 0.2339 = 3.13 mm. Step 2 (Sec.3 [1.1.1] via Sec.8 [3.1]): Sec.4 Table 1 footnote and Sec.3 Table 1 note state that for minimum thicknesses for deckhouses and superstructures, see also Sec.8 [3.1]. Sec.8 [3.1] directs back to Sec.3 minimum thickness requirements. From Sec.3 Table 1 for deckhouse/superstructure side walls: a = 4.0, b = 0.01 (structures in deckhouse and superstructure). t_min = 4.0 + 0.01 × 185 × sqrt(1.0) = 4.0 + 1.85 = 5.85 mm. Also check general shell/side minimum: not applicable here as this is deckhouse side, not main hull side. The governing minimum is max(3.13, 5.85) = 5.85 mm. The proposed 7.0 mm exceeds 5.85 mm, so the plating thickness is acceptable. Step 3 (Sec.6 [3.1] and [3.3]): For the pillar under compressive axial load, the standard check per Sec.6 [3.1] gives σav = 10 × 420 / 28 = 150 N/mm². The buckling check per Ch.8 Sec.4 [5.1] must be performed. However, because the pillar has a significant bending stress of 45 N/mm² at midspan (not negligible), Sec.6 [3.3] applies: for beam-columns with significant additional bending stress at midspan, the buckling utilisation shall also be verified in accordance with Ch.8 Sec.1 [3.4] and DNV-CG-0128 Sec.3 [5.2.3]. Therefore, the pillar requires both the standard axial buckling check (Ch.8 Sec.4 [5.1]) AND the combined axial-plus-bending beam-column buckling check (Ch.8 Sec.1 [3.4] / DNV-CG-0128 Sec.3 [5.2.3]).

question_text: A designer is sizing longitudinal stiffeners for the inner bottom of a bulk carrier. The stiffeners are fabricated T-profiles with a flange plate made from Grade A steel (minimum yield strength 235 N/mm²) and a web made from Grade AH36 steel (minimum yield strength 355 N/mm²). The designer proposes to use the full yield strength of the AH36 web when calculating the section modulus of the stiffener without any additional checks. Is this arrangement acceptable under classification rules, and if not, what additional verification is required?
required_facts: The rules generally assume that the plate flange and web have the same minimum yield strength
When the plate flange has a lower minimum yield strength than the connected stiffener or PSM, an additional check of yield capacity of the plate flange may be required
Grade A steel has a minimum yield strength of 235 N/mm² and AH36 has 355 N/mm², so the flange is weaker than the web
The arrangement as proposed (using full AH36 yield strength without additional checks) is not directly acceptable without further verification
The additional check required is the yield capacity check of the plate flange per Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4]

annotator_grounding.start_clause: Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [symbols / general context on stiffener idealisation]
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec7 defines structural idealisation of stiffeners including the concept of plate flange and web, and references Sec1 [2.1.2] which states that when the plate flange has a lower minimum yield strength than the connected stiffener or PSM, an additional check of yield capacity of the plate flange may be required (see Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4]).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: The designer is working with stiffener idealisation — the stiffener has a plate flange (Grade A, ReH = 235 N/mm²) and a web (AH36, ReH = 355 N/mm²). Step 2: Sec7 symbols define the structural components (plate flange, web, etc.) and the idealisation framework. Step 3: Following the cross-reference chain, Sec1 [2.1.2] states that the rules generally assume flange and web have the same minimum yield strength. When the plate flange has a lower minimum yield strength than the connected stiffener or PSM, an additional check of yield capacity of the plate flange may be required, per Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4]. Step 4: In this scenario, the plate flange (235 N/mm²) is weaker than the web (355 N/mm²), so the arrangement is not straightforwardly acceptable — an additional yield capacity check of the plate flange is required.

question_text: A 280 m bulk carrier is being assessed for hull girder buckling. The upper deck plating consists of elementary plate panels with two distinct plate thicknesses across the panel width: the inner strip has a net thickness t1 = 18 mm over a width ℓ1 = 400 mm, and the outer strip has a net thickness t2 = 24 mm over a width ℓ2 = 600 mm. The two strips are joined by a transverse butt weld. The deck is longitudinally stiffened, and the hull girder bending stress σhg = 180 N/mm² with a hull girder shear stress τhg = 55 N/mm². For the buckling check of this plate panel under hull girder loads, the designer proposes to treat the entire panel as a single uniform panel using an equivalent width approach. (a) What equivalent plate panel width should be used for the buckling check, and which plate thickness is paired with it? (b) For the stress combination that maximises shear demand, what values of σx, σy, and τ should be applied to the panel in a longitudinal stiffening arrangement? (c) The buckling utilization factor for the elementary plate panel is calculated as ηPlate = 0.82, and the allowable utilization factor ηall = 0.85. Is the panel compliant, and what assessment method (SP-A, SP-B, or UP) applies to this deck panel?
required_facts: b_eq ≈ 790 mm (using formula b_eq = ℓ1 + ℓ2·(t1/t2)^1.5), paired with the smaller thickness t1 = 18 mm
For a transverse butt weld joining two thicknesses, the buckling check must be performed separately for each thickness treated as constant over the EPP
Stress combination 2 for longitudinal stiffening gives σx = 0.7·σhg = 126 N/mm², σy = 0, τ = τhg = 55 N/mm² (maximum shear demand case)
ηPlate = 0.82 ≤ ηall = 0.85, so the panel is compliant with the buckling criterion
The applicable assessment method for deck plating in a longitudinal stiffening arrangement is SP-A

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec4 [2.1.2] gives the average thickness formula for direct strength analysis panels, but for hull girder buckling the equivalent panel width approach is governed by Sec3 [1.2.1]–[1.2.2]. The stress combinations for longitudinal stiffening are in Sec3 [2.2], and the plate buckling criterion with SP-A method is in Sec3 [3.2]. The cross-reference from Sec4 Table 3 row (a) explicitly points to Sec3 [1.2.2] for the plate thickness basis in hull girder buckling checks.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Equivalent panel width (Sec3 [1.2.1]): b_eq = ℓ1 + ℓ2·(t1/t2)^1.5 = 400 + 600·(18/24)^1.5 = 400 + 600·(0.75)^1.5 = 400 + 600·0.6495 = 400 + 389.7 ≈ 790 mm, paired with the smaller thickness t1 = 18 mm. Step 2 — Butt weld / transverse thickness change (Sec3 [1.2.2]): because the EPP has different thicknesses joined by a transverse butt weld, the buckling check is made for each thickness treated as constant on the EPP, with stresses estimated at the LCP. Step 3 — Stress combinations for longitudinal stiffening (Sec3 [2.2a]): stress combination 1 (max bending): σx = σhg = 180 N/mm², σy = 0, τ = 0.7·55 = 38.5 N/mm²; stress combination 2 (max shear): σx = 0.7·180 = 126 N/mm², σy = 0, τ = τhg = 55 N/mm². The combination maximising shear demand is combination 2. Step 4 — Buckling criterion and method (Sec3 [3.2]): ηPlate ≤ ηall → 0.82 ≤ 0.85, so the panel is compliant. The assessment method for deck plating (longitudinal structure) per Sec4 Table 1 is SP-A.

question_text: A naval architect is preparing the loading manual for a newly built general cargo vessel. The ship is 88 m in length, has a maximum deadweight of 2,100 tonnes, and a maximum displacement of 4,800 tonnes. The vessel is intended for ocean-going service and falls under the International Convention on Load Lines. The owner asks whether a loading instrument system (loading computer) is also required onboard in addition to the loading manual, and whether the loading manual needs to address longitudinal strength. Assess both questions and justify your conclusions.
required_facts: A loading manual is required because the vessel is covered by Load Lines Reg.10
The deadweight-to-displacement ratio is approximately 43.75%, which exceeds the 30% threshold
Because the 30% deadweight ratio is exceeded, the exemption from longitudinal strength consideration does not apply and the loading manual must address longitudinal strength
A loading instrument system (loading computer) is only mandatory for category I ships of 100 m length and above
At 88 m length, the vessel is below the 100 m threshold and no loading instrument system is required

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec5 [1.1.2] sets out loading manual requirements and references category I/II ship definitions and length thresholds; resolving 'category II ship' and the scope of Pt.3 rules requires reading Sec1 to understand the general application framework and ship categorisation context within Ch.1.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Start at Sec5 [1.1.2]: All ships covered by Load Lines Reg.10 must have an approved loading manual. A loading manual considering longitudinal strength is NOT required for a category II ship with length < 90 m where maximum deadweight does not exceed 30% of maximum displacement. Step 2 — Check the deadweight ratio: 2,100 / 4,800 = 43.75%, which exceeds 30%. Therefore the exemption from longitudinal strength consideration does NOT apply, and the loading manual must address longitudinal strength even though the ship is < 90 m. Step 3 — Loading instrument (loading computer): Required only for category I ships of 100 m length and above. At 88 m, the vessel is below the 100 m threshold, so no loading instrument system is required. Step 4 — Sec1 provides the general application scope confirming these rules apply to monohull welded steel ships and that Pt.3 Ch.1 sets general principles, grounding the category and length-based thresholds used in Sec5.

question_text: A structural engineer is performing a direct strength analysis on a 280-metre bulk carrier. During the FE-based buckling assessment, a longitudinal deck panel between two web frames is identified as a critical element. The panel is made of two plate zones of different thicknesses: a 16 mm net zone of width 420 mm and a 20 mm net zone of width 380 mm, both spanning the same stiffener spacing. The panel is subjected to combined compressive and shear stresses under a static-plus-dynamic load combination (design load scenario AC-II). The computed buckling utilization factor for this panel is η_act = 0.97. Is this panel compliant with the buckling acceptance criteria? Additionally, what equivalent panel width should be used for the buckling check, and what is the allowable utilization factor η_all that applies?
required_facts: For a varying-thickness panel under FE-based / direct-strength buckling assessment, Pt3.Ch8.Sec4 [2.1.2] requires the average net thickness t_avr = Σ A_i t_i / Σ A_i across the panel; with t1 = 16 mm, ℓ_1 = 420 mm and t2 = 20 mm, ℓ_2 = 380 mm: t_avr = (420×16 + 380×20) / (420+380) ≈ 17.9 mm (the equivalent-width formula b_eq = ℓ_1 + ℓ_2(t1/t2)^1.5 belongs to Pt3.Ch8.Sec3 [1.2.1] hull-girder buckling and does not apply here)
The allowable buckling utilization factor η_all for plates and stiffened panels under design load scenario AC-II (S+D) is 1.00
The acceptance criterion is η_act ≤ η_all, i.e. 0.97 ≤ 1.00
The panel is compliant with the buckling acceptance criteria

The buckling check for the varying-thickness panel shall be performed using the average net thickness t_avr ≈ 17.9 mm across the full panel width per Pt3.Ch8.Sec4 [2.1.2], not the smaller plate thickness t1 = 16 mm combined with an equivalent width

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Sec4 (direct strength analysis buckling requirements), which references Sec2 for boundary conditions and Sec3 for equivalent plate panel width formula, which in turn references Sec1 [3.4] for the allowable utilization factor η_all.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec4 [1.1.1]: The panel is subject to buckling assessment under direct strength analysis. Sec4 symbols define η_all as 'allowable buckling utilization factor, as defined in Sec.1 [3.4]', establishing the first cross-reference hop. Step 2 — Sec4 [2.1.2] references the average thickness formula for non-constant plate panels; however, the varying-thickness equivalent panel width formula is found in Sec3 [1.2.1]: b_eq = ℓ1 + ℓ2 × (t1/t2)^1.5, where t1 = 16 mm (smaller), ℓ1 = 420 mm, t2 = 20 mm, ℓ2 = 380 mm. Calculation: b_eq = 420 + 380 × (16/20)^1.5 = 420 + 380 × (0.8)^1.5 = 420 + 380 × 0.7155 = 420 + 271.9 ≈ 692 mm. Step 3 — Sec3 symbols confirm η_all is 'as defined in Sec.1 [3.4]', the second cross-reference hop. Step 4 — Sec1 [3.4] Table 3: For plates and stiffened panels under AC-II (S+D), η_all = 1.00. Step 5 — Acceptance check per Sec1 [3.3.1]: η_act = 0.97 ≤ η_all = 1.00 → panel is compliant.

scenario_parameters.panel_location: longitudinal deck panel between web frames

question_text: A 180-metre general cargo vessel is being classed with a classification society for the first time. The vessel was built under the direct supervision of the society's own surveyors throughout the entire construction process, and all hull, machinery, systems and equipment have been verified to comply with the applicable structural, machinery and equipment rule requirements. The owner wishes to know: (1) which construction symbol will appear in the vessel's class notation, and (2) which main class notation will be assigned? Additionally, the owner is considering a future scenario where a sister ship was instead built under the supervision of a different, recognised classification society and is now being transferred to this society's class — what construction symbol and main class notation would that sister ship receive?
required_facts: The original vessel receives the construction symbol ✠ (solid cross) because it was built under the direct supervision of the Society
The original vessel receives the main class notation 1A because hull, machinery, systems and equipment comply with applicable rule requirements

The sister ship receives the alternative construction symbol (the recognised-society variant, typographically distinct from the solid ✠) because it was built under a recognised classification society's supervision
The sister ship also receives the main class notation 1A upon transfer of class
A vessel not built under either of those two conditions would not be assigned any construction symbol at all

The applicable rules for construction symbols and main class notation are found in the section covering construction symbol and main class notation, not in the general class notations introduction section

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec.1 [1.1.2] states that applicable class notations (including construction symbol and main class notation) are given in Sec.2 to Sec.7, directing the answerer to Sec.2 for the actual assignment rules for construction symbols and main class notation.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec.1 [1.1.2] establishes that class notations are assigned to determine applicable rule requirements, and that the applicable class notations are given in Sec.2 to Sec.7. This cross-reference directs the answerer to Sec.2 for construction symbol and main class notation rules. Step 2 — Sec.2 [1.1.1]: the construction symbol ✠ (built-under-society-supervision symbol) is assigned to vessels built under the direct supervision of the Society — this applies to the original vessel. Step 3 — Sec.2 [2.1.1]: the main class notation 1A is assigned when hull, machinery, systems and equipment comply with applicable rule requirements in Pt.2, Pt.3 and Pt.4 — satisfied here. Step 4 — Sec.2 [1.1.2]: the alternative construction symbol (the dotted/dashed ✠ variant) is assigned to vessels built under the supervision of a recognised classification society and later assigned class with the Society — this applies to the sister ship. Step 5 — Sec.2 [2.1.2]: the main class notation 1A is also assigned to vessels designed and constructed under another classification society's rules and later assigned class — so the sister ship also receives 1A.

scenario_parameters.compliance_status: hull, machinery, systems and equipment all compliant

question_text: A 78-metre general cargo vessel (non-SOLAS convention vessel) is being designed with a diesel-mechanical propulsion system. The designer has proposed the following watertight bulkhead arrangement: one collision bulkhead, one aft peak bulkhead, one bulkhead forward of the engine room, and one bulkhead aft of the engine room — giving a total of four transverse watertight bulkheads. No formal damage stability calculations have been carried out for this vessel. Is this arrangement compliant with the applicable classification rules? If not, state the minimum total number of transverse watertight bulkheads required and identify any other deficiency in the proposed arrangement.
required_facts: The vessel has 4 transverse watertight bulkheads as proposed (collision, aft peak, forward and aft of engine room)
For a ship of 78 m length (65 < L ≤ 85) with no damage stability calculations, Table 1 requires a minimum of 4 transverse watertight bulkheads
The proposed arrangement meets the minimum bulkhead count from Table 1
The mandatory minimum bulkheads under the 'all ships' rule include: one collision bulkhead, one aft peak bulkhead, and one bulkhead at each end of the engine room — all of which are present
As a non-convention vessel, the SOLAS-based subdivision requirements are not strictly mandatory, but the designer must still consider flooding risk and the Society may require defined damage cases
The arrangement is compliant with the minimum numerical requirement, but additional bulkheads may be required to satisfy national regulations or Society-imposed damage cases

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec1 [1.1.3] states that requirements for arrangement given in Sec2 [1] to Sec2 [5] assume SOLAS damage cases and are not mandatory for non-convention vessels, but the designer must still consider risk of flooding per [1.1.2]. However, Sec2 [1.1.1] lists minimum mandatory bulkheads for ALL ships, and Sec2 [1.1.4] with Table 1 gives the minimum total count for vessels without damage stability calculations — the answerer must navigate from the general application clause in Sec1 to the specific bulkhead count table in Sec2.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Sec1 [1.1.3] notes that Sec2 [1] through [5] requirements assume SOLAS damage cases and are not mandatory for non-convention vessels. However, [1.1.2] requires non-convention vessels to be designed with consideration to flooding risk. Step 2: Navigate to Sec2 [1.1.1] — this clause applies to 'all ships' and mandates at minimum: (a) one collision bulkhead, (b) one aft peak bulkhead, (c) one bulkhead at each end of the engine room. The proposed arrangement satisfies [1.1.1] with exactly these four bulkheads. Step 3: Sec2 [1.1.4] states that for vessels where no damage stability calculations have been carried out, the total number of watertight transverse bulkheads shall not be less than given in Table 1. For a ship length of 78 m (65 < L ≤ 85), Table 1 requires a minimum of 4 bulkheads with engine room aft and 4 bulkheads elsewhere — total minimum is 4. Wait: reading Table 1 carefully, for 65 < L ≤ 85, the entry shows 4 bulkheads for engine room aft arrangement and 4 for elsewhere, meaning total minimum = 4. The proposed arrangement has exactly 4 bulkheads, which meets the Table 1 minimum. Therefore the arrangement is compliant with the minimum count. However, the answerer should also note that [1.1.3] requires bulkheads to suit transverse strength, subdivision, floodability and damage stability per national regulations, and that the Society may require additional design damage cases per Sec1 [1.1.2] for non-convention vessels.

question_text: A 180-metre bulk carrier is being designed with a ballast water tank located amidships. The structural designer is sizing the internal web frames (primary supporting members) inside this tank. The tank has a volumetric centre of gravity at z_G = 8.2 m, and the top of the tank (excluding small hatchways) is at z_top = 14.5 m. The air pipe extends 0.5 m above the tank top. During the normal seagoing design load scenario, the designer calculates the dynamic liquid pressure P_ld acting on the tank boundaries and also needs to determine the correct pressure to apply to the web frames themselves (internal structures within the tank). What pressure value, in kN/m², must be used for the design of these internal tank structures such as the web of primary supporting members, and is this value dependent on the calculated dynamic liquid pressure or the tank geometry?
required_facts: P_int = 12 kN/m² is the prescribed pressure for internal structures in tanks
This value applies to the web of primary supporting members inside the tank
P_int is a fixed minimum value, not derived from tank geometry or dynamic liquid pressure
For internal tank structures, normal seagoing operations (Scenario 2) use P_int
P_int is independent of the calculated dynamic liquid pressure P_ld used for tank boundary design

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec7 symbols table defines P_int as the minimum pressure for internal structures in tanks, referencing Sec6 [3.1]. Sec6 [3.1] gives the fixed value P_int = 12 kN/m². The chain requires the answerer to follow the cross-reference from the Sec7 symbol definition into Sec6 to retrieve the actual numeric value.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: In Sec7 (Design Load Scenarios), the symbol table defines P_int as 'minimum pressure for internal structures in tanks as given in Sec.6 [3.1]'. In Table 1, for the normal seagoing S+D scenario, the row 'Internal structures in tanks' shows P_int as the applicable load component. Step 2: Following the reference to Sec6 [3.1], the clause states: 'The pressure, in kN/m², for internal structures in tanks, e.g. web of primary supporting members, shall be taken as: P_int = 12'. Step 3: This value is a fixed prescribed minimum — it is not derived from tank geometry, liquid density, or dynamic pressure calculations. It applies regardless of the computed P_ld for the tank boundaries. Therefore, the web frames of the primary supporting members inside the ballast tank must be designed for P_int = 12 kN/m².

scenario_parameters.structure_being_sized: web of primary supporting members (internal tank structures)

question_text: A RO/RO ferry has a stern door that also serves as a vehicle ramp. The door opening area is 18 m² and the door opens inwards into an enclosed RO/RO space. The lower edge of the door sill is located 180 mm above the uppermost load line (measured at the ship's side). In a damage stability scenario, the deepest equilibrium waterline is 1.4 m above the lower edge of the door opening. The total packing force is 12 kN and the door mass is 8 t. During a pre-approval review, the surveyor notes that the door will become immersed by an intermediate waterplane in the damage condition. What hydrostatic pressure test must be applied to this door, and what head of water (in metres) must be used as a minimum for that test?
required_facts: The door sill at 180 mm above the uppermost load line is below the minimum 230 mm threshold, placing it in a non-compliant position requiring special consideration
Because the door becomes immersed by an intermediate or equilibrium waterplane in the damage condition, a hydrostatic pressure test is mandatory
The minimum head of water for the hydrostatic pressure test is measured from the lower edge of the door opening to the most unfavourable damage waterplane
The minimum test head is 1.4 m (equal to the vertical distance from the lower edge of the door opening to the deepest equilibrium waterline in the damage condition)
The acceptance criterion for the hydrostatic pressure test is no leakage

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Sec5 side/stern door requirements, which establishes the door is below the freeboard deck threshold and leads to damage condition considerations; Sec1 [3.3.3] (reached via the general chapter requirements) specifies the hydrostatic pressure test requirement for doors immersed in damage condition, referencing the head measured from the lower edge of the door opening to the most unfavourable damage waterplane.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 (Sec5 [1.2.3]): The lower edge of the door sill must not be below a line 230 mm above the uppermost load line. Here the sill is only 180 mm above the load line, which is below the 230 mm threshold — so the sill is in a non-compliant position relative to [1.2.3], triggering special consideration under [1.2.4]. Step 2 (Sec5 [1.4.3]): The door opens inwards into an enclosed RO/RO space with area A = 18 m² ≥ 12 m², so sea pressure must be transferred directly to hull coamings per [1.3.3], and the design force F1 applies (inward-opening). Step 3 (Sec1 [3.3.3]): Because the door becomes immersed by an intermediate waterplane in the damage condition, it must be subjected to a hydrostatic pressure test. The head of water for the test must correspond at least to the head measured from the lower edge of the door opening to the most unfavourable damage waterplane. In this scenario, the deepest equilibrium waterline is 1.4 m above the lower edge of the door opening, so the minimum test head is 1.4 m. Acceptance criterion is no leakage.

question_text: A designer is detailing the end bracket connection for a longitudinal shell stiffener on a bulk carrier. The stiffener has a flat bar flange with a free outstand of 60 mm and a net flange thickness of 12 mm. At the transition between the stiffener flange and the integral end bracket, the flange is knuckled rather than curved. The designer proposes to curve the flange instead of fitting additional support, using a radius of 450 mm. Is this arrangement compliant, and if not, what is the minimum acceptable radius? Additionally, when verifying the net flange thickness used in the radius formula, the designer must confirm which scantling definition applies — specifically whether the 12 mm value should be the as-built thickness, the gross offered thickness, or the net offered thickness after deducting corrosion additions. Which thickness definition is correct, and what is the minimum required radius?
required_facts: The minimum required radius is 480 mm (r = 1.6 × 60² / 12 = 480 mm)
The proposed radius of 450 mm is less than the required 480 mm and is therefore not compliant
The free flange outstand b1 = 60 mm is used in the formula as defined by the structural idealisation section
The thickness tf must be the net flange thickness (net offered thickness after deducting corrosion addition), not the as-built or gross offered thickness
The net scantling approach requires corrosion additions to be deducted from as-built thickness to obtain the net offered thickness used in section property calculations

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec6 [2.1.2] gives the curved-flange radius formula r = 1.6 * b1^2 / tf, where b1 is defined by reference to Sec7 [1.3.4] and tf is the net thickness. The net thickness definition requires going to Sec2 [1.3.2] to confirm that net offered thickness (as-built minus voluntary addition minus corrosion addition) is the correct value to use.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec6 [2.1.2]: When the flange transition at an integral bracket is knuckled, the flange may alternatively be curved with radius r = 1.6 * b1^2 / tf, where b1 is the free flange outstand as defined in Sec7 [1.3.4] and tf is the net flange thickness. Step 2 — Sec7 [1.3.4]: Confirms b1 is the free outstand of the flange beyond the web, i.e. 60 mm in this scenario. Step 3 — Sec2 [1.3.2]: The net scantling approach requires that net sectional dimensions of local supporting members are used for strength calculations; tf must therefore be the net offered thickness (as-built thickness minus voluntary addition minus corrosion addition), not the as-built or gross offered thickness. Step 4 — Compute: r = 1.6 * (60)^2 / 12 = 1.6 * 3600 / 12 = 480 mm. The proposed radius of 450 mm is less than the required 480 mm, so the arrangement is not compliant.

question_text: A newbuilding general cargo vessel of 112 m length is being designed for DNV class. The ship is a monohull welded steel vessel with a maximum deadweight of 8,400 tonnes and a maximum displacement of 14,200 tonnes (deadweight is approximately 59% of displacement). The designer has prepared a loading manual covering the standard cargo and ballast conditions. The shipowner asks whether a loading instrument system (loading computer) is also required onboard, and separately, what documentation must be submitted to the classification society to demonstrate compliance with the hull structure design. Specifically: (1) Is a loading instrument system mandatory for this vessel, and if so, what is the basis for that requirement? (2) What category does this ship fall into for the purposes of loading guidance requirements? (3) What plans and supporting calculations must be submitted for approval or information as part of the design assessment, and who bears responsibility for ensuring the program input data and output are correctly transposed?
required_facts: A loading instrument system (loading computer) is mandatory because the vessel is 112 m in length and qualifies as a category I ship of 100 m and above
The deadweight-to-displacement ratio is approximately 59%, which exceeds the 30% threshold, so no exemption from loading instrument requirements applies

Documentation to be submitted includes the general arrangement plan, structural design brief, design load plan, tank and capacity plan, and structural drawings covering decks/inner bottom, transverse and longitudinal bulkheads, fore ship, engine room area, and aft ship
Structural drawings are submitted for approval (AP) while plans such as general arrangement, design load plan, and tank plan are submitted for information (FI)
The responsibility for error-free program input data and correct transposal of output resides with the designer, not the Society

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Sec5 loading manual/instrument requirements, which references Sec1 for ship category definitions and ship length/deadweight thresholds, then follow to Sec3 for documentation submission requirements and designer responsibility for calculation data.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec5 [1.1.2]: All ships covered by Load Line Reg.10 shall have an approved loading manual. A loading instrument is NOT required for a category II ship with length < 90 m where deadweight ≤ 30% of displacement. This vessel is 112 m, so the 90 m exemption does not apply on length alone. Step 2 — Sec5 [1.1.2] and [3.1.1]: All ships of category I of 100 m and above shall be provided with a loading instrument system. The vessel is 112 m, so if it is category I, a loading instrument is mandatory. Step 3 — Sec1 [1.1.1]: The rules apply to monohull welded steel ships — this vessel qualifies. The ship's deadweight is 8,400 t vs displacement 14,200 t, giving DWT/displacement ≈ 59%, which exceeds 30%, so the category II exemption from loading instrument does not apply regardless. At 112 m and category I, the loading instrument system is mandatory per Sec5 [3.1.1]. Step 4 — Sec3 [2.2.1]: For design assessment, documentation as specified in Table 1 must be submitted. Table 1 requires items such as Z010 General arrangement plan (FI), H010 Structural design brief (FI), H020 Design load plan (FI), H030 Tank and capacity plan (FI), H050 Structural drawings for decks/inner bottom, transverse bulkheads, longitudinal bulkheads, fore ship, engine room area, aft ship (AP). Step 5 — Sec3 [2.1]: The responsibility for error-free specification and input of program data and the subsequent correct transposal of output resides with the designer.

question_text: A designer is detailing a longitudinal bulkhead on a 180 m bulk carrier. At one location, the bulkhead has a shallow knuckle with an angle of 8 degrees. The nearest stiffening web running in line with the knuckle is positioned 80 mm away from the knuckle line. The ship's knuckle is located within the 0.6L midship region. The designer proposes to accept this arrangement without any fatigue analysis, arguing that the 80 mm distance is acceptable for shallow knuckles. Is this arrangement compliant with the classification rules? If not, what is the maximum permitted distance between the knuckle and the support stiffening, and what alternative would allow the 80 mm distance to be accepted?
required_facts: The knuckle qualifies as a shallow knuckle because its angle (8 degrees) is less than 10 degrees
The maximum permitted distance between a shallow knuckle and its support stiffening within 0.6L is 75 mm
The proposed 80 mm distance exceeds the 75 mm limit and is therefore not compliant as-designed
The arrangement cannot be accepted without further justification simply because it is a shallow knuckle — the 75 mm cap still applies
The only route to accepting the 80 mm distance without physical modification is to perform a fatigue analysis in accordance with Ch.9
The fatigue analysis requires the material factor k, which depends on the steel grade (ReH) of the bulkhead plating as defined in the materials section of the same chapter

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec6 [2.1.1(f)] sets the 75 mm limit for shallow knuckles within 0.6L, and states that alternative arrangements may be considered based on fatigue analysis in accordance with Ch.9. The material grade and factor k from Sec1 [2.2] feed into the fatigue assessment that would be required to justify the 80 mm distance.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify the knuckle as a shallow knuckle (angle = 8 deg < 10 deg threshold stated in Sec6 [2.1.1(f)]). Step 2: Apply the rule that for shallow knuckles the distance between the knuckle and support stiffening shall not be greater than 75 mm within 0.6L. Step 3: The proposed 80 mm exceeds the 75 mm limit, so the arrangement as-proposed is non-compliant. Step 4: The rule provides one alternative: the arrangement may be accepted if a fatigue analysis in accordance with Ch.9 is performed and supports the larger distance. Step 5: The fatigue analysis per Ch.9 requires knowledge of the material factor k from Sec1 [2.2], which depends on the steel grade and specified minimum yield stress ReH used for the bulkhead plating — this is the cross-section link back to Sec1.

question_text: A general cargo vessel has a freeboard deck with bulwarks forming a well on the port and starboard sides. The bulwark length for the well is 24 m, and the average bulwark height is 1.0 m. The ship has standard sheer in way of the well. The vessel is fitted with weathertight hatch covers on the freeboard deck. During the design review, the surveyor asks whether the hatch covers require function testing before the vessel enters service. Additionally, calculate the minimum required freeing port area on each side of the ship for the freeboard deck well, and confirm whether the bulwark height affects this calculation.
required_facts: Minimum freeing port area per side = 1.68 m² (using A = 0.07 × 24 m)
The formula branch A = 0.07ℓ_b applies because ℓ_b = 24 m > 20 m
No bulwark height adjustment is required because average height of 1.0 m is within the 0.9 m to 1.2 m range
No sheer-based increase is required because sheer is standard
All weathertight hatch covers must be function tested before the vessel enters service
The function testing requirement applies to all weathertight/watertight doors and hatch covers without exception

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Sec10 freeing port area formula for freeboard deck wells, then follow the reference to Sec1 general testing requirements which mandates function testing for all weathertight/watertight doors and hatch covers.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Freeing port area (Sec10 [2.1.1]): Since ℓ_b = 24 m > 20 m, use A = 0.07 × ℓ_b = 0.07 × 24 = 1.68 m² per side. Step 2 — Bulwark height adjustment: Average height is 1.0 m, which is between 0.9 m and 1.2 m, so no adjustment applies (adjustment only triggers below 0.9 m or above 1.2 m). Step 3 — Sheer: Standard sheer, so no increase per [2.1.2]. Minimum freeing port area = 1.68 m² per side. Step 4 — Function testing: Sec10 references Sec1 [3.3.1] for general documentation and testing requirements. Sec1 [3.3.1] states that all weathertight/watertight doors and hatch covers shall be function tested. Therefore the weathertight hatch covers on the freeboard deck must be function tested before the vessel enters service.

question_text: A general cargo vessel is fitted with a machinery space ventilator on the exposed freeboard deck (position 1). The ventilator coaming is 750 mm tall, made of standard carbon steel with an external diameter of 200 mm. The designer proposes a wall thickness of 7.0 mm for the coaming. Is this arrangement compliant with the applicable classification rules? State the minimum required wall thickness for the coaming and whether the proposed 7.0 mm thickness is acceptable.
required_facts: The machinery space ventilator coaming in an exposed position must comply with the ventilator coaming requirements cross-referenced from the machinery space openings rules
The applicable minimum wall thickness for a carbon steel coaming in position 1 with external diameter ≥ 165 mm is 8.5 mm
The proposed wall thickness of 7.0 mm is less than the required 8.5 mm minimum
The arrangement as proposed is not compliant with the classification rules
The coaming height of 750 mm does not exceed 900 mm, so no additional special support is triggered by height alone

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec8 [1.1.2] states that coamings of any machinery space ventilator in an exposed position shall be in accordance with Sec7 [4.3]. Sec7 [4.3] contains the ventilator coaming requirements including the wall thickness table for steel other than stainless (Table 2 in [3.2.2], referenced via [4.3]), which for position 1 and external diameter 165 mm and above requires 8.5 mm minimum gross thickness.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Sec8 [1.1.2] directs that machinery space ventilator coamings in exposed positions must comply with Sec7 [4.3]. Step 2: Navigate to Sec7 [4.3], which covers ventilator coaming and closing arrangements. Step 3: Sec7 [4.3.2] references the wall thickness requirements. For carbon steel (non-stainless) coamings, Table 2 in [3.2.2] applies. Step 4: The ventilator is in position 1, external diameter is 200 mm (which is between 165 mm threshold and above), so the minimum gross wall thickness is 8.5 mm. Step 5: The proposed 7.0 mm is less than the required 8.5 mm, so the arrangement is NOT compliant.

question_text: A shipbuilder based in South Korea has signed a contract with a Norwegian owner on 14 March 2024 to construct a 180-metre general cargo vessel intended for DNV classification. The shipbuilder has not previously worked with DNV and is delivering the vessel for the first time under DNV rules. During the pre-classification meeting, the owner's representative asks two questions: (1) Which edition of the DNV rules governs the design and construction of this vessel — specifically, is it the rules in force on the contract signing date, or can the parties agree to apply a different edition? (2) The shipbuilder's procurement team is sourcing a batch of hull structural steel plates from a sub-supplier. The sub-supplier will issue a material test report rather than a product certificate. Under what conditions may the Society require its surveyors to witness the tests associated with that material test report, and does the shipbuilder need to formally demonstrate its capability to manage the classification project before work begins? Provide a complete compliance assessment addressing both questions.
required_facts: The rules in force on the date the contract to build the vessel is signed (14 March 2024) govern the design and construction, unless the Society and the parties agree otherwise by special consideration.

The date of 'contract for construction' is defined as the date on which the contract to build is signed between the prospective owner and the shipbuilder, and this date must be declared to the Society.
The Society may at any time require to witness tests associated with a material test report and/or check elements of production control.
Because the shipbuilder is unfamiliar to the Society, it must provide evidence of its capability to successfully manage classification projects before work proceeds.

The Society retains the right to agree with the parties to apply a different edition of the rules than those in force at the contract date, but this requires special consideration and mutual agreement.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Sec4 certification requirements (material test report and Society's right to witness tests), which references back to Sec1 for the definition of applicable rules and the date of 'contract for construction', and Sec2 for the builder capability demonstration requirement and the rule-version-selection clause.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec4 [2.1.2] states that where rules require a material test report, the Society may at any time require to witness the tests and/or check elements of production control. This answers part of question (2) about the sub-supplier's material test report. Step 2 — To answer which rules apply (question 1), the answerer must follow the cross-reference from Sec4 [1.1.2] (applicable chapters define extent of certification) back to Sec2 [1.3.1], which states that the rules in force at the date of 'contract for construction' apply, but the Society may upon special consideration and in agreement with the parties decide on different rules. Step 3 — The term 'contract for construction' must then be resolved via Sec2 [1.3.2], which defines it as the date the contract to build is signed between the prospective owner and the shipbuilder — here 14 March 2024. Step 4 — For question (2) on builder capability, Sec2 [1.2.1] requires builders unfamiliar to the Society to provide evidence of their capability to successfully manage classification projects before proceeding.

question_text:
A 145 m general cargo vessel has a forecastle superstructure connected to the main deckhouse by a continuous hatchway side coaming running the full length of the exposed freeboard deck between them. The vessel is assigned as a Type 'B-60' ship. On the exposed freeboard deck forward of the deckhouse, bulwarks form a well of 28 m length. The bulwarks have an average height of 1.05 m. The breadth of the continuous hatchway side coaming is 55% of the ship's breadth. The vessel has standard sheer throughout.

A design engineer proposes fitting side scuttles in the first tier of the enclosed forecastle superstructure. These side scuttles are round openings, each with an area of 0.09 m². The forecastle spaces below the freeboard deck are also fitted with side scuttles of the same size.

For the freeing port arrangement on the freeboard deck well: (1) determine the minimum required freeing port area per side using the appropriate method for this vessel configuration, and (2) confirm whether the proposed side scuttles in the forecastle require hinged inside deadlights, and if so, for which spaces.
required_facts: The continuous hatchway side coaming between superstructures triggers the Table 1 method (coaming/trunk breadth table) rather than the standard freeing port formula
At 55% coaming breadth-to-ship breadth ratio, linear interpolation between 40% (20%) and 75% (10%) gives approximately 15.7% of total bulwark area
The Type 'B-60' requirement of 25% of total bulwark area is more onerous and governs, giving a minimum freeing port area of approximately 7.35 m² per side
The proposed openings qualify as side scuttles (round, area 0.09 m² which is less than 0.16 m²)
Side scuttles in spaces below the freeboard deck require hinged inside deadlights
Side scuttles in the first tier of enclosed superstructures require hinged inside deadlights
Both forecastle locations (below freeboard deck and first tier enclosed superstructure) require hinged inside deadlights

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec10 freeing port rules for a vessel with continuous hatchway side coaming between superstructures trigger the trunk/coaming table method (Sec10 [2.1.3]). The special requirements for Type 'B-60' ships (Sec10 [6.2]) also apply. The side scuttle deadlight question requires navigating from Sec10 context into Sec2 (access openings, which references Sec6 arrangement rules) to find that side scuttles in spaces below the freeboard deck and in the first tier of enclosed superstructures require hinged inside deadlights per Sec6 [3.1.1].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Freeing port area method selection (Sec10 [2.1.3]): The vessel has continuous hatchway side coaming between detached superstructures, so [2.1.1] does NOT apply. Instead, Table 1 in [2.1.3] governs. The coaming breadth is 55% of ship breadth, which is intermediate between 40% and 75%. Linear interpolation: at 40% → 20% of total bulwark area; at 75% → 10% of total bulwark area. At 55%: fraction = (55-40)/(75-40) = 15/35 = 0.4286. Required % = 20% - 0.4286×(20%-10%) = 20% - 4.286% = 15.71% of total bulwark area per side. Total bulwark area per side = 28 m length × 1.05 m height = 29.4 m². Minimum freeing port area = 0.1571 × 29.4 = 4.62 m² per side. Step 2 — Type 'B-60' check (Sec10 [6.2]): For Type 'B-60' ships, freeing port area in the lower part of bulwarks must be at least 25% of total bulwark area = 0.25 × 29.4 = 7.35 m² per side. This is more onerous than the coaming-table result, so 7.35 m² governs. Step 3 — Side scuttle deadlights (Sec6 [3.1.1]): Side scuttles are round openings with area 0.09 m² < 0.16 m², confirming they are side scuttles not windows. Per Sec6 [3.1.1], hinged inside deadlights are required for: (a) spaces below the freeboard deck — YES, the forecastle spaces below freeboard deck require deadlights; (b) spaces within the first tier of enclosed superstructures — YES, the forecastle first tier spaces require deadlights. Both proposed locations therefore require hinged inside deadlights.

side_scuttle_locations: first tier of enclosed forecastle superstructure

question_text: A bulk carrier with a length L_LL of 95 m is being designed with a double bottom extending from the collision bulkhead to the aft peak bulkhead. The naval architect proposes to install small drainage wells in the double bottom beneath the cargo holds. The ship's beam B is 16 m, giving a calculated minimum double bottom height h_DB of 800 mm. One of the proposed drainage wells has its bottom located 380 mm above the keel line. A second drainage well, intended for lubricating oil collection under the main engine, is located 420 mm above the keel line. Evaluate whether each well arrangement complies with the classification rules, and state the minimum permitted vertical distance from the bottom of a drainage well to the keel line plane for this vessel.
required_facts: The minimum permitted vertical distance from the bottom of a drainage well to the keel line is the greater of 500 mm or half the required double bottom height
Half the required double bottom height is 400 mm (800 mm / 2), so the governing minimum is 500 mm
The first drainage well at 380 mm above the keel line does not comply because 380 mm < 500 mm
The second well (lubricating oil under main engine) is subject to a special provision allowing it if equivalent protection to a compliant double bottom is demonstrated
The L_LL >= 80 m threshold is the trigger for the 500 mm / half-height rule, and this vessel at 95 m meets that threshold

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec4 access arrangement references Sec3 compartment arrangement for double bottom well geometry; the well depth limit in Sec3 [2.4] is the governing rule for drainage well placement in ships with L_LL >= 80 m.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — The access arrangement section (Sec4) references Sec3 [2] for well location constraints, specifically noting that wells shall not be located closer to the keel line than the maximum of 500 mm or half the required double bottom height for ships with L_LL >= 80 m. Step 2 — The vessel has L_LL = 95 m, so it falls under the L_LL >= 80 m threshold.
