Step 3 — Navigate to Sec3 [2.4]: for ships with L_LL 80 m or above, the vertical distance from the bottom of a drainage well to the keel line plane shall not be less than 500 mm OR half the required double bottom height, whichever is greater. Step 4 — Half the required double bottom height = 800 mm / 2 = 400 mm. The maximum of 500 mm and 400 mm is 500 mm. Therefore the minimum permitted distance is 500 mm. Step 5 — First drainage well: 380 mm < 500 mm → NON-COMPLIANT. Step 6 — Second well (lube oil under main engine): Sec3 [2.4] states other wells such as for lubricating oil under main engines may be permitted if the arrangement gives protection equivalent to that afforded by a compliant double bottom. This is a special dispensation, so the 420 mm figure is not automatically disqualifying, but it requires demonstrating equivalent protection — it cannot be accepted as-is without that demonstration.

question_text: A 180-metre bulk carrier is being designed with a longitudinally stiffened upper deck. The deck plating is made of a single material with a specified minimum yield stress of 315 N/mm². The designer proposes T-bar longitudinals with a web depth of 300 mm and a net web thickness of 9 mm, and a free flange outstand of 75 mm with a net flange thickness of 10 mm. The deck plating between longitudinals has a net thickness of 14 mm with a stiffener spacing of 800 mm. During the hull girder buckling check under the S+D load component, the maximum compressive hull girder bending stress at the deck is 180 N/mm² and the hull girder shear stress is 60 N/mm². The buckling utilization factor for the deck plate panel under stress combination 1 (longitudinal stiffening) is calculated as 0.88. Determine whether (a) the T-bar proportions are acceptable, (b) the deck plate slenderness is acceptable, and (c) the buckling utilization factor of 0.88 is within the allowable limit for this load component and acceptance criterion AC-I. Show all checks.
required_facts: η_all = 0.80 for AC-I under S load component (from Sec1 [3.4] Table 3)
Buckling utilization factor 0.88 ≤ η_all = 1.00, therefore the deck panel buckling check is acceptable
Minimum required plate net thickness = 800/100 = 8 mm (C = 100 for strength deck, L ≥ 90 m); offered 14 mm is acceptable
Minimum required T-bar web thickness = (300/75) × √(315/235) ≈ 4.64 mm; offered 9 mm is acceptable
Minimum required T-bar flange thickness = (75/12) × √(315/235) ≈ 7.24 mm; offered 10 mm is acceptable
Stress combination 1 for longitudinal stiffening gives σ_x = 180 N/mm², τ = 0.7 × 60 = 42 N/mm²

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Sec3 hull girder buckling criteria, which references Sec1 [3.4] for the allowable utilization factor; Sec1 [3.4] defines the table of η_all values; the slenderness check routes through Sec2 [2.2] and [3.1.1] for plate and stiffener proportions; Sec4 [2] provides boundary conditions for the direct analysis panel definition.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec3 [3.2] states the buckling strength of elementary plate panels shall comply with η_Plate ≤ η_all, where η_all is defined in Sec1 [3.4]. Step 2 — Sec1 [3.4] Table 3: for AC-I under S+D load component, η_all = 0.90. Therefore 0.88 ≤ 0.90 → utilization is acceptable. Step 3 — Sec3 [2.2] stress combination 1 for longitudinal stiffening: σ_x = σ_hg = 180 N/mm², σ_y = 0, τ = 0.7 × 60 = 42 N/mm². This confirms the stress inputs used. Step 4 — Sec2 [2.2] plate slenderness: t_p ≥ b/C. Ship length L = 180 m ≥ 90 m, so C = 100 for outer shell/strength deck. Required t_p ≥ 800/100 = 8 mm. Offered t_p = 14 mm ≥ 8 mm → plate slenderness is acceptable. Step 5 — Sec2 [3.1.1] T-bar web: t_w ≥ (h_w / C_w) × √(R_eH/235). From Table 2, C_w = 75 for T-bars. Required t_w ≥ (300/75) × √(315/235) = 4.0 × 1.159 = 4.64 mm. Offered t_w = 9 mm ≥ 4.64 mm → web is acceptable. Step 6 — Sec2 [3.1.1] T-bar flange: t_f ≥ (b_f-out / C_f) × √(R_eH/235). From Table 2, C_f = 12 for T-bars. Required t_f ≥ (75/12) × √(315/235) = 6.25 × 1.159 = 7.24 mm. Offered t_f = 10 mm ≥ 7.24 mm → flange is acceptable. All three checks pass.

question_text: A general cargo vessel of 82 m in length is being reviewed for classification. The ship's maximum deadweight is 1,850 tonnes and its maximum displacement is 4,200 tonnes. The vessel carries mixed general cargo and is not a bulk carrier or tanker. The owner wishes to know whether an approved loading manual considering longitudinal strength is required for this ship, and if so, what minimum content must it include regarding permissible structural limits.
required_facts: The ship qualifies as a category II vessel (not category I)
The ship's length of 82 m is less than the 90 m threshold
The deadweight-to-displacement ratio is approximately 44% (1850/4200), which exceeds the 30% limit
Because the 30% deadweight/displacement threshold is exceeded, the longitudinal-strength exemption does not apply
An approved loading manual considering longitudinal strength IS required for this vessel
The loading manual must include permissible limits of still water bending moment and shear force

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec5 [1.1.2] states that a loading manual considering longitudinal strength is not required for a category II ship with length less than 90 m where maximum deadweight does not exceed 30% of maximum displacement; the threshold check references Sec4 [3.1.7] for the category II definition and the 30% deadweight/displacement ratio criterion.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec5 [1.1.2]: All ships covered by Load Lines Reg.10 must have an approved loading manual. However, a loading manual considering longitudinal strength is NOT required for a category II ship with length < 90 m where maximum deadweight does not exceed 30% of maximum displacement (reference to Sec4 [3.1.7]). Step 2 — Check ship category: the vessel is a general cargo ship, not a category I ship (tankers, bulk carriers, etc.), so it is category II. Step 3 — Check length threshold: 82 m < 90 m — threshold satisfied. Step 4 — Check deadweight/displacement ratio: 1,850 / 4,200 = 44.0%, which EXCEEDS the 30% limit. Step 5 — Conclusion: Because the deadweight ratio (44%) exceeds 30%, the exemption does NOT apply. A loading manual considering longitudinal strength IS required. The manual must include permissible limits of still water bending moment and shear force, results of still water bending moment and shear force calculations for the design loading conditions, and relevant operational limitations.

question_text: A naval architect is detailing the end bracket connection for a longitudinal stiffener on the inner bottom of a 180 m bulk carrier. The stiffener has a flat bar flange with a free outstand of 75 mm and a net flange thickness of 12 mm. At the transition between the stiffener flange and the integral end bracket, the flange is knuckled rather than curved. The designer proposes to curve the flange instead of fitting additional support, using a radius of 650 mm. Is this arrangement acceptable, and if not, what is the minimum radius required for the curved flange transition to comply with the rules?
required_facts: The minimum required curve radius is r = 750 mm
The formula applied is r = 1.6 × (b1² / tf) with b1 = 75 mm and tf = 12 mm
The proposed radius of 650 mm is less than the required 750 mm
The arrangement as proposed is NOT acceptable
b1 is the free flange outstand as defined in the structural idealisation section of the same chapter
A transition plate is required at the bracket connection if the difference in as-built plate thickness exceeds 50% of the larger plate thickness in the load-carrying direction

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec6 [2.1.2] gives the formula for minimum curve radius at a knuckled flange transition on an integral bracket, and defines b1 as the free flange outstand per Sec7 [1.3.4]. Sec5 [2.4] is reached via the plate thickness transition requirement that governs the insert plate / local reinforcement context around the bracket connection.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec6 [2.1.2]: When the flange transition between a stiffener and an integral bracket is knuckled, the flange may alternatively be curved with radius r = 1.6 × (b1² / tf), where b1 is the free flange outstand (mm) as defined in Sec7 [1.3.4], and tf is the net flange thickness (mm). Step 2 — Sec7 [1.3.4]: b1 is confirmed as the free outstand of the flange from the web face to the free edge. With b1 = 75 mm and tf = 12 mm: r = 1.6 × (75² / 12) = 1.6 × (5625 / 12) = 1.6 × 468.75 = 750 mm. Step 3 — The proposed radius of 650 mm is less than the required 750 mm, so the arrangement is NOT acceptable. Step 4 — Sec5 [2.4]: If the bracket insert plate or local reinforcement at the bracket connection involves plates of differing thickness, a transition plate is required when the difference in as-built plate thickness exceeds 50% of the larger plate thickness in the load-carrying direction; this must also be checked for the bracket-to-inner-bottom connection in this detail.

question_text: A 185-metre bulk carrier is being designed with a hopper-side ballast tank arrangement. During the structural design review, the designer needs to establish the design load scenario for evaluating the primary supporting members of the cargo hold region. The vessel's loading manual includes the following intact loading conditions: full cargo departure (draught 11.2 m), full cargo arrival (draught 10.8 m), ballast departure (draught 6.1 m), and ballast arrival (draught 5.7 m). The designer proposes to define the design loads for the primary supporting members using only the full cargo departure and ballast arrival conditions, arguing these represent the two extremes of global hull girder loading. As part of the load scenario definition, the design still water torsional moment Mst must also be established for use in the combined load table. At a transverse section located 74 metres from the aft perpendicular, the calculated still water torsional moments from the loading conditions are: +18,400 kNm (full cargo departure), −12,600 kNm (ballast arrival), and +22,100 kNm (ballast departure). The designer proposes to use Mst = +18,400 kNm as the design still water torsional moment at this section. Is the designer's approach for selecting loading conditions for primary supporting members acceptable, and is the proposed value of Mst = +18,400 kNm correct for use in the design load scenario table?
required_facts: The designer's approach of using only two loading conditions is not acceptable; all intact loading conditions in the loading manual must be considered for primary supporting members.
The ballast departure condition (draught 6.1 m) must be included in the loading condition set for primary supporting member evaluation.
The design still water torsional moment Mst is the design still water torsional moment in seagoing condition at the hull transverse section being considered, as defined in Sec4 [2.3.1].
At the section 74 m from AP, the maximum absolute still water torsional moment is 22,100 kNm (from the ballast departure condition).
The proposed Mst = +18,400 kNm is incorrect.
The loading conditions must also account for operational limitations and combinations of local and global loading, not just global draught extremes.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec8 [2.1.2] defines what loading conditions must be considered for primary supporting members, requiring all intact loading conditions in the loading manual and consideration of operational limitations and local/global load combinations — not just two extreme conditions. Sec8 [2.1.2] also references Sec7 for the design load scenario table, where Mst appears as a symbol defined by reference to Sec4 [2.3], which specifies how the design still water torsional moment is determined (the maximum absolute value across all loading conditions at the section).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Sec8 [2.1.2]: The loading conditions for evaluation of primary supporting members shall be defined with consideration to all intact loading conditions in the loading manual, operational limitations, and the ship arrangement including possible combinations of local and global loading. The designer's proposal to use only two conditions (full cargo departure and ballast arrival) is therefore not acceptable — ballast departure must also be included at minimum, as it is an intact loading condition in the loading manual.

Step 2 — Sec8 [2.1.2] references Sec7 for the design load scenario table structure, where the symbol Mst is defined as the design still water torsional moment as defined in Sec4 [2.3].

Step 3 — Sec4 [2.3]: The design still water torsional moment at any longitudinal position shall be taken as the maximum absolute value of the still water torsional moments from all design loading conditions. At the section 74 m from AP, the three values are +18,400 kNm, −12,600 kNm, and +22,100 kNm. The maximum absolute value is |+22,100| = 22,100 kNm (from ballast departure). Therefore Mst = +22,100 kNm, not +18,400 kNm as proposed. The designer's proposed Mst is incorrect because it excludes the ballast departure condition, which was also excluded from the loading condition set — both errors stem from the same root cause of not considering all intact loading conditions.

question_text: A general cargo vessel of 120 m length is fitted with a deckhouse on the freeboard deck. The deckhouse contains a stairway leading to spaces below the freeboard deck. The external doors of the deckhouse are weathertight, but the designer proposes to omit fitting the deckhouse doors to the full weathertight door standard, instead relying solely on the fact that the stairway inside the deckhouse is enclosed within a properly constructed companionway fitted with doors meeting the applicable door standard. A sanitary discharge pipe from a toilet space within this deckhouse leads through the shell plating. The inboard end of the discharge pipe is located 0.8 m above the summer load waterline (ship length L = 120 m, so 0.01L = 1.2 m and 0.02L = 2.4 m). The designer proposes to fit two automatic non-return valves without any positive means of closing from above the freeboard deck. Is the proposed arrangement for the deckhouse doors acceptable, and is the proposed valve arrangement for the sanitary discharge compliant? Justify your answer with reference to the applicable door requirements and the discharge valve rules.
required_facts: The deckhouse door arrangement is acceptable because the stairway is enclosed in a companionway with compliant doors, so external doors need not be weathertight
The threshold for permitting two automatic non-return valves without positive closing is when the inboard end exceeds 0.01L above the summer load waterline
0.01L = 1.2 m for this 120 m vessel; the inboard end at 0.8 m does NOT exceed this threshold
The proposed two-valve arrangement without positive means of closing is NOT compliant
The compliant arrangement requires one automatic non-return valve WITH a positive means of closing operable from above the freeboard deck
The door standard referenced in the discharge rule is found in the access openings section governing weathertight doors on the freeboard deck

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec9 [1.1.1] governs discharge valve requirements and conditions them on whether the space is within a superstructure/deckhouse whose doors comply with Sec2 [4.1.1]. The answerer must navigate from the discharge rule to the door standard in Sec2 to determine both the door acceptability and the valve arrangement.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Discharge valve rule (Sec9 [1.1.1]): Discharges led through the shell from within superstructures and deckhouses on the freeboard deck fitted with doors complying with Sec2 [4.1.1] must have efficient non-return valve arrangements. The inboard end is 0.8 m above SWL. Since 0.8 m < 0.01L (1.2 m), the general requirement applies: one automatic non-return valve WITH a positive means of closing from above the freeboard deck. Two automatic non-return valves without positive closing are only permitted when the vertical distance exceeds 0.01L. Since 0.8 m does not exceed 1.2 m, the proposed two-valve arrangement without positive closing is NOT compliant. Step 2 — Door standard (Sec2 [4.1.1]): Sec9 [1.1.1] conditions the discharge rule on doors complying with Sec2 [4.1.1]. The answerer must check Sec2 to find the door requirements. Per Sec2 [1.1.6], if stairways within a deckhouse are enclosed within properly constructed companionways fitted with doors complying with [4.1.1], the external doors need not be weathertight. Therefore the deckhouse door arrangement (external doors not to full standard, but internal companionway doors meeting [4.1.1]) IS acceptable under Sec2 [1.1.6]. Step 3 — Combined conclusion: The deckhouse door arrangement is acceptable. The discharge valve arrangement is not compliant because the inboard end height of 0.8 m does not exceed 0.01L = 1.2 m, so a single automatic non-return valve with positive means of closing from above the freeboard deck is required, not two valves without positive closing.

scenario_parameters.discharge_source: sanitary space within deckhouse on freeboard deck
scenario_parameters.proposed_valve_arrangement: two automatic non-return valves, no positive closing
scenario_parameters.deckhouse_door_arrangement: external doors not full weathertight standard; internal companionway doors compliant

question_text: A 145-metre general cargo vessel has a forecastle superstructure and a poop superstructure, with an open well formed on the freeboard deck between them. Bulwarks run along both sides of this well for a length of 32 metres on each side, with an average bulwark height of 1.4 metres. The ship has standard sheer in way of the well. The designer proposes fitting freeing ports with a total area of 2.35 m² on each side of the well. The vessel is also fitted with side cargo doors located below the freeboard deck, and the designer intends to submit an operating and maintenance manual (OMM) for these doors. The OMM as drafted includes main particulars, design drawings, service conditions (limiting heel/trim for operations and loading), and a maintenance schedule — but does not include any trouble-shooting guidance, acceptance/rejection criteria, or a register of inspections. A surveyor reviewing the submission raises two concerns: (1) whether the proposed freeing port area of 2.35 m² per side is sufficient for the well, and (2) whether the OMM content is adequate for approval. Are both aspects of the design compliant, and if not, what specific deficiencies exist?
required_facts: Minimum required freeing port area per side = 2.496 m² (base 2.24 m² plus 0.256 m² height correction for bulwark exceeding 1.2 m by 0.2 m)
The proposed freeing port area of 2.35 m² per side is insufficient — it falls short of the 2.496 m² minimum
The bulwark height correction applies because the average height of 1.4 m exceeds the 1.2 m threshold, requiring an increase of 0.004 m² per metre of well length per 0.1 m excess height
Side cargo doors below the freeboard deck are shell doors requiring an operating and maintenance manual (OMM)
The OMM must include trouble-shooting guidance and acceptance/rejection criteria in the maintenance section
The OMM must include a register of inspections covering locking, securing and supporting devices, and records of repairs and renewals
The submitted OMM is non-compliant because it omits trouble-shooting, acceptance/rejection criteria, and the register of inspections

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Freeing port area calculation starts at Sec10 [2.1.1], which for the bulwark height adjustment references the same section's formula. The OMM requirement for side doors starts at Sec5 [1.6.1] (side/stern doors application and OMM reference), which points to Sec3 [1.2] for internal door/hatch application scope, which in turn references Sec1 [10.3.3] — but the direct OMM content requirements for shell doors including side doors are in Sec1 [3.2.2] and [3.2.3].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Freeing port area (Sec10 [2.1.1]): ℓ_b = 32 m (> 20 m), so base formula A = 0.07 × 32 = 2.24 m². Bulwark height is 1.4 m, which exceeds 1.2 m by 0.2 m (i.e., 2 increments of 0.1 m). Required increase = 2 × 0.004 × 32 = 0.256 m². Adjusted minimum area = 2.24 + 0.256 = 2.496 m² per side. The proposed 2.35 m² is less than 2.496 m², so the freeing port area is INSUFFICIENT. Step 2 — OMM adequacy (Sec5 [1.6.1] → Sec3 [1.2] → Sec1 [3.2.2] and [3.2.3]): Side doors below the freeboard deck are shell doors covered by Sec5. Sec5 [1.6.1] requires an OMM as described in Sec1 [3.2.2]. Sec1 [3.2.3] states the OMM shall be submitted for approval and the inclusion of necessary information regarding inspections, trouble-shooting, and acceptance/rejection criteria in the maintenance part shall be verified. The draft OMM omits trouble-shooting guidance, acceptance/rejection criteria, and a register of inspections — all required by Sec1 [3.2.2](c) and (d). Therefore the OMM is also NON-COMPLIANT.

question_text:
A new RO/RO passenger ferry is being designed with internal watertight sliding doors fitted in the main watertight bulkheads below the freeboard deck. During the design review, the following items are under discussion:

1. The ship has 14 internal watertight doors, each with a clear opening of 900 mm wide × 2100 mm high. The doors are remotely operated from the bridge and locally operable from both sides. After installation, the shipyard proposes to perform only a visual inspection and a single operational cycle test for each door to confirm function.

2. Several side scuttles (round, 350 mm diameter) are fitted in crew cabins located within the first tier of an enclosed superstructure. The designer proposes to fit these side scuttles without deadlights, arguing that the cabin bulkheads and doors separating the scuttles from direct access leading below are sufficient.

3. One of the side scuttles in the first tier has its sill located 480 mm above the summer load line, measured at the ship's side. The ship's breadth B is 22 m.

For each of the three items above, determine whether the proposed arrangement is compliant with classification rules. For item 1, state what specific additional testing is required beyond a basic function test, and describe the test conditions that must be met. For item 3, calculate the minimum required sill height above the summer load line and state whether the 480 mm sill height is acceptable.
required_facts: The basic single-cycle function test is insufficient for internal watertight doors; an additional function test per the internal doors and hatches section is required
The function test must confirm the door is operable from both sides of the bulkhead
For remotely controlled doors, indicators at the control position showing open/closed status must be verified

Side scuttles in first-tier enclosed superstructure spaces must be fitted with hinged inside deadlights; the cabin bulkhead/door exemption applies only to the second tier and above, so the proposal is non-compliant
Minimum sill height = 2.5% × 22,000 mm = 550 mm (governs over the 500 mm alternative)
The proposed sill height of 480 mm is below the 550 mm minimum and is not acceptable

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec1 [3.3.1] requires internal watertight doors to be function tested per Sec3 [4.1.2]; Sec3 [2.1.3] references Sec2 [1.3] for scantlings of securing devices; Sec6 [3.1] governs deadlight requirements and sill height limits for side scuttles
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Item 1 testing: Pt3.Ch12.Sec1 [3.3.1] states all weathertight/watertight doors shall be function tested, and for each internal watertight door/hatch, function test shall be carried out in accordance with Sec3 [4.1.2] additionally. Navigating to Sec3 [4.1.2]: the function test for internal watertight doors requires the door to be operable from both sides of the bulkhead or deck (Sec3 [4.2.1]), and remotely controlled doors must also be locally operable with open/closed indicators at the control position (Sec3 [4.2.2]). The basic single-cycle operational test is insufficient; the full function test per Sec3 [4.1.2] must be carried out, confirming operability from both sides and remote/local operation with indicators. Step 2 — Item 2 deadlights: Navigating to Sec6 [3.1.1], side scuttles in spaces within the first tier of enclosed superstructures SHALL be fitted with hinged inside deadlights. The exemption in Sec6 [3.1.8] (cabin bulkheads and doors accepted in lieu of deadlights) applies only to the second tier and above, not the first tier. Therefore the proposal to omit deadlights in first-tier cabins is non-compliant. Step 3 — Item 3 sill height: Sec6 [3.1.3] states side scuttles shall not be fitted with sills below a line drawn parallel to the freeboard deck at side having its lowest point 2.5% of breadth B or 500 mm, whichever is greater, above the summer load line. 2.5% × 22,000 mm = 550 mm. Since 550 mm > 500 mm, the minimum sill height is 550 mm. The proposed 480 mm sill height is below 550 mm and is therefore not compliant.

scenario_parameters.side_scuttle_location: first tier enclosed superstructure crew cabins

question_text:
A 145-meter bulk carrier is being designed with transverse web frames acting as primary supporting members in the cargo hold region. At each frame, longitudinal stiffeners on the inner bottom pass through cut-outs in the transverse web frame. The designer has sized the cut-outs at 48% of the web frame depth, with no lug or collar plates fitted. The cut-out breadth is 60 mm. The corner radii of the cut-outs are currently detailed at 10 mm.

The fillet welds connecting the longitudinal stiffeners to the transverse web frames must be sized. The designer intends to use the detailed calculation method (rather than the simplified method) for determining the stiffener-to-PSM connection loads, since the ship exceeds 90 m in length.

For the weld sizing, the designer references a specific sub-article in the chapter on fillet weld calculations. That sub-article (referenced from the detailed connection calculation method) specifies requirements for fillet weld throat thickness based on the shear flow in the connection.

(a) Is the cut-out arrangement (48% depth, no lug/collar plate, corner radius 10 mm) compliant with the structural rules? Identify any non-compliances and state the minimum required corner radius.

(b) Which sub-article on fillet weld sizing applies when using the detailed (non-simplified) stiffener-to-PSM connection calculation method, and how does this differ from the sub-article that would apply under the simplified method?
required_facts: Cut-out depth of 48% is compliant because it does not exceed the 50% limit for cut-outs without lug or collar plate
Minimum required corner radius R = 25 mm (greater of 20% × 60 mm = 12 mm and 25 mm absolute minimum)
The current corner radius of 10 mm is non-compliant and must be increased to at least 25 mm
For the detailed stiffener-to-PSM connection calculation method, fillet weld sizing is governed by Ch.13 Sec.1 [2.5.6]
For the simplified method (ships < 90 m), fillet weld sizing would instead reference Ch.13 Sec.1 [2.5.4]
The detailed method applies here because the ship length (145 m) exceeds 90 m

annotator_grounding.end_clause: Pt3.Ch6.Sec1 [2.5.6] (via Ch.13 Sec.1 [2.5.6] reference in Sec7 [1.2.8])
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec7 [1.2.8] states that fillet weld sizing for the detailed connection method shall be calculated according to Ch.13 Sec.1 [2.5.6], while Sec7 [1.3.4] directs the simplified method to Ch.13 Sec.1 [2.5.4]. The answerer must navigate from the detailed calculation method clause to the correct weld sizing sub-article reference, distinguishing it from the simplified method reference.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Cut-out depth check (Sec7 [1.1.2]): 48% < 50%, so the cut-out depth without lug/collar plate is compliant. Step 2 — Corner radius check (Sec7 [1.1.6]): minimum R = max(20% × b, 25 mm) = max(0.20 × 60, 25) = max(12, 25) = 25 mm. The detailed radius of 10 mm is less than 25 mm, so this is NON-COMPLIANT. Step 3 — Weld sizing for detailed method (Sec7 [1.2.8]): the detailed calculation method directs weld sizing to Ch.13 Sec.1 [2.5.6]. Step 4 — Weld sizing for simplified method (Sec7 [1.3.4]): the simplified method directs weld sizing to Ch.13 Sec.1 [2.5.4]. The answerer must identify that [2.5.6] (not [2.5.4]) applies here because the ship is >90 m and the detailed method is used.

question_text: A bulk carrier of 185 m rule length is being designed. One of the transverse web frames in the cargo hold region acts as a primary supporting member (PSM) spanning between the inner bottom and the deck. The PSM web plating is proposed at a net thickness of 6.5 mm. The ship has a single strength deck and the PSM is located at the boundary of a cargo hold intended for dry bulk cargo. Is the proposed web thickness compliant with the minimum thickness requirement for this PSM, and what is the minimum net thickness required?
required_facts: The applicable minimum thickness formula is t = a + b·L2·sqrt(k) from the primary supporting members minimum thickness requirements
The correct table row is for PSM at boundaries of holds intended for cargo in bulk / single strength deck, giving a = 4.5 and b = 0.015
The minimum net thickness evaluates to approximately 7.28 mm (4.5 + 0.015 × 185 = 7.275 mm) for k = 1.0
The proposed web thickness of 6.5 mm is less than the required minimum of approximately 7.28 mm
The arrangement is not compliant and the web plating must be increased to at least 7.28 mm net thickness

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec6 pillar/PSM scantling requirements reference Sec3 for minimum thickness of PSM web plating; the answerer must navigate from the PSM scantling section to the minimum thickness section and apply Table 3 for the correct location category.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify that the PSM web plating minimum thickness requirement is governed by Pt3.Ch6.Sec3 [3.1.1], which gives t = a + b·L2·sqrt(k). Step 2 — From Table 3 in Sec3, identify the correct row: 'PSM at tank boundaries, boundaries of holds intended for cargo in bulk, single strength deck and shell up to freeboard deck', which gives a = 4.5, b = 0.015. Step 3 — For a bulk carrier, L2 = L1 = 185 m (rule length). Compute t = 4.5 + 0.015 × 185 × sqrt(1.0) = 4.5 + 2.775 = 7.275 mm. Step 4 — Round up: minimum net thickness = 7.28 mm (or 7.3 mm). Step 5 — The proposed 6.5 mm is less than 7.28 mm, so the arrangement is NOT compliant.

scenario_parameters.PSM_location: cargo hold boundary / single strength deck

question_text: A bulk carrier with length L = 180 m, breadth B = 32 m, block coefficient CB = 0.82, and scantling draught TSC = 12.5 m is being assessed for structural strength. The ship is fitted with bilge keels and has a metacentric height GM = 0.07B in the fully loaded condition (TLC = 12.5 m). During the design review, the naval architect needs to determine the roll angle θ to be used in the dynamic load case calculations. Using the standard formula approach (no direct GM calculation has been performed), what is the roll period Tθ and the roll angle θ for the strength assessment under the extreme sea loads design load scenario with no service restriction? Show all intermediate values.
required_facts: Roll radius of gyration kr is to be determined in accordance with Pt.5 for a vessel with the class notation "Bulk carrier" or "Ore carrier", rather than using the general default kr = 0.39B
GM = the Pt.5 bulk-carrier value for the relevant loading condition (the general default GM = 0.07B does not apply)
Roll period Tθ is derived from Tθ = 2.3π·kr / √(g·GM), with kr and GM taken from the bulk-carrier-specific Pt.5 values in Sec.3 [2.1.1].
fBK = 1.0 because the ship is fitted with bilge keels
fp = fps = 1.0 for strength assessment under extreme sea loads design load scenario with no service restriction
Roll angle θ for a bulk carrier is derived from the Sec.3 [2.1.1] roll angle formula using the Pt.5 values of k_r and GM, not the Pt.3 general defaults

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec.2 Symbols section references θ (roll angle) and Tθ (roll period) as defined in Sec.3 [2.1.1]. The answerer must follow this cross-reference to Sec.3 to find the actual formulae for roll period and roll angle, then apply the correct coefficients for the given scenario (bilge keel fitted, strength assessment, extreme sea loads, no service restriction).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec.2 Symbols defines θ = roll angle as defined in Sec.3 [2.1.1], so the answerer must navigate to Sec.3 [2.1.1]. Step 2 — In Sec.3 [2.1.1], roll radius of gyration: kr = 0.39B = 0.39 × 32 = 12.48 m (general default, not a tanker). Step 3 — GM = 0.07B = 0.07 × 32 = 2.24 m (general default). Step 4 — Roll period: Tθ = (2.3π × kr) / √(g × GM) = (2.3π × 12.48) / √(9.81 × 2.24) = (90.13) / √(21.97) = 90.13 / 4.687 ≈ 19.23 s. Step 5 — fBK = 1.0 (bilge keel fitted). Step 6 — fp = fps for strength assessment; fps = 1.0 for extreme sea loads design load scenario with no service restriction (fr = 1.0 for R0). Step 7 — Roll angle: θ = [9000 × (1.4 − 0.035 × Tθ) × fp × fBK] / [(1.15B + 55) × π] = [9000 × (1.4 − 0.035 × 19.23) × 1.0 × 1.0] / [(1.15 × 32 + 55) × π] = [9000 × (1.4 − 0.673)] / [(36.8 + 55) × π] = [9000 × 0.727] / [91.8 × π] = 6543 / 288.4 ≈ 22.7 deg.

question_text: A bulk carrier with a scantling length L = 220 m, block coefficient CB = 0.82, and scantling draught TLC = 14.5 m is being assessed for external sea pressures under the HSM-1 dynamic load case. The structural engineer is evaluating a load point on the ship's side shell located at x = 110 m from the aft perpendicular, y = 8.5 m from the centreline, and z = 9.0 m above the baseline. The moulded breadth at the waterline at this cross-section is Bx = 38 m. The loading condition being assessed has a draught of 13.0 m. For the extreme sea loads design load scenario, determine: (1) the value of fxL at this load point and the corresponding non-linear coefficient fnℓ; (2) the wave coefficient Cw applicable to this vessel; and (3) the x, y, z coordinates of the load point must be measured with respect to which reference origin, and where is that origin defined?
required_facts: fxL = 0.5 (computed as x/L = 110/220, within [0,1])
fnℓ = 0.9 for extreme sea loads at fxL = 0.5 (interpolated between fxL=0.3 and fxL=0.7, both giving 0.9)
Cw ≈ 10.03 using the formula Cw = 10.75 − ((300−L)/100)^1.5 applicable for 90 ≤ L ≤ 300
The x, y, z coordinates are measured with respect to the reference coordinate system defined in the Introduction section of this chapter (Sec1 [1.2.1]), which itself refers to Ch.1 Sec.4
fT = 13.0/14.5 ≈ 0.897 (ratio of loading condition draught to scantling draught, needed for CfT and other coefficients)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec5 defines hydrodynamic pressure formula for HSM load cases using fxL (defined in Sec2), Cw (defined in Sec4), and coordinates x,y,z referenced to the coordinate system defined in Sec1 [1.2.1]
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Start in Sec5 [1.3.2]: The HSM-1 hydrodynamic pressure formula uses fxL, fnℓ, and Cw. The symbols table in Sec5 states fxL is 'ratio as defined in Sec2' and Cw is 'wave coefficient defined in Sec4'. The coordinates x,y,z are stated as 'coordinates of the load point with respect to the reference coordinate system defined in Sec1 [1.2.1]'. Step 2 — Follow to Sec2: fxL = x/L = 110/220 = 0.5, constrained to [0,1]. For extreme sea loads, fnℓ is interpolated: at fxL=0.3 fnℓ=0.9, at fxL=0.7 fnℓ=0.9, so at fxL=0.5 (midpoint) fnℓ=0.9 by linear interpolation. Step 3 — Follow to Sec4: Cw for L=220m falls in range 90≤L≤300, so Cw = 10.75 − ((300−220)/100)^1.5 = 10.75 − (0.8)^1.5 = 10.75 − 0.7155 ≈ 10.03. Step 4 — Follow to Sec1 [1.2.1]: The coordinate system is defined in Ch.1 Sec.4, referenced from Sec1 [1.2.1]. The origin and axis directions are established there — x measured from aft perpendicular, z from baseline, y from centreline.

question_text: A 185 m bulk carrier is being designed with a longitudinally stiffened bottom and inner bottom. The designer proposes to join two bottom shell plates of different thicknesses: a 22 mm plate in the midship region transitioning to a 14 mm plate toward the fore end. No transition plate is planned between these two plates. The difference in as-built plate thickness is assessed purely on the stress level at the connection. Is this arrangement acceptable under classification rules, and what condition must be satisfied for the larger thickness difference to be permitted without a transition plate?
required_facts: The threshold for requiring a transition plate is when the difference in as-built plate thickness exceeds 50% of the larger plate thickness in the load-carrying direction
50% of the larger plate thickness (22 mm) equals 11 mm
The actual thickness difference is 8 mm (22 mm − 14 mm), which does not exceed the 11 mm threshold
No transition plate is required in this specific case because the difference does not exceed 50% of the larger plate thickness
If the difference did exceed 50%, a transition plate would be required unless an evaluation of the stress level at the connection demonstrates acceptability
The same rule applies to local inserts such as insert plates in double bottom girders, floors, and inner bottom

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Structural idealisation section references plating arrangement principles; the plating thickness transition rule in Sec5 [2.4] governs when a transition plate is required and when a larger thickness difference may be accepted based on stress evaluation.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: The designer is dealing with plates of different thicknesses being joined — 22 mm and 14 mm. The difference is 22 - 14 = 8 mm. Step 2: Check the threshold: 50% of the larger plate thickness = 0.5 × 22 = 11 mm. Since 8 mm < 11 mm, the difference does NOT exceed 50% of the larger plate thickness. Step 3: Per Sec5 [2.4], a transition plate is required only when the difference in as-built plate thickness exceeds 50% of the larger plate thickness in the load-carrying direction. Since 8 mm < 11 mm threshold, no transition plate is strictly required by the rule. Step 4: However, the question is framed to test whether the designer correctly understands the rule: if the difference DID exceed 50%, a transition plate would be mandatory unless an evaluation of the stress level at the connection justifies acceptance of the larger difference. The condition for omitting the transition plate when the difference exceeds 50% is that a stress-level evaluation at the connection must be carried out and must demonstrate acceptability.

question_text: A 180-metre general cargo vessel is being designed with a welded steel monohull and conventional stiffened plate construction. The vessel has been assigned the class notation CSR. The designer intends to rely solely on the CSR requirements for all structural chapters and has not submitted any certification-related documentation under the general hull structure rules, arguing that CSR replaces everything in those chapters. The vessel's anchor equipment includes anchor chain joining shackles, and the designer has submitted only a Manufacturer's Declaration (MD) for these shackles rather than a product certificate issued by the Society. Is the designer's documentation approach compliant with the classification rules for this CSR-classed vessel, and what specific certification document is required for the anchor chain joining shackles?
required_facts: CSR notation does not exempt the vessel from certification requirements in the compliance documentation section; those requirements still apply
The designer's approach of omitting certification documentation on the basis of CSR is non-compliant
Anchor chain joining shackles require a material certificate (MC) issued by the Society
A Manufacturer's Declaration (MD) is not sufficient for anchor chain joining shackles
The applicable compliance documentation requirements for anchor equipment remain in force for CSR-classed vessels

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec1 [1.1.2] states that for CSR ships, separate requirements replace Ch.1 to Ch.13 EXCEPT for certification requirements given in Sec.3 [4] and documentation requirements for items in Sec.3 [2.2] not specified in CSR. This forces the answerer to navigate to Sec.3 [4] (equivalence/compliance documentation) and specifically Table 2, which specifies that anchor chain joining shackles require an MC (material certificate) issued by the Society — not an MD from the manufacturer.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Sec1 [1.1.2] establishes that CSR replaces Ch.1–Ch.13 for CSR-classed ships, but explicitly carves out certification requirements in Sec.3 [4] and documentation requirements in Sec.3 [2.2] not covered by CSR. Step 2: The designer's claim that CSR replaces all documentation is therefore incorrect — Sec.3 [4] still applies. Step 3: Navigate to Sec.3 [4], which covers compliance documentation. Table 2 lists required compliance documents for hull equipment including anchor equipment. Step 4: Table 2 specifies that anchor chain joining shackles require document type MC (material certificate) issued by the Society (PC = product certificate, MC = material certificate, MD = material declaration). Step 5: The designer submitted only an MD (Manufacturer's Declaration), which does not satisfy the requirement for an MC issued by the Society. Therefore the documentation approach is non-compliant, and a Society-issued material certificate (MC) is required for the anchor chain joining shackles.

scenario_parameters.required_document: MC (material certificate) issued by the Society

question_text: A new 320-metre two-island container ship is being designed with NV 47 steel upper hull longitudinal structural members. The leading plate thickness of the hatch side coaming structure is 72 mm. During the design review, the NDT plan is being prepared for the block assembly welds. The designer proposes to apply 100% MT and 100% UT to all block-to-block butt joints of the upper hull longitudinal structural members including attached longitudinal stiffeners, and 20% MT to transversely orientated full penetration weld joints (plate butt welds) in the coaming structure. A surveyor questions whether the extent of NDT testing depends solely on the weld type and location, or whether additional vessel-type and joint-location factors must first be established before the minimum testing percentages can be confirmed. What is the correct basis for determining the extent of NDT, and is the proposed NDT scope for the block-to-block butt joints and the transversely orientated full penetration plate butt welds in the coaming structure compliant with the minimum requirements?
required_facts: The extent of NDT testing depends on the type of vessel and the location of the joints, not solely on weld type
NV 47 material with leading plate thickness of 72 mm falls within the 50 < t ≤ 100 mm threshold triggering additional container ship NDT requirements

Block-to-block butt joints of all upper hull longitudinal structural members including attached longitudinal stiffeners require 100% MT and 100% UT (with only UT to be performed for the RT/UT requirement)
The proposed 100% MT and 100% UT for block-to-block butt joints is compliant with minimum requirements
Transversely orientated full penetration plate butt welds in the coaming structure require 20% UT (not 20% MT)
The proposed 20% MT for transversely orientated full penetration plate butt welds is non-compliant; 20% UT is required
The coaming structure NDT scope for transversely orientated full penetration welds applies for the full length of the coaming structure

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec3 [2.1.1] states that the extent of testing depends on the type of vessel and the location of the joints, which cross-references the documentation requirements in Sec2 [2.1.1] regarding ship-type-specific requirements that must be established before the NDT scope can be confirmed.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Start at Pt1.Ch3.Sec3 [2.1.1]: The clause explicitly states 'The extent of testing will depend on the type of vessel and the location of the joints.' This is the gating condition: before applying Table 1 percentages, the vessel type and joint location must be established. Step 2 — The vessel is a two-island container ship, which is a specific vessel type. The cross-reference to Sec2 [2.1.1] confirms that documentation requirements (and by extension NDT scope) are conditioned on ship type notations. Step 3 — Return to Sec3 Table 1: For container ships with NV 47 material and leading plate thickness 50 < t ≤ 100 mm (here t = 72 mm, which falls in this range), the 'Additional for container ships' row applies. Block-to-block butt joints of all upper hull longitudinal structural members including attached longitudinal stiffeners require 100% MT and 100% UT (only UT shall be performed per footnote 3). Step 4 — For transversely or vertically orientated full penetration weld joints (plate butt welds) in the coaming structure, footnote 8 states this scope applies for the full length of the coaming structure, and Table 1 requires 20% UT (RT/UT column), not 20% MT. The designer's proposal of 20% MT for these welds is therefore non-compliant; it should be 20% UT. Step 5 — The 100% MT + 100% UT for block-to-block butt joints is compliant (footnote 3 clarifies only UT shall be performed for the RT/UT column, so 100% UT is required; 100% MT is also required from the MT/PT column). Conclusion: The extent of NDT is correctly governed first by vessel type and joint location per [2.1.1]; the block-to-block butt joint scope is compliant; the transversely orientated full penetration plate butt weld scope is non-compliant (20% MT proposed, but 20% UT is required).

question_text: A designer is detailing the end bracket connection for a longitudinal stiffener on the inner shell of a double-hull tanker. The stiffener has a flat bar flange with a free outstand of 65 mm and a net flange thickness of 12 mm. At the transition between the stiffener flange and the integral end bracket, the flange is knuckled rather than curved. The designer proposes to curve the flange instead of fitting additional support, and wants to know the minimum radius of curvature required for this to be acceptable. Additionally, the stiffener web and the attached plating meet at an angle of 42 degrees. What are the minimum radius of curvature for the curved flange transition, and what additional detailing requirement is triggered by the web-to-plating angle?
required_facts: Minimum flange curve radius r = 1.6 × (65² / 12) ≈ 563–564 mm
The formula parameter b1 = 65 mm is the free flange outstand as defined in the structural idealisation section
Because the web-to-plating angle (42 deg) is less than 50 deg, tripping brackets or carlings are required at spacing not exceeding 4 times the stiffener spacing
The as-built thickness of tripping brackets must be at least 75% of the as-built web thickness of the connected stiffener
For an unsymmetrical stiffener with web-to-plating angle less than 50 deg, the face plate shall be fitted on the open angle side
If the plate flange material has a lower minimum yield strength than the stiffener or PSM, an additional yield capacity check of the plate flange may be required

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec6 [2.1.2] gives the formula for minimum flange curve radius and defines b1 as the free flange outstand per Sec7 [1.3.4]. Sec6 [3.1.2] triggers a tripping bracket requirement when the web-to-plating angle is less than 50 deg, and specifies that the face plate shall be on the open angle side. Sec1 [2.1.2] is reached because the yield capacity check of the plate flange may be required when flange and web materials differ, which is a background material assumption the answerer must confirm is not violated.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Start at Sec6 [2.1.2]: The clause states that if the flange transition at an integral bracket is knuckled, the flange may alternatively be curved with radius r = 1.6 × (b1² / tf), where b1 is the free flange outstand as defined in Sec7 [1.3.4] and tf is the net flange thickness. Step 2 — Navigate to Sec7 [1.3.4]: This clause defines b1 (free flange outstand) for the stiffener cross-section, confirming b1 = 65 mm as given. Step 3 — Apply formula: r = 1.6 × (65² / 12) = 1.6 × (4225 / 12) = 1.6 × 352.08 = 563.3 mm, so minimum radius ≈ 564 mm. Step 4 — Sec6 [3.1.2]: The web-to-plating angle is 42 deg, which is less than 50 deg, so tripping brackets or carlings shall be fitted at spacing not more than 4 times the stiffener spacing, bracket as-built thickness ≥ 75% of stiffener web as-built thickness, and the face plate shall be on the open angle side. Step 5 — Sec1 [2.1.2]: The rules assume flange and web have the same minimum yield strength; if the plate flange has a lower yield strength than the stiffener, an additional yield capacity check per Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4] may be required.

scenario_parameters.connection_type: integral end bracket with knuckled flange transition

question_text: A 145 m general cargo vessel has a forecastle deck forming a well on the freeboard deck. The well is bounded by bulwarks 28 m long and 1.35 m in average height. The ship has no sheer. On the forward bulkhead of the forecastle, there is a side door located below the freeboard deck, with its lower edge sitting 180 mm above the upper edge of the uppermost load line. The door leads to a cargo hold assumed intact in the damage analysis. The door is secured by hydraulic cleating, and the hydraulic system has no mechanical lock-in-closed provision. Assess whether (a) the freeing port area provided on each side of the well is sufficient if 0.95 m² of freeing ports are fitted per side, (b) the side door arrangement is compliant, and (c) the hydraulic cleating arrangement for the door is acceptable.
required_facts: Required freeing port area per side is approximately 3.19 m² (base 1.96 m² increased for bulwark height above 1.2 m, then multiplied by 1.5 for no-sheer condition)
Provided freeing port area of 0.95 m² per side is insufficient — the arrangement is not compliant
The side door lower edge at 180 mm above the uppermost load line does not meet the minimum 230 mm requirement — the door arrangement is not compliant
Because the sill is below the 230 mm line, special consideration is required, such as fitting a second door of equivalent strength and watertightness
Hydraulic cleating without a mechanical lock-in-closed provision in the event of hydraulic failure is not acceptable — the cleating arrangement is not compliant
Scantlings of securing devices for the door are to be determined in accordance with the requirements for hatch cover securing devices on exposed decks

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Freeing port area calculation starts in Sec10, which requires applying the no-sheer 50% uplift from Sec10 [2.1.2] and the bulwark height correction from Sec10 [2.1.1]. The side door minimum sill height is governed by Sec5 [1.2.3]. The hydraulic cleating mechanical lock requirement is in Sec3 [2.1.4], which cross-references securing device scantlings to Sec2 [1.3].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 (Sec10 [2.1.1]): ℓb = 28 m > 20 m, so base area A = 0.07 × 28 = 1.96 m². Bulwark height 1.35 m > 1.2 m, difference = 0.15 m = 1.5 × 0.1 m increments, increase = 1.5 × 0.004 × 28 = 0.168 m². Adjusted base = 1.96 + 0.168 = 2.128 m². Step 2 (Sec10 [2.1.2]): No sheer → increase by 50%. Required area = 2.128 × 1.5 = 3.192 m² per side. Provided 0.95 m² < 3.192 m² → NOT compliant. Step 3 (Sec5 [1.2.3]): Lower edge of cargo door must not be below a line 230 mm above the upper edge of the uppermost load line. Provided clearance is 180 mm < 230 mm → NOT compliant; special consideration required per Sec5 [1.2.4] (e.g. fitting a second door of equivalent strength and watertightness). Step 4 (Sec3 [2.1.4]): Where hydraulic cleating is applied, the system shall remain mechanically locked in closed position in the event of hydraulic system failure. No such provision is fitted → NOT compliant. Scantlings of securing devices are governed by Sec2 [1.3].

question_text:
A 14,000 TEU container ship (L = 340 m, B = 48.5 m, CB = 0.65, CWL = 0.82, scantling draught T = 14.5 m) is being designed with container stacks both in hold (below deck in cell guides) and on deck secured by lashing rods and turnbuckles. The designer is evaluating the hull support structures beneath the deck-mounted container support fittings at a position x/L = 0.45 (amidships region).

The proposed support structure consists of a transverse web frame with a net thickness of 14 mm and a yield strength of 315 N/mm². The design load combinations being applied consider only the vertical reaction forces from the container stacks (Fv1 and Fv2) and horizontal transverse forces (Fq), but the designer has omitted hull girder loads from the strength evaluation on the grounds that the support fittings are local structures.

Additionally, for the containers stowed in cell guides in the hold, the designer has placed doubler plates only at the inner bottom footprints and has not provided any doubler plates at the stringer levels, arguing that stringers are stiff enough without them.

Finally, the design loads for the hull support structures beneath the lashing eye plates have been set to 80% of the certified safe working load (SWL) of the lashings, rather than the full SWL, to allow a design margin.

(a) Is the omission of hull girder loads from the strength evaluation of the deck-mounted container support fitting structures at x/L = 0.45 acceptable? Justify your answer with reference to the applicable load combination requirements and what additional load components must be included.

(b) Is the arrangement of doubler plates for the cell-guided containers in the hold compliant? If not, what is required?

(c) Is the design load for the lashing eye plate hull support structures set correctly? What value must be used?
required_facts: Omitting hull girder loads at x/L = 0.45 is NOT acceptable; hull girder loads must be included in the strength evaluation of hull support structures subject to such loads
At x/L = 0.45 the distribution factor cM for hogging equals 1.0 (peak region, 0.35 ≤ x/L < 0.55), so the full vertical wave bending moment applies and cannot be neglected
The hull girder load inclusion requirement flows from Sec9 through the hull girder strength section and ultimately to the loads section governing wave bending moments and shear forces
Doubler plates for cell-guided containers in hold are required at footprints on inner bottom OR stringers — omitting stringer-level doubler plates where containers bear on stringers is non-compliant
Design loads for hull support structures of lashing eye plates must be based on the full certified safe working load (SWL) of the lashings; using 80% SWL is not permitted

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec9 hull support structure requirements reference Sec8 for design loads (Sec9→Sec8[6]), and Sec9[3.1.3] requires hull girder loads to be included per [4] which in turn references Sec4 for hull girder strength, and Sec4 references Sec3 for the applicable dynamic and static hull girder loads including wave bending moments at x/L=0.45.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Sec9 [3.1.3]: For hull support structures subject to hull girder loads, such loads SHALL be included in the strength evaluation in accordance with [4] (i.e., Sec9[4]) in addition to the design loads in Sec9[3]. At x/L=0.45 (within 0.35–0.55 range), the structure is in the full-moment region and hull girder loads are clearly applicable. The omission is NOT acceptable.

Step 2 — Sec9[4.1.1] references Sec8[7.2] for acceptance criteria, and Sec9[3.2.1] states loads shall be calculated according to Sec8[6]. Following Sec8[6] for the actual load magnitudes, the designer must combine local container reaction forces with hull girder bending moment and shear force.

Step 3 — Hull girder loads come from Sec4 (hull girder strength chapter), which in turn draws on Sec3 for the wave bending moments. At x/L=0.45, the distribution factor cM for hogging = 1.0 (from Sec3 Table 1, range 0.35≤x/L<0.55), meaning the full wave bending moment applies — this is the peak region and cannot be ignored.

Step 4 — Sec9[2.2.2]: For containers stowed in cell guides in hold, doubler plates shall be arranged for the footprints on INNER BOTTOM OR STRINGERS. The 'or' is inclusive of both locations where containers bear; if containers rest on stringers at intermediate levels, doubler plates are required there too. Omitting stringer-level doublers where containers bear on stringers is non-compliant.

Step 5 — Sec9[3.1.2]: Hull support structures for lashing eye plates SHALL be strengthened with respect to the lashings' CERTIFIED SAFE WORKING LOAD (SWL) — the full SWL, not a reduced fraction. Using 80% SWL is not compliant; the full certified SWL must be used.

question_text: During the detail design review of a 180 m general cargo vessel, a structural engineer is evaluating an integral end bracket connection on a shell longitudinal stiffener in the bow flare region. The stiffener has a flat bar flange with a free outstand of 80 mm and a net flange thickness of 12 mm. The designer proposes to curve the flange transition at the bracket rather than fit a tripping bracket, using a radius of 820 mm. The stiffener is located in a ballast water tank on one side and exposed to a void space on the other side. For the net thickness calculation, the designer has applied a corrosion addition of 1.5 mm to the flange. Is the proposed curved flange radius acceptable, and is the corrosion addition applied to the flange correct? Provide the minimum required radius and the correct total corrosion addition for the flange.
required_facts: r_min = 1.6 × 80² / 12 ≈ 853 mm (rounded to nearest mm)
The proposed radius of 820 mm is less than the minimum required 853 mm and is therefore not acceptable
The definition of free flange outstand b1 must be taken from the structural idealisation section of the same chapter
The stiffener corrosion addition is determined by the location of its connection to the attached plating
When a stiffener is affected by more than one corrosion addition value, the largest shall be applied
Correct total corrosion addition = 1.0 (ballast water tank side) + 0.5 (external/void side) + 0.5 (reserve) = 2.0 mm
The designer's applied corrosion addition of 1.5 mm is insufficient; the correct value is 2.0 mm

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec6 [2.1.2] gives the formula for minimum flange curve radius and references Sec7 [1.3.4] for the definition of free flange outstand b1. The corrosion addition for the flange is governed by Sec3, where the stiffener corrosion addition is determined by the location of its connection to the attached plating (Sec3 [1.2.6]), and when affected by more than one value the largest applies (Sec3 [1.2.7]).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Start at Sec6 [2.1.2]: The formula for minimum curve radius at an integral bracket flange transition is r = 1.6 × b1² / tf. The clause states b1 is the free flange outstand as defined in Sec7 [1.3.4], so the answerer must navigate there. Step 2 — Navigate to Sec7 [1.3.4]: Confirm the definition of b1 as the free flange outstand. With b1 = 80 mm and tf = 12 mm, compute r_min = 1.6 × 80² / 12 = 1.6 × 6400 / 12 = 853.3 mm. The proposed radius of 820 mm is less than 853.3 mm, so it is NOT acceptable. Step 3 — Evaluate corrosion addition via Sec3 [1.2.6]: The stiffener's corrosion addition is determined by the location of its connection to the attached plating. The shell plating is on the boundary between a ballast water tank (tc1 = 1.0 mm per side) and external surface (tc1 = 0.5 mm per side). Per Sec3 [1.2.7], when a stiffener is affected by more than one corrosion addition value, the largest shall be applied. Total tc = tc1 (ballast side) + tc2 (void/external side) + tres = 1.0 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 2.0 mm. The designer's applied value of 1.5 mm is therefore insufficient; the correct total corrosion addition is 2.0 mm.

scenario_parameters.stiffener_location: shell longitudinal in bow flare, integral end bracket

question_text: A 180-metre bulk carrier is being designed to DNV class. During the hull girder buckling assessment, the design team is evaluating a longitudinally stiffened bottom shell plate panel located amidships. The panel is subjected to combined hull girder stresses under a static-plus-dynamic (S+D) load case. The calculated buckling utilization factor for the elementary plate panel is η_Plate = 0.97. The designer argues this is acceptable because the load case is dynamic. Is this arrangement compliant, and what is the correct allowable buckling utilization factor η_all that applies to this plate panel under the S+D acceptance criterion?
required_facts: η_all for plates and stiffened panels under AC-II (S+D) load scenario is 1.00
The applicable acceptance criterion for the S+D load case is AC-II
The plate buckling criterion requires η_Plate ≤ η_all
η_Plate = 0.97 does not exceed η_all = 1.00, so the arrangement is compliant
If the load case were S only (AC-I), η_all would be 0.80, and the panel would NOT be compliant at η_Plate = 0.97

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec3 [3.2] states the plate buckling criterion η_Plate ≤ η_all, where η_all is defined in Sec1 [3.4]. Sec1 [3.4] Table 3 gives η_all = 1.00 for plates under AC-II (S+D), so η_Plate = 0.97 is compliant.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec3 [3.2] gives the plate buckling acceptance criterion: η_Plate ≤ η_all, and states that η_all is 'as defined in Sec.1 [3.4]'. Step 2 — Navigate to Sec1 [3.4] Table 3 'Allowable buckling utilization factor η_all'. Step 3 — Locate the row for 'Plates and stiffeners/stiffened panels' and the column for acceptance criterion AC-II with design load scenario S+D. Table 3 gives η_all = 1.00 for this combination. Step 4 — Compare: η_Plate = 0.97 ≤ η_all = 1.00, so the arrangement IS compliant. The designer's conclusion is correct, though the reasoning should be grounded in the specific table value rather than a general claim about dynamic loads.

scenario_parameters.structural_member: longitudinally stiffened bottom shell plate panel
scenario_parameters.designer_claim: acceptable because load case is dynamic

question_text: A shipowner is commissioning a new 85-metre vessel designed specifically for conducting oceanographic surveys, including deployment of autonomous underwater vehicles and towed sensor arrays. The vessel has no cargo-carrying function and does not fit any of the standard ship type notations used by the classification society. The owner wishes to have the vessel's survey purpose formally recognized in the class certificate. The owner also wants to understand whether any specific technical requirements from the classification rules will be imposed as a condition of this recognition. What notation would be assigned to acknowledge the vessel's survey purpose, how is it visually distinguished in the class certificate, and does the assignment of this notation carry any mandatory class requirements that the vessel must satisfy?
required_facts: The vessel would be assigned a descriptive notation (e.g. [Survey vessel] or [Oceanographic survey vessel]) because its purpose is not covered by existing notations
The descriptive notation is visually distinguished by square brackets in the class certificate
There are NO class requirements associated with a descriptive notation
The descriptive notation is assigned upon request to the Society

Additional class notations (under Sec4) are distinct from descriptive notations and DO carry mandatory technical requirements for certain vessel types or equipment — the descriptive notation carries none

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec7 defines descriptive notations for vessels not covered by existing notations, states there are no class requirements associated with them, and notes they are identified by square brackets. The Changes – Historic table in Sec7 references Sec4 for additional class notations, prompting the answerer to consult Sec4 to understand the contrast: Sec4 additional class notations DO carry mandatory requirements for certain vessel types/features, whereas the descriptive notation in Sec7 explicitly does not.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: The vessel does not fit any existing ship type notation (no cargo function, unique survey mission) → Sec7 [1.1] applies: a descriptive notation may be assigned for vessels with purpose not covered by existing notations. Step 2: Sec7 [1.2] confirms the descriptive notation is assigned upon request to the Society. Step 3: Sec7 [1.4] specifies the notation is identified by square brackets, e.g. [Research vessel] — so the survey vessel would receive something like [Survey vessel] or [Oceanographic survey vessel]. Step 4: Sec7 [1.3] explicitly states there are NO class requirements associated with a descriptive notation. Step 5: Cross-check with Sec4 [1.1.1]–[1.1.2]: additional class notations (which are different from descriptive notations) DO carry requirements from Pt6, and certain ones are mandatory for specific installations/features. This contrast confirms that the descriptive notation stands apart — it is purely recognition-based with zero mandatory technical requirements attached.

scenario_parameters.vessel_type: oceanographic survey vessel with AUV deployment capability
scenario_parameters.owner_request: formal recognition of survey purpose in class certificate
scenario_parameters.owner_query: whether mandatory class requirements attach to the recognition notation

question_text: A bulk carrier has a ship length L = 220 m, breadth B = 32 m, and block coefficient C_B = 0.82. The designer needs to compute the vertical still water bending moment at a transverse bulkhead located 88 m from the aft end of the ship (i.e., x = 88 m). The ship is in a seagoing hogging condition. The designer uses the rule minimum guidance formula for the still water hogging bending moment, which requires the wave coefficient C_w and the distribution factor f_sw. To apply the formula correctly, the designer must also determine the x-coordinate of the calculation point using the reference coordinate system defined in the rules. Describe how the x-coordinate should be interpreted, determine C_w, evaluate f_sw at x = 88 m, and compute the minimum permissible still water hogging bending moment M_sw-h-min at that location (ignoring the wave bending moment correction term, i.e. set M_wv-h-mid = 0 for this preliminary estimate). Is the bulkhead location in the region where f_sw = 1.0 applies?
required_facts: The x-coordinate is measured from the aft perpendicular (AP) forward, as defined by the reference coordinate system in the introduction section of the chapter
C_w ≈ 10.03 (using the formula for 90 ≤ L ≤ 300: C_w = 10.75 − ((300 − L)/100)^1.5 with L = 220 m)
x/L = 88/220 = 0.40, which falls within the range 0.3L ≤ x ≤ 0.7L, so f_sw = 1.0
The bulkhead IS in the region where f_sw = 1.0 applies
M_sw-h-min ≈ 4.04 × 10^6 kNm (preliminary estimate with M_wv-h-mid = 0)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec4 symbols define x as the X-coordinate with respect to the reference coordinate system defined in Sec1 [1.2.1]. Sec1 [1.2.1] defines the coordinate system (origin at aft perpendicular, x measured forward). Sec4 [2.2.1] gives the still water bending moment formula using C_w and f_sw. C_w depends on L (from the piecewise table in Sec4 Symbols). f_sw depends on x/L ratios. The dynamic load cases referenced in Sec4 symbols (BSR, BSP, etc.) are defined in Sec2 [2].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Resolve x-coordinate via Sec1 [1.2.1]: The symbol definition in Sec4 states x is the X-coordinate with respect to the reference coordinate system defined in Sec1 [1.2.1]. Sec1 [1.2.1] defines the coordinate system with origin at the aft perpendicular (AP), x measured positively forward. Therefore x = 88 m means 88 m forward of the AP. Step 2 — Compute C_w: L = 220 m, which falls in the range 90 ≤ L ≤ 300, so C_w = 10.75 − ((300 − 220)/100)^1.5 = 10.75 − (0.8)^1.5 = 10.75 − 0.7155 ≈ 10.034. Step 3 — Evaluate f_sw at x = 88 m: x/L = 88/220 = 0.40. Since 0.3L ≤ x ≤ 0.7L (i.e., 66 m ≤ 88 m ≤ 154 m), f_sw = 1.0. Step 4 — Compute M_sw-h-min: M_sw-h-min = f_sw × (171 × C_w × L² × B × (C_B + 0.7) × 10^-3 − M_wv-h-mid). With M_wv-h-mid = 0: M_sw-h-min = 1.0 × 171 × 10.034 × 220² × 32 × (0.82 + 0.7) × 10^-3 = 171 × 10.034 × 48400 × 32 × 1.52 × 10^-3. Intermediate: 171 × 10.034 = 1715.8; 1715.8 × 48400 = 83,044,720; 83,044,720 × 32 = 2,657,431,040; 2,657,431,040 × 1.52 = 4,039,295,181; × 10^-3 ≈ 4,039,295 kNm ≈ 4.04 × 10^6 kNm. Step 5 — Confirm f_sw = 1.0 applies: Yes, x = 88 m = 0.4L falls within the 0.3L–0.7L band.

question_text: A structural engineer is calculating internal liquid pressures for a ballast tank on a 180 m bulk carrier. The tank has its highest point (excluding small hatchways) at z_top = 14.2 m above the keel, and the load point under assessment is located at z = 1.8 m above the keel, y = 9.5 m to starboard, and x = 72 m from the aft end. The tank is fitted with a pressure relief valve set at 35 kN/m². The liquid density for strength assessment is 1.025 t/m³. For the static plus dynamic load scenario, the engineer needs to apply the correct dynamic load combination factors for a BSR-1P load case at a draught ratio f_T = 0.85. What is the static liquid pressure at the load point for normal operations at sea, and which load combination factor applies to the vertical wave bending moment for the BSR-1P load case under strength assessment?
required_facts: Static pressure formula for a tank with pressure relief valve is P_ℓs-1 = f_cd × ρ_L × g × (z_top − z) + P_PV
f_cd = 1.0 for ballast tanks (not oil/oil product cargo with ρ_L ≤ 1.025)
Static pressure at the load point ≈ 159.7 kN/m² (accepting range 158–161 kN/m²)
The coordinate system for z, y, x of the load point is the reference coordinate system defined in the Introduction section of the same chapter
For strength assessment S+D scenarios, dynamic load combination factors are taken from the dynamic load cases section of the same chapter
The load combination factor C_WV for BSR-1P under strength assessment is given by 0.1 − 0.2f_T
With f_T = 0.85, C_WV for BSR-1P = −0.07

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec6 defines static liquid pressure and references Sec1 [1.2.1] for the coordinate system used to define z, y, x of the load point; Sec1 [1.1.5] then directs the reader to Sec2 [2] for the EDW dynamic load combination factors for strength assessment.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Start in Sec6 [1.2.1]: The static pressure for a tank with a pressure relief valve is P_ℓs-1 = f_cd × ρ_L × g × (z_top − z) + P_PV. The coordinates z_top and z are defined with respect to the reference coordinate system defined in Sec1 [1.2.1]. Step 2 — Follow reference to Sec1 [1.2.1]: Confirm the coordinate system origin and that z is measured from the keel upward, validating z_top = 14.2 m and z = 1.8 m. Step 3 — Compute static pressure: For a ballast tank under strength assessment, f_cd = 1.0 (not oil/oil product cargo). P_ℓs-1 = 1.0 × 1.025 × 9.81 × (14.2 − 1.8) + 35 = 1.025 × 9.81 × 12.4 + 35 = 124.65 + 35 ≈ 159.7 kN/m². Step 4 — Follow Sec1 [1.1.5] to Sec2 [2]: For the S+D scenario strength assessment, the EDWs and dynamic load combination factors are listed in Sec2 [2]. Step 5 — In Sec2 [2], locate the BSR-1P load case strength assessment table: C_WV for BSR-1P = 0.4f_T − 0.7. With f_T = 0.85: C_WV = 0.4 × 0.85 − 0.7 = 0.34 − 0.7 = −0.36.

question_text: A 180 m general cargo vessel is being designed with a midship cross-section that includes a longitudinal trunk running continuously for 32 m (approximately 0.18L) along the centreline, supported by two longitudinal bulkheads spaced 3.2 m apart. The trunk deck plating is 14 mm thick and sits 2.1 m above the strength deck. The designer proposes to include this trunk in the hull girder section modulus calculation. Additionally, the same cross-section has a vertically corrugated longitudinal bulkhead with corrugation geometry: sc = 600 mm, a = 350 mm, c = 250 mm. The designer intends to include the full gross thickness of this corrugated bulkhead (t = 16 mm) when computing the total vertical hull girder shear capacity at this section. Is the proposed treatment of both the trunk and the corrugated bulkhead acceptable for the hull girder strength calculation? For the corrugated bulkhead, what effective thickness should be used when calculating the unit shear flow qvi-gr, and what thickness applies when computing the total vertical hull girder shear capacity?
required_facts: The trunk may be included in the hull girder transverse section because it extends more than 0.15L and is effectively supported by longitudinal bulkheads
The vertical corrugations of the longitudinal bulkhead must be excluded from the hull girder transverse section used for bending (section modulus and moment of inertia)
The effective thickness for computing unit shear flow qvi-gr must be obtained by applying Cshr = sc/(a+c) = 600/(350+250) = 1.0, giving an effective thickness of 16 mm

For the total vertical hull girder shear capacity (as defined in the shear strength section), the thickness reduction factor Cshr is NOT applicable and the full gross thickness ti-gr = 16 mm is used directly
The designer's use of full gross thickness for shear capacity is correct, but the corrugated bulkhead cannot contribute to the hull girder bending section modulus

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec1 [2.3] governs whether the trunk may be included (requires effective support by longitudinal bulkheads or PSMs). Sec1 [2.4] allows stiffeners/girders above the strength deck to be included. Sec1 [2.5.1] excludes vertical corrugations from the hull girder transverse section for bending. Sec1 [2.5.2] introduces the Cshr reduction factor for computing qvi-gr (unit shear flow), but explicitly states this reduction is NOT applicable for the hull girder shear capacity ti-gr as defined in Sec2 [2.1].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Trunk inclusion: Sec1 [2.3] states continuous trunks may be included provided they are effectively supported by longitudinal bulkheads or primary supporting members. The trunk here runs 0.18L > 0.15L threshold (Sec1 [2.2] excludes trunks < 0.15L), and it is supported by two longitudinal bulkheads, so inclusion is acceptable. Sec1 [2.4] further confirms that longitudinal stiffeners/girders welded above the strength deck, including the deck of a qualifying trunk, shall be included. Step 2 — Corrugated bulkhead in bending: Sec1 [2.5.1] states vertical corrugations shall NOT be included in the hull girder transverse section for bending purposes. Step 3 — Corrugated bulkhead in shear (unit shear flow): Sec1 [2.5.2] requires applying the reduction factor Cshr = sc/(a+c) = 600/(350+250) = 600/600 = 1.0 to obtain the effective thickness for qvi-gr. In this specific geometry Cshr = 1.0, so effective thickness = 1.0 × 16 = 16 mm (no reduction in this case, but the formula must still be applied). Step 4 — Corrugated bulkhead in shear capacity: Sec1 [2.5.2] explicitly states that for the hull girder shear capacity as given in Sec2 [2.1] (ti-gr), the thickness reduction is NOT applicable, so the full gross thickness of 16 mm is correctly used. Therefore the designer's proposal to use full gross thickness for shear capacity is acceptable, but the vertical corrugations must be excluded from the bending section modulus calculation.

question_text: A 180-metre bulk carrier is being designed for unrestricted worldwide service with a 25-year design life. The fatigue assessment for a critical welded connection at the lower part of a cargo hold uses prescriptive wave-induced loads. The designer proposes to apply an environmental factor of 0.8 and an operational factor of 0.76 in the fatigue damage calculation. The structural detail is located in the lower part of a cargo hold that carries dry bulk cargo, and the detail is assessed using the hot spot stress approach with S-N curve D (FAT 90). During the design review, the Society raises a concern: the ship will spend its entire operational life trading exclusively on North Atlantic routes rather than worldwide routes. Does the proposed environmental factor of 0.8 remain valid for this vessel, and what value should be used instead? Additionally, what is the time in corrosive environment that must be assumed for this structural detail when calculating fatigue damage, and how does the corrosive environment affect the damage calculation?
required_facts: The environmental factor fe = 0.8 is not valid for a vessel trading exclusively on North Atlantic routes
fe = 1.0 must be used for North Atlantic wave environment
The operational factor fR = 0.76 is correct for prescriptive loads
The time in corrosive environment TC,25 for the lower part of a dry bulk cargo hold is 5 years over a 25-year design life
The fatigue damage estimate for the period spent in corrosive environment must be multiplied by two

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec.5 special consideration notes that the Society may require directly calculated loads or modified approaches for specific designs; the scenario triggers review of the environmental factor defined in Sec.4 [4.2], which distinguishes worldwide vs North Atlantic wave environment, and Sec.4 [4.4] which defines the time in corrosive environment for the lower part of a cargo hold for dry bulk cargo.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 – The designer has used fe = 0.8, which per Sec.4 [4.2] is the value for worldwide wave environment. Step 2 – Because the vessel trades exclusively on North Atlantic routes, Sec.4 [4.2] requires fe = 1.0 for North Atlantic wave environment. The proposed value of 0.8 is therefore not valid; fe = 1.0 must be used. Step 3 – The operational factor fR = 0.76 is correct per Sec.4 [4.3] for prescriptive loads. Step 4 – Per Sec.4 [4.4] Table 1, the time in corrosive environment TC,25 for the lower part of a cargo hold for dry bulk cargo is 5 years (same category as water ballast tank and oil cargo tank). Step 5 – The damage estimate for the time in corrosive environment (5 years out of 25) must be multiplied by two, per Sec.4 [4.4].

scenario_parameters.structural_detail_location: lower part of dry bulk cargo hold

question_text: A 175-metre offshore supply vessel with no service area notation is being designed for unrestricted ocean service. The designer has specified a design fatigue life of 25 years. During the structural review, the following two details within the midship region are flagged for fatigue consideration: (1) longitudinal stiffener end connections at transverse frames located 40 metres forward of the aft quarter length, and (2) a large moonpool opening whose coaming ends are situated 20 metres aft of the forward quarter length. The vessel has no special ship-type fatigue notation assigned.
