Which of these structural details must undergo fatigue assessment, what type of assessment applies to each, and is the 25-year design fatigue life sufficient to satisfy the acceptance criterion?
required_facts: The vessel (L = 175 m, no service area notation, no ship-type fatigue notation) falls under the fatigue chapter requirements
Longitudinal stiffener end connections within 0.5L amidships SHALL be assessed using prescriptive fatigue assessment (mandatory)

The moonpool coaming ends within 0.5L amidships are an example of a detail with high longitudinal stresses due to structural discontinuity and MAY require fatigue assessment on a case-by-case basis (not automatically mandatory)
The scope and extent of main class fatigue assessment is determined by referencing the requirements for other details in the same chapter
The 25-year design fatigue life meets the minimum requirement (T_DF must not be less than 25 years), and the acceptance criterion is T_F ≥ T_DF with cumulative damage D ≤ 1.0

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec.1 [1.2] establishes that for vessels L ≥ 150 m with no service area notation and no ship-type fatigue notation, this chapter applies. Sec.1 [1.3] directs the reader to Sec.2 [2] for the scope and extent of main class fatigue assessment. Sec.2 [1] mandates prescriptive fatigue assessment for longitudinal stiffener end connections within 0.5L amidships; Sec.2 [2] states that other details with high longitudinal stresses (including moonpool/large openings) within 0.5L amidships may be required on a case-by-case basis.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec.1 [1.2]: The vessel is 175 m (≥ 150 m) with no service area notation and no ship-type fatigue notation, so the chapter applies in full. Step 2 — Sec.1 [1.3]: The scope and extent of fatigue assessment for main class is defined in Sec.2 [2]. Step 3 — Sec.2 [1]: Longitudinal stiffener end connections at frames within 0.5L amidships SHALL be assessed by prescriptive fatigue assessment. Both details are stated to lie within the 0.5L amidships band, so the stiffener end connections are mandatory. Step 4 — Sec.2 [2]: The moonpool coaming ends are explicitly listed as an example of a detail with high longitudinal stresses due to structural discontinuity; fatigue assessment MAY be required on a case-by-case basis. Step 5 — Sec.1 [1.4]: The acceptance criterion is T_F ≥ T_DF; with T_DF = 25 years (the minimum), the 25-year design fatigue life is sufficient provided T_F ≥ 25 years (D ≤ 1.0).

scenario_parameters.detail_1: longitudinal stiffener end connections at transverse frames, 40 m forward of aft quarter length (within 0.5L amidships)
scenario_parameters.detail_2: moonpool coaming ends, 20 m aft of forward quarter length (within 0.5L amidships)

question_text: A designer is performing a buckling assessment for a stiffened panel forming part of the inner hull of a 180 m bulk carrier. The panel is a longitudinal structure connected to the hopper tank side. During direct strength analysis using finite element methods, the panel is modelled with shell elements and subjected to combined compressive and shear stresses under a static + dynamic load combination. The designer proposes to use boundary condition A for the panel assessment and obtains a buckling utilization factor of 0.97 for the AC-II acceptance criterion. The panel consists of T-bar stiffeners with a web depth of 300 mm and a web net thickness of 9 mm. The yield stress of the stiffener material is 355 N/mm². Is the proposed design acceptable, and what is the minimum required web net thickness for the T-bar stiffeners to satisfy the slenderness requirement?
required_facts: Boundary condition A (BC-A) is correct for inner hull panels connected to the hopper tank side in direct strength analysis
The allowable buckling utilization factor η_all = 1.00 for plates and stiffened panels under AC-II (S+D) load combination
η_act = 0.97 ≤ η_all = 1.00, so the buckling utilization check is satisfied
The minimum required T-bar web net thickness is approximately 4.92 mm, calculated as (300/75) × √(355/235)
The proposed web net thickness of 9 mm exceeds the minimum slenderness requirement of ~4.92 mm
The overall design is acceptable for both the buckling utilization and the stiffener slenderness requirement

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec.1 [2.1.1] directs buckling checks for direct analysis to Sec.4; Sec.4 [2] specifies boundary conditions referencing Sec.1 [3.1] and Table 1 (confirming BC-A for inner hull connected to hopper tank side); Sec.4 also references Sec.3 [3.2.1] for the utilization factor definition; Sec.3 [3.2.1] defines the utilization factor and references the allowable value from Sec.1 [3.4] Table 3 (η_all = 1.00 for AC-II plates/stiffened panels); then Sec.2 [2] is invoked for slenderness requirements of the stiffeners, specifically [3.1.1] for T-bar web thickness.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec.1 [2.1.1]: For direct strength analysis, buckling checks of stiffened panels shall be performed according to Sec.4. Step 2 — Sec.4 [2.1.1]: Boundary condition A (BC-A) applies to longitudinal structures including inner hull connected to hopper tank side, per Table 1. The designer's choice of BC-A is confirmed correct. Step 3 — Sec.4 references Sec.3 [3.2.1] for the utilization factor definition: η_act = W_act / W_u. Step 4 — Sec.3 [3.2.1] defines η and directs to Sec.1 [3.4] Table 3 for the allowable value. For plates and stiffened panels under AC-II (S+D), η_all = 1.00. The computed η_act = 0.97 ≤ 1.00, so the buckling utilization is acceptable. Step 5 — Sec.1 [2.1.1] also directs slenderness requirements to Sec.2. Sec.2 [3.1.1](a) for T-bar web: t_w ≥ (h_w / C_w) × √(R_eH / 235). From Table 2, C_w = 75 for T-bars. t_w_min = (300 / 75) × √(355 / 235) = 4.0 × √1.5106 = 4.0 × 1.2291 = 4.92 mm. The proposed t_w = 9 mm ≥ 4.92 mm, so the slenderness requirement is satisfied.

scenario_parameters.structural_element: inner hull stiffened panel connected to hopper tank side

question_text:
A 175 m bulk carrier with unrestricted service notation is being assessed for hull girder ultimate strength at the transverse section located at the forward end of the engine room. The ship has a double bottom and carries homogeneous cargo in all holds; no alternate loading conditions are specified in the loading manual, and the class notation does not include HC(A), HC(B*), or HC(M). At the section under consideration, the permissible still water bending moment is 4 800 000 kNm in hogging and 3 200 000 kNm in sagging. The vertical wave bending moment is 2 100 000 kNm in hogging and 1 750 000 kNm in sagging. The hull transverse section includes a longitudinal bulkhead with vertical corrugations running the full length of the cargo hold region. The designer proposes to include the full gross sectional area of the vertical corrugations when computing the hull girder section modulus and moment of inertia for the ultimate bending capacity calculation. The computed vertical hull girder ultimate bending capacity is MU = 14 500 000 kNm in hogging and 12 800 000 kNm in sagging.

(a) Is the ship subject to the hull girder ultimate strength check, and at which locations must it be applied?
(b) Determine the total design vertical bending moment M (in kNm) for both hogging and sagging conditions.
(c) Identify the correct partial safety factor γR for both conditions and verify whether the ultimate bending capacity criterion is satisfied.
(d) Is the designer's proposal to include the full corrugated bulkhead area in the section modulus calculation correct? Explain what adjustment, if any, must be made and how it affects the shear capacity assessment.
required_facts: The ship meets all three applicability criteria (unrestricted service, L > 150 m, bulk carrier/single deck) and the ultimate strength check is required at the forward end of the engine room and other specified locations
Design hogging bending moment M = 7 320 000 kNm (= 1.0 × 4 800 000 + 1.2 × 2 100 000)
Design sagging bending moment M = 5 300 000 kNm (= 1.0 × 3 200 000 + 1.2 × 1 750 000)
Hogging γR = 1.21 (γM = 1.1, γDB = 1.1 because no HC(A)/HC(B*)/HC(M) alternate loading applies); sagging γR = 1.10 (γDB = 1.0)
Both hogging and sagging ultimate strength criteria are satisfied (7 320 000 ≤ 11 983 471 kNm and 5 300 000 ≤ 11 636 364 kNm)
The designer's proposal is incorrect: vertical corrugations in longitudinal bulkheads must NOT be included in the hull girder section modulus or moment of inertia used for bending capacity

Vertical corrugations are effective for hull girder shear force, but a thickness reduction factor Cshr = sc/(a+c) must be applied when computing unit shear flow; this reduction does not apply to the shear capacity thickness

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Sec4 ultimate strength check criteria, which requires the hull girder ultimate bending capacity MU computed from the hull transverse section properties. This forces a look-up of Sec1 (strength characteristics of hull girder transverse sections) to determine which members contribute — specifically Sec1 [2.5] on vertical corrugations, which states they must NOT be included in the section modulus/moment of inertia but ARE effective for shear, with a thickness reduction factor Cshr applied. Sec1 [2.5.2] then cross-references Sec3 [4.2] for the shear stress calculation where the reduced thickness applies.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Applicability (Sec4 [1.1.1]): Ship has unrestricted service, L = 175 m > 150 m, and is a bulk carrier (single deck type). All three conditions are met, so the ultimate strength check applies. Required locations include the forward end of the engine room (explicitly listed), forward end of foremost cargo hold, and any locations with significant cross-section changes.

Step 2 — Design bending moment (Sec4 [2.2.1]): M = γS·Msw-U + γW·Mwv, with γS = 1.0 and γW = 1.2.
  Hogging: M = 1.0 × 4 800 000 + 1.2 × 2 100 000 = 4 800 000 + 2 520 000 = 7 320 000 kNm
  Sagging: M = 1.0 × 3 200 000 + 1.2 × 1 750 000 = 3 200 000 + 2 100 000 = 5 300 000 kNm

Step 3 — Partial safety factors (Sec4 [2.1.2]): γR = γM × γDB, with γM = 1.1.
  Hogging: ship does NOT have HC(A), HC(B*), or HC(M) with alternate loading, so γDB = 1.1 (the 'all other cases' branch). γR = 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.21.
  Sagging: γDB = 1.0. γR = 1.1 × 1.0 = 1.10.

Step 4 — Criterion check (Sec4 [2.1.2]): M ≤ MU / γR.
  Hogging: MU/γR = 14 500 000 / 1.21 = 11 983 471 kNm. M = 7 320 000 kNm ≤ 11 983 471 kNm → SATISFIED.
  Sagging: MU/γR = 12 800 000 / 1.10 = 11 636 364 kNm. M = 5 300 000 kNm ≤ 11 636 364 kNm → SATISFIED.

Step 5 — Corrugated bulkhead treatment (Sec1 [2.5.1]): Vertical corrugations in longitudinal bulkheads shall NOT be included in the hull girder transverse section for bending (section modulus and moment of inertia). The designer's proposal is therefore incorrect; the corrugated area must be excluded from the MU calculation.

Step 6 — Shear capacity exception (Sec1 [2.5.2]): Although excluded from bending, vertical corrugations ARE effective for hull girder shear force. However, a thickness reduction factor Cshr = sc/(a+c) must be applied to obtain the effective thickness for shear flow calculations. This reduced thickness is used in the unit shear flow qvi-n50 as referenced in Sec3 [4.2] for shear stress calculations, but the reduction does NOT apply to the shear capacity thickness tI-n50 used in the shear capacity formula in Sec2 [2.1].

question_text: During the structural detail design review of a 180 m general cargo vessel, a shell stiffener in the bow flare region terminates at an integral end bracket. The flange transition between the stiffener and the bracket is knuckled rather than curved. The stiffener has a free flange outstand of 80 mm and a net flange thickness of 12 mm. The designer proposes to avoid fitting tripping support at the knuckle by instead curving the flange with a radius of 800 mm. Is this arrangement acceptable, and if not, what is the minimum radius required for the curved flange transition to be considered compliant?
required_facts: The applicable formula for minimum curve radius is r = 1.6 × (b1² / tf)
b1 = 80 mm (free flange outstand) and tf = 12 mm (net flange thickness)
Minimum required radius r = 1.6 × (80² / 12) ≈ 853 mm
The proposed radius of 800 mm is less than the required minimum of approximately 853 mm
The arrangement as proposed is NOT compliant
To be compliant without tripping support, the curve radius must be at least approximately 854 mm

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec6 [2.1.2] gives the formula for minimum flange curve radius at a knuckled integral bracket, and defines b1 as the free flange outstand 'as defined in Sec.7 [1.3.4]'. The answerer must navigate to Sec7 [1.3.4] to confirm the correct interpretation of b1, then return to apply the formula in Sec6 [2.1.2].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec6 [2.1.2] states that if the flange transition between a stiffener and an integral bracket is knuckled, the flange may alternatively be curved with radius r = 1.6 × (b1² / tf), where b1 is the free flange outstand as defined in Sec.7 [1.3.4] and tf is the net flange thickness. Step 2 — Navigate to Sec7 [1.3.4] to confirm the definition of b1 (free flange outstand). Step 3 — Apply the formula: r = 1.6 × (80² / 12) = 1.6 × (6400 / 12) = 1.6 × 533.33 = 853.3 mm. Step 4 — The proposed radius of 800 mm is less than the required 853.3 mm, so the arrangement is NOT compliant. The minimum required radius is approximately 854 mm (rounding up).

scenario_parameters.location: bow flare region, shell stiffener integral end bracket

question_text: A 185-metre bulk carrier with unrestricted service notation is being assessed for hull girder ultimate strength at the transverse section located at the forward end of the engine room. The ship has a class notation HC(B*) and the loading manual includes alternate loading conditions with empty cargo holds. The permissible vertical still water bending moment in the hogging seagoing condition at this section is 4 200 000 kNm, and the vertical wave bending moment in hogging is 2 800 000 kNm. The calculated vertical hull girder ultimate bending capacity M_U at this section is 14 500 000 kNm. The gross section modulus at the bottom Z_B-gr is 28.5 m³ and the gross section modulus at deck Z_D-gr is 24.8 m³. The permissible hull girder bending stress for the mild steel used throughout the cross-section is 175 N/mm². Does the hull girder ultimate bending capacity satisfy the applicable checking criterion for the hogging condition, and what is the minimum gross section modulus at deck that must be maintained within the 0.4L amidships region to comply with the vertical bending strength requirements?
required_facts: γ_DB = 1.25 applies in hogging because the vessel has HC(B*) notation with empty cargo hold alternate loading conditions in the loading manual
Design bending moment M = 1.0 × 4 200 000 + 1.2 × 2 800 000 = 7 560 000 kNm
Allowable capacity M_U / γ_R = 14 500 000 / 1.375 ≈ 10 545 000 kNm
The hogging ultimate strength criterion is satisfied because 7 560 000 kNm ≤ 10 545 000 kNm

The minimum required gross section modulus at deck from the vertical bending strength check is Z_D-gr,min = |M_sw + M_wv| / σ_perm × 10^-3 = (4,200,000 + 2,800,000) / 175 × 10^-3 = 40.0 m³ (Pt3.Ch5.Sec2 [1.4.1])
The provided Z_D-gr = 24.8 m³ is below the minimum of 40.0 m³ and therefore does not satisfy the vertical bending strength section-modulus requirement

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Sec4 ultimate strength check criteria, which requires computing the partial safety factor γ_R = γ_M × γ_DB; the γ_DB value for hogging depends on vessel type and loading conditions. Then the minimum section modulus requirement is found in Sec2 [1.3], which the answerer must navigate to from the cross-section reasoning context established in Sec4.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify applicability: ship is 185 m > 150 m, unrestricted service, bulk carrier (single deck type) → ultimate strength check applies per Sec4 [1.1.1]. The forward end of the engine room is an explicitly listed check location per Sec4 [1.1.2]. Step 2 — Determine γ_DB for hogging: the vessel has class notation HC(B*) and alternate loading conditions with empty cargo holds are included in the loading manual → γ_DB = 1.25 (the higher value applies). Step 3 — Compute γ_R: γ_R = γ_M × γ_DB = 1.1 × 1.25 = 1.375. Step 4 — Compute design bending moment M: M = γ_S × M_sw-U + γ_W × M_wv = 1.0 × 4 200 000 + 1.2 × 2 800 000 = 4 200 000 + 3 360 000 = 7 560 000 kNm. Step 5 — Check criterion M ≤ M_U / γ_R: M_U / γ_R = 14 500 000 / 1.375 = 10 545 455 kNm. Since 7 560 000 ≤ 10 545 455, the criterion is satisfied. Step 6 — Navigate to Sec2 [1.3] for minimum section modulus at deck: the required gross section modulus at deck must satisfy Z_D-gr ≥ M_sw / (k × σ_perm) where σ_perm = 175 N/mm² for mild steel. Using M_sw = 4 200 000 kNm = 4.2 × 10⁹ Nmm and σ_perm = 175 N/mm²: Z_D-gr-min = 4.2 × 10⁹ / 175 = 24 000 000 cm³ ... applying the formula from Sec2 [1.3] with k=1 for mild steel: Z_D-gr-min = M_sw / (k × σ_perm) = 4 200 000 × 10³ / (1.0 × 175) = 24 000 000 cm³ = 24.0 m³. The provided Z_D-gr = 24.8 m³ > 24.0 m³, so the section modulus at deck is also compliant.

question_text: A general cargo vessel has a freeboard deck with bulwarks forming a well on the weather deck. The bulwark length for the well is 24 m, and the bulwark average height is 1.0 m. The ship has standard sheer in way of the well. The designer proposes to install four freeing port openings on each side of the ship, each measuring 0.35 m wide by 0.40 m tall (total area per side = 0.56 m²). Additionally, the vessel is fitted with internal watertight hatches providing access to spaces below the freeboard deck. The surveyor requires that all weathertight and watertight doors and hatch covers aboard the vessel undergo a specific type of testing before the vessel enters service. What is the minimum required freeing port area per side for the well on the freeboard deck, is the proposed arrangement compliant, and what testing obligation applies to the internal watertight hatches — including any additional test requirement specific to internal watertight hatches beyond the standard function test?
required_facts: Minimum required freeing port area per side = 1.68 m² (using A = 0.07 × 24 m)
No height adjustment applies because bulwark average height of 1.0 m is between 0.9 m and 1.2 m
Proposed freeing port area of 0.56 m² per side is less than the required 1.68 m², so the arrangement is not compliant
All weathertight and watertight doors and hatch covers must be function tested
Internal watertight hatches are subject to an additional function test requirement beyond the standard function test, as referenced in the internal doors and hatches section

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Sec10 freeing port area formula to compute minimum area; then Sec1 [3.3.1] mandates function testing for all weathertight/watertight doors and hatch covers, and further directs that internal watertight doors/hatches must additionally be function tested in accordance with Sec3 [4.1.2].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Compute minimum freeing port area using Sec10 [2.1.1]: since ℓb = 24 m > 20 m, use A = 0.07 × ℓb = 0.07 × 24 = 1.68 m². Bulwark height is 1.0 m, which is between 0.9 m and 1.2 m, so no adjustment applies. Sheer is standard, so no increase per [2.1.2]. Required area per side = 1.68 m². Step 2 — Check proposed area: 4 × (0.35 × 0.40) = 4 × 0.14 = 0.56 m² per side. 0.56 m² < 1.68 m², so the arrangement is NOT compliant. Step 3 — Testing obligation: Sec1 [3.3.1] states all weathertight/watertight doors and hatch covers shall be function tested. For each internal watertight door/hatch, a function test shall additionally be carried out in accordance with Sec3 [4.1.2], which specifies the additional function test requirements for internal watertight hatches.

question_text: A 145 m general cargo vessel has a zero-sheer freeboard deck with bulwarks forming a forward well. The bulwark in way of the well is 25 m long and has an average height of 1.5 m. The designer proposes four freeing port openings on each side of the ship, each 0.45 m wide by 0.30 m high, giving a total freeing port area of 0.54 m² per side. The ship has a stern door located below the freeboard deck that leads to a cargo hold. This stern door, when the vessel is assessed in a damaged stability condition, becomes submerged by an intermediate damage waterplane. The lower edge of the stern door opening is 0.8 m below the damage waterplane at that location. The designer intends to verify the stern door by hose testing only, without any hydrostatic pressure test. Is the proposed freeing port arrangement on the forward well compliant, and is the hose-test-only approach for the stern door acceptable? Provide the minimum required freeing port area per side and state what testing is required for the stern door.
required_facts: Base freeing port area for ℓ_b = 25 m is A = 0.07 × 25 = 1.75 m² per side
Bulwark height of 1.5 m exceeds 1.2 m threshold, requiring an increase of 0.004 × 25 × 3 = 0.30 m², giving an adjusted base of 2.05 m² per side
Zero-sheer condition requires a 50% increase, giving a minimum required freeing port area of 3.075 m² per side
The proposed freeing port area of 0.54 m² per side is non-compliant (less than 3.075 m²)
A stern door submerged by a damage waterplane must be subjected to a hydrostatic pressure test, not hose testing alone
The hydrostatic pressure test head must correspond at least to the head from the lower edge of the door opening to the most unfavourable damage waterplane (minimum 0.8 m in this case)
The acceptance criterion for the hydrostatic pressure test is no leakage

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Freeing port area calculation starts in Sec10 [2.1.1]/[2.1.2] (zero-sheer 50% increase), which leads to Sec5 [1.6.1] for stern door general requirements, which references Sec1 [3.3.3] for damage condition testing obligations, which in turn points to Sec3 [4.1.2] for the hydrostatic pressure test requirement on doors submerged in a damage waterplane.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Freeing port area (Sec10 [2.1.1]): bulwark length ℓ_b = 25 m > 20 m, so base formula A = 0.07 × 25 = 1.75 m². Bulwark height is 1.5 m, which exceeds 1.2 m by 0.3 m (3 increments of 0.1 m), so increase = 3 × 0.004 × 25 = 0.30 m². Adjusted base area = 1.75 + 0.30 = 2.05 m² per side. Step 2 — Zero-sheer correction (Sec10 [2.1.2]): ship has no sheer, so area must be increased by 50%: required area = 2.05 × 1.50 = 3.075 m² per side. Proposed area = 0.54 m² per side — grossly non-compliant. Step 3 — Stern door testing: the stern door is a side/stern door below the freeboard deck, so Sec5 [1.6.1] applies for general closing appliance requirements and refers back to Sec1 for documentation and testing. Sec1 [3.3.3] states that doors and hatch covers which become immersed by an equilibrium or intermediate damage waterplane shall be subjected to a hydrostatic pressure test with head of water corresponding at least to the head from the lower edge of the door opening to the most unfavourable damage waterplane (here 0.8 m). Hose testing alone is not sufficient; a hydrostatic pressure test with at least 0.8 m head is mandatory, with acceptance criterion of no leakage.

question_text: A 180 m bulk carrier is being designed with a longitudinally stiffened upper deck. The deck plating in the midship region consists of two strakes joined by a transverse butt weld: the inboard strake has a net thickness of 14 mm over a width of 320 mm, and the outboard strake has a net thickness of 18 mm over a width of 280 mm. Both strakes are made of the same steel grade with a specified minimum yield stress of 315 N/mm². The deck is subject to hull girder compressive and shear stresses. A designer proposes to check the buckling of this panel using only the thicker strake properties, arguing that the thicker plate governs. Is this approach acceptable? If not, describe the correct procedure for establishing the panel geometry to be used in the buckling check, and determine the equivalent plate panel width (in mm) that must be used in the assessment. Additionally, the designer needs to confirm the allowable buckling utilization factor to apply when checking this panel under the combined still-water and dynamic (S+D) load condition using acceptance criterion AC-II. State the numerical value of this factor.
required_facts: Using only the thicker strake for the buckling check is NOT acceptable; each thickness must be checked separately as a constant-thickness EPP
The equivalent plate panel width is calculated as b_eq = ℓ1 + ℓ2 × (t1/t2)^1.5, combining the smaller thickness t1 = 14 mm with ℓ1 = 320 mm and t2 = 18 mm with ℓ2 = 280 mm
b_eq ≈ 512 mm (accepting answers in the range 511–513 mm)
The equivalent panel width b_eq is used together with the smaller plate thickness t1 = 14 mm for the buckling assessment
The allowable buckling utilization factor η_all for AC-II under S+D load condition is 0.90

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec3 defines the equivalent plate panel concept and references Sec1 [3.4] for the allowable buckling utilization factor. Sec1 [3.4] Table 3 gives the numerical value. Sec3 also references Sec2 implicitly via the slenderness check that must be satisfied before the buckling check is meaningful, and Sec1 [2.1] scopes which sections apply.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec3 [1.2.2]: When an EPP is formed by a transverse butt weld joining plates of different thicknesses, the buckling check must be performed for each thickness treated as constant over the EPP, with stresses estimated at the LCP. The designer's proposal to use only the thicker strake is therefore NOT acceptable; both strakes must be checked. Step 2 — Sec3 [1.2.1]: For the strake with the smaller thickness (t1 = 14 mm, ℓ1 = 320 mm) combined with the larger thickness strake (t2 = 18 mm, ℓ2 = 280 mm), the equivalent panel width is: b_eq = ℓ1 + ℓ2 × (t1/t2)^1.5 = 320 + 280 × (14/18)^1.5. Compute (14/18) = 0.7778; (0.7778)^1.5 = 0.7778 × sqrt(0.7778) = 0.7778 × 0.8819 = 0.6860. So b_eq = 320 + 280 × 0.6860 = 320 + 192.1 = 512.1 mm ≈ 512 mm. This equivalent width is used together with t1 = 14 mm for the buckling check of the thinner-plate EPP. Step 3 — Sec3 symbols / [3.1], [3.2]: The buckling criteria reference η_all, defined in Sec1 [3.4]. Step 4 — Sec1 [3.4] Table 3: For acceptance criterion AC-II under S+D load condition, η_all = 0.90.

question_text: A bulk carrier with scantling length L = 220 m, block coefficient CB = 0.82, and scantling draught TLC = 14.5 m is being assessed for external sea pressures under the HSM-1 dynamic load case. The load point of interest is located on the ship's side shell at x = 110 m from the aft end, y = 0 m (centreline), and z = 8.0 m (below the waterline). The loading condition being assessed has a draught of 12.0 m. The non-linear coefficient fnℓ is required for the HSM pressure formula. At the longitudinal position of the load point, what is the value of fxL, and what is the corresponding fnℓ for the extreme sea loads design load scenario? Show your derivation.
required_facts: fxL is defined in Sec2 (the dynamic load cases section) as fxL = x/L, not to be taken less than 0.0 or greater than 1.0
For the extreme sea loads design load scenario, fnℓ = 0.9 at fxL = 0.3 and fnℓ = 0.9 at fxL = 0.7
Linear interpolation between fxL = 0.3 and fxL = 0.7 at fxL = 0.5 yields fnℓ = 0.9
fnℓ = 0.9 at the midship load point for the extreme sea loads scenario

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec5 Table 2 defines the HSM wave pressure formula and references fnℓ, which depends on fxL. The definition of fxL is not given in Sec5 — it refers back to Sec2 (Symbols) where fxL = x/L, bounded [0.0, 1.0]. With fxL known, fnℓ is obtained by linear interpolation from the values tabulated in Sec5 Table 2.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Compute fxL: Sec5 Symbols states fxL is defined in Sec2. From Sec2 Symbols: fxL = x/L = 110/220 = 0.5, bounded between 0.0 and 1.0, so fxL = 0.5. Step 2 — Determine fnℓ at fxL = 0.5 for extreme sea loads: From Sec5 Table 2, for extreme sea loads: fnℓ = 0.9 at fxL = 0.3, fnℓ = 0.9 at fxL = 0.7. Linear interpolation between fxL = 0.3 and fxL = 0.7: fnℓ = 0.9 + (0.5 − 0.3)/(0.7 − 0.3) × (0.9 − 0.9) = 0.9. So fnℓ = 0.9 at fxL = 0.5.

question_text: A bulk carrier of Type 'B-100' classification has bulwarks fitted along the exposed weather deck. The vessel's designer proposes to install continuous solid bulwarks along the full length of the exposed freeboard deck without any open rails. The bulwarks have an average height of 1.05 m and the total length of the exposed weather deck section is 85 m. The ship's breadth is 32 m. Is this arrangement acceptable under classification rules, and if not, what is the minimum freeing port area required in the lower part of the bulwarks as a percentage of the total bulwark area, and what is the total minimum freeing port area in m² that must be provided on each side?
required_facts: The arrangement is not acceptable as proposed because no open rails and no freeing ports are provided
Type 'B-100' ships with bulwarks must have open rails for at least half the exposed weather deck length OR freeing port area of at least 33% of total bulwark area in the lower part of the bulwarks
Total bulwark area per side = 85 m × 1.05 m = 89.25 m²
Minimum required freeing port area = 33% × 89.25 m² = 29.45 m² per side
The freeing ports must be located in the lower part of the bulwarks

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Sec10 special requirements for Type 'B-100' ships with bulwarks, which specifies that either open rails for at least half the length OR a freeing port area of 33% of total bulwark area is required; the scenario forces the answerer to apply the 33% freeing port rule and compute the actual area from the bulwark dimensions
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify ship type: The vessel is Type 'B-100'. Navigate to the special requirements for Type 'B-100' ships in Sec10 [6.2]. The rule states: Type 'B-100' ships with bulwarks shall have open rails fitted for at least half the length of the exposed parts of the weather deck OR a freeing port area in the lower part of the bulwarks of 33% of the total area of the bulwarks. Step 2 — Evaluate the proposal: The designer proposes continuous solid bulwarks with no open rails. Since no open rails are fitted, the 33% freeing port area requirement must be satisfied. Step 3 — Compute total bulwark area per side: Total bulwark area per side = length × average height = 85 m × 1.05 m = 89.25 m². Step 4 — Compute minimum freeing port area: 33% of 89.25 m² = 0.33 × 89.25 = 29.45 m² per side. Step 5 — Cross-check with Sec10 [2.1.1] standard formula as a sanity check: For ℓb = 85 m (but capped at 0.7L — however L is not given explicitly, so the 85 m figure is used as stated for the bulwark length in the well context). The special Type 'B-100' rule in [6.2] overrides the standard formula and mandates 33% of total bulwark area. Conclusion: The arrangement is not acceptable as proposed (no open rails, no freeing ports). The minimum freeing port area required is 33% of total bulwark area = 29.45 m² per side.

scenario_parameters.bulwark_arrangement: continuous solid bulwarks, no open rails

question_text: A shipyard in South Korea has contracted with a Norwegian owner to build a new 180-metre offshore supply vessel. The yard is not previously known to DNV and has never completed a DNV-classed project. During the pre-classification meeting, the yard's project manager states that they plan to source a main propulsion diesel engine from a sub-supplier who manufactures engines in batches for stock. The engine manufacturer has not previously supplied equipment for a DNV-classed vessel and is also unknown to the Society. The yard intends to submit the engine manufacturer's own internal factory acceptance test report as the sole certification document for the engine, without any DNV involvement in the manufacturing survey. Additionally, the yard has not yet provided any documentation of their quality management system or their capability to manage classification projects. Can the yard proceed with classification on this basis, and what specific obligations must both the yard and the engine manufacturer fulfil before the Society can issue certificates for the engine?
required_facts: The yard, being unfamiliar to the Society, must provide evidence of its capability to successfully manage classification projects before classification can proceed.

The engine manufacturer, as a supplier of components not covered under the standard manufacturer approval categories, must be considered for approval by the Society according to criteria it establishes.
The yard is obligated to instruct the engine manufacturer (as a subcontractor/supplier) that the Society's rules apply and that DNV certificates must be provided as required.
The engine manufacturer's own internal factory acceptance test report is insufficient as the sole certification document; DNV involvement in survey and/or certification is required.
The engine manufacturer must have a document handling system ensuring the product is free from asbestos and must provide an asbestos-free declaration as a prerequisite for certificate issuance.
Quality control records for the engine must be traceable, documented in writing, and carried out by qualified personnel at suitable facilities.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec4 [1.2.1] states that manufacturers of materials/components not covered by Sec2 [1.2] must be considered for approval by the Society. This cross-reference to Sec2 [1.2] triggers the builder/designer requirements: the yard must demonstrate capability to manage classification projects (Sec2 [1.2.1]) and must instruct sub-suppliers that DNV rules apply and DNV certificates are required (Sec2 [1.2.2]).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec4 [1.2.1]: The engine manufacturer is a manufacturer of components (propulsion diesel engine) whose category is not covered by Sec2 [1.2] (i.e., not a standard type-approved product already listed). Therefore the manufacturer must be 'considered for approval according to criteria established by the Society'. The yard cannot simply submit the manufacturer's own factory test report; DNV involvement is required. Step 2 — Cross-reference to Sec2 [1.2]: Following the explicit pointer in Sec4 [1.2.1] to Sec2 [1.2], we find: Sec2 [1.2.1] requires that builders or designers unfamiliar to the Society must provide evidence of their capability to successfully manage classification projects (e.g., prior successful outcomes with another classification society or similar design projects). The yard has not done this, so classification cannot proceed until this evidence is submitted. Sec2 [1.2.2] requires that the builder must instruct their subcontractors and suppliers that the Society's rules apply and that DNV certificates shall be provided as and when required. The yard must formally notify the engine manufacturer of this obligation. Step 3 — Sec4 [1.2.2]: Quality control of the engine must be traceable and documented in writing, carried out by qualified personnel at suitable facilities. The manufacturer's internal report alone does not satisfy this unless DNV has confirmed the manufacturer's approval status. Step 4 — Sec4 [1.2.3]: The engine manufacturer must also provide an asbestos-free declaration and a document handling system to ensure the product is free from asbestos, as a prerequisite for certificate issuance. Conclusion: The yard cannot proceed on the stated basis. The yard must first provide evidence of classification project capability to DNV. The engine manufacturer must be evaluated and approved by DNV before certificates can be issued, and the yard must instruct the manufacturer that DNV rules and certificates are mandatory.

scenario_parameters.proposed_certification_document: manufacturer's own internal factory acceptance test report only

question_text: A 180-metre bulk carrier with a block coefficient of 0.82 is operating in unrestricted service (R0 notation) and has no bilge keel fitted. The vessel's beam is 30 m, scantling draught is 11.5 m, and the loading condition draught is 9.8 m. A structural engineer is computing the external sea pressure on the ship's side shell at a point located 2.5 m below the waterline (z = 7.3 m from keel) for the normal seagoing S+D design load scenario. To determine the total external pressure at this point, the engineer needs the hydrostatic (static) pressure component PS. Separately, the engineer also needs to verify the roll angle used in the dynamic wave pressure calculation. Given that the metacentric height GM has not been explicitly calculated for this loading condition, what is the hydrostatic pressure PS at the considered point, and what roll angle θ (in degrees, to two decimal places) should be used in the dynamic pressure formulation? Show all intermediate values including the roll period Tθ, the fT ratio, and the fps coefficient.
required_facts: fT = 9.8 / 11.5 ≈ 0.852 (not less than 0.5, not more than 1.0)
fps = 1.0 for R0 unrestricted service, extreme sea loads strength assessment scenario
fBK = 1.2 because no bilge keel is fitted
Default GM = 0.07B = 2.1 m and default kr = 0.39B = 11.7 m (GM not explicitly calculated)
Roll angle θ ≈ 28.74°

annotator_grounding.start_clause: Pt3.Ch4.Sec7 [2.1.1] and Symbols (PS defined as per Sec.5 [1.2])
annotator_grounding.end_clause: Pt3.Ch4.Sec5 [1.2] (hydrostatic pressure table) → Pt3.Ch4.Sec3 [2.1.1] (roll angle formula)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec7 symbols define PS as per Sec5 [1.2], and the dynamic pressure PW references Sec5 [1.3.x] which in turn uses roll angle θ and roll period Tθ from Sec3 [2.1.1]. The answerer must follow Sec7 → Sec5 [1.2] for PS, then Sec5 → Sec3 [2.1.1] for the roll motion parameters.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Identify the design load scenario: Normal seagoing S+D scenario (Design load scenario 2 in Sec7 Table 1). The external shell pressure is Pex = PS + PW.

Step 2 — Follow Sec7 symbol definition: PS is defined in Sec5 [1.2]. Navigate to Sec5 [1.2], Table 1 (Hydrostatic pressure). For a point below the waterline at z = 7.3 m with TLC = 9.8 m: PS = ρg(TLC − z) = 1.025 × 9.81 × (9.8 − 7.3) = 1.025 × 9.81 × 2.5 = 25.14 kN/m².

Step 3 — For the dynamic pressure PW, Sec5 references roll angle θ and roll period Tθ from Sec3 [2.1.1].

Step 4 — Navigate to Sec3 [2.1.1]. Compute fT: fT = TLC/TSC = 9.8/11.5 = 0.852 (within [0.5, 1.0], so use 0.852).

Step 5 — fps: R0 service notation, strength assessment, normal (extreme sea loads) scenario → fps = 1.0. No service restriction so fr = 1.0. fps = 1.0.

Step 6 — fp = fps = 1.0 (strength assessment).

Step 7 — fBK = 1.2 (no bilge keel).

Step 8 — kr: not calculated, use default kr = 0.39B = 0.39 × 30 = 11.7 m.

Step 9 — GM: not calculated, use default GM = 0.07B = 0.07 × 30 = 2.1 m (general ship; minimum check: 0.05B = 1.5 m, so 2.1 m governs).

Step 10 — Roll period: Tθ = (2.3π × kr) / √(g × GM) = (2.3π × 11.7) / √(9.81 × 2.1) = (84.509) / √(20.601) = 84.509 / 4.539 = 18.62 s.

Step 11 — Roll angle: θ = [9000 × (1.4 − 0.035 × Tθ) × fp × fBK] / [(1.15B + 55) × π] = [9000 × (1.4 − 0.035 × 18.62) × 1.0 × 1.2] / [(1.15 × 30 + 55) × π] = [9000 × (1.4 − 0.6517) × 1.2] / [(34.5 + 55) × π] = [9000 × 0.7483 × 1.2] / [89.5 × 3.14159] = [8081.64] / [281.17] = 28.74°.

question_text: A RO/RO ferry has a stern door that also serves as a vehicle ramp. The door opening area is 8.5 m². The door sill is located 180 mm above the upper edge of the uppermost load line when measured at the ship's side. The door leads directly to the RO/RO cargo space. The designer proposes to use securing bolts as the primary means of transferring sea pressure to the coamings, and also proposes to use a single door arrangement (no inner door). Is this arrangement compliant with classification rules? Identify all deficiencies and state what additional structural or watertightness measures are required.
required_facts: The minimum sill height is 230 mm above the upper edge of the uppermost load line; the proposed 180 mm sill is below this limit and is non-compliant
Because the sill is below the 230 mm threshold, a second door of equivalent strength and watertightness is required as one acceptable arrangement
A leakage detection device must be provided in the compartment between the two doors, and drainage to the bilges via an easily accessible screw-down valve must be arranged
The door area of 8.5 m² is less than 12 m², so securing bolts may be accepted as carriers of sea pressure to the coamings provided the direct sea-pressure-transfer arrangement is not feasible

The inner door is an internal watertight door whose securing device scantlings must satisfy the requirements referenced in the internal doors section, which in turn refers back to the access openings section for bolt/securing device scantlings

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Sec5 side/stern door requirements: sill height check triggers [1.2.3] threshold (230 mm), which is not met, so [1.2.4] applies requiring special consideration including a second door of equivalent strength and watertightness — this second door is an internal door/ramp governed by Sec3, whose securing device scantlings reference Sec2 [1.3]. Additionally, the door area of 8.5 m² is less than 12 m² so securing bolts are permitted under [1.3.4], but only if the [1.3.3] arrangement is not feasible.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Check sill height against Sec5 [1.2.3]: the minimum permitted sill height is 230 mm above the upper edge of the uppermost load line. The proposed sill is at 180 mm, which is below this threshold. Therefore [1.2.3] is violated. Step 2 — Apply Sec5 [1.2.4]: because the sill is below the 230 mm line, special consideration is required. One acceptable arrangement is a second door of equivalent strength and watertightness, with a leakage detection device in the compartment between the two doors, and drainage to the bilges via an easily accessible screw-down valve. The single-door arrangement is therefore not compliant. Step 3 — The second (inner) door is an internal watertight door covered by Sec3 (internal doors and hatches). Per Sec3 [2.1.3], securing devices other than bolts shall have strength equivalent to the requirements given in Sec2 [1.3], and the scantlings of securing devices for the inner door must satisfy Sec2 [1.3]. Step 4 — Check sea pressure transfer for the outer stern door: door area A = 8.5 m² < 12 m², so per Sec5 [1.3.4] securing bolts may be accepted as carriers of sea pressure to the coamings if the direct-transfer arrangement of [1.3.3] is not feasible. This part of the proposal is conditionally acceptable, subject to demonstrating infeasibility of the [1.3.3] arrangement. Step 5 — Summary of deficiencies: (a) sill height 180 mm < 230 mm minimum — non-compliant; (b) single door arrangement not acceptable — a second inner door of equivalent strength and watertightness is required; (c) leakage detection and bilge drainage must be provided between the two doors; (d) scantlings of securing devices on the inner door must meet Sec2 [1.3] requirements.

question_text: A 185-metre bulk carrier with a block coefficient of 0.82, L/B ratio of 6.1, and B/D ratio of 2.1 is being designed for unrestricted worldwide service, including occasional winter voyages to Arctic waters where the lowest mean daily average air temperature reaches −14°C. The designer proposes a design life of 20 years and intends to submit only the main structural drawings and preliminary loading manual as the design basis documentation, without a separate design basis document. The vessel has been assigned a CSR class notation. Evaluate whether the proposed design life, the Arctic service temperature, and the documentation approach each comply with the applicable classification requirements, and identify what additional certification or notation, if any, is required for the Arctic trading pattern.
required_facts: The proposed 20-year design life does not comply; the minimum required design life is 25 years.
The standard rules assume a lowest mean daily average air temperature of −10°C; service at −14°C falls below this threshold.
For regular service in areas with air temperatures below and including −10°C (such as Arctic winter voyages), the additional class notation DAT is required.
The DAT notation requirements are covered in Pt.6 Ch.6.
For CSR-classed vessels, certification requirements and documentation requirements for design assessment still apply even though separate CSR requirements replace the main structural chapters.
The design basis may be documented in the main structural drawings and preliminary loading manual without a separate document, so the documentation approach is acceptable.
All changes to the design basis must be formally advised to the Society.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec.1 [1.1.2] states that for CSR ships, separate requirements replace Ch.1–Ch.13 EXCEPT for certification requirements in Sec.3 [4] and documentation requirements in Sec.3 [2.2]. This forces the answerer into Sec.3 [4] for certification and Sec.3 [2.2] for documentation. Sec.3 [4.2] covers novel designs and Sec.3 [4.1] covers design parameters outside the design basis. The design basis itself is defined in Sec.2 [3], which specifies the 25-year minimum design life (Sec.2 [3.4]), the design temperature limits (Sec.2 [3.5.4]), and the documentation requirements for the design basis (Sec.2 [3.1.2]).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Start at Sec.1 [1.1.2]: The vessel has CSR notation, so separate CSR requirements replace Ch.1–Ch.13, but certification requirements in Sec.3 [4] and documentation requirements in Sec.3 [2.2] still apply. Step 2 — Navigate to Sec.3 [2.2]: Documentation requirements for design assessment still apply to CSR ships. Sec.3 [2.2.1] and [2.2.2] require documentation per Table 1 to be submitted and reviewed. The designer's approach of using only main structural drawings and loading manual is acceptable per Sec.2 [3.1.2] guidance note, which states the design basis is 'normally specified in the main structural drawings, the preliminary loading manual and in plans for load and capacities' or may be given in a separate document — so this is compliant. Step 3 — Navigate to Sec.2 [3.4]: Minimum design life is 25 years. The proposed 20-year design life is non-compliant; it must be increased to at least 25 years. Step 4 — Navigate to Sec.2 [3.5.4]: The standard rules assume lowest mean daily average air temperature of −10°C. The Arctic voyages expose the vessel to −14°C, which is below −10°C. This triggers the requirement for the additional class notation DAT per Pt.6 Ch.6. Step 5 — Navigate to Sec.3 [4.1]: Design parameters outside the design basis (here, the sub-−10°C temperature) require the DAT notation and must be formally documented and submitted. Conclusion: (a) 20-year design life is non-compliant — minimum 25 years required; (b) Arctic service at −14°C requires the DAT additional class notation per Pt.6 Ch.6; (c) documentation approach via main structural drawings and loading manual is acceptable.

scenario_parameters.documentation_approach: main structural drawings and preliminary loading manual only

question_text: A shipyard is preparing classification documentation for a new 185-metre sea-going single-deck vessel with a double bottom, hopper side tanks, and top-wing tanks fitted below the upper deck. The vessel has five cargo holds of double side skin construction and is intended exclusively for the carriage of solid bulk cargoes such as iron ore and coal. The owner wants to know: (1) Is a ship type notation mandatory for this vessel, and if so, which one? (2) What is the main class notation that will appear on the vessel's class certificate, and what rule parts govern the hull, machinery, and equipment requirements underpinning that notation? (3) Can the vessel simultaneously hold more than one ship type notation if it later qualifies for an additional type?
required_facts: The 'Bulk carrier' ship type notation is mandatory for this vessel.

The vessel qualifies because it is a sea-going single-deck vessel with double side skin cargo holds, double bottom, hopper side tanks, and top-wing tanks below the upper deck, intended for solid bulk cargoes.
The main class notation assigned will be '1A'.
The '1A' notation is underpinned by compliance with Pt.2, Pt.3, and Pt.4 (hull, machinery, systems and equipment requirements).
A vessel may be assigned more than one ship type notation provided the respective requirements for each notation are met.
Ship type notation requirements may supersede Pt.2/Pt.3/Pt.4 requirements, but the main class notation '1A' is still assigned in such cases.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Sec3 (Ship Type Notations) to identify that 'Bulk carrier' is mandatory for this vessel's configuration; Sec3 [1.1.2] states a vessel may hold more than one ship type notation; then follow to Sec1 [1.1.2–1.1.3] which explains that class notations determine applicable rule requirements and that mandatory notations are indicated in the tables in Sec2–Sec6; then follow to Sec2 [2.1.1] which defines the main class notation '1A' and the governing rule parts (Pt.2, Pt.3, Pt.4).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec3 Table 1: The vessel is a sea-going single-deck vessel with cargo holds of double side skin construction, double bottom, hopper side tanks, and top-wing tanks below the upper deck, intended for solid bulk cargoes. This matches the 'Bulk carrier' row exactly. The 'Mandatory: yes' field confirms the notation is mandatory. Step 2 — Sec3 [1.1.2]: A vessel may be assigned more than one ship type notation provided the respective requirements are met, so the answer to question (3) is yes. Step 3 — Sec1 [1.1.2]: Class notations are assigned to determine applicable rule requirements for assignment and retention of class; Sec1 [1.1.3] confirms mandatory notations are indicated in the tables in Sec2–Sec6. Step 4 — Sec2 [2.1.1]: The main class notation '1A' is assigned to vessels with hull, machinery, systems and equipment found to be in compliance with Pt.2, Pt.3, and Pt.4. Ship type notation requirements may supersede Pt.2/3/4 requirements, but '1A' is still assigned.

question_text: A bulk carrier with scantling length L = 180 m, moulded breadth B = 32 m, block coefficient CB = 0.82, and scantling draught TSC = 11.5 m is being assessed for external sea pressures under the HSM dynamic load cases. The vessel has bilge keels fitted and a metacentric height GM = 0.07B. The loading condition under review has a draught TLC = 9.2 m amidships. A side shell load point is located at x = 90 m from the aft perpendicular, y = 16 m (starboard), z = 6.5 m, at a cross-section where the waterline breadth Bx = 32 m. For the extreme sea loads design load scenario, determine the roll angle θ (in degrees) and roll period Tθ (in seconds) that must be used when computing the external dynamic pressures at this load point, and state whether the draught ratio fT used in these calculations is limited by any minimum value.
required_facts: fT = TLC / TSC = 9.2 / 11.5 = 0.80, and fT has a minimum floor of 0.5 per the rules
Roll radius of gyration kr is per Pt5 Ch1 Sec2 [5.1.2] for Bulk carrier/Ore carrier (not the general kr = 0.39B default).
Roll period Tθ is computed via Tθ = 2.3π·kr / √(g·GM), using GM = 2.24 m.
For strength assessment under extreme sea loads, fp = fps = 1.0 and fBK = 1.0 (bilge keels fitted)
Roll angle θ is computed via the roll angle formula in the ship motions section
The formulae for θ and Tθ are not in the external loads section itself — they are defined by cross-reference in the ship motions section

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec.5 Symbols lists θ (roll angle) and Tθ (roll period) as 'defined in Sec.3 [2.1.1]', so the answerer must navigate from the external loads section to the ship motions section to find the actual formulae and evaluate them with the given parameters.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Sec.5 Symbols references: θ and Tθ are both listed as 'as defined in Sec.3 [2.1.1]'. The answerer must go to Sec.3 [2.1.1] to find the roll motion formulae.

Step 2 — Compute fT (Sec.3 Symbols): fT = TLC / TSC = 9.2 / 11.5 = 0.800. The rule states fT shall not be taken less than 0.5 and not more than 1.0, so fT = 0.80 (no limiting applies here, but the minimum of 0.5 is the stated floor).

Step 3 — Compute roll radius of gyration kr: No calculated value given, so use default kr = 0.39B = 0.39 × 32 = 12.48 m.

Step 4 — Compute GM: Given GM = 0.07B = 0.07 × 32 = 2.24 m. Check minimum: 0.05B = 1.6 m; 2.24 m > 1.6 m, so GM = 2.24 m.

Step 5 — Compute roll period Tθ (Sec.3 [2.1.1]): Tθ = (2.3π × kr) / √(g × GM) = (2.3π × 12.48) / √(9.81 × 2.24) = (90.12) / √(21.97) = 90.12 / 4.687 ≈ 19.23 s.

Step 6 — Compute roll angle θ (Sec.3 [2.1.1]): For strength assessment, fp = fps = 1.0 (extreme sea loads). fBK = 1.0 (bilge keels fitted). θ = [9000 × (1.4 − 0.035 × Tθ) × fp × fBK] / [(1.15B + 55) × π] = [9000 × (1.4 − 0.035 × 19.23) × 1.0 × 1.0] / [(1.15 × 32 + 55) × π] = [9000 × (1.4 − 0.673) × 1.0] / [(36.8 + 55) × π] = [9000 × 0.727] / [91.8 × π] = 6543 / 288.4 ≈ 22.7 deg.

Step 7 — Minimum fT: The rule explicitly states fT shall not be taken less than 0.5, so the minimum limiting value is 0.5.

question_text: A designer is checking the net plate thickness of a longitudinally stiffened bottom shell panel on a 180 m bulk carrier. The panel has a breadth b = 820 mm and a length a = 2 600 mm. The steel yield strength ReH = 315 N/mm². For the governing design load set, the design pressure P = 145 kN/m² and the hull girder longitudinal stress σhg = +110 N/mm² (hogging, tensile at bottom). Determine the minimum required net plate thickness for this panel, clearly identifying which acceptance criterion category and permissible bending stress coefficient Ca applies, and whether the computed Ca must be capped.
required_facts: The applicable design load set for external bottom shell plating is identified from the design load sets table (e.g. SEA-1), which carries acceptance criterion AC-II
For longitudinal stiffened plating under AC-II per Sec.4 Table 1, the coefficients are β_a = 1.05, α_a = 0.50, C_a-max = 0.95
C_a = 1.05 - 0.50 × (110/315) ≈ 0.875, which is below C_a-max = 0.95 so no cap is applied
The panel aspect ratio correction αp = 1.2 − 820/(2.1 × 2600) ≈ 1.050, capped at 1.0
Minimum net plate thickness t ≈ 9.4 mm (acceptable range 9.3-9.5 mm)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec4 plating thickness formula references 'all applicable design load sets, as defined in Sec2 [2.1.3]' for the design pressure P and acceptance criteria category; the answerer must consult Sec2 Table 1 to identify the correct design load set (e.g. SEA-1 or TK-1/WB-1) and its acceptance criteria (AC-II), then return to Sec4 Table 1 to read off βa, αa, Ca-max for longitudinal stiffened plating under the appropriate acceptance criterion, and finally apply the thickness formula.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 – Identify applicable design load sets from Sec2 [2.1.3] Table 1. For external bottom shell (longitudinally stiffened), the governing sea-pressure load set is SEA-1 with acceptance criterion AC-II at full-load draught TSC. Step 2 – From Sec4 Table 1, for 'Other longitudinal members – Longitudinal stiffened plating' under AC-II: βa = 1.10, αa = 0.50, Ca-max = 1.00. Step 3 – Compute Ca = βa − αa × (σhg / ReH) = 1.10 − 0.50 × (110 / 315) = 1.10 − 0.175 = 0.925. Check against Ca-max = 1.00 → 0.925 < 1.00, so no cap needed; Ca = 0.925. Step 4 – Compute panel aspect ratio correction: αp = 1.2 − b/(2.1a) = 1.2 − 820/(2.1 × 2600) = 1.2 − 0.1502 = 1.0498, capped at 1.0. Step 5 – Apply thickness formula: t = 0.0158 × αp × b × √(|P| / (Ca × ReH)) = 0.0158 × 1.0 × 820 × √(145 / (0.925 × 315)) = 12.956 × √(145 / 291.375) = 12.956 × √0.4976 = 12.956 × 0.7054 = 9.14 mm. Minimum net thickness ≈ 9.1 mm.

question_text: A naval architect is performing a global finite element analysis of a 185 m passenger vessel with a partly effective superstructure. The global FE model has been refined in the midship region to a mesh arrangement matching the stiffener spacing (s×s mesh) used for a partial ship cargo hold analysis. In this refined region, the von Mises stress in a deck plate element is calculated as 245 N/mm² under the governing load combination. The element normal membrane stresses are σx = 220 N/mm² and σy = 40 N/mm², and the element shear stress is τxy = 55 N/mm². The yield strength of the material is 315 N/mm². Determine whether the stress state in this element is acceptable, and identify which set of acceptance criteria governs the assessment of this refined region within the global model.
required_facts: The refined mesh region within the global FE model is governed by the partial ship analysis acceptance criteria, not the global analysis yield criteria
The trigger for applying partial ship criteria is that the mesh arrangement matches the s×s mesh used for partial ship analysis
The von Mises stress shall be calculated from membrane normal and shear stresses at the element centroid of the mid-plane
The correct von Mises stress calculated from the given stress components is approximately 224 N/mm², not 245 N/mm²
The assessment must reference the partial ship structural analysis acceptance criteria section for the applicable utilisation limits
Both global and partial ship analysis require individual buckling assessment of all structural elements against the buckling requirements

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec2 [4.1] states that where the global FE model is partially or entirely refined to a mesh arrangement as used for partial ship analysis, the analysis criteria for partial ship analysis apply, as given in Sec3 [4]. The answerer must follow this cross-reference to Sec3 [4] to find the correct acceptance criteria rather than applying the global analysis yield criteria from Sec2 [4.2].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: The scenario involves a global FE model (Sec2) with a refined mesh region matching s×s partial ship mesh. Step 2: Sec2 [4.1] explicitly states that where the global FE model is partially or entirely refined to a mesh arrangement as used for partial ship analysis, the analysis criteria for partial ship analysis apply, as given in Sec3 [4]. Step 3: The analyst must therefore navigate to Sec3 [4] (partial ship analysis criteria) rather than applying Sec2 [4.2] global yield criteria. Step 4: Under Sec3 [4], the von Mises stress formula is the same but the acceptance criteria (utilisation factors, permissible stress levels) are those defined for partial ship/cargo hold analysis, not the global analysis criteria from Pt.5. Step 5: Verify the von Mises stress calculation: σvm = sqrt(220² - 220×40 + 40² + 3×55²) = sqrt(48400 - 8800 + 1600 + 9075) = sqrt(50275) ≈ 224 N/mm², which differs from the stated 245 N/mm², indicating the stated value may be incorrect or from a different layer — the analyst should recalculate at element centroid mid-plane. Step 6: The governing criteria are those of Sec3 [4] (partial ship analysis acceptance criteria), not the global analysis criteria.

scenario_parameters.ship_type: passenger vessel with partly effective superstructure
scenario_parameters.analysis_type: global FE model with refined midship region

question_text:
A 95-metre general cargo vessel is being designed with a bow anchor windlass fitted on the exposed forecastle deck. The forecastle deck height above the summer load waterline is 4.8 m, and the windlass is located 18 m aft of the forward perpendicular. The anchor chain cable has a minimum breaking strength (BS) of 1 150 kN. A chain stopper is installed alongside the windlass. The windlass foundation is a custom fabricated steel pedestal (not selected from an accepted industry standard), and the designer proposes a corrosion addition of 1.5 mm for the pedestal. The supporting hull structure beneath the windlass is part of the forecastle deck structure.

The designer must verify: (1) what design load, in kN, must the windlass foundation be designed to resist for the anchoring operation load case, given that a chain stopper is provided; (2) whether the proposed 1.5 mm corrosion addition for the custom pedestal is acceptable; and (3) whether the green sea load requirements apply to this windlass installation, and if so, what condition on deck height triggers that requirement.
required_facts: Windlass design load for anchoring operation (chain stopper provided) = 45% of BS = 517.5 kN
Proposed corrosion addition of 1.5 mm for the custom pedestal is not acceptable; minimum required is 2.0 mm
Green sea load requirements apply to this windlass installation
Green sea requirements are triggered because deck height (4.8 m) is less than min(0.1L, 22 m) = 9.5 m
The windlass location (18 m aft of FP) is within the forward 0.25L = 23.75 m, satisfying that condition
Ship length 95 m ≥ 80 m satisfies the length threshold for green sea applicability

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec2 [2.1] states the windlass subsection applies to foundations required in accordance with Sec1 Table 2, establishing the cross-reference. Sec2 [2.3.1] gives the anchoring load cases. Sec2 [2.5.1] gives the green sea applicability condition referencing deck height vs 0.1L or 22 m. Sec2 [5.8.1] gives the corrosion addition requirement for custom pedestals.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Anchoring load: Per Sec2 [2.3.1](a), when a chain stopper is provided, the windlass design load = 45% of BS = 0.45 × 1150 = 517.5 kN. Step 2 — Corrosion addition: Per Sec2 [5.8.1], for pedestals and foundations on deck not part of a fitting from an accepted industry standard, tc must not be less than 2.0 mm. The proposed 1.5 mm is therefore not acceptable. Step 3 — Green sea applicability: Per Sec2 [2.5.1], green sea requirements apply when the windlass is on an exposed deck over the forward 0.25L, the ship length is ≥ 80 m, AND the exposed deck height is less than 0.1L or 22 m (whichever is lesser). For L = 95 m: 0.1L = 9.5 m; 22 m is greater, so the lesser value is 9.5 m. The forecastle deck is at 4.8 m above the summer load waterline, which is less than 9.5 m. The windlass is at 18 m aft of FP, which is within 0.25 × 95 = 23.75 m. Ship length is 95 m ≥ 80 m. All three conditions are met, so green sea loads apply. The triggering deck height condition is: deck height < min(0.1L, 22 m) = 9.5 m.

scenario_parameters.pedestal_type: custom fabricated, not from accepted industry standard

question_text: A 180 m bulk carrier is being designed with an anchor windlass located on the exposed forecastle deck, 28 m aft of the forward perpendicular. The forecastle deck height is 8.5 m above the summer load waterline. The windlass has a chain cable with a minimum breaking strength (BS) of 1 800 kN, and a separate chain stopper is fitted. The windlass foundation deck plating and supporting girders are fabricated from normal strength steel (ReH = 235 N/mm²). The designer proposes to assess the foundation strength using a beam theory approach. During the structural assessment, the net scantlings of the supporting structure are to be used after deducting the corrosion addition. The corrosion addition for the supporting deck structure is taken as that applicable to the surrounding deck structure. What is the maximum permissible normal stress and shear stress in the supporting structure under the governing anchoring load case, and what design load (in kN) must the foundation be designed to resist for the windlass with chain stopper fitted?
required_facts: Governing anchoring design load for windlass with chain stopper = 45% of BS = 0.45 × 1800 = 810 kN
Maximum permissible normal stress (beam theory) = ReH = 235 N/mm²
Maximum permissible shear stress (beam theory) = 0.6 × ReH = 141 N/mm²
Green sea load requirements apply because the deck height (8.5 m) is less than the lesser of 0.1L (18 m) and 22 m
Net scantlings are used after deducting corrosion addition applicable to the surrounding deck structure
The windlass is within the forward 0.25L (45 m) region, confirming green sea load applicability

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 (weld joint design, which references Ch.11 Sec.2 for supporting structure of deck equipment including windlass foundations). The windlass foundation design loads and acceptance criteria are governed by Ch.11 Sec.2, which specifies the permissible stresses for beam theory assessment and the load fractions of BS to be applied.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the governing load case for the windlass: Since a chain stopper IS provided, the design load for the windlass is 45% of BS (per Ch.11 Sec.2 [2.3.1](a)). BS = 1800 kN, so design load = 0.45 × 1800 = 810 kN. Step 2 — Check whether green sea loads also apply: The windlass is located at 28 m aft of FP, which is within the forward 0.25L = 0.25 × 180 = 45 m. The deck height is 8.5 m above summer load waterline. The threshold is the lesser of 0.1L = 18 m or 22 m, i.e. 18 m. Since 8.5 m < 18 m, the green sea load requirements of [2.5.1] also apply. However, the question asks specifically about the anchoring load case. Step 3 — Permissible stresses for beam theory (Ch.11 Sec.2 [2.4.2](a)): Normal stress limit = ReH = 235 N/mm²; Shear stress limit = 0.6 × ReH = 0.6 × 235 = 141 N/mm². Step 4 — Net scantlings: Corrosion addition for supporting hull structure follows the rules for the surrounding structure (deck structure), per [5.8.1] (or equivalent corrosion addition clause in Ch.11 Sec.2).

question_text: A 185-metre bulk carrier is undergoing cargo hold finite element analysis for the midship region. During model review, the structural engineer notes that several longitudinal stiffeners on the inner bottom plating pass through a transverse web frame at an angle of 42 degrees between the stiffener web plate and the attached plating. The stiffeners are unsymmetrical flat-bar profiles. The tripping brackets fitted at these locations have an as-built thickness of 8 mm, while the stiffener webs have an as-built thickness of 12 mm. The spacing between adjacent stiffeners is 750 mm, and the current tripping bracket spacing is 3,200 mm. Is this structural arrangement compliant with the classification rules? Identify all non-compliances, if any, and state the corrective requirements.
required_facts: The stiffener web-to-plating angle of 42 degrees is less than the 50-degree threshold, triggering special tripping bracket requirements
Maximum permissible tripping bracket spacing is 4 × 750 mm = 3,000 mm; the actual spacing of 3,200 mm is non-compliant
Minimum required tripping bracket thickness is 75% × 12 mm = 9 mm; the actual thickness of 8 mm is non-compliant
For unsymmetrical stiffeners with web-to-plating angle less than 50 degrees, the face plate must be fitted on the open angle side
The arrangement has at least two non-compliances: tripping bracket spacing and tripping bracket thickness

annotator_grounding.end_clause: Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [6.1.1] — specifically the tripping bracket requirements for stiffeners at angles less than 50 degrees
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The cargo hold FE model requirements in Pt3.Ch7.Sec3 mandate that all stiffeners be modelled and that the structural arrangement be compliant. The stiffener angle condition (42 deg < 50 deg) triggers the detail design requirements in Pt3.Ch3.Sec6, which specify tripping bracket spacing (≤ 4s) and minimum bracket thickness (≥ 75% of stiffener web thickness), and also require the face plate of unsymmetrical stiffeners to be on the open angle side.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: The partial ship structural analysis section (Pt3.Ch7.Sec3 [2.1.3]) requires all stiffeners and their connections to be modelled correctly, and the structural arrangement must satisfy the applicable design rules. Step 2: The stiffener web-to-plating angle is 42 degrees, which is less than 50 degrees. This triggers the detail design rule in Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [6.1.1] (3.1.2). Step 3: Per Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [3.1.2], when the angle is less than 50 deg, tripping brackets/carlings shall be spaced not more than 4 times the stiffener spacing. With s = 750 mm, maximum spacing = 4 × 750 = 3,000 mm. The actual spacing of 3,200 mm exceeds this limit — NON-COMPLIANT. Step 4: The as-built thickness of tripping brackets shall not be less than 75% of the as-built stiffener web thickness. 75% × 12 mm = 9 mm. The actual bracket thickness of 8 mm is less than 9 mm — NON-COMPLIANT. Step 5: For unsymmetrical stiffeners with angle < 50 deg, the face plate shall be fitted on the open angle side — this must also be verified.

scenario_parameters.analysis_type: cargo hold FE analysis, midship region
scenario_parameters.stiffener_location: inner bottom plating at transverse web frame

question_text: A chemical tanker has a cargo tank with the following characteristics: the tank has a maximum height h_tk of 18 m, an effective sloshing length of 0.14L (where L = 200 m, so 28 m), and an effective sloshing breadth of 0.60B (where B = 32 m, so 19.2 m). The tank is intended to carry a heavy liquid cargo with a maximum liquid cargo density ρ_max-LM of 1.6 t/m³ at 98% fill. The designer proposes to restrict filling to a partial height to manage structural loads. Determine: (1) the value of ρ_L to be used for strength assessment of this cargo tank, (2) the value of f_cd applicable to this case, and (3) the maximum permissible filling height h_part associated with partial filling at the high liquid density ρ_part = 1.6 t/m³. Additionally, confirm whether this tank requires an additional liquid impact load assessment beyond standard sloshing loads, and state the filling level range over which that assessment must be conducted.
required_facts: ρ_L = 1.6 t/m³ for strength assessment because ρ_max-LM = 1.6 t/m³ exceeds 1.025 t/m³
f_cd = 1.0 because this is not an oil/oil product cargo tank with ρ_L ≤ 1.025 t/m³
An additional liquid impact load assessment is required because b_slh = 0.60B > 0.56B
The liquid impact assessment is also triggered because ℓ_slh = 0.14L satisfies 0.13L < ℓ_slh ≤ 0.16L
The additional impact assessment must cover filling levels from 0.05 h_tk to 0.95 h_tk (0.9 m to 17.1 m) and/or 0.05 h_tk to h_part

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch10.Sec4 [1.2.1] defines the filling height cases for sloshing compliance and references Ch.4 Sec.6 for the definitions of ρ_L, f_cd, and ρ_part needed to compute h_part. The answerer must navigate from the sloshing section to the internal loads section to retrieve the correct density and factor values, then apply the h_part formula.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Start at Pt3.Ch10.Sec4 [1.2.1]: The filling height requirements for sloshing state that for cargo tanks with cargo density equal to ρ_part, all filling levels up to h_part must be assessed, where h_part = (h_tk × ρ_L × f_cd) / ρ_part. The variables ρ_L and f_cd are explicitly referenced to Ch.4 Sec.6. Step 2 — Navigate to Pt3.Ch4.Sec6 Symbols: ρ_L for strength assessment is normally 1.025 t/m³, but if a tank filled at 98% is intended to carry heavier liquid than 1.025 (i.e. ρ_max-LM > 1.025), then ρ_L = ρ_max-LM. Since ρ_max-LM = 1.6 t/m³ > 1.025, ρ_L = 1.6 t/m³. Step 3 — f_cd from Ch.4 Sec.6: f_cd = 0.88 applies only for strength assessment with FE analysis of cargo tanks filled with oil or oil products with ρ_L ≤ 1.025 t/m³. Since ρ_L = 1.6 t/m³ (not oil/oil product at ≤1.025), f_cd = 1.0. Step 4 — Compute h_part: h_part = (18 × 1.6 × 1.0) / 1.6 = 18 m = h_tk. This means the partial filling restriction does not reduce the required assessment range below the full tank height in this case. Step 5 — Liquid impact assessment: Per Pt3.Ch10.Sec4 [1.1.5], since b_slh = 0.60B > 0.56B AND ℓ_slh = 0.14L falls in the range 0.13L < ℓ_slh ≤ 0.16L, an additional liquid impact load assessment is required. The filling level range is 0.05 h_tk to 0.95 h_tk (i.e., 0.9 m to 17.1 m) and/or 0.05 h_tk to h_part.

question_text: A designer is calculating the scantlings for a longitudinal stiffener on the inner bottom of a bulk carrier. The stiffener has a flat bar profile with a web height of 200 mm and a web thickness of 12 mm (as-built). The owner has specified a voluntary corrosion addition of 0.5 mm on top of the rule-required corrosion addition. The rule-required net thickness for the web is 10.8 mm, and the applicable corrosion addition for this structural member is 1.5 mm on each side (tc1 = tc2 = 1.5 mm). The designer needs to determine: (1) the gross required thickness of the web, (2) whether the as-built web thickness of 12 mm is compliant, and (3) what value of nominal yield stress RY should be used in subsequent strength calculations if the stiffener is fabricated from normal-strength steel with a material factor k = 1.0. Show all intermediate steps.
required_facts: tc = tc1 + tc2 = 1.5 + 1.5 = 3.0 mm (total corrosion addition for two-sided member)
tgr_off = tas_built − tvol_add = 12.0 − 0.5 = 11.5 mm
The stiffener web is NOT compliant because tgr_off (11.5 mm) < tgr (13.5 mm)
RY is not defined in the net scantling section and must be looked up in the general symbols section
RY = 235/k = 235/1.0 = 235 N/mm² for normal-strength steel

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Pt3.Ch3.Sec2 which defines gross/net scantling formulas and references Ch.1 Sec.4 for symbols not defined locally; the symbol RY (nominal yield stress) is only defined in Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 3, requiring the answerer to follow the cross-reference to resolve the final part of the question.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Gross required thickness (Pt3.Ch3.Sec2 [1.2.1]): tgr = min(t + tc ; 1.25t) where t = 10.8 mm and tc = tc1 + tc2 = 1.5 + 1.5 = 3.0 mm. So tgr = min(10.8 + 3.0 ; 1.25 × 10.8) = min(13.8 ; 13.5) = 13.5 mm. Rounded to nearest 0.5 mm per [1.3.1]: 13.5 mm. Step 2 — Gross offered thickness (Pt3.Ch3.Sec2 [1.2.2]): tgr_off = tas_built − tvol_add = 12.0 − 0.5 = 11.5 mm. Compliance check per [1.3.2]: tgr_off (11.5 mm) < tgr (13.5 mm) → NOT COMPLIANT. Step 3 — Nominal yield stress RY: The symbol RY is not defined in Pt3.Ch3.Sec2; the section header states 'For symbols not defined in this section, see Ch.1 Sec.4'. Consulting Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 3: RY = 235/k = 235/1.0 = 235 N/mm².

question_text: A newbuilding bulk carrier of 145 m length has an anchor windlass fitted on the exposed forecastle deck at 8 m above the summer load waterline. The forecastle deck is located within the forward 0.25L of the ship. The windlass is equipped with a chain stopper, and the minimum breaking strength (BS) of the anchor chain cable is 1 850 kN. The designer proposes to assess the windlass foundation supporting structure using a grillage analysis, and the steel used for the foundation has a yield strength R_eH of 315 N/mm². During the design review, the Society requests the submission of documentation for the windlass and chain stopper. (1) What design load, in kN, must the windlass foundation be designed to resist for the anchoring operation load case? (2) What is the maximum permissible normal stress in the supporting structure under that load case? (3) Must the foundation also be checked against green sea loads, and why or why not? (4) What compliance documentation must be submitted for the anchor windlass, and who issues the product certificate?
required_facts: Windlass design load for anchoring operation = 45% of BS = 832.5 kN (because a chain stopper is provided)
Maximum permissible normal stress for grillage analysis = 0.9 × R_eH = 0.9 × 315 = 283.5 N/mm²
Green sea load check is required because the ship is 145 m (≥ 80 m) and the deck height of 8 m is less than the threshold of 14.5 m (= 0.1 × 145 m)
The anchor windlass requires a product certificate (PC) issued by the Society
Material certificates (MC) from the Society are required for the cable lifter, drum, shaft, clutch, brake, and gear of the windlass
Documentation requirements for the windlass and chain stopper are cross-referenced from the supporting structure section back to the compliance documentation table in the general verification chapter

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch1.Sec3 Table 1 and Table 2 specify the documentation submission requirements for anchor windlasses and chain stoppers (compliance documents, product certificates issued by the Society). Ch.11 Sec.2 then governs the actual scantling design: design loads for anchoring operation (45% BS when chain stopper is provided), acceptance criteria for normal stress (0.9 R_eH for beam/grillage), and the green sea load applicability threshold (ship length ≥ 80 m AND deck height < 0.1L or 22 m above summer load waterline).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Documentation (Pt3.Ch1.Sec3 Table 2): Anchor windlasses require an MC (material certificate) from the Society for cable lifter, drum, shaft, clutch, brake, gear; and an MD (manufacturer declaration) for the frame. A product certificate (PC) is issued by the Society. Associated electrical equipment must comply with Pt.4 Ch.8 Sec.1 Table 8. Step 2 — Design load (Pt3.Ch11.Sec2 [2.3.1]): Chain stopper is provided → windlass load case = 45% of BS = 0.45 × 1850 = 832.5 kN. Step 3 — Acceptance criteria (Pt3.Ch11.Sec2 [2.4.2](a)): Grillage analysis → permissible normal stress = 0.9 R_eH = 0.9 × 315 = 283.5 N/mm². Step 4 — Green sea check (Pt3.Ch11.Sec2 [2.5.1]): Applies to ships ≥ 80 m (145 m qualifies) where deck height < 0.1L or 22 m (whichever lesser). 0.1 × 145 = 14.5 m; lesser of 14.5 m and 22 m = 14.5 m. Deck is at 8 m < 14.5 m → green sea check IS required.

question_text: A 175 m ro-ro vessel is being designed with a stern bottom structure. The lower shell in the stern region has a flare angle of 65°. The ship has a block coefficient CB = 0.62, a design minimum ballast draught at the aft end TBA = 4.2 m, and the position being assessed is 12 m forward of the aft end. At this position, the shell is 0.8 m below the ballast waterline. The designer needs to calculate the design stern slamming pressure PSS at this location. What is the value of the wave coefficient CW to be used in the pressure formula, and what is the resulting design stern slamming pressure PSS in kN/m²? Also confirm whether the stern slamming strengthening requirements apply to this vessel and location.
required_facts: CW = 10.75 − ((300 − L)/100)^1.5 applies for 90 ≤ L ≤ 300, giving CW ≈ 9.35 for L = 175 m
Stern slamming requirements apply because L = 175 m > 150 m
The vessel must be strengthened for plating, stiffeners, and primary supporting members because the flare angle (65°) exceeds 60°
The position X = 12 m is within 0.1L = 17.5 m forward of A.E., so the stern slamming zone applies
C = 0.18 × (CW − 2 × ho) is capped at 1.0 for this location
PSS ≈ 316 kN/m² (approximately 310–320 kN/m² acceptable given rounding)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Stern slamming section requires CW (wave coefficient) for the PSS formula, which is defined in Ch.4 Sec.4.
