The answerer must navigate from the stern slamming pressure formula to the hull girder loads section to retrieve the correct CW expression for the given ship length.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Check applicability: L = 175 m > 150 m, so stern slamming requirements apply per [1.1.1]. Flare angle = 65° > 60°, so the vessel (ro-ro) must be strengthened per [1.1.2] for plating, stiffeners, and primary supporting members. The position X = 12 m forward of A.E. is within 0.1L = 17.5 m forward of A.E., so [1.1.3] confirms the requirements apply at this location. Step 2 — Find CW: The PSS formula in [2.1] requires CW = wave coefficient as given in Ch.4 Sec.4. From Ch.4 Sec.4 Symbols, for 90 ≤ L ≤ 300: CW = 10.75 − ((300 − L)/100)^1.5. With L = 175 m: CW = 10.75 − ((300 − 175)/100)^1.5 = 10.75 − (1.25)^1.5 = 10.75 − 1.3975 ≈ 9.353. Step 3 — Compute intermediate parameters: ho = −0.8 m (shell is below waterline, but ho is positive downwards from waterline to shell; shell is 0.8 m below waterline means ho = −0.8 m, i.e. shell is submerged). Wait — re-reading: ho = vertical distance positive downwards from waterline TBA to shell. If shell is 0.8 m below the waterline, ho = +0.8 m (downward is positive, shell is below waterline). C = 0.18 × (CW − 2 × ho) = 0.18 × (9.353 − 2 × 0.8) = 0.18 × (9.353 − 1.6) = 0.18 × 7.753 = 1.3955 → capped at maximum 1.0. So C = 1.0. a0 = (3 × CW / L) + 0.16 = (3 × 9.353 / 175) + 0.16 = (28.059 / 175) + 0.16 = 0.1603 + 0.16 = 0.3203. Step 4 — Compute PSS: PSS = 2.2 × C × L × (0.6 + (1.65 × a0 × (0.55L − X) × sin³α) / (CB × L))². With C = 1.0, L = 175, X = 12, α = 65°, CB = 0.62: sin(65°) = 0.9063, sin³(65°) = 0.7451. 0.55L = 96.25 m; 0.55L − X = 96.25 − 12 = 84.25 m. Numerator: 1.65 × 0.3203 × 84.25 × 0.7451 = 1.65 × 0.3203 × 62.77 = 1.65 × 20.10 = 33.17. Denominator: CB × L = 0.62 × 175 = 108.5. Fraction = 33.17 / 108.5 = 0.3058. Inner term = 0.6 + 0.3058 = 0.9058. PSS = 2.2 × 1.0 × 175 × (0.9058)² = 385 × 0.8205 = 315.9 kN/m². Step 5 — Check upper bound: PSS_max = 2.2 × C × L × (0.6 + 1.65 × a0 / (2 × CB))³ = 2.2 × 1.0 × 175 × (0.6 + 1.65 × 0.3203 / (2 × 0.62))³ = 385 × (0.6 + 0.5283 / 1.24)³ = 385 × (0.6 + 0.4261)³ = 385 × (1.0261)³ = 385 × 1.0803 = 415.9 kN/m². Since 315.9 < 415.9, the upper bound does not govern. PSS ≈ 316 kN/m².

question_text: A naval architect is performing a cargo hold finite element analysis for a 175-metre bulk carrier with a conventional midship cargo hold arrangement. The FE model covers three cargo hold lengths and uses a standard s×s mesh throughout. During post-processing, several web girder elements in the mid-hold evaluation area show von Mises stresses approaching the yield acceptance limit. The web girders contain circular cut-outs for pipe passages that were not explicitly modelled in the FE mesh — each cut-out has a diameter of 420 mm in a web of total height 1800 mm, and the effective web height after deducting all openings including stiffener slots is 1350 mm. The element shear stress at these locations reads 95 N/mm² before any correction. The designer argues that because the cut-outs were not modelled, no correction is needed and the raw FE stresses can be used directly against the yield criteria. Is the designer's position correct? What corrected shear stress value must be used for the von Mises yield check at these elements, and what broader design-basis principle governs the requirement to document and submit the assumptions underlying this structural assessment?
required_facts: The designer's position is incorrect — shear stress correction for unmodelled cut-outs is mandatory
h = 1800 mm because the cut-out geometry was not modelled (full web height applies)
h_eff = 1350 mm (effective web height after deducting all openings including stiffener slots)
The corrected shear stress of ~126.7 N/mm² must be used to compute von Mises stress for the yield check
The design basis, including modelling assumptions such as omission of cut-outs, must be documented and submitted as part of design review and approval, and all changes formally advised

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Pt3.Ch7.Sec3 shear stress correction for cut-outs (4.2.7), which requires use of heff from Ch.3 Sec.7 [1.4.7]; the broader obligation to document and submit the design basis — including the assumptions about what is and is not modelled — is governed by Pt3.Ch1.Sec2 [3.1.2].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify that the cut-outs were not modelled in the FE mesh. Pt3.Ch7.Sec3 [4.2.7] states that element shear stress in way of cut-outs in webs shall be corrected for loss in shear area even when the geometry of the opening is not modelled. The formula is τ_cor = (h / h_eff) × τ_elem. Step 2 — Apply the formula: h = 1800 mm (total web height, since the opening geometry is NOT modelled, h is the full web height), h_eff = 1350 mm (effective web height deducting all openings including stiffener slots), τ_elem = 95 N/mm². Therefore τ_cor = (1800 / 1350) × 95 = 1.333 × 95 = 126.7 N/mm². Step 3 — The designer's position is incorrect; the correction is mandatory regardless of whether the cut-out is modelled. Step 4 — Cross-chapter link: Pt3.Ch1.Sec2 [3.1.2] requires that the design basis used for each ship — including all modelling assumptions — shall be documented and submitted as part of the design review and approval, and all changes formally advised. This principle underpins the obligation to declare that cut-outs were omitted from the model and to apply the prescribed correction.

question_text: A newbuilding bulk carrier with a scantling draught of 14.5 m and a design life of 20 years is being reviewed for classification. The designer has proposed using a net scantling approach for the main deck plating, calculating a net required thickness of 14.2 mm. The corrosion addition for the deck plating exposed to weather is 1.5 mm on one side. The designer proposes an as-built thickness of 16.0 mm with no voluntary addition. Is the proposed design life acceptable under the classification rules, and does the gross offered thickness of the deck plating comply with the gross required thickness? Show your derivation of the gross required thickness and the gross offered thickness, and state whether each parameter is compliant.
required_facts: The minimum design life required by the rules is 25 years
The proposed design life of 20 years is non-compliant
Gross required thickness tgr = min(t + tc; 1.25t) = min(15.7; 17.75) = 15.7 mm, rounded to 15.5 mm
Gross offered thickness tgr_off = 16.0 mm (as-built minus zero voluntary addition)
The gross offered thickness of 16.0 mm meets or exceeds the gross required thickness of 15.5 mm — plating is compliant
No credit is given for coatings in the structural capability assessment

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch1.Sec2 [3.4] establishes the minimum design life of 25 years; the designer's proposed 20-year design life is non-compliant. The same section's design basis requirements (Pt3.Ch1.Sec2 [3.1.2]) require the design basis to be documented and submitted. The scantling compliance check then requires navigating to Pt3.Ch3.Sec2 to apply the net scantling approach: gross required thickness is min(t + tc; 1.25t) = min(14.2 + 1.5; 1.25 × 14.2) = min(15.7; 17.75) = 15.7 mm, rounded to nearest 0.5 mm = 15.5 mm (since 15.7 rounds to 15.5 under the rounding rule in [1.3.1]: 15.25 ≤ 15.7 < 15.75 → 15.5 mm). Gross offered thickness = as-built − vol_add = 16.0 − 0 = 16.0 mm. Since 16.0 ≥ 15.5, the plating thickness is compliant. However, the design life of 20 years is non-compliant as it falls below the 25-year minimum.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 (Pt3.Ch1.Sec2 [3.4]): Minimum design life is 25 years. The proposed 20-year design life is below this minimum — non-compliant. Step 2 (Pt3.Ch3.Sec2 [1.2.1]): Gross required thickness tgr = min(t + tc; 1.25t) = min(14.2 + 1.5; 1.25 × 14.2) = min(15.7; 17.75) = 15.7 mm. Step 3 (Pt3.Ch3.Sec2 [1.3.1]): Round to nearest 0.5 mm: 15.25 ≤ 15.7 < 15.75, so tgr = 15.5 mm. Step 4 (Pt3.Ch3.Sec2 [1.2.2]): tgr_off = tas_built − tvol_add = 16.0 − 0 = 16.0 mm. Step 5 (Pt3.Ch3.Sec2 [1.3.2]): 16.0 mm ≥ 15.5 mm — plating thickness is compliant. Conclusion: Design life is non-compliant; plating scantling is compliant.

question_text:
A new-build general cargo vessel has L = 140 m. During detailed design review, the naval architect is sizing the plate stem. The stem plate is stiffened by horizontal breasthooks spaced at S_B = 1.8 m. The steel used for the stem has a minimum yield strength of 315 MPa (k = 0.78). The as-built plate thickness proposed by the builder is 22.0 mm, and the builder has declared a voluntary addition of 0.5 mm on top of the corrosion addition. The corrosion addition t_c for this location is 3.0 mm.

The surveyor needs to confirm two things: (1) whether the net required thickness formula gives a value that, when converted to a gross required thickness, is satisfied by the as-built plate; and (2) whether the gross required thickness must be capped at the upper-bound formula rather than the direct formula result. Determine the net required thickness t, the gross required thickness t_gr, and state whether the as-built plate of 22.0 mm is compliant.
required_facts: Net required thickness t ≈ 16.18 mm (from the plate stem formula with S_B = 1.8 m, L = 140 m, k = 0.78)
The upper-bound cap evaluates to approximately 18.43 mm and does not govern because t < cap
Gross required thickness t_gr = min(t + t_c ; 1.25t) = min(19.18 ; 20.23) ≈ 19.18 mm, rounded to 19.0 mm
Gross offered thickness t_gr_off = 22.0 - 0.5 = 21.5 mm
The as-built plate of 22.0 mm is compliant because t_gr_off (21.5 mm) ≥ t_gr

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch10.Sec6 [1.1.1] gives the net thickness formula for the plate stem and its upper-bound cap. The result is a net required thickness. To check compliance against the as-built plate, the answerer must apply the net scantling approach from Pt3.Ch3.Sec2 [1.2.1], which defines how to convert net required thickness to gross required thickness via t_gr = min(t + t_c ; 1.25t), and then compare against the gross offered thickness derived from the as-built minus voluntary addition.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Compute net required thickness from Pt3.Ch10.Sec6 [1.1.1]:
  t = (0.6 + 0.4 × 1.8) × (0.08 × 140 + 2.7) × sqrt(0.78)
    = (0.6 + 0.72) × (11.2 + 2.7) × 0.8832
    = 1.32 × 13.9 × 0.8832
    = 16.18 mm

Step 2 — Check upper bound cap:
  t_max = 22 × sqrt(0.78) - 1 = 22 × 0.8832 - 1 = 19.43 - 1 = 18.43 mm
  Since 16.18 mm < 18.43 mm, the cap does not govern; net required thickness t = 16.18 mm.

Step 3 — Convert to gross required thickness using Pt3.Ch3.Sec2 [1.2.1]:
  t_gr = min(t + t_c ; 1.25t) = min(16.18 + 3.0 ; 1.25 × 16.18) = min(19.18 ; 20.23) = 19.18 mm
  Rounded to nearest 0.5 mm → t_gr = 19.5 mm (per [1.3.1]).

Step 4 — Determine gross offered thickness:
  t_gr_off = t_as_built - t_vol_add = 22.0 - 0.5 = 21.5 mm

Step 5 — Compliance check:
  t_gr_off (21.5 mm) ≥ t_gr (19.5 mm) → COMPLIANT.

question_text: A naval architect is designing the rudder system for a new 145-metre general cargo vessel. The vessel's maximum continuous rated (MCR) power drives it to a top speed of 16.5 knots in calm water at the scantling draught. The owner's specification lists the 'maximum ahead service speed' as 16.5 knots for use in all rudder scantling calculations. A junior engineer on the team argues that the value to be used in the rudder force calculations should instead be taken as the maximum speed the vessel can physically reach under any condition, which they estimate at 17.8 knots based on model tests in light ballast condition. Which speed value is correct for use in the rudder scantling calculations, what is the precise definition of that speed parameter as it applies to rudder design, and what are the units in which it must be expressed?
required_facts: The correct speed to use in rudder scantling calculations is the maximum ahead service speed V = 16.5 knots, not 17.8 knots.
Maximum ahead service speed is defined as the maximum service speed V, with the definition of V found in the symbols and definitions section of the hull rules.
The symbol V is defined as 'maximum service speed' and its unit is knots.
The 17.8-knot light-ballast model-test speed is not the correct value because it does not correspond to the defined maximum service speed.
The cross-reference from the rudder chapter to the symbols and definitions chapter is required to confirm the precise meaning and units of V.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch14.Sec1 [1.2.2] defines 'maximum ahead service speed' as the maximum service speed V and explicitly cross-references Ch.1 Sec.4 [3.1.8] for the definition of V. Ch.1 Sec.4 Table 2 defines V as 'maximum service speed' in knots — not the maximum physically attainable speed in any loading condition.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Pt3.Ch14.Sec1 [1.2.2] states 'Maximum ahead service speed is the maximum service speed V, see Ch.1 Sec.4 [3.1.8].' Step 2: Navigate to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 and locate [3.1.8] / Table 2 which defines V as 'maximum service speed' in knots. Step 3: The definition ties V to the maximum service speed — not the maximum speed achievable in any loading condition. Step 4: Therefore the owner's specification value of 16.5 knots (maximum ahead service speed at scantling draught) is the correct input, not the 17.8 knots light-ballast model-test figure. Step 5: The units are knots.

scenario_parameters.junior_engineer_basis: model tests in light ballast condition

question_text:
A 185 m ro-ro vessel is being designed with a stern bottom structure. The lower shell in the stern region has a flare angle of 65°. The design minimum ballast draught at the aft end is 3.2 m, and the shell at the position being evaluated sits 0.8 m below that waterline (i.e., the shell is submerged at ballast draught). The position under evaluation is 12 m forward of the aft end. The block coefficient at scantling draught is 0.62, and the wave coefficient CW for this vessel is 9.4.

The designer proposes to use flat bar stiffeners running longitudinally in the stern bottom, supported by transverse web frames. No tripping brackets are currently shown on the drawings.

For the stiffener scantling check, the designer applies a design pressure equal to the full stern slamming pressure PSS. Is this correct? Additionally, are tripping brackets required for the stiffeners and web frames, and what symbol definition source must be consulted for any symbol used in the stern slamming calculations that is not explicitly defined in the stern slamming rules themselves?
required_facts: The stiffener design pressure for stern slamming is 0.5 × PSS, not the full PSS — the designer's assumption is incorrect
Tripping brackets are required for both stiffeners and primary supporting members in the stern slamming zone
The tripping bracket requirement references the bow impact section of the same chapter (Sec.1 [4.1]) for the detailed criteria
Symbols not defined within the stern slamming rules must be sourced from the general Symbols and Definitions section in Chapter 1 of Part 3
The vessel qualifies for the special flare-angle category (65° > 60°) as a ro-ro vessel, triggering strengthening requirements for plating, stiffeners, and primary supporting members

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Stern slamming section (Pt3.Ch10.Sec3) references Sec.1 (Pt3.Ch10.Sec1) for stiffener scantling method and tripping bracket requirements, and references Ch.1 Sec.4 (Pt3.Ch1.Sec4) for symbol definitions not given locally.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Applicability: The vessel is 185 m > 150 m, so stern slamming rules apply. The flare angle is 65° > 60°, so the vessel falls under the special category (ro-ro vessel with flare > 60°), requiring strengthening per [3.1], [3.2.1], and [3.3.1].

Step 2 — Stiffener design pressure: Pt3.Ch10.Sec3 [3.2.1] states that stiffener strengthening shall be according to Sec.1 [3.2] using Pst = 0.5 × PSS, NOT the full PSS. The designer's use of full PSS for stiffeners is therefore incorrect; the correct pressure is 0.5 PSS.

Step 3 — Tripping brackets: Pt3.Ch10.Sec3 [3.4] states that stiffeners and primary supporting members shall be supported by tripping brackets in accordance with Sec.1 [4.1]. Sec.1 here is Pt3.Ch10.Sec1 (Bow Impact section of the same chapter), which contains the tripping bracket requirements at [4.1]. Therefore tripping brackets ARE required.

Step 4 — Symbol definitions: The Symbols preamble of Pt3.Ch10.Sec3 explicitly states 'For symbols not defined in this section, see Ch.1 Sec.4.' This leads to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 (Symbols and Definitions), which provides the master symbol table including primary symbols (Table 1), ship main data (Table 2), materials (Table 3), and loads (Table 4). Any symbol used in the stern slamming pressure formula not locally defined (e.g., CB, ao, general pressure symbol P, etc.) must be looked up there.

question_text: A 180-metre general cargo ship (L = 180 m) is being designed with a sea chest integrated into the side shell at approximately 2.0 m below the scantling draft waterline. The sea chest boundary plating is fabricated from ordinary mild steel (k = 1.0). The longest unsupported panel span on the sea chest boundary is b = 600 mm. The design team proposes a net plate thickness of 9.5 mm for the sea chest boundary plating, citing only the blow-out pressure formula with a blow-out pressure of 2 bar. A surveyor questions whether this thickness is sufficient, noting that sea chest boundaries must also satisfy the general minimum thickness requirements for side shell structure. Determine whether the proposed 9.5 mm net thickness is compliant with all applicable requirements, and state the governing minimum net thickness.
required_facts: Sea chest boundary plating must satisfy both the blow-out pressure formula and the general minimum thickness requirements for side shell / sea chest boundaries
Blow-out pressure formula gives t ≈ 10.2 mm (using b = 600 mm, Po = 2 bar, k = 1.0)
General minimum thickness for sea chest boundaries uses coefficients a = 4.5 and b = 0.035
General minimum thickness = 4.5 + 0.035 × 180 × sqrt(1.0) = 10.8 mm
The governing minimum net thickness is 10.8 mm
The proposed 9.5 mm net thickness is non-compliant with both requirements

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch10.Sec6 [3.2.1] states that sea chest plating strength shall comply with the minimum thickness requirements for side structure in Ch.6 Sec.3, in addition to the blow-out pressure formula in [3.2.2]. The answerer must therefore evaluate the sea chest boundary against Ch.6 Sec.3 Table 1 (sea chest boundaries row: a=4.5, b=0.05) as well as the blow-out formula.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Blow-out pressure formula (Pt3.Ch10.Sec6 [3.2.2]): t = 0.012 × b × sqrt(Po × k) = 0.012 × 600 × sqrt(2 × 1.0) = 7.2 × 1.4142 ≈ 10.18 mm. So the blow-out formula alone already requires ~10.2 mm, which exceeds the proposed 9.5 mm. Step 2 — Minimum thickness per Ch.6 Sec.3 Table 1 (sea chest boundaries): a = 4.5, b = 0.05, L2 = min(L, 300) = 180 m. t_min = 4.5 + 0.05 × 180 × sqrt(1.0) = 4.5 + 9.0 = 13.5 mm. Step 3 — Governing value: max(10.18, 13.5) = 13.5 mm. The proposed 9.5 mm is non-compliant on both counts; the governing requirement is 13.5 mm from the general minimum thickness rule for sea chest boundaries.

question_text: A 95-metre general cargo vessel is being designed with a double bottom extending from the collision bulkhead to the aft peak bulkhead. The ship has a moulded breadth B of 16 m. In the fore peak region, forward of the collision bulkhead, the designer proposes to fit a centreline floor. What is the minimum required depth of that floor at the centreline, and what formula or value governs it? Additionally, confirm whether the minimum double bottom height hDB for this vessel is governed by the formula-derived value or the absolute minimum, and state the numerical result.
required_facts: The minimum fore peak centreline floor depth equals the required double bottom height hDB
hDB is calculated as 1000 · B/20, with a minimum of 760 mm and a maximum of 2000 mm
800 mm exceeds the 760 mm absolute minimum, so the formula-derived value governs
800 mm is below the 2000 mm cap, so no capping applies
The minimum required depth of the centreline floor in the fore peak is 800 mm

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The fore peak floor depth requirement in Pt3.Ch3.Sec5 [6.2.1] explicitly references Ch.2 Sec.3 [2.3] for the required double bottom depth, which contains the hDB formula. The answerer must navigate from the structural arrangement section to the compartment arrangement section to retrieve the formula and compute the result.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec5 [6.2.1] states: 'The minimum depth of the floor at the centreline shall not be less than the required depth of the double bottom, see Ch.2 Sec.3 [2.3].' Step 2 — Navigate to Pt3.Ch2.Sec3 [2.3], which gives hDB = 1000 · B/20, minimum 760 mm, maximum 2000 mm. Step 3 — Compute: hDB = 1000 × 16/20 = 800 mm. Step 4 — Check bounds: 800 mm > 760 mm (minimum), 800 mm < 2000 mm (maximum), so the formula-derived value governs. Step 5 — Therefore the minimum depth of the centreline floor in the fore peak is 800 mm.

scenario_parameters.double_bottom_extent: collision bulkhead to aft peak bulkhead

question_text: A 185 m general cargo vessel is being designed with a pronounced flared bow. At a cross-section located 0.12L from the forward end, the side shell has a flare angle of 44° measured between a vertical line and the tangential plane of the side plating. At 0.17L from the forward end, the same measurement yields a flare angle of 42°. The ship's designer claims that the bow impact strengthening zone need only extend to 0.15L from the forward end. Is this claim correct? Additionally, the structural assessment of the bow region requires a partial ship finite element analysis. The FE model uses rod elements throughout to represent all stiffeners, including primary supporting members and their face plates. Is this modelling approach acceptable under classification rules, and if not, what element types are required for the stiffeners?
required_facts: The bow impact strengthening zone must extend to 0.20L from the forward end if the flare angle at 0.15L from the forward end exceeds 40°
The flare angle α > 40° at 0.15L from F.E. requires extension to 0.20L
The designer's claim that 0.15L is sufficient cannot be confirmed or refuted without the actual flare angle at 0.15L
Stiffeners in the partial ship FE model must be modelled with beam elements having axial, torsional, bi-directional shear and bending stiffness
The eccentricity of the neutral axis must be modelled for stiffeners
Rod elements alone are not acceptable for general stiffeners; only sniped stiffeners and face plates of PSMs and brackets may use beam or rod elements
Shell elements are required to represent plates in the FE model

annotator_grounding.end_clause: Pt3.Ch10.Sec2 [2.1.1] → Pt3.Ch7.Sec3 [4.2] (via model requirements for partial ship FE analysis)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec1 [1.1.3] defines the extent of bow impact strengthening and references Sec2 [2.1.1] for the definition of flare angle α. The extension rules in [1.1.3] require checking α at 0.10L, 0.15L, and potentially 0.20L. Since α > 40° at both 0.12L (proxy for the 0.15L threshold check) and 0.17L, the zone must extend to 0.20L. The FE modelling requirements for partial ship analysis are governed by Pt3.Ch7.Sec3 [2.1.1], which mandates shell elements for plates and beam elements (with full stiffness properties) for stiffeners — rod elements alone are insufficient.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Pt3.Ch10.Sec1 [1.1.3] states the strengthening shall extend forward of 0.1L. If α > 40° at 0.10L from F.E., extend to 0.15L. If α > 40° at 0.15L from F.E., extend to 0.20L. Step 2: The flare angle α is defined in Sec2 [2.1.1] (cross-reference within same chapter). Step 3: At 0.12L the flare angle is 44° > 40°, triggering extension to 0.15L. At 0.17L the flare angle is 42° > 40°, triggering further extension to 0.20L. Therefore the designer's claim that 0.15L suffices is incorrect — the zone must reach 0.20L. Step 4: For the FE modelling question, Pt3.Ch7.Sec3 [2.1.1] (partial ship structural analysis model requirements) states shell elements shall be used for plates, and stiffeners shall be modelled with beam elements having axial, torsional, bi-directional shear and bending stiffness, with eccentricity of neutral axis modelled. Sniped stiffeners and face plates of PSMs and brackets shall use beam or rod elements. Using rod elements for all stiffeners (including primary supporting members) is not acceptable — beam elements with full stiffness properties are required for stiffeners generally.

scenario_parameters.FE_stiffener_element_type_required: beam elements with axial, torsional, bi-directional shear and bending stiffness

question_text: A designer is calculating the total internal pressure acting on the boundary of a ballast tank aboard a 180 m general cargo vessel. The tank has its highest point at z = 14.5 m above the reference coordinate system baseline, and the load point under consideration is located at z = 6.2 m. The tank is fitted with a pressure relief valve, and the design overpressure PPV is set at 30 kN/m². For the static design load scenario (S), the liquid density ρL is taken as 1.025 t/m³ and gravitational acceleration g = 9.81 m/s². The designer also needs to confirm the correct symbol and unit for the total internal pressure Pin that will be used in subsequent structural checks. What is the total static internal pressure Pin acting on the load point, and what are the correct symbol and unit for Pin as used throughout the structural rules?
required_facts: Pin is the symbol for total internal pressure due to liquid, with unit kN/m²
The definition and formula for Pin are found in Ch.4 Sec.6 [1], as cross-referenced from the symbols table
For the static (S) scenario, Pin equals the static liquid pressure Pℓs
For a tank with a pressure relief valve, the static pressure formula is Pℓs = fcd·ρL·g·(ztop − z) + PPV
fcd = 1.0 for ballast water (not oil/oil products with ρL ≤ 1.025 t/m³)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The symbol Pin and its unit are defined in Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 4 (Loads), which references Ch.4 Sec.6 [1] for the definition of total internal pressure due to liquid. The answerer must follow that cross-reference into Ch4.Sec6 to find the actual formula for static pressure Pℓs-1 for a tank with a pressure relief valve, then compute Pin = Pℓs = fcd·ρL·g·(ztop − z) + PPV.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — In Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 4, the symbol Pin is listed as 'total internal pressure due to liquid, see Ch.4 Sec.6 [1]' with unit kN/m². This tells the answerer that the definition and formula live in Ch4.Sec6.

Step 2 — Navigate to Pt3.Ch4.Sec6 [1.1.1]: for the static (S) design load scenario, Pin = Pℓs (the static liquid pressure).

Step 3 — In Pt3.Ch4.Sec6 [1.2.1], for a tank with a pressure relief valve, the static pressure is: Pℓs-1 = fcd·ρL·g·(ztop − z) + PPV.

Step 4 — Identify fcd: for strength assessment with a tank filled with ballast water (not oil/oil products with ρL ≤ 1.025), fcd = 1.0.

Step 5 — Substitute values: Pℓs = 1.0 × 1.025 × 9.81 × (14.5 − 6.2) + 30 = 1.025 × 9.81 × 8.3 + 30 = 83.44 + 30 = 113.44 kN/m² ≈ 113.4 kN/m².

Step 6 — Confirm: Pin symbol has unit kN/m² per Table 4 in Ch1.Sec4.

question_text: A newbuilding bulk carrier has a transverse web frame with an attached side shell plate. The designer proposes an as-built plate thickness of 14.5 mm for this side shell plating. The applicable net required thickness calculated from the structural rules is 11.8 mm, and the corrosion addition for this location is 2.5 mm. The owner has specified a voluntary corrosion margin of 0.5 mm on top of the standard corrosion addition. Determine whether the proposed as-built thickness of 14.5 mm is compliant with the classification rules for plating scantlings, showing the gross required thickness (rounded to the nearest half millimetre), the gross offered thickness after accounting for the voluntary addition, and the net offered thickness.
required_facts: Gross required thickness t_gr = min(11.8 + 2.5, 1.25 × 11.8) = min(14.3, 14.75) = 14.3 mm, rounded to 14.5 mm
Gross offered thickness t_gr_off = 14.5 − 0.5 = 14.0 mm (voluntary addition is deducted from as-built thickness)
Net offered thickness t_off = 14.0 − 2.5 = 11.5 mm
Compliance requires gross offered thickness ≥ gross required thickness, i.e. 14.0 mm ≥ 14.5 mm
The arrangement is NOT compliant because 14.0 mm < 14.5 mm
The voluntary addition (owner's extra margin) is excluded from the compliance comparison and does not count toward meeting the gross required thickness

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 defines the elementary plate panel (EPP) and references Ch.1 Sec.4 for undefined symbols; the structural idealisation section references the net scantling approach in Pt3.Ch3.Sec2, which governs how gross and net thicknesses are defined, calculated, and compared for compliance. The answerer must navigate from the structural idealisation context (Sec7) into the net scantling compliance rules (Sec2) to determine whether the offered thickness satisfies the gross required thickness criterion.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Compute gross required thickness using Pt3.Ch3.Sec2 [1.2.1]: t_gr = min(t + t_c ; 1.25t) = min(11.8 + 2.5 ; 1.25 × 11.8) = min(14.3 ; 14.75) = 14.3 mm. Round to nearest half millimetre per [1.3.1]: 14.3 falls in [14.25, 14.75), so t_gr_required = 14.5 mm. Step 2 — Compute gross offered thickness per [1.2.2]: t_gr_off = t_as_built − t_vol_add = 14.5 − 0.5 = 14.0 mm. Step 3 — Compute net offered thickness per [1.2.3]: t_off = t_gr_off − t_c = 14.0 − 2.5 = 11.5 mm. Step 4 — Apply compliance check per [1.3.2]: gross offered thickness (14.0 mm) must be ≥ gross required thickness (14.5 mm). Since 14.0 < 14.5, the arrangement is NOT compliant. The as-built thickness of 14.5 mm is insufficient once the voluntary addition is excluded from the compliance comparison.

question_text: A 145 m general cargo vessel is being designed with an anchor windlass installed on the exposed forecastle deck, 18 m aft of the forward perpendicular. The forecastle deck is 8.5 m above the summer load waterline. The windlass foundation and supporting girders are fabricated from carbon-manganese steel. The supporting girders are located within the chain locker space on one side and exposed to the external atmosphere on the other side. A finite element analysis is performed to assess the strength of the windlass foundation under anchoring loads. The windlass is fitted with a chain stopper, and the minimum breaking strength of the chain cable is 1 850 kN. Determine the total corrosion addition tc that must be deducted from the gross scantlings of the supporting girder when evaluating net scantlings for the FEA strength check, and confirm whether the Von Mises stress limit used in the FEA is correct at 1.0 ReH.
required_facts: tc is determined by deducting corrosion addition from gross scantlings per the corrosion addition rules in Ch.3 Sec.3
tc = tc1 + tc2 + tres, where tc1 and tc2 are the one-side corrosion additions for each exposed face
The chain locker side contributes tc1 = 1.0 mm (chain locker compartment type)
The external atmosphere side contributes tc2 = 0.5 mm (external surfaces)
The reserve thickness tres = 0.5 mm is always added
Total tc = 2.0 mm for this girder
The Von Mises stress limit of 1.0 ReH for FEA strength assessment is correct

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch11.Sec2 [2.4.1] states that strength assessment shall be based on net scantlings obtained by deducting the corrosion addition tc given in Ch.3 Sec.3 [1.2]. The answerer must navigate to Ch.3 Sec.3 [1.2] to determine the correct tc formula and table values for a girder exposed to chain locker on one side and external atmosphere on the other.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt3.Ch11.Sec2 [2.4.1]: Strength assessment uses net scantlings = gross scantlings minus tc, where tc is taken from Ch.3 Sec.3 [1.2]. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch11.Sec2 [2.4.2(b)]: FEA Von Mises stress limit is 1.0 ReH — confirmed correct. Step 3 — Navigate to Pt3.Ch3.Sec3 [1.2.1]: tc = tc1 + tc2 + tres. Step 4 — From Table 1: chain locker side → compartment type 'Tanks for brine, urea, bilge water, drain storage and chain locker' → tc1 = 1.0 mm. External surface side → 'External surfaces' → tc2 = 0.5 mm. tres = 0.5 mm (always applied). Step 5 — tc = 1.0 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 2.0 mm total corrosion addition. Step 6 — Check [1.2.5] maximum cap: tc_max = 0.2 * tgr_off; this is a designer check but the computed 2.0 mm is the required minimum value before cap. Step 7 — Confirm Von Mises limit 1.0 ReH is correct per [2.4.2(b)].

question_text: A 180 m general cargo vessel has a sea chest integrated into the ship structure on the port side. The sea chest boundary plating is fabricated from standard carbon-manganese steel and is exposed to sea water on the outer face and to a ballast water tank on the inner face. The designer proposes a net plate thickness of 12 mm for the sea chest boundary, with a stiffener spacing of 400 mm and a blow-out pressure of 2 bar. The gross thickness of the boundary plating is 14 mm. The material factor k = 1.0. Is the proposed net plate thickness of 12 mm sufficient, and what total corrosion addition must be applied when converting from net to gross scantlings for this boundary plate?
required_facts: Minimum net plate thickness from the sea chest formula is approximately 6.79 mm (t = 0.012 × 400 × sqrt(2.0 × 1.0)), so the proposed 12 mm net thickness is sufficient
The corrosion addition for the external (sea water) side of the boundary plate is tc1 = 0.5 mm
The corrosion addition for the internal (ballast water tank) side of the boundary plate is tc2 = 1.0 mm
The reserve thickness tres = 0.5 mm must be added regardless of environment
Total corrosion addition tc = 0.5 + 1.0 + 0.5 = 2.0 mm
Required minimum gross thickness = 12 + 2.0 = 14 mm, which matches the proposed gross thickness exactly
The arrangement is compliant with the classification rules

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sea chest plate thickness requirement in Ch10 Sec6 [3.2.2] references Ch3 for general requirements; Ch10 Sec6 [3.1.1] explicitly states Ch.3 applies. The net-to-gross conversion requires the corrosion addition from Ch3 Sec3 [1.2], which depends on compartment type. The sea chest boundary has one side exposed to sea water (external surface, tc1=0.5 mm) and one side exposed to a ballast water tank (tc2=1.0 mm), plus the reserve thickness tres=0.5 mm, giving tc = 0.5 + 1.0 + 0.5 = 2.0 mm. The minimum net thickness from the formula is t = 0.012 × 400 × sqrt(2.0 × 1.0) = 0.012 × 400 × 1.414 = 6.79 mm, so 12 mm net is sufficient. The required gross thickness is 12 + 2.0 = 14 mm, which exactly matches the proposed gross thickness.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Start at the sea chest scantling requirement (Pt3.Ch10.Sec6 [3.2.2]): minimum net plate thickness t = 0.012 × b × sqrt(Po × k), where b = stiffener spacing = 400 mm, Po = 2 bar, k = 1.0. So t = 0.012 × 400 × sqrt(2.0 × 1.0) = 4.8 × 1.4142 = 6.79 mm. The proposed net thickness of 12 mm exceeds this minimum, so the net scantling is adequate. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch10.Sec6 [3.1.1] states that the requirements of Ch.3 apply in addition to the sea chest requirements. This triggers a cross-reference to Ch.11 Sec.2 [2.4.1] (for acceptance criteria of supporting structures, which references Ch.3 Sec.3 [1.2] for corrosion addition) and directly to Ch.3 Sec.3 for corrosion additions. Step 3 — Navigate to Pt3.Ch3.Sec3 [1.2] to determine the total corrosion addition for the boundary plate. The plate has two sides: outer face exposed to sea water (external surface) → tc1 = 0.5 mm; inner face exposed to ballast water tank → tc2 = 1.0 mm. Reserve thickness tres = 0.5 mm. Total tc = tc1 + tc2 + tres = 0.5 + 1.0 + 0.5 = 2.0 mm. Step 4 — Required gross thickness = net thickness + tc = 12 + 2.0 = 14 mm. The proposed gross thickness of 14 mm is exactly at the minimum required value, so the arrangement is compliant.

question_text:
A 110 m bulk carrier is being designed with a forward bottom slamming region. The designer has specified a normal ballast condition minimum forward draught T_F-f = 4.2 m at the forward end. The bottom plating in the slamming region is stiffened by longitudinal flat-bar stiffeners that pass through transverse floors (primary supporting members). At one such intersection, the floor web depth is 900 mm and the cut-out for the longitudinal stiffener has a depth of 480 mm. No lug plate or collar plate is fitted at this cut-out. The cut-out breadth is 60 mm. The designer proposes to use a corner radius R = 18 mm at the cut-out corners.

The ship's block coefficient C_B = 0.78 and service speed V = 14 knots. The bottom slamming pressure P_SL has been calculated as 185 kN/m² at the cross-section under review. The stiffener spacing is 750 mm and the stiffener span between floors is 2.4 m.

(a) Determine the design pressure to be used for sizing the bottom plating at this location against bottom slamming.
(b) Determine the design pressure to be used for sizing the longitudinal stiffeners against bottom slamming.
(c) Is the cut-out arrangement at the stiffener-to-floor intersection compliant with the rules? Specifically, assess whether the cut-out depth is acceptable without a lug or collar plate, and whether the proposed corner radius R = 18 mm is sufficient. State the minimum required corner radius.
required_facts: Design pressure for bottom plating P_pl = P_SL = 185 kN/m²
Design pressure for stiffeners P_st = 0.5 × P_SL = 92.5 kN/m²
The permissible cut-out depth without lug or collar plate is 50% of the PSM (floor) web depth = 0.50 × 900 mm = 450 mm
The proposed cut-out depth of 480 mm exceeds the 450 mm limit, so the arrangement without a lug or collar plate is non-compliant
Minimum corner radius R_min = max(20% × 60 mm, 25 mm) = max(12 mm, 25 mm) = 25 mm
The proposed corner radius R = 18 mm is less than the required 25 mm and is therefore non-compliant

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch10.Sec2 [3.1] directs plating scantlings to Sec.1 [3.1] (i.e. Pt3.Ch10.Sec1 [3.1]) using P_pl = P_SL; Sec.2 [3.2.1] directs stiffener scantlings to Sec.1 [3.2] using P_st = 0.5*P_SL. Sec.2 [3.2.2] directs connection area requirements to Sec.1 [3.2.3]. Pt3.Ch10.Sec1 [3.2.3] references impact pressure connection rules, which in turn point to Pt3.Ch6.Sec7 for the cut-out geometry and corner radius requirements at stiffener-to-PSM intersections.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Pt3.Ch10.Sec2 [3.1]: The design pressure for bottom plating is P_pl = P_SL = 185 kN/m². The plating scantlings shall be determined according to Pt3.Ch10.Sec1 [3.1] using this pressure.

Step 2 — Pt3.Ch10.Sec2 [3.2.1]: The design pressure for stiffeners is P_st = 0.5 × P_SL = 0.5 × 185 = 92.5 kN/m². Stiffener scantlings shall be determined according to Pt3.Ch10.Sec1 [3.2] using this pressure.

Step 3 — Pt3.Ch10.Sec2 [3.2.2] → Pt3.Ch10.Sec1 [3.2.3]: The connection area of bottom stiffeners to floors shall be per Sec.1 [3.2.3] using P = 0.5 × P_SL = 92.5 kN/m². Sec.1 [3.2.3] is the impact pressure connection clause, which directs the designer to Pt3.Ch6.Sec7 for cut-out and connection geometry.

Step 4 — Pt3.Ch6.Sec7 [1.1.2]: The total depth of cut-outs without lug or collar plate shall not be greater than 50% of the depth of the primary supporting member. Floor web depth = 900 mm; 50% = 450 mm. The proposed cut-out depth is 480 mm > 450 mm. Therefore the cut-out depth EXCEEDS the 50% limit and a lug or collar plate is required, OR shear strength and buckling capacity must be demonstrated as sufficient. The arrangement as proposed (no lug/collar plate, no demonstrated shear/buckling check) is non-compliant.

Step 5 — Pt3.Ch6.Sec7 [1.1.6]: Corner radii R shall be at least the greater of 20% of the cut-out breadth b or 25 mm. Cut-out breadth b = 60 mm; 20% × 60 = 12 mm. The governing minimum is therefore max(12 mm, 25 mm) = 25 mm. The proposed R = 18 mm < 25 mm, so the corner radius is also non-compliant. The minimum required corner radius is R_min = 25 mm.

question_text: A Type 'A' bulk carrier has continuous bulwarks along the exposed freeboard deck. The bulwarks form a well between the forecastle and the bridge front. The designer proposes to cut a series of rectangular openings in the lower portion of these bulwarks to serve as freeing ports, rather than fitting open rails. The bulwark height is 1.4 m, the length of the well on each side is 28 m, and the ship has standard sheer. The total area of the bulwark panels on one side of the well (height × length) is 39.2 m². The designer claims that providing freeing port openings totalling 12.9 m² on each side satisfies all applicable requirements. Additionally, the openings are fitted with vertical bars spaced 230 mm apart instead of horizontal rails. Is the proposed arrangement compliant, and what is the minimum freeing port area required on each side?
required_facts: Type 'A' ships with bulwarks must have a freeing port area of at least 33% of the total bulwark area (or open rails for at least half the exposed deck length)
Total bulwark area on one side = 1.4 m × 28 m = 39.2 m²
Minimum required freeing port area = 33% × 39.2 m² = 12.936 m² per side
The proposed 12.9 m² is less than the required 12.936 m² and is therefore non-compliant
Vertical bars spaced approximately 230 mm apart are acceptable in lieu of horizontal rails for openings in bulwarks
The formula-based minimum from the freeing port area formula (adjusted for bulwark height > 1.2 m) is approximately 2.18 m², which is satisfied but does not override the Type 'A' special requirement

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch11.Sec3 [2.1.2] governs openings in bulwarks and requires crew protection equivalent to the horizontal courses specified in Ch.12 Sec.10 [6.1]. Ch.12 Sec.10 [6.1] independently imposes a minimum freeing port area of 33% of total bulwark area for Type 'A' ships, which must also be satisfied.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt3.Ch11.Sec3 [2.1.2]: Openings in bulwarks must provide crew protection at least equivalent to the horizontal courses in Ch.12 Sec.10 [6.1]. Vertical bars at ~230 mm spacing are explicitly accepted in lieu of horizontal rails, so the bar arrangement is acceptable in principle. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch12.Sec10 [6.1]: For Type 'A' ships with bulwarks, open rails must be fitted for at least half the length of the exposed weather deck OR a freeing port area of at least 33% of the total bulwark area must be provided. The designer has chosen the freeing port route. Step 3 — Check the 33% threshold: Total bulwark area on one side = 1.4 m × 28 m = 39.2 m². Required freeing port area = 33% × 39.2 = 12.936 m². The designer proposes 12.9 m², which is less than 12.936 m² — marginally non-compliant. Step 4 — Additionally, Ch.12 Sec.10 [2.1.1] gives a formula-based minimum: for ℓb = 28 m > 20 m, A = 0.07 × 28 = 1.96 m² per side (formula minimum). The bulwark height of 1.4 m exceeds 1.2 m, so the area must be increased by 0.004 m²/m of well length per 0.1 m excess height: excess = 1.4 − 1.2 = 0.2 m → 2 increments × 0.004 × 28 = 0.224 m² additional → formula minimum = 1.96 + 0.224 = 2.184 m². The designer's 12.9 m² easily exceeds the formula minimum, but fails the Type 'A' special requirement of 33% = 12.936 m². Conclusion: The arrangement is not compliant; the minimum required freeing port area is 12.936 m² (≈ 12.94 m²) per side under the Type 'A' special requirement.

question_text:
A bulk carrier (ESP notation) with a length L = 185 m and maximum speed v₀ = 14.5 knots is fitted with a forecastle. The No. 1 cargo hold hatch cover is located with its midpoint at x = 175 m from the aft end of L. The hatch cover is a double-skin steel construction and is designed to carry cargo on deck. The hatch coaming top plate and stopper substructure are made of steel with R_eH = 355 N/mm² and R_m = 490 N/mm².

During the design review, the structural engineer proposes to use MAFI trailers to load cargo onto the No. 1 hatch cover when the ship is at sea. The MAFI trailer has a maximum axle load Q = 18 t, pneumatic tyres with maximum tyre pressure P₀ = 1000 kN/m², double wheels with axle perpendicular to the stiffeners, and n₀ = 2 load areas per axle. The hatch cover top plating stiffeners run longitudinally with spacing ℓ = 0.55 m.

(a) What is the minimum stopper design pressure that must be used for the longitudinal forces on the forward end of the No. 1 hatch cover, and does the presence of the forecastle affect this value?

(b) For the MAFI trailer operating on the hatch cover at sea, calculate the design deck pressure P_wl-2 that must be used for scantling checks of the hatch cover top plating stiffeners, given that the footprint dimensions are not available. Use the vertical acceleration a_z = 3.8 m/s² for the sea-going condition.
required_facts: The ship is a Type-2 vessel (bulk carrier with ESP notation), so the Type-2 stopper requirements apply to the No. 1 hatch cover
The baseline longitudinal stopper pressure for No. 1 hatch cover forward end is 230 kN/m² for Type-2 ships
Because a forecastle is fitted, the stopper pressure for No. 1 hatch cover may be reduced to 175 kN/m²
The effective yield strength R_eH = min(355, 0.7×490) = 343 N/mm², giving an allowable stopper stress of 0.8×343 = 274.4 N/mm²
For the MAFI trailer at sea with double wheels (w = 1.20) and P₀ = 1000 kN/m², the design deck pressure P_wl-2 = (1000/1.20)×(1 + 3.8/9.81) ≈ 1156 kN/m²
Since Q = 18 t exceeds 15 t, footprint data should normally be provided per the heavy vehicle rule; the simplified formula is used here as an approximation only
The load area dimensions are approximately a₁ ≈ 291 mm and b₁ ≈ 364 mm based on k₁ = 0.8 for double wheels with axle perpendicular to stiffeners

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Pt3.Ch12.Sec4 hatch cover stopper requirements for Type-2 ships, which establishes the stopper pressure for No.1 hatch cover and the forecastle reduction condition; then the scenario of MAFI trailers on the hatch cover requires following the wheel loading rules in Pt3.Ch10.Sec5 to compute the design deck pressure for stiffener scantlings.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Classify ship type: The vessel is a bulk carrier with ESP notation, so it is a Type-2 ship per Pt3.Ch12.Sec4 [1.2].

Step 2 — Stopper pressure for No. 1 hatch cover (Pt3.Ch12.Sec4 [6.2.4]): For Type-2 ships, No. 1 hatch cover must be secured against longitudinal forces on the forward end arising from a pressure of 230 kN/m². However, this pressure may be reduced to 175 kN/m² when a forecastle is fitted in accordance with UR S28. Since the ship has a forecastle, the design stopper pressure for longitudinal forces on the No. 1 hatch cover forward end is 175 kN/m².

Step 3 — Effective yield strength for stopper stress check: R_eH_eff = min(355, 0.7×490) = min(355, 343) = 343 N/mm². Allowable equivalent stress in stoppers and welds = 0.8 × 343 = 274.4 N/mm².

Step 4 — MAFI trailer design pressure at sea (Pt3.Ch10.Sec5 [2.1.2]): Footprint dimensions not available, so use the simplified formula. Q = 18 t > 15 t triggers [2.1.3] note that footprint data shall be provided; however, the problem states to use [2.1.2] with given a_z.

Using P_wl-2 = (P₀/w)(1 + a_z/g):
- P₀ = 1000 kN/m² (cargo handling vehicle)
- Double wheels → w = 1.20
- a_z = 3.8 m/s², g = 9.81 m/s²
- P_wl-2 = (1000/1.20)(1 + 3.8/9.81) = 833.33 × (1 + 0.3874) = 833.33 × 1.3874 = 1156.2 kN/m²

Load area dimensions:
- A = g·w·Q / (n₀·P₀) = 9.81 × 1.20 × 18 / (2 × 1000) = 211.896/2000 = 0.10595 m²
- k₁ = 0.8 for double wheels with axle perpendicular to stiffeners
- Check k₂ condition: wQ/(n₀·b₁²)×10⁶ ≥ 100 — need b₁ first; use k = k₁ = 0.8 initially
- a₁ = √(k·A)×10³ = √(0.8×0.10595)×10³ = √0.08476×10³ = 0.2911×10³ = 291.1 mm
- b₁ = √(A/k)×10³ = √(0.10595/0.8)×10³ = √0.13244×10³ = 363.9 mm

Final answer for part (b): P_wl-2 ≈ 1156 kN/m².

question_text: A 180 m LNG-ready tanker has a centreline cargo tank with an internal length of 32 m and an internal breadth of 28 m. The ship's breadth B is 46 m and the ship's length L is 180 m. The tank height h_tk is 18 m. The tank volume is 16 128 m³. During the structural assessment of the tank's internal web frames, the designer needs to determine the minimum required section modulus Z (in cm³) of a vertical web frame that acts as a primary supporting member subjected to liquid impact pressure. The following data apply: liquid impact pressure P_i = 180 kN/m², stiffener spacing s = 0.75 m, loaded length of girder ℓ_p = 3.0 m, bending span ℓ_bdg = 6.5 m, area reduction factor k_p = 0.55, and the steel used has a specified minimum yield stress R_eH = 355 N/mm². What is the minimum required section modulus Z of the web frame, and what is the unit of R_eH that must be used in the formula?
required_facts: The section modulus formula is Z = (1000 · P_i · S · k_p · ℓ_p · ℓ_bdg) / (f_bdg · R_eH)
R_eH must be taken in units of N/mm² as defined in the general symbols table (Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 3)
The symbol R_eH is not defined within the sloshing section itself; the preamble directs the reader to Ch.1 Sec.4 for undefined symbols
Using f_bdg = 8 (simply supported bending moment factor) and the given value of S, Z_min ≈ 510 cm³
The tank volume (16 128 m³) exceeds 100 m³, so the minimum sloshing pressure floor of 12 kN/m² for small tanks does not apply; full impact assessment is required

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The section modulus formula in Pt3.Ch10.Sec4 [3.2.5] uses the symbol R_eH. The section header of Pt3.Ch10.Sec4 states 'For symbols not defined in this section, see Ch.1 Sec.4.' The answerer must navigate to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 3 to confirm that R_eH is the specified minimum yield stress in N/mm², not kN/m² or MPa labelled differently, and apply it correctly in the formula.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the formula: Pt3.Ch10.Sec4 [3.2.5] gives Z = (1000 · P_i · S · k_p · ℓ_p · ℓ_bdg) / (f_bdg · R_eH). Step 2 — Identify f_bdg: the section states f_bdg is the bending moment factor as given in Sec.1 (Ch.6 Sec.6 Table 1); for a simply supported beam f_bdg = 8. Step 3 — Resolve R_eH units: the Symbols preamble of Pt3.Ch10.Sec4 says 'For symbols not defined in this section, see Ch.1 Sec.4.' Navigating to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 3 (Materials) confirms R_eH = specified minimum yield stress in N/mm². Step 4 — Substitute: Z = (1000 × 180 × 0.75 × 0.55 × 3.0 × 6.5) / (8 × 355) = (1000 × 180 × 0.75 × 0.55 × 3.0 × 6.5) / 2840. Numerator = 1000 × 180 × 0.75 = 135 000; × 0.55 = 74 250; × 3.0 = 222 750; × 6.5 = 1 447 875. Z = 1 447 875 / 2840 ≈ 509.8 cm³, so Z_min ≈ 510 cm³. Step 5 — Confirm unit of R_eH is N/mm² (from Ch.1 Sec.4 Table 3), which is essential for dimensional consistency of the formula.

question_text: A 95-metre general cargo vessel is being designed with an anchor windlass located on the exposed forecastle deck, 18 metres aft of the forward perpendicular. The forecastle deck is 1.8 metres above the summer load waterline. The windlass is fitted with a chain stopper, and the chain cable has a minimum breaking strength (BS) of 550 kN. The supporting hull structure beneath the windlass foundation is to be assessed using finite element analysis. A girder web in the supporting structure has a height of 320 mm and contains a small circular cut-out of 60 mm diameter; the cut-out is not modelled in the FE mesh. The FE analysis yields a von Mises stress of 285 N/mm² in the element adjacent to the cut-out, and the material has a yield strength ReH of 315 N/mm². Determine: (1) the design load that must be applied to the windlass foundation for the anchoring operation load case, and (2) whether the FE result for the girder web element is acceptable, accounting for the presence of the unmodelled cut-out.
required_facts: Anchoring design load = 247.5 kN (45% of BS = 0.45 × 550 kN), because a chain stopper is provided
The FE permissible von Mises stress for the supporting structure is 1.0 ReH = 315 N/mm²
The cut-out occupies 18.75% of the web height (60/320), which is less than 40%, so the reduction factor Cr = 0.60 applies for a web opening
The simplified corrected yield utilisation = 285/(315 × 0.60) = 1.508, which exceeds 1.0, so the simplified criterion is not satisfied
The full shear stress correction must be applied: τ_cor = (320/260) × τ_elem
The arrangement's acceptability cannot be definitively determined without the correct Cr, complete shear correction, and full FE stress data

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch11.Sec2 governs windlass foundation design loads and acceptance criteria for FE analysis; the FE acceptance criteria for the supporting structure reference the partial ship structural analysis rules in Pt3.Ch7.Sec3, specifically the shear stress correction procedure for unmodelled cut-outs in girder webs.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Design load (Pt3.Ch11.Sec2 [2.3.1]): Because a chain stopper is provided, the windlass design load is 45% of BS = 0.45 × 550 = 247.5 kN. Step 2 — Green sea applicability (Pt3.Ch11.Sec2 [2.5.1]): The ship is 95 m (≥ 80 m) and the forecastle deck is 1.8 m above the summer load waterline. The threshold is the lesser of 0.1L = 9.5 m or 22 m, i.e. 9.5 m. Since 1.8 m < 9.5 m, the green sea load requirements also apply, but the question focuses on the anchoring load case. Step 3 — FE acceptance criterion (Pt3.Ch11.Sec2 [2.4.2(b)]): For FE assessment the permissible von Mises stress = 1.0 ReH = 315 N/mm². Step 4 — Shear stress correction for unmodelled cut-out (Pt3.Ch7.Sec3 [4.2.6] and [4.2.7]): The cut-out diameter is 60 mm in a web of height 320 mm, giving a cut-out-to-web ratio of 60/320 = 18.75%, which is less than 20%. Per Table 2, the reduction factor Cr = 0.80. The simplified correction gives an adjusted yield utilisation: λ_y,a = λ_y,FE / Cr. The raw utilisation is 285/315 = 0.905. Adjusted utilisation = 0.905 / 0.80 = 1.131 > 1.0, so the simplified criterion is not satisfied. The full shear stress correction per [4.2.7] must then be applied: τ_cor = (h / h_eff) × τ_elem, where h_eff = 320 − 60 = 260 mm. This increases the effective shear stress and hence the von Mises stress beyond the 1.0 ReH limit, meaning the arrangement is not acceptable as-is and scantlings must be increased or the cut-out relocated/reinforced.

question_text: A naval architect is sizing the elementary plate panels (EPPs) on the inner bottom of a 185 m bulk carrier. The inner bottom plating is supported by longitudinal stiffeners spaced 680 mm apart and by transverse floors spaced 2 600 mm apart. The proposed EPP has a length a = 2 600 mm and a breadth b = 680 mm. The designer wants to confirm the aspect ratio of this EPP and determine the correct values of a and b to use in subsequent plate thickness calculations. Which dimension is 'a' and which is 'b' for this EPP, and what is the resulting aspect ratio a/b? Would the aspect ratio change if the stiffener spacing were increased to 2 700 mm while the floor spacing remained at 2 600 mm?
required_facts: a is defined as the longer dimension of the EPP and b is the shorter dimension, per Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [2.1.1]
For the base case (floor spacing 2 600 mm, stiffener spacing 680 mm): a = 2 600 mm and b = 680 mm
The base-case aspect ratio a/b = 2 600 / 680 ≈ 3.82
If stiffener spacing increases to 2 700 mm, the longer side becomes the stiffener spacing, so a and b swap: a = 2 700 mm, b = 2 600 mm
The revised aspect ratio a/b = 2 700 / 2 600 ≈ 1.04, a substantial reduction
The symbol definitions for a and b in Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 explicitly cross-reference Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [2.1.1] for their full definition

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 defines the symbols a and b used throughout Part 3, noting they are 'as defined in [2.1.1]' of Ch.3 Sec.7. The answerer must follow that cross-reference to Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [2.1.1] to find the precise definition of the EPP dimensions a (length, the longer side) and b (breadth, the shorter side), and then apply those definitions to the given panel geometry.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — The symbol table in Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 lists 'a = length, in mm, of EPP as defined in [2.1.1]' and 'b = breadth, in mm, of EPP as defined in [2.1.1]', directing the reader to Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [2.1.1]. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [2.1.1] defines the EPP as the plate panel bounded by stiffeners and primary supporting members, with 'a' being the longer dimension and 'b' the shorter dimension of the panel. Step 3 — For the given panel: one side = 2 600 mm (floor spacing), other side = 680 mm (stiffener spacing). Since 2 600 > 680, a = 2 600 mm and b = 680 mm, giving a/b ≈ 3.82. Step 4 — If stiffener spacing increases to 2 700 mm while floor spacing stays at 2 600 mm, then 2 700 > 2 600, so a and b swap: a = 2 700 mm, b = 2 600 mm, giving a/b ≈ 1.04. The aspect ratio changes significantly and the roles of a and b are exchanged.

question_text: A naval architect is designing a weathertight door for a companionway on the exposed freeboard deck of a 145 m general cargo vessel. The door blade is fabricated from steel with a specified minimum yield stress ReH = 235 N/mm². The door panel has a breadth b = 600 mm and a length a = 900 mm. The design lateral pressure P at the load calculation point is 12.5 kN/m². Calculate the minimum required gross thickness of the door blade, and determine the value of the aspect ratio correction factor αp that must be applied. Is the calculated αp capped at any limiting value, and if so, what is that limit?
required_facts: αp is capped at a maximum value of 1.0 (not to be taken greater than 1.0)
αp = 0.883 is below the cap of 1.0, so no capping is applied
ReH = 235 N/mm² (specified minimum yield stress, units confirmed from the symbols and definitions section)
t_gr = 0.0158 × αp × b × sqrt(|P| / (0.85 × ReH)) is the applicable formula
t_gr ≈ 2.09 mm (minimum required gross door blade thickness)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The door blade thickness formula in Pt3.Ch12.Sec2 [4.3.1] uses the symbol ReH (specified minimum yield stress) and αp (aspect ratio correction factor). The section header explicitly states 'For symbols not defined in this section, see Ch.1 Sec.4', so the answerer must navigate to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 to confirm the definition and units of ReH (N/mm²) from Table 3. Additionally, αp is defined locally but capped at 1.0 — the answerer must recognise this cap applies here since b/a = 600/900 gives αp = 1.2 − 600/(2.1×900) = 1.2 − 0.317 = 0.883, which is below 1.0 so the cap is not triggered, but the question asks whether a cap exists and what it is.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the formula: t_gr = 0.0158 × αp × b × sqrt(|P| / (0.85 × ReH)) from Pt3.Ch12.Sec2 [4.3.1]. Step 2 — Compute αp: αp = 1.2 − b/(2.1a) = 1.2 − 600/(2.1 × 900) = 1.2 − 0.3175 = 0.8825. The section states αp shall not be taken greater than 1.0, so the cap is 1.0; here αp = 0.8825 < 1.0, so no capping needed. Step 3 — Confirm ReH units: the symbol ReH is listed in Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 3 as 'specified minimum yield stress' in N/mm², consistent with its use in the formula. Step 4 — Compute t_gr: t_gr = 0.0158 × 0.8825 × 600 × sqrt(12.5 / (0.85 × 235)) = 0.0158 × 0.8825 × 600 × sqrt(12.5 / 199.75) = 0.0158 × 0.8825 × 600 × sqrt(0.06257) = 0.0158 × 0.8825 × 600 × 0.2501 = 0.0158 × 132.4 = 2.09 mm (approximately). This is the gross thickness requirement; actual plate must meet or exceed this value.

question_text: A 185 m general cargo ship (L1 = 185 m) is being designed with a double-side structure. A longitudinal shell stiffener runs along the side shell at a location 3.2 m above the top of the summer load waterline (TSC). The stiffener web meets the attached shell plating at an angle of 42 degrees. The designer proposes to fit tripping brackets at every fourth stiffener spacing to control lateral-torsional instability, and specifies the tripping brackets with a net thickness of 5.5 mm. The attached shell plating at this location has a net required thickness (from scantling calculations) of 8.0 mm. Is the proposed tripping bracket arrangement and thickness compliant with the classification rules? Specifically: (a) is the spacing of tripping brackets acceptable, (b) is the net thickness of the tripping brackets sufficient given the stiffener web thickness requirement, and (c) what is the minimum net thickness the tripping brackets must satisfy based on the ship's length?
required_facts: The web-to-plating angle of 42 degrees is less than 50 degrees, triggering the tripping bracket requirement
Tripping bracket spacing at every fourth stiffener spacing (= 4× stiffener spacing) is at the maximum permitted limit and is acceptable
The minimum net thickness for tripping brackets is 4.5 + 0.01 × 185 = 6.35 mm
The proposed tripping bracket net thickness of 5.5 mm is less than the required 6.35 mm and is therefore NOT compliant
The tripping bracket web thickness must also not be less than 40% of the net required attached plating thickness: 0.40 × 8.0 = 3.2 mm (this sub-requirement is satisfied by the proposed 5.5 mm)
The arrangement fails on the absolute minimum thickness requirement from the minimum thickness table

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [3.1.2] establishes the requirement for tripping brackets when the web-to-plating angle is less than 50 degrees, specifying spacing (≤4× stiffener spacing) and that tripping bracket as-built thickness shall not be less than 75% of the stiffener web thickness. The minimum net thickness of tripping brackets is governed by Pt3.Ch6.Sec3 [2.1] Table 2, which gives t = 4.5 + 0.01·L1 for tripping brackets.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [3.1.2]: The web-to-plating angle is 42 deg, which is less than 50 deg, so tripping brackets are required. They shall be spaced not more than 4 times the stiffener spacing. The proposal of every fourth stiffener spacing equals exactly 4× spacing, which is at the limit and therefore acceptable. The as-built thickness of the tripping brackets shall not be less than 75% of the as-built thickness of the stiffener webs to which they are connected — this links the tripping bracket thickness to the stiffener web thickness. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch6.Sec3 [2.1] Table 2: The minimum net thickness for tripping brackets is t = 4.5 + 0.01 × L1 = 4.5 + 0.01 × 185 = 4.5 + 1.85 = 6.35 mm. The proposed 5.5 mm is less than 6.35 mm, so it is NOT compliant. Step 3 — Pt3.Ch6.Sec3 [2.1]: Additionally, the net thickness of the web of stiffeners and tripping brackets shall not be less than 40% of the net required thickness of the attached plating. 40% × 8.0 mm = 3.2 mm. The 5.5 mm proposed exceeds this 3.2 mm floor, so this sub-requirement is satisfied. However, the absolute minimum from Table 2 (6.35 mm) governs and is not met.

question_text:
A ro-ro ferry has a stern ramp that also serves as a vehicle loading ramp in harbour. The ramp has a light opening area of 8 m² and is constructed from stiffened steel panels. During the design review, the structural engineer performs a direct strength analysis (FEA) of the ramp structure. The ramp panels include a longitudinal stiffened panel with plate elements of varying thickness: three finite elements with areas of 0.04 m², 0.06 m², and 0.05 m² and net thicknesses of 14 mm, 12 mm, and 10 mm respectively. The panel yield stresses for these elements are 315 MPa, 355 MPa, and 355 MPa respectively.

For the buckling assessment of this ramp-as-ramp harbour condition:
1. Is an additional buckling check beyond basic slenderness requirements mandatory for this ramp, and under what specific condition does this obligation apply?
2. What average plate thickness should be used in the buckling panel assessment?
3. What yield stress value should be assigned to the panel for the buckling check?
required_facts: The additional buckling check per Ch.8 Sec.4 is mandatory because the door acts as a ramp in harbour condition
The additional buckling check is NOT required for doors that do not serve as ramps (harbour condition is the trigger)
Average plate thickness t_avr = 11.87 mm (calculated as area-weighted average of the three elements)
Panel yield stress R_eH_P = 315 MPa (minimum yield stress among all elements in the panel)
Basic slenderness requirements from Ch.8 Sec.2 apply regardless of ramp function

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch12.Sec5 [1.3.7] states that an additional buckling check per Ch.8 Sec.4 is required only for doors acting as ramps in harbour condition. The answerer must then navigate to Ch.8 Sec.4 to find the specific procedures for average thickness (2.1.2) and panel yield stress (2.1.3) used in that buckling assessment.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify that the stern ramp has a light opening area of 8 m² (< 12 m²), so securing bolts may be used for sea pressure transfer. Step 2: Per Pt3.Ch12.Sec5 [1.3.7], slenderness requirements from Ch.8 Sec.2 always apply, but the additional buckling check per Ch.8 Sec.4 is ONLY required when the door acts as a ramp in harbour condition — which this ramp does. So the additional check is mandatory. Step 3: Navigate to Pt3.Ch8.Sec4 [2.1.2] for average thickness: t_avr = (A1*t1 + A2*t2 + A3*t3) / (A1 + A2 + A3) = (0.04*14 + 0.06*12 + 0.05*10) / (0.04 + 0.06 + 0.05) = (0.56 + 0.72 + 0.50) / 0.15 = 1.78 / 0.15 = 11.87 mm. Step 4: Per Pt3.Ch8.Sec4 [2.1.3], the panel yield stress R_eH_P is the MINIMUM of the specified yield stresses of the elements within the panel = min(315, 355, 355) = 315 MPa.

question_text: A structural engineer is calculating external sea pressures on the hull of a 180 m bulk carrier (block coefficient CB = 0.82) operating in unrestricted service. For an HSM-1 dynamic load case, the load point is located at x = 36 m from the aft perpendicular, y = 8.5 m from the ship centreline, and z = 4.2 m above the keel. The moulded breadth at the waterline at that cross-section is Bx = 28 m, and the loading condition draught TLC = 9.8 m. The wave coefficient Cw has been determined as 10.75, and the roll angle θ = 22°. During the pressure calculation, the engineer needs to determine the water head equivalent hW at the waterline and also confirm the correct value of seawater density ρ to use in the formula hW = PW,WL / (ρg). What value of ρ should be used, in t/m³, and what is the resulting fYB ratio for this load point? Is the load point above or below the waterline, and which pressure formula branch applies?
required_facts: ρ = 1.025 t/m³, obtained from the primary symbols table in the general definitions section (not defined locally in the external loads section)
fYB = |2 × 8.5| / 28 ≈ 0.607, which is less than 1.0 so the cap does not apply
The load point at z = 4.2 m is below the waterline at TLC = 9.8 m
The applicable HSM-1 wave pressure branch below the waterline is PW = max(−PHS, ρg(z − TLC))
g = 9.81 m/s² per the primary symbols definition
The symbol ρ is not defined in the external loads symbols list and must be sourced from the cross-referenced general symbols section

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch4.Sec5 Symbols section explicitly states 'For symbols not defined in this section, see Ch.1 Sec.4.' The engineer must follow this cross-reference to resolve ρ (seawater density) and confirm the coordinate system definitions used in the fYB and hW calculations.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — In Pt3.Ch4.Sec5 Symbols, the formula hW = PW,WL / (ρg) uses ρ, but ρ is not defined locally in Sec.5. The section header states 'For symbols not defined in this section, see Ch.1 Sec.4.' Step 2 — Navigate to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 1 (Primary symbols), which defines ρ as 'density of seawater, taken equal to 1.025 t/m³'. Step 3 — Back in Pt3.Ch4.Sec5, compute fYB = |2y| / Bx = |2 × 8.5| / 28 = 17/28 ≈ 0.607, which is less than 1.0, so fYB = 0.607. Step 4 — The load point z = 4.2 m is below TLC = 9.8 m, so the point is below the waterline. For HSM load cases below the waterline, the pressure formula branch PW = PW,WL − ρg(z − TLC) applies (with z < TLC giving a positive addition). Step 5 — g = 9.81 m/s² per Ch.1 Sec.4 Table 1.

question_text: A 180 m bulk carrier is being designed with a longitudinal shell knuckle in the midship region (within 0.6L). The knuckle angle is 8 degrees (a shallow knuckle). The designer proposes to place the nearest support stiffening in line with the knuckle at a distance of 80 mm from the knuckle line, arguing that the shallow angle justifies relaxed tolerances. Additionally, the structural drawings use the symbol 'r' to denote the knuckle support bracket radius, and the designer asks whether this symbol conflicts with any standard symbol definition used throughout the structural rules for this vessel type. Is the proposed 80 mm distance acceptable for this shallow knuckle arrangement, and does the symbol 'r' carry a pre-assigned meaning in the general rules that the designer should be aware of?
required_facts: For shallow knuckles (angle less than 10 degrees), the maximum permitted distance from the knuckle to the support stiffening is 75 mm
The proposed distance of 80 mm exceeds the 75 mm limit for shallow knuckles and is therefore not acceptable as-is
An alternative arrangement may be accepted if supported by a fatigue analysis
The symbol 'r' is defined in the general symbols table (Ch.1 Sec.4 Table 1) as radius of curvature of plating or bilge radius, in mm
Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 explicitly directs the reader to Ch.1 Sec.4 for symbols not defined within that section
The knuckle angle of 8 degrees qualifies as a shallow knuckle (less than 10 degrees), triggering the 75 mm relaxed-but-still-limited distance rule rather than the standard 50 mm rule

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [2.1.1(f)] sets the distance limit for knuckle support stiffening and explicitly states that symbols not defined in Sec6 are defined in Ch.1 Sec.4. The answerer must go to Ch.1 Sec.4 Table 1 to resolve the meaning of 'r'.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify the knuckle distance rule in Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [2.1.1(f)]: for shallow knuckles (angle < 10 degrees), the maximum permitted distance between the knuckle and the support stiffening is 75 mm. The proposed 80 mm exceeds this limit, so the arrangement is NOT acceptable unless a fatigue analysis per Ch.9 is performed. Step 2: The section header of Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 states 'For symbols not defined in this section, see Ch.1 Sec.4.' The symbol 'r' is not defined within Sec6 itself for this context. Step 3: Navigate to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 1 (Primary symbols): 'r' is defined there as 'radius of curvature of plating or bilge radius' in mm. The designer must be aware that 'r' is a reserved primary symbol with a specific structural meaning and should not be reused for a different purpose without explicit redefinition.

question_text: A ro-ro vessel has a car deck fitted with transverse primary supporting members (girders) spaced 3.6 m apart. The deck is designed to carry heavy road transporters with a maximum axle load Q = 18 t. Each axle has two load areas (n_o = 2). The footprint data for the transporters is available and confirmed. During the design review, the structural engineer needs to determine the vehicle load (in kN) to apply as a concentrated force on the girders for scantling purposes. The transporter axles are positioned at the most unfavourable location for girder strength. The vertical acceleration a_z applicable to the at-sea condition is 1.8 m/s². What concentrated force value, in kN, must be used for the girder scantling check under the at-sea design condition, and what is the correct method for determining this concentrated force according to the applicable structural rules?
required_facts: The vehicle load on girders must be taken as a concentrated force, not a distributed load, for primary supporting member scantling under wheel loading rules
The concentrated force formulation requires navigating from the wheel loading section to the external loads section within Part 3
The concentrated force per load area at sea is calculated as F = (Q/n_o) * (g + a_z) * 10^3 N, giving approximately 104.5 kN per load area
The total concentrated axle force for the at-sea condition is approximately 209 kN (using Q=18 t, n_o=2, g=9.81 m/s², a_z=1.8 m/s²)
Because Q = 18 t exceeds 15 t, footprint data must be provided for the vehicle
The axle must be positioned at the most unfavourable location for the girder strength assessment

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Wheel loading rules for primary supporting members (girders) in Pt3.Ch10.Sec5 [3.3.1] explicitly direct the designer to use the vehicle load as a concentrated force per Pt3.Ch4.Sec5 [2.3.2]. The answerer must navigate from the wheel loading chapter to the external loads chapter within the same Part 3 to find the concentrated force formulation.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify that the question concerns girder scantlings on a ro-ro car deck under wheel loading. The relevant starting point is the primary supporting member requirements for wheel loads. Step 2: Pt3.Ch10.Sec5 [3.3.1] states that vehicle loads in kN shall be taken as concentrated force according to Ch.4 Sec.5 [2.3.2]. This is the cross-reference that must be followed. Step 3: Navigate to Pt3.Ch4.Sec5 [2.3.2] to find the concentrated force formulation for vehicle loads. Step 4: Per [2.3.2], the concentrated force F for each axle load area at sea is: F = (Q / n_o) * (g + a_z) * 10^3 [in kN], where Q is in tonnes, g = 9.81 m/s², a_z is the vertical acceleration. Step 5: Substituting values — Q = 18 t, n_o = 2, g = 9.81 m/s², a_z = 1.8 m/s²: F_per_area = (18/2) * (9.81 + 1.8) * 10^3 / 1000 = 9 * 11.61 = 104.49 kN per load area. Total axle concentrated force = 2 * 104.49 ≈ 208.98 kN ≈ 209 kN. Step 6: Confirm that since Q = 18 t > 15 t, footprint data must be provided (which the scenario states is available), satisfying the requirement of [2.1.3]. Step 7: The girder must be checked with this concentrated force at the most unfavourable axle position.

question_text: A 185-metre bulk carrier with class notation ESP is being assessed for structural adequacy. The design team is evaluating the bottom shell plating in the midship region. The ship operates between full load draught (T_SC = 13.2 m) and ballast draught (T_BAL = 6.8 m). The adjacent double bottom tank is a ballast water tank. For the primary supporting members in the double bottom, the scantlings are NOT determined by global FE analysis or partial ship structural FE analysis — they are determined by direct calculation. The FE analysis team later decides to build a partial ship structural FE model for a separate verification exercise. Given that the ship carries the ESP notation, what scantling basis must the FE model use, and how does this differ from the scantling basis that was used for the direct calculation of the primary supporting members under the design load sets?
required_facts: FE models for ships with ESP class notation must be based on net scantlings as defined in Ch.3 Sec.2 Table 1
Without the ESP notation, gross scantlings would be used in FE models
The direct calculation of primary supporting members under design load sets (Ch.6 path) uses gross scantlings
Buckling capacity assessment in the FE model must also be based on net scantlings per Ch.3 Sec.2 Table 1
The Ch.6 design load set requirements apply to primary supporting members precisely because their scantlings are not determined by global FE or partial ship structural FE analysis
The distinction between net and gross scantlings is the key difference between the FE model basis and the direct calculation basis for this ESP-classed ship

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Ch.6 Sec.2 [2.1.1] establishes that design load sets apply to primary supporting members when scantlings are not determined by global FE or partial ship structural FE analysis. Ch.7 Sec.1 [2.1] then specifies that FE models for ESP-classed ships must use net scantlings as defined in Ch.3 Sec.2 Table 1, whereas the direct calculation path (Ch.6) implicitly uses gross scantlings unless otherwise specified — creating a distinction the answerer must identify by crossing from Ch.6 to Ch.7.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Ch.6 Sec.2 [2.1.1] states that the design load set requirements apply to primary supporting members 'if scantlings are not determined by global FE analysis or partial ship structural FE analysis'. This confirms the direct calculation path is in scope for Ch.6 load sets. Step 2: The question then asks about the FE model. Ch.7 Sec.1 [2.1] states: 'FE models for ships with class notation ESP shall be based on the net scantling as defined in Ch.3 Sec.2 Table 1. Otherwise, gross scantlings shall be used in FE models.' Step 3: Since the ship has ESP notation, the FE model must use net scantlings. Step 4: The direct calculation under Ch.6 design load sets uses gross scantlings (the default for non-FE direct calculation). Step 5: Therefore the key distinction is net scantlings for the ESP FE model vs. gross scantlings for the direct calculation — and buckling capacity assessment in the FE context must also use net scantlings per Ch.3 Sec.2 Table 1.

scenario_parameters.region: midship bottom shell and double bottom

question_text: A ro-ro cargo vessel is being designed with a car deck intended to carry road transporters. One of the transporters has a maximum axle load of 12 t, is fitted with double wheels on each axle, and the footprint dimensions for the individual wheels are not available. The designer needs to calculate the design deck pressure for normal operation at sea. During the calculation, the designer encounters the symbol 'g' in the pressure formula and wants to confirm its exact numerical value and units as defined in the governing rules for this vessel type. What is the correct value of g to use, and what is the resulting design pressure (in kN/m²) for normal operation at sea for this axle, assuming a vertical acceleration az = 1.5 m/s², two load areas on the axle (no_o = 2), and standard double-wheel tyre pressure assumptions?
required_facts: g = 9.81 m/s² as defined in the primary symbols table (Ch.1 Sec.4 Table 1)
The symbol g is not defined locally in the wheel loading section and must be looked up in Ch.1 Sec.4
P0 = 120(√Q + 3) applies for road transporters, giving approximately 775.7 kN/m² for Q = 12 t
w = 1.20 for double wheels
Design pressure formula for at-sea operation without known footprint is P_wl-2 = (P0/w)(1 + az/g)
Resulting design pressure P_wl-2 ≈ 745 kN/m² (accepting values in range 740–750 kN/m²)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Wheel loading section defines design pressure formula for pneumatic tyres but defers symbol definitions (including g) to Ch.1 Sec.4, which defines g = 9.81 m/s². The answerer must follow the cross-reference to resolve the symbol before completing the numerical calculation.
