The designer's approach to the partially filled ballast tank is non-compliant: the rules require the tank to be assessed at empty, full, and the intended partial fill level (45%), not only at departure and arrival at the intended fill.

The standard seagoing design loading conditions for this container ship must satisfy both the container-ship-specific requirements and those in the general loading conditions section of the structural rules.
The intact stability requirements of the main class apply to this vessel because its waterline length (280 m) exceeds the 24 m threshold.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 (thick plate / brittle crack arrest rules for container ships), which at [2.2.3] defines brittle crack arrest steels referencing Pt.2 Ch.2 Sec.2 [7], and at [1.1.2] triggers additional requirements for NV 47. The section also references Sec.3 [2.2.3] (loading conditions for container ships), which at [3.1.1] directs to Pt.3 Ch.4 Sec.8 [1] for standard design loading conditions. Pt.3 Ch.4 Sec.8 [1.1.1] in turn references Ch.15 Sec.1 [4.3] for the design loading conditions basis, and Sec.8 [1.2.1] governs partially filled ballast tanks. Pt.3 Ch.15 Sec.1 [1.1.1] establishes the stability applicability threshold of L_LL ≥ 24 m.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.1]: The vessel has class notation 'Container ship', NV 47 steel, and hatch coaming thickness 72 mm (between 50 mm and 100 mm), so this section applies. Step 2 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [2.2.1] and Table 1: With NV 47 and a leading plate thickness of 72 mm, countermeasures are required (specific measures per Table 1 for NV 47 at 72 mm). Step 3 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.2]: Because NV 47 material is applied, the requirements given in [3] shall be applied additionally — this is an extra obligation not triggered for NV 36 or NV 40. Step 4 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [3.1.1]: The standard design loading conditions for container ships shall be considered in addition to those in Pt.3 Ch.4 Sec.8 [1]. Step 5 — Pt3.Ch4.Sec8 [1.2.1]: For a ballast loading condition with a partially filled tank at 45% intended level, it is NOT sufficient to check only departure and arrival at 45%. The rules require that the tank be assessed at empty, full, and the intended partial fill level (45%), and all combinations must be shown within permissible limits. The designer's approach is non-compliant. Step 6 — Pt3.Ch15.Sec1 [1.1.1]: All vessels with L_LL of 24 m and above shall comply with the stability requirements. The ship has L_LL = 280 m ≥ 24 m, so intact stability requirements of the main class apply.

question_text: A 320-metre container ship (unrestricted service, single deck) is being assessed for hull girder ultimate strength. The vessel has a block coefficient of 0.65, a contract speed of 22 knots, and a bow flare angle of 48°. The ship is designed with empty cargo holds in alternate loading conditions, and the loading manual includes these alternate loading conditions. The class notation assigned is HC(M). At the cross-section located 80 m aft of the forward perpendicular, the designer has calculated the following: permissible still water bending moment in hogging M_sw-U = 8,500,000 kNm, vertical wave bending moment M_wv = 4,200,000 kNm, and the computed vertical hull girder ultimate bending capacity M_U = 18,000,000 kNm. Does this cross-section satisfy the hull girder ultimate strength criterion in hogging, and what is the governing value of the combined partial safety factor γ_R that must be applied to M_U?
required_facts: The cross-section at 80 m aft of FE corresponds to 0.25L on a 320 m ship, which is a mandatory check location for container ships

The bow flare angle (48°) and contract speed (22 kn) do not by themselves determine whether the whipping amplification factor γ_WH applies, because α > 55° and V > 25 kn are guidance-note triggers for advanced assessment and the Pt5 Ch2 Sec4 [2.6.2] branch also depends on breadth B
The design bending moment M = 1.0 × 8,500,000 + 1.2 × 4,200,000 = 13,540,000 kNm
γ_DB = 1.15 applies in hogging under Pt5 Ch2 Sec4 [2.6.1] for container ships
The allowable moment M_U / γ_R = 18,000,000 / 1.2075 ≈ 14,907,000 kNm
The cross-section satisfies the hull girder ultimate strength criterion because, using the Pt5 factors, M = 13,540,000 kNm is below the corrected allowable moment M_U / γ_R

annotator_grounding.start_clause: Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.6] (hull girder ultimate strength for container ships)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 directs hull girder strength assessment to Pt3.Ch5, with additional container-ship-specific requirements. The answerer must navigate from the container ship chapter to Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 to find the ultimate strength checking criteria, identify the correct γ_DB factor for the HC(M) notation with alternate loading conditions included, and verify the criterion M ≤ M_U / γ_R.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [1] states that hull girder strength assessment shall be carried out in accordance with Pt3.Ch5, with additional requirements in lieu of particular Pt3.Ch5 requirements. For ultimate strength, the container-ship-specific partial safety factor γ_WH may modify γ_W, but the core checking criterion comes from Pt3.Ch5.Sec4.

Step 2 — Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [1.1.2] confirms that the hull girder ultimate strength requirements apply to the cargo hold area in general and to specific locations; for container ships, locations at or near 0.25L and 0.75L are explicitly listed. The cross-section at 80 m aft of FE on a 320 m ship is at x/L = 80/320 = 0.25L, so this is one of the mandatory check locations.

Step 3 — Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [2.2.1] gives the design bending moment: M = γ_S · M_sw-U + γ_W · M_wv, with γ_S = 1.0 and γ_W = 1.2 (standard value; the container-ship whipping factor γ_WH from Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.6.2] applies when L > 290 m, B > 47 m, α > 55°, V > 25 kn — here α = 48° < 55° and V = 22 kn < 25 kn, so the standard γ_W = 1.2 governs). M = 1.0 × 8,500,000 + 1.2 × 4,200,000 = 8,500,000 + 5,040,000 = 13,540,000 kNm.

Step 4 — Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [2.1.2] gives the criterion M ≤ M_U / γ_R, where γ_R = γ_M · γ_DB.

Step 5 — γ_M = 1.1 (general value).

Step 6 — For hogging condition, γ_DB = 1.25 for vessels with empty cargo holds and class notation HC(A) or HC(B*), or HC(M) if alternate loading conditions are included in the loading manual. The vessel has HC(M) notation AND alternate loading conditions are included in the loading manual, so γ_DB = 1.25.

Step 7 — γ_R = 1.1 × 1.25 = 1.375.

Step 8 — Allowable moment = M_U / γ_R = 18,000,000 / 1.375 = 13,090,909 kNm ≈ 13,091,000 kNm.

Step 9 — Design moment M = 13,540,000 kNm > 13,091,000 kNm. The criterion is NOT satisfied; the cross-section fails the hull girder ultimate strength check in hogging.

question_text: A new 280-metre container ship is being designed with cell guides in the cargo holds and fixed lashing bridges on the upper deck. During the structural review, the design team is assessing a stiffened panel on the inner bottom that forms part of the container foundation structure. The panel consists of finite elements with varying plate thicknesses: three elements each with area 0.12 m² and net thickness 14 mm, and two elements each with area 0.08 m² and net thickness 18 mm. The panel yield stress must be determined for the buckling assessment. Additionally, the buckling check is being performed as part of a direct strength analysis finite element study, and the panel in question is a double bottom floor. The design team needs to confirm: (1) what average thickness should be used for the buckling panel, and (2) which boundary condition assessment method applies to double bottom floors in the direct strength analysis, and (3) what value of yield stress should be assigned to the panel if the 14 mm elements are Grade A steel (ReH = 235 N/mm²) and the 18 mm elements are Grade DH36 steel (ReH = 355 N/mm²)?
required_facts: Average panel thickness t_avr = 15.23 mm (calculated as area-weighted mean: (3×0.12×14 + 2×0.08×18) / (3×0.12 + 2×0.08))
Double bottom floors use assessment method SP-A in the direct strength analysis buckling check
Panel yield stress ReH_P = 235 N/mm² (minimum of the element yield stresses within the panel)
The container ship rules in Part 5 are supplementary to main class rules in Part 3, so Part 3 buckling requirements apply
The panel normal definition for double bottom floors is: length = full web depth, width = between primary supporting members

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 defines container ship scope and references Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [3] for definitions not defined locally; Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 symbols and definitions underpin the structural idealisation in Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [2.1.1] for elementary plate panel geometry (a, b dimensions); Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 structural idealisation feeds into the direct strength analysis buckling requirements of Pt3.Ch8.Sec4, which specifies boundary conditions (Table 1), average thickness formula, and yield stress assignment rules.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.5]: The container ship rules state that for definitions not defined in that section, see Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [3]. This anchors the design to Part 3 definitions and structural rules as supplementary requirements. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch1.Sec4: Provides primary symbols including net thickness t (mm), area A (m²), yield stress ReH (N/mm²), confirming the notation used in the buckling section. Step 3 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [2.1.1]: Defines the elementary plate panel (EPP) dimensions a and b, which establish what constitutes a 'plate panel' for buckling purposes — the panel extent is needed before applying the buckling formulae. Step 4 — Pt3.Ch8.Sec4 [2.1.1] Table 1: For double bottom floors, the boundary condition assessment method is SP-A (with footnote 6), with panel defined as length = full web depth, width = between primary supporting members. Step 5 — Pt3.Ch8.Sec4 [2.1.2]: Average thickness t_avr = (sum of Ai*ti) / (sum of Ai) = (3×0.12×14 + 2×0.08×18) / (3×0.12 + 2×0.08) = (5.04 + 2.88) / (0.36 + 0.16) = 7.92 / 0.52 = 15.23 mm. Step 6 — Pt3.Ch8.Sec4 [2.1.3]: Panel yield stress ReH_P is taken as the minimum value of the specified yield stresses of the elements within the panel = min(235, 355) = 235 N/mm².

scenario_parameters.ship_type: container ship with cell guides and lashing bridges
scenario_parameters.structural_location: double bottom floor (inner bottom container foundation)
scenario_parameters.analysis_type: direct strength analysis FE buckling assessment

question_text: A 310-metre container ship with a service speed of 23 knots is being designed for unrestricted ocean service. The vessel has a single continuous weather deck and large deck openings typical of container ships. During the hull girder ultimate strength review, the designer proposes to check the ultimate bending capacity only at the midship section and at the forward end of the engine room, arguing that no other locations require assessment. The ship's loading manual includes alternate loading conditions for the cargo holds, and the class notation HC(M) is assigned. For the hogging ultimate strength check, the designer applies a combined partial safety factor γ_R = γ_M × γ_DB = 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.21. Is the proposed scope of check locations sufficient, and is the applied partial safety factor γ_R = 1.21 correct for the hogging condition? Provide a full justification including all locations that must be checked and the correct value of γ_R.
required_facts: The check locations are insufficient: for a container ship with large deck openings, ultimate strength must also be verified at or near 0.25L and 0.75L
Additional mandatory locations include the forward end of the foremost cargo hold and any locations with significant changes in hull cross-section or framing system
For container ships, for the hogging condition with class notation HC(M) and alternate loading conditions included in the loading manual, γ_DB = 1.15
The applicable combined partial safety factor is γ_R = γ_M × γ_DB = 1.05 × 1.15 = 1.2075
The designer's decomposition of the applied value γ_R = 1.21 using γ_DB = 1.1 is incorrect for this vessel
For this container-ship check, the Pt5 Ch2 Sec4 requirement governs γ_DB in hogging; the general Pt3 'all other cases' / HC(M) alternate-loading split does not apply

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 states hull girder strength shall be assessed per Pt3.Ch5, with additional requirements. Sec4 [3.3] references the ultimate strength check. Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [1.1.2] defines the mandatory check locations including 0.25L and 0.75L for container ships with large deck openings. Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [2.1.2] defines γ_DB: for hogging with HC(M) and alternate loading conditions in the loading manual, γ_DB = 1.25, giving γ_R = 1.1 × 1.25 = 1.375.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Start at Pt5.Ch2.Sec4: The hull girder strength assessment for container ships shall be carried out in accordance with Pt.3 Ch.5, with Pt5 specifying additional requirements. The ultimate strength check is governed by Pt3.Ch5.Sec4.

Step 2 — Navigate to Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [1.1.2]: This clause lists mandatory check locations for hull girder ultimate strength. For ships with large deck openings such as container ships, checks are required at or near 0.25L and 0.75L in addition to: the cargo hold area in general, forward end of the engine room, forward end of the foremost cargo hold, and any locations with significant changes in hull cross-section or framing system. The designer's proposal to check only midship and forward engine room is therefore insufficient — at minimum 0.25L and 0.75L must also be checked for this container ship.

Step 3 — Navigate to Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [2.1.2]: The partial safety factor γ_R = γ_M × γ_DB. γ_M = 1.1 in general. For the hogging condition, γ_DB = 1.25 applies to vessels with empty cargo holds and class notation HC(A), HC(B*), or HC(M) if alternate loading conditions are included in the loading manual. The ship has HC(M) notation and the loading manual includes alternate loading conditions, so γ_DB = 1.25 applies, not 1.1. Therefore γ_R = 1.1 × 1.25 = 1.375, not 1.21 as proposed. The designer's value of 1.21 is non-conservative and incorrect.

scenario_parameters.deck_type: single continuous weather deck with large deck openings

question_text: A newbuild 320-metre container ship is being designed with NV 47 high-strength steel upper deck plating and hatch side coaming. The hatch coaming structure has an as-built plate thickness of 72 mm, which is the leading plate for brittle crack arrest design purposes. The upper deck longitudinal stiffeners are T-bar profiles with a plate flange minimum yield strength of 355 N/mm² (NV 36), while the connected primary supporting members (PSMs) have a minimum yield strength of 460 N/mm² (NV 47). The designer proposes to use the standard yield capacity check for the plate flange without any additional verification. During the structural assessment of these longitudinal stiffeners, the design pressure P for the governing load set is determined from the static and dynamic lateral pressure components acting on the upper deck in the full-load condition at the scantling draught, combined with the hull girder longitudinal stress at the load calculation point. Is the proposed design approach for the plate flange yield capacity check acceptable, and what additional verification — if any — is required for the stiffener-to-PSM connection given the mismatch in yield strengths? Additionally, identify which load combination scenario governs the hull girder longitudinal stress used in the stiffener assessment for the static-only load component.
required_facts: The proposed design approach may require additional verification

An additional yield capacity check of the plate flange is not required under Pt.3 Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4], because the plate flange minimum yield strength (355 N/mm²) is about 29.6% lower than the connected PSM minimum yield strength (460 N/mm²), which is below the 35% threshold

The additional plate flange yield capacity check requirement is not triggered in this case because the yield strength mismatch between the NV47 flange and AH36 PSM materials is about 30%, below the 35% threshold in [1.1.4]
For the static load component S, the hull girder longitudinal stress is taken as σ_hg = σ_hg-sw (stress due to vertical still water bending moment only, with no dynamic wave contribution)
For a container ship with large deck openings, the still water bending moment stress is determined from the relevant large-deck-opening provisions rather than the standard formula
The 72 mm leading plate thickness for NV 47 coaming places this vessel in a range requiring brittle crack arrest countermeasures under the applicable table

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [2.1.4] directs material grade selection to Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.3]; Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.2] flags that when plate flange yield strength is lower than connected PSM, an additional yield capacity check per Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4] may be required; Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4] references the design pressure P as defined in Sec.2 [1], which is Pt3.Ch6.Sec2 [1.1.1] for the hull girder longitudinal stress under static load component S.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [2.1.4]: The material grade selection for the NV 47 upper hull longitudinal structural members on this container ship must follow Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.3]. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.2]: This clause explicitly states that the rules generally assume flange and web material have the same minimum yield strength. When the plate flange has a LOWER minimum yield strength than the connected stiffener or PSM, an additional check of yield capacity of the plate flange may be required, referencing Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4]. Here, the plate flange is NV 36 (355 N/mm²) and the PSM is NV 47 (460 N/mm²), so the condition is triggered. Step 3 — Pt3.Ch6.Sec5 [1.1.4]: This clause governs the additional yield capacity check for the plate flange in such mixed-yield-strength configurations. The design pressure P used in the stiffener assessment is defined in Sec.2 [1] (i.e., Pt3.Ch6.Sec2 [1]). Step 4 — Pt3.Ch6.Sec2 [1.1.1]: For the static load component S, the hull girder longitudinal stress σ_hg = σ_hg-sw, i.e., the stress due to vertical still water bending moment only (no dynamic wave component). For a container ship with large deck openings, the reference is Ch.5 Sec.3 [3]. Conclusion: The proposed approach (standard check without additional verification) is NOT acceptable. An additional yield capacity check of the plate flange is required per Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4] because the plate flange yield strength (355 N/mm²) is lower than the connected PSM yield strength (460 N/mm²). The governing hull girder longitudinal stress for the static-only load component S is σ_hg = σ_hg-sw (still water bending moment stress only).

question_text: A 310-metre container ship (breadth B = 48.5 m, block coefficient C_B = 0.65, contract speed 22 knots at 85% MCR and 15% sea margin) is being assessed for hull girder strength. The structural designer has computed the following net section properties at the amidships cross-section: net moment of inertia about the horizontal neutral axis I_y = 980 m⁴, neutral axis height above baseline z_NA = 14.2 m, deck height above baseline z_deck = 27.8 m, and keel distance below neutral axis z_keel = 14.2 m. The design still water hogging bending moment at amidships is M_SW = +4 800 000 kNm, and the vertical wave bending moment in hogging (M_WVH) at amidships is 3 200 000 kNm. The partial safety factor for the additional whipping contribution γ_WH has been calculated by the designer as 1.28, and the designer claims this value is acceptable as-is. A deck longitudinal stiffener at the amidships section has a compressive hull girder stress σ_hg that the designer wishes to use as input to a hull girder buckling check. For the buckling capacity check, the designer applies a corrosion addition factor α = 0.5 when computing the net offered thickness of the deck plating. Is the designer's claimed γ_WH value of 1.28 acceptable, and is the corrosion addition factor α = 0.5 correct for the buckling capacity check? Provide the minimum permissible γ_WH, the correct α for buckling capacity, and explain how the hull girder compressive stress at the deck used in the buckling check is derived.
required_facts: γ_WH = 1.28 is NOT acceptable because it falls below the mandatory minimum floor of γ_WH ≥ 1.3 specified for the whipping contribution partial safety factor
The minimum permissible γ_WH is 1.3
The corrosion addition factor α = 0.5 is incorrect for the buckling capacity check; the correct value is α = 1.0
α = 0.5 applies only to section property calculations (stress determination), not to buckling/collapse capacity

The hull girder compressive stress at the deck (σ_hg-cp) used in the buckling check is derived from the hull girder yield check formulae: Pt3.Ch5.Sec3 [2] for ships without large deck openings or Pt3.Ch5.Sec3 [3] for ships with large deck openings
The permissible still water bending moments M_sw-h and M_sw-s used in the stress derivation are defined in Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 [2.2.2]

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 governs hull girder strength for container ships and specifies the whipping factor floor (γ_WH ≥ 1.3) and the corrosion addition factor α for different analysis types (Table 1). The buckling capacity check requires α = 1.0 (not 0.5). The hull girder compressive stress at the deck for the buckling check is obtained from Pt3.Ch5.Sec3 [2] (ships without large deck openings) or [3] (ships with large deck openings), which in turn requires the permissible still water bending moments defined in Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 [2.2.2].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Whipping factor floor (Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.6.2]): The formula gives γ_WH = 1 + c_L[3.8×10⁻⁷(L+1100)(V+4.1)²(tan(α·π/180)−0.19)] ≥ 1.3. The designer computed 1.28, which is below the mandatory floor of 1.3. Therefore γ_WH = 1.3 must be used as the minimum. Step 2 — Corrosion addition factor for buckling capacity (Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.1.1] Table 1): Table 1 lists α = 0.5 for section properties (stress determination) but α = 1.0 for buckling/collapse capacity. The designer used α = 0.5, which is only correct for section property calculations, not for the buckling capacity check. The correct value is α = 1.0. Step 3 — Hull girder compressive stress derivation (Pt3.Ch8.Sec3 [2.2] symbol definition): The symbol σ_hg-cp used in the buckling check of deck primary supporting members is defined as the maximum compressive stress in the deck based on Pt3.Ch5.Sec3 [2] for ships without large deck openings and Pt3.Ch5.Sec3 [3] for vessels with large deck openings. Step 4 — Still water bending moment input (Pt3.Ch5.Sec3 symbols and Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 [2.2.2]): The hull girder yield check in Pt3.Ch5.Sec3 uses M_sw-h and M_sw-s defined as the permissible vertical still water bending moments for hogging and sagging respectively in seagoing condition, which are defined in Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 [2.2.2]. These permissible values (not the actual loading manual values) feed into the stress calculation used for the buckling check.

question_text: A new 320-metre container ship is being designed with a class notation 'Container ship'. The upper deck plating amidships is fabricated from NV 47 steel with an as-built thickness of 62 mm. The structural designer proposes to apply ISO 5817 quality level C for all welded joints in the upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships, arguing that this meets the minimum workmanship standard. For the hull girder strength assessment, the upper deck is exposed to atmosphere on its top surface and to a container hold on its underside. The designer calculates the net offered thickness using a corrosion addition factor α = 0.5 for the strength assessment section properties, with a one-side corrosion addition of 1.0 mm for the atmosphere-exposed face and 1.0 mm for the container hold face. Is the proposed ISO 5817 quality level acceptable for this application, and what is the net offered thickness of the upper deck plate if the voluntary addition t_vol_add is zero?
required_facts: ISO 5817 quality level C is not acceptable; level B is required for container ships in the upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships

The upper deck qualifies as an upper hull longitudinal structural member per the cross-referenced definition covering upper deck, sheer strake, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate and attached longitudinals
The corrosion addition factor α = 0.5 is correct for strength assessment section properties
The container hold face has a one-side corrosion addition of 1.0 mm (same as atmosphere), giving t_c = 2.0 mm total
The net offered thickness t_off = 62 − 0 − 0.5 × 2.0 = 61.0 mm

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2] mandates ISO 5817 level B (not C) for container ships in upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships, and cross-references Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3] to define what 'upper hull longitudinal structural members' means. Separately, Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.1.1] and Table 1 define the corrosion addition factor α for net scantling calculations, and Table 2 gives the one-side corrosion additions by compartment type.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Workmanship quality level: Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2] states that ISO 5817 quality level B (not C) shall be applied to container ships for upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships. The designer's proposal of level C is therefore not acceptable. Step 2 — Definition of upper hull longitudinal structural members: To confirm the upper deck falls within scope, the reader must follow the cross-reference in Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2] to Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3], which defines upper hull longitudinal structural members as including the upper deck, sheer strake, uppermost strake of longitudinal bulkhead, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate and all attached longitudinals. The 62 mm NV 47 upper deck plate is explicitly within this definition and within the 0.4L amidships zone, so ISO 5817 level B is mandatory. Step 3 — Net offered thickness: From Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.1.1], t_off = t_as_built − t_vol_add − α·t_c. For strength assessment section properties, Table 1 gives α = 0.5. The total corrosion addition t_c = t_c1 + t_c2. From Table 2, the atmosphere-exposed face gives t_c1 = 1.0 mm and the container hold face gives t_c2 = 1.0 mm (container holds are listed at 1.0 mm in Table 2). So t_c = 1.0 + 1.0 = 2.0 mm. With t_vol_add = 0: t_off = 62 − 0 − 0.5 × 2.0 = 62 − 1.0 = 61.0 mm.

question_text: A 310-metre container ship (block coefficient CB = 0.65, waterplane coefficient CWL = 0.78, breadth B = 48.5 m, scantling draught d = 14.2 m) is being designed for unrestricted ocean service. The design team has established the following loading conditions for the hull girder strength assessment: (1) a homogeneous full-load departure condition at maximum draught with bunker tanks at 95% capacity, (2) a homogeneous full-load arrival condition with bunker tanks at 10% capacity, (3) a ballast departure condition, and (4) a ballast arrival condition. The structural designer claims that these four conditions are sufficient to satisfy the loading condition requirements for the longitudinal strength assessment, and that no additional loading conditions need to be considered. The ship has no sequential ballast water exchange procedure. Is the designer's claim correct? Identify any mandatory loading conditions that are missing, and explain what departure and arrival assumptions must be applied to consumables in each seagoing design loading condition.
required_facts: The designer's claim is incorrect — the four listed conditions are not sufficient on their own.

The hull girder strength loading conditions must include all standard design loading conditions from the intact stability requirements (Pt3.Ch15.Sec1 [4.3]) as a mandatory baseline, in addition to the container-ship-specific conditions.
At departure, bunker tanks shall be taken as not less than 95% full and other consumables at 100% capacity.
At arrival, bunker tanks shall be taken as not more than 10% full and other consumables at 10% capacity.
Any intermediate voyage stage that is more severe than departure or arrival must also be submitted and included in the loading manual.
The Pt5 container-ship conditions (homogeneous full load and ballast) are additive to, not a replacement for, the Pt3 baseline loading conditions.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.2] requires still water bending moments to be calculated for design loading conditions as specified in Sec.3 [3]; Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [3.1.1] states that standard design loading conditions given there are in addition to those in Pt.3 Ch.4 Sec.8 [1]; Pt3.Ch4.Sec8 [1.1.1] states that design loading conditions as specified in Ch.15 Sec.1 [4.3] shall be provided as design basis; Pt3.Ch15.Sec1 [4.3] defines the full set of standard intact stability loading conditions that must be covered.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.2]: The hull girder strength assessment requires still water bending moments MSW and shear forces QSW to be calculated for 'design loading conditions as specified in Sec.3 [3]'. This sends the reader to Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [3].

Step 2 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [3.1.1]: States that 'the standard design loading conditions given in this subsection shall be considered in addition to the standard loading conditions given in Pt.3 Ch.4 Sec.8 [1]'. The Pt5 conditions for container ships are: homogeneous cargo loading at maximum draught and ballast loading conditions. But these are additive to Pt.3 Ch.4 Sec.8 [1], so the reader must also go there.

Step 3 — Pt3.Ch4.Sec8 [1.1.1]: States that 'design loading conditions as specified in Ch.15 Sec.1 [4.3] shall be provided as design basis in addition to, if applicable, design load conditions required by Pt.5'. This sends the reader to Pt3.Ch15.Sec1 [4.3] for the base set of loading conditions.

Step 4 — Pt3.Ch15.Sec1 [4.3]: Defines the standard intact stability loading conditions (full load departure and arrival, ballast departure and arrival, and potentially others such as partial load conditions). These form the mandatory baseline.

Step 5 — Pt3.Ch4.Sec8 [1.1.1] also specifies that all design loading conditions shall be evaluated for at least departure and arrival, with departure bunkers ≥ 95% full and other consumables at 100%, and arrival bunkers ≤ 10% full and other consumables at 10%.

Conclusion: The designer's claim is incorrect. The four conditions listed cover the Pt5 container-ship-specific conditions, but the full set from Pt3.Ch15.Sec1 [4.3] must also be included as the baseline. Additionally, Pt3.Ch4.Sec8 [1.1.2] requires that any intermediate voyage stage that is more severe than departure or arrival must also be submitted. The consumable assumptions (bunkers ≥ 95% / other consumables 100% at departure; bunkers ≤ 10% / other consumables 10% at arrival) are mandatory for every seagoing design loading condition.

question_text: A 310-metre container ship is undergoing classification review. The structural design team has completed a cargo hold finite element analysis for the midship region. During the yield strength assessment of the inner bottom plating and double bottom girders, the FE mesh used is a standard cargo hold mesh with element size s×s. The calculated von Mises stress at a double bottom girder connection exceeds the standard cargo hold mesh acceptance threshold, and the designer proposes to use a finer mesh sub-model for that localised geometry to demonstrate compliance. The sub-model covers an area of 450 mm × 450 mm around the connection. The area-weighted von Mises stress extracted from the fine mesh over that region is 285 N/mm² against a yield stress of 315 N/mm² for the material used. Is this arrangement and stress result acceptable under the classification rules, and what specific stress averaging procedure must be applied when using a finer mesh in this context?
required_facts: Yield verification for the cargo hold FEA must follow the requirements in the general FE rules for partial ship structural analysis (not just the container ship chapter alone)
When stress in the standard cargo hold mesh exceeds acceptance criteria and geometry cannot be adequately represented, a finer mesh sub-model is permitted
The finer mesh result must be evaluated as the area-weighted von Mises stress over an area equivalent to the standard s×s mesh element area
The area-weighted von Mises stress of 285 N/mm² is below the material yield stress of 315 N/mm², so the connection is acceptable under the yield criterion
The acceptance criteria applied to the fine mesh stress are the same as those specified for the cargo hold mesh yield check (i.e. the [4.2.3] criteria), not a relaxed limit
The permissible utilisation framework (WSD method with utilisation factor η_i applied to characteristic capacity R) underpins the yield acceptance criteria used in this assessment

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec6 [2.4.1] mandates yield verification per Pt3.Ch7.Sec3 [4.2]; within Pt3.Ch7.Sec3, clause [4.2.8] governs use of finer mesh when geometry cannot be adequately represented and stress exceeds cargo hold mesh acceptance criteria, requiring area-weighted von Mises stress over an area equivalent to s×s to comply with [4.2.3]; the design basis and acceptance framework underpinning these criteria traces back to Pt3.Ch1.Sec2 [4.2] which defines the WSD/PSF methodology and permissible utilisation factors used to calibrate the acceptance criteria.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — The container ship FEA yield check is governed by Pt5.Ch2.Sec6 [2.4.1], which states verification against yield criteria shall be carried out according to Pt3.Ch7.Sec3 [4.2]. Step 2 — Navigating to Pt3.Ch7.Sec3 [4.2.8]: when geometry cannot be adequately represented in the cargo hold model and stress exceeds the cargo hold mesh acceptance criteria, a finer mesh may be used. The area-weighted von Mises stress within an area equivalent to that specified in [2.1.2] (i.e. the standard s×s mesh area) shall comply with requirements given in [4.2.3]. Step 3 — The acceptance criteria in [4.2.3] are calibrated using the WSD method as defined in Pt3.Ch1.Sec2 [4.2], where the permissible utilisation factor η_i is applied to the characteristic structural capacity R (yield stress). For the standard cargo hold mesh yield check the permissible stress is typically η × R_eH. Step 4 — With yield stress 315 N/mm² and a typical permissible utilisation factor of ~1.0 for the fine mesh condition (area-weighted), 285 N/mm² < 315 N/mm², so the result is acceptable provided the area-weighted averaging is correctly applied over an area equivalent to the s×s mesh footprint as required by [4.2.8].

scenario_parameters.mesh_type: standard cargo hold s×s mesh with fine mesh sub-model
scenario_parameters.structural_member: double bottom girder connection at inner bottom

question_text: A naval architect is performing a cargo hold finite element analysis for a 310-metre container ship with a standard midship hold arrangement (two 40 ft bays per hold, one non-watertight support transverse bulkhead between bays). The analysis includes a damaged flooding condition where the centre cargo hold is one of the flooded compartments. For the BSP load cases in this FE analysis, the designer proposes to apply the hydrodynamic sea pressures without any modification factor, arguing that the standard external pressure formulation is sufficient. Additionally, for the fatigue assessment of welded structural details in the cargo hold region, the designer intends to use an operational factor of 1.0 when combining with prescriptive loads from the wave load chapter. The ship trades worldwide and no direct hydrodynamic analysis has been performed. Are either of these two design decisions compliant with the classification rules? Provide the correct values or corrections required for each.
required_facts: The BSP hydrodynamic pressures in the cargo hold FEA must be multiplied by the container ship correction factor f_bCS = 0.9, not applied without modification.
The correction factor f_bCS = 0.9 applies specifically to BSP load cases for container ships as stated in the cargo hold FEA load combination requirements.
The operational factor f_R for prescriptive wave loads in fatigue assessment is 0.76, not 1.0.
f_R = 0.76 applies when using prescriptive loads from the wave load chapter for worldwide trade without a direct hydrodynamic analysis.
Both design decisions are non-compliant with the classification rules.
The f_R factor is defined in the fatigue strength calculations section under operational factor requirements for prescriptive loads.

annotator_grounding.start_clause: Pt5.Ch2.Sec6 Table 1 Note 3 and final paragraph
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec6 Table 1 (cargo hold FEA load combinations for container ships) explicitly references Pt3.Ch4.Sec5 [1.3.6] for BSP hydrodynamic pressures and requires a correction factor; the symbol f_R used in Pt3.Ch4.Sec5 is defined by cross-reference to Pt3.Ch9.Sec4 [4.3], which specifies the operational factor for prescriptive loads.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Start at Pt5.Ch2.Sec6 Table 1: The standard design load combinations for cargo hold FEA include BSP load cases. The final paragraph of Table 1 states that hydrodynamic pressures for BSP load cases according to Pt3.Ch4.Sec5 [1.3.6] shall be multiplied by the correction factor for container ships f_bCS = 0.9. Therefore the designer's proposal to apply BSP pressures without modification is non-compliant; the correct factor is 0.9 (a 10% reduction). Step 2 — Pt3.Ch4.Sec5 [1.3.6] defines the wave pressure formulation for BSP load cases and references the operational factor f_R as defined in Ch.9 Sec.4 [4.3]. Step 3 — Pt3.Ch9.Sec4 [4.3] states that for prescriptive loads calculated in Ch.4, the operational factor shall be f_R = 0.76. The designer's use of f_R = 1.0 is therefore non-compliant; the correct value is 0.76 for worldwide trade with prescriptive loads.

scenario_parameters.hold_arrangement: two 40 ft bays per hold, one non-watertight support transverse bulkhead

question_text:
A newbuild container ship of 320 m length is being designed with upper hull longitudinal structural members fabricated from NV 47 steel plates. The hatch side coaming plates have an as-built thickness of 68 mm. During the structural fabrication review, the shipyard proposes to apply ISO 5817 quality level C welding throughout the entire upper hull longitudinal structure, including the 0.4L amidships region. The designer also proposes to use a material grade selection approach for the 68 mm NV 47 plates that does not reference the rolled steel material grade requirements for structural application.

Is the proposed welding quality level acceptable for the upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships on this vessel? What minimum welding quality level is required, and which structural members are covered by that requirement? Additionally, which material grade selection standard must govern the 68 mm NV 47 coaming plates, and what is the significance of the 50 mm thickness threshold for this ship type?
required_facts: ISO 5817 quality level B (not C) is required for the upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships on container ships
The shipyard's proposal to apply ISO 5817 level C throughout the upper hull longitudinal structure is not acceptable
Upper hull longitudinal structural members include the uppermost strake of longitudinal bulkhead, sheer strake, upper deck, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate, and all attached longitudinals
The 50 mm thickness threshold triggers the thick-plate regime for container ships using NV 36, NV 40, or NV 47 steel; the 68 mm NV 47 coaming plates exceed this threshold and fall within scope
Material grade selection for the 68 mm NV 47 plates must follow the rolled steel material grade requirements for structural application in the hull materials section (Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.3])
The thick-plate section (Pt5.Ch2.Sec10) explicitly cross-references the hull materials section for material grade selection, making it a mandatory cross-volume requirement

annotator_grounding.start_clause: Pt3.Ch9.Sec5 [1] (special consideration for fatigue, innovative designs, and workmanship)
annotator_grounding.end_clause: Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.3] (material grade selection for rolled steels)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Pt3.Ch9.Sec5 (fatigue special considerations) → Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2] (workmanship/welding quality level requirement referencing Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3]) → Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3] (definition of upper hull longitudinal structural members for container ships with thick plates >50 mm) → Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.3] (material grade selection requirements for rolled steels)
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2]: The workmanship section states that ISO 5817 quality level C applies to all ship types as a minimum, but ISO 5817 quality level B is required for container ships for the upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships and critical areas. The reference for 'upper hull longitudinal structure' is explicitly given as Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3]. Therefore the shipyard's proposal to use level C throughout is not acceptable for this container ship.

Step 2 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3]: This clause defines 'upper hull longitudinal structural members' as: uppermost strake of longitudinal bulkhead, sheer strake, upper deck, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate, and all attached longitudinals. The section applies to container ships with thick steel plates exceeding 50 mm (up to 100 mm) of steel strength groups NV 36, NV 40, and NV 47. The 68 mm NV 47 coaming plates fall squarely within this scope (50 mm < 68 mm ≤ 100 mm, NV 47 group). The 50 mm threshold is the trigger for the entire Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 regime.

Step 3 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [2.1.4] → Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.3]: Clause 2.1.4 of Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 explicitly states that material grade selection shall be according to Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.3]. This cross-volume reference (Pt5 → Pt3) means the designer cannot use an independent approach; the rolled steel material grade requirements in Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.3] are mandatory for the 68 mm NV 47 plates.

question_text: A 185-metre container ship is being designed with fixed cell guides at the bulkheads, fixed container foundations on the inner bottom, and fixed lashing appliances on the upper deck. The ship has a double-bottom ballast tank located beneath the forward cargo hold. The tank has its volumetric centre of gravity at coordinates xG = 42 m, yG = 0 m, zG = 1.8 m (measured from the reference coordinate system). The highest point of the tank (excluding small hatchways) is at ztop = 2.9 m, and the load point under assessment is at z = 0.4 m. The tank is fitted with a pressure relief valve set at 35 kN/m². The tank is intended to carry seawater ballast only. For the static design load scenario during normal operations at sea, what is the static internal pressure acting on the tank boundary at the load point described, and what liquid density value must be used in the calculation?
required_facts: The applicable formula for a tank fitted with a pressure relief valve is P_ℓs-1 = fcd · ρL · g · (ztop − z) + PPV
The liquid density ρL must be taken as 1.025 t/m³ for ballast tanks in strength assessment
fcd = 1.0 applies here (not an oil/oil product cargo tank assessed by FE analysis)
PPV = 35 kN/m² is used directly as the design overpressure (within the permitted 25–70 kN/m² range)
The static pressure at the load point is approximately 60.1 kN/m² (= 1.0 × 1.025 × 9.81 × 2.5 + 35)
Cargo hold FE analysis is mandatory for this ship because L = 185 m exceeds the 150 m threshold

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 defines the container ship scope and references Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [3] for definitions not defined locally. Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 defines symbols including density ρ and references the coordinate system. Pt3.Ch7.Sec3 governs partial ship structural analysis (cargo hold analysis) applicable to ships L > 150 m, which mandates FE analysis and references load inputs. Pt3.Ch4.Sec6 provides the internal loads formulae including static liquid pressure for normal operations at sea, specifying the density to use for ballast tanks and the pressure relief valve formula branch.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.5]: The question involves a container ship as defined in this section. For definitions not defined locally, the rules direct the reader to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [3]. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch1.Sec4: Confirms symbols and definitions including ρ (density of seawater = 1.025 t/m³), z coordinates, and g = 9.81 m/s². The density symbol ρL for liquid in tanks is defined in Pt3.Ch4.Sec6 symbols. Step 3 — Pt3.Ch7.Sec3 [1.3.1]: The ship is 185 m (L > 150 m), so cargo hold analysis is mandatory. This section governs the structural analysis framework and references load cases from Pt3.Ch4. Step 4 — Pt3.Ch4.Sec6 [1.2.1]: For normal operations at sea, the static pressure on a tank boundary is: P_ℓs-1 = fcd · ρL · g · (ztop − z) + PPV for tanks with pressure relief valves. For ballast tanks, ρL = 1.025 t/m³ (per the symbols section of Pt3.Ch4.Sec6, fatigue: ρL = 1.025 for ballast tanks; for strength assessment ρL = 1.025 for all liquids). fcd = 1.0 for cases other than FE analysis of oil/oil product cargo tanks with ρL ≤ 1.025. PPV = 35 kN/m² (given, within the 25–70 kN/m² range). Calculation: P_ℓs-1 = 1.0 × 1.025 × 9.81 × (2.9 − 0.4) + 35 = 1.025 × 9.81 × 2.5 + 35 = 25.138 + 35 ≈ 60.1 kN/m².

question_text: A designer is sizing longitudinal stiffeners on the inner bottom of a 150 m container ship. The stiffeners are continuous with fixed ends and span between primary supporting members. The plate flange of the inner bottom has a specified minimum yield strength of 235 N/mm², while the attached longitudinal stiffeners are fabricated from high-strength steel with a specified minimum yield strength of 355 N/mm². The designer proposes to use the plate flange yield strength directly in the stiffener section modulus calculation without any additional checks. Is this approach acceptable under classification rules, and if not, what additional verification is required?
required_facts: The approach is not acceptable because the plate flange yield strength (235 N/mm²) is lower than the stiffener yield strength (355 N/mm²), triggering a mandatory additional check
When plate flange has lower minimum yield strength than the connected stiffener, an additional yield capacity check of the plate flange is required
The additional check is governed by the stiffener yield capacity requirements in the stiffener scantling section (Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4])
The check requires design pressure P determined from the applicable design load sets
Hull girder longitudinal stress σhg must be included, defined as the stress due to vertical still water bending moment for static load component S, plus dynamic wave bending for S+D load components
The designer cannot simply use the plate flange yield strength directly in the stiffener section modulus calculation without performing this additional verification

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.3] flags that when plate flange has lower yield strength than the connected stiffener, an additional yield capacity check of the plate flange may be required, referencing Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4]. Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4] governs the stiffener yield check and uses design pressures P and hull girder stress σhg as defined in Sec.2 [1], which is Pt3.Ch6.Sec2 [1].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.3]: The rules generally assume material in flange and web have the same minimum yield strength. When the plate flange has a lower minimum yield strength than the connected stiffener or PSM, an additional check of yield capacity of the plate flange may be required, per Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4]. Here the plate flange is 235 N/mm² and the stiffener is 355 N/mm², so the condition is triggered. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch6.Sec5 [1.1.4]: This clause specifies the additional yield capacity check for the plate flange when the mismatch condition from Ch.3 Sec.1 [2.3] applies. The check uses design pressure P from the applicable design load sets and hull girder longitudinal stress σhg. Step 3 — Pt3.Ch6.Sec2 [1]: The hull girder longitudinal stress σhg is defined here — for static load component S it equals σhg-sw (stress due to vertical still water bending moment), and for S+D load components it includes the dynamic wave bending contribution. The designer must apply the correct load combination from the design load sets in Sec.2 Table 1 to obtain P and σhg for the inner bottom location. Conclusion: The proposed approach is not acceptable. Because the plate flange yield strength (235 N/mm²) is lower than the stiffener yield strength (355 N/mm²), an additional yield capacity check of the plate flange is mandatory, using design pressures and hull girder stresses determined from the load application rules.

question_text: A new 320-metre container ship is being designed with the class notation 'Container ship'. The upper deck plating within the 0.4L amidships region uses NV 40 steel with a gross plate thickness of 58 mm. The hatch coaming top plates in the same region are also 58 mm thick NV 40 steel. At the forward corner of a cargo hatchway located at 0.45L from the aft perpendicular, the strength deck has a hatch corner between a longitudinal deck strip and a closed area (HC1 type). The longitudinal deck girder alongside the hatchway has a breadth b_L = 2.8 m, and there are no large deck openings forward or aft of any superstructure contributing additional length. The gross moment of inertia of the hull section at this location (without insert plate) is I_y-gr = 980 m^4, the neutral axis is at z_O = 11.2 m above baseline, the hatch corner plate is at z_D = 22.5 m above baseline, the gross thickness of the hatch corner plate t_i = 58 mm, the gross thickness of the longitudinal structural member t_D = 58 mm, the material factor k_i = 1.47, and the total longitudinal bending moment at the forward edge of the relevant cross deck strip is M_T = 12,500,000 kNm. The distribution factor c_s applies at x/L = 0.55. (a) What ISO 5817 weld quality level is required for the fabrication of the upper hull longitudinal structure in this region, and why does the plate thickness trigger a specific additional requirement? (b) Calculate the minimum required hatch corner radius r for this HC1-type corner. (c) If the calculated radius requires an insert plate, what is the minimum longitudinal dimension 'a' of that insert plate, given that the gross deck plate thickness t_gr = 52 mm?
required_facts: ISO 5817 quality level B is required (not level C) for the upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships because the ship is a container ship
The 58 mm NV 40 plate thickness exceeds 50 mm, triggering the thick-plate brittle crack arrest requirements for upper hull longitudinal structural members
Upper hull longitudinal structural members include the upper deck, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate and attached longitudinals as defined in the container ship rules
The minimum required hatch corner radius is r ≈ 1.02 m (approximately 1.016 m), which exceeds r_min = 0.15 m
The coefficient c1 = 1.12 (using f_D = 0.40 with L_13 = 300 m and b_L = 2.8 m, with ℓ = 0)
The minimum longitudinal insert plate dimension a = 350 mm (governed by a_min, since the formula gives 318 mm < 350 mm)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2] mandates ISO 5817 level B for container ship upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships and references Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3] for the definition of those members. Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.1] establishes that the 58 mm NV 40 plate triggers the thick-plate regime (>50 mm, ≤100 mm). Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [6.3.6] / [7.3.5] directs that hatch corners of ships with large deck openings (container ships) shall be assessed per Pt.5 Ch.1 and Pt.5 Ch.2. Pt5.Ch2.Sec2 [2.1.1] provides the hatch corner radius formula and insert plate sizing rules.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Weld quality (Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2]): The ship is a container ship. The upper deck and hatch coaming top plate are 'upper hull longitudinal structural members' as defined in Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3] (uppermost strake of longitudinal bulkhead, sheer strake, upper deck, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate and all attached longitudinals). The location is within 0.4L amidships. Therefore ISO 5817 quality level B applies (not the default level C). Additionally, Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.1] is triggered because the plate thickness is 58 mm (>50 mm, ≤100 mm) for NV 40 steel in upper hull longitudinal members — this activates the thick-plate brittle crack arrest requirements of Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [2]. Step 2 — Hatch corner radius (Pt5.Ch2.Sec2 [2.1.1]): The corner is HC1 type (between longitudinal deck strip and closed area). Formula: r ≥ c1 · c2, with r ≥ r_min = 0.15 m. Compute c1: f_D = 0.25 + L_13/2000; L_13 = min(max(L,100),300) = 300 m; f_D = 0.25 + 300/2000 = 0.25 + 0.15 = 0.40. No large deck openings forward/aft of superstructure so ℓ = 0. c1 = (f_D + ℓ/750) · b_L = (0.40 + 0) · 2.8 = 1.12. Compute c2: c_s at x/L = 0.55 → 0.3 ≤ x/L < 0.7 → c_s = 1.0. t_D/t_i = 58/58 = 1.0 (within [0.65, 1.0]). k_i = 1.47; k_i^(1/4) = 1.47^0.25 ≈ 1.101. c2 = [M_T · (z_D − z_O)] / [I_y-gr · 175 × 10^3 · c_s] · (t_D/t_i) · k_i^(1/4) = [12,500,000 · (22.5 − 11.2)] / [980 · 175,000 · 1.0] · 1.0 · 1.101 = [12,500,000 · 11.3] / [171,500,000] · 1.101 = 141,250,000 / 171,500,000 · 1.101 = 0.8237 · 1.101 ≈ 0.907. r = c1 · c2 = 1.12 · 0.907 ≈ 1.016 m. Since 1.016 m > r_min = 0.15 m, the required radius is r ≈ 1.016 m (≈ 1.02 m). Step 3 — Insert plate dimension 'a' (Pt5.Ch2.Sec2 [2.1.1]): a = 3·(t_i − t_gr) + 300 with a ≥ a_min = 350 mm. a = 3·(58 − 52) + 300 = 3·6 + 300 = 18 + 300 = 318 mm. Since 318 mm < 350 mm, a = a_min = 350 mm.

question_text: A newbuilding RO/RO ferry is under construction at a shipyard. The vessel has a contract for construction signed on 15 March 2024. The design includes several internal watertight doors fitted in transverse watertight bulkheads. During the outfitting phase, the shipyard proposes the following testing programme for these internal watertight doors: (1) a standard function test to verify mechanical operation of each door, and (2) a hydrostatic pressure test for doors that become submerged in the worst-case damage waterplane. The shipyard claims that the function test alone satisfies all classification requirements for internal watertight doors, and that no additional testing beyond the hydrostatic pressure test is needed for damaged-condition doors. The chief surveyor questions whether the function test procedure for internal watertight doors must meet any specific additional requirements beyond simply confirming the door opens and closes. Separately, the owner asks which edition of the classification rules governs this vessel's design — the rules in force when the contract was signed in March 2024, or a newer edition published in October 2024. Is the shipyard's testing claim correct, and which rules apply to this vessel?
required_facts: The function test for internal watertight doors must be carried out in accordance with the additional requirements for internal watertight doors (cross-referenced from Pt3.Ch12.Sec1 [3.3.1] to Sec.3 [4.1.2]), not merely a basic open/close check
The shipyard's claim that a standard function test alone satisfies all requirements is incorrect — an additional function test per Sec.3 [4.1.2] is mandatory for each internal watertight door
Internal watertight doors must be operable from both sides of the bulkhead
Remotely controlled internal watertight doors must also be locally operable, with open/closed indicators at the control position
The rules in force at the date of contract for construction (15 March 2024) govern this vessel's classification — not the October 2024 edition
The date of contract for construction is the date the contract to build the vessel is signed between the prospective owner and the shipbuilder, which is 15 March 2024 in this scenario

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch12.Sec1 [3.3.1] requires function testing for internal watertight doors and cross-references Sec.3 [4.1.2] for additional function test requirements; Sec.3 [4.1.2] in turn references Sec.2 [1.3] for scantlings of securing devices; the applicable rules question resolves via Pt1.Ch1.Sec2 [1.3.1] which states rules in force at date of contract for construction apply.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Pt3.Ch12.Sec1 [3.3.1] states all weathertight/watertight doors shall be function tested, AND for each internal watertight door/hatch, the function test shall be carried out in accordance with Sec.3 [4.1.2] additionally. This means the shipyard's claim that a standard function test alone suffices is incomplete — there is a mandatory additional requirement cross-referenced to Sec.3 [4.1.2]. Step 2: Navigating to Pt3.Ch12.Sec3 [4.1.2], this clause specifies the detailed function test procedure for internal watertight doors, including operability requirements from both sides of the bulkhead/deck (Sec.3 [4.1.1] and [4.2.1]). Step 3: Sec.3 [2.1.2] references Sec.2 [1.3] for scantlings of securing devices, confirming the cross-section dependency. Step 4: For the applicable rules question, Pt1.Ch1.Sec2 [1.3.1] states that the rules applying for assignment of class to a new vessel are generally those in force at the date of 'contract for construction'. Since the contract was signed 15 March 2024, the rules in force on that date govern — not the October 2024 edition.

scenario_parameters.door_type: internal watertight doors in transverse watertight bulkheads
scenario_parameters.shipyard_claim: standard function test alone satisfies all classification requirements for internal watertight doors

question_text: A naval architect is designing a two-island container ship with the following characteristics: ship length L = 320 m, breadth B = 48.2 m, depth D = 27.5 m, and the engine room front bulkhead is located 56 m from the aft end of L. The hull cross-section at 0.5L uses AH36 steel (specified minimum yield stress R_eH = 355 N/mm²) for the upper deck plating, with a net plate thickness of 22 mm as-built. The designer proposes to also use A47 steel (R_eH = 460 N/mm²) for highly stressed deck longitudinals in the same cross-section to reduce scantlings. The hull girder yield check at 0.5L requires combining vertical bending, horizontal bending, and warping stresses. For the warping stress calculation, the net sectorial moment of inertia I_ω-n50 = 4 800 m⁶, the net torsional moment of inertia I_T-n50 = 0.0045 m⁴, and the characteristic torsion length ℓ_c = 0.71 × 320 = 227.2 m. The design still water torsional moment M_st at 0.5L is 850 000 kNm. Is the proposed use of A47 steel (460 N/mm²) for the deck longitudinals permissible for this vessel, and what material factor k should be applied for the A47 steel in the hull girder scantling calculations? Additionally, what is the warping factor λ (in m⁻¹) for this cross-section, and what is the distribution coefficient c_d at x = 0.5L?
required_facts: The use of A47 steel with R_eH = 460 N/mm² is permissible because this vessel qualifies as a Container ship (two-island design), which is the required class notation for applying extra high strength steel at this yield level
The material factor k for A47 steel (R_eH = 460 N/mm²) is k = 0.62
The warping factor λ = sqrt(I_T-n50 / (2.6 × I_ω-n50)) = sqrt(0.0045 / 12480) ≈ 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ m⁻¹
The distribution coefficient c_d = 1.0 at x/L = 0.5 (midship region, plateau zone)

The symbol definitions for R_eH and k used in the hull girder yield check are defined in the materials section (Ch.3 Sec.1 [2]), reached via the symbols cross-reference in the hull girder yield check section
For vessels other than those with the Container ship class notation, application of 460 N/mm² steel is considered on a case-by-case basis only

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt1.Ch3.Sec2 introduces the revised bi-moment formula for two-island container ships and references Pt3.Ch5.Sec3 [3] for the hull girder yield check. Pt3.Ch5.Sec3 defines symbols and references Ch.1 Sec.4 for coordinate system and symbol definitions. Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 defines material symbols (R_eH, k) and references Ch.3 Sec.1 [2] for material factor k and yield stress definitions. Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.5] restricts use of 460 N/mm² steel to ships with the Container ship class notation, and [2.2] gives the material factor k table.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt1.Ch3.Sec2: The revision note establishes that for two-island container ships, the bi-moment formula in Pt3.Ch5.Sec3 [3] applies with the modified (≈20% reduced) formula. The warping factor λ = sqrt(I_T-n50 / (2.6 × I_ω-n50)) = sqrt(0.0045 / (2.6 × 4800)) = sqrt(0.0045 / 12480) = sqrt(3.606×10⁻⁷) ≈ 6.005×10⁻⁴ m⁻¹. The distribution coefficient c_d at x/L = 0.5 falls in the range 0.45 ≤ x/L ≤ 0.55 (midship plateau), so c_d = 1. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch5.Sec3: The hull girder yield check section references Ch.1 Sec.4 for all undefined symbols, including material-related symbols such as R_eH and k. Step 3 — Pt3.Ch1.Sec4: The symbols section defines R_eH as specified minimum yield stress (see Ch.3 Sec.1 [2]) and k as material factor (see Ch.3 Sec.1 [2]), directing the reader to Pt3.Ch3.Sec1. Step 4 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.5]: Extra high strength steel with R_eH = 460 N/mm² is limited to ships with the class notation 'Container ship' as defined in Pt.5 Ch.2. Since this vessel IS a two-island container ship (and thus carries the Container ship notation), the use of A47 (460 N/mm²) steel IS permissible. Step 5 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.2], Table 2: The material factor k for A47 steel (R_eH = 460 N/mm²) is not explicitly listed in Table 2 which shows k = 1.00 for 235 N/mm², k = 0.78 for 315 N/mm², k = 0.72 for 355 N/mm². For 390 N/mm² k = 0.66 by interpolation, and for 460 N/mm² k = 0.57 (as given in the full table for A47/D47/E47/F47 grades). The material factor k = 0.57 applies for A47 steel.

question_text: A 185 m container ship is being designed with fixed cell guides at the bulkheads, fixed container foundations on the inner bottom, and fixed lashing appliances on the upper deck. The ship has a double-bottom ballast tank with the following geometry: the top of the tank is at z = 1.8 m, the load point under assessment is at z = 0.3 m, and the volumetric centre of gravity of the tank is at coordinates (x_G = 92 m, y_G = 4.5 m, z_G = 0.9 m). The tank is fitted with a pressure relief valve set at 30 kN/m². For the static design load scenario during normal operations at sea, the tank is filled with seawater ballast (density 1.025 t/m³). The designer needs to determine the static internal pressure acting on the inner bottom plating at the load point. What is the correct static liquid pressure at that load point, and what density value must be used for the ballast tank in this calculation?
required_facts: The ship qualifies as a Container ship under the classification rules based on its fixed cell guides, container foundations on inner bottom, and fixed lashing appliances
The density ρ_L for a ballast tank must be taken as 1.025 t/m³ for both strength and fatigue assessments
For a tank fitted with a pressure relief valve, the static pressure formula is P_ℓs-1 = f_cd · ρ_L · g · (z_top − z) + P_PV
The factor f_cd = 1.0 applies here because the tank is a ballast tank (not an oil/oil product cargo tank with ρ_L ≤ 1.025 t/m³)
The static liquid pressure at the load point is approximately 45.1 kN/m² (= 1.0 × 1.025 × 9.81 × 1.5 + 30)
The design overpressure P_PV = 30 kN/m² is within the permitted range of 25 to 70 kN/m² and is applied directly in the formula

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 defines the container ship scope and directs undefined terms to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [3] for definitions; Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 defines symbols including density ρ and coordinates; Pt3.Ch4.Sec6 [1.2.1] provides the static liquid pressure formula for normal operations at sea, referencing the symbol definitions from Pt3.Ch1.Sec4
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Establish ship type: The vessel has cell guides at bulkheads, fixed container foundations on inner bottom, and fixed lashing appliances on upper deck, matching the application criteria in Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.3]. It qualifies as a Container ship. Step 2 — Locate definitions: Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.5] states that for definitions not defined in that section, see Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [3]. This directs the designer to the general symbols and definitions section for coordinate system, density symbols, and other parameters used in load calculations. Step 3 — Identify relevant symbols from Pt3.Ch1.Sec4: ρ (density of seawater) = 1.025 t/m³; z = z-coordinate of load point; z_top = Z coordinate of highest point of tank; g = 9.81 m/s²; P_PV = design overpressure from pressure relief valve. Step 4 — Apply Pt3.Ch4.Sec6 [1.2.1] for static pressure during normal operations at sea. For a tank fitted with pressure relief valves: P_ℓs-1 = f_cd · ρ_L · g · (z_top − z) + P_PV. Step 5 — Determine density: Per Pt3.Ch4.Sec6 symbols, for fatigue assessment ρ_L = 1.025 for ballast tanks; for strength assessment ρ_L = 1.025 for all liquids. So ρ_L = 1.025 t/m³. Step 6 — Determine f_cd: The tank is a ballast tank (not an oil/oil product cargo tank), so f_cd = 1.0. Step 7 — Calculate: z_top = 1.8 m, z = 0.3 m, so (z_top − z) = 1.5 m. P_PV = 30 kN/m² (within the 25–70 kN/m² permitted range). P_ℓs-1 = 1.0 × 1.025 × 9.81 × 1.5 + 30 = 1.025 × 9.81 × 1.5 + 30 = 15.09 + 30 = 45.09 kN/m².

question_text:
A newbuild container ship of 320 m length is being designed with NV 47 high-strength steel plates in the hatch side coaming structure. The coaming plates have an as-built thickness of 72 mm. During structural design review, the design team proposes using flat bar longitudinals welded to the coaming as the attached longitudinals. The plate flange of these flat bar longitudinals has a specified minimum yield strength of 355 N/mm², while the connected primary supporting members (PSMs) have a minimum yield strength of 460 N/mm². The ship will operate in unrestricted service. 

Is the proposed arrangement of flat bar longitudinals with the lower-yield-strength plate flange acceptable without additional checks? If not, what additional verification is required, and what design load scenario table must be applied when performing the yield strength check for these stiffeners?
required_facts: The section on very thick steel plates (Pt5.Ch2.Sec10) applies because the coaming plates are NV 47 with thickness 72 mm, which exceeds 50 mm and does not exceed 100 mm, on a container ship.
Material grade selection for these plates is governed by Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.3].
Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.2] states that when the plate flange has a lower minimum yield strength than the connected PSM, an additional yield capacity check of the plate flange is required.

The condition is not triggered here because the yield-strength difference between the plate flange (355 N/mm²) and the connected PSM (460 N/mm²) is about 29.6%, which is below the 35% threshold for an automatic additional check.
The additional check is specified in Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4] (yield capacity of plate flange for stiffeners subject to lateral pressure).
The design load scenarios to be applied in that yield check are the principal S and S+D load scenarios defined in Ch.4 Sec.7 [1.1.2], Table 1.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [2.1.4] directs material grade selection to Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.3]; Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.2] flags that when plate flange yield strength is lower than connected PSM, an additional yield capacity check per Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4] is required; Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4] in turn requires the design load scenarios to be applied per Ch.4 Sec.7 [1.1.2].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.1]: The ship is a container ship with NV 47 plates of 72 mm thickness (>50 mm, ≤100 mm) in upper hull longitudinal structural members (hatch side coaming). The section applies. Step 2 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [2.1.4]: Material grade selection shall be according to Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.3]. Step 3 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.2]: The rules generally assume material in flange and web have the same minimum yield strength. When material in plate flange has a lower minimum yield strength than the connected stiffener or PSM, then an additional check of yield capacity of plate flange may be required — see Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4]. Here the plate flange is 355 N/mm² and the PSM is 460 N/mm², so the condition is triggered. Step 4 — Pt3.Ch6.Sec5 [1.1.4]: The yield capacity check of the plate flange must be performed. The design load scenarios to be used for this check are those defined in Ch.4 Sec.7 [1.1.2], which specifies that for strength assessment the principal design load scenarios consist of S (static) or S+D (static+dynamic) loads as tabulated in Table 1 of that section.

scenario_parameters.structural_location: hatch side coaming (upper hull longitudinal structural member)

question_text:
A shipyard signed a contract on 15 March 2021 to build a series of five ro-ro cargo vessels for a Norwegian owner. The contract explicitly lists hull numbers 101 through 105. The yard now wishes to add two additional sister vessels (hull numbers 106 and 107) via a contract amendment signed on 10 September 2022. All seven hulls are built to the same approved classification plans with no design alterations affecting classification matters.

The vessels are fitted with internal hydraulic ramp covers that separate a cargo hold from a ballast tank. The ramp covers use hydraulic cleating as the sole means of securing. The securing devices (bolts and wedges) for the hatch coamings are sized to a bolt diameter of 22 mm at a spacing of 600 mm, and the designer claims this satisfies the applicable scantling requirements.

For the purposes of DNV classification:
1. Which edition of the rules applies to hull numbers 106 and 107 — those in force on 15 March 2021 or those in force on 10 September 2022?
2. For the hydraulic cleating arrangement on the internal ramp covers, what additional mechanical requirement must be satisfied?
3. The scantlings of the securing devices (bolts, wedges) for the internal ramp covers are governed by a specific set of requirements — identify what those requirements are and where they are found within the same chapter.
required_facts: Hull numbers 106 and 107 are subject to the rules in force on 10 September 2022, because a contract amendment adding vessels is treated as a new contract for construction.
The date of 'contract for construction' for amended/additional vessels is the date the amendment is signed, not the date of the original contract.
Hydraulic cleating on internal ramp covers must remain mechanically locked in the closed position in the event of hydraulic system failure.

Scantlings of securing devices (bolts, wedges, etc.) for internal hatch/ramp covers are governed by the requirements in the section covering access openings in freeboard and exposed decks within the same chapter (Pt3.Ch12.Sec2 [1.3]).
Hull numbers 101–105 remain subject to rules in force on 15 March 2021, as they were covered by the original contract.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch12.Sec3 [2.1.2] states scantlings of securing devices are given in Sec.2 [1.3]; Sec.3 [2.1.4] imposes a mechanical lock requirement for hydraulic cleating. The question of which rules apply to the amendment vessels requires following the cross-volume reference from Pt3.Ch12.Sec2 [1.3] back to Pt1.Ch1.Sec2 [1.3], which defines 'contract for construction' and how amendments are treated as new contracts.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Pt3.Ch12.Sec3 [2.1.2]: 'Scantlings of securing devices are given in Sec.2 [1.3].' This directs the reader to Pt3.Ch12.Sec2 [1.3], which contains the bolt/wedge scantling requirements for securing devices on access openings in freeboard and exposed decks.
Step 2 — Pt3.Ch12.Sec3 [2.1.4]: 'Where hydraulic cleating is applied, the system shall remain mechanically locked in closed position in the event of failure of the hydraulic system.' This is a direct requirement at the start section.
Step 3 — Pt3.Ch12.Sec2 [1.3] references Pt1.Ch1.Sec2 [1.3] for the applicable rules question. Pt1.Ch1.Sec2 [1.3.1] states: 'The rules that apply for assignment of class to a new vessel are generally those in force at the date of contract for construction.' Pt1.Ch1.Sec2 [1.3.2] para 3 states: 'If a contract for construction is later amended to include additional vessels or additional options, the date of contract for construction for such vessels is the date on which the amendment to the contract is signed... The amendment to the contract is to be considered as a new contract.' Therefore hull numbers 106 and 107 are subject to rules in force on 10 September 2022, not 15 March 2021.

question_text: A 220 m container ship is being designed with NV 47 steel plates of 68 mm thickness used for the hatch side coaming structure within the cargo hold region. The shipyard proposes to use Option B brittle crack arrest design (high toughness welds with increased sensitivity NDT). The bilge keel ground bar is fabricated from the same NV 47 steel as the adjacent bilge strake, and the bilge keel ends are welded to the hull using a fillet weld with a leg length of 8 mm. The ground bar has an as-built thickness of 16 mm, while the bilge strake has an as-built thickness of 18 mm. The bilge keel web ends are tapered at a ratio of 2.5:1. Is the overall arrangement compliant with classification requirements? Identify all non-compliances, including any additional welding detail requirements that apply specifically because of the NV 47 material used in the upper hull longitudinal structural members, and state what minimum taper ratio is required for the bilge keel web ends.
required_facts: The 220 m ship exceeds 150 m, so the additional bilge keel requirements for ships above 150 m apply
The minimum taper ratio for bilge keel web ends on ships above 150 m is 3:1
The proposed taper ratio of 2.5:1 is non-compliant (less than the required 3:1 minimum)
NV 47 steel plates of 68 mm thickness in the hatch side coaming trigger the application of Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 for container ships
Because NV 47 material is used, the additional requirements in the thick plate section apply, which reference detail design rules for upper hull longitudinal structural members
Welding requirements for bilge keel ends are governed by the weld joint design section referenced from the bilge keel appendage rules
The arrangement is not fully compliant due to at least the non-conforming taper ratio

annotator_grounding.end_clause: Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 (detail design requirements reached via Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [5.1] and Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [3.2.4])
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Bilge keel appendage rules (Pt3.Ch11.Sec4) reference welding requirements in Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [5.1]; the container ship NV47 thick plate rules in Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 impose additional requirements referencing Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 for detail design of welded connections in upper hull longitudinal members.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Start at Pt3.Ch11.Sec4 (bilge keel appendages). Clause [1.1.3] states the ground bar and bilge keel shall be tapered or rounded towards the bilge keel ends, and directs the reader to Ch.13 Sec.1 [5.1] for welding requirements. Clause [1.2.3] (ships >150 m, so 220 m qualifies) states tapering shall be gradual with a minimum ratio of 3:1. The proposed 2.5:1 taper ratio is non-compliant — minimum required is 3:1. Step 2 — Follow the reference to Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [5.1] for welding requirements applicable to bilge keel ends. This section governs weld joint design for hull structures. The fillet weld leg length and ground bar thickness must satisfy the weld sizing rules there. Step 3 — Because the ship has the Container ship class notation and uses NV 47 plates of 68 mm thickness (>50 mm, ≤100 mm) in upper hull longitudinal structural members (hatch side coaming qualifies per Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3]), Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 applies. Clause [1.1.2] states that the requirements in [3] shall additionally apply when NV 47 material is used. Clause [3.2.4] references Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 for detail design requirements — specifically the weld joint detailing and knuckle/stiffener connection rules that must be satisfied for the structural members in the upper hull region. Step 4 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 provides detail design rules including stiffener end connections, knuckle reinforcements, and bracketed connections. These impose additional detailing obligations on the NV 47 upper hull members beyond the standard bilge keel rules. Non-compliances identified: (a) taper ratio of 2.5:1 is less than the required 3:1 minimum for ships >150 m; (b) additional detail design requirements per Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 apply to the NV 47 upper hull structural members due to the Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [3.2.4] cross-reference, which the design must satisfy.

question_text:
A naval architect is reviewing the structural detail design for a new 310-metre container ship. In the upper deck structure, a longitudinal shell strake transitions through a knuckle where the plating changes angle. The knuckle is located within the 0.6L midship region. The designer has proposed placing the in-line support stiffener at 65 mm from the knuckle line, arguing this is close enough to provide adequate out-of-plane stiffness. Additionally, at one location a transverse stiffener intersects the knuckle at an angle of approximately 12 degrees (a shallow angle), and the designer proposes interrupting this stiffener at the knuckle with a backing bracket fitted to the attached plating on the opposite side only.

The ship is primarily intended for the carriage of containers, equipped with cell guides at bulkheads, fixed container foundations on the inner bottom, and fixed lashing appliances on the upper deck.

(a) Is the proposed 65 mm support stiffener offset from the knuckle acceptable for this location on the ship?
(b) Is the proposed arrangement for the stiffener intersecting the knuckle at 12 degrees — interrupted with a bracket on the opposite side only — compliant with the applicable structural rules?
(c) What is the maximum permitted distance between the knuckle and the in-line support stiffening for a standard (non-shallow) knuckle within the 0.6L region, and what alternative distance applies for shallow knuckles (angles less than 10 degrees)?
required_facts: The 65 mm offset between the knuckle and the in-line support stiffener is NOT acceptable within the 0.6L region
The maximum permitted distance between a standard knuckle and its in-line support stiffening within 0.6L is 50 mm
For shallow knuckles (angles less than 10 degrees), the permitted distance increases to 75 mm
The 12-degree intersection angle does NOT qualify as a shallow knuckle (threshold is less than 10 degrees), so the 50 mm limit applies
The proposed interrupted stiffener arrangement with a bracket fitted only on the opposite side of the attached plating does NOT constitute proper end support at the knuckle and is not compliant
