Proper end support at the knuckle requires a carling, bracket, or equivalent fitted at the knuckle itself (not on the opposite side of the plating)

The container ship classification under Pt5.Ch2 is supplementary to main class rules, and the knuckle detail design requirements derive from the main class structural rules referenced via the definitions cross-reference chain

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Container ship rules (Pt5.Ch2.Sec1) direct undefined terms to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [3] for definitions; Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 symbols section references Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [2.1.1] for EPP geometry; Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 symbols direct to Ch.1 Sec.4 for undefined symbols, and the structural idealisation rules feed into detail design requirements in Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [2.1.1] for knuckle reinforcement.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Establish ship type: The vessel is a sea-going ship primarily intended for carriage of containers with cell guides, fixed foundations, and lashing appliances → qualifies under Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.3] as a Container ship. Rules in Pt5.Ch2 are supplementary to main class rules.

Step 2 — Locate definitions: Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.5] states 'For definitions not defined in this section, see Pt.3 Ch.1 Sec.4 [3].' This directs the reviewer to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 for general structural terminology including geometric definitions used in detail design.

Step 3 — Structural idealisation link: Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [2.1.1] defines the elementary plate panel (EPP) dimensions (a = length, b = breadth of EPP). The symbols section of Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 explicitly states 'For symbols not defined in this section, see Ch.1 Sec.4.' This confirms the cross-reference chain from Pt5 → Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 → Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 → Pt3.Ch3.Sec6.

Step 4 — Apply knuckle detail design rules from Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [2.1.1]:
  (a) Clause 2.1.1(f): 'the distance between the knuckle and the support stiffening in line with the knuckle shall not be greater than 50 mm within 0.6L.' The proposed 65 mm offset EXCEEDS the 50 mm limit → NOT acceptable.
  (b) Clause 2.1.1(d): Where stiffeners intersect the knuckle at a narrow angle, interrupting the stiffener may be accepted 'provided that proper end support in terms of carling, bracket or equivalent is fitted.' However, Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [3.1] and the effective bending span rules (Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [1.1.2]) clarify that a bracket fitted only on the opposite side of the attached plating does NOT reduce the effective span and does not constitute proper end support at the knuckle itself → the arrangement as described (bracket on opposite side only) is NOT compliant; a carling, bracket, or equivalent must be fitted at the knuckle.
  (c) Standard knuckle within 0.6L: max 50 mm. Shallow knuckle (angle < 10 degrees): max 75 mm is acceptable per clause 2.1.1(f). The 12-degree angle in the scenario does NOT qualify as a shallow knuckle (threshold is < 10 degrees), so the 50 mm limit applies.

scenario_parameters.ship_type: container ship with cell guides, fixed foundations, lashing appliances
scenario_parameters.knuckle_location: within 0.6L midship region, upper deck longitudinal shell strake
scenario_parameters.bracket_position: opposite side of attached plating only

question_text: A 320-metre container ship is being designed with class notation 'Container ship'. The upper deck plating within the 0.4L amidships region uses NV 40 steel plates with a gross thickness of 58 mm. The structural designer proposes to apply ISO 5817 quality level C to all welded joints in this region during fabrication, arguing that level C is the standard minimum for all ship types. Additionally, the hatch side coaming in the same region is fabricated from the same 58 mm NV 40 plate. During the buckling check of the upper deck plating under combined longitudinal compression and shear (design load scenario combining static and dynamic loads), the calculated buckling utilization factor η_act comes out to 0.92. The designer claims this is acceptable because it is below 1.0. Is the proposed fabrication quality level correct for this vessel and region, and is the buckling utilization factor of 0.92 acceptable for the upper deck plating under the described load scenario? Justify your answer with reference to the applicable thresholds.
required_facts: ISO 5817 quality level B (not C) is required for container ships for upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships
Upper hull longitudinal structural members include the upper deck and hatch side coaming, as defined in the container ship rules for thick plate application
The 58 mm NV 40 plate exceeds the 50 mm thickness threshold that triggers the thick-plate upper hull requirements for container ships
Buckling checks must be performed on net scantlings (gross thickness minus corrosion addition t_c), not gross thickness
For plates and stiffened panels under AC-II (S+D load scenario), the allowable buckling utilization factor η_all = 1.00
η_act = 0.92 is acceptable under AC-II (η_all = 1.00) but would be non-compliant under AC-I (η_all = 0.80)
The fabrication quality level proposal of ISO 5817 level C is non-compliant for this vessel type and region

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Fatigue workmanship requirements for container ships reference upper hull longitudinal structure definition in Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3]; that section's scope triggers corrosion addition rules in Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [6.3.6] for net scantling context; buckling allowable utilization factors for plates under AC-II (S+D) are governed by Pt3.Ch8.Sec1 [3.4] Table 3.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Fabrication quality level: Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2] states that ISO 5817 quality level B (not C) shall be applied to container ships for upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships. The designer's proposal of level C is therefore non-compliant for this vessel type and region.

Step 2 — Identify 'upper hull longitudinal structural members': Following the cross-reference in Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2] to Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3], upper hull longitudinal structural members include the upper deck, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate, sheer strake, uppermost strake of longitudinal bulkhead, and all attached longitudinals. The 58 mm NV 40 upper deck plating and hatch side coaming both fall within this definition, and since thickness exceeds 50 mm, the section Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.1] applies to this vessel.

Step 3 — Net scantling basis for buckling: Pt3.Ch8.Sec1 [1.1.3] states buckling strength is based on net scantling (gross thickness minus corrosion addition t_c as defined in Ch.3, i.e. Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [6.3.6]). The designer must deduct t_c from the 58 mm gross thickness before performing the buckling check.

Step 4 — Allowable buckling utilization factor: Pt3.Ch8.Sec1 [3.4] Table 3 defines η_all for plates and stiffened panels under AC-II (S+D load scenario) as 1.00, and under AC-I (S only) as 0.80. The described load scenario combines static (S) and dynamic (D) loads, which corresponds to AC-II. Therefore η_all = 1.00 for AC-II, and η_act = 0.92 ≤ 1.00 is technically acceptable under AC-II. However, if the designer had incorrectly classified this as AC-I (static only), η_all = 0.80 and 0.92 would exceed the limit and be non-compliant.

Conclusion: (a) ISO 5817 level C is NOT correct — level B is required for container ships in the upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships; (b) η_act = 0.92 is acceptable only if the load scenario is correctly classified as AC-II (S+D), giving η_all = 1.00; under AC-I the limit would be 0.80 and the design would fail.

scenario_parameters.region: upper deck and hatch side coaming within 0.4L amidships

question_text: A 230 m bulk carrier with large deck openings (as defined by the classification society's rules for ships with large deck openings) is being designed. The strength deck has a series of cargo hatchways. At one hatch corner located on the strength deck, the following parameters apply: the hatch corner is of type HC1 (between a longitudinal deck strip and a closed area), the breadth of the longitudinal deck girder alongside the hatchway is bL = 2.8 m, the relevant length of large deck openings forward and aft of superstructure is ℓ = 46 m, the rule length L13 = 230 m, the gross moment of inertia of the hull section at the hatch corner (without insert plate) is Iy-gr = 180 m⁴, the total longitudinal bending moment MT = 4 200 000 kNm, the distance of the hatch corner from baseline zD = 18.5 m, the distance of the neutral axis from baseline zO = 9.2 m, the gross thickness of the hatch corner plate ti = 22 mm, the gross plate thickness of the longitudinal structural member tD = 22 mm, and the material factor ki = 1.0. The hatch corner is located at x/L = 0.55 along the ship length. A designer proposes a corner radius of r = 0.55 m with no insert plate. Is this arrangement compliant, and what is the minimum required corner radius? Additionally, the primary supporting members (PSMs) in the cargo hold region are subjected to lateral pressure. For one transverse web frame acting as a PSM with both ends fixed (load model A), the hull girder longitudinal stress at the load calculation point must be determined. The designer states that the load calculation point for the hull girder longitudinal stress σhg is taken at the mid-span of the PSM. Is this correct, and if not, where should it be taken?
required_facts: The minimum required hatch corner radius is approximately r ≥ 1.48 m (from c1 · c2 ≈ 1.194 × 1.240)
The proposed radius of r = 0.55 m does not comply with the minimum required radius
The arrangement is not compliant and an insert plate is required
The fD coefficient for the strength deck is 0.365 (= 0.25 + 230/2000) and c1 = 1.194 m for HC1 corner type
The load calculation point for hull girder longitudinal stress σhg in PSM scantling checks is defined in Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [5.1], not at mid-span as the designer assumed
Ships with large deck openings must have hatch corners assessed per the special requirements in Pt.5 Ch.2 (cross-volume reference triggered by Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [7.3.5])
rmin = 0.15 m for hatch corners in the strength deck, but the governing requirement is c1 · c2 ≈ 1.48 m

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The symbol definition for σhg in Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 references Ch.3 Sec.6 [5.1] for the load calculation point. Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [7.3.5] then directs ships with large deck openings to Pt.5 Ch.2 for hatch corner treatment, landing at Pt5.Ch2.Sec2 [2.1.1] for the hatch corner radius formula.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — PSM hull girder stress location: In Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 Symbols, σhg is defined as 'calculated at the load calculation point as defined in Ch.3 Sec.6 [5.1]'. The designer's claim that mid-span is the load calculation point must be checked against Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [5.1], which specifies the actual location (typically at the support or a defined reference point, not mid-span). This is the first cross-reference hop.

Step 2 — Hatch corner applicability: The ship is a bulk carrier with large deck openings (L = 230 m). Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [7.3.5] states that for ships with large deck openings, hatch corners shall be specially considered per Pt.5 Ch.1 and Pt.5 Ch.2. This triggers the cross-volume hop to Pt5.

Step 3 — Hatch corner radius formula (Pt5.Ch2.Sec2 [2.1.1]): The required radius is r ≥ c1 · c2 with r ≥ rmin. For HC1 corner type: c1 = (fD + ℓ/750) · bL. With L13 = 230 m (capped at 300 m, not less than 100 m, so L13 = 230): fD = 0.25 + 230/2000 = 0.25 + 0.115 = 0.365. Then c1 = (0.365 + 46/750) · 2.8 = (0.365 + 0.0613) · 2.8 = 0.4263 · 2.8 = 1.194 m.

Step 4 — Compute c2: c2 = [MT · (zD − zO)] / [Iy-gr · 175 · 10³ · cs] · (tD/ti) · ki^(1/4). At x/L = 0.55 (strength deck, 0.3 ≤ x/L < 0.7): cs = 1.0. tD/ti = 22/22 = 1.0 (within [0.65, 1.0]). ki = 1.0, so ki^(1/4) = 1.0. c2 = [4 200 000 · (18.5 − 9.2)] / [180 · 175 000 · 1.0] · 1.0 · 1.0 = [4 200 000 · 9.3] / [31 500 000] = 39 060 000 / 31 500 000 = 1.240.

Step 5 — Required radius: r ≥ c1 · c2 = 1.194 · 1.240 = 1.481 m, and r ≥ rmin = 0.15 m. So r_required ≈ 1.48 m. The proposed r = 0.55 m is far below the required 1.48 m — the arrangement is NOT compliant. An insert plate is also required.

Step 6 — PSM load calculation point conclusion: Per Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [5.1], the load calculation point for hull girder longitudinal stress is not at mid-span; the designer's assumption is incorrect.

question_text:
A newbuild container ship of 280 m length is being designed with the class notation 'Container ship'. The upper deck plating in the cargo hold region uses NV 47 steel with an as-built thickness of 72 mm. The shipyard proposes to connect the hatch side coaming top plate to the upper deck using a continuous fillet weld. The coaming top plate is also NV 47 steel with a yield strength ReH = 460 N/mm² and as-built thickness of 68 mm. The weld deposit has a specified minimum yield strength ReH_weld = 400 N/mm².

During detail design review, the structural engineer notes that the coaming top plate has a knuckle transition where it meets a longitudinal bracket. The knuckle angle is 15 degrees, and the free flange outstand b1 at the knuckle is 120 mm with a net flange thickness tf of 18 mm. The shipyard proposes to curve the flange at the knuckle rather than fit a tripping bracket.

Two questions arise:
1. Given the plate thickness and steel grade, what additional brittle crack arrest design measures (if any) are required for the hatch coaming structure in the cargo hold region, and which option or options are available to the shipyard?
2. For the curved flange transition at the knuckle on the coaming top plate bracket, what is the minimum radius of curvature r (in mm) that must be achieved to avoid fitting a separate tripping bracket support at the knuckle?
required_facts: The hatch side coaming top plate qualifies as an upper hull longitudinal structural member, so the thick-plate brittle crack arrest rules apply to the 68 mm NV 47 coaming top plate
Because NV 47 material is used with thickness exceeding 50 mm, the additional requirements for NV 47 (beyond those for NV 36/NV 40) must also be applied per the container ship thick-plate section

The shipyard may satisfy brittle crack arrest design via Option A (design approach: block joint shift, crack arrest plates/inserts, crack arrest holes or equivalent) or Option B (welding quality control with high-toughness welds and enhanced NDT)
The minimum radius of curvature for the curved flange transition at the knuckle is r = 1.6 × b1² / tf
Substituting b1 = 120 mm and tf = 18 mm gives r = 1.6 × 120² / 18 = 1280 mm
If the curved radius of at least 1280 mm is achieved, a tripping bracket at the knuckle is not required; otherwise effective tripping support must be fitted

This directs the answerer to Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 for container ships with thick NV 47 plates (>50 mm, ≤100 mm) in upper hull longitudinal structural members including hatch coaming. Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [3.2.4] specifies the brittle crack arrest design requirements for NV 47 material. The hatch coaming top plate is an upper hull longitudinal structural member per [1.1.3]. The weld design for the coaming connection is governed by Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [2.6], which covers fillet weld sizing. The knuckle detail at the coaming bracket flange is governed by Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [2.1.2], which gives the minimum radius formula r = 1.6 × b1² / tf for a curved flange transition as an alternative to tripping bracket support.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Pt3.Ch11.Sec2 [6.1.3]: The miscellaneous deck fittings and supporting structure section notes that requirements related to ship types and class notations are covered in Pt.5 and Pt.6. Since this is a container ship, the answerer is directed to Pt.5 Ch.2.
Step 2 — Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [2.6]: The weld design for the coaming connection must satisfy fillet weld requirements; the weld factor and throat thickness are determined here for the NV 47 / ReH_weld = 400 combination.
Step 3 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [3.2.4]: For container ships with NV 47 steel plates between 50 mm and 100 mm thick in upper hull longitudinal structural members (which explicitly includes hatch side coaming and coaming top plate per [1.1.3]), brittle crack arrest design measures are required. The additional requirements of [3] apply specifically when NV 47 material is used per [1.1.2]. The shipyard may choose Option A (design approach: shift in block joints, crack arrest plates/inserts, crack arrest holes or equivalent) or Option B (welding quality control: high toughness welds with increased sensitivity NDT or multi-pass increased toughness welds with advanced NDT or equivalent).
Step 4 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [2.1.2]: For the curved flange transition at the knuckle on the coaming top plate integral bracket, the minimum radius is r = 1.6 × b1² / tf = 1.6 × 120² / 18 = 1.6 × 14400 / 18 = 1280 mm. If this radius is achieved, a separate tripping bracket at the knuckle is not required. If not, effective support (tripping bracket) must be fitted.

question_text: A 320-metre container ship with a block coefficient of 0.65 and a contract speed of 22 knots is being assessed for hull girder ultimate strength. The vessel operates on unrestricted service. The designer has calculated a permissible vertical still water hogging bending moment of 8,500,000 kNm at the midship section. The hull girder ultimate bending capacity in hogging, MU, has been computed as 12,000,000 kNm. The partial safety factor for material and geometric uncertainties is taken as 1.1, and the vessel has no empty cargo holds with class notation HC(A) or HC(B*). The design loading condition results in a vertical wave hogging bending moment of 4,200,000 kNm at midship. Does the midship section satisfy the hull girder ultimate strength criterion, and what is the minimum required ultimate bending capacity MU (in kNm) to just meet the criterion, given the applied bending moment M derived from the permissible still water and wave bending moments?
required_facts: The hull girder ultimate strength criterion requires M ≤ MU / γR, where γR = γM × γDB
γM = 1.1 and γDB = 1.0 for this hogging case (no empty HC(A)/HC(B*) holds), giving γR = 1.1
The total applied bending moment M = permissible still water hogging moment + wave hogging bending moment = 8,500,000 + 4,200,000 = 12,700,000 kNm
The permissible still water bending moment used in M is defined by reference to the hull girder loads section (Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 [2.2.2])
MU / γR = 12,000,000 / 1.1 ≈ 10,909,091 kNm, which is less than M = 12,700,000 kNm, so the criterion is NOT satisfied
The minimum required ultimate bending capacity is MU_min = 12,700,000 × 1.1 = 13,970,000 kNm

annotator_grounding.start_clause: Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.6] (hull girder ultimate strength for container ships)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 directs hull girder ultimate strength assessment to Pt3.Ch5. Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [1.1.2] defines the locations and [2.1.2] gives the checking criterion M ≤ MU/γR. The symbols section of Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 references Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 [2.2.2] for the permissible still water bending moment Msw-h used in computing M.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 states hull girder ultimate strength shall be assessed in accordance with Pt3.Ch5, with Pt5 requirements applied in lieu of particular Pt3.Ch5 requirements. For container ships, Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [1.1.4] confirms Pt5.Ch2 supplements this section. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [1.1.1] confirms applicability: unrestricted service, L=320m > 150m, container ship (single deck / required in Pt5). Step 3 — Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [2.1.2] gives the criterion: M ≤ MU / γR, where γR = γM × γDB. γM = 1.1 (given). γDB for hogging with no empty HC(A)/HC(B*) holds = 1.0 (standard case), so γR = 1.1 × 1.0 = 1.1. Step 4 — M is the total vertical bending moment = Msw-h + Mwv-h = 8,500,000 + 4,200,000 = 12,700,000 kNm. The permissible still water bending moment Msw-h is defined in Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 [2.2.2] (referenced in the Symbols of Pt3.Ch5.Sec4). Step 5 — Check: MU / γR = 12,000,000 / 1.1 = 10,909,091 kNm. Since M = 12,700,000 kNm > 10,909,091 kNm, the criterion is NOT satisfied. Step 6 — Minimum required MU = M × γR = 12,700,000 × 1.1 = 13,970,000 kNm.

question_text:
A 155 m container ship in unrestricted service is being assessed for classification. The vessel has a single deck configuration and a block coefficient of 0.65. During the structural review, the designer notes that the side shell in the midship region omits transverse stringers between frames, resulting in relatively low lateral bending stiffness at the longitudinal stiffener end connections. The designer proposes to calculate the additional stresses at these end connections using relative displacements obtained from a cargo hold finite element analysis, following the method described in DNV-CG-0129. Separately, the hull girder ultimate strength check is being prepared. The permissible still water bending moment at the midship section is 4 800 000 kNm (hogging) and the vertical wave bending moment is 2 100 000 kNm (hogging). The vessel carries bulk cargo in alternate loading conditions and has class notation HC(M) with alternate loading conditions included in the loading manual.

(a) Is the vessel subject to prescriptive fatigue strength assessment for the longitudinal stiffener end connections in the side shell, and is the proposed calculation approach for additional stresses due to relative deflections acceptable?

(b) For the hull girder ultimate strength check at the midship section in hogging, calculate the design vertical bending moment M and identify the correct partial safety factor γ_R (= γ_M × γ_DB) that must be applied. Is the ultimate strength check mandatory for this vessel, and at which locations along the ship length must it be performed?
required_facts: Prescriptive fatigue assessment applies because L = 155 m ≥ 90 m and the vessel is a container ship
Additional stresses due to relative deflections must be considered for the low-stiffness side shell, and the proposed FE-based approach per DNV-CG-0129 Sec.4 [7] is acceptable
Hull girder ultimate strength check is mandatory: L = 155 m > 150 m, unrestricted service, single deck
For container ships, the ultimate strength check must be performed at or near 0.25L and 0.75L in addition to other specified locations
Design bending moment M = 1.0 × 4 800 000 + 1.2 × 2 100 000 = 7 320 000 kNm (hogging)
γ_DB = 1.25 for hogging with HC(M) notation and alternate loading conditions in the loading manual

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec7 governs fatigue for container ships ≥90 m and references DNV-CG-0129 Sec.4 [7] for relative displacement stresses. Pt5.Ch2.Sec7 [2.1.2] triggers the cross-reference to DNV-CG-0129. Separately, Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 states hull girder strength shall be carried out per Pt.3 Ch.5, and Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [1.1.1] sets the application threshold (L > 150 m, unrestricted service, single deck or if required in Pt.5) and [1.1.2] lists the mandatory check locations including 0.25L and 0.75L for container ships. [2.1.2] and [2.2.1] give the checking criteria and load formula.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Fatigue scope (Pt5.Ch2.Sec7 [1.1.1]): Rule length L = 155 m ≥ 90 m and ship type is container ship → prescriptive fatigue assessment applies. Step 2 — Additional stresses (Pt5.Ch2.Sec7 [2.1.2]): Side shell with omitted stringers has low lateral bending stiffness → additional stresses due to relative deflections must be considered. The calculation shall follow DNV-CG-0129 Sec.4 [7] using relative displacements from FE analysis → proposed approach is acceptable. Step 3 — Hull girder ultimate strength applicability (Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 + Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [1.1.1]): Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 says hull girder strength per Pt.3 Ch.5. Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [1.1.1] requires: unrestricted service ✓, L > 150 m (155 m > 150 m) ✓, single deck ✓ → check is mandatory. Step 4 — Check locations (Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [1.1.2]): For container ships, mandatory locations include cargo hold area in general, forward end of engine room, forward end of foremost cargo hold, significant cross-section changes, framing system changes, and locations at or near 0.25L and 0.75L. Step 5 — Design bending moment (Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [2.2.1]): M = γS × Msw-U + γW × Mwv = 1.0 × 4 800 000 + 1.2 × 2 100 000 = 4 800 000 + 2 520 000 = 7 320 000 kNm. Step 6 — Partial safety factor γ_R (Pt3.Ch5.Sec4 [2.1.2]): γ_M = 1.1. For hogging with HC(M) and alternate loading conditions included in loading manual → γ_DB = 1.25. Therefore γ_R = 1.1 × 1.25 = 1.375.

scenario_parameters.class_notation: HC(M) with alternate loading conditions in loading manual
scenario_parameters.side_shell_feature: omitted transverse stringers — low lateral bending stiffness

question_text: A 320-metre container ship is being designed with NV 47 steel (ReH = 460 N/mm²) upper deck plates of 72 mm as-built thickness in the cargo hold region. The hatch coaming structure uses the same NV 47 material at 68 mm thickness. The designer proposes to use a weld deposit with a specified minimum yield stress of 360 N/mm² for connecting these upper deck plates to the hatch side coaming. The welding procedure qualification tests have been completed. Is the proposed weld deposit yield strength acceptable for this application, and what is the minimum permissible ReH_weld for this connection? Additionally, what material grade selection standard must be followed for the thick plate application, and does the use of NV 47 at this thickness trigger any additional structural countermeasures beyond the standard thick-plate requirements?
required_facts: The proposed weld deposit ReH_weld of 360 N/mm² is NOT acceptable; the minimum required ReH_weld for welding extra high strength steel (ReH = 460 N/mm²) is 400 N/mm².
Material grade selection for the 72 mm NV 47 upper deck plates must follow Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.3] as mandated by the thick-plate application rules for container ships.

Because NV 47 material is applied to upper hull longitudinal structural members exceeding 50 mm thickness, the additional brittle crack arrest design requirements (Section 3 of the thick-plate rules) are triggered.
Brittle crack arrest countermeasures (Option A or Option B) are required within the cargo hold region for the hatch coaming structure at 68 mm NV 47.
NV 47 steel with ReH = 460 N/mm² is classified as extra high strength steel; its application is limited to ships with the Container ship class notation.
The upper deck plates at 72 mm and hatch coaming at 68 mm both fall within the 50–100 mm thickness range covered by the thick-plate application rules for NV 36, NV 40 and NV 47 strength groups.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Weld design symbols in Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 define ReH_weld thresholds; the thick-plate section Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 governs NV 47 application on container ships and references Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.3] for material grade selection; Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.2] adds extra requirements when NV 47 is used.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Weld deposit acceptability (Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 Symbols): For welding of high strength steel with ReH = 390 N/mm², ReH_weld = 400 N/mm². NV 47 has ReH = 460 N/mm², which is extra high strength steel (ReH > 390). The symbol table states ReH_weld shall not be taken greater than 371/k^(2/3). For NV 47, k must be determined from Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 Table 2 (k for ReH = 460 is 0.66 by interpolation or as tabulated). The proposed 360 N/mm² deposit must be checked against the minimum: for ReH = 460 (above the 390 threshold), the minimum ReH_weld = 400 N/mm². Therefore 360 N/mm² is below the minimum of 400 N/mm² and is NOT acceptable. Step 2 — Material grade selection (Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [2.1.4] → Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.3]): Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [2.1.4] states that material grade selection shall be according to Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.3], which gives the material grade requirements based on thickness and service temperature for hull structural steel. The designer must follow those grade requirements for the 72 mm NV 47 upper deck plates. Step 3 — Additional NV 47 countermeasures (Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.2]): Because NV 47 material is applied per [1.1.1], the requirements of [3] (brittle crack arrest design) shall be applied additionally. The hatch coaming at 68 mm with NV 47 falls within the cargo hold region, so brittle crack arrest countermeasures (Option A or Option B per Table 1) are required in addition to the standard thick-plate measures. Step 4 — Cross-reference to Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.7] (end of chain): Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.7] covers material requirements for extra high strength steel application, confirming that NV 47 (ReH = 460 N/mm²) is classified as extra high strength steel and its application on container ships is governed by Pt5.Ch2 as referenced in [2.1.5].

scenario_parameters.location: cargo hold region, upper hull longitudinal structural members

question_text:
A newbuild container ship of 285 m length is being designed with NV 47 high-strength steel plates in the upper hull longitudinal structural members. The hatch side coaming plates have an as-built thickness of 68 mm. The shipyard proposes to use full-penetration butt welds at the block joints in the cargo hold region without any additional crack arrest measures, relying solely on standard welding procedures qualified under normal production conditions. The coaming top plate and sheer strake are also 68 mm NV 47 material.

During the design review, the classification surveyor raises concerns about the weld joint design for these thick plates. Specifically, the surveyor asks whether the proposed welding procedure qualification is sufficient, and whether the weld deposit yield strength used in calculating the weld factor is appropriate given that the abutting plates are NV 47 steel (ReH = 460 N/mm²).

(a) Is the shipyard's proposed approach — standard welding procedures without dedicated brittle crack arrest measures — acceptable for this vessel and plate configuration?

(b) What is the maximum value of ReH_weld that may be used when calculating the weld factor for these NV 47 coaming joints, and what minimum yield strength of weld deposit does the rule specify for welding high-strength steel with ReH = 390 N/mm²? (Use k = 0.62 for NV 47 material.)

(c) The welding procedure qualification tests (WPQT) must comply with which overarching requirement, and does the hull local scantling calculation for the coaming plating use the standard permissible bending stress coefficients or modified ones?
required_facts: The section on very thick steel plates applies because the vessel is a container ship with NV47 plates of 68 mm thickness (exceeding 50 mm but not greater than 100 mm) in upper hull longitudinal structural members.
Because NV47 material is used, the additional requirements for NV47 (beyond those for NV36/NV40) must also be applied.

The shipyard's proposal is not acceptable: brittle crack arrest design measures (Option A or Option B) are mandatory in the cargo hold region for this plate thickness and steel strength group; standard welding procedures alone do not satisfy this requirement.
Welding procedure qualification tests (WPQT) must be qualified in accordance with the requirements of Pt.2 Ch.4 Sec.5, not merely standard production welding procedures.
The maximum permissible ReH_weld for the weld factor calculation is capped at ReH_weld = 371 / k^(2/3); with k = 0.62 this gives approximately 510 N/mm².
The rule specifies a minimum weld deposit yield strength of ReH_weld = 400 N/mm² for welding high-strength steel with ReH = 390 N/mm².

Hull local scantling calculations for the coaming plating must use the modified permissible bending stress coefficients (Ca, βa, αa, Ca-max) from the container ship hull local scantlings table, not the unmodified Pt.3 general values.

annotator_grounding.end_clause: Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [2.6] (weld factor / ReH_weld cap); Pt5.Ch2.Sec5 [3] (hull local scantlings for container ship plating)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 triggers for container ships with NV47 plates >50 mm; [1.1.2] mandates additional requirements in [3] for NV47; [2.1.3] requires WPQT per Pt.2 Ch.4 Sec.5; [3.2.4] references weld joint design back to Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 for the ReH_weld cap formula; hull local scantlings for the coaming plating are governed by Pt5.Ch2.Sec5 which modifies Pt3 coefficients.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.1]: Section applies because vessel is a Container ship with NV47 plates of 68 mm thickness (50 mm < 68 mm ≤ 100 mm) in upper hull longitudinal structural members (hatch side coaming, coaming top plate, sheer strake). Step 2 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.2]: Because NV47 material is applied per [1.1.1], the additional requirements of [3] must also be applied. Step 3 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [2.2.1] / Table 1: The brittle crack arrest design measures (Option A or Option B) are mandatory within the cargo hold region for the applicable thickness/strength group combination. Standard welding without dedicated crack arrest measures does NOT satisfy this requirement — the shipyard's proposal is not acceptable. Step 4 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [2.1.3]: WPQT must be qualified according to Pt.2 Ch.4 Sec.5 (not merely standard production welding procedures). Step 5 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [3.2.4] → Pt3.Ch13.Sec1 [2.6]: For the weld factor calculation, ReH_weld for NV47 (k = 0.62) is capped at ReH_weld_max = 371 / k^(2/3) = 371 / (0.62)^(2/3). Compute: (0.62)^(2/3) = exp((2/3)·ln(0.62)) = exp((2/3)·(−0.4780)) = exp(−0.3187) ≈ 0.7269. So ReH_weld_max ≈ 371 / 0.7269 ≈ 510 N/mm². The rule also specifies ReH_weld = 400 N/mm² as the minimum for welding high-strength steel with ReH = 390 N/mm². Step 6 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec5 [3]: Hull local scantlings for the coaming plating (a container ship structural member) are governed by Pt5.Ch2.Sec5, which provides modified permissible bending stress coefficients (Ca, βa, αa, Ca-max from Table 1) that deviate from the plain Pt3 values — the answerer must apply the Pt5 table rather than the generic Pt3 coefficients.

question_text: A 230-metre container ship is being designed with a deckhouse-mounted containerized equipment unit (a self-contained laboratory module in an ISO freight container) permanently installed on the exposed weather deck. The module is manned during sea voyages. The designer needs to verify the structural scantlings of the side plating of this containerized unit. The deckhouse side plating is being assessed under the SEA-1 design load set. The design pressure PA for the aft and forward external bulkheads of the deckhouse walls is to be applied. The plate panel has a length a = 900 mm and a breadth b = 600 mm. The material used has a specified minimum yield stress ReH = 315 N/mm². Is the containerized equipment unit subject to the same structural scantling requirements as a deckhouse, and what correction factor αp applies to this plate panel?
required_facts: The containerized equipment unit is subject to deckhouse scantling requirements because it is manned during sea voyages
The applicable rule condition triggering deckhouse compliance is that the containerized equipment space is manned
The correction factor αp = 1.2 − b/(2.1a) applies to the plate panel
αp = 0.883 (less than 1.0, so the cap of 1.0 does not apply)
The design pressure PA for deckhouse bulkheads under SEA-1 is defined in the external loads section for aft and forward external bulkheads of superstructure and deckhouse walls

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 defines container ship scope and references Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 for definitions; Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 defines general symbols used throughout; Pt3.Ch4.Sec5 provides the external load formulas (PA for deckhouse bulkheads); Pt3.Ch6.Sec8 governs superstructure/deckhouse scantlings including containerized equipment, and defines the αp correction factor formula
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.3] establishes this is a container ship. Sec1 [1.5] states that for definitions not defined in that section, see Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [3]. This directs the reader to the general definitions and symbols framework in Part 3.

Step 2 — Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 provides the primary symbols and definitions used across Part 3 structural rules, including coordinate systems and material symbols. This is the intermediate node confirming the cross-volume link from Part 5 into Part 3.

Step 3 — Pt3.Ch4.Sec5 [3.4] defines the design pressure PA for aft and forward external bulkheads of superstructure and deckhouse walls under the SEA-1 design load set. This is the load input needed for the scantling check.

Step 4 — Pt3.Ch6.Sec8 [1.1.3] explicitly states that containerized equipment shall comply with the requirements for deckhouse given in [2.2] and [3] IF the containerized equipment space is manned (condition satisfied here — the module is manned during sea voyages). Therefore the manned ISO container module IS subject to deckhouse scantling requirements.

Step 5 — Pt3.Ch6.Sec8 Symbols section defines αp = 1.2 − b/(2.1a), not to be taken greater than 1.0. With a = 900 mm and b = 600 mm: αp = 1.2 − 600/(2.1 × 900) = 1.2 − 600/1890 = 1.2 − 0.317 = 0.883. Since 0.883 < 1.0, αp = 0.883.

scenario_parameters.containerized_unit: manned ISO freight container laboratory module on weather deck

question_text: A newbuild container ship of 320 m length is being designed with the class notation 'Container ship'. The upper deck plating and hatch side coaming in the amidships cargo hold region are fabricated from NV 40 steel with an as-built thickness of 58 mm. The shipyard proposes to apply ISO 5817 quality level C welding throughout the entire vessel, including the upper hull longitudinal structure within the 0.4L amidships region. During the fatigue design review, the attending surveyor also notes that the hatch coaming top plate longitudinals in this region are welded using standard production welds with no enhanced quality control measures. Is the proposed welding quality level acceptable for the upper hull longitudinal structure of this vessel? What minimum welding quality level is required, and which structural members are considered part of the upper hull longitudinal structure for this purpose?
required_facts: ISO 5817 quality level C is not acceptable for the upper hull longitudinal structure of this container ship in the 0.4L amidships region
ISO 5817 quality level B is required for container ships in the upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships
The vessel qualifies as a critical area because NV 40 steel has ReH = 390 N/mm² and/or the plate thickness of 58 mm exceeds 50 mm
Upper hull longitudinal structural members include: uppermost strake of longitudinal bulkhead, sheer strake, upper deck, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate, and all attached longitudinals
The 58 mm plate thickness exceeds the 50 mm threshold that triggers the thick plate and critical area provisions

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Pt3.Ch9.Sec5 (special fatigue considerations), which leads to Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2] (workmanship/welding quality requirements for fatigue), which references Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3] (definition of upper hull longitudinal structural members for container ships), which in turn connects back to Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 for detail design context of those structural members.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Pt3.Ch9.Sec5: The vessel is a container ship with thick plates (58 mm > 50 mm) in the upper hull region, triggering special fatigue consideration. The section notes that for certain structural details, a reduced permissible cumulative fatigue damage or additional verification may be required, and directs the assessor to consider workmanship quality.

Step 2 — Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2]: The workmanship clause states that ISO 5817 quality level C applies to all ship types as a minimum. However, ISO 5817 quality level B shall be applied to container ships for the upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships and critical areas. The guidance note clarifies that critical areas include structural members made of material with yield strength ReH = 390 N/mm² and above, or with thickness more than 50 mm. NV 40 steel has ReH = 390 N/mm², and the plate thickness is 58 mm (> 50 mm), so both criteria are met — this is a critical area. Therefore ISO 5817 level B is required, not level C as proposed by the shipyard.

Step 3 — Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3]: To determine which members constitute 'upper hull longitudinal structural members' (as referenced in Pt3.Ch9.Sec3 [2]), the assessor must follow the cross-reference to Pt5.Ch2.Sec10 [1.1.3]. This clause defines upper hull longitudinal structural members as: uppermost strake of longitudinal bulkhead, sheer strake, upper deck, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate, and all attached longitudinals.

Step 4 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec6: The detail design requirements for these structural members (knuckle reinforcements, stiffener end connections, etc.) are governed by Pt3.Ch3.Sec6, which provides the fabrication and arrangement standards that must be met in conjunction with the elevated welding quality level.

Conclusion: ISO 5817 level C is NOT acceptable. ISO 5817 level B is required for the upper hull longitudinal structure (upper deck, hatch side coaming, coaming top plate, sheer strake, uppermost strake of longitudinal bulkhead, and all attached longitudinals) within 0.4L amidships, because the NV 40 material at 58 mm thickness meets the critical area criteria.

scenario_parameters.region: upper hull longitudinal structure within 0.4L amidships

question_text:
A 180-metre bulk carrier is being designed with a double-side skin construction. The ship has a yield strength of 315 N/mm² (grade AH32 steel, k = 0.78). One of the structural panels under review is a longitudinal stiffened plating panel forming the boundary of a ballast water tank on the inner side of the double skin. The panel has a breadth b = 750 mm and a length a = 2400 mm. The design pressure for the governing load condition is P = 85 kN/m², and the hull girder longitudinal stress at the load calculation point is σ_hg = 110 N/mm².

The designer proposes a net plate thickness of 14.5 mm for this panel. The design is being assessed under the acceptance criteria applicable to ballast tank boundaries (the most demanding static + dynamic load scenario for normal seagoing operations).

Determine whether the proposed 14.5 mm net thickness is sufficient. In your answer, identify the applicable permissible bending stress coefficient Ca, compute the minimum required net thickness, and state whether the design is compliant.
required_facts: The applicable thickness formula is t = 0.0158 × αp × b × √(|P| / (Ca × ReH)), sourced from the general plating rules cross-referenced by the bulk carrier hull scantling requirements

The permissible bending stress coefficient Ca must be taken from the bulk-carrier-specific override table (not the general plating table), using the AC-II row for ballast tank boundaries under S+D loading
For AC-II, longitudinal stiffened plating (longitudinal members): βa = 1.05, αa = 0.50, Ca-max = 0.95
The panel aspect ratio correction αp = 1.2 − 750/(2.1 × 2400) ≈ 1.051, capped at 1.0
The minimum required net thickness is approximately 6.6 mm
The proposed 14.5 mm net thickness is compliant (exceeds the minimum required thickness)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec5 [2.1] directs the designer to use the thickness formula in Pt3.Ch6.Sec4 [1.1.1] but with the Ca coefficients (βa, αa, Ca-max) overridden by Table 1 of Pt5.Ch2.Sec5. The applicable design load scenario (S+D, normal seagoing, ballast tank boundary) is identified via Pt3.Ch4.Sec7 [1.1.2], which classifies the governing load set as scenario 2 (Static + Dynamic). The answerer must navigate from the Pt5 ship-type chapter to the Pt3 plating formula, then back to Pt3 load scenario definitions to confirm which acceptance criteria row applies.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Identify applicable rules: The ship is a bulk carrier, so Pt5.Ch2 applies. Pt5.Ch2.Sec5 [2.1] states that net thickness of plating subjected to lateral pressure shall be derived from Pt3.Ch6.Sec4 [1.1.1], but with Ca defined by Table 1 of Pt5.Ch2.Sec5 (not the standard Pt3 table).

Step 2 — Identify the design load scenario: The panel is a ballast tank boundary under normal seagoing S+D conditions. Per Pt3.Ch4.Sec7 [1.1.2], this is a Static + Dynamic (S+D) load scenario (scenario 2 in Table 1). The acceptance criteria for ballast tank boundaries under S+D is AC-II.

Step 3 — Determine Ca coefficients from Pt5.Ch2.Sec5 Table 1: For AC-II, longitudinal stiffened plating, longitudinal members: βa = 1.05, αa = 0.50, Ca-max = 0.95.

Step 4 — Compute Ca: Ca = βa − αa × (σ_hg / ReH) = 1.05 − 0.50 × (110 / 315) = 1.05 − 0.1746 = 0.8754. Check against Ca-max = 0.95: 0.8754 < 0.95, so Ca = 0.8754.

Step 5 — Compute αp (panel aspect ratio correction): αp = 1.2 − b/(2.1a) = 1.2 − 750/(2.1 × 2400) = 1.2 − 0.1488 = 1.0512, but capped at 1.0, so αp = 1.0.

Step 6 — Apply Pt3.Ch6.Sec4 [1.1.1] formula: t = 0.0158 × αp × b × √(|P| / (Ca × ReH)) = 0.0158 × 1.0 × 750 × √(85 / (0.8754 × 315)) = 11.85 × √(85 / 275.75) = 11.85 × √(0.3083) = 11.85 × 0.5552 = 6.58 mm.

Wait — ReH for AH32 is 315 N/mm², k = 0.78. The formula in Pt3.Ch6.Sec4 uses ReH directly. Let me recheck: t = 0.0158 × 1.0 × 750 × √(85 / (0.8754 × 315)) = 11.85 × √(0.3083) ≈ 6.58 mm.

The proposed 14.5 mm exceeds the minimum required ~6.6 mm, so the design is compliant. However, the key pedagogical point is that the answerer must correctly identify Ca from the Pt5 override table (not the Pt3 default table), use the S+D scenario classification from Pt3.Ch4.Sec7, and apply the Pt3.Ch6.Sec4 formula — a genuine three-node chain.

scenario_parameters.panel_location: longitudinal stiffened plating, inner side of double skin, ballast tank boundary

question_text: A 310 m container ship is being designed with cell guides at the bulkheads, fixed container foundations on the inner bottom, and fixed lashing appliances on the upper deck. The structural engineer needs to calculate the external sea pressure acting on the ship's side shell at a load point located 3.2 m below the design waterline, at a transverse coordinate y = 8.5 m from the centreline, where the local moulded breadth at the waterline Bx = 38 m. During the design review, a question arises about the correct interpretation of the symbol 'TLC' used in the external pressure formulation, and whether the hydrostatic pressure component Ps at this submerged load point should account for the full water head from the load point up to the waterline. Specifically: (1) What does the symbol TLC represent in the context of the pressure calculation, and (2) What is the hydrostatic pressure Ps, in kN/m², at this load point for the static design load scenario, assuming seawater density ρ = 1.025 t/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s²?
required_facts: TLC is defined as the draught at the considered loading condition, found in the symbols and definitions section of the hull rules (Pt3.Ch1.Sec4)
The definition of TLC is reached by following the cross-reference from the container ship rules (Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.5]) to the general definitions section
For the static design load scenario, the external pressure equals the hydrostatic pressure Ps
The hydrostatic pressure formula for a submerged load point is Ps = ρg(TLC − z)
The transverse coordinate y and local breadth Bx are not needed for the hydrostatic component Ps (they affect the wave pressure Pw only)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.5] states that for definitions not defined in that section, see Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [3]. The symbol TLC (draught at considered loading condition) is defined there. Pt3.Ch4.Sec5 [1.2] then gives the hydrostatic pressure formula Ps = ρg(TLC − z), which uses TLC as defined in Pt3.Ch1.Sec4.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify ship type: The vessel has cell guides, fixed container foundations, and fixed lashing appliances → qualifies as a Container ship under Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.3]. Step 2 — Definitions: Pt5.Ch2.Sec1 [1.5] directs the reader to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [3] for definitions not given locally. In Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 2, TLC is defined as the draught at the considered loading condition (in metres). Step 3 — External pressure formula: Pt3.Ch4.Sec5 [1.1] states that for the static (S) design load scenario, Pex = Ps. Pt3.Ch4.Sec5 [1.2] and Table 1 give Ps = ρg(TLC − z) for load points below the waterline (z < TLC). Step 4 — Numerical calculation: The load point is 3.2 m below the design waterline, so (TLC − z) = 3.2 m. Ps = 1.025 × 9.81 × 3.2 = 32.17 kN/m².

question_text: A 14,000 TEU container ship (L = 366 m, B = 51 m, CB = 0.65, CWL = 0.82) is being designed for worldwide trade with a 25-year design life. The structural design team is performing a fatigue assessment of the hatch-corner welded details at the midship region. The ship's loading manual includes three seagoing loading conditions: (1) homogeneous full load at scantling draught with GM = 2.1 m, (2) a 60% homogeneous load condition at T = 11.5 m with GM = 3.4 m, and (3) a ballast condition at T = 8.2 m with GM = 5.8 m. The container securing arrangement plan submitted for approval states a minimum GM of 1.8 m. The fatigue analyst proposes to use the world-wide wave environment with the prescriptive load approach and applies an operational factor fR = 0.76 and an environmental factor fe = 0.8. For the hatch-corner hot spot stress assessment, the analyst selects S-N curve E (FAT 80) arguing it is more conservative than FAT 90 for the hot spot approach. The hatch-corner detail is located in the upper deck plating, which is not a ballast tank or cargo hold. The corrosion protection is standard coating, and the analyst assigns a time in corrosive environment of TC,25 = 2 years. Is the fatigue assessment setup fully compliant with the classification rules? Identify any non-compliant choices and state the correct values or curves that must be used.
required_facts: For the hot spot stress approach on welded joints, S-N curve D (FAT 90) is mandatory; S-N curve E (FAT 80) is not the correct prescribed curve and must be replaced with FAT 90.
The environmental factor fe = 0.8 for worldwide wave environment with prescriptive loads is correct.
The operational factor fR = 0.76 for prescriptive loads is correct.

The container securing arrangement plan minimum GM (1.8 m) must not be less than the minimum GM in the approved trim and stability booklet for the respective draught; if the booklet requires a higher value, the plan is non-compliant.
The standard seagoing design loading conditions for container ships must include at minimum a homogeneous cargo loading condition at maximum draught and a ballast loading condition.
The metacentric height GM for each loading condition is a required input parameter for the fatigue strength calculations.

The time in corrosive environment TC,25 must be taken from the prescribed table based on the structural location; the analyst must verify the correct value for upper deck details against the tabulated values.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The container securing arrangement plan (Pt5.Ch2.Sec8) requires a minimum GM value consistent with the approved trim and stability booklet; the loading conditions for container ships must follow Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 which mandates homogeneous and ballast conditions and references Pt3.Ch9.Sec4 for the fatigue basis including S-N curve selection, environmental factor, operational factor, and corrosion time.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Container securing plan GM check (Pt5.Ch2.Sec8 [1.1.1]): The container securing arrangement plan states a minimum GM of 1.8 m. The rule requires that the GM value in the plan shall not be less than the minimum GM in the approved trim and stability booklet for the respective draught. The analyst must verify that 1.8 m is consistent with the stability booklet; if the booklet requires a higher minimum GM at scantling draught, the plan is non-compliant. This is a gating condition that links the securing plan to the stability booklet. Step 2 — Loading conditions for fatigue (Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [3.1.2]): For container ships, the standard seagoing design loading conditions that must be included are homogeneous cargo loading at maximum draught and ballast loading conditions. The three conditions described (full homogeneous, partial homogeneous, ballast) satisfy the minimum requirement, but the partial condition is optional per the guidance note. The GM values for each condition (2.1 m, 3.4 m, 5.8 m) feed into the fatigue assessment per Pt3.Ch9.Sec4 [2(j)]. Step 3 — S-N curve selection (Pt3.Ch9.Sec4 [4.1]): For welded joints assessed by the hot spot stress approach, the rule mandates S-N curve D (FAT 90). The analyst's choice of S-N curve E (FAT 80) is NON-COMPLIANT — FAT 80 is more conservative in terms of lower allowable stress range, but the rules prescribe FAT 90 (curve D) specifically for the hot spot approach. Using a different curve, even a nominally 'more conservative' one, is not permitted without explicit rule basis. Correct curve: S-N curve D (FAT 90). Step 4 — Environmental factor (Pt3.Ch9.Sec4 [4.2]): For prescriptive loads in worldwide wave environment, fe = 0.8. The analyst's value of fe = 0.8 is COMPLIANT. Step 5 — Operational factor (Pt3.Ch9.Sec4 [4.3]): For prescriptive loads, fR = 0.76. The analyst's value of fR = 0.76 is COMPLIANT. Step 6 — Time in corrosive environment (Pt3.Ch9.Sec4 [4.4], Table 1): The hatch-corner detail is in the upper deck, not a ballast tank or cargo hold. Table 1 lists TC,25 = 5 years for water ballast tanks and TC,25 = 2 years for cargo holds (except lower part). Upper deck details not in those categories are covered by the general corrosion protection assumption. The analyst assigns TC,25 = 2 years; this needs to be checked against Table 1 — upper deck exposed details may have a different value. If the detail is in an exposed or unprotected location, the correct TC,25 from Table 1 must be applied. The analyst must confirm the correct row in Table 1 for the specific structural location.

question_text: A 310-metre container ship (block coefficient CB = 0.65, breadth B = 48.2 m, contract speed 22 knots at 85% MCR with 15% sea margin, bow flare angle α = 58°) is being assessed for hull girder buckling strength. The ship has no bilge keel and operates without any service restriction. The designer proposes to use a net plate thickness of 18 mm for a bottom shell plate panel located in a ballast water tank. The as-built thickness is 20 mm and the voluntary addition is 0.5 mm. During the buckling strength check, the designer needs to determine the lateral pressure to combine with hull girder stresses at the load calculation point. The ship is in a fully loaded departure condition with a draught TLC = 14.8 m and scantling draught TSC = 15.2 m, GM = 3.6 m, and the roll radius of gyration kr = 0.39B. Determine: (a) whether the net plate thickness of 18 mm is correctly derived for the buckling capacity check, and (b) what roll angle θ (in degrees) should be used when computing the transverse acceleration for the lateral pressure determination in the buckling design load set, given that the ship has no bilge keel.
required_facts: For the buckling capacity check, the corrosion addition factor α = 1.0 (not 0.5)
The correct net thickness for buckling capacity is 18.5 mm (= 20 − 0.5 − 1.0×1.0), so the designer's 18 mm is incorrect
The hull girder buckling design load sets require lateral pressure from Pt3 Ch4 at the load calculation point
Roll period Tθ ≈ 22.9 s, computed using kr = 0.39B and the given GM
The roll angle θ ≈ 18.7° using fBK = 1.2 (no bilge keel) and fps = 1.0 (no service restriction)
The corrosion addition tc = 1.0 mm for a ballast water tank (one side exposure)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 defines net scantlings for hull girder assessment with α=1.0 for buckling capacity, and references Pt3.Ch3.Sec3 for corrosion addition tc. Pt3.Ch8.Sec3 [1.1.3] requires the buckling check to use design load sets from Pt3.Ch6.Sec2 [2], which in turn requires lateral pressures from Pt3.Ch4. Pt3.Ch4.Sec3 [2.1.1] gives the roll angle formula needed to compute transverse accelerations for the lateral pressure.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 (Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.1.1]): For buckling capacity check, α = 1.0. The corrosion addition tc for a ballast water tank (one side) = 1.0 mm per Table 2. The net offered thickness for buckling capacity = t_as_built − t_vol_add − α·tc = 20 − 0.5 − 1.0×1.0 = 18.5 mm. The designer's proposed 18 mm is therefore NOT correctly derived for the buckling capacity check; the correct value is 18.5 mm. Note: for section properties (stress determination) α = 0.5, giving t_off = 20 − 0.5 − 0.5×1.0 = 19.0 mm, but for buckling capacity α = 1.0. Step 2 (Pt3.Ch8.Sec3 [1.1.3]): The hull girder buckling check requires combination of hull girder stress and lateral pressure using design load sets defined in Pt3.Ch6.Sec2 [2]. Step 3 (Pt3.Ch6.Sec2 [2.1.1]): The design load sets require lateral pressures determined according to Pt3.Ch4 at the load calculation point. Step 4 (Pt3.Ch4.Sec3 [2.1.1]): Roll period Tθ = 2.3π·kr/√(g·GM). kr = 0.39×48.2 = 18.798 m. GM = 3.6 m. Tθ = 2.3π×18.798/√(9.81×3.6) = 135.87/5.940 = 22.87 s. Roll angle θ = 9000(1.4 − 0.035×Tθ)·fp·fBK / ((1.15B+55)π). fp = fps = 1.0 (no service restriction, extreme sea loads). fBK = 1.2 (no bilge keel). θ = 9000×(1.4 − 0.035×22.87)×1.0×1.2 / ((1.15×48.2+55)×π) = 9000×(1.4−0.8005)×1.2 / (110.43×π) = 9000×0.5995×1.2 / 346.8 = 6474.6/346.8 ≈ 18.67°. Also note: the ship characteristics (L=310m > 290m, B=48.2m > 47m, α=58° > 55°, V=22 kn < 25 kn) trigger the guidance note in Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.6.2] recommending advanced whipping/springing assessment, though V < 25 kn means not all four criteria are met simultaneously.

question_text:
A 280 m bulk carrier with large deck openings is being designed with a cargo hatch on the strength deck. The hatch corner is located between a longitudinal deck girder strip and a closed area (HC1 type). The longitudinal deck girder alongside the hatchway has a breadth bL = 2.8 m, and the relevant length of large deck openings forward and aft of the superstructure is 45 m. The hatch corner plate has a gross thickness ti = 22 mm, while the longitudinal structural member plate thickness tD = 20 mm. The gross moment of inertia of the hull section at the hatch corner (without insert plate) is Iy-gr = 980 m⁴, and the total longitudinal bending moment at the relevant cross deck strip edge is MT = 8 500 000 kNm. The hatch corner is located 12 m above the baseline, and the neutral axis of the hull section is at 9.5 m above the baseline. The hatch corner is positioned at x/L = 0.55 along the ship length. The material factor ki = 1.0.

A primary supporting member (PSM) in the cargo hold supports the strength deck plating. The PSM spans between two transverse bulkheads with a full span of 18.5 m. Brackets are fitted on both sides of each bulkhead connection, each bracket having a horizontal length of 0.9 m measured along the PSM span. The PSM is subjected to a design pressure P = 35 kN/m² (AC-II load set), with a PSM spacing S = 4.2 m. The load model is type A (both ends fixed, uniformly distributed load). The hull girder longitudinal stress at the load calculation point on this PSM is σhg = 42 N/mm², and the material yield stress ReH = 315 N/mm².

(a) Is the hatch corner arrangement subject to special consideration under the rules for ships with large deck openings, and what minimum corner radius r (in m) is required?

(b) For the PSM, confirm whether the section modulus formula applies directly or whether an alternative assessment path is required, and — if the formula applies — calculate the minimum required section modulus Z (in cm³) using the appropriate bending moment distribution factor.
required_facts: The hatch corner is subject to special consideration because the ship has large deck openings, requiring application of the hatch corner radius formula from the rules for such ships
The minimum required hatch corner radius is governed by rmin = 0.15 m (the computed value c1·c2 ≈ 0.142 m is less than rmin)
The PSM section modulus formula applies directly because the hull girder longitudinal stress σhg = 42 N/mm² does not exceed the threshold 0.15·ReH = 47.25 N/mm²
The effective bending span ℓbdg = 16.7 m after deducting the bracket lengths (0.9 m each end) from the full span of 18.5 m
The applicable bending moment distribution factor is fbdg = 24.0 (load model A, mid-span field position) with Cs = 0.85 for AC-II
The minimum required section modulus Z ≈ 6 381 cm³

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: PSM scantling check in Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 references load calculation point definition in Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [4.1] and hull girder stress point in Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [5.1]; the hatch corner special consideration for large-deck-opening ships in Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [7.3.5] directs to Pt5.Ch2.Sec2 [2.1.1] for the radius formula.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Hatch corner applicability (Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [7.3.5]): The ship has large deck openings (280 m bulk carrier). Pt3.Ch3.Sec6 [7.3.5] states that for ships with large deck openings the corners of cargo hatchways shall be specially considered on the basis of stresses due to longitudinal hull girder bending, torsion and transverse loads, and directs to Pt.5 Ch.1 and Pt.5 Ch.2.

Step 2 — Hatch corner radius formula (Pt5.Ch2.Sec2 [2.1.1]): The applicable formula is r ≥ c1·c2 with r ≥ rmin. rmin = 0.15 m for strength deck corners.

Compute c1 (HC1 type, between longitudinal deck strip and closed area):
  fD = 0.25 + L13/2000, where L13 = max(100, min(280,300)) = 280 m
  fD = 0.25 + 280/2000 = 0.25 + 0.14 = 0.39
  c1 = (fD + ℓ/750)·bL = (0.39 + 45/750)·2.8 = (0.39 + 0.06)·2.8 = 0.45·2.8 = 1.26

Compute c2:
  cs at x/L = 0.55 (strength deck, 0.3 ≤ x/L < 0.7): cs = 1.0
  c2 = [MT·(zD − z0)] / [Iy-gr · 175·10³ · cs] · (tD/ti) · (ki)^(1/4)
  = [8 500 000·(12 − 9.5)] / [980 · 175 000 · 1.0] · (20/22) · 1.0
  = [8 500 000 · 2.5] / [171 500 000] · 0.909
  = 21 250 000 / 171 500 000 · 0.909
  = 0.12390 · 0.909
  = 0.1126 m

  Check tD/ti = 20/22 = 0.909, which is within [0.65, 1.0] ✓

  r = c1·c2 = 1.26 · 0.1126 = 0.1419 m
  r_min = 0.15 m → governs
  Required r ≥ 0.15 m

Step 3 — PSM section modulus applicability check (Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 [1.1.2]): The section modulus formula in [2.1.1] is NOT applicable for longitudinal PSMs where hull girder longitudinal stress exceeds 0.15·ReH. Check: 0.15·315 = 47.25 N/mm². σhg = 42 N/mm² < 47.25 N/mm², so the formula DOES apply.

Step 4 — Load calculation point for P (Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [4.1]): P is calculated at the load calculation point as defined in Ch.3 Sec.7 [4.1]. P = 35 kN/m² is given.

Step 5 — Effective bending span (Pt3.Ch3.Sec7 [1.1.6] / [1.1.8]): For PSM with brackets on both sides, the effective bending span ℓbdg is reduced from the full span. Per [1.1.8], ℓbdg = ℓ − bracket reductions. With brackets of 0.9 m on each end: ℓbdg = 18.5 − 0.9 − 0.9 = 16.7 m (exact reduction rule per figure, but using the bracket length directly as a first approximation consistent with the referenced sub-article).

Step 6 — Section modulus calculation (Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 [2.1.1]): Load model A, both ends fixed → fbdg at field (mid-span) = 24.0 (from Table 1, position 2). Cs = 0.85 for AC-II.
  Z = 1000·|P|·S·ℓbdg² / (fbdg·Cs·ReH)
  = 1000·35·4.2·16.7² / (24.0·0.85·315)
  = 1000·35·4.2·278.89 / (6426)
  = 1000·41 000.7 / 6426
  ≈ 6 381 cm³
  Minimum required section modulus Z ≈ 6 381 cm³.

scenario_parameters.ship_type: bulk carrier with large deck openings
scenario_parameters.hatch_corner_type: HC1 (longitudinal deck strip to closed area)

question_text: A 310-metre container ship is being designed with a rule length L of 310 m and a contract speed of 23 knots. The side shell structure in the midship region omits intermediate stringers, resulting in relatively low lateral bending stiffness between transverse web frames. The designer proposes to calculate the additional stresses at longitudinal stiffener end connections due to relative deflections of the supporting transverses using relative displacements taken from a cargo hold finite element analysis. The hull girder section modulus and shear strength are to be assessed using net scantlings, with the deck plating exposed to atmosphere and the inner bottom plating bounding a ballast water tank. For the net thickness calculation, the designer applies a corrosion addition factor α = 0.5 to both the deck plating and the inner bottom plating for the section properties used in the strength assessment. The vertical hull girder bending strength check uses a permissible still water bending moment Msw derived from the seagoing condition. Is the proposed design approach fully compliant with classification requirements? Specifically: (a) is the method for calculating additional stresses at the longitudinal stiffener end connections acceptable, and what reference document and sub-section governs the calculation procedure? (b) is the corrosion addition factor α = 0.5 correct for both the deck plating and the inner bottom plating when assessing section properties for hull girder strength? (c) does the hull girder bending strength assessment need to account for any harbour/sheltered water condition, and if so, what correction factor applies?
required_facts: The method of calculating additional stresses at longitudinal stiffener end connections using relative displacements from cargo hold FE analysis is acceptable per the fatigue requirements for container ships with L ≥ 90 m.
The governing calculation procedure for relative displacement stresses is DNV-CG-0129 Sec.4 [7].
For hull girder strength assessment (section properties), the corrosion addition factor α = 0.5 is correct for both deck plating and inner bottom plating.
The one-side corrosion addition tc = 1.0 mm applies to both the deck plating (exposed to atmosphere) and the inner bottom plating (ballast water tank boundary).
The hull girder bending strength assessment must also satisfy the harbour/sheltered water condition using the correction factor fhar = 0.5.

The hull girder strength assessment for container ships is governed by the general vertical bending and shear strength rules, with Pt5 container ship requirements applied in lieu of specific Pt3 paragraphs where stated.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec7 fatigue section for container ships references DNV-CG-0129 Sec.4 [7] for the relative displacement stress calculation method. Pt5.Ch2.Sec7 [2.1.2] also triggers a look at Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 for hull girder strength requirements (net scantlings, corrosion factors), which in turn defers to Pt3.Ch5.Sec2 for the bending and shear strength criteria including harbour/sheltered water permissible bending moments.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Fatigue / stiffener end connections: Pt5.Ch2.Sec7 [2.1.2] states that additional stresses due to relative displacement shall be calculated as described in DNV-CG-0129 Sec.4 [7], based on relative displacements from global or cargo hold FE analysis. The proposed method (cargo hold FE) is therefore acceptable. Step 2 — Net scantlings / corrosion factor: Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [2.1.1] Table 1 shows that for strength assessment (section properties), α = 0.5 is correct. Table 2 gives the one-side corrosion addition tc: deck plating exposed to atmosphere → tc = 1.0 mm per side; inner bottom plating bounding a ballast water tank → tc = 1.0 mm per side. So α = 0.5 applied to tc = 1.0 mm is consistent for both plates; the factor itself is correct at 0.5 for section property strength assessment. Step 3 — Harbour/sheltered water bending moment: Pt3.Ch5.Sec2 [1.7] (referenced via Pt5.Ch2.Sec4 [1] which states hull girder strength shall be per Pt3.Ch5) requires that permissible still water bending moments for harbour/sheltered operations comply with a separate criterion using fhar = 0.5 (unless otherwise defined in Pt.5). The designer must therefore also check the harbour/sheltered water condition with fhar = 0.5.

scenario_parameters.side_structure: no intermediate stringers, low lateral bending stiffness
scenario_parameters.condition_checked: seagoing only (harbour condition omitted by designer)

question_text: A 14,000 TEU container ship (each TEU rated at 14 t) has the following principal dimensions: L = 366 m, B = 51 m, scantling draught T = 15.5 m, block coefficient C_B = 0.66, and a waterplane coefficient C_WL = 0.88 (waterplane area A_W = 16,400 m²). The bow flare geometry gives A_DK = 3,200 m² and A_WL = 2,850 m² (both measured from 0.8L forward), with a freeboard z_f = 9.2 m at the forward end. For the midship cross-section (x/L = 0.5), the designer needs to determine the design vertical wave bending moment in hogging for the extreme sea loads strength assessment. As part of this calculation, the factor f_R must be obtained from the hull girder loads section of the general ship rules, and the symbols used in that calculation (including the wave coefficient C_w and the reference coordinate system) must be interpreted using the general definitions chapter. What is the numerical value of the hogging vertical wave bending moment M_WV-Hog at x/L = 0.5, and which value of f_R applies for a standard unrestricted ocean-going service? Show all intermediate parameters including C, f_NL-Hog, c_M, and f_Bow.
required_facts: f_R = 0.85 for strength assessment, obtained from Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 [3.1.1] as referenced by Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2.2.3] in the container ship loads section
The wave parameter C ≈ 1.00 because L = 366 m is marginally below L_ref ≈ 368 m, placing the ship in the L ≤ L_ref branch
f_NL-Hog = 0.3 · (C_B / C_WL) · sqrt(T) ≈ 0.886 (below the 1.1 cap), using C_B = 0.66, C_WL = 0.88, T = 15.5 m
c_M = 1.0 at x/L = 0.5 in hogging (falls in the 0.35 ≤ x/L < 0.55 range of Table 1)
f_Bow ≈ 0.52, computed from the projected deck area and waterplane area forward of 0.8L and the freeboard z_f
M_WV-Hog at x/L = 0.5 is approximately 10,100 MNm (≈ 10.1 × 10⁶ kNm)
The general Pt3 vertical wave bending moment formula does NOT apply to this container ship; the Pt5.Ch2 formula supersedes it per Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 [1.1.3]

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 gives the container-ship-specific vertical wave bending moment formula, which references Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 [3.1.1] for f_R; Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 in turn references Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 for symbol definitions (C_w, coordinate system); and Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 [3] is also where the general vertical wave shear/bending moment baseline lives, which Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2.2.1] explicitly supersedes for container ships, completing the cross-volume chain.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Start at Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2.2.3]: The formula for M_WV-Hog = +1.5 · f_R · f_p · L³ · C · c_M · C_WL · (B/L)^0.8 · f_NL-Hog applies. Identify all parameters needed.

Step 2 — Compute wave parameter C (Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2.2.2]): L_ref = 315 · C_WL^(-1.3) = 315 · (0.88)^(-1.3). (0.88)^1.3 ≈ 0.856, so L_ref ≈ 315 / 0.856 ≈ 368 m. Since L = 366 m < L_ref = 368 m, use C = 1 − 1.50·(1 − sqrt(366/368))^2.2. sqrt(366/368) = sqrt(0.9946) ≈ 0.9973. (1 − 0.9973) = 0.0027. (0.0027)^2.2 ≈ very small ≈ 0.00028. C ≈ 1 − 1.50 · 0.00028 ≈ 0.9996 ≈ 1.00.

Step 3 — Obtain f_R: Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2.2.3] states f_R = as given in Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 [3.1.1] for strength assessment. Navigate to Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 [3.1.1]: for unrestricted ocean-going service f_R = 1.0.

Step 4 — Obtain f_p: from Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [3.1.1], f_p = 1.0 for strength assessment (standard design load scenario).

Step 5 — Compute f_Bow (Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2.2.3]): f_Bow = (A_DK − A_WL) / (0.2 · L · z_f) = (3200 − 2850) / (0.2 · 366 · 9.2) = 350 / 673.4 ≈ 0.520.

Step 6 — Compute f_NL-Hog for strength assessment: f_NL-Hog = 0.3 · (C_B / C_WL) · sqrt(T) = 0.3 · (0.66 / 0.88) · sqrt(15.5) = 0.3 · 0.750 · 3.937 = 0.886. Check: not greater than 1.1 → f_NL-Hog = 0.886.

Step 7 — Obtain c_M at x/L = 0.5 (hogging, Table 1 of Pt5.Ch2.Sec3): range 0.35 ≤ x/L < 0.55 → c_M = 1.0.

Step 8 — Symbols check via Pt3.Ch1.Sec4: C_w (wave coefficient) is defined in Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 symbols preamble; coordinates x, y, z defined in Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 1 and Table 2. Note that in the Pt5 formula the wave parameter is called 'C' (not C_w), so no confusion with the Pt3 wave coefficient C_w.

Step 9 — Compute M_WV-Hog: (B/L)^0.8 = (51/366)^0.8 = (0.1393)^0.8. ln(0.1393) = −1.970; × 0.8 = −1.576; e^(−1.576) ≈ 0.2069. M_WV-Hog = 1.5 · 1.0 · 1.0 · (366)³ · 1.00 · 1.0 · 0.88 · 0.2069 · 0.886. (366)³ = 49,027,896 m³. Product: 1.5 · 49,027,896 · 0.88 · 0.2069 · 0.886 ≈ 1.5 · 49,027,896 · 0.1614 ≈ 1.5 · 7,912,101 ≈ 11,868,000 kNm ≈ 11,870 MNm.

Step 10 — Cross-reference note: Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 [1.1.3] confirms that for container ships the Pt5.Ch2 vertical wave bending moment supersedes the Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 [3] general formula, completing the chain.

question_text: A designer is scantling-checking the deck structure of a 185 m bulk carrier (no large deck openings). The ship has a longitudinally stiffened main deck. The deck plating is 18 mm thick and made of NV A36 (yield strength 355 N/mm²), while the attached longitudinal stiffeners are fabricated from NV A40 material (yield strength 390 N/mm²), giving the plate flange a lower minimum yield strength than the connected stiffeners. During the yield capacity check of the stiffeners under combined lateral pressure and hull girder bending, the designer wants to know whether the standard stiffener yield formula can be applied directly, or whether an additional check is required because of the material mismatch between the plate flange and the stiffener. If an additional check is required, identify what that check is and which structural parameter it targets. Furthermore, once the stiffener scantlings are confirmed, the designer must also verify that the deck longitudinals satisfy hull girder buckling requirements along the full ship length — state the stress combinations that must be evaluated for a longitudinally stiffened arrangement and confirm whether the buckling check applies only within 0.4L amidships or over the full ship length.
required_facts: The plate flange (NV A36, 355 N/mm²) has about 9.9% lower minimum yield strength than the connected stiffeners (NV A40, 390 N/mm²), which is below the 35% threshold
The additional check targets the yield capacity of the plate flange, not just the stiffener web or section modulus
For a longitudinally stiffened arrangement, stress combination 1 uses σx = σhg, σy = 0, τ = 0.7τhg
For a longitudinally stiffened arrangement, stress combination 2 uses σx = 0.7σhg, σy = 0, τ = τhg
The hull girder buckling strength requirements apply along the full length of the ship, not only within 0.4L amidships

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.2] flags that when plate flange yield strength is lower than the connected stiffener, an additional yield capacity check of the plate flange may be required and explicitly cross-references Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4]. Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4] provides the combined axial/bending/shear stiffener yield check including the Cm coefficient that accounts for hull girder stress. That section in turn references Ch.8 Sec.3 for buckling compliance of longitudinal members. Ch.8 Sec.3 [1.1.2] states the hull girder buckling strength requirements apply along the full length of the ship, and [2.2] defines the stress combinations for longitudinally stiffened arrangements.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.1.2]: The rules note that when the plate flange has a lower minimum yield strength than the connected stiffener or PSM, an additional check of the yield capacity of the plate flange may be required, with an explicit pointer to Ch.6 Sec.5 [1.1.4]. This is triggered here because the deck plate is NV A36 (355 N/mm²) while the stiffeners are NV A40 (390 N/mm²). Step 2 — Pt3.Ch6.Sec5 [1.1.4]: This clause governs the yield check of stiffeners under combined lateral pressure and hull girder stress. The Cm coefficient in the web thickness and section modulus formulae accounts for the interaction of hull girder longitudinal stress with bending and shear. The additional check targets the yield capacity of the plate flange, ensuring the lower-yield-strength plate is not overstressed when the stiffener is sized to the higher yield strength. Step 3 — Pt3.Ch8.Sec3 [1.1.2] and [2.2]: Once stiffener scantlings are set, hull girder buckling must be verified. Clause [1.1.2] explicitly states the requirements apply along the full length of the ship — not just 0.4L amidships. Clause [2.2] defines two stress combinations for a longitudinally stiffened arrangement: combination 1 with σx = σhg, σy = 0, τ = 0.7τhg; and combination 2 with σx = 0.7σhg, σy = 0, τ = τhg. Both must be evaluated for all applicable loading conditions.

question_text:
A 185-metre container ship is being designed with NV 47 steel upper hull longitudinal structural members. The hatch side coaming top plate has an as-built thickness of 72 mm, and the horizontal coaming plate has an as-built thickness of 65 mm. During the structural arrangement review, the designer proposes to terminate several deck longitudinals at a transverse bulkhead within the 0.8L amidships region, rather than running them continuously through it. The hull girder longitudinal stress at the relevant deck plating is calculated as 145 N/mm², and the permissible hull girder stress for that deck is 210 N/mm². The ship has two continuous decks above 0.7D from baseline.

For the block-to-block butt joints of the upper hull longitudinal structural members at this coaming, the designer proposes to apply 100% MT and 100% UT. Additionally, for transversely oriented full penetration plate butt welds in the same region, the designer proposes 20% RT.

Are the proposed NDT methods and extents compliant? Is the proposed termination of deck longitudinals at the transverse bulkhead acceptable, and what welding requirements apply if those longitudinals are made non-continuous under high tensile hull girder stress conditions?
required_facts: The leading plate thickness is 72 mm (hatch side coaming top plate is thicker than the 65 mm horizontal coaming plate), which falls in the 50 < t ≤ 100 mm range for NV 47, triggering the enhanced NDT requirements.
For transversely oriented full penetration plate butt welds in the NV 47 upper hull region, only UT (not RT) is permitted; the proposed 20% RT is non-compliant.
For block-to-block butt joints, 100% MT and 100% UT is required and the proposed scope is compliant.

The exception permitting deck longitudinals to be terminated at transverse members requires BOTH more than two continuous decks above 0.7D AND σhg ≤ 0.5·σhg-perm; neither condition is satisfied here (only two decks, and 145 N/mm² > 0.5 × 210 = 105 N/mm²).
The proposed termination of deck longitudinals at the transverse bulkhead within 0.8L amidships is NOT acceptable under the structural arrangement rules.
If deck longitudinals under high tensile hull girder stress are nonetheless made non-continuous, the applicable welding requirements are those given in Ch.13 Sec.1 [2.4.6].

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at Pt1.Ch3.Sec3 NDT requirements for container ship upper hull members, which references material grade and thickness thresholds. Then navigate to Pt3.Ch3.Sec1 [2.3] for material grade definitions and upper hull structural member context. Then to Pt3.Ch6.Sec3 for minimum thickness rules. Then to Pt3.Ch3.Sec5 [4] for structural arrangement rules on deck longitudinal continuity and the welding cross-reference.
